stories.title: The high risk of seeing double in Toronto’s mayoral race
stories.summary: Braeden Chow and Olivia Chow share a surname but are running very different campaigns
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
In his promotional photos, Braeden Chow dons mayoral chic: button-down shirt and loose tie. On this day, with a Globe photographer present, he opts for black Ray-Bans, a black leather jacket and black pants. He’s become the Toronto election’s man of mystery. Why not embrace the part?

With the Toronto mayoral race tightening in recent days, neither of the front-runners can afford miscast ballots. That scrutiny has wrenched Mr. Chow’s candidacy out of obscurity. He shares a last name with the incumbent, Mayor Olivia Chow, and appears immediately above her on the ballot, creating the real possibility of Ms. Chow losing voters to Mr. Chow, political scientists told The Globe.

“It’s a serious issue,” said York University politics professor Dennis Pilon. “If the numbers even up, then suddenly a candidate that surprisingly gets a few thousand votes could be decisive.”

But who is the unknown Chow?

His was a inconspicuous candidacy until Ms. Chow emerged from early voting on Tuesday to speak with reporters. They wanted to ask about Chris Alexander, the former federal candidate who had dropped out of the race that morning. She had something else on her mind.

“I just noticed there is two Chows on the ballot and there is one before me,” she said, admitting she’d nearly voted for the wrong person.

Toronto’s budget hole looms over mayoral race

Her campaign followed up with a social media post and a statement reminding voters to mark the right Chow on their ballots. Reddit commenters soon labelled him a decoy candidate, a plant and a spoiler – someone whose last name alone could siphon enough votes away from Ms. Chow to allow her main challenger, Brad Bradford, to win an ever-tightening contest.

“I’d feel bad for sure if that happened,” said Mr. Chow, who insisted nobody recruited him to the race while sitting on a bench outside the Art Gallery of Ontario and sipping a double-double. “But I’d also say Olivia could join forces with me. If I win, she’s on my team for sure.”

That’s a stretch – for a few reasons. His support has failed to register in polling.

What’s more, they have incompatible political philosophies (he wants to fund city services through donations from the rich and train 100 police to be Navy Seals, “like GI Joe and GI Jane,” he said).

And then there’s the family matter.

He insists he’s the mayor’s second cousin.

But, according to the mayor’s campaign team, that’s simply not true.

“We can confirm that Braeden Chow is not related to Olivia Chow,” said campaign spokesman Zeus Eden in a statement to The Globe. “We have no idea where he comes from. Our campaign is encouraging all voters to look to Olivia Chow, who is number 9 on the ballot.”

No hard feelings. He says he endorses Ms. Chow all the same and hopes she wins. It’s an unconventional campaign.

She could use the support. Ms. Chow’s odds of winning appeared to narrow this week, with Mainstreet Research releasing a poll on Friday showing she leads Mr. Bradford by just 2.9 points among decided and leaning voters. The poll of 1,000 people carries a margin of error of 3.1 per cent 19 times out of 20 and was conducted Oct. 6 and 7, after Mr. Alexander had withdrawn.

Researchers have found that minor candidates can pick up as much as two-tenths of a per cent if they appear next to a major candidate, said Charles Tessier, expert in citizen behavior at Tact, a Quebec-based public affairs firm and a ballot-order researcher.

Chris Alexander drops out of Toronto mayoral race

Fifty-three candidates are vying to be Toronto’s chief magistrate. That’s down considerably from the 102 who ran in 2023, but far greater than other Canadian cities. The upcoming Vancouver election has eight mayoral candidates while Winnipeg has 12.

“The decision in Toronto is more prone to that kind of mistake because there are so many candidates,” he said. “If the election is decided by a few votes, it could have an effect.”

Some jurisdictions put candidate names in random order to avoid side-by-side name duplication. Others place pictures next to the candidates. Still others place high fees and endorsement requirements on anyone applying to be a candidate. In Toronto, mayoral aspirants need endorsements from 25 people and a $200 filing fee to enter the race.

Mr. Chow said he got 25 names when he filed his candidacy in May, but some endorsers messed up the form. He had to ask strangers outside City Hall to complete the list.

Since then, he hasn’t done much campaigning. He says he was homeless for about a week last month, showering at GoodLife Fitness. He’s also been taking care of a friend’s cats and working on registering a charity, the Nora Foundation, which will provide free groceries, laundry, transportation to those in need, according to a website he registered in June. He isn’t certain yet how it will accomplish those lofty goals.

“Honestly, that’s a ChatGPT site,” he said. “But I had the homeless week, and the taking care of cats and I’m landscaping in the summer. I haven’t had time to open a location and all that. But soon.”

stories.title: Steven Galloway testifies his book sales ‘cratered’ because of sexual-assault allegations
stories.summary: Former UBC professor faces first day of cross-examination at defamation trial at B.C. Supreme Court
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Steven Galloway’s follow-up to The Cellist of Sarajevo sold a fraction of the copies that the 2008 international bestseller had, and he received much lower Canadian advances for his next planned endeavour.

But Mr. Galloway testified in British Columbia Supreme Court Friday that these metrics don’t prove his career as a writer was on the downslope before a former student’s accusation that he sexually assaulted her led to his suspension from teaching in 2015 and near-immediate exile from Canada’s literary world.

During the first day of his cross-examination at the defamation trial he has been pursuing for eight years, the former chair of University of British Columbia’s creative-writing program disputed the assertion by a defendant’s lawyer that 2014’s The Confabulist was a flop for selling 8,390 total copies in Canada compared with the 132,256 of his smash hit.

Steven Galloway accuser threatened to sue UBC for up to $3-million, defamation trial hears

“Cellist was a zeitgeist book, and this was just a book,” he explained to Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for the woman who made the allegations, known only as A.B. because of a publication ban on her name.

Mr. Beddoes took the novelist through months of financial records and posited that sales had already fallen off before his client’s allegations ignited an online and industry firestorm over his suspension and eventual dismissal from UBC.

Mr. Galloway pushed back, saying The Confabulist had not enjoyed a run of success from paperback sales because these books were put on stands around the time of his fall from grace.

“It had a paperback life without an author,” he said.

Mr. Galloway maintained that his sales had “cratered” because of the allegations made by A.B., whom he is suing for defamation along with three other women who publicly repeated the allegations of sexual assault.

The trial will not hear testimony from A.B. Mr. Beddoes told the court that her defence no longer includes an assertion that she was assaulted, but rather that she reported the alleged assaults. Mr. Beddoes has said A.B. has twice tried to kill herself in recent months because of the stress of the ordeal.

A retired judge hired by the university to investigate her complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime, but he was fired without severance in 2016 due to breach of trust.

Marsha Lederman: The Steven Galloway trial demonstrates how hot takes can set fire to people’s lives

Earlier Friday, Mr. Galloway testified that there was no official prohibition on sexual relationships between students and faculty, and that he knows of “numerous instances” of similar relationships in the university’s faculty of arts.

He testified that it was normal for other professors to attend a regular night at a Vancouver legion to hang out and drink with students.

Mr. Beddoes questioned Mr. Galloway about a voicemail that he left for A.B. shortly before his suspension that offered an apology that said he was ashamed and was working to be a better person and “turn over a new leaf.”

He told the court that he is ashamed for having an affair with the student and cheating on his then-wife, but he didn’t think he would be fired for violating the university’s conflict-of-interest policy.

The court heard how in November, 2015, Mr. Galloway had repeatedly called both A.B. and fellow faculty member Keith Maillard, whom had received an e-mail where A.B. had described feeling at risk and “unsafe.”

Mr. Beddoes suggested that the numerous calls were Mr. Galloway “panicking,” but Mr. Galloway said that he wanted to disclose the pair’s past affair himself to Mr. Maillard, a mentor and “father figure.”

Gary Mason: Is Steven Galloway finally getting justice?

Mr. Galloway testified that no other faculty members had ever been terminated for similar conduct, though he says he should not have cheated on his wife, especially with a student.

Mr. Beddoes asked Mr. Galloway if he kept having sexual relationships with students, bringing up the fact that his current wife, screenwriter Katie Wagner, met him while attending the creative-writing program. But Mr. Galloway said she had not been a student for “well over a year” when they got together.

The original defamation suit included almost two dozen defendants, most of whom settled. Only A.B. and three others remain: Mandi Gray, Dana Kagis and Glynnis Kirchmeier.

Lawyers for the defendants will resume their cross-examination of Mr. Galloway on Tuesday.

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: With Alberta referendum in sight, the nine other ballot questions are capturing attention
stories.summary: Some federalist leaders, claiming early victory on independence, have shifted their energy to persuading Albertans to vote against Smith’s proposals
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
With little more than a week until the Alberta referendum, campaigners on both sides of the separation question have turned an eye toward the nine other ballot proposals around immigration, voter ID and constitutional issues – but they are doing it for different reasons.

Some federalist leaders, claiming early victory on the question around independence, have shifted their energy to persuading Albertans to vote against the nine proposals and have pitched their campaign as a proxy war against Premier Danielle Smith. On the flipside, some separatist camps are suggesting voters boycott the nine questions, arguing their participation would be capitulating to federalism.

The nine questions propose new fees for non-permanent residents accessing health care and education, limiting non-permanent residents’ access to other social supports and working to reopen the Canadian Constitution with the aim of wresting more power from Ottawa.

“We are very likely to reject the premise that we should be a separate country, but the other nine questions remain very much in play,” said Stephen Carter, a political strategist who has organized a campaign around the slogan, “Stay in Canada, no to the nine.”

On Friday, the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project posted to social media: “Ignore THE 9, Vote Option 2,” referring to the choice on the 10th question for a binding independence referendum.

Alberta’s referendum campaign has been subsumed by the ballot question asking voters whether they wish to remain in Canada or begin working toward a second, binding secession referendum. Support for separation has held steady during the campaign, floating between 20 per cent and 25 per cent.

The nine other questions, meanwhile, have received less scrutiny and face greater odds of winning public support.

The provincial government has offered little detail how it would enact the proposals if approved by voters.

Ms. Smith says the nine questions will give her a mandate and is focused on successfully having them pass. The government has dedicated a $4-million advertising budget to the campaign – nearly seven times what third-party advertisers are legally allowed to receive or spend during the referendum period.

Ms. Smith has characterized the proposals as a tool for leverage over Ottawa, the same argument some separatist camps have made in their pitch for voters to endorse a binding secession referendum.

Mr. Carter, the political strategist, said he’s pivoting away from the separation question to campaign exclusively on the nine others for the final week. Unlike the separation question, there are still swaths of undecided voters on the remaining questions, he said.

His campaign is attempting to frame a rejection of the questions as a rebuke of Ms. Smith’s leadership.

“It’s up to us to make sure that people understand that they can oppose these questions and oppose Danielle Smith at the same time,” he said.

Ms. Smith has said she will vote for Alberta to remain in Canada and her government has vigorously campaigned on the nine other questions, with brochures and advertising deployed across the province. Asked on Thursday how she and her United Conservative Party will be working to get out the federalist vote, she said: “Well, I want people to vote for our nine questions.”

“We want to seek a mandate on that, and if people want to change the relationship with Ottawa, that’s the best way to do it.”

Ms. Smith has said the proposals would help boost Alberta’s autonomy within Canada.

Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said in an interview that he’s “disgusted” by the nine questions, though he May vote for the proposals he believes are “pertinent.”

“I haven’t really taken a chance to inform myself on anything but the one directly related to us,” Mr. Sylvestre said.

Not all movement leaders agree, however. Keith Wilson, a lawyer and co-founder of separatist group Let Alberta Decide, called the nine proposals a “political gimmick” but said refusing to vote for them would be foolish.

“I still think they send a message,” Mr. Wilson told The Globe.

Despite bubbling interest in the nine questions, they appear likely to continue to take a back seat to the question of national unity.

Thomas Lukaszuk, leader of Forever Canadian, said he has planned rallies with “very interesting speakers” next Thursday and Friday in Calgary and Edmonton, and he’s planning a get-out-the-vote drive that will encourage his list of 1.5 million electors.

“Our campaign has always been about remaining in Canada, so that’s our primary focus,” he said.

The Alberta NDP will be hosting rallies on Tuesday and Wednesday, and it has bought advertising slots that will air during Edmonton Oilers and Calgary Flames games.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Friday that he’ll be campaigning in Alberta next week “to keep our country united.”

Ms. Smith’s office said she will be in southern Alberta next week, and will be urging Albertans to vote with new campaign literature.

Let Alberta Decide’s Mr. Wilson, meanwhile, is organizing a pro-independence rally next Saturday at the Alberta legislature, and Mr. Sylvestre is planning to activate the roughly 250,000 people in the Prosperity Project’s database ahead of referendum day. He said he’s unsure if he’ll attend Mr. Wilson’s rally.

stories.title: B.C. parties pitch contrasting income-tax proposals in the third week of election campaign
stories.summary: Tax hikes proposed by NDP, Greens could raise less revenue than projected, while Conservatives’ cuts could put province further in debt, economists say
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
British Columbia’s three largest political parties are proposing different approaches to how the province should raise and spend public money, pitching contrasting income-tax proposals in the third week of the election campaign .

The fiscally focused election promises tap into some of voters’ top concerns – affordability, health care and the province’s finances. But as B.C. faces a projected $13.8-billion deficit, the differing approaches from each of the three main parties come with their own risks. Economists say tax hikes proposed by the NDP and Greens could raise less revenue than projected and discourage economic activity, while the Conservatives’ tax cut could put B.C. further in the red.

NDP Leader David Eby said his government, if re-elected, would increase income taxes for the province’s highest earners to fund health care services, while Green Leader Emily Lowan said she would target the ultra-wealthy with a “fair share” tax to fund public services and drive down the provincial debt. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has pledged to put cash back into the pockets of British Columbians by cutting income taxes.

An Angus Reid Institute Poll released Oct. 5 found 57 per cent of respondents said the cost of living was their top concern; 42 per cent, health care; and 24 per cent the provincial deficit.

At a campaign stop in Victoria on Oct. 4, Mr. Eby said his party would raise income taxes by 2 percentage points on the top two brackets; the portion of income between $190,405 and $265,545 would be taxed at 18.8 per cent, and the portion between $265,545 and $1-million at 22.5 per cent. A new bracket of 24.5 per cent would apply to income above $1-million.

The progressive taxation plan, which would start in the 2027 tax year, would generate $1-billion by 2028-29, Mr. Eby said. The changes would apply only to income earned over each tax bracket threshold and affect only the top 4 per cent of earners in B.C.

A person who makes $250,000 a year, for example, would pay an extra $2,169 per year, for a total of $28,649 in provincial income tax – which would still be $5,250 less than they would pay in Ontario. Those earning $190,000 or less would see no changes.

“We’re going to ask those who are the wealthiest to pay a little bit more so that we can deliver the care that you and your family deserve,” Mr. Eby said.

Trevor Tombe, a professor of economics at the University of Calgary, said the Ndp’s projected gains May be overly optimistic. Using a Statistics Canada tax-modelling tool, he estimated the proposed increases would raise about $700-million by 2027 and affect about 175,000 British Columbians.

The actual amount could be much lower because those high-income earners could change their consumption, production and investment decisions as a result.

“Economists call this the behavioural effect of a tax change, and it offsets some of the mechanical effect of a tax change,” Prof. Tombe said.

“It’s sometimes possible that the behavioural changes are so large that tax increases lower revenues.”

He cited a Fraser Institute 2022 paper that suggested a rate increase in B.C. would generate approximately one-quarter of what the mechanical effect suggests, which would shrink his $700-million estimate to less than $200-million and the Ndp’s $1-billion estimate to $250-million.

Mr. Eby’s proposed new tax bracket of 24.5 per cent on income over $1-million, combined with the federal income tax of 33 per cent, would put B.C.’s combined marginal rate at 57.5 per cent – the highest in the world, Prof. Tombe said. But over all, B.C. would still be one of the lowest-tax jurisdictions in Canada, the third-lowest on incomes of $400,000 and the second-lowest on incomes of $250,000.

Ms. Lowan, of the Green Party, said Mr. Eby’s plan fails to reflect that the ultra-wealthy grow their fortunes in stocks and real estate, and not paycheques. One day after the NDP announcement, Ms. Lowan announced that her party would introduce a one-time tax of 5 per cent on net wealth above $50-million, 10 per cent above $100-million and 20 per cent above $1-billion. This would raise an estimated $22.2-billion after accounting for administrative costs and behavioural responses, the party said.

An ongoing annual tax of 2 per cent on net wealth above $50-million, 3 per cent above $100-million, and 5 per cent above $1-billion would then generate about $5.4-billion each year, according to the Greens.

Jared Walker, executive director of the non-profit, non-partisan organization Canadians for Tax Fairness, said such progressive taxation plans are in line with successful policy pushes to tax the rich across North America.

In Massachusetts, for example, an additional tax of 4 per cent on income above US$1-million, introduced in 2022, generated US$3.4-billion in fiscal year 2026.

“Asking fewer people than it takes to sell out BC Place to pay a bit more tax so we can keep hospitals running for millions of British Columbians is both good policy and common sense,” Mr. Walker said in an Oct. 6 statement.

Conservative Leader Mr. Doerkson, meanwhile, announced on Oct. 8 that his party would raise the province’s personal income tax exemption level to $32,000, from $13,216, saving most workers $1,000 a year.

“With a $1,000 tax cut, British Columbia will be well on its way to becoming the most affordable, competitive province in Canada,” Mr. Doerkson said at a campaign stop at a Surrey grocery store on Thursday.

Mr. Doerkson did not answer a reporter’s question about how much his plan would cost and instead spoke generally of growing the economy. But Prof. Tombe said the plan would take $2.5-billion a year out of the province’s coffers – raising questions about how the Conservatives would offset the lost revenue while addressing the deficit and honouring Mr. Doerkson’s earlier campaign pledge to freeze taxes across the board for as long as he’s premier.

The NDP also raised the $2.5-billion price tag and added that Mr. Doerkson’s plan would give $190-million to B.C.’s top 4 per cent of earners.

Prof. Tombe said all policy has tradeoffs, and reasonable people will reach different conclusions based on the outcomes they give most weight to.

“I’d note that B.C. has a long-term fiscal challenge, so raising the basic personal amount by this much will make that challenge more difficult,” he said of the Conservative plan.

“I’d also note that B.C., like Canada, has a large economic and productivity growth challenge, so raising income tax rates – especially at the top – risks making that challenge more difficult, too.”

stories.title: Incoming Parti Québécois eyes friends and foes across the aisle
stories.summary: Minority government needs collaboration from across the political spectrum, but finding independence help is unlikely
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Two parties at opposite ends of Quebec’s ideological spectrum have been thrust into the national spotlight after an election that leaves the province’s political future – and possibly the unity of Canada – in their hands.

The left-wing Québec solidaire and right-wing Conservative Party both won enough seats in Monday’s vote to potentially decide whether the incoming minority Parti Québécois government stays in power long enough to launch an independence referendum.

With the PQ at 59 seats, five shy of a majority, premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to collaborate across the aisle, while his rival party leaders are starting to hint at what they will demand in return.

“It will be a context of rivalry and contention on many issues,” said André Lamoureux, a political-science lecturer at the University of Quebec at Montreal.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has promised not to hold a referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump is in the White House, and throughout the campaign spoke little about sovereignty, which is currently unpopular in Quebec.

But during his victory speech Monday, he reaffirmed his commitment to fighting for independence.

The premier-designate suggested that opposition lawmakers could help realize his plan to hold a vote on secession, though he has also made clear that sovereignty will not be among his early priorities. In reality, partisan jockeying May well bring down his government long before he can hold an independence vote.

The Quebec Liberal Party will retain its position as Official Opposition with 40 seats, though it seems least inclined to collaborate with its old adversaries in the PQ. Although there are some areas that the two parties agree on, such as trimming bureaucracy and building housing, the animosity between the federalists and sovereigntists runs deep, noted Mr. Lamoureux.

The Liberals May have their first chance to clash with the government over its plans to abolish the role of lieutenant-governor, which Leader Charles Milliard said was “constitutionally an issue” and “not a priority for Quebeckers” in a postelection interview with Montreal radio station Cjad.

The government’s most likely partner in its goal of separating from Canada is Québec solidaire, with its nine seats concentrated in the cores of Montreal and Quebec City. The PQ needs a majority of votes in the National Assembly to adopt a referendum question.

But the two sovereigntist parties are not natural allies. QS was born in 2006, partly out of frustration with the PQ’s drift to the right on economic and identity issues, and they diverge sharply on everything from immigration to the question of how to bring about independence.

The left-wing party describes its vision of separation as “inclusive” and proposes a four-year process that would involve consulting minorities on a proposed constitution, which would then be put to a referendum, at a cost of $840-million. The PQ wants a more pared-back constitutional consultation at far less cost.

Despite these differences, party leaders have collaborated before, including on a “roadmap” to independence in 2017, when both were in opposition.

Their bases are deeply at odds, however, ON ideological grounds and have blocked attempted reconciliations in the past, including when QS members voted down a proposed alliance with the PQ ahead of the 2018 election.

Despite its iron-clad commitment to independence, QS draws major support from urban progressives who like its environmental and social policies but are not interested in separation. Polls show that only a minority of the party’s supporters would vote Yes in a referendum.

QS is also conscious of avoiding the fate that befell the NDP in last year’s federal election, when the New Democrats were decimated after propping up a minority Liberal government. The QS caucus will include Alexandre Boulerice, a former NDP MP now representing the Montreal riding of Gouin in the National Assembly.

“Politically, it wasn’t a winning choice for the NDP,” said Quentin Janel, QS director of communications. “And we have fundamental disagreements with the PQ on immigration and inclusivity, which makes it out of the question to strike a formal pact with the government on that level.”

The most likely dance partner for the PQ on many bread-and-butter issues is the provincial Conservative Party, founded in 2009, which had never won a seat in the National Assembly and now has 19, clustered in the Quebec City area. (An earlier iteration of the party dissolved in 1936).

The breakout star of the 2026 election was Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, who campaigned on the cost of living and voters’ dissatisfaction with the Coalition Avenir Québec government’s management of public funds.

Mr. Duhaime promised to act as a watchdog on behalf of taxpayers if voters gave his party the balance of power, and during a press conference in Quebec City on Wednesday, he said his caucus members are united by their commitment to fiscal conservatism.

“These are people fighting for individual freedom, for civil liberties, for democracy, and also for more money in your pockets – a smaller government that’s tightening its belt,” he said. “That’s the Quebec version of conservatism today.”

Shortly before the campaign, Mr. Duhaime unveiled a plan to cut government spending by $47-billion over five years, in part by eliminating 20,000 public-service jobs.

The proposal was the cornerstone of his campaign, and it set the narrative for an election that saw most parties announce measures to shrink the size of the bureaucracy, said Rudy Husny, a political analyst and former federal Conservative adviser.

There is considerable common ground between the Conservatives and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s PQ, the most “centre-right” version of the party that Quebec has seen, Mr. Husny said.

Both parties want to scrap the sales tax on used goods and to abolish Santé Québec, a Crown corporation created by the CAQ government to operate Quebec’s health care network, which critics have labelled as little more than a new layer of bureaucracy. On Wednesday, Mr. Duhaime said he also supports the PQ’s plan to freeze the salaries of elected officials.

But the Conservative Leader has been adamant that his party wants nothing to do with a vote on sovereignty. “Our position is non-negotiable,” said spokesperson Cédric Lapointe in a statement. “There will be no referendum.”

Mr. Husny said it’s very unlikely the PQ will launch the process to hold a referendum in this mandate, especially given Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s promise to wait until Mr. Trump leaves office in 2029. Quebec’s two previous minority governments survived less than two years.

This election campaign was primarily about change, he said.

“The next one will certainly be about the referendum.”

stories.title: Ex-UBC prof Steven Galloway cross-examined at defamation trial about repeated phone calls to accuser
stories.summary: Lawyer for A.B., former student of Steven Galloway, questioned him about why he repeatedly called her and a fellow faculty member.
stories.author: Susan Lazaruk
stories.content:
The former head of the University of B.C.’s creative writing department, who is suing a former student for defamation, testified that he was worried about the news of the affair coming out.

Steven Galloway was under cross-examination Friday by the lawyer for A.B., a former graduate student in his department with whom he had a relationship for two years, during the trial in B.C. Supreme Court.

In late 2015, two years after the affair had ended, A.B. sent an email to another UBC faculty member, Keith Maillard, to discuss a sexual assault allegation in a separate UBC faculty, A.B.’s lawyer, Arden Beddoes, told Justice Neena Sharma. In it, she asked Maillard not to forward the email to others because she felt “very unsafe for reasons of my own,” court heard.

A.B. had copied Galloway on the email and he said he called A.B. to ask her about it. He said she was short with him before ending the call.

Galloway had testified earlier that A.B. had been posting on social media about “power dynamics” and imbalances in relationships, and he worried that she was characterizing their consensual relationship to Maillard as one in which he had taken advantage of her.

Galloway then called both A.B. and Maillard a number of times — Beddoes said Maillard had 34 calls that day from an unknown number and A.B. during the same time had repeated calls from an unknown number.

After being unable to reach A.B. by phone that day, Nov. 11, 2015, Galloway left a voicemail for her, a transcript of which was read in court.

Galloway told her on the message that he wanted to apologize to her and “to take responsibility for our relationship” and to “turn myself in.” He told her he was “pretty ashamed of the way I acted,” that he had “turned over a new leaf” and was “trying to be a good person.”

“It does seem you’re in distress?” Beddoes asked him. “Your concern is she was talking about a consensual affair?” he asked.

He agreed and said he was worried that she felt there was a power imbalance in the relationship and was fearful how news of their consensual affair would affect Maillard, a good friend, and he wanted the chance to speak with him first.

“And that’s because you were panicking?” because of fear of losing his job, asked Beddoes.

But Galloway said a sexual relationship with a student wasn’t a firing offence and he was instead worried instead about how that news was going to be upsetting to Maillard, who was like a father figure to him.

In reference in his voice message to being ashamed about the affair, Beddoes asked: “That was the only thing you were ashamed of?”

“I should not have been cheating on my wife and I should not have been doing it with a student,” he said.

Beddoes also asked Galloway about regularly drinking with students at the Legion pub and questioned whether other faculty did the same, as Galloway maintained.

Much of the cross-examination Friday focused on the money Galloway made from his four novels and about a $100,000 advance he was offered by his publisher to write a series of three lighter books about Pepatone, a ventriloquist detective, around the time the allegations came out and that were never written.

The trial continues.

stories.title: Nova Scotia shelter serves up 2,000 Thanksgiving dinners
stories.summary: A rescue mission in Nova Scotia served 2,000 Thanksgiving meals to visitors on Friday as the community celebrated the holiday weekend.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - Souls Harbour Rescue Mission provides food, shelter and other forms of assistance for Nova Scotians each day. But on Friday, the non-profit facility started the holiday weekend early.

“Today was Thanksgiving at Souls Harbour,” said CEO Michelle Porter, as everyone who visited received a midday, multi-course, free turkey dinner with all the fixings.

By noon, the dining room was jampacked with a lineup outside of people waiting to enter.

“The message is, we all belong and this is about gratitude and celebration,” Porter said. “And we all celebrate together.”

At a time when the need has increased to provide food for people who cannot afford groceries, the facility typically feeds hundreds each week. Provincewide, Porter said on Friday alone, they were providing more than 2,000 Thanksgiving meals for men, women and children.

“Big picture, Souls Harbour has 14 locations in Nova Scotia and nine of our drop-in centres are having a Thanksgiving dinner,” said Porter, who acknowledged the non-profit now provides food for more people than ever before.

“This year, we opened two new Nova Scotia-based drop-in centres in Yarmouth and Dartmouth, and this will be their first Thanksgiving,” she said. “It does warm my heart that we can do that, but it also means that there is a cost-of-living factor that is impacting our neighbours.”

Laurie Thibodeau comes to Souls Harbour for food, usually each day. She knows the volunteers and staff are there to serve, and she expressed her gratitude for the continued assistance.

“They make you feel welcome and feel at home,” said Thibodeau, who added the festive Thanksgiving vibe made the day feel even more special. “I am really happy, with honest and amazing appreciation and I am grateful for that.”

Porter said the pre-holiday weekend event captured what she believed to be the true meaning of Thanksgiving – showing generosity toward people who live in the community and often go hungry.

“The best part of my job is to be able to serve more than 2,000 people a Thanksgiving meal,” she said. “Never in my life did I think we would get numbers like that here in Nova Scotia, and it saddens me.

“But at the same time, it brings me joy to know we are helping that many people,” she added.

stories.title: Charges laid after 19-year-old dies of carbon monoxide poisoning in Sudbury area
stories.summary: Sudbury - Two people and a company have been charged after a 19-year-old died of carbon monoxide poisoning in the Sudbury area.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Local police responded to a home in May 2025 after someone was reportedly found unresponsive.

Ontario Provincial Police say Roch Renaud died in hospital.

A 59-year-old from Sheguiandah on Manitoulin Island and a 53-year-old from the Sudbury area were each charged with criminal negligence causing death.

Article continues below

A Sudbury-area business, Sunswim Pool Concepts and Design Ltd., was also charged with the same offence.

OPP say both accused people have been released and are set to appear in court in January.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Politics Insider: Paul Godfrey ousted from Order of Ontario advisory council
stories.summary: Also in this issue, Poilievre to deliver Canadian unity speech in Alberta and Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu gets ready to lead trip to India
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Former Postmedia chairman Paul Godfrey has been removed from the advisory council to the Order of Ontario, days after accusing Premier Doug Ford’s office of trying to use the potential extension of a government contract with a company run by Godfrey’s son as “political leverage.”

Laura Stone and Jeff Gray report that the Ontario government confirmed today that the 87-year-old Godfrey, a longtime Progressive Conservative, is no longer on the council that evaluates nominees and makes recommendations for the Order of Ontario , the province’s highest civilian honour.

Godfrey’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.

The longtime political powerbroker, himself a member of both the Order of Ontario and the Order of Canada, waded into a tangled legal battle this week between the province and a technology company called Keel Digital Solutions Corp., chaired by his son, Rob Godfrey. The company, which faces an Ontario Provincial Police probe, was put into receivership this week over unpaid debts.

In an allegation that has been denied by both the Premier’s Office and Postmedia, Godfrey says he felt pressured to ask his former newspaper chain to print an op-ed by the Premier before last year’s snap provincial election – in return for help from a senior official to hurry the approval of a new three-year government contract for Keel.

In other news, Canada’s economy posted a second consecutive month of job losses in September, pushing up the unemployment rate and offsetting what had been a hot streak for the labour market earlier in the year.

Statistics Canada said today that the economy lost 68,000 positions in September, coming off a loss of 42,000 roles in August.

All the best for the holiday weekend. There will be no newsletter on Thanksgiving Monday.

Poilievre to deliver Canadian unity speech in Alberta ahead of referendum: Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told a news conference in Burlington, Ont. today he will be doing “additional campaigning on the ground” in Alberta next week.

Ottawa declassifies new details about CIA’s role in resettling Nazi war criminals in Canada: The newly declassified information sheds more light on the role American intelligence agencies played in facilitating the settlement of Nazi collaborators in Canada, in some cases by providing false identity papers.

Industry optimistic as Defence Investment Agency pursues new business model, but questions remain: New legislation to transform Ottawa’s Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation is a positive step, industry members say, but concerns about slow-moving procurement remain as the agency pursues a new business model.

Canada signs on to pledge to fight subsidized overproduction of EVs, batteries and solar panels: In all, 14 countries plus the EU signed on to this communiqué, which warned of the increasing harms that factory overproduction “created, sustained, or contributed to by government policies or interventions” is causing to the signatories’ domestic industries.

Ottawa negotiating deal with Angola as trade diversification efforts expand: Canadian mining companies could be among the beneficiaries of the federal government’s push for an economic agreement with resource-rich Angola, one of the first African targets in Ottawa’s global trade diversification campaign.

On our radar

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney did not have any public events today.

Party Leaders: In Burlington Ontario, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre held a news conference. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May attended the sitting of the House of Commons. NDP Leader Avi Lewis met, in Toronto, with the NDP caucus. No schedule available for Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet.

Ministers on the Road:

In the Quebec township of Orford, Canadian Identity Minister Marc Miller announced today $334,750 in funding over four years to support the annual Orford Musique festival and its year-round concert programming.

In the Quebec city of Beaupré, Public Works Minister Joël Lightbound , joined with Québec International to meet with Quebec company Ferreol Skis and visit its innovation laboratory.

In the Nova Scotia community of Hacketts Cove, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab highlighted the new Productivity Mega Deduction, which will provide immediate expensing for a broad-based range of depreciable property on a permanent basis.

In Edmonton, Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski announced more than $15.6-million through the Humanitarian Workforce Program to strengthen the Canadian Red Cross’s readiness to respond when disasters occur.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu is leading a Team Canada trade mission, with about 300 delegates, to India from next Monday to Saturday. Stops will include Mumbai and Bengaluru.

“What we need to do is focus on saving Canadians money and jobs, giving young people hope they will be able to have homes and start families.” - Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre , during a news conference in Burlington today, responds to a question from The Globe and Mail about members of his caucus who are leaving politics, and what he is doing to ensure the exits don’t continue.

Human rights pioneer Navi Pillay was today named the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize. Before Lester Pearson’s run as prime minister between 1963 and 1968, he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957. What did he do to earn the honour?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Perspectives

The Liberals are right to restrict MAID

The Liberals are to be commended for backing away from one ill-advised expansion of MAID. They should make sure that they are not embarking on another. — The Globe and Mail Editorial Board

The Alberta referendum: a pointless, futile stunt, just like the last one

Let us come, then, to the latest exercise in knife-at-the-throat democracy, the gargantuan, 10-question ballot the government of Danielle Smith, Mr. Kenney’s successor, has seen fit to place before the voters. — Andrew Coyne, Columnist

Alberta used AI to draft its whisky act, giving Canada’s legal community a buzz

Alberta’s use of AI to draft its whisky law is proof of the tech’s evolving potential. But governments must use it with a peg of prudence or risk finding themselves on the rocks. — Rita Trichur, Senior Business Writer and Columnist

Follow along for our stories on Canada-U.S. relations as news develops

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question:

Following a 1956 attack on Egypt by Great Britain, France and Israel, Pearson, as Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs, secured support for sending a United Nations emergency force to the region to separate the parties in conflict. His efforts earned him the peace prize.

stories.title: Another Marineland whale dies at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago
stories.summary: It's the sixth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., theme park to die after a massive relocation of whales and dolphins over the summer.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Another whale shipped out of Marineland has died at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago.

The aquarium says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga, died on Wednesday despite efforts to save her.

It’s the sixth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., theme park to die after a massive relocation of whales and dolphins over the summer.

Four other belugas and one dolphin from Marineland have died since they were moved out of the former tourist attraction.

Shedd says Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels. The park added that her blood had become “dangerously acidic.”

The aquarium says those findings helped the veterinary care team understand how sick the beluga was, but they did not establish a cause of death.

Shedd says Caspian was on life support for nearly four hours before she died.

Shedd recently performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.

Shedd and four other aquariums in the United States and Spain helped Marineland relocate all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins over the course of six weeks this summer.

Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada.

A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

stories.title: Port Stanley celebrates Arrival Day with Oneida First Nation
stories.summary: It was a day to celebrate First Nations in Port Stanley. The Elgin County village on Friday played host to Oneida Arrival Day, an event to commemorate the Oneida Peoples’ journey across Lake Erie nearly two centuries ago.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
It was a day to celebrate First Nations in Port Stanley. The Elgin County village on Friday played host to Oneida Arrival Day, an event to commemorate the Oneida Peoples’ journey across Lake Erie nearly two centuries ago.

Among the hundreds on hand to take in the sights and sounds at Little Beach was Oneida Elder, 82 year old Rog Cornelius.

“We’re a welcoming people. We share what we have, whether there’s a little bit, or plenty,” he said.

Oneida Arrival Day marks the story of how in 1840 First Nations were forced from their home in Oneida, New York.

200 crossed Lake Erie by boat and landed on what would become the shores of Elgin County, Ontario.

Oneida elected councillor Alizabeth George-Antone says each member bought and paid for land to establish the Oneida First Nation community we know today.

“We have a very unique story because Oneida came here and purchased our land in 1840 before Canada was fully a country at that time. So Oneida has unique status with our land,” George-Antone explained.

Arrival Day is filled with art, food, and music. A celebration of First Nations culture shared by Oneida community members. Leaders from both Port Stanley and Oneida say it also plays a big role in fostering Truth and Reconciliation.

“And I think what’s happening right now is a great demonstration of Truth and Reconciliation. We’re coming together. Doors are open. Hands are open. And we’re going to learn from each other,” said Tonya Antone, a musician and MC for the Oneida Community Band.

“It’s an understanding day. It’s a day for us to learn about the Oneida people, and also to have some fun as a community,” said Central Elgin Mayor Andrew Sloan.

As for one elder on this Arrival Day, Rog Cornelius’s message is simple.

“We’re human. We should get along and do everything toward that.”

stories.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional
stories.summary: The Court found that, among other things, the act still grants the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction.
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional, following a second court challenge of the federal legislation.

The act, otherwise known as Bill C-69 , was first passed by the Liberals under former prime minister Justin Trudeau to set out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines.

In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction.

The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction.

“While Parliament May have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the (Impact Assessment Act) creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects,” the court wrote.

“This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, ON the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction.”

The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren’t constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction.

“The decision maker May regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project,” the court wrote.

Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta’s legal challenge.

The Impact Assessment Act has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the “no more pipelines act.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was “yet another big win for Alberta.”

“I’m calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country,” she said.

Friday’s ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast.

Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa’s new Building Canada Act.

And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed.

Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator.

The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn’t be found at the Impact Assessment Agency.

Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions of the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews.

In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps.

”To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The (Impact Assessment Act) is fundamental to the advancement of this work,” wrote press secretary Amy Falkner.

”The (Court of Appeal) opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

— With files from Lauren Krugel in Calgary.

“The decision maker May regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project,” the court wrote.
Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta’s legal challenge.
The Impact Assessment Act has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the “no more pipelines act.”
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was “yet another big win for Alberta.”

“I’m calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country,” she said.
Friday’s ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast.
Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa’s new Building Canada Act.

And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed.

Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator.

The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn’t be found at the Impact Assessment Agency.

Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions of the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews.
In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps.

”To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The (Impact Assessment Act) is fundamental to the advancement of this work,” wrote press secretary Amy Falkner.
”The (Court of Appeal) opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism.”

stories.title: Encampment removal in Saskatoon ‘very sad,’ but necessary, advocate says
stories.summary: Thursday's removal of a Saskatoon encampment at 20th Street and Avenue K South has left many residents seeking resources from Saskatoon outreach groups, they say.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The removal of a Saskatoon encampment earlier this week was upsetting, but necessary, a local outreach advocate said.

The reaction comes following the City of Saskatoon’s decision to remove the encampment on city-owned private property at 20th Street and Avenue K South on Thursday. In a news release that evening, the city said 120 people left the site.

Eighty tents were removed from the encampment, the City of Saskatoon added.

“It was very sad for us to see the encampments go down, but to be honest, they needed to. There has been a lot of violence,” Shirley Isbister, president of the Central Urban Métis Federation Inc. (Cumfi), told Global News.

“There was alcohol, drugs being moved in and that’s not a good environment for safety for the people in the encampments or for the people in the community.”

Following the cleanup of the encampment, Cumfi’s president said a large number of its residents arrived at the Saskatoon nonprofit and set up in its area.

Many of them set up close to the nearby railroad tracks, she said, adding two previous encampment residents sought shelter in the group’s Mobile Housing and Community Resource Centre Bus. The bus has Wi-Fi, as well as contact information for people to get housing.

“We have a lot of encampments here. And we have the bathrooms, and we have the showers but it’s also getting cold,” Isbister said, noting that those facilities are expected to close at the end of this month in anticipation of winter weather.

“That tells me that there’s a lot of people who aren’t ready to be housed yet,” she continued.

“People gather and they stay in the encampments because that’s where they’re happy.”

Isibister said the charity will continue providing support and resources, such as clothing and blankets, to people who reach out, including those who have established encampments around Cumfi.

Melissa Zimmer, president and founder of Bridge City Warmth, a volunteer group who distributes supplies to people who are homeless in Saskatoon said her group was visiting the encampment on 20th Street multiple times a day in recent weeks to hand out business cards.

She said Thursday’s takedown led to the group assisting in finding housing for five people.

“Since the encampment’s been taken down, we’ve had all kinds of calls, text messages, emails just looking for assistance with housing, and just we’re finding that there’s just so many barriers for those looking for housing,” Zimmer said.

On Thursday night, the nonprofit had a street patrol which observed many residents from the encampment who needed a hot meal or new supplies, she continued. Those living at the now-removed site are scattered across the city – including some who found spots in shelters before they filled.

“When we showed up last night at our street patrol, we left with nothing. People need stuff. They’re cold, they’re hungry, they’re tired,” Zimmer said.

Ahead of the winter, the group has put out a call for highly requested items, such as blankets and jackets.

stories.title: Canadians’ mental health is at a decade low: Western prof explains why, and what May help
stories.summary: Western University professor Eric Collins reflects on mental health worsening in Canada, and what could be done to tackle the problem.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
In Canada, almost a third of the population rated their mental health fair or poorlast year, an increase from five years earlier. By the age of 40, one in two Canadians will have had, or be living with, a mental illness.

Mental health has only worsened since the COVID-19 pandemic, and reflects a pattern of declining rates across the globe. We’re in the midst of a systemic mental health crisis that has evolved over the past several decades, explained Western University’s Eric Collins.

A professor of health studies within the Faculty of Health Sciences, Collins specializes in teaching and researching mental illness. Today’s crisis is the culmination of an ever-shifting notion of mental health, he said, and the policies that have sprung forth from those views.

In the ancient world, mental illness was often framed as a supernatural curse or moral failure, laying the groundwork for centuries of stigma and cruelty to those affected. With the discovery of brain networks and neurochemistry, the 20 th century brought a modern understanding of mental health, rooted in science. Advancements in technology have further unearthed its complexity.

We still haven’t got it figured out, Collins stressed.

An over-emphasis on the biological mechanisms of the brain has turned mental health into a checklist, he says, where “people are labelled as mentally ill or having a diagnosis because of how they check off a number of boxes in a diagnostic manual. It is a mistake to think of our mental health in isolation from our physical environment, from our social relationships, our workplace, and all these factors,” he added.

Mental health is a collection of our emotional, psychological and social capacity – which, together, allow us to deal with adversity and tough times, Collins said.

But external factors are weighing on us more than ever. Collins considers the current affordability crisis one of the greatest contributors to our worsening mental state.

“It’s impossible to ignore because of the implications it has on an everyday basis. We need bread, we need vegetables, we need somewhere to live,” he said. “If those things are out of reach or putting us into debt, that affects us every single day.”

Even more pervasive, and just as influential, is social media. Collins points to the slew of mixed content that floods feeds, often filled with violent and graphic imagery, as taking a significant toll on our well-being. And while this negative content stirs up immediate feelings of angst, aspirational content from influencers showcasing their fitness or wealth lifestyle can be equally as disheartening.

“It’s become, for many people, the benchmark they’re trying to reach. And if they’re not there, they feel at a deficit through this comparison,” Collins said.

While extending our ability to connect with people online, Collins also recognizes how internet culture has re-shaped our social lives, an irreplaceable ingredient to happiness.

“We’re not machines or robots. We’re designed to connect with one another in-person, in real life,” he stressed. “If our existence is not structured to facilitate that, we pay a price.”

The price is an all-encompassing weight on our well-being, extending to our physical health as well.

Our bodies are always responding in a way to try to help us survive, and in many cases, thrive, he said. “When our mental health is poor, it can be difficult to get off the couch, get out of bed, find the energy to do the things we know would help.”

This is why reframing mental health holistically – as an experience deeply responsive to the web of our surroundings – is an important starting point for understanding and effectively addressing this crisis, Collins said. Not only does it take pressure off the individual, “it exposes many societal problems contributing to our well-being.”

As long as these pressures – soaring affordability costs, constant exposure to harmful social media content and the absence of meaningful in-person social connection – continue to dominate daily life, solving the mental health crisis will be difficult, Collins believes. But he remains hopeful. On a systemic level, he sees expanding access to high-quality, community-based mental health support as an essential, timely strategy that can provide immediate relief to those most in need while broader social reforms are implemented.

Because specialized mental health care is largely privatized and out of reach, many Canadians are left navigating years-long public waitlists. In the absence of timely professional care, some people use harmful coping strategies, such as substance misuse, chronic gambling or other high-risk behaviours for temporary relief, Collins said.

Encouraging young adults to choose a career in the mental health care field, amid a shortage in the industry, and ensure there is available services for those who need them, is a possible solution to democratizing care, Collins said.

“You need to have the bricks and mortar, the hospitals, the clinics, the institutions available to house people or patients, but also the trained experts to work. All this lowers barriers to access.”

On a personal level, he encourages people to center the fundamentals, and take it step by step.

“If you’re fortunate enough to have a home that has a roof over it and has a refrigerator and shower, try your best to take care of yourself that way,” he said.

Collins’ Tips:

Get good quality sleep.

Limit your exposure to social media.

Try to eat nutritious food.

Take care of your hygiene.

Try to exercise.

Connect with others in-person.

“I am optimistic that we’re figuring it out, painfully, but in a way that’s moving us in a positive direction,” Collins said.

Reflecting on his childhood and adolescence, Collins experienced his own mental health struggles. He credits the support of people around him, access to quality mental health care and a relentless determination, with leading him to recovery. This triumph gave him invaluable insight into what mental health means, and how we can all navigate it.

“I’ve learned that there is a pathway to recovery. I’ve lived it, and it’s possible for others as well,” he said.

“It’s inevitable that we’ll experience adversity in our personal lives, we’re all recovering from something – but in that, we can find deep meaning and establish connections that really make it all worth it.”

Our bodies are always responding in a way to try to help us survive, and in many cases, thrive, he said. “When our mental health is poor, it can be difficult to get off the couch, get out of bed, find the energy to do the things we know would help.”

This is why reframing mental health holistically – as an experience deeply responsive to the web of our surroundings – is an important starting point for understanding and effectively addressing this crisis, Collins said. Not only does it take pressure off the individual, “it exposes many societal problems contributing to our well-being.”

As long as these pressures – soaring affordability costs, constant exposure to harmful social media content and the absence of meaningful in-person social connection – continue to dominate daily life, solving the mental health crisis will be difficult, Collins believes. But he remains hopeful. On a systemic level, he sees expanding access to high-quality, community-based mental health support as an essential, timely strategy that can provide immediate relief to those most in need while broader social reforms are implemented.

Because specialized mental health care is largely privatized and out of reach, many Canadians are left navigating years-long public waitlists. In the absence of timely professional care, some people use harmful coping strategies, such as substance misuse, chronic gambling or other high-risk behaviours for temporary relief, Collins said.

Encouraging young adults to choose a career in the mental health care field, amid a shortage in the industry, and ensure there is available services for those who need them, is a possible solution to democratizing care, Collins said.
“You need to have the bricks and mortar, the hospitals, the clinics, the institutions available to house people or patients, but also the trained experts to work. All this lowers barriers to access.”
On a personal level, he encourages people to center the fundamentals, and take it step by step.
“If you’re fortunate enough to have a home that has a roof over it and has a refrigerator and shower, try your best to take care of yourself that way,” he said.
Collins’ Tips:

items: Limit your exposure to social media.

content_blocks.text: “I am optimistic that we’re figuring it out, painfully, but in a way that’s moving us in a positive direction,” Collins said.

Reflecting on his childhood and adolescence, Collins experienced his own mental health struggles. He credits the support of people around him, access to quality mental health care and a relentless determination, with leading him to recovery. This triumph gave him invaluable insight into what mental health means, and how we can all navigate it.
“I’ve learned that there is a pathway to recovery. I’ve lived it, and it’s possible for others as well,” he said.

“It’s inevitable that we’ll experience adversity in our personal lives, we’re all recovering from something – but in that, we can find deep meaning and establish connections that really make it all worth it.”

stories.title: All evidence heard in trial of former babysitter charged in toddler’s death
stories.summary: Following 49 days of testimony, lengthy legal arguments and numerous adjournments all of the evidence is now in at the trial of a former Strathroy area babysitter charged in the death of a toddler.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Following 49 days of testimony, lengthy legal arguments and numerous adjournments all of the evidence is now in at the trial of a former Strathroy area babysitter charged in the death of a toddler.

Meggin Van Hoof, 47, has plead not guilty to one charge of manslaughter in connection to the death of Nathaniel McLellan.

The 15-month-old boy had been in the care of Van Hoof on the day he was rushed to hospital by his mother 11 years ago.

He died in October 2015 after suffering blunt force trauma to the head.

Van Hoof would not be charged until six years later.

After the Crown closed its case on Friday, the defence said it was not calling any evidence and that the accused herself would not be testifying.

Justice Michael Carnegie then told the court, “It is the Crown that bears the burden of proving the offence beyond a reasonable doubt.”

The matter has now been put over until Oct. 28 to set a date for closing submissions which May not be heard until February of next year.

stories.title: 7 Alberta referendum signs vandalized in Fort McMurray
stories.summary: More than half of the signs encouraging Albertans to vote to have a second, binding referendum to leave Canada were vandalized in Fort McMurray over the past week.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Treason. No to the nine. Not your land.

Those are just some of the words spray-painted this week on several Alberta referendum political signs placed throughout Fort McMurray.

Wood Buffalo RCMP were alerted Thursday about the damage to more than half of the signs promoting Alberta separatism in the northern Alberta community.

RCMP said they received a report that seven signs relating to the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum had been damaged with spray paint, sometime between Sept. 29 and Oct. 4.

Elections Alberta granted permission for 11 signs from third-party campaign group Let Alberta Decide to be placed around the community.

The signs were all spray painted with various graffiti, bearing messages like “No Treason Gtfo!!!” and one said “Go 2 America!”

It’s a criminal offence to destroy, damage or steal election signs, which RCMP has pointed out several times over the years when signs in other elections have been vandalized or gone missing.

The vandalism happened to two signs along Thickwood Boulevard, two along Confederation Drive, and one each on Hospital Street, MacKenzie Boulevard and along Highway 63 across from the dump station.

The Let Alberta Decide campaign is promoting Albertans selecting option two on the tenth question being asked in the Oct. 19 referendum.

It states: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

The RCMP said the signs have since been repaired and are now asking for the public’s assistance in identifying those responsible for damaging them.

Anyone who witnessed suspicious activity near any of the above-mentioned locations, has relevant surveillance or dash camera footage, or has information that could help the investigation is asked to call Wood Buffalo RCMP at 780-788-4040.

stories.title: Family of Walkerton crash victim pushing for school transportation and grief counselling reform
stories.summary: It’s been more than a year since four Walkerton high school softball players and their coach were taken in a tragic crash near London.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
It’s been more than a year since four Walkerton high school softball players and their coach were taken in a tragic crash near London.

Coach and teacher Mat Eckert was driving the SUV carrying Olivia Rourke, Rowan McLeod, Danica Baker, and Kaydance Ford when it collided with a transport truck on May 23, 2025.

While she holds no blame towards Coach Eckert, Kaydance Ford’s mother believes the practice of teachers or coaches driving students to off-site sports, or school sanctioned activities should no longer be happening.

“A lot of the time there’s teachers and coaches who are driving students and that should not be the norm. It shouldn’t be common. I don’t know why it was ever made a thing because it’s not in their job description. They should not be responsible to transfer students to a school sanctioned event. That never should have been a thing,” said Jessica Ford, Kaydance Ford’s mother.

Jessica has submitted a 14 point Student Grief and Traumatic Loss Reform Proposal to the Bluewater District School Board. At it’s core, she’s calling for a school sanctioned school bus or coach bus to be the main source of transportation for students to off-site activities.

“I want to see not necessarily a bus for every single school sanctioned event, but for most of them, if it makes sense to fund a bus then fund a bus. If there’s no funding then ask parents if they can pay for the bus. We used to do that all the time when I was young, so there’s really no reason why we can’t do it again,” she said.

Jessica is also calling for a more standardized framework for death and traumatic loss through the school board, including long term student grief counselling, and a bereaved family liaison to help families navigate help and support during their darkest days.

“Yes, the initial tragedy needs fast support, but not just after that first week or first month. It needs to be ongoing. And it can’t be that the student has to be responsible for reaching out to ask for that. We shouldn’t have to ask for grief support when we’re grieving,” she said.

She wants better communication for the next family that faces a tragedy like theirs. As an example, she says her family wasn’t informed the school was making “memorial tables” for the crash victims until they were already in place.

“Because we didn’t learn about the memorial tables until later, we very well could have been the only family that their daughter’s table didn’t have personal things. And that hurt us, but it also would have ended up hurting her friends, and other students and staff,” she said.

The Bluewater District School Board says they are looking over Jessica’s reforms. While they are proud of their response in the wake of the crash tragedy, they acknowledge more could possibly be done in the future.

As far as student transportation to off-site activities goes, the school board says they too want school bus transportation for all students but that’s not always possible.

“Efforts are made to secure bus transportation for trips and excursions where possible. However, there are limitations and unique circumstances that must be considered and applying this approach consistently to all trips across more than 40 school locations presents some challenges. We will continue to review all options available to us while prioritizing the safety of our students and staff,” said a Bluewater District School Board statement.

Jessica has met with school board officials regarding her proposed changes to trauma response, and off-site school transportation.

“I really hoped that we would learn from our tragedy. We can’t change what happened to our family, but we can advocate for changes to happen before something else happens to another family because we don’t live in a perfect world.

This wasn’t the first tragedy, and it won’t be the last. So we need to learn from it. And we really need to look at how we transport our children. I don’t want to see another family go through the added trauma or the added stress that we have.

And I in a perfect world, it wouldn’t happen again. But in reality, we live in an imperfect world. So I want to see something in place that can prevent as much of this as possible,” said Jessica.

To learn more about Jessica’s Student Grief and Traumatic Loss Reform Proposal, you can visit the Kaydance Ford Athletic and Trades Foundation website .

The full response to Ford’s proposal, from the Bluewater District School Board.

“Bluewater District School Board has received the proposal and is reviewing its recommendations with staff in the applicable portfolios.

When it comes to critical incidents affecting our schools, we are continually learning, refining our practices, and looking for meaningful ways to strengthen our existing supports and communication practices. The tragedy impacting Walkerton District Community School in May 2025 was significant.

Our school and system-level staff closely followed our established tragedy response and crisis communications processes that have guided us through many previous school-based incidents. This included consulting and working closely with other experts outside of our organization, such as the Center for Trauma Informed Practices (Ctip) and Victim Services.

These are living documents that will continue to be refined through our direct experiences in managing situations involving tragedy. While our primary focus has been to support the students and staff of a school when they experience a traumatic event, we are exploring ways to better support directly impacted families in our approach, which is one of the key areas outlined in the proposal.

Regarding student transportation for trips and events, we follow board policy BP 5602-D Field Trips and Excursions and its accompanying procedure AP 5602-D Field Trips and Excursions – Approval Process . As outlined in the procedure, it is currently a requirement that any volunteer drivers who are transporting students must first obtain appropriate formal authorization.

Our broader transportation policy, BP 6501-D Transportation , indicates the intent to provide transportation (i.e., busing) for school-sponsored educational, sports, and general-interest programs, within the limits established by the annual budget.

In accordance with the policy, efforts are made to secure bus transportation for trips and excursions, where possible. However, there are limitations and unique circumstances that must be considered and applying this approach consistently to all trips across more than 40 school locations presents some challenges.

We will continue to review all options available to us while prioritizing the safety of our students and staff.”
