stories.title: Halton police in Ontario uses AI in hiring, training 911 call takers
stories.summary: Halton regional police in Ontario say they are using artificial intelligence in the recruitment and training of 911 call takers and dispatchers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
They say American AI firm GovWorx provides the technology to create emergency call simulations to help 911 applicants improve their decision-making, communication and crisis management skills.

Halton police say the use of AI in the hiring of 911 communicators reduces candidate evaluation time by 50 per cent.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

They say the force is the first in Canada to use AI in training for 911 call takers and dispatchers.

Halton police started using another AI technology called Sara AI to take certain types of non-emergency phone calls.

They say the bot has answered 95,367 calls so far this year and sent more than 2,470 text messages to people to report events through alternate means like websites or the collision reporting centre.

stories.title: Charges laid after ‘Code Silver’ at St. Thomas hospital
stories.summary: A 40-year-old London resident is facing multiple charges after an alleged threat against an employee at St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital prompted a lockdown Thursday.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 40-year-old London resident is facing multiple charges after an alleged threat against an employee at St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital prompted a lockdown Thursday .

St. Thomas police say officers were called to the hospital on Thursday after reports that a suspect had threatened a hospital employee.

As a precaution, the hospital issued a Code Silver, locking down the building while police investigated.

Police said a 40-year-old London resident was arrested and charged with two counts of uttering threats to cause death, possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, administering a noxious substance with intent to endanger life, and mischief causing damage to property.

The accused was being held in police custody and was scheduled to appear in court Friday morning.

Police have not released the identity of the accused.

stories.content:
ST. John’s - Shell Canada has agreed to buy a 30 per cent stake in the proposed Bay du Nord oil project off the East Coast of Newfoundland from Norwegian energy giant Equinor, which will continue to lead the $14-billion development.

Equinor is expected to decide early next year whether it will proceed with what would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada.

stories.title: Buying a home with points, where our cities are shrinking and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Oct. 9
stories.summary: Plus, this week’s lowest fixed and variable mortgage rates in Canada
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: A way to buy a home with rewards points, and the parts of our fastest-growing cities that are actually shrinking. Plus, a clash over discipline for a real-estate scandal, and one home worth a look.

Rewards programs can help you travel, get cash back or even enjoy a free birthday treat, but what about buying a home? A new company offers a way for your everyday spending and even paying your rent on time to earn you points towards perhaps the biggest purchase of your life – no credit card required.

Quarters connects to all your bank accounts and credit cards, awarding you 1 per cent on most purchases that you can use to cover a realtor’s broker fee, potentially saving you thousands on closing costs. As Salmaan Farooqui reports, co-founder Romir Joshi says the program helps aspiring homeowners feel their goal is within reach, realtors get referrals for reliable clients, and institutional landlords attract tenants who are further incentivized to pay rent on time. “We just literally need to show them the property, sign a couple pieces of paper, and they [the realtors] can get paid,” Joshi told Salmaan.

But should you use Quarters? It’s gotten a couple of glowing reviews, with one user saying he saved $8,000, largely through purchases on Uber Eats, a partner app. Calgary-based rewards expert Patrick Sojka says the program is worth it because it allows you to stack your rewards on top of existing credit card rewards like Rbc’s Avion or Blue Rewards (formerly Air Miles). However, it’s common for rewards programs to start out strong and then cut back benefits, so read Salmaan’s piece and keep an eye out for diminishing returns down the road.

Has the solution to the housing crisis been right in front of us all along? Toronto and Vancouver’s populations have doubled in the last 50 years, but there are pockets where the population has shrunk since 1970s – sometimes by as much as 40 per cent. One of those neighbourhoods is affluent Kerrisdale, where my weekend bike rides take me by more and more shuttered shops. And as Alex Bozikovic reports with Yang Sun’s data analysis , the west-side Vancouver neighbourhood is far from an anomaly.

Using census data on clusters of a few blocks, the data shows something you can’t see from the street. In the Vancouver region, 21 per cent of these clusters declined in population between 1971 and 2021, losing 76,424 people in total, and many others failed to keep up with growth. The pattern is even more stark in and around Toronto: Almost three-quarters of those established areas had declined, shedding a total of 540,789 people. Statistics Canada advises against such a granular analysis because boundaries change over time, but, as Yang told me, “that is the level urban planners, demographers, cartographers or journalists often want to see how a place has changed.”

So what’s going on in your neighbourhood, and could building more into these shrinking areas help us avoid urban sprawl? Experts say they could absorb more residents and at a lower cost than building new communities, but as Alex writes, it’s not as simple as that. Read the story to see where cities are gaining or losing population , and why some see a solution to the housing crisis in the data.

Things are getting heated in the Prairies. The decision to allow two real estate agents who broke provincial and Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission rules dozens of times to keep their licenses has the Saskatchewan Realtors’ Association riled up over the “wholly inadequate” punishment and calling for an overhaul at the regulator. And as Shane Dingman reports, the disagreement is renewing attention on the scandal and how realtors are disciplined.

Paul Chavady and Jerry Hallgrimson failed to represent the interests of buyers when representing both buyers and sellers on 67 occasions, failed to remove conditions on sales contracts and, in one case, failed to disclose the presence of asbestos in a home they sold in dual agency, according to the commission’s recent disciplinary decision. The two business partners held key roles at Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

Their punishment? Each must pay $100,000 in fines and serve a six-month suspension, staggered so that at least one can continue practising real estate while the other is suspended. The SRA says it’s not harsh enough to uphold the trust consumers place in realtors, and has called for an inquiry and overhaul at the Srec. However the commission defended its decision, saying the evidence didn’t demonstrate the criminality required to permanently revoke their licenses. Read more about the scandal and why the two bodies are at odds over how to regulate realtors.

What’s old is new, and that goes for your home, too. But how can you actually turn good bones into something fit for this millennium? These three heritage home renovations took different approaches to balancing original character and modern comforts, but all got beautiful results. From opening up a vaulted ceiling in a 1920s Tudor in Toronto to preserving a neo-Georgian’s stunning woodwork in Quebec, take a peek inside the transformations to get inspired.

And while these projects weren’t necessarily on a budget, designers told Silvana Longo there are plenty of ways to keep a home’s character without breaking the bank. You might think it’s cheaper to gut everything, but read their tips for preserving your home’s history and your finances before you get out the sledgehammer.

816 248 St., Langley, B.C. – Full gallery here

This historic home offers a lesson in creative vision. Built in Langley’s farm country in 1922, the original one-room schoolhouse was expanded in 1970, shuttered in 1983 and became a private residence in 1987, with many haphazard renovations following. But carpenter Alex Oosthoek and his wife Jill, an artist, saw through the peculiarities to the cozy space it would become for their two daughters to grow up.

After taking it down to the studs, harmonizing the rooflines of the expansion and turning the covered former play area into an in-law suite, the vision started to come to life. The 1970s addition was once the school office, but now houses the kitchen, three bathrooms and lounging and dining areas with a wood stove and exposed beams on the ceiling. There is a modern farmhouse feeling throughout the inside of the four-bedroom, 2,724-square foot home, but vestiges of the former classroom remain, including panelled ceiling and walls painted white in the entry area. Outside, cedar shake siding gives it a distinctly West-Coast feel.

Sitting on an acre whose designation protects against urban sprawl, the property is surrounded by large equestrian estates and, save for the stars, “black, black, black” at night, said Mr. Oosthoek. But while the family enjoyed the quiet, the surrounding community’s connection to the schoolhouse – and, sometimes, their escaped cows – also made living there special. Inspired by the school’s pancake breakfast every Christmas, the Oosthoeks hosted a holiday potluck for neighbours, former students and retired teachers. “The school was a community hub, and it was really nice to do that again,” Ms. Oosthoek said.

content_blocks.text: Quarters connects to all your bank accounts and credit cards, awarding you 1 per cent on most purchases that you can use to cover a realtor’s broker fee, potentially saving you thousands on closing costs. content_blocks.text: The population is declining in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we built more housing there?
content_blocks.html: The population is declining in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we built more housing there?

content_blocks.text: Has the solution to the housing crisis been right in front of us all along? Toronto and Vancouver’s populations have doubled in the last 50 years, but there are pockets where the population has shrunk since 1970s – sometimes by as much as 40 per cent. One of those neighbourhoods is affluent Kerrisdale, where my weekend bike rides take me by more and more shuttered shops. And as Alex Bozikovic reports with Yang Sun’s data analysis , the west-side Vancouver neighbourhood is far from an anomaly.

Toronto and Vancouver’s populations have doubled in the last 50 years, but there are pockets where the population has shrunk since 1970s – sometimes by as much as 40 per cent. One of those neighbourhoods is affluent Kerrisdale, where my weekend bike rides take me by more and more shuttered shops. And as Alex Bozikovic reports with Yang Sun’s data analysis, the west-side Vancouver neighbourhood is far from an anomaly.

content_blocks.text: Using census data on clusters of a few blocks, the data shows something you can’t see from the street. In the Vancouver region, 21 per cent of these clusters declined in population between 1971 and 2021, losing 76,424 people in total, and many others failed to keep up with growth. The pattern is even more stark in and around Toronto: Almost three-quarters of those established areas had declined, shedding a total of 540,789 people. Statistics Canada advises against such a granular analysis because boundaries change over time, but, as Yang told me, “that is the level urban planners, demographers, cartographers or journalists often want to see how a place has changed.”

content_blocks.text: Things are getting heated in the Prairies. The decision to allow two real estate agents who broke provincial and Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission rules dozens of times to keep their licenses has the Saskatchewan Realtors’ Association riled up over the “wholly inadequate” punishment and calling for an overhaul at the regulator. And as Shane Dingman reports, the disagreement is renewing attention on the scandal and how realtors are disciplined.
content_blocks.html: Things are getting heated in the Prairies. The decision to allow two real estate agents who broke provincial and Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission rules dozens of times to keep their licenses has the Saskatchewan Realtors’ Association riled up over the “wholly inadequate” punishment and calling for an overhaul at the regulator. And as Shane Dingman reports, the disagreement is renewing attention on the scandal and how realtors are disciplined.

content_blocks.text: Paul Chavady and Jerry Hallgrimson failed to represent the interests of buyers when representing both buyers and sellers on 67 occasions, failed to remove conditions on sales contracts and, in one case, failed to disclose the presence of asbestos in a home they sold in dual agency, according to the commission’s recent disciplinary decision. The two business partners held key roles at Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

The two business partners held key roles at Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

content_blocks.text: Their punishment? Each must pay $100,000 in fines and serve a six-month suspension, staggered so that at least one can continue practising real estate while the other is suspended. The SRA says it’s not harsh enough to uphold the trust consumers place in realtors, and has called for an inquiry and overhaul at the Srec. However the commission defended its decision, saying the evidence didn’t demonstrate the criminality required to permanently revoke their licenses. Read more about the scandal and why the two bodies are at odds over how to regulate realtors.

stories.title: Did Canada add jobs in September? StatCan to release data
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada has kept its key lending rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent for about a year, but market expectations have been shifting lately.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Statistics Canada is set to report its latest jobs numbers Friday.

A Reuters poll of economists predicts employers added 9,200 positions in September, a slight bounce back after roughly 42,000 jobs were lost in August.

The consensus among economists is the unemployment rate ticked up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent.

The August job losses snapped a hot streak for the labour market, but economists weren’t overly concerned and instead pointed to the relatively stable unemployment rate as a sign the labour market wasn’t taking a major step back.

The jobs data will be the Bank of Canada’s last look at the labour market before its next interest rate decision on Oct. 28.

The central bank has kept its key lending rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent for about a year, but market expectations have been shifting lately, with slightly higher odds we’ll see a hike coming sooner rather than later.

stories.title: Permanent resident who left sex assault victim 'choking on blood' gets 12 years, could get deported
stories.summary: Kepra Udup Bang, an Ethiopian immigrant, was convicted of the aggravated sexual assault of a woman in 2019 thanks largely to DNA evidence.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A man who brutally beat and raped a woman, leaving her unrecognizable and “choking on blood” in the bushes of a Calgary subdivision, was sentenced to 12 years in prison last month.

Alberta Court of Justice Judge Allan Fradsham convicted Kepra Udup Bang, 27, earlier this year of the 2019 aggravated sexual assault of the woman identified as MM in court documents under a publication ban to protect her identity.

“It was a crime of egregious violence which grossly violated the victim’s sexual integrity and left her with significant, life-altering injuries,” Fradsham wrote in his recently published decision.

Although the decision does not mention it, under Canadian law, Udup Bang, a permanent resident who immigrated to Canada from Ethiopia with his family in 2017, could face deportation after serving his time.

Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act , anyone found guilty of an offence under federal law and sentenced to more than six months is automatically deemed inadmissible to Canada, which can lead to a removal order and deportation. That complex legal process begins with a Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) admissibility report, followed by a hearing with the Immigration Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB). If deemed inadmissible, a removal order is issued and can’t be appealed for sentences of six months or more.

As highlighted by a different Alberta judge’s sentencing of another Ethiopian man in Calgary earlier this year for pointing a loaded handgun at someone during a road rage incident, a stay of removal could be granted due to recurring political violence in the African nation.

At present, the nation is not on Canada’s list of countries where administrative deferral of removal measures are in place for situations of humanitarian crisis. Nor is it on Cbsa’s temporary suspension of removal list of countries where “general conditions, such as armed conflict or an environmental disaster, pose a risk to the entire civilian population.” Tsr’s are only in place for Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Iraq, per the Cbsa website.

“Individuals with serious inadmissibility, such as national security and criminality, do not benefit from a stay of removal under these provisions,” the agency writes online. “However, no one is removed from Canada without consideration for their individual needs for protection. When the situation in a country stabilizes, the deferral and suspension of removals can be lifted, and the Cbsa will resume removals for all individuals who have an enforceable removal order.”

Cbsa does not comment on individual cases due to privacy laws. National Post has contacted the agency for more information on current policies regarding removal orders to Ethiopia. Ircc deferred to Cbsa for comment.

During trial last December, the court heard that police were called to a Forest Lawn neighbourhood around 5 a.m. on July 14, 2019, ON reports of someone being attacked and the sound of screaming.

“I could tell he was raping her,” testified one witness who looked out her window to see a man with his pants down holding up a woman from behind.

“After a few minutes of searching, the attending officer heard sounds of someone choking and struggling to breathe” and found MM lying on her back with no clothes below her waist, her legs spread open and her face a mess of blood.

“The officer said that the facial trauma which MM had suffered was so extensive that even if he had found photo identification with the victim… he would not have been able to identify her using it,” Fradsham wrote.

The victim, then a 28-year-old transient with drug addiction issues, was taken to hospital where she remained unconscious for eight days and underwent surgeries to reconstruct her nose, fix her orbital bone and repair a laceration under her chin over the next three months.

As a result of her severe traumatic brain injury, she did not recognize her own mother for several weeks after waking up, lost a month of memory after the attack, and to this day has no recollection of it. Today, she lives at her mother’s house with her husband and 10-year-old child. While now “clean and sober,” she’s unable to work and “does not often leave the residence because she is bothered by noise and collections of people.”

“This aggravated sexual assault has had severe and permanent detrimental effects on MM and her family,” Fradsham noted.

Udup Bang, now a father of two with a common-law partner, wasn’t charged until 2025 after DNA he’d submitted as part of a separate criminal investigation in 2024 — a break-in conviction, according to CBC — matched the samples obtained from MM and a wristband found at the scene of her attack in 2019.

Under questioning by police, he initially alleged that he did not recognize MM when shown a photo of her, but during trial testified that he and MM had met at a child’s birthday party a month before, connected via Snapchat and then engaged in consensual sex on a night in July he was unsure of. The victim maintained all along that she did not know Udup Bang.

“He explained that he lied to police because he had been arrested for aggravated sexual assault resulting in another person being injured, which he understood to be very serious, and was afraid that admitting he knew MM would lead to the police concluding he was guilty,” Fradsham wrote in his March verdict.

That lie and the DNA evidence led Fradsham to dismiss Udup Bang’s version of events and find him guilty. His lack of a criminal record at the time was his only mitigating factor and the judge decided the evidence didn’t support his race as a “significant mitigating weight… on his moral blameworthiness.”

The Crown wanted Udup Bang to spend 10-12 years behind bars, while the defence argued for seven to nine. Fradsham respectfully disagreed, noting the Crown’s “does not adequately address denunciation and deterrence, and gives insufficient weight to the degree of responsibility of the offender.”

As for the defence submission, the judge said he was “mindful of his difficult time growing up” — Udup Bang was born in a refugee camp and “described an unstable upbringing marked by frequent relocations, multiple school changes, and exposure to conflict” — but said none of the evidence allowed him “to conclude that his experiences would materially diminish his moral culpability.’

Udup Bang, in custody since his arrest, was granted credit for 893 days, leaving him with roughly nine years and seven months in prison.

In his pre-sentence report, Udup Bang said “his short-term goal is to become a book publisher within five years,” and long-term goals include “owning an online store… and developing a food-production company within” the next decade.

“He plans to return to school, complete high school, and pursue post-secondary education with the intention of obtaining degrees in business and law,” the report states, per Fradsham.

The victim, then a 28-year-old transient with drug addiction issues, was taken to hospital where she remained unconscious for eight days and underwent surgeries to reconstruct her nose, fix her orbital bone and repair a laceration under her chin over the next three months.

As a result of her severe traumatic brain injury, she did not recognize her own mother for several weeks after waking up, lost a month of memory after the attack, and to this day has no recollection of it. While now “clean and sober,” she’s unable to work and “does not often leave the residence because she is bothered by noise and collections of people.”
“This aggravated sexual assault has had severe and permanent detrimental effects on MM and her family,” Fradsham noted.

Udup Bang, now a father of two with a common-law partner, wasn’t charged until 2025 after DNA he’d submitted as part of a separate criminal investigation in 2024 — a break-in conviction, according to CBC — matched the samples obtained from MM and a wristband found at the scene of her attack in 2019.

That lie and the DNA evidence led Fradsham to dismiss Udup Bang’s version of events and find him guilty. His lack of a criminal record at the time was his only mitigating factor and the judge decided the evidence didn’t support his race as a “significant mitigating weight… on his moral blameworthiness.”

content_blocks.text: Although the decision does not mention it, under Canadian law, Udup Bang, a permanent resident who immigrated to Canada from Ethiopia with his family in 2017, could face deportation after serving his time.

Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act , anyone found guilty of an offence under federal law and sentenced to more than six months is automatically deemed inadmissible to Canada, which can lead to a removal order and deportation. That complex legal process begins with a Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) admissibility report, followed by a hearing with the Immigration Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB). If deemed inadmissible, a removal order is issued and can’t be appealed for sentences of six months or more.

stories.title: New assignments for an old schoolhouse in Langley, B.C.
stories.summary: Creative couple saw potential in the property, despite the rough interior and some peculiarities
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
816 248 St., Langley, B.C.

Asking price: $2,750,000

Taxes: $4,904.45 (2026)

Lot size: One acre

Agents: Carolyn Glazier and Sabrina Glazier, Angell, Hasman & Associates Realty

Most of the trappings of education had vanished from the former South Otter Elementary School when Alex and Jill Oosthoek first saw the property for sale in 2008.

The Oosthoek’s were feeling cramped in their tiny mill worker’s cottage in New Westminster, B.C., as their daughters Hailey and Jenna grew.

They had already explored the rural landscape and equestrian farms of South Langley during family outings to the area.

This one-room schoolhouse, built in 1922 to educate the children of the surrounding farming community, was expanded in the 1970s, then shuttered in 1983.

The building languished for a few years before it was converted into a private residence in 1987.

When the Oosthoek’s toured the home, some improvements had been made by the owner, who worked on sets for the film industry.

“He had a vision for what he wanted to achieve, but it was all done very haphazardly,” Mr. Oosthoek says.

The interior was rough, but the couple are both creative: Ms. Oosthoek is an artist, and Mr. Oosthoek is a carpenter who works on high-end residential projects. Together they could see the potential, despite some peculiarities.

“There were really bizarre props in the yard. And later we found out that kids had scratched obscenities into the stucco,” Mr. Oosthoek says with a laugh.

As the Oosthoek family settled in, they were surprised at the outpouring of goodwill from neighbours and passersby who shared memories of their connection to the community landmark.

“Everyone was expecting that we were going to bulldoze it,” Mr. Oosthoek says.

In the 1970s, a reclaimed building of similar shape and size had been joined to the original schoolhouse with a smaller portion bridging the two.

Mr. Oosthoek’s first task was to rebuild and harmonize three different rooflines.

Outside, a covered playground for the students had been enclosed by the previous owner, who invited musicians over for jam sessions in the stand-alone structure.

The couple decided to transform the former play area into an in-law suite for Ms. Oosthoek’s father.

Some unexpected quirks soon turned up: The former one-room schoolhouse had been converted into three bedrooms, but they still shared the same electrical circuit. When family members turned on the lights in one room, they came on in all of them.

There was no choice but to take the interior back to the studs in order to redo the wiring and the plumbing.

“We were all living like refugees in the main house,” Mr. Oosthoek recalls. “There was quite a period of time when the whole family was camped out in the living room, around the wood stove.”

Along the way, the couple discovered vestiges of scholastic life: The burlap bags used for potato sack races were stored in the attic and lost tin soldiers were embedded in the soil outside.

In the 1970s, the addition housed the school’s offices; today it provides the kitchen, bathrooms, and areas for lounging and dining in the 2,724-square-foot home.

The couple enlisted the next-door neighbour to build the kitchen. Mr. Oosthoek looks back with amusement at the occasional disruptions in farm country.

“Some of his cows would get loose into our yard and we had to chase them around together.”

Once the interior became more comfortable, the couple added cedar shake siding and outdoor sitting areas to the exterior.

Ms. Oosthoek created gardens filled with lavender and perennials.

As the couple and their daughters heard more stories about the school, they learned that it was the venue for a pancake breakfast each Christmas.

The family decided to host a Christmas potluck for neighbours, former students and retired teachers.

“The school was a community hub, and it was really nice to do that again,” Ms. Oosthoek says. “We have a lot of fond memories of 10- and 12-foot Christmas trees.”

The couple has continued to gradually undertake new projects throughout their time there. The in-law suite eventually became a short-term rental, and then an art studio and gym.

“To take on a project like this you have to be really romantic and a little bit naive,” Mr. Oosthoek says. “It’s not really a renovation – it’s a lifestyle.”

The one-acre property sits within a zone designated as an Agricultural Land Reserve, which protects the area against urban sprawl.

Large equestrian estates surround the home, and no street lights illuminate the roads.

“It’s black, black, black here at night,” Mr. Oosthoek says of the peaceful setting, where they sometimes hear owls hooting from inside tall stands of fir trees.

He recalls the time not long after the family arrived when the homeowner across the road decided to nail shut the openings in his antique barn – to the vexation of five or six barn owls that roosted inside.

“The owls flew around for about a week – screeching – until he opened up the barn again,” he says with a laugh.

stories.title: Eby’s election promise to tax unsold condos in B.C. draws industry criticism
stories.summary: Proposal will make it hard for the development community to trust the Premier again, housing experts say
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
B.C. Premier David Eby’s election promise to slap developers with a tax on unsold condos has been met with outrage from developers who’ve already paid hefty fees to build and who are paying substantial carrying costs on units they can’t sell.

Housing experts say the proposal will make it hard for the development community to trust the Premier again, if he is re-elected on Oct. 24. And policy analysts and experts outside that community are also divided, with many perplexed and even opposed to the tax, which would kick in by the second year of vacancy at 2 per cent of the assessed value, then go up by 1 per cent each year it remains unsold. The Premier said his new tax would target 5,000 vacant unsold condo units in Metro Vancouver.

At a news conference, the Premier told reporters he’d also increase the speculation and vacancy tax to 2 per cent for domestic homeowners and 5 per cent for foreign owners.

Simon Fraser University finance professor Andrey Pavlov said he was shocked by the move, which could drop prices in the short term, but have severe unintended consequences, he said.

“No one wants to hold because they want to sell – that’s how they make their money, and then they deploy the money for the next project. To add to those carrying costs, sure, that will incentivize developers to sell even faster.

“And some of them May say, ‘Fine, whatever, I’ll take the loss and move on.’ So, some condos might be sold at a lower price than other ones. But the problem is, this is a very short-term effect. And once you look past that horizon, the issue, of course, is that no one will ever want to build.”

If building in B.C. becomes more expensive and riskier, developers will be forced to build expensive homes, Prof. Pavlov said.

“That investment needs to have some rate of return. And when you make it riskier, you must increase the rate of return.

“And that makes most projects uneconomical, so they never start. And the ones that do start, they need to offer a huge rate of return, which means basically luxury buildings. And that’s not the type of housing we need. So, we’re doing exactly the opposite.”

“They’re punishing the people who build homes,” he said. “This is a penalty for completing projects at completely the wrong time in the cycle. Lenders will treat it as extra risk. Economist and policy expert Mike Moffatt, founding director of Ottawa-based Missing Middle Initiative, called the tax plan “bad policy” that could have the temporary effect of reducing prices but creating more harm than good.

“It May end up helping motivate a few sales, but for the most part, I wouldn’t expect it to accomplish a whole lot,” said Mr. Moffatt. “There can be many reasons why a developer might not be able to sell. “If you have a building that’s not completely sold, maybe you wait a little bit, try and sell more units before obtaining an occupancy permit,” Mr. Moffatt said.

“We have to pay 5 per cent GST to the federal government if we rent them. Perhaps our provincial government could lobby the federal government on this front rather than proposing yet another punitive tax on housing?” he said in an e-mail.

“Imagine taxing an automobile manufacturer, a heat-pump manufacturer or virtually any other business simply because it had finished inventory that had not yet sold,” he added.

The result would not be increased production, he said.

stories.title: Massive soil pile sparks dispute, damages London property
stories.summary: A London couple is calling on city hall to reconsider an exemption in a municipal bylaw they say allowed damage caused by a large pile of fill dumped in a neighbour’s backyard.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A London couple is calling on city hall to reconsider an exemption in a municipal bylaw they say allowed damage caused by a large pile of fill dumped in a neighbour’s backyard.

Standing along her property line in southwest London, Lisa Davis said the pile of earth towers above her.

Davis said dump trucks began depositing loads of soil and stone in her neighbour’s backyard in 2023, in what she believes was an effort to level a steep slope on the property.

She said wooden shipping skids placed along the property line were not enough to prevent the fill from slumping onto her property and against her deck stairs.

“The only way to really fix the problem is to either remove the grade or build a retaining wall,” Davis told CTV News. “It would be in excess of $100,000 just for the retaining wall.”

An engineering report concluded the weight of the loose fill pressing against the home’s second-storey deck stairs compromised the structure’s integrity.

A city-issued Order to Make Safe, issued in April, prohibits use of the deck and stairs and requires they be removed or reinforced.

According to the order, “DC Buck Engineering found the cause of the damage was due to the debris and fill that was placed in the neighbouring property.”

“Those stairs provide us access to the side of the house, but we’re not allowed to use them,” Davis said. She added the family can no longer use the space for gatherings and visits with grandchildren.

Davis and her husband, Neil Mutch, have been involved in a legal dispute with their neighbour over the fill pile for several years.

They said city staff informed them that London’s Site Alteration Bylaw, which governs the use of fill for grading purposes, includes an exemption for residential properties smaller than 0.5 hectares.

Davis said she would like to see the city amend the bylaw to allow for earlier intervention before neighbouring properties are damaged.

In an emailed statement, London’s director of municipal compliance, Amanda Pfeffer, said the city has received complaints regarding the property and has several active bylaw enforcement files under investigation.

Pfeffer said a Property Standards Order related to fence and erosion concerns was issued to the property owner and has been registered on title because deficiencies remain uncorrected. Penalties have also been issued.

She added municipal compliance has arranged debris removal through a contracted service provider and issued additional penalties for repeated bylaw violations.

Despite those measures, Davis said the large pile of fill remains in place.

“It’s the most stressful thing I’ve ever gone through in my life,” she said. “The amount of money to fix the damages, the length of time slowly watching our property deteriorate.”

CTV News contacted the owner of the neighbouring property, but they did not agree to an interview.

Davis alleges the pile contains concrete, asphalt and other mixed materials, and fears it could shift further.

“We just have no protection from our homeowners’ insurance and no protection from the city,” she said.

stories.title: Why Ottawa plans to allow Maid for people incapable of consenting moments before death
stories.summary: Advance requests allowing doctors to administer euthanasia without the person's final expressed consent could be the next Maid battleground.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Just as one debate over euthanasia is being settled, another is emerging over Canada’s plans to allow people to consent to medical aid in dying (Maid) at some future date when they are no longer of sound mind.

In a surprise move this week, federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced the Liberal government is fine-tuning a bill to be introduced sometime this fall that, in addition to placing an indeterminate hold on Maid for mental illness alone, would decriminalize “advance requests” for doctor-administered death.

Critics say the government is preparing to cross a new line, this one based on the fundamental principle of consent.

Performing euthanasia on the basis of a person’s advance request “will mean that people will receive Maid when they no longer understand what is happening to them,” said Trudo Lemmens, a University of Toronto professor of health law and policy.

Another thorny ethical concern: who makes the final call that it’s time to act on an advance request once the person has lost the capacity to decide for themselves?

The Criminal Code generally requires that a person have the capacity to consent to receive Maid immediately before death is administered.

The Liberal government is proposing to change that.

Here’s a look at why that’s making some people nervous.

Advance requests would allow people who have been diagnosed with a serious and incurable disease that will eventually lead to incapacity to draft a document outlining the specific conditions under which they would prefer to die, which would then be provided after they have lost capacity.

In its report following a “national conversation” on the issue, the federal government offered the hypothetical example of a man named “Charlie” who, after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, “decides that should his health decline rapidly and he starts experiencing intolerable suffering after he has lost capacity to make health care decisions, he would like to have Maid provided.”

His advance request would set out conditions that, for Charlie, would constitute “endurable and intolerable suffering,” a formal criterion for Maid. That could include not being able to feed himself, get out of bed or recognize his children.

If these conditions were to arise, the advance request would state that it would be his explicit wish to be provided Maid.

The Criminal Code currently requires that a person have capacity to give explicit, final consent before death. The only exception involves people who are close to a natural death and have already been approved for Maid and have a date set, but are at risk of losing capacity before the scheduled date. In those cases, people can sign a waiver of final consent.

In March, Alberta became the only province to explicitly ban advance requests for Maid. Fraser said it will be up to provinces to decide whether to allow people to make advance requests.

On Oct. 30, 2024, Quebec joined the Netherlands in accepting advance requests for people diagnosed with dementia and other serious conditions that will lead to incapacity.

However, as the Montreal Gazette’s Aaron Derfel has reported, with no amendment to the Criminal Code, many Maid providers in Quebec are anxious about being prosecuted, despite the province’s directive to criminal prosecutors that pursuing doctors who comply with the provincial law would “not be in the public interest.”

Even then, about 3,000 advance requests have now been added to a Quebec registry; between 30 to 40 deaths have been performed under the directives so far.

According to the federal government’s recently conducted national conversation on the issue , an online questionnaire completed by more than 46,000 adults between December 2024 and February 2025 found 69 per cent supported advance requests for people diagnosed with a serious or incurable condition that will lead to a loss of capacity.

Twenty-six per cent said they oppose them.

Some participants in roundtable discussions said final consent is “an essential guardrail. Without it they said that vulnerable individuals would be at risk,” according to the report. Some questioned how people can make a truly informed decision, given they don’t know for certain what they’ll be experiencing in the future.

Likewise, some wondered how to manage circumstances “where the person meets the conditions set out in their advance request but appears to refuse Maid after they have lost capacity.”

“Euthanasia for people who are incapacitated is a very, very delicate matter,” Montreal family physician Laurence Normand-Rivest said this week at a press conference on Parliament Hill organized by the Euthanasia Prevention Coalition. “They don’t have the privilege to consent at the moment where we kill them,” Normand-Rivest said.

“They show a lot of resistance. They need to be sedated. They don’t want an injection, and to have an IV … People think it will be a peaceful death but in fact we see a lot of struggle and battle when doctors euthanize incapacitated patients,” she said.

Dr. Laurent Boisvert, a Maid provider and president of Quebec’s Dying with Dignity association, said that, in his experience, deaths performed under advance requests aren’t nearly so disturbing.

He has personally performed three or four such Maid provisions. “I didn’t have this type of problem, but I know that at some point I can be in front of a patient who is quite aggressive, who doesn’t want to be touched and we need to sedate this patient” in order to insert the IV, Boisvert said.

“But calling this a distressing procedure, I don’t think so.”

People can appoint one or two trusted people — a spouse, an adult child — to make sure their advance request is respected, he said.

In conversations with colleagues, “it seems that it has worked well (with) no big problems at this time,” Boisvert said.

On the morning of her death, the doctor secretly slipped a sedative into the woman’s coffee. She did not tell the woman she was about to die. Despite the sedative, the woman appeared to try to get up in the middle of the procedure and “resisted physically,” the doctor initially reported to the euthanasia committee. The woman’s son-in-law laid her back down so the doctor could inject her. The doctor was eventually acquitted of breaking Dutch euthanasia laws after a judge ruled the woman’s prior written request was sufficient and that there was no legal requirement for the doctor to verify the “current death wish,” BBC reported.

Dying with Dignity Canada said the proposed legislation would only decriminalize advance requests in provinces and territories that also pass legislation permitting them, creating at best a patchwork system across Canada. “At worst, some people in Canada May never have access to advance requests in their province or territory,” CEO Helen Long said.

Fraser, the federal justice minister, said advance requests would allow people at risk of losing their decision-making capacity “to live out their remaining years, rather than being put in a position where they fear they have to take that decision prematurely.”

While he can understand the appeal they hold for some, psychiatrist Dr. Sonu Gaind said there are several unresolved concerns, including how people, once they lose capacity, could withdraw their consent.

“Meaning that, if they change their mind, and they’ve lost capacity, what do you do? How do you deal with it? How do you know?” It’s a concern reflected in the coffee case in the Netherlands, he said.

Advance requests are also based on what people think they would and would not want in the future. “We’re not very good at knowing how we’ll actually deal with things and cope with things” months or years later, said Gaind, a University of Toronto professor. What’s not talked about enough, he said, is what gets “projected into the decision” to end a person’s life.

paragraphs: Just as one debate over euthanasia is being settled, another is emerging over Canada’s plans to allow people to consent to medical aid in dying (Maid) at some future date when they are no longer of sound mind.

In a surprise move this week, federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced the Liberal government is fine-tuning a bill to be introduced sometime this fall that, in addition to placing an indeterminate hold on Maid for mental illness alone, would decriminalize “advance requests” for doctor-administered death.
Critics say the government is preparing to cross a new line, this one based on the fundamental principle of consent.

Performing euthanasia on the basis of a person’s advance request “will mean that people will receive Maid when they no longer understand what is happening to them,” said Trudo Lemmens, a University of Toronto professor of health law and policy.
Another thorny ethical concern: who makes the final call that it’s time to act on an advance request once the person has lost the capacity to decide for themselves?
The Criminal Code generally requires that a person have the capacity to consent to receive Maid immediately before death is administered.
The Liberal government is proposing to change that.
Here’s a look at why that’s making some people nervous.

Advance requests would allow people who have been diagnosed with a serious and incurable disease that will eventually lead to incapacity to draft a document outlining the specific conditions under which they would prefer to die, which would then be provided after they have lost capacity.

In its report following a “national conversation” on the issue, the federal government offered the hypothetical example of a man named “Charlie” who, after being diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, “decides that should his health decline rapidly and he starts experiencing intolerable suffering after he has lost capacity to make health care decisions, he would like to have Maid provided.”

His advance request would set out conditions that, for Charlie, would constitute “endurable and intolerable suffering,” a formal criterion for Maid. That could include not being able to feed himself, get out of bed or recognize his children.
If these conditions were to arise, the advance request would state that it would be his explicit wish to be provided Maid.

The Criminal Code currently requires that a person have capacity to give explicit, final consent before death. The only exception involves people who are close to a natural death and have already been approved for Maid and have a date set, but are at risk of losing capacity before the scheduled date. In those cases, people can sign a waiver of final consent.
In March, Alberta became the only province to explicitly ban advance requests for Maid. Fraser said it will be up to provinces to decide whether to allow people to make advance requests.
On Oct. 30, 2024, Quebec joined the Netherlands in accepting advance requests for people diagnosed with dementia and other serious conditions that will lead to incapacity.

However, as the Montreal Gazette’s Aaron Derfel has reported, with no amendment to the Criminal Code, many Maid providers in Quebec are anxious about being prosecuted, despite the province’s directive to criminal prosecutors that pursuing doctors who comply with the provincial law would “not be in the public interest.”
Even then, about 3,000 advance requests have now been added to a Quebec registry; between 30 to 40 deaths have been performed under the directives so far.

According to the federal government’s recently conducted national conversation on the issue , an online questionnaire completed by more than 46,000 adults between December 2024 and February 2025 found 69 per cent supported advance requests for people diagnosed with a serious or incurable condition that will lead to a loss of capacity.
Twenty-six per cent said they oppose them.

Some participants in roundtable discussions said final consent is “an essential guardrail. Without it they said that vulnerable individuals would be at risk,” according to the report. Some questioned how people can make a truly informed decision, given they don’t know for certain what they’ll be experiencing in the future.
Likewise, some wondered how to manage circumstances “where the person meets the conditions set out in their advance request but appears to refuse Maid after they have lost capacity.”

“Euthanasia for people who are incapacitated is a very, very delicate matter,” Montreal family physician Laurence Normand-Rivest said this week at a press conference on Parliament Hill organized by the Euthanasia Prevention Coalition. “They don’t have the privilege to consent at the moment where we kill them,” Normand-Rivest said.

“They show a lot of resistance. They need to be sedated. They don’t want an injection, and to have an IV … People think it will be a peaceful death but in fact we see a lot of struggle and battle when doctors euthanize incapacitated patients,” she said.
Dr. Laurent Boisvert, a Maid provider and president of Quebec’s Dying with Dignity association, said that, in his experience, deaths performed under advance requests aren’t nearly so disturbing.

He has personally performed three or four such Maid provisions. “I didn’t have this type of problem, but I know that at some point I can be in front of a patient who is quite aggressive, who doesn’t want to be touched and we need to sedate this patient” in order to insert the IV, Boisvert said.
“But calling this a distressing procedure, I don’t think so.”
People can appoint one or two trusted people — a spouse, an adult child — to make sure their advance request is respected, he said.
In conversations with colleagues, “it seems that it has worked well (with) no big problems at this time,” Boisvert said.

On the morning of her death, the doctor secretly slipped a sedative into the woman’s coffee. She did not tell the woman she was about to die. Despite the sedative, the woman appeared to try to get up in the middle of the procedure and “resisted physically,” the doctor initially reported to the euthanasia committee. The woman’s son-in-law laid her back down so the doctor could inject her. The doctor was eventually acquitted of breaking Dutch euthanasia laws after a judge ruled the woman’s prior written request was sufficient and that there was no legal requirement for the doctor to verify the “current death wish,” BBC reported.

Dying with Dignity Canada said the proposed legislation would only decriminalize advance requests in provinces and territories that also pass legislation permitting them, creating at best a patchwork system across Canada. “At worst, some people in Canada May never have access to advance requests in their province or territory,” CEO Helen Long said.

Fraser, the federal justice minister, said advance requests would allow people at risk of losing their decision-making capacity “to live out their remaining years, rather than being put in a position where they fear they have to take that decision prematurely.”

While he can understand the appeal they hold for some, psychiatrist Dr. Sonu Gaind said there are several unresolved concerns, including how people, once they lose capacity, could withdraw their consent.

“Meaning that, if they change their mind, and they’ve lost capacity, what do you do? How do you deal with it? How do you know?” It’s a concern reflected in the coffee case in the Netherlands, he said.

It would fall onto an assessor, yet the Maid literature shows the personal views and values of the assessor influences the end-of-life decisions that are made, Gaind said.

“You risk having an illusion that, ‘Oh, we’re compassionately fulfilling patient autonomy,’ but in fact are we now, in some of these situations, allowing internalized ableism of assessors to get projected onto these assessments of patients who’ve, at this point, lost capacity?”

stories.title: Seven Canadian provinces trail behind most U.S. states on economic performance: study
stories.summary: A study comparing economic performance in Canadian provinces and U.S. states has found that seven of the 10 lowest-ranking are in Canada.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A new study comparing economic performance in all of the Canadian provinces and U.S. states has found that, of the 60 jurisdictions, seven of the 10 lowest-ranking are in Canada.

The research by the Fraser Institute looked at living standards, incomes, private sector employment and labour productivity to compare the economic growth of the two countries. It found that, in every category, Canadians have fallen further behind Americans.

In 2024 (the most recent year of comparable data), seven of the 10 lowest rates of gross domestic product (GDP) per person were Canadian provinces. New Brunswick ranked lowest, followed by Prince Edward Island (at number 59), Nova Scotia (58), Manitoba (56), Quebec (55), Newfoundland and Labrador (52) and Ontario (51).

B.C. ranked 49th, while Saskatchewan ranked 35th, and Alberta — the only province in the top half — ranked 25th.

For comparison, in 1999 six Canadian provinces ranked among the bottom 10 in terms of GDP per person, while Alberta, which has remained Canada’s top-ranked province, was 7th-highest.

In the U.S., Mississippi ranked the lowest, at number 57, between Nova Scotia and Manitoba, followed by West Virginia (54) and Arkansas (53), both of which were sandwiched between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador.

At the top of the table for GDP per person is New York, followed by Washington, Massachusetts and California.

Jake Fuss, director of fiscal studies at the Fraser Institute and co-author of the new research study, said in a news release: “By comparing important economic outcomes in Canadian provinces and American states, it’s easy to see how Canadians stack up to their counterparts south of the border, and in recent years, Canadians have been falling further behind.”

Meanwhile, the study also found that most U.S. states out-earned most Canadian provinces. Inflation-adjusted median employment income — wages and salaries — increased faster in most states than in Canadian provinces in recent years and, in 2024, median employment incomes in all 50 states were higher than in all ten Canadian provinces.

In 2010, meanwhile, only eight Canadian provinces ranked among the bottom 10 in terms of median employment income, while Canada’s top province (Alberta again) ranked 12th-highest. By 2024, Alberta was the only jurisdiction in both countries where median income had declined and now ranks 51st.

Prince Edward Island was the jurisdiction with the lowest median employment income in 2024, followed by Manitoba and then Newfoundland and Labrador.

Maryland, Massachusetts and North Dakota are at the top of the table.

Elsewhere, the research found that from 1999 to 2024 every Canadian province experienced a decline in private-sector employment as a share of total employment, meaning the government sector outgrew the private sector in every province. This was not the case for most U.S. states, where 31 out of 50 saw an increase in private-sector employment between 1999 and 2024.

And from 2007 to 2024, all but five U.S. states experienced stronger labour productivity growth than every Canadian province. Meanwhile, Prince Edward Island was the only jurisdiction in both countries where labour productivity declined.

“The evidence is clear,” Fuss said. “The 21st century has, so far, not belonged to Canadians, who have seen their living standards and incomes fall further behind those of Americans.”

The latest Fraser Institute study is the second in a two-part series looking at whether Canada’s economic growth will outpace that of the U.S. in the 21st century.

The first part of the research compared Canada and the U.S. nationally, and similarly found that Canada’s economic performance has fallen further behind that of the U.S. over the past quarter century.

In 1999, inflation-adjusted GDP per person in Canada was $48,076, while in the U.S. it was $58,842. By 2024, GDP per person had grown to $83,286 in the U.S. compared to just $59,529 in Canada — meaning the gap had widened from $10,766 to $23,757 over 25 years.

And in 2010 (the earliest year of comparable data), inflation-adjusted median employment income was $6,126 higher in the U.S. than in Canada. But by 2024, that gap had increased to $8,663.

The Fraser Institute outlined three factors that explain the widening gap in economic performance between the two countries: a decline in private sector employment as a share of total employment in Canada, slower growth in labour productivity (a key driver of income growth, according to the think tank), and changes in business investment in Canada.

The research found that business investment in Canada — which equips workers with the tools and technology they need to produce goods and services — dropped from nearly 90 cents per worker for every dollar invested in the U.S. to 54 cents between 2007 and 2024.

The Fraser Institute suggests in its research that “serious and fundamental fiscal and economic reforms need to occur” for there to be any hope of Canada’s economic growth outpacing the U.S.

The latest Fraser Institute study is the second in a two-part series looking at whether Canada’s economic growth will outpace that of the U.S. in the 21st century.

The first part of the research compared Canada and the U.S. nationally, and similarly found that Canada’s economic performance has fallen further behind that of the U.S. over the past quarter century.

And in 2010 (the earliest year of comparable data), inflation-adjusted median employment income was $6,126 higher in the U.S. than in Canada. But by 2024, that gap had increased to $8,663.

The Fraser Institute outlined three factors that explain the widening gap in economic performance between the two countries: a decline in private sector employment as a share of total employment in Canada, slower growth in labour productivity (a key driver of income growth, according to the think tank), and changes in business investment in Canada.

The research found that business investment in Canada — which equips workers with the tools and technology they need to produce goods and services — dropped from nearly 90 cents per worker for every dollar invested in the U.S. to 54 cents between 2007 and 2024.
The Fraser Institute suggests in its research that “serious and fundamental fiscal and economic reforms need to occur” for there to be any hope of Canada’s economic growth outpacing the U.S.

stories.title: Canada unexpectedly sheds 68,000 jobs in September; jobless rate climbs to 6.5%
stories.summary: Losses concentrated in the public sector and split between full- and part-time work
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s labour market stumbled in September, posting a second consecutive monthly decline and reinforcing forecasts that the Bank of Canada will hold interest rates steady later this month.

Employment fell by 68,000 in September, adding to a loss of 42,000 jobs in August, Statistics Canada reported on Friday. The unemployment rate nudged up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent.

The economy has faced serious headwinds over the past couple years, most notably tariffs imposed by the United States. The trade war has intensified with the introduction of new tariffs in recent weeks and negotiations between Ottawa and Washington have been suspended since August.

“A second consecutive month of sizable job losses washes away the surprising strength reported in Canada’s job market through the early summer,” said Douglas Porter, Bank of Montreal’s chief economist, in a research note.

“On balance, we continue to believe that the appropriate stance by the Bank of Canada is watchful waiting, particularly so with employment suddenly clouding over.”

The Bank of Canada is widely anticipated to resume raising interest rates in the coming months, with several hikes expected by next summer.

The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time this year. Central bankers are wary of how higher energy prices resulting from the Iran war could feed into more widespread inflation.

The Bank of Canada’s key interest rate is 2.25 per cent, and its next decision is on Oct. 28.

Friday’s jobs report showed that the biggest decline last month was in the public sector, where there was a loss of 70,000 positions, with half of those attributed to education services in Quebec. This is the fourth consecutive month showing a decline in the public sector, which is down 119,000 jobs year-over-year.

Health care and social assistance also saw their first monthly decrease since December, 2022, while September also saw a decline in manufacturing.

The loss in the manufacturing sector May be, according to Mr. Porter, “an early warning of the weight from the amped-up trade tussle.”

Regionally, Quebec saw the biggest drop in employment at 49,000 jobs, with British Columbia and Ontario following with a loss of 20,000 jobs apiece, and 4,400 job losses in Manitoba. In comparison, Alberta saw an increase of 23,000 last month. Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island also saw job gains.

Andrew Hencic, a senior economist at Toronto-Dominion Bank, said in a note to clients that the unemployment rate is expected to “tread water in coming months, as trade frictions and higher [interest] rates weigh on activity.”

Mr. Hencic added that the one positive takeaway from Friday’s report was a steady employment rate in the private sector.

The jobless rate for women between the ages of 25 and 54 rose to 5.3 per cent from 5 per cent both because fewer women in this cohort were working, and more were actively searching for a job. The unemployment rate for men in the same age bracket fell slightly to 5.8 per cent.

Employment for youth aged 15 to 24 declined by 48,000 jobs in September for a second consecutive monthly loss, although the rate remained little changed at 13 per cent.

Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said in a research note that the slight increase in the unemployment rate “could have been worse, were it not for a drop in the participant rate to its lowest level in almost 30 years.”

The labour participation rate – the proportion of the population aged 15 and above that is working or actively looking for work – fell to 64.8 per cent, the lowest level since December, 1997, excluding the early parts of the pandemic. The agency attributed this trend to aging demographics, though more recently, the country’s population growth has been meagre after strong immigration from 2022 to 2024.

“Overall, the decline in employment and hours worked, combined with the increase in the unemployment rate, point to a shift in economic momentum. After a solid first half of the year, it looks like economic activity has cooled off,” Mr. Mendes added.

stories.title: ‘Nightmare’: Homeowner blames bylaw loophole after neighbour dumps tonnes of earth in backyard
stories.summary: A London couple is calling on city hall to reconsider an exemption in a municipal bylaw they say allowed damage caused by a large pile of fill dumped in a neighbour’s backyard.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A London couple is calling on city hall to reconsider an exemption in a municipal bylaw they say allowed damage caused by a large pile of fill dumped in a neighbour’s backyard.

Standing along her property line in southwest London, Lisa Davis said the pile of earth towers above her.

Davis said dump trucks began depositing loads of soil and stone in her neighbour’s backyard in 2023, in what she believes was an effort to level a steep slope on the property.

She said wooden shipping skids placed along the property line were not enough to prevent the fill from slumping onto her property and against her deck stairs.

“The only way to really fix the problem is to either remove the grade or build a retaining wall,” Davis told CTV News. “It would be in excess of $100,000 just for the retaining wall.”

An engineering report concluded the weight of the loose fill pressing against the home’s second-storey deck stairs compromised the structure’s integrity.

A city-issued Order to Make Safe, issued in April, prohibits use of the deck and stairs and requires they be removed or reinforced.

According to the order, “DC Buck Engineering found the cause of the damage was due to the debris and fill that was placed in the neighbouring property.”

“Those stairs provide us access to the side of the house, but we’re not allowed to use them,” Davis said. She added the family can no longer use the space for gatherings and visits with grandchildren.

Davis and her husband, Neil Mutch, have been involved in a legal dispute with their neighbour over the fill pile for several years.

They said city staff informed them that London’s Site Alteration Bylaw, which governs the use of fill for grading purposes, includes an exemption for residential properties smaller than 0.5 hectares.

Davis said she would like to see the city amend the bylaw to allow for earlier intervention before neighbouring properties are damaged.

In an emailed statement, London’s director of municipal compliance, Amanda Pfeffer, said the city has received complaints regarding the property and has several active bylaw enforcement files under investigation.

Pfeffer said a Property Standards Order related to fence and erosion concerns was issued to the property owner and has been registered on title because deficiencies remain uncorrected. Penalties have also been issued.

She added municipal compliance has arranged debris removal through a contracted service provider and issued additional penalties for repeated bylaw violations.

Despite those measures, Davis said the large pile of fill remains in place.

“It’s the most stressful thing I’ve ever gone through in my life,” she said. “The amount of money to fix the damages, the length of time slowly watching our property deteriorate.”

CTV News contacted the owner of the neighbouring property, but they did not agree to an interview.

Davis alleges the pile contains concrete, asphalt and other mixed materials, and fears it could shift further.

“We just have no protection from our homeowners’ insurance and no protection from the city,” she said.

Standing along her property line in southwest London, Lisa Davis said the pile of earth towers above her.
Davis said dump trucks began depositing loads of soil and stone in her neighbour’s backyard in 2023, in what she believes was an effort to level a steep slope on the property.
She said wooden shipping skids placed along the property line were not enough to prevent the fill from slumping onto her property and against her deck stairs.

content_blocks.alt: london home - dirt pile - oct 2026
content_blocks.caption: A pile of earth deposited in the backyard next door to Lisa Davis and Neil Mutch’s property in southwest London (Daryl Newcombe/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: “The only way to really fix the problem is to either remove the grade or build a retaining wall,” Davis told CTV News. “It would be in excess of $100,000 just for the retaining wall.”
An engineering report concluded the weight of the loose fill pressing against the home’s second-storey deck stairs compromised the structure’s integrity.
A city-issued Order to Make Safe, issued in April, prohibits use of the deck and stairs and requires they be removed or reinforced.
According to the order, “DC Buck Engineering found the cause of the damage was due to the debris and fill that was placed in the neighbouring property.”

“Those stairs provide us access to the side of the house, but we’re not allowed to use them,” Davis said. She added the family can no longer use the space for gatherings and visits with grandchildren.
Davis and her husband, Neil Mutch, have been involved in a legal dispute with their neighbour over the fill pile for several years.
They said city staff informed them that London’s Site Alteration Bylaw, which governs the use of fill for grading purposes, includes an exemption for residential properties smaller than 0.5 hectares.
Davis said she would like to see the city amend the bylaw to allow for earlier intervention before neighbouring properties are damaged.

In an emailed statement, London’s director of municipal compliance, Amanda Pfeffer, said the city has received complaints regarding the property and has several active bylaw enforcement files under investigation.

Pfeffer said a Property Standards Order related to fence and erosion concerns was issued to the property owner and has been registered on title because deficiencies remain uncorrected. Penalties have also been issued.

content_blocks.alt: london home - dirt pile - oct 2026
content_blocks.caption: Leaning pillars meant to support the second storey deck attached to Lisa Davis and Neil Mutch’s home. (Daryl Newcombe)/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: She added municipal compliance has arranged debris removal through a contracted service provider and issued additional penalties for repeated bylaw violations.
Despite those measures, Davis said the large pile of fill remains in place.
“It’s the most stressful thing I’ve ever gone through in my life,” she said. “The amount of money to fix the damages, the length of time slowly watching our property deteriorate.”
CTV News contacted the owner of the neighbouring property, but they did not agree to an interview.
Davis alleges the pile contains concrete, asphalt and other mixed materials, and fears it could shift further.
“We just have no protection from our homeowners’ insurance and no protection from the city,” she said.

stories.title: Everybody rock your body: Backstreet Boys tickets on public sale Friday
stories.summary: Ticket for the Backstreet Boys residency at the Rogers Centre in February, 2027 go on public sale on Oct. 9, 2026.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
If you want it that way , today’s the day: tickets for the Backstreet Boys Toronto residency at the Rogers Centre go on public sale Friday.

After massive public demand during ticket presales that started on Oct. 5, the initial four-date run of shows presented by Rogers was extended twice to expand to a nine-date stretch over three weekends in February, 2027. After public sales opened, the unprecedent interest in tickets led to the addition of two more dates to include the first weekend of March, 2027, making it a substantial 11-date series of concerts in Toronto.

Into the Millenium – Homecoming: Live in Canada will take over the Rogers Centre for the record resicency on the weekends of Feb. 12, 13 and 14, Feb. 19, 20 and 21, Feb. 26, 27 and 28 and March 5 and 6.

In an Instagram post, the band thanked fans, saying “we truly didn’t know the demand would be THIS BIG” and they were adding more shows “so as many of you as possible can experience “Into the Millennium – HOMECOMING: Live in Canada” with us!”

The shows will be the iconic 90s boy band’s only 2027 North American stadium concerts. The group has had it going on in Canada from the early years of their careers, where they marked their first major breakthrough in North America back in 1995.

Group member Brian Littrell said Canada has shown them the shape of their hearts from day one, and they’re excited that Backstreet’s back in the country after four long years.

“Canada was one of the first places to embrace us, and the love and support we’ve received from our fans there has meant so much from the very beginning,” said Brian Littrell. “Coming back feels incredibly special. It is a chance for all of us to celebrate the memories we’ve made together and create some new ones.”

For Rogers customers who still haven’t made the call to buy tickets, they have one more chance to quit playing games and purchase a limited number of reserved tickets by using their presale code during the public sale.

To get the code:

Go to your MyRogers app. (My Rogers (Shaw) app in Western Canada)

Click on the Backstreet Boys banner to claim your code – it will save in the messages section of the app

Log in to Ticketmaster on Oct. 9 at least 15 mins before the sale starts and enter your code

Rogers customers and fans will also have the chance to win thousands of tickets including grand prizes with airfare and accommodation in Toronto, with contests already live on Rogers radio stations 98.1 CHFI and KISS 92.5 social media channels.

“Fans from around the world are excited to see this iconic group live, so we jumped at the opportunity to bring the Backstreet Boys to Canada – and add a record number of shows for one artist at Rogers Centre given the incredible demand,” said Terrie Tweddle, Chief Brand and Communications Officer at Rogers. “For more than three decades, the Backstreet Boys have built a passionate fan base and sold-out arenas around the world, and we’re excited to create unforgettable opportunities for fans and our customers.”

stories.title: Montreal couple takes on marathon together following ALS diagnosis
stories.summary: Years after an ALS diagnosis changed their lives, a Montreal couple is taking on the Montreal Marathon together.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Elizabeth Zogalis
stories.content:
A Montreal couple is preparing to take on the Montreal Marathon together this weekend, years after an ALS diagnosis dramatically changed their lives.

Spencer Levine will run the 42.2-kilometre course while pushing his wife, Amanda Tam, in a specially adapted wheelchair.

The idea came last spring, when Tam went to cheer on Levine at an Ironman competition and the couple saw another person with a disability participating with assistance.

“We actually saw a (person with a disability) being pushed and they were attached to the bike, they were on a kayak for the swimming portion and Spencer thought it would be a cool idea to do the same,” Tam told Global News on Thursday.

The high school sweethearts, who married in 2024, bought a specialized running wheelchair in June and have since trained more than 600 kilometres for the Montreal Marathon.

“We have trained all throughout the summer from June until now,” Levine said. “We’ve run 623 kilometres as of today.”

Tam, a McGill University graduate, was 20 years old when she was diagnosed with ALS.

Dr. Angela Genge, clinical research program director at the McGill Neurological Institute, described Tam as remarkably upbeat.

“She is one of these kids that in another circumstance would have flown,” Genge said.

The neurodegenerative disease has taken away much of Tam’s autonomy, leaving her reliant on Levine, who is also her primary caregiver.

Claudine Cook, executive director of the Quebec ALS Society, said the couple have become “incredible ambassadors.”

“Having a care partner like Spencer along her side is just … they’ve been really incredible ambassadors,” Cook said.

The couple has been determined to share their experiences, and their marathon effort is also raising money for ALS Quebec.

“Just because I was dealt an unlucky hand or the fact that I have a death sentence, I mean, it doesn’t mean that you have to stop living,” Tam said.

Training for the marathon has also given the couple more time together.

“As someone who trains 10 to 15 hours a week, having those extra six to 10 hours a week with her is just so meaningful and has made us grow so much closer as a couple,” Levine said.

But even getting to the starting line at Parc Jean-Drapeau could pose a challenge, with Berri-Uqam Metro station not fully accessible.

“I love the fact that we have this huge marathon, but if you have a wheelchair category … make it at least accessible to get to,” Tam said.

With 20,000 people expected at the starting line, the couple also wants to avoid traffic.

Tam said she uses social media in part to draw attention to accessibility issues in Montreal while encouraging others to continue living their lives despite difficult circumstances.

“That is also why I have social media, to bring awareness to, I guess, accessibility around the city and to also to keep living life no matter what,” she said.
