stories.title: Diplomat Ian Hamilton led operation to save desperate refugees afloat on the South China Sea
stories.summary: The immigration official, who was haunted by what he had witnessed, said the crisis was ‘probably the greatest human tragedy of our time’
stories.author: Alan Freeman
stories.content:
It was an image that caught the world’s attention: A rusty freighter, the Hai Hong, appeared off Port Klang on the coast of Malaysia in early November 1978, its filthy decks teeming with 2,500 refugees from Vietnam.

It had been three years since the fall of Saigon and the collapse of the South Vietnamese regime to the communist forces. There had been an initial outflow of refugees fleeing the country but by 1978 that stream had turned into a torrent, creating what became known as the “boat people” crisis, as tens of thousands of Vietnamese boarded any watercraft, no matter how flimsy, to escape their homeland, heading out across the South China Sea. They were joined by victims of repression in Cambodia and Laos.

Malaysia, already overwhelmed by the influx of refugees, wanted nothing to do with the Hai Hong’s human cargo and threatened to tow the ship and its desperate passengers out to sea. The country’s Malay majority was hostile to the ethnic Chinese people on board. And Malaysian authorities claimed the passengers weren’t real refugees because they had paid for their passage.

As international pressure grew for wealthy countries to do something, the Canadian government decided to act. Immigration minister Bud Cullen announced that Canada would take 600 of the ship’s refugees for resettlement.

The officer in charge of Canada’s tiny immigration office in Singapore was Ian Hamilton, a seasoned 42-year-old official, who was sent to Kuala Lumpur to lead what became a heroic operation that saved thousands over the coming months. Tall, charming and rugged-looking with an infectious sense of humour, Mr. Hamilton, who died in Ottawa on Sept. 15 at the age of 89, was also determined and dedicated to the task at hand.

Malaysian officials wanted the Hai Hong and its passengers to leave their country’s waters, but nonetheless threw roadblocks in front of Mr. Hamilton’s small team. They wouldn’t allow the freighter to dock or permit the Canadians to board it. But, according to the 2017 book Running on Empty: Canada and the Indochinese Refugees, 1975-80 , Mr. Hamilton persuaded the officials to allow him to set up shop on a Malaysian minesweeper, anchored near the Hai Hong, to conduct his screening.

Armed Malaysian police escorted small contingents of the refugees to the deck of the naval ship where the immigration officers, plus a doctor and an interpreter, assembled a rudimentary office consisting of two wooden tables and a few chairs under a tarpaulin to protect them from the scorching tropical sun. The refugees were short of food and traumatized by their days at sea, with the Hai Hong refused entry by neighbouring countries.

“It was an appalling situation, probably the greatest human tragedy of our time,” Mr. Hamilton told a CBC film crew.

“The pressure of saying yes and no just squashes you,” Mr. Hamilton said 10 years later in an interview with The Ottawa Citizen, recalling how frail and terrified the refugees were. “You’re doing the best job that you can and you’re just being eaten up by the decision-making process. You want to say yes, but obviously you can’t.”

He did what he could, sometimes bending the rules to save lives. Dick Martin, who was No. 2 in the Singapore immigration office, remembers an incident where a woman slipped and fell to her death on the Hai Hong. The next day, her son, who was seven or eight and now an orphan, appeared before the Canadian immigration officers with a group of other refugees. Alone.

“I told Ian the story and he was overcome. He already had in front of him a young family, a mother, father and two children,” Mr. Martin recalled in an interview with The Globe. “Ian looks at them and says, ‘are you taking your nephew with you?’” Perplexed, the father initially said he didn’t have a nephew, but Mr. Hamilton insisted, gesturing to the little boy in the queue. The man relented, and his new-found nephew was on his way to life in Canada.

Despite the awful conditions, Mr. Hamilton and his crew interviewed and accepted as many as 356 refugees on a single day in an era when the standard was 12 interviews a day. By the end of November, the first Boeing 707 full of refugees from the Hai Hong arrived in Montreal. Three more flights followed. In all, 604 Vietnamese from the Hai Hong restarted their lives in Canada. The remaining refugees were taken by the U.S., France, Germany, Belgium and Switzerland.

Over the next two years, Canada welcomed 60,000 Southeast Asian refugees, many of them under the pioneering private sponsorship program, where church and other groups got together to support newcomers as they adapted to Canadian life. After the Hai Hong, Mr. Hamilton travelled throughout the region processing thousands of refugees at wretched refugee camps, renting fishing boats and leaning on reluctant bureaucrats to facilitate his work, armed with nothing more than a stack of Maple Leaf pins, which he distributed widely.

“He was a real leader, a mentor, the kind of guy who set an example,” said Scott Mullin, who as a 21-year-old junior immigration officer in Hong Kong, was assigned to work with Mr. Hamilton. “He was a superb guy. I loved working with him,” added Florent Fortin, who represented the Quebec government, which had recently signed an immigration agreement with Ottawa, and was part of the team.

“They were young and they were tough,” said Mike Molloy, a senior Immigration official at the time who worked on co-ordinating the refugee influx from Ottawa and co-wrote Running on Empty .

“Ian was a really compassionate person,” Mr. Molloy told The Globe. “There are people who are really good and Ian was one of those people, in terms of being compassionate and caring about people.”

Ian Stewart Hamilton was born on Sept. 23, 1936 in Ottawa, the eldest of three children of John Hamilton, a vice-president of the E.B. Eddy forest products company, and his wife, the former Shirley Stewart. Ian grew up in Aylmer, Que., and attended boarding school in Ontario, winding up at Valley Forge Military Academy in Pennsylvania, where he completed high school.

He earned a degree in psychology at Curry College, a small liberal-arts institution near Boston and began work as a psychologist for Corrections Canada. After two years, he joined Canada’s foreign service as an immigration officer, posted successively to Cologne, Stockholm, Sydney and Madrid before moving to Singapore in 1977. By that time, he was married and had three sons.

After the Hai Hong, Mr. Hamilton continued his resettlement work in refugee camps along the Malaysian coast, gaining considerable media attention for his work. “Hamilton has waded out to tossing boats carrying dead and dying in his arms,” read one account in The Toronto Sun. “There are lines of fatigue around his eyes where the laugh lines were once etched. It comes from tropical diseases, from endless days of interviewing in the filth and heat of a refugee camp.”

By the summer of 1979, the ceaseless work proved too much. Mr. Hamilton had contracted hepatitis. “It was hard on him physically. It was hard on him emotionally,” his eldest son, Shawn, said. Mr. Hamilton and his family moved back to Canada. Soon after, he and his wife separated.

Mr. Hamilton was honoured with a Public Service Award in 1979 but remained in Ottawa for the rest of his career, working in immigration and consular affairs, never venturing out on another foreign assignment.

“He did not want to travel again. It was a purposeful choice,” Shawn said. “He was done. He just wanted to find peace and tranquillity.” Mr. Hamilton retired in the early 1990s, spending lots of time in nature, ON extended camping trips in Quebec’s La Verendrye Park and salmon fishing on the Miramichi River.

He seldom talked about his time in Southeast Asia, only opening up as he aged. Shawn says he discovered 80 per cent of what he knows about that crucial period of his father’s life in the last two or three years. “The veil lifted.”

Mr. Hamilton’s role wasn’t forgotten by the people most important to him, members of Canada’s Vietnamese community, who would send him greeting cards on his birthday and Christmas. He befriended Can Le, a retired Ottawa economist and a leader of the Vietnamese-Canadian community who has been working for years to erect a Boat People Museum in Ottawa.

Last March, Mr. Le invited Mr. Hamilton to a fundraising event for the project in Ottawa. “He gave a very eloquent and moving speech,” Mr. Le said. Mr. Hamilton recalled how he was haunted by the awful things he had seen in the refugee camps after he returned to Canada decades ago. Distraught, he would walk through Ottawa’s Chinatown neighbourhood and found solace in seeing how the newly arrived refugees were adapting well to their new home.

“I love you all dearly,” Mr. Hamilton told the crowd. “I’m proud of what I did. And you are the ones who are building our country.” The crowd gave him a standing ovation.

Mr. Hamilton leaves his sons, Shawn, Matthew and Nicholas; five grandchildren; and his sister, Susan. Bonnie Boyle, his wife of 41 years, died in 2013. His first marriage ended in divorce.

Mr. Molloy said he recalled that Mr. Hamilton was once asked how he decided on whether a displaced family should be accepted for resettlement or not. “He replied, ‘by the light of their children’s eyes.’”

He seldom talked about his time in Southeast Asia, only opening up as he aged. Shawn says he discovered 80 per cent of what he knows about that crucial period of his father’s life in the last two or three years. “The veil lifted.”

Mr. Hamilton’s role wasn’t forgotten by the people most important to him, members of Canada’s Vietnamese community, who would send him greeting cards on his birthday and Christmas. He befriended Can Le, a retired Ottawa economist and a leader of the Vietnamese-Canadian community who has been working for years to erect a Boat People Museum in Ottawa.

Last March, Mr. Le invited Mr. Hamilton to a fundraising event for the project in Ottawa. “He gave a very eloquent and moving speech,” Mr. Le said. Mr. Hamilton recalled how he was haunted by the awful things he had seen in the refugee camps after he returned to Canada decades ago. Distraught, he would walk through Ottawa’s Chinatown neighbourhood and found solace in seeing how the newly arrived refugees were adapting well to their new home.
“I love you all dearly,” Mr. Hamilton told the crowd. “I’m proud of what I did. And you are the ones who are building our country.” The crowd gave him a standing ovation.
Mr. Hamilton leaves his sons, Shawn, Matthew and Nicholas; five grandchildren; and his sister, Susan. Bonnie Boyle, his wife of 41 years, died in 2013. His first marriage ended in divorce.

Mr. Molloy said he recalled that Mr. Hamilton was once asked how he decided on whether a displaced family should be accepted for resettlement or not. “He replied, ‘by the light of their children’s eyes.’”

content_blocks.text: It had been three years since the fall of Saigon and the collapse of the South Vietnamese regime to the communist forces. There had been an initial outflow of refugees fleeing the country but by 1978 that stream had turned into a torrent, creating what became known as the “boat people” crisis, as tens of thousands of Vietnamese boarded any watercraft, no matter how flimsy, to escape their homeland, heading out across the South China Sea. They were joined by victims of repression in Cambodia and Laos.

content_blocks.text: Malaysia, already overwhelmed by the influx of refugees, wanted nothing to do with the Hai Hong’s human cargo and threatened to tow the ship and its desperate passengers out to sea. The country’s Malay majority was hostile to the ethnic Chinese people on board. And Malaysian authorities claimed the passengers weren’t real refugees because they had paid for their passage.

content_blocks.text: The officer in charge of Canada’s tiny immigration office in Singapore was Ian Hamilton, a seasoned 42-year-old official, who was sent to Kuala Lumpur to lead what became a heroic operation that saved thousands over the coming months. Tall, charming and rugged-looking with an infectious sense of humour, Mr. Hamilton, who died in Ottawa on Sept. 15 at the age of 89, was also determined and dedicated to the task at hand.

content_blocks.text: Malaysian officials wanted the Hai Hong and its passengers to leave their country’s waters, but nonetheless threw roadblocks in front of Mr. Hamilton’s small team. The refugees were short of food and traumatized by their days at sea, with the Hai Hong refused entry by neighbouring countries.

content_blocks.text: Despite the awful conditions, Mr. Hamilton and his crew interviewed and accepted as many as 356 refugees on a single day in an era when the standard was 12 interviews a day. By the end of November, the first Boeing 707 full of refugees from the Hai Hong arrived in Montreal. Three more flights followed. In all, 604 Vietnamese from the Hai Hong restarted their lives in Canada. The remaining refugees were taken by the U.S., France, Germany, Belgium and Switzerland.

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives drop candidate over ‘racist’ social media posts
stories.summary: Screenshots shared by NDP show Joachim Agou saying car that drove through pro-Palestine protest ‘should have reversed’ over demonstrators
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Interim leader of the British Columbia Conservatives Lorne Doerkson has swiftly dumped a candidate in the provincial election over online posts that the NDP called racist.

Doerkson said Thursday that the posts by Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate Joachim Agou cannot be tolerated and if he is elected, he will not be part of the Conservative caucus.

Agou’s ejection from the Conservative election slate was announced about 90 minutes after Agou’s posts on social media platform X were highlighted by the NDP.

Although Agou’s account has now been deleted, screenshots shared by the NDP show him saying last year that a car that drove through a pro-Palestine protest “should have reversed” over the demonstrators, and he also shared a meme while using an expletive to describe Pakistan.

Agou did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent to his campaign.

The Conservative website describes Agou as a professional engineer and small-business owner with more than 15 years of experience in engineering research and industry.

His biography says he was born in France, studied in the United States and came to Canada in 2011.

He is also the interim vice-president of the Victoria Conservative Association.

Doerkson said in a statement that there is “no excuse” for the posts.

He told reporters at an event earlier in the day that he hadn’t seen the allegations, but he “of course” would never support the comments.

“Trust me when I say this, I’ll be looking into them the second I leave this podium.” he said about an hour before Agou’s removal was made public.

NDP candidate Amna Shah had shared the screenshots and called on Doerkson to fire Agou immediately for what she called “horrific racism.”

Victoria-Beacon Hill is consistently considered a safe NDP riding, with the party winning the seat in every provincial election since 2005.

stories.title: Countering drones is ‘critical’ as warfare evolves, Canada’s military says
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces has been spending on both building its drone warfare capabilities and defending operations from 'unmanned aerial systems.'
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The increasing availability of sophisticated drone technology has led the Department of National Defence (DND) to move to take “critical” steps to counter “unauthorized drone activity” that could threaten Canadian military installations.

Global News reported last week the department was looking to purchase anti-drone defences for military facilities on Canadian soil, similar to the protection given to Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) personnel deployed in Europe.

The story was based on federal procurement documents, but the records provided no detail on what systems DND is looking to purchase, or what threat the department envisions deploying drones on Canadian soil.

In a statement this week, a DND spokesperson said that as drone technology becomes more widespread and capable, “defence and security organizations (are examining) how best to address the risks.”

“(Counter-drone) capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to Global News.

“DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering (drone) threats, building on existing measures and capabilities. This work forms part of broader efforts to support the Caf’s ability to effectively respond to evolving operational and security requirements and enhance the security of defence establishments.”

2:01 UN condemns Russian attacks on Ukraine civilians after fatal bus strike kills 33

McIntyre-Grills noted that due to operational security reasons, the department would not comment on specifics, and that some aspects of the procurement will be subject to a national security exception and kept from public release.

As part of the Canadian Nato deployment in Latvia aimed at deterring Russian aggression, Canadian military leaders have closely watched the evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces have deployed low-cost but highly-effective drones in the efforts to push back Russia’s invasion force. Reuters reported earlier this year that drone-related casualties in the conflict have jumped from 10 per cent of the total in 2022 to roughly 80 per cent in 2025.

The skies above Ukraine’s battlefields are now haunted by the unmanned machines, making troop and artillery movement much more dangerous. Both Ukraine and Russia deploy drones to strike at the opposing side’s territory. On Oct. 8, a Russian drone blitz killed four and injured 19 others in Kyiv and led to emergency energy shutdowns, according to the Kyiv Independent.

This year the Canadian military embarked on a multi-year research and procurement project to boost Canada’s drone capabilities, called the Drone Defence Initiative (DDI). Through the project, the Canadian government hopes to “accelerate” research, development, adaptation and production of drones for use by both the CAF and the Canadian Coast Guard.
paragraphs: The increasing availability of sophisticated drone technology has led the Department of National Defence (DND) to move to take “critical” steps to counter “unauthorized drone activity” that could threaten Canadian military installations.

Global News reported last week the department was looking to purchase anti-drone defences for military facilities on Canadian soil, similar to the protection given to Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) personnel deployed in Europe.

The story was based on federal procurement documents, but the records provided no detail on what systems DND is looking to purchase, or what threat the department envisions deploying drones on Canadian soil.
In a statement this week, a DND spokesperson said that as drone technology becomes more widespread and capable, “defence and security organizations (are examining) how best to address the risks.”
“(Counter-drone) capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to Global News.

“DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering (drone) threats, building on existing measures and capabilities. This work forms part of broader efforts to support the Caf’s ability to effectively respond to evolving operational and security requirements and enhance the security of defence establishments.”

McIntyre-Grills noted that due to operational security reasons, the department would not comment on specifics, and that some aspects of the procurement will be subject to a national security exception and kept from public release.
As part of the Canadian Nato deployment in Latvia aimed at deterring Russian aggression, Canadian military leaders have closely watched the evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces have deployed low-cost but highly-effective drones in the efforts to push back Russia’s invasion force. Reuters reported earlier this year that drone-related casualties in the conflict have jumped from 10 per cent of the total in 2022 to roughly 80 per cent in 2025.

The skies above Ukraine’s battlefields are now haunted by the unmanned machines, making troop and artillery movement much more dangerous. Both Ukraine and Russia deploy drones to strike at the opposing side’s territory. On Oct. 8, a Russian drone blitz killed four and injured 19 others in Kyiv and led to emergency energy shutdowns, according to the Kyiv Independent.

This year the Canadian military embarked on a multi-year research and procurement project to boost Canada’s drone capabilities, called the Drone Defence Initiative (DDI). Through the project, the Canadian government hopes to “accelerate” research, development, adaptation and production of drones for use by both the CAF and the Canadian Coast Guard.

stories.title: Alberta’s Cold Lake First Nations seek judicial review of Pacific Link pipeline designation
stories.summary: Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under t…
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under the Building Canada Act. The goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so that construction can begin next September.

Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko previously told The Canadian Press his community was left out of consultations on the pipeline designation, despite the fact that his community is situated in the oilsands region.

In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations’ lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

“Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of Clfn members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty no. 6,” the application said.

“Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on Clfn’s Luechogn Tue Denesuline treaty rights.”

The First Nation is asking the court to quash the national interest designation and to declare that Canada has a duty to consult with the community on the pipeline.

The Assembly of First Nations previously told The Canadian Press it had identified “many red flags” in the pipeline’s national interest designation and says the federal government appears to be predetermining outcomes and approving projects in advance of meaningful consultations.

Prime Minister Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada’s obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

stories.title: Two house explosions shake Hamilton, send three people to hospital
stories.summary: Hamilton - Firefighters in Hamilton say two house explosions shook the city on Thursday, sending three people to the hospital with burns.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hamilton - Firefighters in Hamilton say two house explosions shook the city on Thursday, sending three people to the hospital with burns.

Hamilton Fire Chief David Cunliffe says the explosions, which took place within hours of each other, were unrelated and investigators are still trying to determine the causes.

Cunliffe says fire crews arrived at the scene of the first explosion at 182 Springside Dr., and found a large debris field and what was believed to be a garage on fire.

A victim believed to have been inside the garage when it exploded was taken to the hospital in serious condition.

Cunliffe says it was a “significant blast” that tore through the building and the explosion was felt at nearby fire stations and a police station.

While the fire was quickly brought under control, Cunliffe says two adjacent homes were significantly damaged.

Cunliffe says the second explosion at 8 Lampton Place sent up a large plume of smoke that was visible to firefighters as they raced to the scene.

The fire chief says two people were inside the home when it exploded and neighbours ran into the burning building to rescue them.

The occupants were both hospitalized, Cunliffe says, one with serious injuries and the other in stable condition.

Cunliffe says gas provider Enbridge is working with authorities as neighbours reported smelling natural gas prior to the blast.

Part of the house collapsed in the approximately 30 minutes it took for firefighters to beat back the blaze, Cunliffe says, causing an estimated $750,000 worth of damage.

Cunliffe says the twin explosions are an anomaly in Hamilton.

“We don’t get a lot of buildings that explode and quite frankly to have two in the same day within hours is really not something that we see a lot,” he told reporters at the scene.

The Ontario Fire Marshal’s office and Hamilton police are investigating the causes of the twin explosions.

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath thanked firefighters, police and first responders for their quick response to the explosions and said her thoughts are with those who were impacted.

“I sincerely hope that everyone that was hurt is going to recover completely; and my heart goes out to those facing uncertainty and distress as a result of these incidents,” she wrote in a social media post.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Arrests and detentions of Canadians spike in the U.S. Travel registrations surge, too
stories.summary: Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.

The department’s annual report on consular cases , published today, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026, despite a 25 per cent decline in visits by Canadians to the U.S.

The report does not explain what caused the increase, though U.S. President Donald Trump has expanded immigration raids and Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials.

Overall, the report tracks a one-fifth increase in the number of arrests of Canadians around the world, including a threefold increase in the number of arrests in Thailand.

Global Affairs Canada has warned in recent years that the growing frequency of wars and natural disasters is resulting in more consular cases that are more complex and expensive to manage.

The data also shows an increase in the number of Canadians voluntarily registering with the department when they go abroad, which helps Ottawa send safety advice and co-ordinate evacuations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Polar bear cub ready for visitors at Winnipeg zoo, as poll opens for his name
stories.summary: A young polar bear cub who arrived at Winnipeg's Assiniboine Park Zoo in late August is ready for visitors and needs a name, the Assiniboine Park Conservancy said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The orphaned polar bear who arrived at the Assiniboine Park Zoo this summer can now be viewed by the public, the park conservancy announced.

The cub, who has not been named yet, arrived at Winnipeg’s zoo in August. He is less than a year old and arrived in the city from Churchill, Man., where he was found orphaned after his mother died.

Since then, a team of animal care, veterinary and conservation experts have managed his care and helped him transition to this new home at the Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre. The team helped him build trust and adjust at his own pace, to ensure he was ready for the public to visit, Assiniboine Park Conservancy said in a news release.

He is the first cub to arrive in years, Jackie Enberg, an animal care curator at Assiniboine Park Conservancy, told Global News in an interview.

“His mom had taught him, probably, to stay away from people. So, it takes some time and that first day we started building a relationship with him,” Enberg said.

The foundation of that relationship is based on the cub’s love for food, she added. His care team provided him with snacks to gain his trust, which helped him associate people with calm behaviour, she said.

“We just keep building that relationship every day,” Enberg added.

“He’s really calm today. He is even rolling around and actually choosing to be where groups of people are. He can go inside as many times as he wants. He took a couple swims today, played with some toys and played with a pumpkin.”

That behaviour, Enberg said, is a good sign.

Currently, no other polar bears are in his enclosure, and he will not get to chill with the others in the centre until he’s grown up, she continued. The cub is in the zoo’s transition centre for polar bears, as he acclimates to his new home and continues training with his care team.

One element of that training will be teaching him to respond to his name – but first, one must be selected, Enberg said. To credit the cub’s connection to the Polar Bear Capital of the World, the zoo has four potential name options – Duke, Marly, Fletcher and Mantayo.

His name will be determined based on an online vote that closes Tuesday, Oct. 13.

Duke comes from the Duke of Marlborough School, a school in Churchill that serves students from kindergarten to Grade 12. Marly also honours that school and its student body, according to the release.

“We are proud to partner with the Town of Churchill and students of the Duke of Marlborough School, whose thoughtful name selections reflect the love and care the community has shown for this bear since the very beginning,” Laura Caback, the senior director of marketing and communications at Assiniboine Park Conservancy, said in the news release.

The third option, Fletcher, is named for Fletcher Lake, a waterway southeast of Churchill in Wapusk National Park, Enberg said. The park is a common place for polar bear mothers to den with their cubs.

The final of the four options, Mantayo, represents the Cree name for Churchill’s River of Strangers, it added. Mantayo means “strangers” in Cree.

He will join seven other rescued polar bears at the polar bear conservation site in Winnipeg. The cub, Storm, Nanuq, York, Kaska, Willow and Star will help connect visitors to Churchill and the Arctic from the city, the release said.
paragraphs: The orphaned polar bear who arrived at the Assiniboine Park Zoo this summer can now be viewed by the public, the park conservancy announced.
The cub, who has not been named yet, arrived at Winnipeg’s zoo in August. He is less than a year old and arrived in the city from Churchill, Man., where he was found orphaned after his mother died.

Since then, a team of animal care, veterinary and conservation experts have managed his care and helped him transition to this new home at the Leatherdale International Polar Bear Conservation Centre. The team helped him build trust and adjust at his own pace, to ensure he was ready for the public to visit, Assiniboine Park Conservancy said in a news release.
He is the first cub to arrive in years, Jackie Enberg, an animal care curator at Assiniboine Park Conservancy, told Global News in an interview.
“His mom had taught him, probably, to stay away from people. So, it takes some time and that first day we started building a relationship with him,” Enberg said.

The foundation of that relationship is based on the cub’s love for food, she added. His care team provided him with snacks to gain his trust, which helped him associate people with calm behaviour, she said.
“We just keep building that relationship every day,” Enberg added.

“He’s really calm today. He is even rolling around and actually choosing to be where groups of people are. He can go inside as many times as he wants. He took a couple swims today, played with some toys and played with a pumpkin.”
That behaviour, Enberg said, is a good sign.

Currently, no other polar bears are in his enclosure, and he will not get to chill with the others in the centre until he’s grown up, she continued. The cub is in the zoo’s transition centre for polar bears, as he acclimates to his new home and continues training with his care team.

One element of that training will be teaching him to respond to his name – but first, one must be selected, Enberg said. To credit the cub’s connection to the Polar Bear Capital of the World, the zoo has four potential name options – Duke, Marly, Fletcher and Mantayo.
His name will be determined based on an online vote that closes Tuesday, Oct. 13.

Duke comes from the Duke of Marlborough School, a school in Churchill that serves students from kindergarten to Grade 12. Marly also honours that school and its student body, according to the release.

“We are proud to partner with the Town of Churchill and students of the Duke of Marlborough School, whose thoughtful name selections reflect the love and care the community has shown for this bear since the very beginning,” Laura Caback, the senior director of marketing and communications at Assiniboine Park Conservancy, said in the news release.

The third option, Fletcher, is named for Fletcher Lake, a waterway southeast of Churchill in Wapusk National Park, Enberg said. The park is a common place for polar bear mothers to den with their cubs.
The final of the four options, Mantayo, represents the Cree name for Churchill’s River of Strangers, it added. Mantayo means “strangers” in Cree.

He will join seven other rescued polar bears at the polar bear conservation site in Winnipeg. The cub, Storm, Nanuq, York, Kaska, Willow and Star will help connect visitors to Churchill and the Arctic from the city, the release said.

stories.title: Carney points to federal review when asked about restricting access to SKS rifle
stories.summary: Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney indicated Thursday the federal government will look at the advice of an arm's-length panel studying firearms classification before making any decision on the status of the SKS rifle.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney indicated Thursday the federal government will look at the advice of an arm’s-length panel studying firearms classification before making any decision on the status of the SKS rifle.

He made the remarks as his public safety minister declined to explain why such a weapon might have been returned to the teenage shooter in the Tumbler Ridge mass killing, after having previously been confiscated by the RCMP.

That claim is contained in an FBI complaint filed in a Washington state court that says the killer talked about having an SKS and a “switch” for this type of rifle, which likely referred to a machine-gun conversion device.

Eighteen-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people in the Feb. 10 attack before taking her own life, is also cited in the complaint as saying she intended to use the SKS returned by police in the attack.

The federal government is undertaking a review of Canada’s firearms classification regime that will include consultations on the SKS rifle.

At an event in Sherbrooke, Que., Carney said the government needed advice from professionals and the RCMP before making further decisions on firearms classification.

He cited “constant changes” in firearms that necessitated input from police and others.

The government has been heavily criticized by gun control advocates for not including the semi-automatic SKS on its list of banned firearms.

The FBI complaint released this week is in support of a charge of conspiracy to murder in a foreign country against 30-year-old James Bryant, who is accused of advising and supporting Van Rootselaar for months as she planned then carried out the murders.

It includes excerpts of conversations between the two where Van Rootselaar allegedly says she stole guns and ammunition from her family’s gun safe.

The complaint also quotes Van Rootselaar as telling Bryant that police confiscated the SKS and damaged the sights, so when they returned it, the weapon was firing “high and to the left.”

“So, it’s a lot of work and I May end up doing my plan with a gun with sights that are super off,” she is quoted as saying, adding that she knows how the gun fires and “I’m sure I can still do fine.”

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree declined Thursday to “opine” on why guns were apparently returned to the shooter’s home before the massacre.

He said the RCMP investigation was ongoing and had been careful not to speculate until it was complete.

Anandasangaree said at an unrelated news conference in Ottawa that the government was focused on supporting the community of Tumbler Ridge.

“Their ultimate demand is about making sure that we have the right answers, and it is premature, in my opinion, to offer and opine on those answers without having the full benefit of the information that the investigation will reveal,” he said when asked about the guns.

Anandasangaree said that as recently as two months ago, he did not believe there would be an arrest made and the charging of Bryant this week showed the investigation was progressing.

“And we see now that is a reality and we want to see justice being served, and we will continue to monitor and support both the investigation as well as the community as the investigation concludes,” he said, directing any questions about the guns to the B.C. RCMP.

A spokeswoman for the Mounties said in an email that information about the firearms mentioned in the FBI complaint is “subject to ongoing court processes in Canada.”

“As the firearms are subject to this publication ban, I cannot provide any context at this time into the firearms that are depicted in the criminal complaint until the courts make a determination on disclosure,” Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said.

The FBI complaint also says Van Rootselaar had been institutionalized twice, having been deemed a danger to herself.

— With files by Brieanna Charlebois in Vancouver

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Cold Lake First Nations push for judicial review of Pacific Link pipeline designation
stories.summary: Chief Kelsey Jacko has said community was left out of consultations despite being situated in oilsands region
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
An Alberta First Nation is taking Ottawa to court over the government’s decision to designate the planned Pacific Link oil pipeline a priority in the national interest, the first legal challenge to the federal push to fast-track the project.

At the heart of the application for judicial review, filed by Cold Lake First Nations on Thursday, is the community’s concerns about a lack of consultation over the pipeline, which would carry one million barrels of oil a day from Bruderheim, Alta., to Roberts Bank, B.C. Another focus of the application is a massive carbon capture project planned for the oil sands.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has repeatedly tied approval of the pipeline to that carbon capture project, called Pathways, which would include a 400-kilometre pipeline that would transport carbon trapped at oil-sands facilities to an underground hub near Cold Lake, Alta.

Cold Lake First Nations sits in the middle of oil sands development in Northern Alberta . While the community supports responsible resource development, Chief Kelsey Jacko said in a statement, it wants to ensure activity is “done right, with meaningful consultation and clear answers about the long-term impacts of projects in the region.”

The legal challenge from Cold Lake is the first against Pacific Link, which would give Alberta oil access to more international markets and garner higher prices.

Pacific Link last week became the first major project to be designated a national priority under the federal Building Canada Act, new legislation that is a marquee element of Mr. Carney’s economic agenda.

The pipeline is also a priority of the Alberta government, which has cited it as an example of co-operation with Ottawa in the lead-up to the province’s referendum on separation this month.

The act provides an accelerated pathway through regulatory approvals, but has been criticized by Indigenous groups over concern that a faster approval process could trample their treaty rights.

Other First Nations leaders have also voiced concerns about the new pipeline, including Terry Teegee, Regional Chief of the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations, and the Coldwater Indian Band, in B.C.

Ottawa has said Pacific Link will create 140,000 jobs, generate more than $20-billion in GDP per year and $100-billion in government revenue by 2060.

Opinion: Is it really a good idea for the government to subsidize a pipeline?

The government is aiming to finish the project’s federal review process, including consultations, by Sept. 1, 2027, in hopes of having it operational by 2032. Its expected price tag is between $35.2-billion and $43.7-billion.

Cold Lake has been raising concerns with the federal government since 2023 “about the potential environmental, geological and safety risks” related to the proposed Pathways carbon storage hub, “as well as the cumulative impacts of oil sands development in its territories,” Mr. Jacko said.

Yet Ottawa moved ahead with the designation despite repeated requests from Cold Lake for meaningful and timely engagement about the pipeline and Pathways, he added.

While the legal action “does not close the door to working with Canada,” he said, “responsibility to take the first step outside the courtroom now rests with Canada.”

In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations’ lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

“Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of CLFN members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty No. 6,” the application said.

“Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on CLFN’s Luechogh Tue Denesuline treaty rights.”

Federal officials have acknowledged the possibility of legal challenges to Pacific Link and its designation, but Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said in a recent interview he’s confident the government is using best practices.

“What we see in pretty much any project these days, is somebody decides to challenge them. Whether they’ll be successful or not is a very different question,” Mr. Hodgson said last week.

The minister’s office did not provide a comment on the legal challenge when The Globe and Mail reached out on Thursday.

With a report from The Canadian Press

Ottawa has said Pacific Link will create 140,000 jobs, generate more than $20-billion in GDP per year and $100-billion in government revenue by 2060.

The government is aiming to finish the project’s federal review process, including consultations, by Sept. 1, 2027, in hopes of having it operational by 2032. Its expected price tag is between $35.2-billion and $43.7-billion.

Yet Ottawa moved ahead with the designation despite repeated requests from Cold Lake for meaningful and timely engagement about the pipeline and Pathways, he added.
While the legal action “does not close the door to working with Canada,” he said, “responsibility to take the first step outside the courtroom now rests with Canada.”
In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations’ lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

“Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of CLFN members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty No. 6,” the application said.
“Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on CLFN’s Luechogh Tue Denesuline treaty rights.”

Federal officials have acknowledged the possibility of legal challenges to Pacific Link and its designation, but Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said in a recent interview he’s confident the government is using best practices.
“What we see in pretty much any project these days, is somebody decides to challenge them. Whether they’ll be successful or not is a very different question,” Mr. Hodgson said last week.
The minister’s office did not provide a comment on the legal challenge when The Globe and Mail reached out on Thursday.

stories.title: Potential rain through region overnight Thursday
stories.summary: London is seeing seasonal temperatures heading into the holiday weekend, in the mid to upper teens.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London is seeing seasonal temperatures heading into the holiday weekend, in the mid to upper teens.

CTV Meteorologist Gary Archibald says weather is fair into the evening, but it will change overnight.

“This massive system of low pressures lingering across northern parts of Ontario into eastern Ontario and parts of the Bruce Peninsula, as well as the Georgian Bay shores and the eastern shores of Lake Huron have seen some scattered showers,” he said.

“It’s been light, the worst of it is well to our north, working east and so that bodes well for the most part across southern Ontario proper. The next 12 to 18 hours, we’re not likely to see a lot of active weather.”

Here’s a full look at your forecast:

Thursday night: Partly cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers, becoming clear overnight. Low 4 C.

Friday: Sunny. Wind becoming northwest 20 km/h, gusting to 40 near noon. High 17 C.

Saturday: Sunny. High 22 C.

Sunday: Periods of rain. High 20 C.

Monday: Cloudy. High 22 C.

stories.title: Cold Lake First Nations push for judicial review of pipeline designation
stories.summary: Chief Kelsey Jacko previously said his community was left out of consultations for the pipeline designation, despite his community being situated in the oilsands region.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under the Building Canada Act.

The designation as a project of national interest does not eliminate the requirement for the government to consult with First Nations on the impact of the project itself. Rather, the goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so construction can begin next September.

Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko has told The Canadian Press his community was left out of consultations on the pipeline designation, despite the fact that his community is situated in the oilsands region.

In an interview Thursday, Jacko said his community was left with no choice but to turn to the courts because the federal government and Carney have ignored their concerns.

“I’m here to protect the best interests of my people and for the ones yet to come,” he said. “They’re going to use my backyard as a garbage dump.”

In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations’ lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

“Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of CLFN members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty no. 6,” the application said.

“Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on CLFN’s Luechogn Tue Denesuline treaty rights.”

The First Nation is asking the court to quash the national interest designation and to declare that Canada has a duty to consult with the community on the pipeline.

Indigenous communities along the route for the pipeline were given just two months for consultations on whether the pipeline should be designated a project of national interest — and that was still more than the government had planned.

At first, the consultations were to take place over one month. They were extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups denounced what they called a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

The Assembly of First Nations told The Canadian Press last week it had identified “many red flags” in the pipeline’s national interest designation and said the federal government appeared to be predetermining outcomes and approving projects in advance of meaningful consultations.

“The government’s decision today is coming only 12 days after the consultation deadline. As we have said on many occasions, First Nations support economic development and prosperity for all, but not at the expense of our rights, the planet, and the government’s legal obligations to our people,” the statement from the Assembly of First Nations said.

Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada’s obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous leaders have warned his government risks violating their rights with “national interest” designations through the Major Projects Office and the controversial Building Canada Act.

The United Nations declaration — which Canada adopted — outlines the need for free, prior and informed consent before decisions are made that could adversely affect the rights and lands of Indigenous communities and people. Indigenous communities also have recognized rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.

The UN declaration is cited in the pipeline consultation document, which says Ottawa’s engagement efforts were designed with those principles in mind.

Cold Lake First Nations is also concerned about the Pathways Project, a multibillion-dollar plan to transport and store oilsands greenhouse gas emissions. The carbon capture and storage project is linked to the pipeline; Ottawa and Alberta have said that one would not be able to proceed without the other.

The court filing says if the national interest designation for the pipeline stands, Ottawa will have granted pre-approval of Pathways without meaningfully consulting with Cold Lake.

“Since March 2023, CLFN has repeatedly written to Canada seeking engagement with the relevant federal ministers regarding the Pathways Project. Canada has not responded in any substantive or meaningful way,” the filing says.

It also says Cold Lake First Nations raised concerns about Pathways to the government’s major projects office, which responded by saying Canada would not consider the effects of that project or the doubling of oilsands production in its assessment of the pipeline designation.

In a statement, NDP MP Leah Gazan said Carney’s major projects plan is failing and the legal challenge from Cold Lake is only the start.

“The government clearly needs a legal reminder that free, prior and informed consent and the duty to consult and accommodate is not a constitutional option,” she said. “It’s unfortunate that in only a year and a half, this government has taken us back decades in our path to reconciliation.”

The court filing says Cold Lake First Nations has made multi-generational sacrifices for Canada’s “national interest” through the relocation of the community for military training, and through Canada’s failure to share resource revenue generated in their territory.

“We trusted them before and now we’re expected to trust them again?” Jacko said. “We’re trying to work with Canada. We keep trying, but nobody’s trying with us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Author Galloway says his defenders lost jobs, friends after letter opposed suspension
stories.summary: Vancouver - Author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says people who signed a letter criticizing the university’s handling of a misconduct case against him were subjected to “extremely hurtful” comments, and suffered socially and professionally.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Author and former UBC creative writing professor Steven Galloway wept as he testified that he can no longer write since unproven allegations of sexual assault derailed his career.

“I just can’t do it anymore. I wish I could,” he said in court on Thursday in the defamation case he brought against his accuser and others.

Galloway told the B.C. Supreme Court judge that writing had been the “greatest part” of his life.

The lawsuit was launched by Galloway after a former student, known only as A.B., alleged he sexually assaulted her, while others spread the claim on social media.

A.B.‘s lawyer said Wednesday that his client’s defence no longer includes an assertion that Galloway sexually assaulted her, but only that she reported he had done so.

A.B. is not testifying in the case, and her identity is protected by a publication ban.

After Justice Neena Sharma allowed for a short break in testimony on Thursday, Galloway stood and briefly rested his head on a concrete wall behind the witness box.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, asked him about the “biggest changes” to his life since the allegations against him surfaced in November 2015.

“Whatever it holds, I’m not particularly excited by it. I don’t know what my life will be, but you know, probably scrape together a living till I’m old enough to retire. Or I’ll be one of those old guys bagging groceries, which is nothing against them, but I don’t think anyone wants to be that old guy bagging groceries,” he said.

“I don’t particularly like the person I have to be now. I don’t want to be me.”

He now sells boats for a living.

The court heard he’d been writing a comedy novel to be part of a three-book deal with a major publisher, and a paperback version of his novel “The Confabulist” was in the works, before the allegations.

He said his income from book royalties had since “cratered” to about $5,000 to $10,000 a year “tops,” and he hasn’t received any invitations for speaking engagements since the woman, with whom he had an affair, accused him of rape, and sexual and physical assault.

He estimated he’d made between $1.3 million and $1.5 million in royalties worldwide, and told the court that “The Cellist of Sarajevo” had been optioned for a movie adaptation that never materialized.

Galloway has long denied A.B.‘s allegations and did so again during his testimony on Wednesday.

On Thursday, his lawyer questioned him about the state of his career.

“I, like every writer, got plenty of bad reviews, and it ruins your lunch, but not your supper,” he said. “I’ve never had my humanity torn apart the way this process has done that.”

Galloway testified earlier Thursday that people who signed a letter criticizing the university’s handling of the misconduct case against him were subjected to “extremely hurtful” comments, and suffered socially and professionally.

The letter, known as “UBC Accountable,” was published in November 2016 with signatories from the literary community, including Margaret Atwood, but Galloway said many removed their names after a wave of vitriolic criticism online.

He said people lost jobs and friendships were ruined, and one signatory called him in tears, saying her daughter was never going to speak to her again.

A number of friends, even those who believed in his innocence, would not talk to him anymore because being associated with him would be “career suicide,” he said.

Galloway told the court that “UBC Accountable” became a hashtag that spread widely online, and became an “all encompassing” term referring to him, and that he reacted with disgust, dismay and horror to the thousands of vitriolic social media posts that were published.

He told the court that a reporter from The Canadian Press had phoned him “relentlessly” and came to his home and left messages in his mailbox, seemingly having access to confidential information.

Galloway said he had attended a hospitality suite during a writers festival in October 2016, against his “better judgment,” and said some people spoke to him and others saw him and walked out.

He said an article in the Walrus magazine reported that he was given a “standing ovation” at the festival, which he said didn’t happen and he contacted the publication’s editor about the inaccuracy.

Galloway said the article portrayed the Canadian literature scene as “a den of rapists and rape apologists” who applauded him after his public shaming and firing.

“I still don’t quite understand how the editors at the Walrus didn’t fact check that,” he said.

He said after he’d won an arbitration award from the university, he “briefly had the hope” the social media storm would subside, but the posts continued.

Galloway did not get his job back as part of the arbitration.

“I wouldn’t have gone back for a million dollars a year to that place,” Galloway said.

He said journalists had been pursuing him for interviews “since Day 1,” and he decided to grant one to Globe and Mail columnist Gary Mason, thinking it May cause people to leave him alone.

“The Gary Mason article didn’t do anything. If anything, it made it worse,” he said. “One thing I’ve learned through all this is that when a mob starts coming for you, it doesn’t matter what you do.”

He said he learned about an art show being held in New York in 2018 through defendant Mandi Gray’s Twitter account, a “rape narrative” exhibition that didn’t mention him by name but included the “UBC Accountable” hashtag.

Burnett later took the court through documents, including evidence that UBC had given A.B. a $30,000 bursary after her graduation.

Galloway said the sum “eclipses the entire bursary program for the entire creative writing program. There’s no academic reason to have given this. After having endured UBC accuse me of a whole manner of crime to see them do this was flabbergasting,” he said.

The documents, which came out in the earlier arbitration proceedings, also included the draft of a lawsuit from A.B. in relation to the alleged assaults. It was never filed.

Galloway said the claim was for millions of dollars.

He said learning that A.B. was still “perpetuating” the allegations — after both his firing and a report by a former judge had determined that the allegations against him were unsubstantiated — was “another kick in the teeth.”

He said near the end of his testimony on Thursday that now his “world is small,” with few friends and only his family, isolating himself from social life.

The court heard he got a job cleaning and fixing swimming pools, writing online marketing advertisements, and he currently works as a boat broker, working as a subcontractor and paid on sales commissions.

Galloway’s cross-examination is set to begin on Friday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Arrests, detentions of Canadians in U.S. up 60 per cent, Ottawa says
stories.summary: The department's annual report on consular cases, published Thursday, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press

Posted October 8, 2026 2:14 pm

The number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent, Global Affairs Canada says.

The department’s annual report on consular cases, published Thursday, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026, despite a 25 per cent decline in visits by Canadians to the U.S.

The report does not explain what caused the increase, though U.S. President Donald Trump has expanded immigration raids and Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials.

3:14 ‘This is Trump’s America’: Protests erupt in Austin, Texas after ICE agent shoots man

Overall, the report tracks a one-fifth increase in the number of arrests of Canadians around the world, including a threefold increase in the number of arrests in Thailand.

Global Affairs Canada has warned in recent years that the growing frequency of wars and natural disasters is resulting in more consular cases that are more complex and expensive to manage.

The data also shows an increase in the number of Canadians voluntarily registering with the department when they go abroad, which helps Ottawa send safety advice and co-ordinate evacuations.

stories.title: Air Canada CEO Michael Rousseau rebuked over English-only message
stories.summary: The commissioner's annual report says the office received a large number of complaints after Michael Rousseau posted a four-minute video that only included two French words.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie
stories.content:
The Commissioner of Official Languages of Canada is rebuking Air Canada’s outgoing CEO for a condolence message he delivered almost entirely in English after a deadly plane crash in New York earlier this year.

The commissioner’s annual report says the office received a large number of complaints after Michael Rousseau posted a four-minute video that only included two French words — “bonjour” and “merci.”

“The intensity of the reactions and the high volume of complaints received in response to this video show that both of our official languages genuinely matter to the Canadian public and that we must continue to protect them,” Burke told reporters in Ottawa, adding that the complaints are still under investigation.

2:17 Business Matters: Air Canada names new, French-speaking CEO

“This situation illustrates that bilingualism is an essential skill for any leader, whether in politics, federal public service, or even in the private sector.”

Rousseau’s video message came after an Air Canada regional jet that took off in Montreal, collided with a fire truck crossing the runway at LaGuardia Airport in New York on March 22, killing two pilots and sending more than 40 people to hospital.

Quebecer Antoine Forest and Mackenzie Gunther, from Ontario, were the two pilots killed in the collision .

Burke’s report says it’s important for Canadians to hear and see their leaders speaking equally in both official languages in times of crisis, “and not solely through an interpreter or subtitles.”

Seven days after Air Canada posted Rousseau’s video, the company’s board of directors announced that he would retire by the end of the third quarter of 2026 and that it was considering a number of criteria for his successor, including the ability to communicate in French.

The commissioner’s office said in an email that it received 2,425 complaints on the video, including 98 that arrived after the end of the current financial year on March 31.

Burke’s 31-page report also touched on a number of other issues, including concern over how federal budget cuts could impact the government’s language obligations and minority language communities.

“In the past, spending on official languages-related activities has often been targeted during periods of fiscal restraint,” the report read.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to cut the size of the public service, relying mainly on attrition.

Burke said it’s still too soon to measure the impacts of the 2025 federal budget, which laid out a plan to save tens of billions of dollars over five years in budget cuts and government efficiency measures.

“We’re watching the government’s actions closely on this subject, and we’re waiting to see how the cutbacks will actually play out within the administration, so we can then assess how the government has addressed the concerns we raised at the beginning,” Burke said.

2:10 Air Canada CEO Rousseau to retire amid language controversy

The report also cited what it saw as positive developments, including $150 million in funding announced for CBC/Radio-Canada in the 2025—2026 fiscal year and a Supreme Court decision in June that ruled that New Brunswick’s lieutenant-governor must be bilingual.

This decision “represents a step forward for the province’s language rights and a major victory for official language minority communities,” the report read.

The report also dedicated several pages to the issued raised by the use of artificial intelligence.

It noted that AI has potential to be used as a tool for translation and interpretation, as well as promoting bilingualism and language learning.

But Burke noted that AI is prone to errors, and has a “language bias” towards English due to the predominance of English-language “content and perspectives” on the internet.

The commissioner recommended that the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat incorporate official languages to its artificial intelligence strategy and other documents by March 2027, “so that they are systematically taken into account during the development, implementation and use of any tools, training, programs, policies or guidelines aimed at deploying artificial intelligence across the public service.”

stories.title: Quebec Conservatives are celebrating wins for the party — and its ideas
stories.summary: Éric Duhaime's party won over 20 per cent of the votes and a whopping 19 seats on Monday, mostly in the Quebec City area.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Plessisville, QC — “Plessisville is Conservative. He’s wasting his time here.”

Samuel Côté, a country music DJ, and his girlfriend Mélanie Lévesque, a social worker, were eating lunch on their porch, just steps away from where Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was trying to shore up support before the Quebec election.

Clearly, the PQ did not have their vote. Their lawn sign showed they instead supported their Conservative candidate, Tarek Henoud, who would end up winning the riding of Arthabaska—L’Érable, located between Montreal and Quebec City, ON Monday.

This is also one of the handful of seats that would end up costing the PQ its coveted majority, having underestimated the voter turnout for their Conservative opponents.

“To begin with, I’m not a huge separatist,” said Côté, who also goes by the alias DJ Sammy. “I used to vote for Québec Solidaire when I was much younger — like a lot of young people in the 18-to-25 age range. But I really lost interest in them during COVID.”

Côté said he was skeptical of the “medical conspiracies” during the pandemic and refused to get vaccinated. It was during that time that he subscribed to follow Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime who was not shy to address those questions.

“That’s what made me move from the far left to a less extreme right, I’d say.”

One example that spoke to them was the promise to abolish the provincial tax on used goods. Lévesque said it makes no sense to pay taxes on a used car, for instance, when those same taxes were already paid for when that same car was brand-new.

Côté also said Duhaime’s promise to abolish Quebec’s “carbon tax” appealed to him. The province remains the only jurisdiction in Canada to have maintained its carbon pricing system, which is adding to the already bloated price at the pump.

The PQ government has promised to abolish the provincial tax on used goods. It also intends to cut the provincial tax on gas by half for one year and reimburse it completely for individual Quebecers earning less than $40,000 per year with a cheque of $125.

Côté said he was happy to see the ideas promoted by the Quebec Conservatives be adopted by other parties — and in this case, make their way to government.

“The important thing is for the ideas to get through — not for the Conservative government to get elected. No. The goal is for the ideas to get through,” he said.

While lots of ink has been spilled on the referendum issue, many Quebecers have expressed they just want to get by. And Duhaime was able to pound that message.

As a result, the Quebec Conservatives are making a noticeable comeback in the National Assembly with over 20 per cent of the votes and a whopping 19 seats. They won 15 out of the 18 seats in Quebec City, spilling into central Quebec and the Eastern Townships. Their navy blue seats now form a large blot on a map of Quebec.

“It exceeded our expectations,” said director of communications Cédric Lapointe.

Duhaime has said he built on the lessons of the past campaign, where his party won no seats despite finishing with 13 per cent of the popular vote. So, he focused his efforts on the Quebec City area, campaigning in surrounding regions as his support grew.

Lapointe said the idea was to develop their brand as the “party of taxpayers” by focusing on people’s purchasing power. He said it was a clear contrast with the PQ and the Quebec Liberals, which were more focused on constitutional debates.

“We were considered by many people as an alternative to the old parties,” he said.

The Quebec Conservatives were not immune to criticism, however. Some of their candidates made headlines for recent comments on vaccines, abortion or Canada becoming the 51st state. Duhaime dismissed those comments as “distractions.”

His campaign was also overshadowed by revelations that 62 per cent of his most recent book, “Destination Autonomy: Expanding Quebec’s Powers within the Canadian Confederation,” was written with artificial intelligence.

Duhaime argued that AI is a tool like any other and those were still his ideas.

In the last stretch of the campaign, Duhaime called on voters who were disappointed by the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec government to instead opt to vote for the Conservatives to block a PQ majority and a possible third referendum.

Duhaime made that ultimate appeal in front of a garage with two buses — one with a “Yes” sign and the other with a “No” sign.

“There is only one party that can stop them from leaving the garage,” he said.

The Quebec Conservatives were aiming for at least 12 seats and form a recognized party at the National Assembly. Poll aggregators were showing there would be close races with the PQ in many ridings which could reduce it to a minority government.

The race in Arthabaska—L’Érable was especially personal for both parties.

The PQ had won a byelection in the riding in 2025 with former journalist Alex Boissonneault against Duhaime, who had asked Henoud, who was also their candidate in 2022, to step aside in an attempt to finally win a seat at the National Assembly.

St-Pierre Plamondon had even promised, days before the vote, to name Boissonneault as one of his ministers in a PQ government. In the end, it wasn’t even close.

Henoud won 41 per cent of the vote against Boissonneault’s 33 per cent.

Duhaime mentioned this accomplishment in his speech the night of the election.

“Tonight, we made history. For the first time in (nearly) 100 years, Quebecers have decided to send a large caucus of Conservative members to the National Assembly.”

“And just think about this: we defeated six incumbent ministers, and we even defeated a Parti Québécois minister, believe it or not,” he added.

That comment prompted loud boos from the PQ supporters on their election night.

Duhaime said the rise of his party on Monday night is certainly no accident.

“It is about a political family — about values ​​deeply rooted in our identity, our history, and our regions,” he said.

“Individual freedom, entrepreneurship, the importance of family, regional autonomy, Quebec’s autonomy within the Confederation — in short, the pride of being Québécois,” he continued.

During an unrelated announcement in Sherbrooke on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney would not comment on the rise of the Quebec Conservatives at the provincial level.

“For us, at the federal level, we take messages from byelections and federal elections,” he said.

In that sense, he said he was “very encouraged” that his own party won over 50 per cent of the votes in a Quebec byelection back in August.

“That’s what made me move from the far left to a less extreme right, I’d say.”

stories.title: Covert U.S. effort led to Canada's acceptance of dubious postwar immigrants: study
stories.summary: Newly released passages of a landmark 1986 study say at least 35 people with apparently suspect backgrounds came to Canada after the Second World War through a covert program set up by U.S. intelligence agencies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Newly released passages of a landmark 1986 study say at least 35 people with apparently suspect backgrounds came to Canada after the Second World War through a covert program set up by U.S. intelligence agencies.

The previously secret details appear in a recently released version of a study on the resettlement of alleged Nazi war criminals in Canada during the Cold War era.

B’nai Brith Canada fought for years to see more of the report by researcher Alti Rodal, which was conducted for Canada’s inquiry on war criminals led by Jules Deschenes in the 1980s.

The Federal Court last month ordered the release of some long-concealed portions of Rodal’s study.

The Canadian Heritage Department did not appeal the decision and Library and Archives of Canada provided B’nai Brith with the latest public version of the Rodal report.

Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s chief executive officer, calls it a historic outcome, adding in a statement the organization is pleased the information has been made available to historians, survivors of the Holocaust and their descendants, and the public.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta government tells Edmonton to dump infill rules, cites parking, property value
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government says it's ordering the city of Edmonton to revert to its old rules for infill housing development.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith says the city’s policies, which have largely been in place since 2024, are too permissive and are harming homeowners by reducing property values and creating parking headaches.

The 2024 changes paved the way for housing redevelopment across much of Edmonton in an effort to increase density and manage population growth.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Smith says the goal can’t just be to build more housing, and that more attention needs to be paid on making sure new developments are properly integrated into the existing community.

She says Edmonton city council will have three months to comply, after which it will be required to review and consult on its land use rules.

The province is also ordering Calgary to maintain its current rules after that city’s council backtracked on its own zoning policies earlier this year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.
