stories.title: Ottawa records 60 per cent spike in arrests, detentions of Canadians in United States
stories.summary: Ottawa - Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens in the United States jumped 60 per cent in the last fiscal year compared to the year before.

“A lot of Canadians are caught up in this dragnet,” said Len Saunders, an immigration lawyer based in Blaine, Wash., just south of Vancouver.

“These are not people that live in Canada and come shopping down here. These are people like me who live here, who work here and who have green cards, and they’re concerned about their status now.”

Global Affairs published its annual report on consular cases Thursday. It recorded 577 cases of Canadians arrested or detained in the U.S. between April 2025 and March 2026, up from 361 a year prior.

Over that same period, the number of visits by Canadians to the U.S. dropped 25 per cent, from 26.8 million visits in 2024-25 to 20 million visits in 2025-26.

The report does not explain what drove the increase in arrests and detentions.

U.S. President Donald Trump ramped up immigration raids after he returned to the White House in January 2025.

Since then, Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials and cases have emerged of Canadians being detained by U.S. immigration officials for minor infractions.

Saunders said most of his clients are Canadian and many facing deportation have been U.S. residents for decades. He said some of his clients are married to Americans or have American children, while some receive U.S. pensions.

He said some of the people he represents thought they were legally residing in the U.S. until they got a visit from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

Others drove up to Vancouver or Windsor, Ont., for a day and were flagged for questioning upon their return to the U.S., he said.

Saunders said he suspects the Trump administration has shifted from a focus on raids targeting illegal low-wage workers to using voting rolls and databases to identify people who might be deportable — just as the Department of Homeland Security receives more funding.

He said Canadians might find themselves on a fast track to deportation because of decades-old sentences relating to assault, drug possession or drunk driving. Others, he said, have overstayed on temporary visas, sometimes for decades.

“In the past, a lot of these people immigration would just turn a blind eye (to), unless it really became something on their radar. But now you hear of ICE going out and scooping up these people, and some of them have lived in this country as permanent residents for decades,” Saunders said.

Many of his clients have voted illegally in the U.S., Saunders said, particularly in states like Washington where voters can make a self-declaration of eligibility.

“A lot of Canadians are naive and don’t realize that as a permanent resident, they actually can’t vote in the United States,” he said.

“I’ve been contacted by half a dozen Canadians in the last two weeks who’ve been put in deportation proceedings for past voting.”

In the past, he said, such people could seek American citizenship and sign a declaration acknowledging an illegal vote, expressing remorse and apologizing.

“There would be no problem and they would naturalize them as Americans,” he said.

Saunders said he now cautions clients to make sure they have no criminal convictions or immigration violations “because I don’t want to put someone in the position that they get deported over applying for U.S. citizenship.”

In Thursday’s report, Global Affairs tracked 1,981 arrests or detentions of Canadians around the world between April 2025 and March 2026 — a one-fifth increase over the prior year and a 43 per cent increase over two years prior.

The number of arrests of Canadians in Thailand jumped threefold. The report does not explain this increase, though the number of direct flights between Canada and Thailand has scaled up in recent years.

The report also notes a 25 per cent jump in consular cases involving children and family over the past three years, with 804 cases involving things like custody disputes, forced marriage or surrogacy. Those cases most commonly involve the U.S., India and Pakistan.

Global Affairs Canada has warned in recent years that the growing frequency of wars and natural disasters is resulting in more complex and expensive consular cases.

Thursday’s report says the federal government fielded a total of 7,436 consular cases over the fiscal year, a 7 per cent increase over two years prior. Those cases ranged from car crashes to child abductions.

It notes that Cuba’s energy crisis — spurred by U.S. attempts to cut off fuel supplies to the island state — resulted in Ottawa working with airlines to return 28,000 people to Canada as companies cut their flights.

Cartel-related violence in the Mexican beach city of Puerto Vallarta and evacuations related to the U.S. war on Iran were other sources of consular demand, the report said.

The data also shows a rise in the number of Canadians voluntarily registering with the department when they go abroad, which helps Ottawa send safety advice and co-ordinate evacuations.

The department tracked an increase in registrations of 27 per cent over the previous fiscal year, resulting in 574,338 registrations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said Global Affairs recorded 557 cases of Canadians being arrested or detained in the United States between April 2025 and March 2026. In fact, it was 577 cases.

stories.title: Trump’s steel tariffs likely here for ‘long term:’ Canadian industry group
stories.summary: The Canadian Steel Producers Association vice president says we need to deal the world as it is, not as we would like it to be, as U.S.-owned Hamilton plant lays off workers.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
A representative for the Canadian steel industry says he worries that U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs are here to stay for the “long term” as he urged the federal government to strengthen Buy Canadian rules to support the industry.

Speaking at the Senate’s foreign affairs committee Thursday, John Cuddihy, a vice president with the Canadian Steel Producers Association, said the American steel industry has profited greatly from Trump’s trade war with Canada.

And Cuddihy said he doesn’t anticipate the situation changing any time soon.

“The underpinnings of the current situation suggest that tariffs could be with us for awhile,” said Cuddihy.

“From a financial perspective, where the United States is at suggests it May be difficult for them to remove tariffs across the board. So in terms of treating the world as it is as opposed to how we’d like it to be, as we look at the world we’re anticipating that tariffs will be … in play for the long term. ”

Cuddihy declined to answer questions about the impact of U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs decision to lay off roughly 350 employees at Hamilton’s Stelco plant.

Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the U.S. company of “betraying” Canadian workers and suggested federal funds were available to keep employees working at the Hamilton plant.

But Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told Global News in an interview that “no amount of money” would’ve changed the factors that led to the company’s decision.

“There’s no market in Canada for the amount of galvanized steel we produce in Canada. We need to export … to the United States,” said Goncalves, who has supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Goncalves denied his support and donations to Trump played a factor in his decision.

“I have been in this business for 45 years, so I have worked with so many different persons, Republicans and Democrats. Trump, then Biden, then Trump,” Goncalves said.

He also denied that he was holding out for a better financial support package from the Canadian government.

“I did not ask for a blank cheque to the tune of billions with no conditions, that’s absolutely wrong,” Goncalves said.

On Monday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly sent Stelco president Paul Simon a letter detailing “extreme disappointment” in the company’s layoff plans, noting that Cleveland-Cliffs takeover of Stelco in 2024 was conditional on maintaining the number of unionized and non-unionized employees.

Those conditions remain regardless of “business strategy or market conditions,” Joly wrote.

With files from Global’s Colin D’Mello and the Canadian Press.

stories.title: Major government economic legislation C-39 clears first vote
stories.summary: Ottawa — A key piece of economic legislation, Bill C-39, has passed its first vote in the House of Commons and the 243-page bill will now be studied by a special committee.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A key piece of the Carney government’s economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons Thursday when Conservatives voted with the majority Liberals to send the bill for study by a special committee.

The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government’s one-project, one-review, within one-year approach to major infrastructure projects to apply to other projects across the country.

The legislation is a core part of the Liberals’ plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets.

Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to a committee study in order to propose amendments to what he called a “weak, watered-down, long-delayed” bill.

Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers’ rights.

He also said Conservatives would seek to eliminate the industrial carbon price and create shovel-ready zones with pre-permitting for developments.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has said it plans to strike a special committee to study the sweeping legislation but the exact makeup of that committee has not been announced.

It won’t include representation from the NDP, which does not have official party status in the House of Commons, a requirement for automatic inclusion on standing committees.

NDP House leader Don Davies said he asked the government to allow his party to participate in the committee but Government House leader Steven MacKinnon turned him down, a move Davies called “fundamentally undemocratic.”

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she also asked for committee standing but was denied.

She said the bill is the “omnibus of omnibuses” and threatens to trample the environment in order to build things quickly.

“What is currently happening, this Prime Minister’s Office is more contemptuous of Parliament and less concerned about transparency and accountability than any previous PMO,” May said, in a scrum with reporters before question period.

At a press conference Thursday with labour and First Nations leaders, Davies and NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the legislation must not pass as written because of what it does to labour and treaty rights.

Lewis said the bill “must be scrapped” because of the massive changes it would unleash and because the government failed to consult adequately with Indigenous groups and others affected by the legislation. He compared it to omnibus bills tabled during the Harper administration.

On Tuesday, B.C. Liberal MP Patrick Weiler took some shots at his own government’s bill during debate in the House of Commons.

Weiler said while he agrees with the overall direction of the bill, he’s not comfortable with C-39 giving cabinet the power to fast-track project timelines. He also warned the one-year project timelines under the bill could undermine the government’s duty to consult with Indigenous communities.

Lewis said Weiler took a “courageous stand” and he’s heard similar concerns from Liberal voters on the doorstep.

“There are people in the progressive Liberal universe who are dismayed by this legislation and I encourage more of them to speak up before it’s too late,” Lewis said.

Poilievre was asked how he would enforce the tight timelines he proposes while giving Indigenous communities and other stakeholders enough time to consider the proposals.

He said Indigenous peoples have already given their consent to an aggressive infrastructure agenda.

“Indigenous people want to build, and I believe that Indigenous Canadians can be the richest people anywhere on earth if we unblock our resources, get the government out of the way and get building,” Poilievre said.

Also on Thursday, Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court for a judicial review of Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest. The First Nation accuses the government of failing to adequately consult with them on the project.

Chief Shelly Moore-Frappier, of the Teme Augama Anishinabek nation, told Thursday’s press conference with Lewis her community is not anti-development but this legislation must not pass as written.

She said she wants to see the bill amended to compel the government to obtain Indigenous consent for developments, to eliminate the legislation’s deadlines on consultation, and to require companies to clean up former industrial sites.

“Last year I told the Senate that Bill C-5 was economic coercion. Ottawa used the threat of tariffs to push First Nations into line, and we got painted as the problem. We were told the fast-track was temporary. C-39 takes it and makes it permanent,” Moore-Frappier said.

She said her community is home to deposits of copper, cobalt, platinum and other critical minerals — along with inactive mines that have been left unremediated.

The government insists it will uphold its duty to consult with Indigenous groups on projects and argues the legislation does not threaten the right to strike.

Bill C-39 proposes new rules on when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute affecting a federally regulated sector.

Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, called C-39 an attack on workers’ rights at a press conference Thursday.

Bruske said changes to clarify a minister’s power to scuttle a work stoppage when the “national interest” is at stake completely undermine unions’ ability to use the threat of a strike to extract gains at the bargaining table.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the federal government will not compromise workers’ rights to strike, but she did not answer directly when asked at the Senate earlier this week whether the bill could impose limits on that right.

The Liberals argue changes proposed to the Canada Labour Code in the bill will put “guardrails” around the minister’s ability to intervene in a labour dispute.

Poilievre said the Conservatives will also introduce amendments at committee to protect workers’ rights but offered no specifics.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

David Baxter and Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Do not bring Canadian alcohol across the border for Thanksgiving, trade lawyer advises
stories.summary: Thinking of bringing your favourite bottle of Canadian whisky over the border this fall? Don’t risk it, says one Canadian expert.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Thinking of bringing your favourite bottle of Canadian whisky over the border this Thanksgiving? Don’t risk it, says one Canadian expert.

Trump’s ban on most Canadian alcohol exports is “comprehensive,” international trade lawyer Rambod Behboodi said, and not to be trifled with.

“My approach with any time you try to cross the border, is minimize hassle,” he told CTVNews.CA on Thursday.

His comments follow more than a week after the ban, announced on Sept. 8, came into effect. The ban bars Canadian exports of more than 30 different alcohol products including packaged beer, sparkling wine, table wines, cider, sake and spirits such as whiskies, vodka and gin. It also barred different whey products, some types of molasses, non-alcoholic beer and some motorcycles.

Trump announced the ban in response to Canada’s retaliation measures on nearly $28 billion of U.S. imports, announced the same day.

A day before the ban was implemented, the Canadian Snowbird Association (CSA) put out its own advisory , warning those crossing the border to avoid packing Canadian alcoholic beverages and some dairy products for their trips.

Bringing alcohol over the border

The ban targets retail-sized packaging of alcohol with exemptions for bulk shipments.

“The better option is not to take any alcohol with you,” Behboodi said.

The CSA advised travellers to keep the ban in mind when crossing the border and to “check their vehicles, RVs and luggage.”

“Do not bring Canadian-origin products that are subject to the new import bans. All food, agricultural products and alcohol must be declared to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP),” the organization warned.

Most probably, the bottles will be seized and destroyed, Behboodi said.

The severity of the consequences depends on a few factors: whether the alcohol was declared, mistakenly carried over or intentionally smuggled.

“If the product hasn’t been declared, there’s a secondary inspection,” he said. “(If) the product is discovered and you genuinely cannot demonstrate that you didn’t know there was a ban,” there could be fines.

On Sept. 29, a truck carrying “over 1,000 bottles of spirits” was denied entry into the U.S. by border officials at the St. Stephen-Calais crossing between New Brunswick and Maine, despite the driver holding a U.S. customs permit.

Border officials said then the cargo violated the recently-implemented import restrictions.

Tensions between U.S. and Canada

Regardless of political climate, it’s never worth attempting to flout the law and less so for a bottle of alcohol.

“Don’t break the law over a bottle of rye or vodka or a two-four of beer,” Behboodi said. “It’s not worth it. Not to mention, just don’t break the law.”

He also strongly advised against taking a risk in the hopes of encountering a U.S. customs officer who May be more lax.

An officer “May,” for instance, believe that a traveller is acting in good faith if they can prove that a bottle was accidentally brought to the border.

“But would I actively take a product that is prohibited at the border in the hope that there is a customs officer who will look the other way? I wouldn’t,” Behboodi said.

Canada and the United States have been embroiled in a protracted tariff war after trade talks broke down in late August. On Aug. 21, Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion of Canadian goods.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on Sept. 29 that trade talks aren’t currently underway, but officials from both countries are still in contact.

“The basic rule of thumb is expect stricter, stronger enforcement at the border,” Behboodi said.

Bringing American booze into Canada

Most Canadian provinces, excluding Alberta and Saskatchewan, have instituted their own ban on retail stores selling U.S. alcohol.

The ban does not apply to travellers purchasing and bringing their own supplies of American-made alcohol into Canada.

“What you can expect at the border is, like anything else, if you’re within limits, it’s OK,” he said. “... If it’s above limits, then you pay duty and taxes that are applicable.”

With files from CTV News Atlantic’s Melanie Price and The Canadian Press

Trump announced the ban in response to Canada’s retaliation measures on nearly $28 billion of U.S. imports, announced the same day.

A day before the ban was implemented, the Canadian Snowbird Association (CSA) put out its own advisory , warning those crossing the border to avoid packing Canadian alcoholic beverages and some dairy products for their trips.
Bringing alcohol over the border
The ban targets retail-sized packaging of alcohol with exemptions for bulk shipments.
“The better option is not to take any alcohol with you,” Behboodi said.
The CSA advised travellers to keep the ban in mind when crossing the border and to “check their vehicles, RVs and luggage.”

“Do not bring Canadian-origin products that are subject to the new import bans. All food, agricultural products and alcohol must be declared to U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP),” the organization warned.
Most probably, the bottles will be seized and destroyed, Behboodi said.
The severity of the consequences depends on a few factors: whether the alcohol was declared, mistakenly carried over or intentionally smuggled.

“If the product hasn’t been declared, there’s a secondary inspection,” he said. “(If) the product is discovered and you genuinely cannot demonstrate that you didn’t know there was a ban,” there could be fines.

On Sept. 29, a truck carrying “over 1,000 bottles of spirits” was denied entry into the U.S. by border officials at the St. Stephen-Calais crossing between New Brunswick and Maine, despite the driver holding a U.S. customs permit.
Border officials said then the cargo violated the recently-implemented import restrictions.
Tensions between U.S. and Canada
Regardless of political climate, it’s never worth attempting to flout the law and less so for a bottle of alcohol.
“Don’t break the law over a bottle of rye or vodka or a two-four of beer,” Behboodi said. “It’s not worth it. Not to mention, just don’t break the law.”
He also strongly advised against taking a risk in the hopes of encountering a U.S. customs officer who May be more lax.
An officer “May,” for instance, believe that a traveller is acting in good faith if they can prove that a bottle was accidentally brought to the border.
“But would I actively take a product that is prohibited at the border in the hope that there is a customs officer who will look the other way? I wouldn’t,” Behboodi said.

Canada and the United States have been embroiled in a protracted tariff war after trade talks broke down in late August. On Aug. 21, Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion of Canadian goods.
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said on Sept. 29 that trade talks aren’t currently underway, but officials from both countries are still in contact.
“The basic rule of thumb is expect stricter, stronger enforcement at the border,” Behboodi said.
Bringing American booze into Canada
Most Canadian provinces, excluding Alberta and Saskatchewan, have instituted their own ban on retail stores selling U.S. alcohol.
The ban does not apply to travellers purchasing and bringing their own supplies of American-made alcohol into Canada.
“What you can expect at the border is, like anything else, if you’re within limits, it’s OK,” he said. “... If it’s above limits, then you pay duty and taxes that are applicable.”
With files from CTV News Atlantic’s Melanie Price and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Fuel tax pause will help higher-income families the most: budget watchdog
stories.summary: Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan said in a new report Thursday that the total tax pause will save the average family $276 over the course of the roughly one year.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Ottawa’s gas tax pause is offering a bigger break at the pumps to the households that earn the most largely because they buy more fuel, the parliamentary budget officer says in a new report.

The federal government temporarily suspended the federal excise tax on gasoline, diesel and jet fuel in April. The pause was supposed to end on Sept. 7, but the government announced last month it would extend that pause into 2027.

Half the tax rate will be reapplied starting Feb. 1 and the tax will be restored to the full rate on April 1.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan said in a new report Thursday that the total tax pause will save the average family $276 over the course of the roughly one year it’s in place.

But those savings increase for families in higher tax brackets. The PBO estimates that families in the highest income quintile can expect to save an average of $468, while those in the lowest quintile would see just $132 in relief.

Fuel costs often make up a bigger share of lower-income families’ total budgets but households that earn more also typically spend more at the pumps.

The Liberals paused the fuel excise tax to offer Canadians relief from a global energy shock driven by the war in Iran.

The government has not provided a per-family estimate of tax savings from the program. Ottawa says the suspension removes roughly 10 cents from a litre of gasoline and four cents from a litre of diesel.

John Fragos, spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said the fuel tax pause is a blanket measure that applies evenly to all Canadians based on how much they’re driving.

The Liberals’ other major affordability program, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, is income-tested and proportionally benefits lower-income households with direct payments, he noted.

Fragos also said that the relief on diesel costs can also pass through Canadian supply chains. Those savings per fuel litre can cut costs for businesses and bring down final prices for consumers on store shelves, he argued.

The PBO noted its estimates assume total savings from the tax break are passed on by producers, but those projections could be affected if corporations retain those savings.

The budget office expects the total cost of the fuel tax pause will be $4.9 billion, just under the federal government’s estimate of $5.3 billion.

The federal Conservatives attempted to pass a motion this week to extend the tax break and cut other fees associated with diesel production, but the proposal was voted down by other parties in the House of Commons on Wednesday.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - The Quebec coroner’s office says it ordered an investigation into the deaths by suicide of five doctors in the province over five months in 2026.

Oct. 8, 2026

By The Canadian Press

Coroner Géhane Kamel will look over each case to identify whether there were common contributing factors.

In September, over 1,500 Quebec physicians signed an open letter calling for an inquest into the deaths of doctors who died by suicide.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

The coroner’s office says it conducted an in-depth analysis of the request and decided to appoint Kamel to investigate the five cases and decide whether to issue recommendations.

The signatories wrote that doctors face death and suffering every day, take on significant responsibility, and sometimes do so without adequate support.

They also said some doctors avoid seeking help for mental health issues because they fear professional repercussions.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

stories.title: Ontario narrows out-of-country drug funding rules after cancer patient court victory
stories.summary: An Ontario man with Stage 4 melanoma says the province has blocked access to funding for out-of-country drug treatments in response to his attempts to seek therapy in the U.S.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
An Ontario man with Stage 4 melanoma says the province has effectively blocked access to public funding for out-of-country drug treatments in response to his attempts to urgently seek therapy in the United States.

Alex Shved, a 37-year-old father of two young children, took the province to court over Ontario Health Insurance Plan rejections.

Ohip denied his oncologist’s request for Shved to receive tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy in Florida at an approximate cost of US$600,000, largely citing the fact that the therapy is under consideration for public funding in Ontario.

The executive officer of Ontario public drug programs wrote in his denial that routinely funding out-of-country drug therapies while they are undergoing review in Ontario would “undermine the incentive structure that encourages manufacturers to participate in Canada’s drug review processes.”

A Divisional Court ruling found that Ohip offered no real basis for that reasoning and ordered Ohip to reconsider.

Following that ruling, Ohip has now rejected Shved’s request for a third time and Health Minister Sylvia Jones announced that the province has amended regulations to clarify that drugs will only be funded out of country if they are already funded within the province but access is temporarily unavailable or delayed.

She also says the government is exploring a “mutually satisfactory resolution” in Shved’s individual case.

stories.title: Five well-known works from Nobel literature prize winner Anne Carson
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadian Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadian Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday.

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson’s work often combines prose, poetry and drama.

Throughout her career, the Toronto-born writer has gained a devoted readership and critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

Here are five of Carson’s best-known works.

“Eros the Bittersweet: An Essay”

Published in 1986, it’s the first book of criticism by Carson. The work traces the concept of eros — an Ancient Greek word that referred to being in love — through its use in classical philosophy and literature, examining it as an experience of both pain and pleasure.

“Autobiography of Red”

Published in 1998, the verse novel is considered one of Carson’s standout works and earned praise from the literary world. The novel reimagines the plot of the fragmentary poem “Geryoneis” by ancient Greek poet Stesichorus, which recounted the myth of Heracles killing the winged monster known as Geryon, to steal his cattle.

Carson’s version is set in present day and recasts the myth as a love triangle, with Geryon as a gay teenager with wings who falls in love with a young, rebellious Heracles.

“Men in the Off Hours”

Published in 2000, the book of poems and prose won Carson the inaugural Griffin Poetry Prize in 2001. The work was praised for its individuality as it reinvented figures such as Oedipus and Emily Dickinson. The work also includes personal pieces about Carson’s parents.

“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos”

Published in 2001, the poetry collection won Carson the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize, making her the first woman to take home the honour. The work, told in 29 parts called tangos, tells the story of a marriage, while also taking on John Keats’ idea that beauty is truth.

Published in 2013, the quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red” combines poetry, prose and drama and resumes the characters’ stories as adults. The work earned Carson her second Griffin Poetry Prize in 2014.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada declines to hear appeal of man sanctioned over ties to Moscow
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada will not hear the appeal of a man sanctioned by Ottawa over his ties to Moscow.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada will not hear the appeal of a man sanctioned by Ottawa over his ties to Moscow.

The decision is the latest legal setback for Igor Viktorovich Makarov, who made billions of dollars through his business activities in Russia.

Ottawa has sanctioned hundreds of individuals and organizations over Moscow’s attack on Ukraine, prohibiting financial dealings linked to Canada.

Canada said Makarov benefited from close associations with top government officials in Russia while brokering energy deals, helping to generate revenues the Kremlin has used to lay the groundwork for its foreign aggression.

Makarov asked Canada’s foreign affairs minister to remove him from the sanctions list, but the minister refused.

The Federal Court dismissed Makarov’s appeal and the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the decision, prompting him to seek a hearing in the Supreme Court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Belleville officer ‘improving each day’ after synagogue shooting: chief
stories.summary: A Belleville, Ont., police officer who was injured in a shootout near a synagogue last month is “improving each day,” the chief of police says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The Belleville, Ont., police officer who was injured in a shootout outside a synagogue last month is “improving each day,” the chief of police says.

Const. Jeff Smith is making “steady progress” and has undergone multiple surgeries, Belleville police Chief Murray Rodd said in a statement Wednesday.

Smith was stationed outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue during Yom Kippur celebrations on Sept. 20 when the shooting unfolded.

Police say Sean Ward, a 29-year-old man from Quinte West, shot at Smith. The officer was rushed to hospital in critical condition. Ward was also injured but died in hospital a day after the shooting.

“I am pleased to share that Constable Smith continues to make steady progress and is improving each day. His treatment has included multiple surgeries, and he continues to receive ongoing medical care. Considering the extent of his injuries, he is doing remarkably well, and we remain encouraged by his resilience and recovery,” Rodd said.

“Every message, letter, card, and well wish received from across Ontario and beyond has been deeply appreciated.”

Rodd added police have met with officials, community and public safety leaders since the incident and have “reaffirmed our commitment” to protecting the community from hate and violence.

Smith was shot multiple times, Rodd has previously said, with the first round hitting him before he even exited his vehicle to return fire.

It was less than three minutes before a second officer engaged in the situation. That officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, did not sustain any injuries.

Smith noticed Ward passing by earlier in the day but was not alarmed, police said during a Sept. 24 news conference. He was then “ambushed on a second pass.”

Smith suffered from multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body.

The officer’s wife posted a message on Facebook on Sept. 23, thanking the community for the “outpouring of love and support.” She also extended her condolences to the Jewish community and the residents of Belleville.

Police said on Sept. 24 they had evidence the shooting was motivated by hate.

“The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd said at the time.

About two dozen people were inside the synagogue at the time of the attack. No one inside was injured, police said.

Police showed a video recording from the area of the shooting in which the shooter appears to tell Smith, “You are going to die for the Jews.”

Rodd said that police have evidence that will corroborate the intent “in more detail,” but did not provide any specifics. He said there were materials in the shooter’s car that would be considered “combustible.”

The investigation remains ongoing.

The province’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, is also completing its own investigation into the conduct of the officers as is customary when actions taken May have resulted in death, serious injury or the discharge of a firearm.

Const. Jeff Smith is making “steady progress” and has undergone multiple surgeries, Belleville police Chief Murray Rodd said in a statement Wednesday.
Smith was stationed outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue during Yom Kippur celebrations on Sept. 20 when the shooting unfolded.
Police say Sean Ward, a 29-year-old man from Quinte West, shot at Smith. The officer was rushed to hospital in critical condition. Ward was also injured but died in hospital a day after the shooting.

“I am pleased to share that Constable Smith continues to make steady progress and is improving each day. His treatment has included multiple surgeries, and he continues to receive ongoing medical care. Considering the extent of his injuries, he is doing remarkably well, and we remain encouraged by his resilience and recovery,” Rodd said.
“Every message, letter, card, and well wish received from across Ontario and beyond has been deeply appreciated.”
Rodd added police have met with officials, community and public safety leaders since the incident and have “reaffirmed our commitment” to protecting the community from hate and violence.
Smith was shot multiple times but still engaged suspect
Smith was shot multiple times, Rodd has previously said, with the first round hitting him before he even exited his vehicle to return fire.
It was less than three minutes before a second officer engaged in the situation. That officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, did not sustain any injuries.
Smith noticed Ward passing by earlier in the day but was not alarmed, police said during a Sept. 24 news conference. He was then “ambushed on a second pass.”
Smith suffered from multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body.

The officer’s wife posted a message on Facebook on Sept. 23, thanking the community for the “outpouring of love and support.” She also extended her condolences to the Jewish community and the residents of Belleville.

content_blocks.text: Why police say shooting was ‘hate-motivated’
Police said on Sept. 24 they had evidence the shooting was motivated by hate.
content_blocks.html: Police said on Sept. 24 they had evidence the shooting was motivated by hate.

content_blocks.text: “The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd said at the time.
About two dozen people were inside the synagogue at the time of the attack. No one inside was injured, police said.
Police showed a video recording from the area of the shooting in which the shooter appears to tell Smith, “You are going to die for the Jews.”

Rodd said that police have evidence that will corroborate the intent “in more detail,” but did not provide any specifics. He said there were materials in the shooter’s car that would be considered “combustible.”
The investigation remains ongoing.

The province’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, is also completing its own investigation into the conduct of the officers as is customary when actions taken May have resulted in death, serious injury or the discharge of a firearm.

stories.title: Nearly 1 in 4 Canadians and half of Gen Z have a side hustle, survey finds
stories.summary: Nearly one in four (23 per cent) of Canadians say they have a side hustle, averaging 13 hours a week on their secondary job, a recent survey has found.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Caught between the high cost of living and mounting debt, Canadians are resorting to side hustles to get by, a new survey has found.

Nearly one in four (23 per cent) of Canadians say they have a side hustle, averaging 13 hours a week on their secondary job, an Ipsos survey conducted for incorporation and business registration platform Ownr found on Thursday.

The proportion rises to nearly half (47 per cent) when you add those who are considering getting a side hustle soon.

Younger Canadians are more likely to have a side hustle, with nearly half (46 per cent) of Gen Z respondents saying they currently have a side hustle of some sort.

The biggest motivation for having a second job was the need to supplement regular income (39 per cent), followed by those who were most concerned about the rising cost of living (33 per cent).

More than a quarter (26 per cent) said they took on a side hustle to pay down debt.

While many start a side hustle out of financial stress, it could also be an entrepreneurial opportunity, said Ownr CEO Jordan Casey.

“There’s a lot of entrepreneurial ambition in Canada, and this data proves that even more of it May be hiding in plain sight,” Casey said.

Around one in five (19 per cent) said they are likely to leave their primary job and turn their side hustle into a full-time business, rising to 29 per cent among Gen Z side hustlers.

More than half of Gen Z respondents said they consider their side hustle a legitimate business.

However, many still face challenges when it comes to forming an exit plan.

“What starts as extra income often becomes a realization: ‘I’m actually good at this.’ Then comes the thought, ‘I could do this full-time.’ That’s where it gets hard,” said Casey.

Four in 10 (40 per cent) of all respondents said they aren’t sure whether or not to incorporate their side hustle as a business, while another 40 per cent said they don’t understand the legal requirements of starting a business.

The “confidence gap” is larger among women, with only 58 per cent of women saying they know when they need to register their business, compared with 69 per cent of men.

stories.title: Allergic to gold jewelry? Western study shows earrings can dissolve under certain conditions
stories.summary: Buying high-quality jewelry is better for your skin because cheap jewelry often hides reactive nickel beneath a thin surface.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Gold has a reputation for being chemically untouchable. But according to Western University chemist Yolanda Hedberg, that reputation is a little misleading – gold is not unreactive so much as selective about what it reacts with.

“Every material has their own enemy. Its own kryptonite,” said Hedberg, Canada Research Chair in Corrosion Science. “For gold, one of those enemies is sulphur.”

That distinction helps explain what Hedberg and her collaborators at Surface Science Western and the University of Copenhagen found when they tested five pairs of 10K and 14K gold earrings purchased from a jeweller.

After a week in cysteine-modified artificial sweat, all five pairs released measurable amounts of gold. Cysteine is an amino acid, or protein building block, made naturally by the body that contains sulphur, which binds to gold.

The amounts were tiny, and the findings do not show that the released gold is enough to cause an allergic reaction. But the study, published by the journal Contact Dermatitis, demonstrates gold in jewelry can become chemically available under the right conditions – a finding that helps explain how exposure to gold can occur at the skin.

In the study, none of five earrings purchased from professional jewellers released detectable nickel, distinguishing them from the inexpensive gold-plated earrings bought from e-commerce sites like Temu that were examined in a previous study. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Gold, silver and platinum are known as noble metals because they do not readily react with oxygen. That resistance to oxidation is a big part of gold’s reputation for stability. But, Hedberg says, it does not mean the metal is universally unreactive.

“Gold reacts to different things,” said Hedberg, a chemistry professor in Western’s Faculty of Science. “Gold doesn’t react much with oxygen, but it can react with sulphur and some amino groups.”

And for some people, that reaction poses a problem.

“Gold allergy is real, although it is less common than nickel allergy. But for a metal to trigger an allergic response, some of that metal has to become chemically available to the body,” said Hedberg. “So we wanted to understand how that might happen when gold jewelry is in contact with skin.”

Sweat contains amino acids and other compounds that can interact with metals. The researchers added cysteine, an amino acid containing sulphur, to an artificial sweat solution and exposed the earrings to it for 168 hours at about 30 C. The team then measured the metals released into the solution using highly sensitive mass spectrometry, a scientific technique used to weigh molecules.

There is no standard artificial-sweat test specifically designed to capture how gold behaves in the presence of sulphur, so Hedberg added cysteine to the solution to create conditions that would reveal whether gold could become soluble.

“The experiment was designed around a simple chemical principle. For a metal to cause an allergic response, it first has to become chemically available,” said Hedberg.

Gold was detected in the release solution from all five pairs of earrings.

Only tiny amounts of gold were released over the week-long test, with a median of 0.057 micrograms per square centimetre. The amount varied among the earrings, ranging from 0.016 to 0.15 micrograms.

Copper was released in much greater amounts, exceeding gold in every sample. The median copper release was 0.53 micrograms per square centimetre per week. Copper is generally considered harmless for humans and has beneficial antibacterial properties. Its higher release was expected, since the earrings were alloys, meaning gold was combined with other metals. Surface analysis showed the materials consisted mainly of gold, copper, silver and zinc, with only small amounts of nickel detected at the surface.

But unlike the inexpensive gold-plated earrings purchased from businesses like e-commerce site Temu, which Hedberg and colleagues examined in an earlier study, none of the five jeweller-purchased earrings released detectable nickel under the conditions of the new experiment.

Gold-plated jewelry can have a thin gold coating over one or more underlying layers that May contain nickel. In the earlier study on inexpensive earrings, nickel was detected in the artificial sweat in which all 10 inexpensive gold-plated earrings were tested, often at levels that exceeded European regulatory limits for jewelry sold for pierced body parts.

Element-specific spectroscopy showed gold throughout the material, rather than just a thin surface coating for the jewelry-store earrings, while the Temu earrings, if they contained any gold, had only a thin-plated layer.

“The chemistry and composition can vary widely, and price alone doesn’t tell you whether a material will cause an allergic reaction. In this particular comparison, however, the distinction between thin-plated earrings and the more expensive gold-alloy earrings from the jewelry store helps explain why nickel behaved so differently,” said Hedberg.

The study measured how much gold became soluble (able to dissolve in a liquid) under specific laboratory conditions. It did not measure how much gold reaches or remains on a person’s skin during actual wear, nor does it establish a dose at which gold jewelry triggers dermatitis.

Hedberg says the very small amounts of gold detected in the study would probably not be enough to trigger an allergic reaction in most circumstances. But that does not make the result irrelevant to someone who already knows they are allergic to gold.

“If I had a gold allergy, I still wouldn’t take the chance,” said Hedberg. “Jewelry moves against your skin, sweat chemistry varies and friction can increase the release.”

For most people, however, nickel remains a more immediate concern with inexpensive jewelry, rather than gold. In the earlier study of cheap gold-plated earrings, nickel was detected in every release solution. In the new study of jeweller-purchased 10K and 14K gold earrings, nickel was below the detection limit in every sample.

“This study doesn’t show that gold jewelry is causing widespread allergic reactions. What it shows is something narrower, but chemically important. Gold can be released from jewelry under conditions that make the metal soluble, so there is a potential pathway for exposure,” said Hedberg.

stories.title: Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canadian poet and essayist
stories.summary: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature Thursday “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian poet Anne Carson, whose work blends the ancient with the avant-garde, has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy, said she reached Carson Thursday in Iceland, where she was “listening to the wind.”

“She was taken by surprise, but very happy,” Carlberg said. “I could hear that in her voice.”

Carlberg said the academy rewarded Carson for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica whose body of work constitutes a genre unto itself.

With a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts, Carson has defied literary conventions.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T. S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

But as her poetic profile has grown over more than three decades, the particulars of Carson’s personal life have remained notoriously elusive.

Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”

View this post on Instagram

Various accounts suggest that Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.

The Swedish Academy confirmed some of those details, but offered few others.

“In 1981, she published her doctoral thesis in Classics entitled Odi et Amo Ergo Sum , and has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee for literature.

“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning.”

After her thesis, Carson made her publishing debut in 1986 with her academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

She gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Bronte sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.

Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography of Red,” which recasts the legend of Hercules as a modern-day love triangle.

Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Men in the Off Hour” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T. S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.

In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red.”

At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

She also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.

Her more recent works include 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win. The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.

One of the earliest congratulations to Carson came Thursday morning from her Canadian publisher, Penguin Random House Canada.

“It is a true honour for all of us at Penguin Random House Canada to bring her groundbreaking work to Canadians, and to congratulate her on this recognition for the way that work has changed the perspectives of readers the world over,” said CEO Kristin Cochrane in a press release.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica whose body of work constitutes a genre unto itself.
With a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts, Carson has defied literary conventions.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T. S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.
But as her poetic profile has grown over more than three decades, the particulars of Carson’s personal life have remained notoriously elusive.
Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”
View this post on Instagram

Various accounts suggest that Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.
The Swedish Academy confirmed some of those details, but offered few others.

“In 1981, she published her doctoral thesis in Classics entitled Odi et Amo Ergo Sum , and has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee for literature.
“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning.”
After her thesis, Carson made her publishing debut in 1986 with her academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

She gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Bronte sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.
Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography of Red,” which recasts the legend of Hercules as a modern-day love triangle.
Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Men in the Off Hour” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T. S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.
In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red.”

At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

She also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.
Her more recent works include 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win. The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.
One of the earliest congratulations to Carson came Thursday morning from her Canadian publisher, Penguin Random House Canada.

“It is a true honour for all of us at Penguin Random House Canada to bring her groundbreaking work to Canadians, and to congratulate her on this recognition for the way that work has changed the perspectives of readers the world over,” said CEO Kristin Cochrane in a press release.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.
Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Regulator publishes guidance on extended trading as it comes to Canada
stories.summary: Toronto - The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization says extended trading hours can offer more flexibility by allowing investors to react to new developments outside of regular hours, but it also comes with risks.
stories.author: Daniel Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization says extended trading hours can offer more flexibility by allowing investors to react to new developments outside of regular hours, but it also comes with risks.

Ciro made the comments in new guidance on the risks and benefits of extended trading as a new alternative trading platform brings after-hours access to investors.

Stock markets typically hold trading hours between 9:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. ET. After-hours trading broadens the times when investors are permitted to buy and sell securities.

“It gives additional choice and flexibility to retail investors, but I think the retail investor really needs to just understand and make conscious decisions of whether this is right for them,” Kevin McCoy, senior vice-president of market regulation at Ciro, said in an interview.

“For a certain segment of investors, this is going to probably be perceived as something that’s really good, but it’s not a one-size-fits-all where every investor is going to benefit from it.”

In publishing the guidance, McCoy said Ciro is aiming to ensure transparency regarding the risks when trading outside typical hours, which could lead to “better decision making” among investors as to whether after-hours trading is appropriate for them.

“Dealer members should consider whether additional controls, disclosures, policies and procedures are appropriate when providing clients with access to extended hours trading,” the guidance reads.

Ciro said extended hours could involve lower trading volumes, greater price volatility and increased reactions to events like earnings, economic reports or other news. It also said trade prices could differ significantly from those during regular trading.

“There’s less trading, there’s less volume. That May result in the prices at which somebody is willing to buy, or the price at which somebody is willing to sell; the difference between those two prices May be significantly greater than you May see in the regular trading session,” McCoy said.

Ciro said investors should keep in mind that extended hours are not available through all investment dealers.

McCoy said the U.S. is furthest along on extended trading. The Nasdaq Stock Market is preparing to implement trading 23 hours a day, five days a week, in early December.

Meanwhile, CIX Trading Inc. is a new marketplace that recently launched in Canada with extended trading hours. CIX Trading currently offers market hours between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET and plans to expand those hours to between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m. ET in the fourth quarter.

Ciro also reminded dealers that they are “equally obliged” to abide by all of the requirements and securities legislation as normal trading hours.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: List of Canadians who have won the Nobel Prize
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto-born writer Anne Carson is the latest Canadian to be awarded a Nobel Prize. The celebrated poet, essayist and translater earned the literature prize Thursday for “bold and inventive” works.

Here is a list of Canadians who have been recognized over the years with a Nobel.

1923: Frederick G. Banting, Nobel Prize in medicine for the “discovery of insulin.”

1949: William F. Giauque, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “contributions in the field of chemical thermodynamics, particularly concerning the behaviour of substances at extremely low temperatures.”

1957: Former prime minister Lester Bowles Pearson, Nobel Peace Prize for his role in defusing the 1956 Suez crisis.

1966: Charles B. Huggins, Nobel Prize in medicine for “his discoveries concerning hormonal treatment of prostatic cancer.”

1971: Gerhard Herzberg, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his contributions to the knowledge of electronic structure and geometry of molecules, particularly free radicals.”

1976: Saul Bellow, Nobel Prize in literature for “the human understanding and subtle analysis of contemporary culture that are combined in his work.’’

1981: David H. Hubel, Nobel Prize in medicine for “discoveries concerning information processing in the visual system.”

1983: Henry Taube, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his work on the mechanisms of electron transfer reactions, especially in metal complexes.”

1986: John Polanyi, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “contributions concerning the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.

1989: Sidney Altman, Nobel Prize in chemistry for discovery of catalytic properties of RNA.

1990: Richard E. Taylor, Nobel Prize in physics for “investigations concerning deep inelastic scattering of electrons on protons and bound neutrons, which have been of essential importance for the development of the quark model in particle physics.”

1992: Rudolph A. Marcus, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his contributions to the theory of electron transfer reactions in chemical systems.”

1993: Michael Smith, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his fundamental contributions to the establishment of oligonucleotide-based, site-directed mutagenesis and its development for protein studies.”

1994: Bertram N. Brockhouse, Nobel Prize in physics for “the development of neutron spectroscopy.”

1996: William Vickrey, Nobel Prize in economic sciences for “contributions to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information.”

1997: Myron S. Scholes, Nobel Prize in economic sciences for “a new method to determine the value of derivatives.”

1999: Robert A. Mundell, Nobel Prize in economic sciences for “his analysis of monetary and fiscal policy under different exchange rate regimes and his analysis of optimum currency areas.”

2009: Jack W. Szostak, Nobel Prize in medicine for “the discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase.”

2009: Willard S. Boyle, Nobel Prize in physics for “the invention of an imaging semiconductor circuit _ the CCD sensor.

2011: Ralph M. Steinman, Nobel Prize in medicine for “his discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity.”

2013: Alice Munro, Nobel Prize in literature for being the “master of the contemporary short story.”

2015: Arthur B. McDonald, Nobel Prize in physics for “the discovery of neutrino oscillations, which shows that neutrinos have mass.”

2018: Donna Strickland, Nobel Prize in physics for co-developing a “method of generating high-intensity, ultra-short optical pulses.”

2019: James Peebles, Nobel Prize in physics for physical cosmology, for laying out the chemical makeup of the universe at its beginning and later explaining the way that galaxies are formed.

2021: David Card shared the Nobel Prize in economic sciences for pioneering research on labour-market impacts of minimum wage, immigration and education.

2024: Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “godfather of AI,” shared the Nobel Prize in physics for work that laid the foundation for machine learning and neural networks.

2025: Peter Howitt, shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics for “having explained innovation-driven economic growth.”

2026: Anne Carson, Nobel Prize in literature, for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Fact File: Headlines falsely claim woman approved for Maid because she couldn't cook
stories.summary: This week, media headlines and social media posts claimed a Canadian woman was approved for medical assistance in dying because she lost her ability to cook.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
This week, media headlines and social media posts claimed a Canadian woman was approved for medical assistance in dying because she lost her ability to cook. The claim stems from an opinion article written by two Canadian psychiatrists who recount the woman’s story.

But the article’s co-author says the woman had an underlying condition that meant she qualified for Maid, and her story was meant to highlight how psychological factors influenced her decision to choose the procedure, a decision she eventually delayed.

The claim A headline this week in the British tabloid The Daily Mail reads, “Canada approved woman’s euthanasia request because she could no longer cook for her family, as country’s leading doctors warn the system is far too permissive.” The claim was shared several times on the X platform, as well as on Instagram, including a post that claimed the government “almost killed” the woman because she couldn’t cook for her family.

The Daily Mail article drew from an opinion piece published Monday by the New York Times, in which two University of Toronto professors of psychiatry argue that medical providers should “pause” in order to help patients who are considering medical assistance in dying.

The authors share anecdotes involving two patients, including a woman in her 70s who “sought and received approval for assisted dying after she lost the ability to cook,” as she felt she had lost value to her family. The other patient, a man in his 80s, said he chose a medically assisted death because the choice gave him agency as a Holocaust survivor.

However, the authors say both patients changed how they viewed the process after counselling and conversations that helped them understand alternatives to suffering or confront the psychological factors behind their decisions.

The woman ultimately chose to delay ending her life, while the man initially delayed and later chose the procedure, the authors say. The facts Medical assistance in dying, also known as Maid, lets adults end their life with the help of a medical practitioner if they meet specific requirements spelled out in federal law.

A key condition is that the person must have a grievous and irremediable medical condition that causes unbearable physical or mental suffering. There are separate tracks for people whose natural death is reasonably foreseeable, and those whose death is not reasonably foreseeable but who meet the other eligibility requirements.

The federal government said Wednesday it would not extend Maid to people seeking it on the basis of mental illness alone. Dr. Gary Rodin, a co-author of the New York Times article, said the claim that the woman was approved for medical assistance in dying because she lost the ability to cook is wrong.

“This patient had an underlying health condition that qualified her for Maid,” Rodin said in an email Tuesday. He did not elaborate on what her condition was, although in their article, he and co-author Madeline Li introduce themselves as psychiatrists who work with patients with advanced cancer.

The authors describe the woman as a matriarch who made Sunday dinners, and Rodin explained that her loss of function affected her sense of value as a person. Being unable to cook for her family “affected her will to live,” Rodin said.

“The patient clearly met criteria for Maid. The anecdote was meant to illustrate how psychological factors can affect patients’ decisions about the timing of proceeding with it,” he said. Some critics of Maid argue the procedure has been fast-tracked without adequate safeguards and that a focus on approval ignores that not everyone needs Maid; others believe the practice is unethical.

The authors of the New York Times opinion piece, who have counselled patients about medical assistance in dying, caution that too many patients are getting the procedure without the opportunity to think carefully about it with a health provider.

“A society that permits assisted dying should also ask whether it has done enough to help people sustain their sense of dignity and meaning in life,” they write. “Death must not become the only kind of relief people can imagine.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct.

7, 2026. Marissa Birnie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Terror groups drawn to recruit in Canada because of multiculturalism, academic says
stories.summary: "There are some people always that feel left out, so they tend to engage in crass stereotypes," says professor Arne Kislenko.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The recent slew of hate-motivated incidents in Canada had myriad alleged motivations, from Islamism to white supremacy. The terror groups that promote such ideologies were likely drawn to recruit in Canada because of its multiculturalism, says one academic.

“Most Canadians are big fans of multiculturalism. We celebrate it. It’s part of our existence,” says Arne Kislenko, a professor of international relations at Trinity College, University of Toronto and in Toronto Metropolitan University’s history department.

But, he said, there’s also that friction that exists. “There are some people always that feel left out, so they tend to engage in crass stereotypes.”

Recent weeks have seen incidents across Canada: a shooting at a synagogue in Belleville motivated by antisemitism, the arrest of three people in Ontario in separate incidents related to antisemitic and anti-Muslim threats made online, the arrest of an Alberta teen in relation to the 764 network , which is classified as a terrorist group in Canada, the arrest of a man in Quebec for allegedly planning to attack Canadians with chemical weapons, and antisemitic flyers handed out in Belleville nearly two weeks after the shooting.

There are currently 89 terror groups listed in Canada, including Hamas, Isis, Al Qaeda, Proud Boys and the Bishnoi Gang.

Kislenko said it’s no different than Germans in the 1930s. Despite some of them being highly educated, they started to think that Jewish or Slavic people “were somehow not human or that they had evil designs.” Today, there’s a similar sentiment of placing blame on others, he said.

Another reason why terror groups might recruit in Canada? From the outside, at least, it appears to be an “easygoing” society. It’s “safe place” where they can operate.

One way recruiters acquire targets is to find someone who has made a comment on a mainstream platform, like Instagram or Twitter. Recruiters from terror groups with similar ideologies to whatever post the person commented on then bombard them with messages. Eventually, the person May be put in contact with like-minded people, who might recruit them.

“We saw that with Isis. It’s super sophisticated, targeted propaganda — high-tech recruitment videos with music and the promise of everything you could imagine,” said Kislenko.

Radical ideologies can also spread on encrypted and unmoderated forums and game sites, according to Dr. Valarie Findlay. She is an Ottawa-based expert in extremism and ideological violence. She founded non-profit resource network IVY , dedicated to supporting youth.

Forums like Discord, Gab, Telegram, 4chan, 8kun (formerly 8chan) and game sites like Roblox and Rimworld “all operate in a similar fashion” and are places where “anyone can create groups focused on hate movements, extremism and social violence,” Findlay told National Post.

Groups like the 764 network coerce youth and “psychologically manipulate them to do the most abhorrent, terrifying crimes towards themselves, their own family, to family pets,” she said.

“Once you’re out of that situation, you realize what you’ve done and how horrifying it is, and that now somebody knows about it, somebody has that evidence or proof, then you have a sort of responsibility to yourself to try and maintain that ‘friendship’ on an even keel, so they never use it against you,” said Findlay.

“But they’re going to use it against you. That was the plan all along. It’s a very slippery slope.”

She said it’s a red flag when someone online becomes increasingly interested in your personal life. “It’s the unfortunate thing about social media. It’s great for the friends that you already have, but it is the worst place to actually make enduring, trustful friendships,” she said.

Both Findlay and Kislenko said that recruiters seek out vulnerable and isolated youth.

“They’re still trying to understand the world. They’re trying to experience it,” said Findlay. “Well-formed adults who are very socially intelligent and have developed their principles — they don’t want to talk to them because those are the folks that will poke holes in their theories, because logic ruins those narratives.”

The young people who do get targeted are often looking for the simplest explanation for complicated issues, said Kislenko.

“People blame Jewish people for everything. It’s a convenient scapegoat. Or you blame big government, or you blame women, right? And that’s what a lot of these newer terrorists are engaging in,” he said. “If you’re deeply antisemitic, you’re probably focusing on Israel and what it’s doing in Palestine, even if you don’t know what that means or have an opinion about it. You see it on the news, and certain narratives play into that.”

Findlay said that although it May seem like there are more hate-motivated attacks now, it’s been going on “for a long time.”

“How it manifests and how it channels and how (terror groups) establish their reach obviously has changed because of the advent of technology from the 1970s roughly onward. It has really made everything look like it’s happening more often in a way,” she said.

“And (terror groups) really do attach to waves of prosperity and economic decline, as well as the rise of conspiracy theories. They follow trends. When things are not looking so great … these things kind of seem to flourish a little bit more.”

Kislenko said just because it’s hard to police against recruitment, it doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t. He recommends an educational approach and possibly putting some restrictions on social media.

“We should empower law enforcement and intelligence not with more authority, but with a better capacity and more funding and training to look for these (recruiters),” he said.

“We should be judicious in prosecution…because it is hate and it is terrorism, and they are closely connected, and that leads to (the shooting in) Belleville, amongst other places.”

Groups like the 764 network coerce youth and “psychologically manipulate them to do the most abhorrent, terrifying crimes towards themselves, their own family, to family pets,” she said.

“Once you’re out of that situation, you realize what you’ve done and how horrifying it is, and that now somebody knows about it, somebody has that evidence or proof, then you have a sort of responsibility to yourself to try and maintain that ‘friendship’ on an even keel, so they never use it against you,” said Findlay.
“But they’re going to use it against you. That was the plan all along. It’s a very slippery slope.”

content_blocks.caption: Police investigate a shooting outside of Belleville’s Sons of Jacob Synagogue, on Tuesday, September 22, 2026. Photo by Peter J. Thompson/National Post

content_blocks.text: She said it’s a red flag when someone online becomes increasingly interested in your personal life. “It’s the unfortunate thing about social media. It’s great for the friends that you already have, but it is the worst place to actually make enduring, trustful friendships,” she said.
Both Findlay and Kislenko said that recruiters seek out vulnerable and isolated youth.

“They’re still trying to understand the world. They’re trying to experience it,” said Findlay. “Well-formed adults who are very socially intelligent and have developed their principles — they don’t want to talk to them because those are the folks that will poke holes in their theories, because logic ruins those narratives.”
The young people who do get targeted are often looking for the simplest explanation for complicated issues, said Kislenko.

“People blame Jewish people for everything. It’s a convenient scapegoat. Or you blame big government, or you blame women, right? And that’s what a lot of these newer terrorists are engaging in,” he said. “If you’re deeply antisemitic, you’re probably focusing on Israel and what it’s doing in Palestine, even if you don’t know what that means or have an opinion about it. You see it on the news, and certain narratives play into that.”
Findlay said that although it May seem like there are more hate-motivated attacks now, it’s been going on “for a long time.”

“How it manifests and how it channels and how (terror groups) establish their reach obviously has changed because of the advent of technology from the 1970s roughly onward. It has really made everything look like it’s happening more often in a way,” she said.

“And (terror groups) really do attach to waves of prosperity and economic decline, as well as the rise of conspiracy theories. They follow trends. When things are not looking so great … these things kind of seem to flourish a little bit more.”
Kislenko said just because it’s hard to police against recruitment, it doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t. He recommends an educational approach and possibly putting some restrictions on social media.
“We should empower law enforcement and intelligence not with more authority, but with a better capacity and more funding and training to look for these (recruiters),” he said.
“We should be judicious in prosecution…because it is hate and it is terrorism, and they are closely connected, and that leads to (the shooting in) Belleville, amongst other places.”
