stories.title: The population is shrinking in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we put more housing there?
stories.summary: Some neighbourhoods have been depleted by up to 40 per cent, a Globe analysis of census data finds
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic, Data analysis by Yang Sun
stories.content:
Kerrisdale looks much the same as ever. In this affluent pocket of Vancouver’s west side, gable-roofed houses stand behind tall hedges and shelter under mature maples.

Yet a subtle change has occurred: In many corners of the neighbourhood, there are fewer people.

On the side streets of Kerrisdale, many blocks have lost between 10 and 30 per cent of their population since the 1970s. One section near the Marine Drive Golf Club fell from 1,010 residents to 630 – down 380 people, or 38 per cent.

This is not an anomaly. Over the past half-century, both the Vancouver and Toronto regions have doubled in population.

But a Globe and Mail analysis of census data shows that within these growing metropolises, there are shrinking cities: established areas where populations have fallen as much as 40 per cent.

This trend of local population declines has been largely overlooked, even as Canadian governments work to create more homes and build the infrastructure – pipes, roads, community facilities – to serve the people who will occupy them.

In last year’s federal budget, the government promised $50-billion toward such projects.

In March, Prime Minister Mark Carney pledged $4.4-billion to “housing-related infrastructure” in Ontario, and in June, the government pledged $1.6-billion over 10 years for such projects in British Columbia.

But experts suggest some of this spending could be put to better use, or avoided entirely.

That is because governments rarely ask a fundamental question: Where do we have unused capacity? Many urban neighbourhoods have water systems, roads, parks and schools that were built for larger populations than today’s.

As new houses have been built across the Lower Mainland and the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, as apartment towers have swelled the populations of formerly desolate industrial districts, each city has maintained an archipelago of neighbourhoods where neighbours have become increasingly scarce.

The Globe compared figures from the 1971 and 2021 censuses for both Toronto and Vancouver, examining the population of “dissemination areas” – each one an area of a few blocks, typically home to about 500 people.

In the Vancouver region, 21 per cent of those areas declined in population over those 50 years, losing 76,424 people in total. Many other areas failed to keep up with the quick growth of the region.

In the Toronto region, the pattern is much more stark: Almost three-quarters of those established areas had declined by 2021, shedding a total of 540,789 people.

This pattern is hard to discern on the streetscape; these prosperous cities generally do not have crumbling, empty buildings or vacant lots. But the declines are subtly reflected in empty public-school classrooms, a lack of foot traffic and the closing of neighbourhood retailers.

The history of growth and shrinkage is shaped by a combination of demographic changes and specific urban planning policies. But nothing is set in stone: Experts say these places could yet absorb more residents, often at a lower cost than building entirely new communities.

Several demographic trends contribute to the pattern of the shrinking city. Canadians today are living longer, having fewer children and occupying more square footage than previous generations.

Roland Haebler is a case in point. A general contractor, he was raised on the west side of Vancouver. He and his wife raised their two sons in a 3,400-square-foot house in Kerrisdale; they remain there as empty nesters, though their son’s dog Hershy is often around the house. “We live in the same space as when we had two boys who walked to school,” said Mr. Haebler, 65. Their pandemic project was to convert their coach house into a music studio. “And now we have a spare bedroom, and I’ve moved my study from the basement into one of the other bedrooms.”

Prof. Maxwell Hartt, a geographer at Queen’s University who studies population decline, says that this story is quite typical. In the shrinking zones of Toronto and Vancouver, “there aren’t a lot of vacant homes,” he said. “It is fewer people in the same amount of places.”

Canadians are having fewer children. Young parents often choose to move from cities to suburbs. And seniors – whose lifespan has increased from an average of about 75 to 82 in the past four decades – are largely remaining in place, by choice or by necessity.

The COVID-19 pandemic prompted thousands of people to migrate out of large cities, particularly Toronto and its adjacent communities. However, that pattern was outweighed until 2025 by high levels of international migration; both the Toronto and Vancouver metro areas have continued to grow in each year of the past decade except for last year.

“There are, I’m sure, many retired people who would be happy to move down,” Dr. Hartt said, “but there isn’t a condo or an apartment nearby to move into in their community.”

Mr. Haebler was surprised to learn that most blocks in his neighbourhood have lost people. Some of his neighbours have divided up their lots to make room for new apartments, often for their children. “Everybody’s got a laneway suite now, and everybody’s got a basement suite,” he remarked.

“There’s multiple generations living in homes where there was only one before.”

Such small-scale additions to the neighbourhood, which planners describe as “gentle density,” don’t trouble Mr. Haebler. But these building projects are outnumbered by changes in the other direction. Empty nesters are more numerous; families are often smaller; and buildings are being converted from rooming houses or apartments into single-family homes.

To reverse the current trend in Kerrisdale would require big, visible change, with mid-rise or even tall buildings permitted across a wider area.

“In Burnaby, there are high-rises going up everywhere,” Mr. Haebler mused. If such large buildings were permitted in Kerrisdale, “I don’t think I would like that very much.”

Mr. Haebler has no interest in selling his house to a developer, and would not support larger buildings on his block.

Such attitudes are common. And while new buildings generate political friction, nobody really notices when existing buildings shed some of their occupants.

The latter trend is common enough in Vancouver, but far more pronounced in Toronto. A large zone of the old City of Toronto, running along Bathurst Street westward to High Park and north to Eglinton Avenue, has seen declines of up to 40 per cent.

Through the 19th century, houses here were home to larger families, and it was common for homeowners to take in tenants. The crowding increased as immigrants arrived in large numbers following the Second World War: Among them were Italians, Portuguese, Poles and Ukrainians, who each settled the west side of the city and then in many cases became homeowners, often raising large families.

As these latter groups became wealthier and more established, they largely moved to the new suburbs of Metro Toronto and beyond. The side streets near the core continued to hold two- and three-storey houses, but those houses gradually became emptier.

The two solitudes of Toronto in 1959: Downtown, the city was growing fast with new immigration and a baby boom, and in North York, the suburbs of Don Mills were taking shape. John Boyd/The Globe and Mail

On one side of the road, farm fields. On the other side, a concrete apartment tower rising 15 storeys from the new neighbourhood of North York.

This was the northern border of Metropolitan Toronto in the late 1960s, when the rapid growth of the city ran into strict boundaries.

The Metropolitan Toronto Planning Board enforced a vision of “urban contiguity,” as the historian Richard White puts it . Within a defined area, “development would be welcomed, but outside that designated urban area, development would be tightly controlled.”

This pattern continued, imperfectly, from 1954 until the early 1970s, when the economic and political pressure for suburbanization won out. The regions around Toronto grew explosively through the 1980s and 90s, largely in the form of houses, while the City of Toronto stagnated.

The last quarter-century has seen another reversal, pushing back against sprawl. In the 1990s, the Toronto region saw increasing gridlock as cities experienced fiscal pressure; at the same time, environmentalists gained popular support to protect green space, especially on the Oak Ridges Moraine north of Toronto. In response, a Liberal government in 2006 introduced the Growth Plan for the Greater Golden Horseshoe, which sought to reverse sprawl by focusing new housing within urbanized areas. Toronto and its neighbouring municipalities were forced to accept more density.

Likewise, Metro Vancouver’s Urban Containment Boundary has directed almost all new growth inward since 1979, and the Regional Growth Strategy , implemented in 1996, reflected a similar attitude.

This “intensification” policy was driven in part by the understanding that the older city neighbourhoods had capacity to hold more people, said Victor Doyle, a planner who spent two decades with Ontario’s Ministry of Municipal Affairs.

“In house neighbourhoods, the population had declined dramatically from seven people in a house to two or three,” he said. “So the housing stock itself could accommodate lots of new people.”

And with the addition of new buildings, he added, “these zones could accommodate a lot more.” They had “soft infrastructure” such as parks and schools, and they were close to downtown jobs, particularly in Toronto.

But in each case, there was a catch. New residents moved into existing cities – but regional and provincial planning generally didn’t dictate where they should go within those cities.

So, as in many other North American cities, a grand bargain was struck: New housing was pushed into the places where few people lived, principally industrial districts near downtown, while house neighbourhoods remained unchanged. In Toronto, the King-Spadina and Liberty Village districts rapidly transformed from industrial uses to high-density neighbourhoods with tens of thousands of residents.

“We protected certain neighbourhoods, so a lot of the geography of the city was insulated from change,” said Josh White, the City of Vancouver’s chief planner. “Those weren’t just geographic realities; those were geographic realities combined with political choices that we made.”

This has generated an uneven pattern of growth sometimes described as “tall and sprawl.” In Vancouver, that has meant high-rise residential buildings within the city’s downtown peninsula, and clusters in the suburban downtowns of Surrey and Burnaby. It has also meant mid-rise buildings focused on particular major streets, but not on the streets next to them.

As an example, Mr. White cited the Cambie Corridor Plan that added new housing when the Canada Line transit route was completed in 2009.

Development “is heavily concentrated physically on Cambie Street, to the exclusion of a lot of density even blocks away,” Mr. White explained. “That’s been the typical pattern of growth in Vancouver for the last couple generations. And that’s one of the patterns we’re trying to shift now.”

The city’s new Official Development Plan, which took effect in March, opened up the potential for new middle-density housing across a much larger swath of the city, organized into 17 new “villages.” The goal was to permit townhouses and small apartment buildings in areas that have seen little construction for decades, and to even out the city’s peaks and valleys in population.

However, Vancouver City Council decisively rejected the villages idea in July. Councillor Sarah Kirby-Yung described the public response as “a landslide of opposition.”

Reversing the patterns of the past 50 years will be difficult, and there are serious political headwinds. Questions around new housing – how much should be added, where and in what form – have dominated Vancouver politics for a generation. Housing has not dominated Toronto’s politics to the same degree, but change remains unpopular.

Still, intensification could pay fiscal and social benefits.

The environs of Christie subway station and Bickford Park are among the shrinking districts of Toronto, The Globe’s analysis found. Laura Proctor/The Globe and Mail

In central Toronto, Darlene Varaleau remembers when the schoolyard at Bickford Park High School was full of action.

“This place used to be busy,” recalled Ms. Varaleau, gesturing at the high school and community centre across the street from her house near Bloor and Christie Streets. “All the children used to go to after-school programs and have swimming lessons here. And then the kids grew up, and most of them left.”

The high school sat in the public park of the same name. Now called Bickford Centre, the building opened in 1965 to serve a growing population of immigrants and local baby boomers alongside a city-run public facility called Bob Abate Community Recreation Centre.

It rises five storeys high and includes a gym, swimming pool and auditorium. But the school that once served 1,000 students is largely quiet. In the last academic year, according to a Toronto District School Board spokesperson, Bickford Centre housed four small specialty high schools with a total of 77 students, while 386 adult students attended short-term programs.

At any given time, this facility is mostly empty. Ms. Varaleau, 74, is advocating for new community programs to make use of the building.

The school board offers one visible example of underused infrastructure in our big cities. For two decades, TDSB and Ontario’s Ministry of Education have argued over funding of its facilities.

This tension is connected to the city’s pattern of growth and shrinkage. In a few places, TDSB schools are oversubscribed. But the board has 301,366 classroom spaces and only 234,514 students, leaving nearly 69,000 empty seats. These are largely located in areas whose population has been declining for years.

Ms. Varaleau’s block, steps from the Christie subway station, had about 750 people in 1971. As of 2021, it had roughly 500, and that number is shrinking.

“There was a migration out of this area,” Ms. Varaleau explained. “You know, these were big families. There were a lot of people in these houses. And now, this is a desirable place to live, so you’ve got two people where there were five or more.”

Indeed, the average household size across Canada has shrunk significantly over the past two generations, from 3.5 in 1971 to 2.4 in 2021. In Toronto, and particularly in older districts such as Ms. Varaleau’s, the change is still more pronounced.

Children in Toronto today are heavily concentrated in a few places – largely the zones where many new homes have been built in condominium apartments. When young couples in those areas have children, many of them will stay in place or else move to the suburbs in search of more space. Houses in the central city, which remain more expensive, can be financially out of reach.

A similar phenomenon is occurring in Vancouver. The downtown Olympic Village neighbourhood, which has many young families, has seen calls for a new school for a decade. A new elementary school is now slated to open in 2029. At the same time, the Vancouver School Board’s buildings in many other downtown areas are below capacity . Meanwhile, suburban boards are booming. Last year, the Surrey Board of Education approved a $5.7-billion, five-year capital plan including 27 new schools.

In both cities, particularly in Toronto, schools are maintaining empty space while new school buildings are being constructed from scratch.

New suburban development generally requires all-new infrastructure. And the cost of building it, in places where homes are spread out, is high.

A 2021 study by Hemson Consulting for the City of Ottawa found that when low-density suburban houses are built, they create a deficit: Their property taxes do not cover the cost of the public infrastructure such as water mains, each home leaving the city worse off by $465 a year. Conversely, infill growth generated a surplus of $606 per home – property taxes cover all the costs of infrastructure, and then some.

That holds true even in places where water infrastructure is aging and under strain, said Kerry Black, an associate professor and Canada Research Chair in the Department of Civil Engineering at the University of Calgary.

Calgary has coped with two water-main failures – on the same pipe, the 50-year-old Bearspaw South Feeder Main – in the past two years. But Dr. Black said such failures are about aging infrastructure, not heavy use. “In many cases we’re not using these systems to their full capacity,” she said. “But they are at their end of life and will need major repairs anyway.”

Expanding cities out into new territory does not reduce that cost, she says; it simply adds new infrastructure that is costly and that will also need to be maintained and repaired.

“Imagine it in the context of a house,” she said. “I’ve got an old house, and now I’m going to buy a new one because it seems like it needs less maintenance.” But government, in this metaphor, keeps the old place and takes care of both.

The better solution, she suggested, is “to fix the existing house, to get the value for our money that we put into it at the outset.” Repairs or replacements to existing water infrastructure, she added, can also add more capacity in any places where it is needed.

Constructing all sorts of infrastructure “is far less expensive” in urban areas than it is in newly built neighbourhoods, said Shoshanna Saxe, associate professor of civil and mineral engineering at the University of Toronto.

Dr. Saxe argued that intensification could focus on neighbourhoods built after 1950. Many of these have similar patterns of population decline to those in older neighbourhoods.

And generally, Dr. Saxe said, these postwar suburbs have “overbuilt” networks of roads and water infrastructure. “It’s not just that there used to be more people there,” she said. “It’s that we have capacity within our networks to add more people because of things like fire requirements.”

Water supply systems are designed to deliver pressure to meet peak demand – which is determined by requirements for fire trucks pumping water to fight a fire, typically ten times the pressure required for normal demand. “In almost all suburban neighbourhoods you have more water capacity than you need to serve the people there,” Dr. Saxe explains. “You could add lots of people before you needed more water pipes.”

Their roads, meanwhile, “are hugely overbuilt” relative to the populations they support, Dr. Saxe said. These road networks can accommodate more people if certain streets were consolidated and if more road space was shifted from driving to mass transit, such as bus lanes and cycling.

In short, use what you have.

To back up the idea that more compact cities are more cost-effective, Canadians would need to take stock of existing infrastructure. How do we do that?

“We don’t,” Dr. Saxe said. “If there are comprehensive studies, I’m not aware of them.”

Generally, Canadian governments build infrastructure in response to population growth; they do not count their existing assets.

But there is one exception, an existing model in Canada for directing growth to where the capacity is: transit-oriented development. Ontario’s 2024 provincial planning statement directs new housing to transit stations. British Columbia has an analogous transit-oriented development policy, introduced in 2023.

Transit-oriented development is a well-established policy across the country – although it has not been widely implemented outside the Vancouver region. Now, there are signs that this tool could start to open the door to change in existing house neighbourhoods.

Jason Thorne, the City of Toronto’s chief planner, pointed to recent planning changes that favour small “multiplex” apartments, and newly updated zoning that would open up broader zones around transit stations.

“We are starting to see more housing permissions in neighbourhoods than has ever been the case” since the beginnings of land-use planning 80 years ago, he said. This will make the decisions “about where we put infrastructure much more complex and complicated,” he said, because growth patterns may be less focused and less predictable.

Complicated – but possible. Could we simply redirect much of the new housing, and new people, across existing neighbourhoods? Dr. Saxe suggested yes, with a caveat.

“The infrastructure could take it,” she said, “but the buildings will look different.”

Because today’s families are smaller than those of past generations, houses will need to be replaced by apartments. “There will be different types of units, different types of living, which will require construction.”

What might this look like? For specific examples, we can look back to how Canadian central cities grew in the 1950s and 60s – with clusters of mid-rise and high-rise apartment buildings.

The City of Vancouver allowed the intensification of the West End; there, more than 220 high-rise apartment towers were added between 1962 and 1975, adding about 10,000 people. Toronto saw a similar but more dispersed pattern: Several central neighbourhoods, including the Annex, saw substantial apartment construction between 1954 and 1972.

Individual houses were replaced, often one or two at a time, by buildings containing many more homes. (Across the Toronto region, more than 1,000 mid-rise and high-rise apartment towers were built in that postwar period, and they now house a total of a million people.) In both the Toronto and Vancouver cases, the street networks and public spaces remained largely intact as the housing stock changed.

Repeating this model on a larger scale could mean designating particular urban areas for redevelopment, as Vancouver tried to do with its rejected Villages initiative.

Or it could mean a more widespread adoption of density – altering regulations for big cities, or their most central neighbourhoods, rather than making new rules block-by-block. Instead of focusing around transit stations, a central-city policy would emphasize the general presence of amenities and transit.

This would represent a rethink in planning and in municipal politics. The generational compromise of “tall-and-sprawl,” block-by-block planning would be replaced by a different pattern, one that would allow growth across urban centres.

Within those chosen zones, large new buildings and houses would stand alongside one another. Allowing private builders, and non-profit housing developers, to construct apartments across a much wider territory would shake up the markets for development land and for housing.

Politically, this would be very difficult – as evidenced by Mr. Haebler’s reaction to seeing apartments in his neighbourhood, and the public outcry that led Vancouver politicians to pause the city’s plan.

Still, Dr. Saxe suggested that some form of more focused metropolitan growth would generate serious benefits through building on the cities we already have. “We can take advantage,” she said, “of a massive, expensive, underused infrastructure.”

Alex Bozikovic: Welcome to the age of the land grab. How can we balance great power with great responsibility?

But experts suggest some of this spending could be put to better use, or avoided entirely.

That is because governments rarely ask a fundamental question: Where do we have unused capacity? Many urban neighbourhoods have water systems, roads, parks and schools that were built for larger populations than today’s.

As new houses have been built across the Lower Mainland and the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area, as apartment towers have swelled the populations of formerly desolate industrial districts, each city has maintained an archipelago of neighbourhoods where neighbours have become increasingly scarce.

The Globe compared figures from the 1971 and 2021 censuses for both Toronto and Vancouver, examining the population of “dissemination areas” – each one an area of a few blocks, typically home to about 500 people.
In the Vancouver region, 21 per cent of those areas declined in population over those 50 years, losing 76,424 people in total. Many other areas failed to keep up with the quick growth of the region.
In the Toronto region, the pattern is much more stark: Almost three-quarters of those established areas had declined by 2021, shedding a total of 540,789 people.

This pattern is hard to discern on the streetscape; these prosperous cities generally do not have crumbling, empty buildings or vacant lots. But the declines are subtly reflected in empty public-school classrooms, a lack of foot traffic and the closing of neighbourhood retailers.

The history of growth and shrinkage is shaped by a combination of demographic changes and specific urban planning policies. But nothing is set in stone: Experts say these places could yet absorb more residents, often at a lower cost than building entirely new communities.
Several demographic trends contribute to the pattern of the shrinking city. Canadians today are living longer, having fewer children and occupying more square footage than previous generations.

Roland Haebler is a case in point. A general contractor, he was raised on the west side of Vancouver. He and his wife raised their two sons in a 3,400-square-foot house in Kerrisdale; they remain there as empty nesters, though their son’s dog Hershy is often around the house. “We live in the same space as when we had two boys who walked to school,” said Mr. Haebler, 65. Their pandemic project was to convert their coach house into a music studio. “And now we have a spare bedroom, and I’ve moved my study from the basement into one of the other bedrooms.”

Prof. Maxwell Hartt, a geographer at Queen’s University who studies population decline, says that this story is quite typical. In the shrinking zones of Toronto and Vancouver, “there aren’t a lot of vacant homes,” he said. “It is fewer people in the same amount of places.”

Canadians are having fewer children. Young parents often choose to move from cities to suburbs. And seniors – whose lifespan has increased from an average of about 75 to 82 in the past four decades – are largely remaining in place, by choice or by necessity.

The COVID-19 pandemic prompted thousands of people to migrate out of large cities, particularly Toronto and its adjacent communities. However, that pattern was outweighed until 2025 by high levels of international migration; both the Toronto and Vancouver metro areas have continued to grow in each year of the past decade except for last year.
“There are, I’m sure, many retired people who would be happy to move down,” Dr. Hartt said, “but there isn’t a condo or an apartment nearby to move into in their community.”

Mr. Haebler was surprised to learn that most blocks in his neighbourhood have lost people. Some of his neighbours have divided up their lots to make room for new apartments, often for their children. “Everybody’s got a laneway suite now, and everybody’s got a basement suite,” he remarked.
“There’s multiple generations living in homes where there was only one before.”

Such small-scale additions to the neighbourhood, which planners describe as “gentle density,” don’t trouble Mr. Haebler. But these building projects are outnumbered by changes in the other direction. Empty nesters are more numerous; families are often smaller; and buildings are being converted from rooming houses or apartments into single-family homes.
To reverse the current trend in Kerrisdale would require big, visible change, with mid-rise or even tall buildings permitted across a wider area.
“In Burnaby, there are high-rises going up everywhere,” Mr. Haebler mused. If such large buildings were permitted in Kerrisdale, “I don’t think I would like that very much.”
Mr. Haebler has no interest in selling his house to a developer, and would not support larger buildings on his block.
Such attitudes are common. And while new buildings generate political friction, nobody really notices when existing buildings shed some of their occupants.

The latter trend is common enough in Vancouver, but far more pronounced in Toronto. A large zone of the old City of Toronto, running along Bathurst Street westward to High Park and north to Eglinton Avenue, has seen declines of up to 40 per cent.

Through the 19th century, houses here were home to larger families, and it was common for homeowners to take in tenants. The crowding increased as immigrants arrived in large numbers following the Second World War: Among them were Italians, Portuguese, Poles and Ukrainians, who each settled the west side of the city and then in many cases became homeowners, often raising large families.

As these latter groups became wealthier and more established, they largely moved to the new suburbs of Metro Toronto and beyond. The side streets near the core continued to hold two- and three-storey houses, but those houses gradually became emptier.

The two solitudes of Toronto in 1959: Downtown, the city was growing fast with new immigration and a baby boom, and in North York, the suburbs of Don Mills were taking shape. John Boyd/The Globe and Mail
On one side of the road, farm fields. On the other side, a concrete apartment tower rising 15 storeys from the new neighbourhood of North York.
This was the northern border of Metropolitan Toronto in the late 1960s, when the rapid growth of the city ran into strict boundaries.

The Metropolitan Toronto Planning Board enforced a vision of “urban contiguity,” as the historian Richard White puts it . Within a defined area, “development would be welcomed, but outside that designated urban area, development would be tightly controlled.”

This pattern continued, imperfectly, from 1954 until the early 1970s, when the economic and political pressure for suburbanization won out. The regions around Toronto grew explosively through the 1980s and 90s, largely in the form of houses, while the City of Toronto stagnated.

The last quarter-century has seen another reversal, pushing back against sprawl. In the 1990s, the Toronto region saw increasing gridlock as cities experienced fiscal pressure; at the same time, environmentalists gained popular support to protect green space, especially on the Oak Ridges Moraine north of Toronto. In response, a Liberal government in 2006 introduced the Growth Plan for the Greater Golden Horseshoe, which sought to reverse sprawl by focusing new housing within urbanized areas. Toronto and its neighbouring municipalities were forced to accept more density.
Likewise, Metro Vancouver’s Urban Containment Boundary has directed almost all new growth inward since 1979, and the Regional Growth Strategy , implemented in 1996, reflected a similar attitude.

This “intensification” policy was driven in part by the understanding that the older city neighbourhoods had capacity to hold more people, said Victor Doyle, a planner who spent two decades with Ontario’s Ministry of Municipal Affairs.
“In house neighbourhoods, the population had declined dramatically from seven people in a house to two or three,” he said. “So the housing stock itself could accommodate lots of new people.”

And with the addition of new buildings, he added, “these zones could accommodate a lot more.” They had “soft infrastructure” such as parks and schools, and they were close to downtown jobs, particularly in Toronto.
But in each case, there was a catch. New residents moved into existing cities – but regional and provincial planning generally didn’t dictate where they should go within those cities.

So, as in many other North American cities, a grand bargain was struck: New housing was pushed into the places where few people lived, principally industrial districts near downtown, while house neighbourhoods remained unchanged. In Toronto, the King-Spadina and Liberty Village districts rapidly transformed from industrial uses to high-density neighbourhoods with tens of thousands of residents.

“We protected certain neighbourhoods, so a lot of the geography of the city was insulated from change,” said Josh White, the City of Vancouver’s chief planner. “Those weren’t just geographic realities; those were geographic realities combined with political choices that we made.”

This has generated an uneven pattern of growth sometimes described as “tall and sprawl.” In Vancouver, that has meant high-rise residential buildings within the city’s downtown peninsula, and clusters in the suburban downtowns of Surrey and Burnaby. It has also meant mid-rise buildings focused on particular major streets, but not on the streets next to them.
As an example, Mr. White cited the Cambie Corridor Plan that added new housing when the Canada Line transit route was completed in 2009.

Development “is heavily concentrated physically on Cambie Street, to the exclusion of a lot of density even blocks away,” Mr. White explained. “That’s been the typical pattern of growth in Vancouver for the last couple generations. And that’s one of the patterns we’re trying to shift now.”

The city’s new Official Development Plan, which took effect in March, opened up the potential for new middle-density housing across a much larger swath of the city, organized into 17 new “villages.” The goal was to permit townhouses and small apartment buildings in areas that have seen little construction for decades, and to even out the city’s peaks and valleys in population.
However, Vancouver City Council decisively rejected the villages idea in July. Councillor Sarah Kirby-Yung described the public response as “a landslide of opposition.”

Reversing the patterns of the past 50 years will be difficult, and there are serious political headwinds. Questions around new housing – how much should be added, where and in what form – have dominated Vancouver politics for a generation. Housing has not dominated Toronto’s politics to the same degree, but change remains unpopular.
Still, intensification could pay fiscal and social benefits.
The environs of Christie subway station and Bickford Park are among the shrinking districts of Toronto, The Globe’s analysis found. Laura Proctor/The Globe and Mail
In central Toronto, Darlene Varaleau remembers when the schoolyard at Bickford Park High School was full of action.

“This place used to be busy,” recalled Ms. Varaleau, gesturing at the high school and community centre across the street from her house near Bloor and Christie Streets. “All the children used to go to after-school programs and have swimming lessons here. And then the kids grew up, and most of them left.”

The high school sat in the public park of the same name. Now called Bickford Centre, the building opened in 1965 to serve a growing population of immigrants and local baby boomers alongside a city-run public facility called Bob Abate Community Recreation Centre.

It rises five storeys high and includes a gym, swimming pool and auditorium. But the school that once served 1,000 students is largely quiet. In the last academic year, according to a Toronto District School Board spokesperson, Bickford Centre housed four small specialty high schools with a total of 77 students, while 386 adult students attended short-term programs.
At any given time, this facility is mostly empty. Ms. Varaleau, 74, is advocating for new community programs to make use of the building.
The school board offers one visible example of underused infrastructure in our big cities. For two decades, TDSB and Ontario’s Ministry of Education have argued over funding of its facilities.

This tension is connected to the city’s pattern of growth and shrinkage. In a few places, TDSB schools are oversubscribed. But the board has 301,366 classroom spaces and only 234,514 students, leaving nearly 69,000 empty seats. These are largely located in areas whose population has been declining for years.
Ms. Varaleau’s block, steps from the Christie subway station, had about 750 people in 1971. As of 2021, it had roughly 500, and that number is shrinking.

“There was a migration out of this area,” Ms. Varaleau explained. “You know, these were big families. There were a lot of people in these houses. And now, this is a desirable place to live, so you’ve got two people where there were five or more.”

Indeed, the average household size across Canada has shrunk significantly over the past two generations, from 3.5 in 1971 to 2.4 in 2021. In Toronto, and particularly in older districts such as Ms. Varaleau’s, the change is still more pronounced.

Children in Toronto today are heavily concentrated in a few places – largely the zones where many new homes have been built in condominium apartments. When young couples in those areas have children, many of them will stay in place or else move to the suburbs in search of more space. Houses in the central city, which remain more expensive, can be financially out of reach.

A similar phenomenon is occurring in Vancouver. The downtown Olympic Village neighbourhood, which has many young families, has seen calls for a new school for a decade. A new elementary school is now slated to open in 2029. At the same time, the Vancouver School Board’s buildings in many other downtown areas are below capacity . Meanwhile, suburban boards are booming. Last year, the Surrey Board of Education approved a $5.7-billion, five-year capital plan including 27 new schools.
In both cities, particularly in Toronto, schools are maintaining empty space while new school buildings are being constructed from scratch.
New suburban development generally requires all-new infrastructure. And the cost of building it, in places where homes are spread out, is high.

A 2021 study by Hemson Consulting for the City of Ottawa found that when low-density suburban houses are built, they create a deficit: Their property taxes do not cover the cost of the public infrastructure such as water mains, each home leaving the city worse off by $465 a year. Conversely, infill growth generated a surplus of $606 per home – property taxes cover all the costs of infrastructure, and then some.

That holds true even in places where water infrastructure is aging and under strain, said Kerry Black, an associate professor and Canada Research Chair in the Department of Civil Engineering at the University of Calgary.

Calgary has coped with two water-main failures – on the same pipe, the 50-year-old Bearspaw South Feeder Main – in the past two years. But Dr. Black said such failures are about aging infrastructure, not heavy use. “In many cases we’re not using these systems to their full capacity,” she said. “But they are at their end of life and will need major repairs anyway.”
Expanding cities out into new territory does not reduce that cost, she says; it simply adds new infrastructure that is costly and that will also need to be maintained and repaired.

“Imagine it in the context of a house,” she said. “I’ve got an old house, and now I’m going to buy a new one because it seems like it needs less maintenance.” But government, in this metaphor, keeps the old place and takes care of both.

The better solution, she suggested, is “to fix the existing house, to get the value for our money that we put into it at the outset.” Repairs or replacements to existing water infrastructure, she added, can also add more capacity in any places where it is needed.

Constructing all sorts of infrastructure “is far less expensive” in urban areas than it is in newly built neighbourhoods, said Shoshanna Saxe, associate professor of civil and mineral engineering at the University of Toronto.
Dr. Saxe argued that intensification could focus on neighbourhoods built after 1950. Many of these have similar patterns of population decline to those in older neighbourhoods.

And generally, Dr. Saxe said, these postwar suburbs have “overbuilt” networks of roads and water infrastructure. “It’s not just that there used to be more people there,” she said. “It’s that we have capacity within our networks to add more people because of things like fire requirements.”

Water supply systems are designed to deliver pressure to meet peak demand – which is determined by requirements for fire trucks pumping water to fight a fire, typically ten times the pressure required for normal demand. “In almost all suburban neighbourhoods you have more water capacity than you need to serve the people there,” Dr. Saxe explains. “You could add lots of people before you needed more water pipes.”

Their roads, meanwhile, “are hugely overbuilt” relative to the populations they support, Dr. Saxe said. These road networks can accommodate more people if certain streets were consolidated and if more road space was shifted from driving to mass transit, such as bus lanes and cycling.
In short, use what you have.
To back up the idea that more compact cities are more cost-effective, Canadians would need to take stock of existing infrastructure. How do we do that?
“We don’t,” Dr. Saxe said. “If there are comprehensive studies, I’m not aware of them.”
Generally, Canadian governments build infrastructure in response to population growth; they do not count their existing assets.

But there is one exception, an existing model in Canada for directing growth to where the capacity is: transit-oriented development. Ontario’s 2024 provincial planning statement directs new housing to transit stations. British Columbia has an analogous transit-oriented development policy, introduced in 2023.

Transit-oriented development is a well-established policy across the country – although it has not been widely implemented outside the Vancouver region. Now, there are signs that this tool could start to open the door to change in existing house neighbourhoods.

Jason Thorne, the City of Toronto’s chief planner, pointed to recent planning changes that favour small “multiplex” apartments, and newly updated zoning that would open up broader zones around transit stations.

“We are starting to see more housing permissions in neighbourhoods than has ever been the case” since the beginnings of land-use planning 80 years ago, he said. This will make the decisions “about where we put infrastructure much more complex and complicated,” he said, because growth patterns may be less focused and less predictable.
Complicated – but possible. Could we simply redirect much of the new housing, and new people, across existing neighbourhoods? Dr. Saxe suggested yes, with a caveat.
“The infrastructure could take it,” she said, “but the buildings will look different.”

Because today’s families are smaller than those of past generations, houses will need to be replaced by apartments. “There will be different types of units, different types of living, which will require construction.”
What might this look like? For specific examples, we can look back to how Canadian central cities grew in the 1950s and 60s – with clusters of mid-rise and high-rise apartment buildings.

The City of Vancouver allowed the intensification of the West End; there, more than 220 high-rise apartment towers were added between 1962 and 1975, adding about 10,000 people. Toronto saw a similar but more dispersed pattern: Several central neighbourhoods, including the Annex, saw substantial apartment construction between 1954 and 1972.

Individual houses were replaced, often one or two at a time, by buildings containing many more homes. (Across the Toronto region, more than 1,000 mid-rise and high-rise apartment towers were built in that postwar period, and they now house a total of a million people.) In both the Toronto and Vancouver cases, the street networks and public spaces remained largely intact as the housing stock changed.
Repeating this model on a larger scale could mean designating particular urban areas for redevelopment, as Vancouver tried to do with its rejected Villages initiative.

Or it could mean a more widespread adoption of density – altering regulations for big cities, or their most central neighbourhoods, rather than making new rules block-by-block. Instead of focusing around transit stations, a central-city policy would emphasize the general presence of amenities and transit.

This would represent a rethink in planning and in municipal politics. The generational compromise of “tall-and-sprawl,” block-by-block planning would be replaced by a different pattern, one that would allow growth across urban centres.

Within those chosen zones, large new buildings and houses would stand alongside one another. Allowing private builders, and non-profit housing developers, to construct apartments across a much wider territory would shake up the markets for development land and for housing.

Politically, this would be very difficult – as evidenced by Mr. Haebler’s reaction to seeing apartments in his neighbourhood, and the public outcry that led Vancouver politicians to pause the city’s plan.

Still, Dr. Saxe suggested that some form of more focused metropolitan growth would generate serious benefits through building on the cities we already have. “We can take advantage,” she said, “of a massive, expensive, underused infrastructure.”
Alex Bozikovic: Welcome to the age of the land grab. How can we balance great power with great responsibility?

content_blocks.text: This pattern continued, imperfectly, from 1954 until the early 1970s, when the economic and political pressure for suburbanization won out. The regions around Toronto grew explosively through the 1980s and 90s, largely in the form of houses, while the City of Toronto stagnated.

content_blocks.text: The last quarter-century has seen another reversal, pushing back against sprawl. In the 1990s, the Toronto region saw increasing gridlock as cities experienced fiscal pressure; at the same time, environmentalists gained popular support to protect green space, especially on the Oak Ridges Moraine north of Toronto. In response, a Liberal government in 2006 introduced the Growth Plan for the Greater Golden Horseshoe, which sought to reverse sprawl by focusing new housing within urbanized areas. Toronto and its neighbouring municipalities were forced to accept more density.

content_blocks.text: So, as in many other North American cities, a grand bargain was struck: New housing was pushed into the places where few people lived, principally industrial districts near downtown, while house neighbourhoods remained unchanged. stories.title: Should you shop around? We tested the old advice on a Thanksgiving feast
stories.summary: Is it possible to make Thanksgiving dinner for less than $40? It depends on exactly what you’re making
stories.author: Bianca Thompson
stories.content:
Global food prices reached their highest level in nearly four years last month, bad news for Canadians headed into holiday entertaining. Large gatherings such as Thanksgiving and Christmas can add another layer of pressure for households trying to keep grocery costs down.

A study from Dalhousie University’s Agri-Food Analytics Lab found that a Thanksgiving dinner for four will cost $35.72 this year, up 10 per cent from $32.48 in 2025. But that estimate included a seven-pound turkey and basic side dishes, only factoring in the cost of potatoes, carrots, stuffing, gravy, cranberries, dinner rolls and a pumpkin pie.

So what’s the cost of a more typical spread? The Globe set out to price a traditional, yet cost-conscious, dinner for six people at Loblaws, No Frills, Walmart and Real Canadian Superstore in midtown Toronto.

For this experiment, the goal was to get a sense of what it costs to put Thanksgiving dinner on the table for six, with a larger turkey, familiar sides and a couple of desserts, while testing whether shopping around to save is worth the extra effort.

These stores were selected based on proximity and price, with Loblaws, No Frills and Walmart being the closest options, and Real Canadian Superstore added as another major grocer expected to offer competitive deals. Other brands were considered, but were noticeably more expensive. (All shopping was completed by Oct. 5th. Prices May vary as Thanksgiving approaches and grocery stores adjust promotions and availability.)

The basket included a 16-pound (7-to-9 kilogram) turkey, potatoes, green beans, carrots, corn on the cob, stuffing, cranberry sauce, gravy, dinner rolls, butter, milk, onions, garlic, rosemary, thyme, an apple pie, a pumpkin pie, Cool Whip and vanilla ice cream.

Households making dishes from scratch, serving alcohol or planning a more elaborate spread could see different totals.

Adam Chapman, a certified financial planner at Yes Money in London, Ont., recommends making a grocery list and estimating the total before heading to the store, so shoppers have a sense of what they are about to spend and aren’t surprised at the checkout.

He says the goal isn’t to be overly frugal during a special occasion but to decide what is worth spending more on.

“Pick that one thing that really matters, splurge on that, and then if you’re trying to cut back, cut back on everything else that’s maybe a little bit less important to the experience.”

After comparing all four stores, No Frills had the cheapest one-stop cart at $105.20 before tax. The same basket came to $124.15 at Loblaws, $131.09 at Walmart and $133.93 at Real Canadian Superstore, a difference of $28.73 between the cheapest and most expensive options.

This gap ultimately came down to the cost of the bird.

A 7-to-9 kilogram frozen turkey cost $30 at No Frills and $32.05 at Loblaws. A similarly sized turkey was $53 at Real Canadian Superstore and $57 at Walmart.

Choosing the cheapest turkey alone could save as much as $27. Sides varied too, with a 10-pound bag of yellow potatoes costing $1.99 at No Frills, versus $5.94 at Walmart and $6 at both Loblaws and Real Canadian Superstore.

The Globe picked the cheapest version of each item across the four stores to build a “deal-hunter” basket and determine whether shopping around was actually worth it.

For items sold by weight, the same amount was compared at each store. For example, two pounds of green beans cost about $5.90 at Walmart, compared with $7.98 at No Frills. Walmart’s corn was also cheaper, with a four-pack of corn on the cob costing just 94 cents, compared with $5 at No Frills.

The final deal-hunter basket came to $92.60 before tax, $12.60 less than buying everything at No Frills, the cheapest one-stop shop.

Compared with Loblaws, the savings grew to $31.55. Compared with Walmart, they grew to $38.49 and more than $40 compared with Real Canadian Superstore. But getting the lowest bill comes with a trade-off: time.

“There’s a cost to effort,” Chapman said. “If that includes shopping all over the place, you’re almost kind of ruining your own experience of Thanksgiving because you’re so exhausted by the time you get to the meal.”

On a Sunday morning in midtown Toronto, hitting several stores added up to more than 40 minutes of driving before factoring in time for parking, shopping and lineups. There are also costs for gas, transit or Ubers to consider.

For anyone trying to keep holiday spending down, Chapman suggests hosting a potluck. The host can provide a main dish, while guests bring sides, desserts or drinks.

The best deal, he suggests, is not always the cheapest but the one that saves money without costing excess time or energy.

Are you a young Canadian with money on your mind? To set yourself up for success and steer clear of costly mistakes, listen to our award-winning Stress Test podcast .

stories.title: When AI causes harm, who’s responsible?
stories.summary: Host Maria Kestane is speaking with Takara Small, a technology journalist, about who's held to account for AI's mass destruction, and why top-down legislation isn't the end-all be-all for a solution.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
In today’s The Big Story podcast, when a person hacks a government website, it’s illegal. But when a rogue AI agent does it, it’s an incident that needs ‘further investigation’.

Canada has invested billions of dollars into AI infrastructure and education, and although safety is a top priority according to Ottawa, robust legislation and regulation to govern the software has not kept up with the momentum.

Host Maria Kestane is speaking with Takara Small, a technology journalist, about who’s held to account for AI’s mass destruction, and why top-down legislation isn’t the end-all be-all for a solution.

You can subscribe to The Big Story podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

stories.title: ‘We don’t want to do a rinse and repeat’: Where Tiff’s big-bet market goes from here
stories.summary: The challenge will be finding the identity of the market, how it’s useful to those who it should be useful to, market head Charles Tremblay says
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
Last month, organizers behind the inaugural edition of the Toronto International Film Festival ’s official market proclaimed that the event was a success across the board, with organizers hailing “strong attendance, sold-out sessions and marquee sales.”

Yet the numbers behind the market, which gathered buyers and sellers of film, television and interactive content for seven days of hopeful deal-making inside the Metro Toronto Convention Centre (Mtcc) – and which was made possible by $23-million in federal funding – tell a different story.

And that’s a story that Tiff’s market head Charles Tremblay wants to clarify. Sitting down with The Globe last week for a wide-ranging interview, Tremblay discussed the highs and lows of the organization’s biggest bet since the 2010 opening of its Lightbox headquarters.

What were the main takeaways you heard from attendees?

Will you allow me to shed light on a few things you said in your article the other week?

Yes, let’s start with those numbers. Tiff said the convention floor contained 238 exhibitors, but I could only count about 100.

The number of stands was around 100. But the reason why we get to 238 is that many of those stands are umbrella sites. Screen Australia might have had like 20 companies, Unifrance had about 10.

Last December, Tiff said it’d provide 650 market screening slots, but the release said just 196 were booked, suggesting a lack of appetite compared with inventory.

The 650 number included the combined press and market screenings that every festival title gets, but the total number got cut down to 450 around March. The reason for that is we had planned on building three theatres inside the Mtcc, and those plans were dropped because it was too heavy a lift for our first year, logistically and operationally. So that brought our inventory down. The actual number is 196 paid market screenings, and then 255 press and market screenings for a total around 450. That’s how we get to those numbers, but I get that it requires an explanation.

The other number was market delegates. You said there were 7,010 this year, a 40-per-cent increase compared with Tiff’s ‘informal, previous offering, which typically drew 5,000 people to the city.’ But materials published by Tiff last year noted 6,000 industry delegates at the 2025 festival, making the attendance jump this year just 16 per cent.

What I can say is that ever since I started, we’ve always worked with 5,000. Not to dismiss it, but the number that matters to me is 7,000. That’s a very solid number for the first year, and an increase regardless. From an operational point of view, we met our revenue target as far as badge sales go.

What was that revenue target?

I will have to get back to you on that. [Reached afterward, a Tiff representative said they were “not at liberty to share the revenue target data.”]

Are you confident you’ll get to the previously stated target of 12,000 delegates by 2030?

Hard to say – I think those were projections from way back. It’s conceivable. For me, the important thing for the market is to become what it needs to be for the industry. I know that sounds vague, but it feels like as long as it’s useful for the people who are interested and need it, then we’re good. It’s not growth for the sake of growth. The market could be a very good service to the industry even if it’s 10,000 or 9,500. It needs to be for the Canadian industry first, and then whatever the international industry needs it to be.

In terms of that service, what have you been hearing from Canadians, and the international side, ON what they need?

There are two components to market attendance. The core of it is sellers and buyers, who represent about a third of the delegates. The other part, the vast majority, are there for the programming. They attend the market to network, go to talks, etcetera. Those two contingents have quite different objectives. The availability of market screenings and the quality of the venues are of no concern to the vast majority of the people there for the programming. The people mostly there for the programming, the feedback is overwhelmingly positive. We doubled the number of sessions, 40 to 85. The number of speakers doubled. Attendance almost tripled from around 6,000 to 16,000.

Doesn’t that include a new partnership with the Access Canada media summit, which has been held parallel to the festival for years? And the programming side has already been running for more than 15 years as part of Tiff’s industry offering.

Yes, but it doubled roughly in one year, so that’s not nothing. And the quality was still there. We had capacity crowds of almost 1,200 at the John Bassett Theatre inside the Mtcc. We also wanted to find a way to make the market, which is a B2B thing, open to the public. So you could buy tickets to see the panels with Gary Oldman or Seth Rogen. The market doesn’t exist in a vacuum, so it needs to reflect the personality of what makes the festival so special. The challenge will be finding the identity of the market – how it’s useful to those who it should be useful to. We don’t want to do a rinse-and-repeat of this year.

There were technical issues, with hours-long lineups for badge pickup ...

I don’t want to sugar-coat it, the badge situation was unfortunate. It was a kind of a perfect storm of printers breaking down, software issues. In our defence, we worked through the night to resolve it, and we pivoted as many people as we could to the digital pass on the app.

In terms of being a place where business gets done, we only saw two sales of note: Universal paying US$10-million to acquire River , which was kind of a buy-back situation, and Sony securing key markets for The Surgeon , which we don’t have a number for. Do you have an update on how much other business was sparked from market activity?

I don’t. To be honest, sales agents don’t call us every time they make a sale. You have those big splashy deals that make it into the trade publications, and then smaller things. What I can say is that a lot of sales agents I talked to were surprisingly pleased by the number of good meetings that they had, the number of them and the quality. As for the volume of business, we’re sending out a survey in the next couple of days, and we’ll see how much they’re willing to share. As you know, the American Film Market is upcoming, so some of the discussions started here will maybe close in L.A.

In terms of business volume, is the plan still to subsidize travel and accommodation for about 200 international buyers for future editions of the market?

It’s very early days. I would think that if the budget permits in the second year, there would be invited buyers. Two hundred? I don’t think so, that’s a big chunk of money.

We’re talking a lot about the film side, but this was launched with the intention of being a content market, with a focus on TV and interactive projects, too. But we haven’t heard much about business on that side.

I would say it’s the first year and markets in general are geared toward films. In programming, we had a good chunk of TV projects. Is there room to grow that sector? I think so. I’m pleased with the immersive hub we had. But yes, I won’t deny the larger part was film. That’s bound to change over the years.

In terms of the Mtcc space that was available to the market for pavilions, did Tiff reach the number of bookings it was hoping to secure?

We had more space than we ended up selling, we had room available. We’ll look at how the space is laid out. It’s a big space.

But the plan is still to return to the Mtcc?

As of today, as far as I know, yes. I don’t want to be non-committal, but it’s just very early.

Do contracts need to be signed in terms of reserving that space less than a year out?

I would think, based on last year’s experience, that this is something that happens before Christmas.

A big reason that this market exists is because of federal money. What kind of return on investment was Ottawa looking for, and do you think that they found it in the inaugural edition?

I believe they did. It was in terms of quality and substance. There wasn’t a set target that they needed in terms of revenue. What they wanted was a content market that would deliver for the Canadian industry and bring the world here. We haven’t had an official review with them, but I’m fairly confident that they would be quite happy. I know Telefilm was thrilled with the activity they had at their stand. And the labs, the IP exchange, the project market, all these programs had majority Canadian participation.

If Ottawa doesn’t renew its investment, which expires in March, can the market be self-sustaining?

The earned revenue component is pretty substantial, but I don’t know of many similar markets that are completely without public funding. It can be successful with probably a lower share of investment. Without any? I think it would be difficult.

I’ve heard from those inside Tiff about tensions between the festival and the market teams, which might be a larger problem as the market inevitably grows.

For tensions, it’s a high-pressure environment, so people worked really hard. But overall, to the contrary, I feel good about how those two teams in a very short time came together and delivered the market.

What do the next 11 months look like in building next year’s edition?

It’s one foot in front of the other. I can’t decide that we’re going to do this or that, though, before we secure some amount of government funding. Now, we’re focused on the postmortem, making sure all the learnings are tracked and discussed. We have to determine the big priorities and vision for the upcoming year and then execute it.

Yet the numbers behind the market, which gathered buyers and sellers of film, television and interactive content for seven days of hopeful deal-making inside the Metro Toronto Convention Centre (Mtcc) – and which was made possible by $23-million in federal funding – tell a different story.

And that’s a story that Tiff’s market head Charles Tremblay wants to clarify. Sitting down with The Globe last week for a wide-ranging interview, Tremblay discussed the highs and lows of the organization’s biggest bet since the 2010 opening of its Lightbox headquarters.
What were the main takeaways you heard from attendees?
Will you allow me to shed light on a few things you said in your article the other week?
Yes, let’s start with those numbers. Tiff said the convention floor contained 238 exhibitors, but I could only count about 100.
The number of stands was around 100. But the reason why we get to 238 is that many of those stands are umbrella sites. Screen Australia might have had like 20 companies, Unifrance had about 10.
Last December, Tiff said it’d provide 650 market screening slots, but the release said just 196 were booked, suggesting a lack of appetite compared with inventory.

The 650 number included the combined press and market screenings that every festival title gets, but the total number got cut down to 450 around March. The reason for that is we had planned on building three theatres inside the Mtcc, and those plans were dropped because it was too heavy a lift for our first year, logistically and operationally. So that brought our inventory down. The actual number is 196 paid market screenings, and then 255 press and market screenings for a total around 450. That’s how we get to those numbers, but I get that it requires an explanation.

What was that revenue target?
I will have to get back to you on that. [Reached afterward, a Tiff representative said they were “not at liberty to share the revenue target data.”]
Are you confident you’ll get to the previously stated target of 12,000 delegates by 2030?

Hard to say – I think those were projections from way back. It’s conceivable. For me, the important thing for the market is to become what it needs to be for the industry. stories.title: Did Christine Frechette face a ‘glass cliff’? Expert points to broader political pattern
stories.summary: Research suggests women are more likely to lead political parties during times of crisis, while facing higher expectations and greater scrutiny than men.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Women who rise to the top of political parties are often doing so in circumstances where the odds of success are already stacked against them, according to a University of Calgary political scientist who studies gender and politics.

The phenomenon is often described as a “glass cliff” — a term borrowed from business research that refers to women being elevated to leadership positions when organizations or political parties are already in crisis. But Melanee Thomas says that concept can oversimplify what is happening.

In an interview with Global News Wednesday, Thomas said she prefers the term “gendered political opportunity structure,” arguing that women are not passive participants being set up to fail. Rather, she says they are political actors who recognize that opportunities to lead are often more available when parties are struggling.

Thomas said political leadership positions, particularly those in government, are among the most coveted jobs in politics. Yet when parties are thriving, leadership contests tend to attract a familiar profile of candidates, often men with traditional political resumes. Women, she said, face steeper barriers when competing in those circumstances.

Instead, opportunities frequently arise when parties are electorally vulnerable or attempting to recover from scandal, internal turmoil or voter dissatisfaction.

The discussion has resurfaced following the recent election loss and resignation of former Quebec premier Christine Fréchette, who became leader of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) party months before an election after the departure of longtime premier François Legault.

Support for the CAQ was at an all-time low and the party had been plagued by scandals and troubled projects, including the SAAQclic fiasco, a controversial bill to change doctors’ pay, the failed Northvolt project and more.

Thomas said any leader would have faced significant challenges trying to rebrand a party that had been defined for years by scandal and its previous premier.

But she said it would be wrong to ignore the role gender plays in determining who gets selected to lead parties during difficult periods, pointing to former Quebec premier Pauline Marois as an example.

Thomas said Marois had long-standing leadership ambitions and extensive cabinet experience, but only became leader of the Parti Québécois after the party had entered a period of crisis.

“Women want the power jobs in politics,” Thomas said. “I think they are strategic enough to read the room and know what their chances are going to be when things are really good, and know that their only chance might be when things aren’t great.”

She drew comparisons to former prime minister Kim Campbell, who became Progressive Conservative leader and prime minister shortly before the party suffered a historic defeat in the 1993 federal election.

“Was it Kim Campbell’s fault? No,” Thomas said. “But do people still blame her specifically for it? Not everyone, but some absolutely do.”

Research suggests women politicians often face different standards than their male counterparts, Thomas said. She cited experimental studies showing some voters continue to hold stereotypical views about women’s suitability for political office. Other studies have found female candidates are often required to demonstrate stronger qualifications than men to receive similar evaluations.

“Women candidates have to be significantly more credentialed,” she said. “They have to have way better CVs to be evaluated the same way as men.”

Even when women secure leadership roles in favourable political conditions, research suggests they can face greater pressure and are more likely to be pushed out sooner than male leaders, Thomas said.

Still, the political scientist argues that women should not avoid leadership opportunities simply because success is uncertain.

Politics is inherently competitive and most candidates, regardless of gender, do not win, she argued. Participation remains essential to a healthy democracy, she told Global News over the phone.

She added that young women and girls need to see examples of women bidding for roles, sometimes getting them and succeeding, but also failing, surviving that failure and continuing their careers. “(Women) have to be willing to participate and lose. That is a core feature of democracy.”

“Anybody who wants to do it should go for it.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Anybody who wants to do it should go for it."

Research has shown that as more women are elected, girls and women are more likely to see politics as a space where they belong, she said.

Instead of focusing solely on whether female leaders succeed or fail, the University of Calgary professor said the more important question is why women continue to be viewed differently than men when navigating the same political challenges.

“Many politicians do good things, and many do things people think are dumb. The fact that when women do those things it is seen as a reflection of women as a whole, while men are not seen as a reflection of all men, shows exactly why this pattern persists.”

On Monday, 57 women were elected to Quebec’s national assembly — about 45 per cent of the 127 seats — slightly down from the number elected in 2022.

stories.title: Hockey N.S. launches pilot program to teach young players about consent, hazing
stories.summary: The organization has teamed up with a local non-profit that provides services to survivors of sexual assault to create the program.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
The head of a provincial body that governs organized hockey in Nova Scotia is touting a new educational program that targets players after a series of hazing incidents and assaults have rocked the sport.

“There’s been several incidents in hockey over the years and it’s been an area of need,” said Michael Field, the executive director of Hockey Nova Scotia in an interview.

The organization has teamed up with a local non-profit that provides services to survivors of sexual assault to create the program. It aims to teach 13- and 14-year-old players about how to engage in healthy team bonding exercises and how to avoid crossing the line.

“We feel there’s a need to educate players on team culture,” Field said. “Some teams do a great job at it and some team sports don’t. We just want to do all we can to ensure that … team culture is being built in a healthy manner.”

Field said more than 2,000 minor hockey players of all genders will participate in the mandatory program.

It emerged as families and coaches reacted to news reports last February about a hazing incident and sexual assault involving a junior hockey team in Nova Scotia.

A number of them sent emails expressing their concerns about the issue to Avalon, the non-profit that is now working with the hockey association, explained Kailee Wakeman, the director of operations at the centre.

Two under-15 minor hockey players in Colchester County, northeast of Halifax, were charged with sexual assault following the incident during a team sleepover last fall.

One of the accused players changed his plea to guilty last month, while the other pleaded not guilty in May.

Wakeman said Avalon hosted a webinar in February to teach parents and coaches how to discuss consent and hazing with young players.

Field said his association then reached out to Avalon to see if it could develop a version of the webinar for players.

Wakeman said the new program aims to teach players how to recognize discrimination, harassment, pressure, hazing and coercion.

“We’re hoping … that we can help change team cultures because sports cultures can often include hazing in ways that people think it strengthens a team and there’s so much research that shows that it doesn’t,” Wakeman said in an interview Wednesday.

The players will participate in two sessions, said Wakeman. The first will teach them about bodily autonomy, respecting boundaries and consent, while the second will teach them how to respond to situations that May cause harm to their teammates.

“So many people call that bystander intervention, but we’re going to frame it through the lens of a caring team environment,” she said. “Looking out for one another rather than placing each other in harmful situations.”

Wakeman said educating the under-15 age group is an important place to start when trying to change behaviours that can lead to a toxic culture.

“We are hoping to reach athletes young enough that … we can start to change the narrative early,” she said.

Dee Dooley, an education adviser with Dalhousie University’s sexual violence prevention program, is helping to facilitate the pilot program along with varsity hockey players in the province.

Dooley, who has also researched sexual violence prevention among varsity student-athletes, said culture in sport is often passed down between generations.

“The importance of peer influence and peer leadership can’t be overstated,” she said. “Culture is really created by the people within it.”

Hazing and sexual violence have plagued hockey in Canada for decades.

In 2023, a Quebec Major Junior Hockey League player filed an application for a class-action lawsuit against the league alleging he was abused during hazing rituals in the 1990s.

The year prior, Hockey Canada came under fire after it was revealed that an undisclosed settlement had been paid to a woman who alleged she was sexually assaulted by members of Canada’s 2018 World Junior hockey team. Five players were charged with sexual assault in 2024 related to the incident and were acquitted of all charges last year.

Jaqueline Moore, a research assistant with the project and a former varsity athlete, said while educating players is an important part of changing hockey’s culture, everyone needs to play a role.

“We also need coaches involved, we need administration involved, we need parents involved,” she said. “It’s really going to take a community.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: A border town on the front lines of the trade war
stories.summary: Sault Ste. Marie’s economic core is a steel plant, which has faced steep tariffs from the U.S.
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland, Patrick White
stories.content:
Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., is on the front lines of Canada’s trade war with the U.S.. The city lies just a few kilometres away from the U.S., across a river from a city with the same name in Michigan. Its core economic industry is steel, which has been hit with U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs.

The Globe and Mail’s staff reporter, Patrick White , recently went to ‘The Soo’ to see how the residents are faring after layoff notices and previous years of economic hardship.

Questions? Comments? Ideas? E-mail us at thedecibel@globeandmail.com
