stories.title: Ontario cancer patient who was denied coverage for U.S. treatment dismayed by province’s revised rules
stories.summary: Alex Shved had previously challenged the province’s decision to deny him coverage that would allow him to access tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy
stories.author: Alanna Smith, Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
An Ontario father of two with Stage 4 melanoma says he is heartbroken that the provincial government’s revised rules for out-of-country medical coverage will continue to bar access to a treatment that could save his and others’ lives.

Previously, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in September quashed the province’s decision to refuse to cover that treatment for 37-year-old Alex Shved.

On Tuesday, the provincial government announced amendments to its health insurance legislation to clarify when it will cover treatments abroad. Under the revised rules, Mr. Shved’s treatment will still not qualify.

The province said funding will only be available under certain conditions, including that the drug and its administration are already funded in Ontario, the treatment is performed in Ontario, access is temporarily unavailable, and travelling is necessary to avoid death or medically significant, irreversible tissue damage.

On Wednesday, Mr. Shved said it is “incredibly disappointing” that Ontario has taken this path, rather than helping residents like himself access vital treatments in a timely manner.

“I hoped this court battle would move things in the right direction. I didn’t realize how easily they could change the rules so that the result is still the same,” he said, expressing frustration with Premier Doug Ford and Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“Over all, I am very disappointed with the end result.”

In a statement, Ontario said it needed to clarify its out-of-country drug funding policy, in place since 2011, because it could expose the province to financial risk.

Failing to update the regulation could cost Ontario’s drug plan $5.2-billion yearly and “create a back door for global pharmaceutical companies to avoid negotiating directly with the province to achieve more competitive pricing,” it said.

In response to the September court decision, the government said it is “exploring all available options,” including an appeal or seeking a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with Mr. Shved.

The Etobicoke father is desperate to access tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte, or TIL, therapy, which is a treatment for metastatic melanoma that uses the cells of one of his own tumours.

Mr. Shved applied to Ontario’s out-of-country program to see whether the province would pay for him to be treated in the United States.

His application was rejected and he was told the program isn’t intended to be used as an interim funding route for drugs that could eventually qualify for public coverage.

In August, 2025, Health Canada approved a commercial version of TIL therapy called lifileucel. A single treatment of lifileucel costs US$515,000, not including the cost of a stay at a U.S. hospital. It is not available in Canada outside of clinical trials because it is still being reviewed for public funding.

Ms. Jones said in a statement that the regulatory change strikes a balance between protecting Ontario taxpayers and providing access to life-saving medications.

She said the change “supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions” and “protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process.”

Decisions about coverage will continue through the established application process.

In the Ontario Superior Court of Justice ruling, justices Jean‑Marc Labrosse and Sharon Shore said the province’s reasons for denying funding to Mr. Shved were unreasonable and inadequately explained, adding that he will “likely be dead by Christmas” without the requested treatment.

They sent the matter back to the executive officer of the Ontario Public Drug Programs and requested a new decision with an expedited timeline.

A third judge, David Corbett, concurred that the decision should be nullified but disagreed on the approach supported by his colleagues. He wrote that he would have directed the executive officer to recommend treatment and would have instructed the general manager of the Ontario Health Insurance Plan to expedite a funding decision.

stories.title: Alberta, Saskatchewan premiers shut down Elon Musk’s call for separation
stories.summary: The trillionaire tech businessman said on his social media platform X that Quebec would benefit from independence, as would the two Prairie provinces.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan are shutting down a suggestion from U.S. tech titan Elon Musk that the two provinces should split from Canada.

The trillionaire tech businessman and former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump said on his social media platform X that Quebec would benefit from independence, as would the two Prairie provinces.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe had a concise response to Musk on social media: “No.”

Moe has said he’s a true Canadian but wouldn’t halt a public vote on separation in Saskatchewan if residents petitioned for a plebiscite.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who states she’s voting to stay in Canada in an upcoming provincial referendum, says she also strongly disagrees with Musk’s opinion.

On Oct. 19, Albertans go to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.

While born in South Africa, Musk holds Canadian citizenship and has lived in several parts of the country.

His mother was born and raised in Saskatchewan, where the tech titan spent time working on a family farm as a teenager.

He moved on to Vancouver before attending Queen’s University in Ontario, where he met his first wife .

stories.title: Arkells sell Tdsb hats to support school nutrition programs
stories.summary: Proceeds from sales will go to the Toronto Foundation for Student Success
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
Max Kerman, frontman of the Canadian rock band Arkells, likes vintage fashion and loves – really loves – public education.

His mom was a special education teacher in Toronto. Reflecting back on his high school years, he said his time at Harbord Collegiate Institute helped shape who he is today.

In his view, public school is one of the great democratic institutions deserving of much more boosterism. A few years ago, Mr. Kerman worked with the band’s merchandise designer to make a vintage-looking hat featuring the Toronto District School Board ’s logo of an apple.

He’s been wearing it periodically ever since. It starts a lot of conversations with people, many of whom don’t even know he’s in a band.

“They just see the hat and they want to talk about their school. They want to talk about their education,” Mr. Kerman said. “Teachers feel really seen by it, teachers really appreciate it, so I figured let’s make this for sale a little bit more widely.”

This week, with the board’s permission, the band began selling two versions of the hat online for preorder, for $40 each. There is a green rope hat, featuring a thin decorative cord stretched across the front, and a floppy grey version.

Proceeds from the sales will go to support the nutrition programs at Toronto Foundation for Student Success.

So far, the hats have received some high-profile endorsements from Canadian indie-rock luminaries. Jim Cuddy of Blue Rodeo has been seen sporting one. So, too, has former Barenaked Ladies member Steven Page.

Dan Levy, of Schitt’s Creek fame, has reached out to the band to say he’d love to get one.

Mr. Kerman, 39, said his first inspiration for the hat was his mother, who used to teach at Central Technical School in the Harbord Village area of Toronto, near where he attended high school.

Thanks to her, Mr. Kerman gained his appreciation for public education as a great equalizer.

“I’ve always thought about sort of the randomness of luck when it comes to a child’s upbringing, and how amazing a great public school system can be,” he said. “That no matter who your parents are, no matter what postal code you live in, or no matter what your parents’ job is, every kid can come through the same doors and get to share time with each other.”

The hat is a celebration of everyone working in public school, especially teachers, Mr. Kerman said.

Part of its appeal, is that unlike a Harvard sweatshirt or a Ferrari hat, the brand it’s repping – the idea of public school itself – is the antithesis of exclusivity.

“Given how much social isolation there is, given how much division the algorithmic social media channels offer us ... what is a place where we can all just see each other for the humans that we are?” he said. “That is a public school.”

The choice to support student nutrition programs came to Mr. Kerman by way of his niece and nephew, who attend high school in Toronto. They had told him about the healthy breakfast program at their school, accessible to all students.

“I thought, yeah, this is a good place because kids need to be well-fed if they’re going to have a good day at school,” he said.

The Toronto Foundation for Student Success supports nearly 1,000 school nutrition programs that provide 284,000 healthy meals to students every school day.

Across the country, nearly one-third of children under the age of 18 – 2.4 million kids – live in food insecure households, according to Statistics Canada data.

The hats are not just a celebration of public school in support of a good cause – they’re also a reminder of the responsibility to care for everyone that public education is founded on, Mr. Kerman said.

“We need to look out for each other. So sure, there are some schools that are in more well-to-do neighbourhoods, but we’re going to use our resources to support schools that don’t have as much, or whose parents are working three jobs and don’t have disposable income to be supporting school fundraisers,” he said.

“That needs to be our duty, right? We need to be in service of each other all the time.”

stories.title: Trial hears of two mysterious phone calls the day $22M in gold and cash stolen from Toronto Pearson airport
stories.summary: The specific impact of those calls on the gold heist was left hanging by court by the end of the third day in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Shortly before a large shipping crate of gold bars and cash worth more than $22 million was stolen from Toronto’s Pearson airport, a worker inside the Air Canada cargo warehouse where it was stored received two mysterious phone calls.

They seem mysterious now, when revealed in court and knowing what was about to happen — the largest gold heist in Canadian history — at the time, though, it all seemed normal, the employee testified. Court heard on Wednesday from several staff who moved the crate stuffed with gold and cash — seemingly unknowingly — around the large facility without anything seeming suspicious.

It was business as usual, cargo workers said.

So much so that nobody realized the crate of gold and cash had been stolen until hours later when the real customer — armed Brink’s guards in an armoured truck — arrived to collect it, and no one could find it for them.

“It was just a regular day, doing the duties, like day to day, whatever was required of me,” said Vatsal Vaid, who helped run the computer end of facility’s automated sorting and moving machinery.

Vaid was one of several workers at the warehouse testifying on the third day of the trial for Parmpal Sidhu, one of those accused of pulling off the notorious Pearson airport gold heist on April 17, 2023.

At the time of the heist, Vaid, 27, was working inside Air Canada’s cargo warehouse for Katlyn International, a third-party contractor to the airline that provided the automation equipment to manage the movement of freight through the facility at Canada’s busiest airport.

The system allows cargo to move around the warehouse on a device not unlike an enormous baggage carousel for passengers at the airport terminal.

Vaid was a controls technologist working in the Hub Operations Control Centre, known as Hocc, which is the control centre for incoming and outgoing cargo. He sat in an office with Air Canada cargo managers providing system assistance and solving problems that came up to ensure containers kept moving to where he was told they should go.

“They would reach out me if there’s any technical problem, otherwise, everything worked automatically most of the times,” Vaid said.

'Curious' Air Canada IT worker tried to think like a crook to trace how airport gold heist was pulled off

India's search for missing loot from Toronto airport gold heist prevents alleged inside man from returning to Canada for trial

The system was automated to take cargo that is specially tagged to the appropriate pit, a staging area for containers where they are unpacked into their component packages, if that’s what the codes told the workers to do, and moved into a storage space until picked up by a client.

Cargo that must be kept cold, such as food, flowers or pharmaceuticals, goes to one place, called the cool-chain; cargo marked high-value goes to a secure area; those marked priority go to a pit where they are dealt with first by warehouse workers. Containers that aren’t specially coded wait their turn and are distributed randomly to one of five pit areas, court heard.

Vaid testified that after he learned of the gold heist, he thought back to the day before. Police investigators asked him to tell them what he remembered, he said.

He said he got a phone call from inside the building, from a container processing area called Pit 5, sometime after 6 p.m. It seemed a routine call.

The caller said a shipment was going into the system in about half an hour — there “were a couple units ahead of it,” he recalled him saying. The caller said something like “this is a high value cargo going into the system. Tell the managers working at the desk.”

About half an hour later, he received a second phone call, Vaid said. This one appeared to come from the cargo manager’s office phone saying that an import manager required a unit to go down to Pit 1 and told him to generate the appropriate command in the conveyer system, “because the customer is here to pick that unit up, and it’s a priority unit.”

Vaid told court he didn’t know who was on the phone. It was a male voice, he said.

The caller, he said, “knew what they were doing, or they had an idea of the system and everything, like how to approach or do some certain stuff within the system, so I was just following the orders in my job.”

The specific impact of those phone calls on the gold heist was left hanging by court by the end of the day. It was not even said whether the phone calls were legitimate or nefarious, but Vaid said he wanted police to know about them.

John Iheme, who worked as a station attendant within the cool-chain, testified about his unfortunate position of unknowingly delivering the crate of gold to the driver of the heist crew and even helped him load it onto the truck that hauled it away, never to be seen again.

He didn’t know of his role until he was called in to speak with Peel Regional Police investigators.

“When I was called to the police station to go give a statement, I was shown a video and that’s when I realized that I had served the driver that came in to pick up the shipment,” he told court.

“If someone needs help, I just step up and help… the gentleman came to the back and needed help, so, I just got up and went and helped,” he said of the man who came to collect the shipping crate.

Court watched video of Iheme, wearing a bright orange safety vest and a ball cap, striding through the loading bay to a man standing beside the open back of a truck that had backed into one of the loading docks.

In the video, he greets the driver with a fist bump. The driver’s face is covered.

“I can’t even remember dealing with the gentleman to be honest, but on the video, I can see myself serving him.”

Police were interested in the fist bump. It could suggest familiarity. Iheme said he was just being friendly. “I do it with everyone,” he said. “I’ve never seen them before.”

He was asked about the driver’s mask.

“I don’t know why he would be masked up,” he said. “It’s not my job to check what people wear and how they’re dressed. I serve you and I move on. He could be sick. I don’’t know.”

He said there was nothing peculiar about the delivery. He took the air waybill from the driver, which is a receipt for picking up a shipment, and looked at it “to make sure it’s got the stamps that you need,” he said. “There was no stamps missing.”

He then went back to find the container; it wasn’t hard, it was already in the cool-chain area.

“I didn’t have to go and get it out, it was already there and I picked it up,” he said. Video shows him navigating a forklift to raise the hefty crate. He said he didn’t know what was inside — staff aren’t to open containers unless they’re told to.

He drove the forklift back to the loading bay, helped the driver load it into the truck and said goodbye.

Court heard previously that somebody had used Air Canada’s internal computer systems and login credentials for various Air Canada employees to change the routing tags in the systems that tracked and automated cargo handling while the crate was in the air from Zurich, Switzerland.

The tag that it was high-value cargo was deleted, which prevented the automated machines from directing it to the secure storage area, which is locked and guarded. Court heard that the digital hygiene at the facility was dreadful and workers routinely shared logins and passwords and workstations were left logged for weeks, month, or years.
paragraphs: Shortly before a large shipping crate of gold bars and cash worth more than $22 million was stolen from Toronto’s Pearson airport, a worker inside the Air Canada cargo warehouse where it was stored received two mysterious phone calls.

They seem mysterious now, when revealed in court and knowing what was about to happen — the largest gold heist in Canadian history — at the time, though, it all seemed normal, the employee testified. Court heard on Wednesday from several staff who moved the crate stuffed with gold and cash — seemingly unknowingly — around the large facility without anything seeming suspicious.
It was business as usual, cargo workers said.

So much so that nobody realized the crate of gold and cash had been stolen until hours later when the real customer — armed Brink’s guards in an armoured truck — arrived to collect it, and no one could find it for them.
“It was just a regular day, doing the duties, like day to day, whatever was required of me,” said Vatsal Vaid, who helped run the computer end of facility’s automated sorting and moving machinery.

Vaid was one of several workers at the warehouse testifying on the third day of the trial for Parmpal Sidhu, one of those accused of pulling off the notorious Pearson airport gold heist on April 17, 2023.

At the time of the heist, Vaid, 27, was working inside Air Canada’s cargo warehouse for Katlyn International, a third-party contractor to the airline that provided the automation equipment to manage the movement of freight through the facility at Canada’s busiest airport.
The system allows cargo to move around the warehouse on a device not unlike an enormous baggage carousel for passengers at the airport terminal.

Vaid was a controls technologist working in the Hub Operations Control Centre, known as Hocc, which is the control centre for incoming and outgoing cargo. He sat in an office with Air Canada cargo managers providing system assistance and solving problems that came up to ensure containers kept moving to where he was told they should go.
“They would reach out me if there’s any technical problem, otherwise, everything worked automatically most of the times,” Vaid said.

Cargo that must be kept cold, such as food, flowers or pharmaceuticals, goes to one place, called the cool-chain; cargo marked high-value goes to a secure area; those marked priority go to a pit where they are dealt with first by warehouse workers. Containers that aren’t specially coded wait their turn and are distributed randomly to one of five pit areas, court heard.
Vaid testified that after he learned of the gold heist, he thought back to the day before. Police investigators asked him to tell them what he remembered, he said.
He said he got a phone call from inside the building, from a container processing area called Pit 5, sometime after 6 p.m. It seemed a routine call.

The caller said a shipment was going into the system in about half an hour — there “were a couple units ahead of it,” he recalled him saying. The caller said something like “this is a high value cargo going into the system. Tell the managers working at the desk.”

About half an hour later, he received a second phone call, Vaid said. This one appeared to come from the cargo manager’s office phone saying that an import manager required a unit to go down to Pit 1 and told him to generate the appropriate command in the conveyer system, “because the customer is here to pick that unit up, and it’s a priority unit.”
Vaid told court he didn’t know who was on the phone. It was a male voice, he said.

The caller, he said, “knew what they were doing, or they had an idea of the system and everything, like how to approach or do some certain stuff within the system, so I was just following the orders in my job.”

The specific impact of those phone calls on the gold heist was left hanging by court by the end of the day. It was not even said whether the phone calls were legitimate or nefarious, but Vaid said he wanted police to know about them.

stories.title: Premier Smith brushes off Ndp’s Alberta voter list court battle, says legislation coming
stories.summary: Prior to new rules released last month, Elections Alberta was allowed to provide political parties lists with full names, addresses, phone numbers and unique voter I.D. numbers.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith on Wednesday brushed off a court battle launched by the Opposition NDP over her government’s changes to Elections Alberta voter list rules.

Smith told reporters in Edmonton that the new restrictions were called for by elections officials earlier this year after a major data breach involving a separatist group and the pro-Independence Republican Party of Alberta.

“That’s what we’ve done,” Smith said at an unrelated news conference.

“We have said that no one is going to get access to detailed private information of Albertans until we have a chance to legislate some guardrails around this in the fall.

“That includes the Republican Party. That includes the NDP. And it includes our party as well.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That includes the Republican Party. That includes the NDP. And it includes our party as well."

The new voter list rules, published last month, say that Elections Alberta can now only provide political parties with the number of voters in each voting area and municipality.

Prior to that, it could offer lists with full names, addresses, phone numbers and unique voter identification numbers.

The government has said the rules are temporary. The regulation is set to expire at the end of the year.

Smith said Wednesday that the NDP had also asked for the changes, but the Opposition said that’s not the case.

NDP house leader Christina Gray said they wanted to see consequences for those involved in the data breach. She criticized the government for not acting sooner and said the new policy risks the integrity of the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum, which features a question on Alberta’s place in Canada.

“If she was interested in protecting Albertans, there should have been consequences months ago, but she chose to protect her separatist friends,” Gray said in a statement.

“Her decision to temporarily restrict access to the voter list during the referendum period weakens election oversight and undermines confidence in the integrity of our democratic institutions.”

The NDP is challenging the new voter list rules in court.

A lawyer for the party argued in a hearing Tuesday that the government acted beyond its power by changing the voter list rules through regulation rather than legislation, and that the new policy undermines provincial law.

Mandy England, a government lawyer, rejected that argument. She told court the province was within its rights to change the rules the way it did and argued that the Ndp’s challenge amounted to a policy disagreement.

She also disputed NDP concerns about how the new rules will limit the ability of party scrutineers to properly observe the ballot count for the referendum.

A decision on the challenge is expected soon.

Smith also said Wednesday that she hoped the NDP would support government legislation coming this fall to introduce new safeguards on voter information.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Changes made to Alberta registered voter list'

content_blocks.text: The government has said the rules are temporary. The regulation is set to expire at the end of the year.
Smith said Wednesday that the NDP had also asked for the changes, but the Opposition said that’s not the case.

NDP house leader Christina Gray said they wanted to see consequences for those involved in the data breach. She criticized the government for not acting sooner and said the new policy risks the integrity of the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum, which features a question on Alberta’s place in Canada.
“If she was interested in protecting Albertans, there should have been consequences months ago, but she chose to protect her separatist friends,” Gray said in a statement.
“Her decision to temporarily restrict access to the voter list during the referendum period weakens election oversight and undermines confidence in the integrity of our democratic institutions.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Separatist leader behind voter list leak ‘not cooperating’: Elections Alberta'

content_blocks.text: The NDP is challenging the new voter list rules in court.

A lawyer for the party argued in a hearing Tuesday that the government acted beyond its power by changing the voter list rules through regulation rather than legislation, and that the new policy undermines provincial law.

Mandy England, a government lawyer, rejected that argument. She told court the province was within its rights to change the rules the way it did and argued that the Ndp’s challenge amounted to a policy disagreement.
She also disputed NDP concerns about how the new rules will limit the ability of party scrutineers to properly observe the ballot count for the referendum.
A decision on the challenge is expected soon.
Smith also said Wednesday that she hoped the NDP would support government legislation coming this fall to introduce new safeguards on voter information.

stories.title: After an alarming rise in battery fires, one fire service takes safety message to the big screen
stories.summary: After an alarming increase of lithium-ion battery fires across the country, one fire service is taking its safety message to the big screen.
stories.author: Katie Griffin
stories.content:
After an alarming increase of lithium-ion battery fires across the country, one fire service is taking its safety message to the big screen.

“These real stories have proven to work on social media so the next step was bringing it to a new platform that is powerful, which is Landmark’s platform,” said Nick DeFazio, public information officer with OFS.

“You have people who have their phones in their pockets before a movie, they’re not distracted, they can’t swipe away from your message and the message is being projected on a massive screen.”

The ad features an Ottawa family who lost their home in March after a blaze sparked by a lithium-ion battery in a power bank that was charging a phone in a bed.

The batteries are in everything from cellphones and power tools to laptops and e-bikes.

“We’re still faced with a lot of aftermarket batteries… people buy batteries that are not approved or certified,” said Ottawa Fire Chief Paul Hutt. “When they do go into thermal runaway, where they overheat and that chemical reaction occurs, it’s very violent.”

So far this year, Toronto has had 108 lithium-ion battery fires, already surpassing last year’s total with three months to go.

“This is the fastest-growing public fire safety risk in Canada’s largest city,” said Toronto Fire Chief Jim Jessop. “We really need the federal government to expedite their process and the Office of the Fire Marshal to expedite their process and introduce regulations that will at least reduce the probability and the consequence of these fires.”

It’s an issue fire services are grappling with across the country.

A national strategy has been something the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs (Cafc) has been calling for. It would mean changes to the National Fire Code and the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act.

“That’s everything from a societal means of operating, charging, purchasing, discarding, recycling, all of those pieces are really critical,” said Cafc president Paul Boissonneault.

“And then we’re also looking at code changes such as heat alarms in residential garages or in garages of multi-residential units because obviously these garage areas are where tools and batteries are often left charging and there can be differentiation of heat and/or extreme cold temperatures, which causes strain on charging systems.”

The battery fires are unpredictable and more challenging for firefighters to put out. The Cafc also highlighted issues around lack of formalized training and specialized equipment.

“Fire prevention really has to be our first line of defence,” Hutt said. “And it’s that proactiveness of how we can communicate to the public to make the public safe and to keep our firefighters safe on a daily basis as well.”

Right now there are no specific regulatory requirements for lithium-ion batteries in Canada.

The next update to the National Fire Code won’t be until 2030, but individual provinces can make changes to their own codes sooner.

In Ontario, the Office of the Fire Marshal (OFM) said it is considering enhancements.

“As we examine potential regulatory and Ontario Fire Code changes, our goal is to strike the right balance between supporting the safe use of these technologies and ensuring the protection of the public and first responders from emerging fire risks,” the OFM wrote in a statement.

Health Canada says it received “broad support for the introduction of mandatory safety requirements,” when it sought public input earlier this year, adding “international harmonization, costs to industry, and transition timelines were other key considerations raised by respondents.”

Health Minister Marjorie Michel offered no specifics or a timeline when asked about potential regulations this week.

“We are doing consultation now at Health Canada and we are working closely with Minister MacKinnon at Transport Canada. We will keep you informed,” Michel said.

Fire officials say to:

Only use a charger approved for your device

Charge on a hard, flat surface

Never charge on a bed, couch or under a pillow

Stop using the device if it feels hot, smells or swells

Unplug once fully charged

DeFazio said the hope is to expand the ad to theatres across the province and the country with the goal of changing behaviour, preventing fires, injuries and saving lives.

stories.title: Alleged racist assault sparks outrage in Kincardine
stories.summary: Two 14-year-old boys, were allegedly spat on, kicked, punched, assaulted, and called racial slurs including the N-word, by a group of fellow students, because of the colour of their skin.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Kincardine’s downtown is bustling on a beautiful fall day. But, last week something ugly allegedly happened in Kincardine’s core.

Two 14-year-old boys, were allegedly spat on, kicked, punched, assaulted, and called racial slurs including the N-word, by a group of fellow students, because of the colour of their skin.

Andrea Clarke is a Kincardine based lawyer, representing the boy’s who were allegedly assaulted. She sent out a news release about this incident late last week.

“One of the things I’ve heard recently out there was, by saying this out loud, it makes our town look like we’re racist. And that’s certainly not what I’m saying. But if we don’t call things out as they are, the behavior doesn’t change. You can love a place like I do with this municipality and still say it’s not perfect,” said Clarke.

Police are investigating the alleged assault, but no charges have been laid, as of yet.

While many students encouraged the altercation, allege the two boys, the assault was eventually ended by an adult bystander who called police and the school.

Clarke says the alleged race-based assault should be a wake-up call to all of Kincardine’s residents, that racism is unfortunately alive and well, in their community.

“Let’s rally together as adults within the community, whatever role we play in children’s lives. Let’s ensure that we’re a positive role model. Sometimes these instances allow us to almost hold a mirror and say, am I doing something that my kids are learning?” said Clarke, who was the former Deputy Mayor for the Municipality of Kincardine.

Both the Municipality of Kincardine and the principal of Kincardine District Senior School have responded to the alleged racist assault condemning the alleged actions.

“Building an inclusive community requires commitment, compassion, and the collective courage to speak up against hate and bullying. When one member of our community is targeted, it affects all of us,” said Ken Craig, mayor of the Municipality of Kincardine.

“These conversations are not always comfortable, but they are necessary. Students who experience discrimination of any kind need to know that the adults responsible for their safety see it, name it and take it seriously,” said Don Burns, principal of Kincardine District Senior School.

Clarke says the victim’s families are seeking a clear safety plan for their children to return to school. Clarke says those discussions are ongoing, but a broader community conversation is necessary.

As Kincardine has grown, it has become more diverse, but Clarke questions if diversity has equaled belonging, for Kincardine’s racial minorities.

“It’s much greater than a single incident. Let’s come together as a community and have a conversation that’s probably long overdue. If we continue to shove it under the rug, whether that’s an inappropriate joke, whether that’s a dismissive comment that goes to dehumanizing an individual, we allow that type of conversation discourse to grow,” said Clarke.

stories.title: 1 in 3 food banks, shelters forced to turn away people due to demand: survey
stories.summary: The federal government says it is reviewing the survey and said it will be responsive as Canadians navigate uncertainty in food costs.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Even as more Canadians turn to them for help, food banks and shelters say they’re struggling to keep up with a new survey showing some are having to turn people away.

The State of Food Charity in Canada, produced by the National Network of Non-Profits and conducted by Ipsos, shows 89 per cent of non-profits across the Second Harvest network saw an increase in demand for food in the past year.

Yet 33 per cent said they have a waitlist for providing support, and 35 per cent had to turn people away either due to limited food available or lack of resources.

“The demand is so high for food right now that it breaks my heart and everybody when we have to say we have a waiting list,” said Vivian Etuka with Bethel Outreach Community Services in Etobicoke, Ont.

Second Harvest works with nearly 2,500 organizations across the country, including food banks and shelters, to help feed people. More than 1,600 responded to the survey.

Among those organizations that had a waitlist, the survey reports the average number of people was 878.

It was estimated that of those who turned people away, two in five had to refuse more than 50 people. According to Second Harvest, an average of 269 people were turned away.

“When we talk about people that come to food banks, these are your neighbours, your coworkers; we’re seeing nurses at the food bank,” said Etuka. “I’ve never seen more teachers.”

It’s not just working adults either.

Jamie Seabrook, a researcher and professor in epidemiology and biostatistics, said there’s a diversity of food bank clients, young and old, and working and not working.

“It (the survey) dispels the myth that those who use food banks are all unemployed,” Seabrook said. “People that are earning an income are not getting enough income to support the rising cost.”

According to Second Harvest, 49 per cent of the groups surveyed don’t access food or other supports through the federal, provincial or regional food bank network.

What the survey also showed was 36 per cent of the food that’s available at the organizations surveyed comes from Second Harvest and 91 per cent say the network helps them offer more food. Another 80 per cent say Second Harvest provides more healthy and nutritious food.

“Canada has enough food to come out of this situation, but too much good food is still going to waste while organizations supporting people are struggling to keep up with demand,” said Lori Nikkel, CEO of Second Harvest, in a statement.

Both Second Harvest and the organizations surveyed urged action as Canadians continue to struggle with food insecurity, saying affordable housing and matching social assistance to rising prices takes time.

By helping food banks now, those who rely on them will also get help, they said.

“When we put families, or when we see wait lists or we have to turn somebody around, hunger doesn’t go on a wait list; that parent is still hungry, that parent still has to provide for the family,” Etuka said.

The federal government says it is reviewing the survey and said it will be responsive as Canadians navigate uncertainty in food costs.

— with files from Global News Nathaniel Dove

stories.title: Premier Moe shuts down Elon Musk's encouragement for Saskatchewan separation: 'No'
stories.summary: Regina - U.S. tech titan Elon Musk says as Quebec's new Parti Québécois government foreshadows a vote to leave Canada, Saskatchewan and Alberta should cut ties with Confederation, too.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Regina - The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan are shutting down a suggestion from U.S. tech titan Elon Musk that the two provinces should split from Canada.

Musk, the trillionaire tech businessman and former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, says on his social media platform X that Quebec would benefit from independence, as would the two Prairie provinces.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe had a concise response to Musk on social media: “No.”

Moe has said he’s a true Canadian but wouldn’t halt a public vote on separation in Saskatchewan if residents petitioned for a plebiscite.

“It’s exceptionally important that all elections that are held in Canada and all votes are held are free and fair,” the prime minister said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who states she’s voting to stay in Canada in an upcoming provincial referendum, says she also strongly disagrees with Musk’s opinion.

On Oct. 19, Albertans go to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Full patch member of the Outlaws Motorcycle Club allowed to keep alcohol delivery licence in Ontario
stories.summary: “The registrar has not met its burden in establishing that the appellant’s conduct ... should disentitle him to a licence,” said the ruling.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A full patch member of the Outlaws Motorcycle Club (OMC) can keep his Trenton, Ont., liquor delivery service licence, despite three recent run-ins with police.

The registrar of Ontario’s Alcohol and Gaming Commission issued a notice of proposal in March revoking Adam Bridge’s liquor delivery service licence for Big Deal Delivery because he “is a full patch member of the OMC,” according to a recent decision from the Ontario Licence Appeal Tribunal.

“The registrar argues that the appellant’s membership, influence and participation in the OMC constitutes reasonable grounds for belief that he will not carry on business in accordance with law and with integrity and honesty.”

The registrar argued that Bridge’s “affiliation with the OMC, which it considers to be a criminal organization and whose members are required to uphold a code of non-cooperation with police and law enforcement, is incompatible with holding a licence in Ontario’s regulated liquor industry, and three recent interactions the appellant had with police further demonstrates his disentitlement to a licence.”

The registrar argued unsuccessfully “that revocation is the only appropriate remedy under the circumstances.”

That didn’t fly with tribunal member Bruce Stanton, who directed the registrar not to carry out the proposal.

“The registrar has not met its burden in establishing that the appellant’s conduct, in the form of his full patch membership in the OMC and the three interactions with police should disentitle him to a licence,” Stanton wrote in a Sept. 22 decision.

Bridge told the tribunal that “licensing should be based on actual conduct, not assumptions based on association,” said the decision.

Outlaws Motorcycle club flexing its muscles and opening new club house in London, Ontario

“He argues that his activities as a licensee are unimpeachable and he has always acted in accordance with the law and with integrity and honesty.”

Bridge told the tribunal “that he provides lawful regulated services to customers including pharmacies, restaurants and other regulated premises,” said the decision.

“He submits that he has never wavered in upholding the obligations of his licence including never selling alcohol illegally or acting dishonestly, and his customers rely on him and are confident in his services.”

Bridge pointed out that his three recent interactions with police did not result in any charges “and did not implicate him in any unlawful activity.”

The tribunal heard Bridge was at a restaurant in Picton, Ont., ON Sept. 2, 2024, when police were called.

“The owner of a restaurant there called police because they thought ‘a couple of bikers are getting into it’ and ‘it looks like it will be physical,’” said the decision.

Police responded to the scene and separated the club members to “figure things out,” in this case two Red Devils and Bridge, who was then a probationary member of the OMC, accompanied by a friend.

OPP Det. Laura Empey, a biker expert, testified “that the situation was ‘not good’ because Picton is an area controlled by Hells Angels. She testified that the Red Devils are a support club of the Hells Angels.”

Bridge, who was wearing his OMC colours, and his friend “were initially obstructing police and refusing to identify themselves while video recording the officers,” said the decision.

Bridge told the tribunal he didn’t identify himself to police because the law does not require him to do so.”

Empey “described the incident as a provocation because the OMC members were in an area known to be controlled by the Hells Angels and Red Devils,” said the decision.

Bridge testified that “he was just having lunch with a friend when two Red Devils approached and started yelling at him. He stated that the situation had calmed down by the time the police arrived. He submits that no charges were laid, there was no altercation and he was simply standing up for his rights.”

On Sept. 4, 2024, police were called to the Trenton Downtown Business Improvement Agency after its executive director, who had previously complained about Big Deal Delivery overcharging her son for a food order, dialled 911 when Bridge showed up in her office.

Bridge testified that he was there “to clear up the misunderstanding and ‘things did not go well.’”

Bridge returned to the same office later that day “and proceeded to video-record elements of the interior,” said the decision, noting that prompted the executive director to dial 911 again.

When police arrived, Bridge told them “that he was uploading video to YouTube, he would not identify himself and that he would not answer any questions of police.”

Police had to use Bridge’s licence plate to identify him.

Bridge “said he posed no threat” to the executive director, who “refused to speak with him and told him to leave.”

Then on Feb. 27, 2026, police pulled Bridge over in Quinte West after he turned onto a side street to avoid a police checkpoint looking for impaired drivers.

When a cop asked Bridge why he avoided the checkpoint, “he said he did not feel like stopping to talk to them,” said the decision, which notes his breath sample showed he had not been drinking and no charges were laid.

Stanton found Bridge’s three police encounters demonstrated he was “following the Omc’s unwritten rule requiring that he avoid talking to law enforcement officers,” said the decision.

“Each of the encounters were resolved peacefully and seemingly without violence or risk to public safety. Accordingly, I find there is insufficient compelling and credible information to find that the appellant’s conduct in these three interactions reaches the level of reasonable grounds for belief that he will not carry on business in accordance with the law and with integrity and honesty.”

stories.title: Lawyer seeks order forcing Quebec legislature members to swear oath to the King
stories.summary: Lawyers are seeking an emergency order from Quebec Superior Court that would require newly elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Lawyers are asking Quebec Superior Court to grant an emergency order that would force the new crop of elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.

Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group are asking the court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional.

The Quebec legislature adopted the law after Parti Québécois members were temporarily barred from taking their seats after they refused to swear allegiance to King Charles.

David argues that politicians who don’t swear the oath won’t be constitutionally entitled to sit in the legislature, and the laws they pass will have no legal effect.

David has already filed a challenge against the law, and believes its application should be suspended to make incoming legislature members take the oath until the case is heard on its merits.

The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Monday’s election, and leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already said he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to the King.

The PQ leader also said he’s seeking legal advice on how to further cut ties with the monarchy, including stripping the lieutenant-governor of her roles and funding.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he told reporters Tuesday. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”

Bill 4, adopted in 2022, amended a section of the 1867 Constitution Act to exempt Quebec from the section that requires the oath.

David argues that the law infringes on Quebecers’ right to vote and right to effective representation, because they’ll be represented by politicians “who are not constitutionally qualified to hold office and whose votes on legislation and other activities in the National Assembly are constitutionally void,” the stay application reads.

He believes the constitutional amendment included in the law requires the consent of the federal government and all Canadian provinces.

David said the hearing date for his stay request hasn’t yet been set, but he will ask for a decision to be delivered before the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

David is also prepared to file more legal challenges if the Parti Québécois follows up on its plans to break from the monarchy, “including any attempt to unilaterally abolish the office of lieutenant governor,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto mayoral race narrows to Chow-Bradford showdown
stories.summary: A head-to-head battle between the two has been brewing for weeks, as no other clear front-runners have managed to break through to voters, according to recent polling.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford now appear to be locked into a heated, two-person matchup in Toronto’s mayoral race, after Chris Alexander dropped out mere hours before he was set to join them in a major candidate debate.

A head-to-head battle between the two has been brewing for weeks, as no other clear front-runners have managed to break through to voters, according to recent polling.

Alexander leaving the campaign trail “gives a bit more of a clear distinction to voters and changes some of the dynamics between Bradford and Chow,” said Zachary Spicer, an associate professor in the school of public policy and administration at York University.

Alexander announced the revocation of his candidacy the morning of Oct 6. The debate held that evening at Toronto Metropolitan University resulted in an unexpected face-off between only Bradford and Chow that saw the two be more pointed in their criticisms of each other. Those changes could indicate a possible reshaping of the campaign period in the final weeks before election day, according to political analysts.

Low polling made it difficult to see a path to victory, which resulted in the decision to exit the campaign, Alexander told reporters Tuesday.

“Our path to success, it became clear to me over this weekend, was not obvious and perhaps not there at all,” he told reporters.

Alexander conceded that polls indicate support for him has remained static since the onset of the campaign and he wanted to step back before advanced voting got underway.

Myer Siemiatycki, a professor emeritus of politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University, said Alexander “just could not get the traction he needed to be a serious contender.”

A Liaison Strategies poll published Tuesday, prior to Alexander dropping out, had placed him at nine per cent support, while Chow reached 48 per cent and Bradford at 40 per cent.

Alexander is best known for being a key member of then-Prime Minister Stephen Harper’s cabinet as the federal immigration minister from 2013 to 2015. Yet Alexander’s policy proposals during the campaign period seemed somewhat closer on the political spectrum to Chow, who was previously a long-time NDP MP. He proposed increasing arts funding to $62 million over ten years— higher than Chow’s proposal of $35 million.

On Tuesday night’s debate stage, the remaining candidates were questioned on how they would approach the housing crisis, increased affordability, transit and public safety.

Chow was noticeably more confrontational during the debate toward Bradford than in previous weeks, said Spicer.

When discussing transit and cycling, Chow accused Bradford of previously supporting fare increases and supporting Premier Doug Ford in his bid to rip out the city’s bike lanes. “How could anyone trust you?” she said.

Bradford replied that Chow was “fearmongering.”

With Bradford now positioning himself as the sole candidate who has a shot at challenging Chow, she will have to be more aggressive in the coming weeks if she wants to hang on to the mayorship, Spicer explained.

“Chow realizes the challenge without Chris Alexander it’s a little bit different…it’s now more of an evaluation of her first term,” he said. Bradford does not need to win on every policy point, but he does needs to make the case the city is heading in the “wrong direction,” to win, which isn’t difficult to hammer home for some groups, said Spicer.

In turn, Chow needs to depict Bradford as a risk for the city while highlighting her accomplishments, he said.

However, there is uncertainty about which candidate Alexander’s supporters will choose now that he is no longer an option, said Siemiatycki.

“This could be very good news for Brad Bradford because, like Bradford, Alexander’s campaign was predicated on time for a change,” he said. “People who were turning to Chris Alexander for that reason, you might think, might be inclined to transfer over to Brad Bradford,” he said.

“There is this kind of discomfort that Torontonians are conveying to pollsters about how they feel about Bradford’s political persona, style etcetera, and that could lead some of Alexander’s supporters to go with Olivia Chow,” he said. “His votes are up for grabs.”

However, as Alexander dropped out fairly late in the race, his name will still be on the ballot. Siemiatycki warns that many people aren’t following the race closely and might not be aware that Alexander has stepped aside.

“What we know for certain is we’ve got a heavyweight final bought ahead of us for the next two weeks plus. That should generate increased public attention and maybe even higher voter turnout than usual,” he said.

With files from The Canadian Press.

stories.title: London politician, author Gord Hume dies
stories.summary: Gord Hume, an icon of local politics, radio, and a prolific writer died on Tuesday at age 76.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Gord Hume, an icon of local politics, radio, and a prolific writer died on Tuesday at age 76.

Hume was elected to city council four times, and served on the former Board of Control.

Longtime friend and political colleague Cheryl Miller says, “One of the things we don’t realize is how much Gord changed London. Gord was a visionary. Gord saw things differently and he had a blueprint for the city. He loved London so much. There are pieces of Gord all over London.

Hume spearheaded moving the central library to its current Dundas Street location, he also pushed for the construction of Canada Life Place and the new Covent Garden Market.

During his time in office he chaired a number of prominent boards including the London Police Services Board, the London Public Library Board, London’s Creative City Task Force, London’s Creative City Committee, and the Small Business Task Force.

Hume started his career in radio in the late 1960s and came to London in 1980.

He authored seven non-fiction books on local government, designing and building great cities, and improving the quality of life in communities.

His career also included stints as a professor at Western University, an instructor at Conestoga College, and a guest lecturer around the world.

Hume shared some “final thoughts” for Londoners:

And so I have departed. I hope it was a good death.

I despise the usual obits, so I am offering some final thoughts. To my remaining family, I loved you dearly although I didn’t say that often enough.

I was fortunate to have three very special women be part of various stages of my life. Each was smart, beautiful and lovely in every way, and enriched my life. I treasured our time together.

I tried to live a life of adventure and discovery–intellectually and personally. I was fortunate to travel to many parts of the world and taste the cultures of many nations. It was not a timid life.

I loved the passion of creating—my books, newspaper and magazine articles, record albums, radio and TV shows and more. I hope generations to come will always discover their creative skills.

Unknown to most, I spent much of my life in pain and endured ten major surgeries with as much dignity and stoicism as possible. It was not always a happy time. The lesson is to be resilient; everybody has tough times.

I believe that public service is noble and that I left my city a little better than when I began. I don’t think London is reaching its potential. The city needs to have a passionate conversation about its priorities and future.

I liked most of my life. We make difficult decisions in our lives and must accept the consequences with grace. A lot of good people touched my life and I am grateful to each of them, especially my sisters Lorraine Harvie and Valerie Jean (VJ) Hume and dear friend Carol Stephenson.

stories.title: Saskatoon Tribal Council inks $269M federal contract for child and family services
stories.summary: A group representing seven Saskatoon-area First Nations has entered a regional agreement with Ottawa to reform the child and family care system and keep kids in their family home.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The Saskatoon Tribal Council (STC) has entered a $269 million regional agreement with the federal government to advance culturally sensitive family and child services and support.

The contract commits $269 million to be spent over the next seven years, with funds going towards reforming the First Nations Child and Family Services Program, with an emphasis being placed on keeping kids at home or in their communities to reclaim First Nations jurisdiction over their children.

STC represents seven First Nations, all within a 200-kilometre radius of Saskatoon. Tribal Chief Mark Arcand and member nation chiefs signed the deal, alongside Minister of Indigenous Services Canada (ISC) Mandy Gull-Masty, at a news conference Wednesday.

“Today is another significant milestone for the seven nations,” Arcand said, noting he couldn’t receive this kind of investment in language, identity, and culture growing up.

“We look at it as an opportunity. We look at it as a challenge to keep helping our people because we see our people need help each and every day, especially our young people.”

The cash will be tailored to the needs of the First Nations represented by the STC.

The ISC minister described the steady stream of income over the next seven years as predictable, adding that the stability will allow the communities to invest in a full continuum of care.

This care will include prevention services and housing support to manage challenges early and keep children in their homes. It will also ensure there are First Nation representative supports for children and families dealing with the family care system, as well as helping provide support for youth who are aging out of care.

Part of the money will also go towards capital projects and building and maintaining facilities to support families, according to a joint news release shared by ISC and the STC.

“We don’t want to see our children, our grandchildren, in addictions. We don’t want to see them incarcerated,” Arcand said.

“It hurts (caregivers) to see their kids go through what their grandparents and great-grandparents went through at residential schools and the negative outcomes that came of that. That’s the system, and this investment is going to help change people’s lives for the next seven years and beyond.”

Exact details on the implementation of the funding will be determined by the tribal council’s principles, the news release said.

ISC said in a separate email $190 million would go directly to the First Nation communities for programming, while $79 million would be directed towards a family service agency.

Arcand expanded on this, saying the First Nations would be supported by the STC in developing a work plan for programming and putting it into practice. He said there would be a wide range of services eligible for intervention prevention funding, including access to out-of-town programming.

“They could be coming to the city to access hockey programs, soccer programs, to keep their kids active because they don’t have it in their nation,” he said.

“The goal is to really focus on keeping kids in a positive frame of mind.”

Gull-Masty also spoke at Wednesday’s event, saying she hopes to execute this type of regional deal with First Nations across Canada.

Stc’s is the first regional agreement of its kind in Saskatchewan, and the first signed outside of Ontario.

“We are targeting systemic change to ensure there are fewer children in care, ideally none, fewer children entering care for the first time, shorter stays when intervention is needed,” Gull-Masty said.

“And more children growing up surrounded by their families, their culture, and their communities.”

She said the regional agreement with the STC is a first step in a program that will have a lasting impact on generations of First Nations and empower self-determination in the involved communities.

“They are truly reclaiming something that should have always been yours – the power to make decisions for your children. The power to ensure that families are doing work and being supported according to your culture, your values and your priorities,” the minister continued.

The regional agreement being directed by its community members will ensure children receive appropriate and prompt care, instead of waiting for the system to catch up to them and their needs, Gull-Masty said.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge conspiracy complaint puts focus on messaging and social media firms
stories.summary: NDP Leader David Eby says social media and other companies must be held accountable to report conversations about causing harm after an FBI complaint detailed extensive online conversations involving the Tumbler Ridge shooter as she planned her deadly attack.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Social media and other companies must be held accountable to report conversations about causing harm after an FBI complaint detailed extensive online conversations involving the Tumbler Ridge shooter as she planned her deadly attack, NDP Leader David Eby said on Wednesday.

The complaint against James Bryant, a resident of Bellingham, Wash., alleges conspiracy to murder as Bryant and killer Jesse Van Rootselaar spent months discussing tactics, locations and weaponry for the attack on the Discord messaging platform before they attempted to livestream the murders on Twitch.

The FBI said Van Rootselaar communicated online with Bryant, even sending photos on the chat website Discord showing what she was wearing for the attack.

Heidi Tworek, professor of international history and public policy at the University of B.C., said on Wednesday that the latest developments from the tragedy reveal a “long-standing and broader phenomena of platforms being used for co-ordination of violence.”

Emily Laidlaw, a Canada Research Chair in cybersecurity law at the University of Calgary, said regulating private messaging platforms is “controversial” due to concerns that it would undermine privacy.

“There are some obligations when it comes to child exploitation material for certain types of platforms, but for problematic content like precisely the Tumbler Ridge scenario, there’s no mandatory reporting,” said Laidlaw.

“Clearly what we saw here was a failure, and something should have been reported to the police,” she added.

Mike Harrington, special agent in charge with the FBI in Seattle, told a news conference on Tuesday that Van Rootselaar met Bryant after being “randomly matched” about three years ago on the now-defunct Omegle messaging app.

Van Rootselaar was about 15 at the time, while Bryant was about 27, and the app that enabled conversations with strangers was closed down not long afterwards over lawsuits about child safety.

Megan Kay, senior communications manager with Twitch, said it’s co-operating with law enforcement but declined to go into details.

Eby said government lawyers will be looking at the Bryant complaint and legal obligations to report wrongdoing need to be placed on tech companies “because they will not and have not done the right thing.”

The B.C. government is already suing artificial intelligence firm OpenAI over its alleged role in helping Van Rootselaar plan the Feb. 10 attack that claimed the lives of eight victims, including six children.

“While the police investigation continues, and I’m glad it’s holding people accountable who were involved, and while that continues, we need Ottawa to step up and impose minimum regulation,” said Eby, speaking Wednesday in his role as the premier at an unrelated B.C. election campaign news conference in Surrey.

“And yes, not just on OpenAI. But on all of the social media companies, ON all the AI companies, that if you become aware of a conversation between users about causing harm, violence against children or anybody, that you should have an obligation to report that to police, just like anybody who overheard a conversation applauding violence in their community would naturally call 911.”

Tworek said social media platforms don’t have a blanket mandatory reporting duty to law enforcement for different types of harmful user content.

She said that’s due to concerns about overreporting and potential policing of vulnerable groups and individuals.

There are many cases where someone might say words like ‘I’m going to kill them,’ but they mean it rhetorically, said Tworek.

“The question is, what are the mechanisms within the companies? How are they approaching trust and safety?” said Tworek. “It depends on the individual platforms.”

Twitch was used to livestream a mass shooting in Buffalo, N.Y., ON May 14, 2022, leaving 10 people dead and three others injured.

David Tindall, a professor in the department of sociology at the University of British Columbia, said evolving technology helps people share common interests to communicate, while it also allows bad actors to collaborate.

“Some of the functions on these platforms allows them to do it in privacy,” said Tindall. “In sociology, there’s a term for this that is called dark networks.”

Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd told the news conference on Tuesday in Seattle that the chats were provided by Discord to the FBI after it obtained subpoenas and search warrants.

Discord did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tworek said Discord functions as a space to allow users to create different communities, like a hybrid app between Slack and Reddit.

Discord was initially built for gamers, but it’s now used for many different purposes. Tworek, who is also a Canada Research Chair, said some professors used the platform for their classes.

Discord’s website says it collects certain information from users, including content users created.

“We generally do not store the contents of video or voice calls or channels. If we were to change that in the future (for example, to facilitate content moderation), we would disclose that to you in advance. We also don’t store streaming content when you share your screen, but we do retain the thumbnail cover image for the stream for a short period of time,” it said.

Federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Wednesday that the information in the FBI complaint was “rather outrageous and seriously worrisome.”

“It speaks to broader issues around the use of social media, the use of collaboration online, issues that I think we’re trying to address through Bill C34,” he told reporters in Ottawa, referring to proposed online safety legislation.

Asked whether Discord should be covered by the legislation, Anandasangaree said the law would establish an independent body to make such decisions.

— With files by Ashley Joannou in Vancouver and David Baxter in Ottawa

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Hundreds attend London job fair as employment seekers and employers agree face-to-face beats AI
stories.summary: More than 500 people attended a London job fair in its first hour on Wednesday.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
More than 500 people attended a London job fair in its first hour on Wednesday.

The figure is seen as a sign of challenging economic times, but also of the desire for face-to-face contact with employers in the age of AI job screening.

The event held at two locations on Horton Street, was organized by Pathways Employment Help Centre (Pehc) and Goodwill Industries.

Hundreds of job seekers spoke with representatives from more than 25 companies representing a half-dozen sectors.

Jacob Lawlor was among the crowd. He is retraining in security after a career in agriculture.

Unlike many, he has had some replies to the hundreds of applications he has sent out. But he is still looking to secure his first role.

“It is tough in certain areas. I’ve been struggling a little bit,” he conceded.

Employment experts tell CTV News Lawlor is not alone in a job market that filters resumes with AI.

“ Especially if you’re on the job boards, clicking that ‘Apply Now’ button. You don’t get any feedback. You’re like, is anybody even getting my resume?” said Michelle Moran, an employment specialist at Pehc.

And feedback is what job seekers crave, according to Cassy Rose. She has recently retrained in administration after a career in fast food.

Rose expressed elation at the change to meet employers face-to-face.

“You can get the language off of somebody, so that you can understand where they’re coming from, and you get a better idea of the insight of a person, when it is not online.”

While employers are ready to give up AI tools, some agreed job fairs remain beneficial.

“We prefer having the in-person interactions with the candidate,” said Tugce Ongel, an HR generalist with Bayshore Home Health, who added, “It further gives the candidate the opportunity to ask any questions and get instant feedback from us, and, as well as for us, we get to have that initial conversation and get to know them.”

But Moran said even with face-to-face contact, it can take time to generate leads and hopefully a job in 2026.

“You can be doing everything right, and it still can take months to go from where you’re starting to onboarding in a new company.”

But Rose believes perseverance can still pay off for positive job seekers.

“We’re all after the same goal. We want to get started!”

stories.title: Writer K.D. Miller crafted stories that glittered like a polished knife edge
stories.summary: Her fiction, which can be blazingly funny or unsettlingly dark, often explores religious themes while marrying pristine linguistic technique with an instinct for drama
stories.author: Steven Beattie
stories.content:
For much of her adult life, author K.D. Miller had a writing ritual. She would rise at 5 a.m., brew a pot of coffee, and head to her desk for two hours before she had to get ready for what she euphemistically referred to as her “day job.”

Fellow writer and good friend Mike Barnes describes Ms. Miller’s writing habit as “monastic,” an appropriate term that hints at the overlap, so central to her identity, between writing and religion. Raised Presbyterian, Ms. Miller was baptized and confirmed in the Anglican Church in 1990, following a period of self-described atheism. On several occasions Ms. Miller, who died in Toronto on Sept. 14 of complications from cancer at the age of 75, described herself as a “default” or “accidental” Christian. It’s the same way her character Robbie describes himself to his friend, the writer Raymond Mayhugh, in the early story A Litany in Time of Plague – a testament to the way Ms. Miller covertly insinuated material from her own life into her fiction.

The title of the story is evidence of Ms. Miller’s preoccupation. On the surface a reference to the poem of the same name by Elizabethan poet Thomas Nashe, the word “litany” carries religious connotations that are unavoidable. And while she eschewed proselytizing about her beliefs – “She was very undogmatic in her approach to spirituality,” Mr. Barnes said – they were an inextricable part of who she was as a person and, importantly, a writer. “Writing stories is the way I pray,” she insisted in her 2001 essay collection Holy Writ , about the confluence between artistic creation and spirituality. One of her later collections, 2014’s All Saints , is a series of linked stories featuring characters associated with the title church.

If religion was one indelible wellspring for Ms. Miller, the other was the theatre. Trained as an actor, she received a BA in drama from the University of Guelph and a master’s in directing from the University of British Columbia, where her thesis was a production analysis of Tennessee Williams’s The Glass Menagerie. In a biographical essay included in the 2003 anthology Writers Talking, she described her mother, the late Isabel Milne Barclay, as “a talented artist and a frustrated actress”; she went on to compare the writing process to Rosalind Russell’s observation that “[g]ood acting is standing up naked and turning around very slowly.”

Writing, for Ms. Miller, involved a similar combination of risk and abandon, something admirers frequently compare to a theatrical performance. “I think it all went back to that early training that she had on stage,” said John Metcalf, who edited her early work. “You had to immerse yourself in [her writing], you had to join the performance. That was what made her so different from many writers in recent years who are firmly outside what they are presenting.”

Novelist Russell Smith also finds aspects of the theatre in Ms. Miller’s work. “She writes these wonderful, humorous but dark monologues. That obviously is the theatrical influence,” he said. It was an influence that was equally apparent in her live readings, which often resembled theatrical performances. This, perhaps, made her the perfect person for that necessary day job: training volunteers at the Cnib in reading books for the blind.

Ms. Miller could be blazingly funny in print: The title story from 2018’s Late Breaking features a pair of competing literary awards – the Biggar Prize and the Olympia Featherstone Award for Fiction – that repeatedly try to one-up each other on the size of their purse. (Somewhat ironically, the book was both a Governor-General’s Literary Award finalist and a Giller Prize nominee.)

But she was also, as Mr. Smith attests, unafraid to present bleak and dark material. In one of her best stories, Magnificat from All Saints , an aged religious spinster witnesses a covert public sex act that crosses the boundary into assault.

“It gets quite gothic and creepy sometimes,” Mr. Smith said about this aspect of Ms. Miller’s fiction. “Who does that remind you of? [Alice] Munro, right away.”

It’s a sentiment with which literary critic Jeet Heer agrees. “There’s the tradition of the Canadian short story where Alice Munro looms very large. K.D. Miller is part of that tradition,” Mr. Heer said. “There’s the idea of the Southern Ontario gothic. I think she was more gothic than most. She did have a sensibility that was partially shaped by things like horror writing.” He points specifically to the 2011 collection The Other Voice as a book that reflects her affinity for writers like Poe and Hawthorne, as well as the uncanny realism of Alex Colville, who served as the inspiration for the stories in Late Breaking. “It’s the idea of realism that’s also a bit unsettling,” Mr. Heer said.

Kathleen Daisy Miller was born on March 6, 1951 in Hamilton, where she lived with her parents and her older brother, Robert Miller. “There was a large family in Hamilton,” says Leah Wallace, Ms. Miller’s sister-in-law. “The Barclays on her mother’s side, the Millers on her father’s side. They actually all lived within walking distance of each other.”

The acting bug bit early. At age 12, Ms. Miller was cast as Annie Sullivan in a school production of The Miracle Worker, and she won the 1967 Hamilton District Collegiate Drama Festival’s award for best actress in Impromptu. She left for Guelph in 1969, graduating with a BA in drama in 1973. She finished her master’s in 1978, “more out of spite than anything else,” she wrote. While in B.C., she met an actor whom she married in 1979; the two divorced in 1986.

Ms. Miller’s first publication was the short story Now, Voyager , which appeared in Flare and won first prize in the magazine’s literary contest. Her first story collection, A Litany in Time of Plague , was published by the Porcupine’s Quill in 1994; the small press in Erin, Ont., also brought out a second collection, Give Me Your Answer (1999), and the essay collection Holy Writ: A Writer Reflects on Creation and Inspiration (2001). A novel, Brown Dwarf, and a story collection, The Other Voice, followed. All Saints was shortlisted for the Rogers Writers’ Trust Award for Fiction, and Late Breaking was a finalist for the Governor-General’s Literary Award, nominated for the Giller, and shortlisted for the Trillium Prize.

An unpublished collection, Alice Walks , is currently under contract with Dundurn Press.

She had three core communities, according to Ms. Wallace: the community of St. Clement’s Anglican Church, in North Toronto, where she served on various committees and attended service every Sunday; the community at Stanley Knowles Housing Co-operative, where she lived; and the literary community. A group of close friends from university that includes Ms. Wallace and goes by the moniker “The Sisterhood” met regularly over the years.

But she also fiercely guarded her privacy and withheld personal aspects of herself from public view, something Mr. Barnes, the writer, believes goes back to an aspect of performing on stage. “She had a real sense of performance; that’s what made her such a dramatic reader,” he said. “But she had a very firm line she drew: A performance was a performance and then off the stage, that’s your private life. The audience is entitled to your very best on stage, but nothing more than that.”

At her very best, she was at the pinnacle of writers in this country, combining pristine linguistic technique with a theatre impresario’s instinct for drama. Her painstaking craft – honed morning after morning beginning at 5 o’clock, often before the sun rose – resulted in prose that glittered like a polished knife edge. And like a knife, it could cut deep. That said, Ms. Miller herself was not reticent to admit writerly self-doubt. “I don’t think I’m ‘important as a writer’ yet,” she wrote in 2003, “and have no idea if I ever will be. I do know that I’m happy as a writer.”

One person who is certain Ms. Miller’s writing will endure is her former editor, Mr. Metcalf. “Her stories are acted out vigorously in marvellous dialogue. And very funny, some of them,” he said. “The stories were very vital and quite unusual within the body of Canadian writing. She has a place within the literature that will always be remembered.”
