stories.title: Carney says 'more work to do' on behalf of Jewish Canadians on Oct. 7 anniversary
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said “there is more work to do” to make Jewish Canadians feel safe and thrive in Canada.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – On the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attacks against Israel, Prime Minister Mark Carney said “there is more work to do” to make Jewish Canadians feel safe and thrive in Canada.

“The government has been taking actions at home to protect the Jewish community, protect all Canadians, but particularly the Jewish community,” said Carney, ON his way into a caucus meeting in Ottawa on Wednesday.

“And it’s above and beyond protection, it’s about the ability to truly thrive, live their lives freely and openly, and thrive as Jewish people in Canada,” he added.

The prime minister outlined measures his government has taken, since the “unspeakable tragedy” three years ago. These measures include anti-hate legislation and $75 million through the Canada Community Security Fund, to protect Jewish community centres, synagogues and day schools.

Carney noted that protection has become necessary, given the recent gunman attack against the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., which was thwarted by Belleville police. One of the police officers, Const. Jeff Smith, is recovering from his injuries and the suspect died from his injuries sustained in the shootout. The attack took place on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, Yom Kippur.

“There’s more work to do,” said Carney. “This is a job for all Canadians to ensure that all Canadians can live freely and openly in our society.”

Israelis gathered on Wednesday to mark the anniversary of the deadliest attack in its history, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 people taken hostage by the Hamas terrorist group.

The ensuing Israel-Hamas war in Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, with the Israeli military controlling over half of the Gaza strip, following a tentative ceasefire announced last fall.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the Jewish Canadian community has experienced the consequences of the war here in Canada.

“The hatred that fuelled October 7th did not remain on foreign shores,” said Poilievre. “Right here in Canada, far too many synagogues, Jewish businesses and institutions have been the targets of harassment and hate.”

“This is not, and cannot become, normal,” added Poilievre. “Conservatives will always fight against antisemitism and all forms of hatred: protecting our schools, communities and places of worship so that Canadians of all faiths can live in peace and security.”

According to data from Statistics Canada, police-reported hate crimes against Jewish Canadians jumped from 492 in 2021, to 788 in 2025. The number of incidents were higher in 2023 and 2024, at 959 and 943 incidents respectively.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) has noted that despite Jewish Canadians representing just one per cent of the population, they were the target of 71 per cent of religion-motivated hate crimes in 2025.

“Today, Prime Minister Carney unequivocally condemned Hamas and recognized that October 7 was a Canadian tragedy, taking the lives of Canadians and leaving a Jewish community here at home still deeply impacted by the terrorist attacks and the devastating resurgence of antisemitism that followed,” said Cija CEO Noah Shack, in a statement.

“We appreciate the prime minister’s renewed commitment to strengthen public safety and combat hate, with new laws and resources to stop extremism before it takes root,” he added.

stories.title: Liberals announce bill to prohibit Maid for mental illness alone
stories.summary: The federal government intends to permanently bar people with mental illness alone from accessing an assisted death.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi, Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government intends to permanently bar people with mental illness alone from accessing an assisted death, settling a decade-long controversial debate.

But the Liberal government is moving forward to allow people to make advance requests for Maid if diagnosed with an illness that would threaten their ability to provide final consent, up to the last moments before the lethal injection. They will do so by decriminalizing the act for doctors who administer Maid to patients who made an advance request.

The announcement was made Wednesday by Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Health Minister Marjorie Michel on the same day the House of Commons is set to vote on a Conservative bill on the topic.

The ministers said they intend to table legislation this fall that will maintain the exclusion of medical assistance in dying (Maid) for people seeking it on the sole basis of a psychiatric illness. The exclusion, set to expire next March, will be maintained “on an indeterminate basis,” Fraser announced.

“While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time,” he said.

On the separate issue of advance requests, Fraser said the legislation will grant access to Maid “to people who have provided consent at a time when they still have capacity but know that they have been diagnosed with an illness that will take that capacity from them subsequently.

“These are not easy decisions. But we believe they are the correct ones,” Fraser said.

The minister did not commit to a date for the legislation beyond the fall. He said the bill was being drafted and promised that the substance would not differ from what he announced Wednesday.

Whether to open up euthanasia to people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness has been one of the most heated issues in the history of legalized assisted death in Canada.

In June, a special parliamentary committee recommended the Liberal government draw a line in the sand and indefinitely exclude people with mental illness alone from eligibility for Maid. Expanding Maid for mental illness, set to take effect March 17, 2027, had already been deferred, twice.

The joint committee of MPs and senators said key issues haven’t been addressed, including whether it’s possible to predict with any certainty whether a person’s mental illness is incurable. Dr. Sonu Gaind, past chief of psychiatry at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, told the committee that doctors are right less than half the time, comparing the ability to predict long-term prognosis to a coin toss.

Current and former chairs of psychiatry departments at universities across Canada warned the committee that making Maid available to people with depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, substance abuse and other mental illnesses would facilitate avoidable deaths and erode suicide prevention efforts.

The committee said “grave concerns and deep divisions” continue to exist. A recurring theme was the pressing need for better access to mental health services and concerns long waits for care could exacerbate suffering, driving Maid requests. The committee also heard stories of “questionable conduct” by some Maid providers, as well as doctors “with a seemingly cavalier attitude toward ending a life,” committee co-chair Liberal MP Marcus Powlowski wrote in a supplemental opinion.

However, the committee’s decision wasn’t unanimous. Three senators as well as a Bloc Québécois MP, Luc Thériault, wrote dissenting opinions and called on the government to bring the question of expansion to the Supreme Court of Canada.

After Fraser’s announcement, Conservative MPs blasted the move as playing politics as the House of Commons was set to vote on a bill they said did substantially the same thing the government was now promising to do.

They also criticized Fraser’s decision to bundle the issues of Maid for mental illness and allowing for advance requests in the same bill.

“What the minister has announced today is eroding that consensus and introducing division into a very complex subject,” charged Conservative MP Andrew Lawton. “We agree that Maid should not extend to people with only a mental illness.”

Earlier this week, Fraser told reporters he’d heard “a range of different views” since the committee’s report was released in June and that he wanted to take the time “to line things up the appropriate way” in deciding on such a serious issue.

First legalized in 2016 for people whose deaths are “reasonably foreseeable,” Canada’s Maid law was amended in 2021 to remove the “reasonably foreseeable” provision. The amendments under Bill C-7 also included a restriction on mental illness alone as a qualifying condition for Maid, an exclusion that was originally set to expire on March 17, 2023, but was later pushed back to 2024 and then again, to March 2027.

Currently, dementia is an eligible diagnosis for Maid in Canada, provided people have the capacity to make a reasoned request and don’t lose that capacity before they want their lives ended. Dementia is considered a neurological disorder, not a mental illness.

Canadian children’s author Robert Munsch revealed in a New York Times profile last year that, shortly after being diagnosed with dementia in 2021, he applied and was approved for Maid.

Munsch said he would have to pick the moment “when I can still ask for it,” otherwise his wife risks being “stuck with me being a lump.”

Outside Quebec, euthanizing someone in the absence of capacity is a serious offence in the absence of a valid waiver of final consent.

The new bill will amend the Criminal Code to reflect that a doctor who provides Maid to someone who is suffering an incurable illness and who has complied with provincially legislated safeguards “will not be treated as a criminal in Canada going forward,” Fraser said. Provinces would decide whether to permit it. Alberta has already banned advance requests.

Alex Schadenberg, executive director of the Euthanasia Prevention Coalition, said consent can become uncertain under advance request scenarios, because someone else will have to decide when the person is experiencing conditions under which they would have wanted their lives ended.

“It’s really a problematic situation, and then who makes the decision in the end? Some family member, some doctor who says, ‘Oh, I guess this was requested in the end,'” Schadenberg told reporters on Parliament Hill Wednesday.

“To me, it’s almost very eugenic.”

“An advance request is written by someone who cannot know what their future will hold,” said Krista Carr, CEO of Inclusion Canada. “Consent at the time is the most basic protection a person has. Parliament should not take it away.”

A recurring theme was the pressing need for better access to mental health services and concerns long waits for care could exacerbate suffering, driving Maid requests. The committee also heard stories of “questionable conduct” by some Maid providers, as well as doctors “with a seemingly cavalier attitude toward ending a life,” committee co-chair Liberal MP Marcus Powlowski wrote in a supplemental opinion.

However, the committee’s decision wasn’t unanimous. Three senators as well as a Bloc Québécois MP, Luc Thériault, wrote dissenting opinions and called on the government to bring the question of expansion to the Supreme Court of Canada.

After Fraser’s announcement, Conservative MPs blasted the move as playing politics as the House of Commons was set to vote on a bill they said did substantially the same thing the government was now promising to do.
They also criticized Fraser’s decision to bundle the issues of Maid for mental illness and allowing for advance requests in the same bill.

“What the minister has announced today is eroding that consensus and introducing division into a very complex subject,” charged Conservative MP Andrew Lawton. “We agree that Maid should not extend to people with only a mental illness.”

Earlier this week, Fraser told reporters he’d heard “a range of different views” since the committee’s report was released in June and that he wanted to take the time “to line things up the appropriate way” in deciding on such a serious issue.

First legalized in 2016 for people whose deaths are “reasonably foreseeable,” Canada’s Maid law was amended in 2021 to remove the “reasonably foreseeable” provision. The amendments under Bill C-7 also included a restriction on mental illness alone as a qualifying condition for Maid, an exclusion that was originally set to expire on March 17, 2023, but was later pushed back to 2024 and then again, to March 2027.

Currently, dementia is an eligible diagnosis for Maid in Canada, provided people have the capacity to make a reasoned request and don’t lose that capacity before they want their lives ended. Dementia is considered a neurological disorder, not a mental illness.
Canadian children’s author Robert Munsch revealed in a New York Times profile last year that, shortly after being diagnosed with dementia in 2021, he applied and was approved for Maid.
Munsch said he would have to pick the moment “when I can still ask for it,” otherwise his wife risks being “stuck with me being a lump.”
Outside Quebec, euthanizing someone in the absence of capacity is a serious offence in the absence of a valid waiver of final consent.

The new bill will amend the Criminal Code to reflect that a doctor who provides Maid to someone who is suffering an incurable illness and who has complied with provincially legislated safeguards “will not be treated as a criminal in Canada going forward,” Fraser said. Provinces would decide whether to permit it. Alberta has already banned advance requests.

Alex Schadenberg, executive director of the Euthanasia Prevention Coalition, said consent can become uncertain under advance request scenarios, because someone else will have to decide when the person is experiencing conditions under which they would have wanted their lives ended.

“It’s really a problematic situation, and then who makes the decision in the end? Some family member, some doctor who says, ‘Oh, I guess this was requested in the end,'” Schadenberg told reporters on Parliament Hill Wednesday.
“To me, it’s almost very eugenic.”

“An advance request is written by someone who cannot know what their future will hold,” said Krista Carr, CEO of Inclusion Canada. “Consent at the time is the most basic protection a person has. Parliament should not take it away.”

stories.title: Person injured after exchanging shots with Quebec provincial police
stories.summary: Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes says police received a call about an armed person in crisis in a residence in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec’s police watchdog is investigating after a person was shot and injured by provincial police during an intervention west of Montreal.

The Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes says police received a call at around 4:30 p.m. Tuesday about an armed person in crisis in a residence in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield.

The watchdog says the suspect fired at the responding officers outside the home, and they returned fire.

The person was taken to hospital where they are in critical condition.

The watchdog says Montreal police officers have been asked to support the investigation.

The BEI is also asking anyone who witnessed or has video of the incident to reach out online or to visit the mobile command centre near the site of the shooting.

stories.title: Canada won’t expand Maid for mental illness alone, minister says
stories.summary: Currently, the law excludes Maid for people seeking it on grounds of mental illness, but the exception is set to expire in March 2027.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada will not extend medical assistance in dying (Maid) for people who are seeking it on the basis of mental illness alone, Justice Minister Sean Fraser said.

Currently, the law excludes Maid for people seeking it on the grounds of mental illness as a sole criteria, but that rule is set to expire in March 2027. The federal government plans to table legislation this fall that will maintain that exclusion “on an indeterminate basis,” Fraser said.

“Canada has made a decision not to move forward with the expansion that is scheduled in the Criminal Code of medical assistance in dying in circumstances where mental illness is the sole basis,” he said.

A parliamentary committee was tasked with studying whether people with mental illness alone should have access to medical assistance in dying. In a June report, the committee concluded that the controversial planned eligibility expansion should not move ahead.

The previous Liberal government passed legislation in 2021 that revised eligibility criteria for Maid, but gave an additional two-year extension for mental illness eligibility to allow for further study.

That 2023 deadline was extended three more times, with the expansion previously set to come into effect in March 2027.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

“ While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time,” Fraser said.

The federal government “dug into” the report of the special committee and found “very real concerns about people who were living [in] communities with inadequate access to mental health services,” he added.

The Conservatives called for more transparency from Fraser.

“We have no idea what his bill is going to say. He’s telling us all sorts of things. He hasn’t even seen the bill himself,” Conservative MP Tamara Jansen told reporters after Fraser’s announcement.

The Bloc Quebecois welcomed the announcement but said limiting further expansion would be “abandoning patients who are suffering.”

“We have a responsibility to those who are suffering, and it is our duty not to let them down and to continue the dialogue,” Bloc MP Luc Theriault said in a statement in French.

1:00 Canada to exclude people who solely suffer from mental illness from MAiD

Advance directives for medical assistance in dying

Fraser also said the government will “grant access to medical assistance in dying to people who have provided consent at a time when they still have capacity but know that they have been diagnosed with an illness that will take that capacity from them subsequently.”

This is sometimes referred to as “advance directive” or “advance request” in medical parlance. It often involves a competent person making a written request for Maid, with the intention that it would be honoured later, if and when they lose the capacity to make the decision for themselves: for example, in people suffering from worsening Alzheimer’s or dementia.

Currently, Canadians cannot make these decisions ahead of time.

1:45 Maid should not be allowed solely for mental illness, committee recommends

More details on the new bill would follow in the coming days, Fraser said, but added that it would include changes to the Criminal Code to ensure that a doctor who provides medical assistance in dying to someone who is eligible on an advance directive “will not be treated as a criminal in Canada going forward.”

Fraser said the federal government was following the committee’s recommendations, but some advocates have said the report had its limitations.

Advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada raised concerns about the testimony heard by the committee. It claimed the committee selected witnesses who were opposed to allowing Maid for people with mental illness and chose not to hear from people with mental disorders who wanted to speak about why they would seek a Maid assessment.

“Canada has made a decision not to move forward with the expansion that is scheduled in the Criminal Code of medical assistance in dying in circumstances where mental illness is the sole basis,” he said.

A parliamentary committee was tasked with studying whether people with mental illness alone should have access to medical assistance in dying. In a June report, the committee concluded that the controversial planned eligibility expansion should not move ahead.

The previous Liberal government passed legislation in 2021 that revised eligibility criteria for Maid, but gave an additional two-year extension for mental illness eligibility to allow for further study.
That 2023 deadline was extended three more times, with the expansion previously set to come into effect in March 2027.

“ While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time,” Fraser said.

The federal government “dug into” the report of the special committee and found “very real concerns about people who were living [in] communities with inadequate access to mental health services,” he added.
The Conservatives called for more transparency from Fraser.
“We have no idea what his bill is going to say. He’s telling us all sorts of things. He hasn’t even seen the bill himself,” Conservative MP Tamara Jansen told reporters after Fraser’s announcement.
The Bloc Quebecois welcomed the announcement but said limiting further expansion would be “abandoning patients who are suffering.”
“We have a responsibility to those who are suffering, and it is our duty not to let them down and to continue the dialogue,” Bloc MP Luc Theriault said in a statement in French.

Advance directives for medical assistance in dying

Fraser also said the government will “grant access to medical assistance in dying to people who have provided consent at a time when they still have capacity but know that they have been diagnosed with an illness that will take that capacity from them subsequently.”

This is sometimes referred to as “advance directive” or “advance request” in medical parlance. It often involves a competent person making a written request for Maid, with the intention that it would be honoured later, if and when they lose the capacity to make the decision for themselves: for example, in people suffering from worsening Alzheimer’s or dementia.
Currently, Canadians cannot make these decisions ahead of time.
1:45 Maid should not be allowed solely for mental illness, committee recommends

More details on the new bill would follow in the coming days, Fraser said, but added that it would include changes to the Criminal Code to ensure that a doctor who provides medical assistance in dying to someone who is eligible on an advance directive “will not be treated as a criminal in Canada going forward.”
Fraser said the federal government was following the committee’s recommendations, but some advocates have said the report had its limitations.

Advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada raised concerns about the testimony heard by the committee. It claimed the committee selected witnesses who were opposed to allowing Maid for people with mental illness and chose not to hear from people with mental disorders who wanted to speak about why they would seek a Maid assessment.

stories.summary: When an elderly woman was found dead in a Quebec seniors home, paramedics police, and a doctor originally determined it was an accident.
stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
When an elderly woman was found dead in a Quebec seniors home, paramedics police, and a doctor originally determined it was an accident.

And it May have stayed that way, if not for the help of her niece.

Montreal Gazette crime reporter Paul Cherry joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss what authorities missed, how the woman’s niece uncovered the truth, and what happened to the woman’s killer.

stories.title: Woman dead after fire at Montreal homeless encampment
stories.summary: Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada says the woman's death at the encampment serves as a reminder of the importance of eliminating homelessness.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A woman in her 50s is dead after a fire broke out in a homeless encampment in Montreal-Nord early Wednesday morning.

Montreal police say the fire was first reported just before 5 a.m. after a resident of the encampment alerted the local police station nearby.

Upon arrival, police say they found an unconscious woman who was taken to hospital in critical condition. She later died at hospital.

Firefighters were called, but authorities say the fire was put out before they arrived.

It is not clear what caused the fire or what caused the woman’s death, but the police’s arson unit is investigating.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada says the death serves as a reminder of the importance of eliminating homelessness.

stories.title: Fixer-uppers, commutes: Many making trade-offs to buy homes, report says
stories.summary: Nearly two-thirds of Canadians say they are willing to make a compromise to be able to afford a larger home or one more suitable for their family, a Remax survey has found.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
It’s no secret that buying a home feels like a distant dream for a large chunk of Canadians, but many are looking to get a foot through the housing market by going for homes that need a little time, love and commitment.

Nearly two-thirds (65 per cent) of Canadians say they are willing to make a compromise to be able to afford a larger home or one more suitable for their family, a survey by real estate firm Remax has found.

This includes either living farther from a city centre or considering an older home that requires renovations, it adds.

“Rather than giving up on homeownership, Canadians are making different choices about how to get there,” said Don Kottick, president of Remax Canada.

“For some, that means looking outside their current community or reconsidering the type of home they buy. For others, it means making different financial choices. Buyers are identifying what matters most and where they have room to be flexible,” he said.

Location is the biggest area of flexibility, with nearly half (47 per cent) saying they would be willing to move up to an hour from their current community and 16 per cent saying they would move even further.

Nearly one-third (31 per cent) said they would move away from the city centre, while 21 per cent said they would live far from shops, restaurants and other amenities to be able to afford a home.

But many are considering the property itself. One in five (20 per cent) say they would consider buying an older property that requires significant renovations.

Canadians are also making financial trade-offs, with 41 per cent saying they would cut discretionary spending such as travel or dining out to afford a home and nearly a quarter (24 per cent) saying they would consider a longer amortization period to be able to afford monthly payments.

The Bank of Mom and Dad remains important for many, with 20 per cent saying they would accept help from family. On the other hand, 17 per cent said they would take on a second job to be able to afford a home, and a similar percentage said they would delay their retirement or other long-term savings plans.

In some markets, homebuying is becoming easier for new entrants but challenges remain, Remax says.

In 81 per cent of the markets analyzed in the Remax report, home sales have been declining between January and June of 2026. However, home prices have steadily increased for more than half (56 per cent) of these housing markets.

stories.title: Fire displaces 30 people, injures 3 in Park Extension area of Montreal
stories.summary: William Murray, a section chief with the department, told Global News that the building was a first-floor commercial, second-floor residential structure.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
About 30 people have been forced from their homes and three people have been injured after a fire erupted early Wednesday morning in the Park Extension neighbourhood.

The Montreal Fire Department said crews started getting calls shortly after 2 a.m. to a two-storey building on St-Roch Street between De L’Epee Avenue and Querbes Avenue.

The fire started at the ground level of the building, officials said, which is home to a grocery store.

William Murray, a section chief with the department, told Global News that the building was a first-floor commercial, second-floor residential structure.

A total of 30 people were evacuated from the building and are now in the care of the Canadian Red Cross.

Murray said as of late Wednesday morning, the fire was under control and firefighters were waiting for a mechanical bulldozer to bring down what’s left of the building.

An investigation is ongoing, and authorities say they are looking into whether any criminality was involved.

— with files from Global News’ Brayden Jagger Haines

stories.title: Key dates in the evolution of Canada’s medically assisted dying laws
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canadian Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Health Minister Marjorie Michel announced two major decisions for the "path forward" in medically assisted dying on Wednesday. Fraser said the government has decided not to proceed with expanding Maid to people whose sole underlying condition is mental illness. He also said the government would table legisl…
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canadian Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Health Minister Marjorie Michel announced two major decisions for the “path forward” in medically assisted dying on Wednesday. Fraser said the government has decided not to proceed with expanding Maid to people whose sole underlying condition is mental illness. He also said the government would table legislation to allow people to give advance consent to Maid if they are suffering from an incurable illness that will take away their capacity to give consent later.

Here are some key dates in the evolution of Maid legislation in Canada:

1892: Canada’s first Criminal Code included a provision that barred people from aiding and abetting suicide and carried a sentence of life in prison. It also criminalized suicide.

1972: The federal government under Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau repealed the Criminal Code section that criminalized suicide. The government left in place the provision that made it a criminal offence to aid or abet a person ending their life, and another provision that said no person could consent to their life being ended.

1991-2010: The House of Commons debated six private member’s bills seeking to decriminalize assisted suicide. None passed.

1993: Sue Rodriguez, a woman diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or ALS, challenged the Criminal Code provision banning assisted suicide in the country’s highest court. The Supreme Court of Canada ruled against her in a 5-4 decision. Rodriguez died with the help of an anonymous physician in 1994.

1995: A Senate committee released a special report on euthanasia and assisted suicide.

While members of the committee held different views on how to deal with the suffering of people who are dying, their report said all had “deep concerns about the implications of permitting assisted suicide.”

Those who supported it suggested minimum safeguards. They said that a person receiving assisted death must be competent, must be suffering from an irreversible illness that has reached an intolerable stage, and must have made a free and informed request without coercion.

2009: The Collège des médecins du Québec released a discussion paper that concluded euthanasia could be a final step in end-of-life care under exceptional circumstances, like uncontrollable pain or interminable suffering.

2010: By this time, some form of assisted dying was legal in the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Colombia and the U.S. states of Oregon, Washington and Montana.

2011: The British Columbia Civil Liberties Association filed a lawsuit challenging the two sections of the Criminal Code outlawing assisted death, arguing they violated the Section 7 guarantee in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms of “life, liberty and security of the person.”

This case, brought on behalf of Lee Carter, Hollis Johnson, William Shoichet and Gloria Taylor, became known as Carter v. Canada.

2012: The Supreme Court of British Columbia ruled in favour of the British Columbia Civil Liberties Association in the Carter case. The federal government under Prime Minister Stephen Harper appealed.

2012: A committee of Quebec’s National Assembly released a report on “dying with dignity” after two years of work that included expert opinions, public consultation and travel to France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

The report concluded that medical aid in dying, or Maid, should be an additional option for end-of-life care in Quebec for a consenting adult patient suffering from a serious, incurable disease who is in an advanced state of decline.

2013: The Carter case went to the Court of Appeal for British Columbia.

The Appeal Court overturned the lower court’s ruling, finding the judge should have upheld the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision in Rodriguez. The B.C. Civil Liberties Association sought leave to appeal at the Supreme Court of Canada.

2014: Quebec’s National Assembly passed a law to allow medical aid in dying for adults in the province who are at the end of their lives, suffering from a serious and incurable illness and in an advanced state of irreversible decline. The law would take effect the following year.

2015: In a unanimous decision, the country’s top court struck down two sections of the Criminal Code — the prohibition on aiding and abetting suicide and the section stating that no one can consent to have death inflicted on them.

The written decision stated it was “cruel” to deprive people of the ability to seek help from a physician to end their lives.

The Court ruled the laws violated the Section 7 Charter rights of “competent adults who seek such assistance as a result of a grievous and irremediable medical condition that causes enduring and intolerable suffering.”

The Supreme Court invalidated the sections of the Criminal Code and gave Parliament one year to create a legal framework for assisted dying. The one-year grace period ended in February 2016.

2015: The Canadian Medical Association began developing training on medical assistance in dying for physicians.

In October, the Liberals won the federal election. Justin Trudeau’s government asked the Supreme Court for a six-month extension to the deadline. The court granted four extra months, ending in June 2016.

2016: The House of Commons passed Bill C-14 in June, making it legal for doctors to help a person end their life if they had a terminal illness. The Senate tried to expand the right to die beyond those whose deaths were deemed “reasonably foreseeable,” but members of Parliament voted against those amendments.

2019: The Superior Court of Quebec ruled that limiting Maid to people whose natural deaths were reasonably foreseeable was unconstitutional in a case involving two plaintiffs — Jean Truchon and Nicole Gladu — who were living with incurable and degenerative conditions.

The federal Liberal government and the Quebec government both chose not to appeal the decision.

2021: Parliament passed a law removing the requirement that a person’s death had to be reasonably foreseeable, creating “track 1” and “track 2” Maid.

People whose deaths were not reasonably foreseeable — those in track 2 — had to meet additional eligibility criteria that included a 90-day assessment period and involvement of a practitioner with expertise in the condition causing the applicant’s suffering.

In response to the Truchon case, the law allowed patients in some circumstances to waive final consent under an advance consent arrangement.

The law also excluded people whose sole underlying condition was a mental illness because of the complexity of those cases. The bill ordered an independent expert review to be done within a year. The exclusion covering cases of mental illness was set to last two years, until March 2023.

2022: The expert panel on Maid and mental illness made recommendations to Parliament that included developing Maid practice standards, requiring independent assessments and creating a model of prospective oversight.

2023: The Liberal government extended the exclusion for people with mental illness by one year to “provide additional time to prepare for the safe and consistent assessment and provision of Maid” and allow the government to consider a report from a special committee of MPs and senators studying Maid.

Quebec’s National Assembly passed amendments to its own assisted dying laws to allow people to draft an advance request, which would come into force in the event that they lose capacity to request Maid.

2024: The government once again delayed eligibility for people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness until March 2027.

2026: On June 17, a parliamentary committee recommended the federal government indefinitely exclude people with mental illness from becoming eligible for Maid. Some dissenting senators on the committee criticized the process as “fundamentally flawed” and called for the government to refer the question to the Supreme Court of Canada.

Oct. 7, 2026: Justice Minister Sean Fraser announces that despite those criticisms, the government will move forward with the committee’s recommendation to exclude people whose sole underlying condition is mental illness from receiving Maid indefinitely and will table legislation to that effect.

Fraser said that legislation will also grant access to Maid to people suffering from an incurable illness who have given advance consent, knowing that their illness will take away their capacity to give consent later. Fraser noted that this change will be reflected in the Criminal Code.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Expert explainer: Why does Thanksgiving cause so much stress?
stories.summary: Western family studies expert Lara Descartes explains why Thanksgiving family stress happens and shares tips for navigating holiday conflict.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
While Thanksgiving presents the opportunity to wind down, reconnect with family , and celebrate the holidays with those we love, it can also become a point of stress.

Whether it’s pressure to make the perfect meal or tensions that arise from family disagreements, conflict can turn our holiday expectations upside down. Lara Descartes, family studies professor in the Faculty of Health Sciences, explains what’s at the root of Thanksgiving tensions, and how we can navigate the challenges this upcoming season.

Lara Descartes (LD) : Expectations can be very high. Media and advertisements often present these lovely family holidays where everyone’s laughing, having a good time, sharing and appreciating one another. When reality doesn’t match that, it often leads to disappointment.

There can be a lot of pressure to present the perfect holiday: the perfect meal, perfect decorations, perfect harmony among family members. When you’re aiming for perfection, it always makes everything more stressful.

LD: There are so many sources of possible tension because holidays are symbolically important to us. We know that they’re cultural institutions: everyone is taking part, which can lead us to imagine that everyone else is doing it with more fun, more togetherness and more joy.

We also often see conflict around identity. A change of identity is hard for families to accept, which is why there can be tension when students return home. Thanksgiving is the first time back for many students since leaving in the summer. You’re returning from the university environment where you have your own identity, which has likely changed from the one you had in high school or the one you have in relation to your family.

Change is hard no matter what – whether it’s good or bad – and families May not react the way an individual wants. While we’re hoping for this wonderful return and to be embraced in the bosom of our family, everyone May need some time to adjust to big or little changes.

LD: They May not be small to the people involved. While the person who upset another May feel it was a small issue they can explain away, to the person at whom it was directed it can hold much more weight. For example, say somebody cooked the whole Thanksgiving meal – which can take days – and then everyone sits down and dad says, ‘boy, this is dry’. That would be very hurtful. The amount of labor and emotion going into this ritualized experience can make interactions more loaded than normal.

Things like food might seem small, but food is identity! It’s rooted in tradition and culture. Because the holidays centre around meals, it can definitely become a touchstone for conflict. Whether it’s people expressing their own boundaries around food, or the experience they had making it, it certainly holds a lot of emotional weight.

LD: We often see conflict being resolved quickly on our screens. For example, the 22-year-old talks seriously to dad about whether he’s accepting her new partner, and he sees the error of his ways. People don’t work like that, which can set up unrealistic expectations that I don’t particularly like as a family studies scholar, because we can’t expect easy resolutions. Change, and accommodation to change, takes time.

Part of the perfectionism and idealism we feel around Thanksgiving can come from media – not just sitcoms, but cooking shows and commercials too. They present these wonderful, picturesque dishes, and the reality is that our food might not even be warm all at the same time! It’s part of their business model, to present these images which make us aspire to more and to buy their product.

What they do get right, though, is that people come back for the holidays because they care so deeply about their families, and want to see them happy. Some people travel thousands of kilometers, and some families put a lot of pressure on everyone to come home for Thanksgiving. It’s certainly an important family ritual.

LD: Conflict is normal. But families are resilient, and most can weather that conflict. There May be anger, guilt and rejection for some time, but over time circumstances and attitudes change, and resolution unfolds.

Family dynamics are so central to how we feel, and it’s easy to be really hurt by someone close to us. But we have to put ourselves into their shoes, and consider their perspective. Does this person need time to adjust? Does this person have a poor memory and just isn’t remembering something that is important to me?

Trusting that over time things will probably resolve, even if we’re not happy with them right now, can go a long way.

LD: Lower your expectations. Don’t expect it to be perfect, because it’s too much pressure on you and your family.

We need to relieve the expectations we have of our families acting a certain way, because that’s not fair. People are their own individuals with their own histories and beliefs. Some of them May never mesh with our own, but it’s part of life! Accepting this can let us take responsibility for our own emotional state. We just have to be who we are.

If we can set a goal to experience rather than achieve perfection, that leaves more space for the good that is there. And there will be good. It May not be as joyful as we might have hoped, but that’s OK.

LD: Many families have rituals that bring them joy. The board games after dinner, the football game, the hike. These moments tend to bring us joy even if there May be disagreements throughout the day.

The holidays are also a chance to show your family how you have changed. It’s a chance to meet new family members. It’s an opportunity to make new memories.

Appreciate what is there, and the fact that you get to share time with the people you love. Even if there’s some conflict, we are all here together. Life can change very quickly, so try to appreciate it for what it is at that moment.
paragraphs: While Thanksgiving presents the opportunity to wind down, reconnect with family , and celebrate the holidays with those we love, it can also become a point of stress.

Whether it’s pressure to make the perfect meal or tensions that arise from family disagreements, conflict can turn our holiday expectations upside down. Lara Descartes, family studies professor in the Faculty of Health Sciences, explains what’s at the root of Thanksgiving tensions, and how we can navigate the challenges this upcoming season.

Lara Descartes (LD) : Expectations can be very high. Media and advertisements often present these lovely family holidays where everyone’s laughing, having a good time, sharing and appreciating one another. When reality doesn’t match that, it often leads to disappointment.

There can be a lot of pressure to present the perfect holiday: the perfect meal, perfect decorations, perfect harmony among family members. When you’re aiming for perfection, it always makes everything more stressful.

LD: There are so many sources of possible tension because holidays are symbolically important to us. We know that they’re cultural institutions: everyone is taking part, which can lead us to imagine that everyone else is doing it with more fun, more togetherness and more joy.

We also often see conflict around identity. A change of identity is hard for families to accept, which is why there can be tension when students return home. Thanksgiving is the first time back for many students since leaving in the summer. You’re returning from the university environment where you have your own identity, which has likely changed from the one you had in high school or the one you have in relation to your family.

Change is hard no matter what – whether it’s good or bad – and families May not react the way an individual wants. While we’re hoping for this wonderful return and to be embraced in the bosom of our family, everyone May need some time to adjust to big or little changes.

LD: They May not be small to the people involved. While the person who upset another May feel it was a small issue they can explain away, to the person at whom it was directed it can hold much more weight. For example, say somebody cooked the whole Thanksgiving meal – which can take days – and then everyone sits down and dad says, ‘boy, this is dry’. That would be very hurtful. The amount of labor and emotion going into this ritualized experience can make interactions more loaded than normal.

Things like food might seem small, but food is identity! It’s rooted in tradition and culture. Because the holidays centre around meals, it can definitely become a touchstone for conflict. Whether it’s people expressing their own boundaries around food, or the experience they had making it, it certainly holds a lot of emotional weight.

LD: We often see conflict being resolved quickly on our screens. For example, the 22-year-old talks seriously to dad about whether he’s accepting her new partner, and he sees the error of his ways. People don’t work like that, which can set up unrealistic expectations that I don’t particularly like as a family studies scholar, because we can’t expect easy resolutions. Change, and accommodation to change, takes time.

Part of the perfectionism and idealism we feel around Thanksgiving can come from media – not just sitcoms, but cooking shows and commercials too. They present these wonderful, picturesque dishes, and the reality is that our food might not even be warm all at the same time! It’s part of their business model, to present these images which make us aspire to more and to buy their product.

What they do get right, though, is that people come back for the holidays because they care so deeply about their families, and want to see them happy. Some people travel thousands of kilometers, and some families put a lot of pressure on everyone to come home for Thanksgiving. It’s certainly an important family ritual.

stories.title: Jessie Reyez, Drake to be honoured for songwriting at Socan Awards
stories.summary: Toronto - Jessie Reyez and Drake will be toasted with special achievement honours at the 2026 Socan Awards.
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Jessie Reyez and Drake will be toasted with special achievement honours at the 2026 Socan Awards.

The two Toronto hip-hop and R&B heavyweights are among the artists being celebrated at the annual gala for Canadian songwriters, composers and music publishers.

Reyez will receive the international achievement award for “representing Canada on the global stage” and “influencing music and culture with her talent.” The Canadian-Colombian artist has won several Juno Awards and collaborated with superstars including Eminem and Beyoncé.

Drake will claim his fifth consecutive award for songwriter of the year in the performer category for “his unmatched influence on music worldwide.”

The Toronto rap star made history earlier this year by shattering several Billboard records with his triple-album release, including the longstanding title previously held by Michael Jackson for most No. 1s by a solo male artist.

The Socan Awards will take place Oct. 26 at Rebel nightclub in Toronto, and will be hosted by actor Andrew Phung and TV personality Arisa Cox.

Socan, which stands for the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada, is a non-profit that manages licensing fees and protects the rights of homegrown songwriters.

Among other honourees this year are Toronto rapper Maestro Fresh Wes and producers Anthony Davis and Peter Davis for their 1989 hit “Let Your Backbone Slide.”

Socan says the song, which was the first single from a Canadian hip-hop artist to go gold in the country, is a “global success story.”

Quebec singer-songwriter Peter Peter will take home the global impact award for composing the original music for Crave’s hit hockey romance “Heated Rivalry.”

Calgary singer-songwriter-producer Jenna Andrews will receive the songwriter of the year award in the non-performer category for co-writing and co-producing several songs on the soundtrack for Netflix’s hit animated film “KPop Demon Hunters.”

Toronto’s Nathan Micay will get the breakout composer award for making waves by scoring Hbo’s hit high-finance drama “Industry.”

Victoria singer-songwriter Jade LeMac will be presented the breakout songwriter award for being “one of the most exciting new voices in Canadian music.”

All winners receive “The Socan,” a trophy that also functions as a musical instrument. Its five custom bronze crotales will be tuned this year to the notes from “Let Your Backbone Slide.”

Last month, Socan launched a lawsuit against U.S. artificial intelligence company Suno, alleging the AI music generator copied songs in its repertoire without permission or compensation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Rents in Canada have fallen for 24 consecutive months, report says
stories.summary: The average asking rent for all residential properties in Canada was $2,034 in September, down 4.2 per cent compared to the month in 2025.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Average rents across Canada fell for the 24th consecutive month, marking two full years of rent declines and one of the longest downturns for the Canadian rental market in recent history, a report by Rentals.CA and Urbanation said.

The average asking rent for all residential properties in Canada was $2,034 in September, down 4.2 per cent compared to the month in 2025. This marked the lowest level of average asking rents for September since 2022.

Average asking rents in Canada reached a record high of $2,202 in May 2024. After hitting $2,142 in September 2024, rents have steadily declined across the country.

Last month, rents were 7.3 per cent below September 2024 levels and 9.2 per cent below the peak of May 2024.

“Two straight years of falling rents is the longest downturn the Canadian rental market has seen in recent history,” said Shaun Hildebrand, president of Urbanation.

The key driver of falling rents is over-supply in key rental markets like Toronto and Vancouver, he added.

“Rents in both cities have trended higher over the past six months, and annual declines have narrowed significantly as renters come off the sidelines. Where Toronto and Vancouver go, the rest of the country follows,” Hildebrand said.

Condos saw the sharpest decline in rents, with rents falling to $2,052 for all condo types, a drop of 7.8 per cent compared to September 2025. Studio condos saw an even sharper decline, with a 9.6 per cent drop.

Other secondary housing units, such as houses and townhomes, saw rents fall by 7.4 per cent to $2,016.

Purpose-built rents remained the most resilient of all property types, down 2.7 per cent to $2,036.

stories.title: California man sentenced to 10 years in major Canada-U.S. drug trafficking conspiracy
stories.summary: According to court docs, Singh was identified as the leader of a conspiracy that coordinated large-scale drug transactions in Canada.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
A California man who led a cross-border drug trafficking operation involving cocaine, heroin, opium and ketamine has been sentenced to 10 years in federal prison and ordered to forfeit $2 million.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office announced that Parampreet Singh, 60, of Davis, Calif., was sentenced by a U.S. District Judge after pleading guilty to conspiring to distribute and possess with intent to distribute multiple controlled substances.

According to court documents, Singh was identified as the leader and organizer of a conspiracy that coordinated large-scale drug transactions in Canada. Prosecutors said Singh and several co-conspirators operated the scheme from California, using encrypted cellphone applications to arrange narcotics deals involving cocaine, heroin, opium and ketamine.

Authorities said Singh worked alongside co-defendants Ranvir Singh, 43, of Sacramento, Calif., and Amandeep Multani, 38, of Roseville, Calif., among others, to facilitate the drug transactions.

Between October 2020 and April 2021, the group coordinated sales to undercover officers totalling approximately 10 kilograms of cocaine, 1.5 kilograms of opium, two kilograms of ketamine and multiple heroin samples. The transactions generated approximately $637,600 CAD and $75,190 USD through deals conducted in Canada and Sacramento.

Prosecutors also alleged that between September 2020 and April 2021, Singh and his co-conspirators repeatedly offered to sell up to 100 kilograms of cocaine, 25 kilograms of heroin, 100 kilograms of opium and 200 kilograms of ketamine.

Singh pleaded guilty on Sept. 9, 2025.

The investigation was led by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), with assistance from Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, York Regional Police (YRP), the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), and the Placer County Special Investigations Unit.

One of Singh’s co-defendants, Multani, pleaded guilty on Dec. 13, 2022, and agreed to cooperate fully with U.S. authorities. He was sentenced to time served on Dec. 10, 2025, after spending more than four years and eight months in custody.

Meanwhile, Ranvir Singh was found guilty by a jury on Oct. 15, 2025, of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and ketamine and one count of cocaine distribution. He is scheduled to be sentenced on Dec. 1, 2026.

Federal prosecutors said Ranvir Singh faces a maximum statutory penalty of life imprisonment and a $10 million fine. Any sentence will ultimately be determined by the court after considering federal sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.

stories.title: Lotto Max jackpot climbs to $80M ahead of Thanksgiving holiday
stories.summary: The Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation said Wednesday millions were won in Tuesday’s draw, but that the big prize continues to grow.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The Lotto Max jackpot for the final draw before the Thanksgiving long weekend has climbed to $80 million.

The Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) said Wednesday millions were won in Tuesday’s draw, but that the big prize continues to grow.

With the $80 million jackpot up for grabs on Oct. 9, players will also have a chance to win an estimated 14 Maxmillions prizes worth $1 million each and 80 Maxplus prizes worth $100,000 each.

The OLG said that means $102 million in top prizes will be available for Friday’s draw.

Draws happen every Friday and Tuesday.

stories.title: Israeli flags set on fire in Toronto, police investigating as suspected hate-motivated attack
stories.summary: Police are investigating a suspected hate-motivated act following reports of Israeli flags being set alight in Toronto on Wednesday morning.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Police are investigating a suspected hate-motivated act following reports of several Israeli flags being set alight in Toronto on Wednesday morning.

Police have said that officers were called to the area of Sunrise Avenue and O’Connor Drive in North York at approximately 1:30 a.m.

Toronto Fire said crews were able to extinguish the outdoor fire at 65 Sunrise Avenue, which is the address for the Word of Faith International Christian Centre.

A police spokesperson confirmed to National Post that the incident is currently being investigated by TPS’ Hate Crime Unit. There were no reported injuries and no arrests have been made at this time.

It comes on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) and UJA Federation of Greater Toronto issued a joint statement on Wednesday, calling the incident “disturbing.”

“Faith International Christian Centre has stood with the Jewish community and with Israel. To see that solidarity answered with fire is a disturbing reminder that hatred does not stop with Jews. Increasingly, those who stand beside us are being targeted too,” the statement read.

It went on to say that Cija and UJA are “deeply grateful” for the “friendship and solidarity” from the Faith International Christian Centre, and calls on leaders at every level of government to condemn the attack and “confront the extremism that is making intimidation and violence increasingly commonplace.”

“When simply standing with the Jewish community carries a cost — when allies are intimidated, threatened, or attacked because they refuse to turn away — this is no longer only a Jewish problem,” the two organizations said. “It is a threat to the kind of country we all want Canada to be.”

Meanwhile, mayoral candidate and city councillor Brad Bradford commented on the incident in North York on social media, describing it in a post on X as “an act of intimidation.”

“I’m thinking today of Jewish families across Toronto who have spent 3 years watching this kind of thing move closer to their homes, their schools and their synagogues, and who are tired of being told it’s being taken seriously while it keeps happening,” he wrote.

“Hate directed at any community is a threat to every community, and the people responsible for this need to be found and charged,” Bradford added.

“We will continue to invest in keeping communities safe and strong and will take action until every Torontonian can practice their faith without fear,” she added.

And Toronto Police said in a statement regarding the Oct. 7 anniversary that there will be “an increased police presence today and in the coming days,” including at synagogues and other places of worship.

“We remain committed to working with communities across Toronto, addressing hate, and ensuring people are safe,” the statement continued.

stories.title: Weston family to buy British retailer Boots for $8.9-billion with Fairfax backing
stories.summary: Wittington Investments to acquire the drug-store chain from U.S. private equity fund; Fairfax to take significant stake
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
The Weston family is returning to British retailing by acquiring drug-store chain Boots for US$8.9-billion, including assumed debt, with financial backing from Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. FFH-T

The Toronto-based Weston family’s holding company, Wittington Investments Ltd., is buying the 1,800-store Boots chain from U.S. private equity fund Sycamore Partners, which acquired the British business as part of a US$24-billion leveraged buyout of U.S. drug-store company Walgreens in 2025.

Wittington is also buying out another billionaire family, headed by Stefano Pessina. Mr. Pessina is the former chair of Boots. He acquired the chain in 2007, then sold the majority of the company to Sycamore, while retaining an ownership stake.

Toronto-based asset manager Fairfax, led by value investor Prem Watsa, is backing Wittington’s investment by paying US$2.3-billon for a 50-per-cent stake in Boots. Wittington will have operating control of the chain.

Galen Weston, chairman of Wittington and Loblaw and CEO of holding company George Weston Ltd. WN-T , will become the chair of Boots after the acquisition closes.

“As Canada builds stronger ties around the globe, we are delighted to welcome the UK’s most iconic pharmacy, health, and beauty business into our group of companies,” Mr. Weston said in an e-mail.

“Once complete, we look forward to Boots both benefiting from, and contributing to our collective expertise in retail, beauty, and the growing role of pharmacists who are making care more accessible in our communities,” he said.

Wittington expects to close the Boots acquisition in the first quarter of 2027.

In the fiscal year ended Aug. 31, 2025, Boots’ revenue grew by 3.2 per cent to £7.5-billion ($14.1-billion,) according to the most recent filing available from the U.K. government’s Companies House . The retailer’s operating profit rose by nearly 30 per cent that year, to £355-million.

Fairfax’s Mr. Watsa said in a press release: “For many years, the Westons have grown and developed some of the most successful retail brands in Canada, including pharmacy and beauty, and we are confident Wittington will be an excellent steward of the Boots business.”

In Canada, Fairfax owns retailers Sporting Life Group and Sleep Country as part of a $110-billion investment portfolio.

Through Wittington, the Weston family controls publicly listed Canadian grocery giant Loblaw Companies Ltd. L-T , parent to Shoppers Drug Mart, and privately holds luxury retailer Holt Renfrew.

In addition to owning Canada’s largest pharmacy chain, the Weston family has long had a strategic focus on health care businesses. Wittington’s venture capital unit has invested in a number of startups in the space.

Those investments occasionally cross over into the Westons’ retail empire. For example, Wittington invested in digital startup League Inc., which built Loblaw’s PC Health app that launched in 2020. The app allows customers to manage prescriptions, and offers appointments for health services at its pharmacies – a growing part of the business.

Shoppers Drug Mart has invested in building more on-site clinics offering consultations on minor health conditions, and other services such as travel vaccinations and cholesterol screening.

Wittington occasionally introduces leaders from the technology startups it invests in to Loblaw executives, when it believes the services could help the retail business. That technological know-how could theoretically apply to Boots as well.

Boots chief executive officer Alex Baldock said in a press release the company plans to deepen its customer relationships under its new owners.

“For all of our social impact and commercial success to-date, the opportunity ahead is even greater,” Mr. Baldock said. “I look forward to making the most of that opportunity and building a world-class Boots.”

Boots owns one of Britain’s leading beauty brands, the No7 family, and will continue to invest in building its stable of products.

Boots has been working to refresh its store network, renovating 40 of its stores and 180 of its in-store cosmetics sections known as “beauty halls” in fiscal year 2025.

That is another area where the Westons’ retail experience could prove informative, since Shoppers Drug Mart has had considerable success expanding the “Beauty Boutique” sections of its stores. That product category brings in higher profit margins than other parts of the stores, and will likely be a priority for the Boots business to find growth.

Boots, like Shoppers, has a massive customer loyalty program with 17 million members and the new owners plan to invest in this part of the business. Loblaw’s PC Optimum loyalty program has 18 million members and is considered the strongest domestic brand in the sector.

In 2022, Wittington sold British department store chain Selfridges for approximately $6.9-billion after successfully turning around the business.

Boots was founded in 1849 in Nottingham, in central England, as an herbalist store, selling alternatives to traditional medicines. The founder, John Boot, turned over control to his son, who bult a retailer that dominates high streets across Britain.

Mr. Pessina has been an investor in Boots for two decades. In a press release, he said: “We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage.”

stories.title: Dog jumping into front seat causes car crash, driver charged: OPP
stories.summary: A 66-year-old man is facing charges for reportedly crashing his vehicle into a tree after a dog jumped into the front seat, Ontario Provincial Police say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 66-year-old man is facing charges for reportedly crashing his vehicle into a tree after a dog jumped into the front seat, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) say.

The OPP said officers were called to Kippen Road in Huron East just after 7 p.m. on Oct. 4 for reports of a single-vehicle crash.

Emergency services found a damaged SUV that had left the roadway and hit a tree stump.

The impact caused the airbags to deploy and left the vehicle inoperable. The driver was treated for minor injuries by paramedics at the scene.

“During the police investigation, it was discovered that a canine companion inside the vehicle had jumped into the front seat of the SUV, distracting the driver, who then lost control of the vehicle, left the roadway, and collided with the tree,” police said in a news release.

The 66-year-old driver from St. Thomas was charged with careless driving under the Highway Traffic Act.

Police are reminding motorists who travel with animals that they need to ensure the driver of the vehicle can safely operate it without distraction and that they are not obstructed or crowded by an animal.

“Failing to do so can result in a loss of control of their vehicle, obstructed views from the driver’s seat, injury to themselves, other vehicle occupants, and the animal(s),” police said.

“Please do your part to ensure animals are secured with seatbelt harnesses or are safely behind a vehicle pet barrier.”

stories.title: $14 milk and $64 diapers: The reality facing some families as Canada rolls out groceries benefit
stories.summary: Eligible Canadians have begun receiving their second payment under the new Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, but some say the extra money does little to ease the pressure of rising food and household costs.
stories.author: Tammy Ibrahimpoor
stories.content:
Eligible Canadians have begun receiving their second payment under the new Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit , but some say the extra money does little to ease the pressure of rising food and household costs.

The benefit, formerly known as the GST/HST credit, provides quarterly payments to lower-income Canadians based on factors including income, marital status and the number of children in a household.

A single person without children can receive up to $679 annually, while households with four or more children can receive up to $1,826.

CTVNews.CA asked readers if the benefit helped their families make ends meet. Through email responses, some said it was not enough to make a meaningful difference, while others said they do not qualify, despite facing financial pressure.

‘Spit in the ocean’

For some seniors and people living on disability benefits, the extra money is welcome, but quickly disappears.

“This barely helps me at all,” Allen Mayes of Armstrong, B.C., wrote, adding that the maximum annual benefit for a single person amounts to only a handful of grocery trips for him.

The 73-year-old said he lives on both the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and Old Age Security (OAS), and spends about $150 every two weeks on basic food.

“(The payment is) less than 20 per cent of my basic food for the year. That’s not a drop in the bucket — it’s spit in the ocean,” Mayes wrote. He said he relies on inexpensive staples such as beans, frozen peas and corn, rice and flour, and bakes his own bread to save money.

Guy Helwig, of Southampton, Ont., said the benefit helps “somewhat,” but argued that rising costs extend far beyond groceries.

Helwig, who said he is retired and living on a fixed income, pointed to higher rent, property taxes, water and sewer rates, as well as phone, cable and internet costs.

“People are drowning in higher bills!” he wrote.

‘Tired of never being heard’

Jodie McAuley of Vancouver Island said the amount she received is far too little to make a significant difference.

“$127 for groceries for a senior is just sad,” she wrote. “If you do the math, that works out to $1.41 a day between payments. A can of soup is more expensive.”

It’s a similar situation for Liz Carter.

“While I am appreciative of any extra money I get it really is just ‘a drop in the bucket,’” the native of Red Deer, Alta., wrote.

The 72-year-old said she has little food in her fridge and pantry, and has had to cut back on what she eats because of rising prices.

“I primarily live on canned light tuna and frozen grilled chicken strips,” she wrote.

Mike Van Damme, of Sarnia, Ont., said he receives about $1,200 a month through CPP.

He said people living on disability benefits are struggling to afford basic necessities and deserve more dignity.

“I never asked to be born with a genetic defect that affected my heart,” he wrote. “We all talk about affordability, but little is done, and people on disability are tired of never being heard.”

‘I feel the government left us out’

For some readers, geography and circumstance adds another layer to the problem.

Arlene Campbell, who is from Patuanak, Sask., said residents in her northern Saskatchewan community do not have access to large grocery chains such as Walmart or Superstore.

“We have to buy from Northern Store, and the price of freight is included in the prices, which (comes at an) extremely higher cost,” Campbell wrote.

She said a jug of milk can cost nearly $14, while a box of diapers can go for $64.

While Campbell appreciates the grocery rebate, she said it’s ”not much of a benefit.”

Not everyone who responded to the callout receives the benefit.

Cindy Hitch, based out of Winnipeg, said she was laid off in 2025 after her employer went bankrupt and has been living on employment insurance.

She said she believes the benefit calculation, based on her previous income, has left people like her behind.

With files from CTV News’ Daniel Otis

“People are drowning in higher bills!” he wrote.
‘Tired of never being heard’
Jodie McAuley of Vancouver Island said the amount she received is far too little to make a significant difference.
“$127 for groceries for a senior is just sad,” she wrote. “If you do the math, that works out to $1.41 a day between payments. A can of soup is more expensive.”
It’s a similar situation for Liz Carter.
“While I am appreciative of any extra money I get it really is just ‘a drop in the bucket,’” the native of Red Deer, Alta., wrote.
The 72-year-old said she has little food in her fridge and pantry, and has had to cut back on what she eats because of rising prices.
“I primarily live on canned light tuna and frozen grilled chicken strips,” she wrote.
Mike Van Damme, of Sarnia, Ont., said he receives about $1,200 a month through CPP.
He said people living on disability benefits are struggling to afford basic necessities and deserve more dignity.
“I never asked to be born with a genetic defect that affected my heart,” he wrote. “We all talk about affordability, but little is done, and people on disability are tired of never being heard.”
‘I feel the government left us out’
For some readers, geography and circumstance adds another layer to the problem.
Arlene Campbell, who is from Patuanak, Sask., said residents in her northern Saskatchewan community do not have access to large grocery chains such as Walmart or Superstore.
“We have to buy from Northern Store, and the price of freight is included in the prices, which (comes at an) extremely higher cost,” Campbell wrote.
She said a jug of milk can cost nearly $14, while a box of diapers can go for $64.
While Campbell appreciates the grocery rebate, she said it’s ”not much of a benefit.”

stories.title: Canadian buoy found on shore of Irish island after journey across Atlantic
stories.summary: Officials in northwestern Ireland say they're working to recover a large Canadian buoy that floated across the Atlantic Ocean and washed up on a coastal island.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
By Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press

Posted October 7, 2026 8:32 am

Officials in northwestern Ireland say they’re working to recover a large Canadian buoy that floated across the Atlantic Ocean and washed up on a coastal island.

A news release from Mayo County Council says the mariner marker, weighing in at roughly 3.5 tonnes, came ashore on Achill Island, known for its rugged mountains and bright sandy beaches.

It says council was told by the Canadian Coast Guard that its buoys, while “very friendly,” have quite the habit of drifting far from home.

The council is looking to recover the buoy so as to prevent it from floating away and becoming a hazard to vessels or coastal infrastructure.

The release says the unusual visitor to the island can carry a navigation light and make a distinctive wave-powered whistling sound to alert nearby vessels.

The council adds the discovery is a lighthearted reminder of Mayo County’s connection to Canada through generations of emigration, before demanding a blithe bit of a ransom.

“Should the Canadians wish to see their buoy again, they May have to make a special trip to Mayo to collect it,” the release said.

stories.title: FBI depicts Tumbler Ridge shooter’s guns, including ‘SKS’ once confiscated by RCMP
stories.summary: An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter gives new details about the guns that May have been used.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter for months provides extensive new details about the guns that May have been used in the attack, and how the teenage killer May have obtained them.

The complaint sworn by an FBI agent in Seattle says James Bryant, who is charged with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country, told officers that Jesse Van Rootselaar stole firearms and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and hid them in her room “in preparation for a mass shooting.”

4:39 Decision not to identify firearm in Tumbler Ridge shooting not political: Public safety minister

It also says in claims not tested in court that 18-year-old Van Rootselaar told Bryant in online chats that she had convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf, and that one of the weapons she intended to use had been returned after previously being confiscated by the RCMP.

Van Rootselaar killed eight victims on Feb. 10, including her mother and brother at their home, and five students and an educational assistant at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The RCMP criminal investigation into the shooting is ongoing, despite Van Rootselaar having killed herself at the school.

2:14 American charged in connection with Tumbler Ridge school shooting

Assistant RCMP Commissioner Elija Rain, who is acting commanding officer in B.C., says “investigators have made substantial progress in the criminal investigation.”

Rain says in a statement that the RCMP’s release of information about the case has recently been limited “because of the need to ensure our investigative theories and actions were not compromised.”

The FBI complaint released on Tuesday says Van Rootselaar told Bryant on the Discord platform that she possessed a 3D-printed foregrip, firearm magazines and a “switch” device for an SKS rifle, which the FBI says likely referred to a “machine-gun conversion device.”

Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, Wash., allegedly told the FBI that Van Rootselaar “ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

A photo in the complaint depicts a person the FBI says is Van Rootselaar, posing on their knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings, while holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic sight on the morning of the attack.

On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, decorated in the blue, white and pink bands of the transgender Pride flag.

Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Bryant identifies as female.

The FBI says that in December 2025, Van Rootselaar discussed a gun she said she was planning to use in the attack.

“The police knocked my SKS sights off zero a lil bit when they roughly confiscated it, so the gun has been hitting high and to the left,” she allegedly told Bryant.

Adjusting the sights would be “a lot of work and I May end up doing my plan with a gun with sights that are super off,” Van Rootselaar allegedly said, before adding “I’m sure I can still do fine.”

3:06 New details in U.S. indictment about Tumbler Ridge shooting

Another photo shows a Canuck-branded shotgun that Van Rootselaar said would also be used in the attack.

It is decorated with a sticker, also in blue, white and pink.

Bryant allegedly tells Van Rootselaar: “Love the stickers … stickers would be so funny to be seen in photos of the incident.”
