stories.title: Polytechnique looks to revive nuclear studies as Quebec’s only reactor turns 50
stories.summary: "Slowpoke" is a suitable name for Quebec's only working nuclear reactor. It only produces about 20 kilowatts of thermal energy, or enough to power six or seven toasters.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie
stories.content:
“Slowpoke” is a suitable name for Quebec’s only working nuclear reactor. It only produces about 20 kilowatts of thermal energy , or enough to power six or seven toasters.

But scientists and administrators at Polytechnique Montréal hope the reactor, which turns 50 this year, will help spur a revival of nuclear science research in a province where it’s been slowly fizzling out.

Slowpoke, which stands for Safe Low-Power Kritical Experiment, looks nothing like the images most people would associate with a nuclear reactor. It’s described as a “sealed-container in-pool type research reactor,” and, as the description suggests, it sits in a deep pool, with no cooling towers. A steady mechanical hum fills a small room in Polytechnique where only the top of the opening can be seen, flanked by orange-painted concrete blocks.

Over the years, it’s been used both for research purposes and to train generations of aspiring scientists, said Nicolas Godbout, the director of engineering physics at Polytechnique Montréal.

“I think that our biggest legacy is the hundreds of highly qualified personnel that have been formed, the expertise,” he said. “And we see a real need to redevelop and ensure that this expertise continues.”

Continuing that expertise will take some work, however.

Fifty years ago, Canada was “pretty much in a leadership position” in the field of nuclear engineering, Godbout said.

The engineering school was also a big part of that expertise, with personnel supporting operations at the now-decommissioned Gentilly-2 nuclear power facility in Bécancour, Que., and contributing research used to design the country’s Candu reactors.

But today, the generation of researchers who once led the field are “pretty much all retired,” Godbout said.

Foutse Khomh, vice-president of research and innovation at Polytechnique Montréal, says the school is taking steps to reinvigorate its nuclear studies.

The university is receiving a $1-million donation over five years from the engineering company AtkinsRéalis in order to create a new nuclear engineering research chair, and Khomh is hoping more industry players will also contribute.

Even as some sectors of society remain opposed, there is a renewed interest in nuclear energy, driven by growing energy needs and climate targets. That includes in Canada, where Ontario, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick and Alberta signed a plan to develop small reactors in 2022. Last month, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe announced he’s looking at building two large reactors somewhere in the province’s northwest by 2042.

But Khomh points out that nuclear research has uses in a wide variety of fields, beyond energy.

“There are a lot of medical applications,” he said. “You also have applications, for example, in mineral exploration and exploitation and so on.”

Regardless of what energy choices are made, “our role as a university is to make sure that we train the engineers that will be ready to answer the call of the society,” he said, adding that the school hopes to hire five professors in the coming years.

The experts at Polytechnique say the Slowpoke reactor can play an important role in research and training, despite its age.

The reactor is currently used to provide quality assurance for companies by measuring the elements in different products or materials through a process called neutron activation analysis, reactor manager Darren Hall says.

He explains that samples are placed into the reactor, where they become lightly radioactive. They are then removed and placed on a detector. By looking at the “energy signature” coming from the radiation, researchers can then quantify the different elements in the material, Hall says.

“Kind of like when you’re looking at your cereal box at home and you look at the side ingredients and you see sodium, 10 per cent,” he said. “We essentially do the same thing.”

As examples, he said the process can be used to detect materials such as arsenic in recycled plastics, or to measure the presence of critical minerals in a mining sample, he said. It can also be used for medical purposes.

Hall says the low-power reactor is also designed with safety features, including shutting off on its own if it reaches a certain temperature.

While Polytechnique’s reactor is turning 50, Hall says it’s far from the oldest in Canada. In comparison, McMaster University’s reactor in Hamilton has been operating since 1959.

“We still have about 25 years left of fuel, so we could operate for the next 25 years,” Hall said.

stories.title: A jerky start as home buyers and sellers in the GTA hit the brakes
stories.summary: U.S. trade tensions, renewed conflict in the Middle East and the Federal Reserve’s rate hike are unsettling consumers again, agent says
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Angst is permeating the Toronto-area real estate market this fall as buyers and sellers hit pause in September.

Sellers are reluctant to list if they won’t fetch the price they are hoping for, says Pritesh Parekh, real estate agent with Century 21 Legacy. Buyers are hesitant to sign a deal if prices have farther to fall.

Mr. Parekh says escalating trade tensions with the United States, renewed conflict in the Middle East and the U.S. Federal Reserve’s interest rate hike are some of the factors unsettling consumers again.

“The conversation has changed from affordability to urgency,” Mr. Parekh says. “Is this urgent or not?”

Sales in the Greater Toronto Area dropped 9 per cent in September from the same month last year, while new listings fell 14.4 per cent in the same period.

The average price declined 5.1 per cent last month from September, 2025, to stand at $1,006,409.

Sales last month decreased 5.2 per cent on a seasonally adjusted basis from the tepid pace in August.

While rare properties sold with multiple offers, many sellers failed to land a deal on nights reserved for viewing offers.

Mr. Parekh recently worked with one set of buyers who were in no rush to move, but they were willing to pounce if they found a larger house at a tempting price.

A renovated three-bedroom house near Christie Street and St. Clair Avenue West was listed with an asking price above the $1.9-million mark early this year, then reduced to $1.8-million.

The semi-detached house at 150 Rushton Rd. was then relisted with an asking price of $1.65-million and an offer deadline.

The house was clearly a cut above the properties the couple had been looking at in that price range, says Mr. Parekh, and the clients were keen on the location in the area near Wychwood Park.

Home Run: With a $1.5-million budget for a new home, what did this expecting Toronto couple buy?

Still, the couple was reluctant to pay a large amount above asking and they didn’t want to waste time with a lowball offer.

Mr. Parekh recommended that the couple submit a bid at the price they were willing to pay without worrying about the competition.

No rival bidders came to the table, says Mr. Parekh, whose clients secured the house for $1.675-million, or $25,000 above asking.

He figures the listing might have appeared stale to some buyers because the property had languished at higher prices.

The deadline for submitting bids likely discouraged house hunters who figured the homeowners were expecting a large premium to the asking price.

“All of these factors lined up to us being the only ones who put in an offer.”

He notes that the original asking price was not a glaring misjudgment because a comparable home in the area had recently sold above $1.9-million.

“This is a common story in 2026,” he says of the vicissitudes of the market.

Mortgage broker Leah Zlatkin, an expert for LowestRates.CA, says buyers are tussling with tough decisions at the moment. She receives many calls from clients who have their financing lined up but wonder if home prices in Ontario have reached bottom after a lengthy downturn.

“I do have people who are preapproved and have been preapproved for two years. They call me every single week and say, ‘do you think we’re at the bottom yet?’”

Ms. Zlatkin points out that recoveries in real estate are rarely V-shaped and the market can remain flat for some time before a renewed upswing.

Values have decreased by more than 25 per cent from the heights of 2022 for many properties in the GTA. That dynamic often provides an opportunity for existing homeowners to move up because a larger buyer pool typically supports the value of entry-level homes more than those in higher price brackets.

In today’s uncertain environment, many people who have the option to trade are cautious about taking the leap, she says.

Meanwhile, Ms. Zlatkin points out, fixed-term mortgages have been getting more expensive in recent weeks, and she expects that trend to continue based on rising yields for long-term bonds, which in turn influence the rates that lenders set.

Mortgage rates for loans with fixed terms of three or five years have recently been hovering around 4.24 per cent at the low end, says Ms. Zlatkin, but mainstream lenders have been offering rates closer to 5 per cent.

Ms. Zlatkin says some buyers are holding off because they figure they May get a lower home price or mortgage rate in the future, but that’s an unpredictable outcome.

Buyers who are in a stable financial position are likely better off jumping in when they find the right house, in her opinion.

“The lowest price possible and lowest mortgage rate might not line up.”

Homes have been sitting on the market for longer stretches in many areas and price brackets, and many sellers with properties listed at the moment need to sell.

People with a down payment saved up have a chance to buy at a lower price, she points out.

“They have a huge opportunity to negotiate,” she says, adding that motivated sellers might be willing to take less than they were hoping for just to get a property sold.

Mr. Parekh says the uneven results are making many potential sellers wary.

Homeowners who have bought in recent years are asking if they can sell for more than they paid, Mr. Parekh says.

Those who have had time to build up equity question whether trading up to a new property is worthwhile.

“They can trade up – but should they? There are a lot of doubts.”

The uncertainty arises from “what ifs” in the macroeconomic outlook, says Mr. Parekh, as people ponder what would happen if they lose their job or interest rates rise or real estate prices continue to decline.

Long-time owners, meanwhile, are still holding out for a turnaround after prices entered a slump in the first quarter of 2022.

Last year at this time many people delayed listing as they gambled that the market would improve. But the pace of new listings has slowed even more because many homeowners figure they won’t fetch the price they want, Mr. Parekh says.

Mr. Parekh is hearing from some clients who are prepared to move but they have put off listing until early 2027.

“Now it’s even slower, and there is even more uncertainty, so I think people are waiting.”

stories.title: Sellers resigned to getting less than they paid for Hamilton home
stories.summary: Two-bedroom bungalow with an in-law suite sells for $13,900 below the asking price
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
133 Beland Ave. S., Hamilton

Asking price: $574,900 (June, 2026)

Selling price: $561,000 (June, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $580,000 (July, 2021); $175,000 (October, 2006)

Taxes: $4,422 (2026)

Days on the market: 11

Listing agents: Michael St. Jean and John Martin, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

Buyers’ agent: Michael St. Jean, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

Considering rising supply levels and declining property values around this two-bedroom bungalow in Hamilton, agent Michael St. Jean knew it was unlikely it would sell for the amount his clients paid when they bought it at the height of the market in 2021. He was frank with the sellers, who agreed to an asking price that was $5,100 less than what they had paid.

“Looking at the current market and comparable sales in the neighbourhood, we wanted to be realistic,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“We had to keep in mind we had some competition. In this neighbourhood, the inventory level was standard, although compared to three or four years ago, it’s higher.”

Properties were taking 30 to 45 days to sell on average, but this roughly 60-year-old bungalow was a hit with buyers who Mr. St. Jean was already working with in their house hunt. Within two weeks, the house was sold for $561,000 – $13,900 below the asking price.

“The buyers were looking for a bit, and when this one popped up, they fell in love pretty quickly with the location, the basement in-law suite and the updates that had been done,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“It worked for them.”

This brick bungalow has 917 square feet of living space, including an eat-in kitchen, living and dining rooms, two bedrooms and one bathroom.

The basement was recently refinished with two bedrooms and a recreation area, plus a kitchen, bathroom and new laundry machines.

The roof and heating and cooling systems were replaced six years ago.

A garage and private driveway are on the 40- by 100-foot lot.

“It’s very close to Red Hill [Valley] Parkway and you can get onto the QEW to go to Niagara, Halton/Peel/Toronto area pretty quickly,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“You’re downtown, but not downtown, kind of tucked away, very close to the escarpment and Stoney Creek.”

stories.title: Saskatchewan real-estate regulator and province’s realtors at odds over disciplinary decision
stories.summary: Realtor association calls for overhaul of regulator over ‘wholly inadequate’ sanctions and suspensions for two local realtors who breached provincial and commission rules
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
A disciplinary decision related to a multimillion-dollar real-estate scandal in Saskatchewan has kicked off a war of words between the provincial regulator and the professional realtor association.

Saskatchewan Realtors Association (SRA) chief executive Chris Guérette is calling for an inquiry and overhaul of the Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission over what she called “wholly inadequate” sanctions and suspensions for two local realtors who breached provincial and commission rules.

The two men, Paul Chavady and Jerry Hallgrimson, are business partners who performed key roles for Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

“Real estate is built on trust,” Ms. Guérette said in an e-mail to her association’s members on Oct. 1, criticizing the penalties faced by Mr. Chavady and Mr. Hallgrimson. “That trust depends on consumers knowing that the people participating in our profession are held to meaningful standards of ethics, accountability and transparency, and that there are meaningful consequences when those standards are breached.”

According to consent agreements released on Oct. 1, the real-estate regulator found that on 67 occasions, Mr. Chavady and Mr. Hallgrimson violated its own bylaws and the provincial Real Estate Act by failing to represent the interests of buyers when they were acting in dual agency for both buyer and seller. Consent agreements are typically a substitute for formal hearings and judgments, and are negotiated with participation from those facing the allegations.

The consent agreements detailed dozens more violations related to failing to remove conditions on sales contracts, and in one case, failing to disclose the presence of asbestos in a home they sold in dual agency.

The two realtors are each required to pay $100,000 in cumulative fines to the commission and serve a six-month suspension. Mr. Hallgrimson’s suspension begins immediately, but Ms. Guérette noted Mr. Chavady’s suspension does not begin until six months later in March. She said this allows at least one of the two business partners to continue practising real estate while the other is suspended.

“What the SRA states to be a ‘wholly inadequate response’ are the most punitive sanctions on record in Saskatchewan,” the regulator’s executive director and registrar Aaron Tetu said in a statement on Oct. 2, responding to Ms. Guérette’s concerns. “The evidence demonstrated that Mr. Chavady and Mr. Hallgrimson’s conduct constituted a complete lack of basic professional duties and representation but fell short of demonstrating criminality.”

In an e-mail to The Globe and Mail, Mr. Tetu said that Saskatchewan’s legislation does not require proof of criminality to permanently revoke the licence of a realtor. He said the six-month, staggered suspensions fell “within the range of reasonableness for the hearing panel.” He suggested the negotiated agreement was a better outcome than a hearing, given the large amount of evidence in the case that could have taken more time to sort through “and May have yielded a less predictable result.”

Before its collapse, Epic Alliance bought and sold more than 700 homes in Saskatoon and North Battleford, Sask., with funds borrowed from investors. No one has been charged criminally. However, the two founders, Rochelle Laflamme and Alisa Thompson, agreed to a settlement in 2024 with the province’s Financial and Consumer Affairs Authority to pay $300,000 in fines and accept a 20-year ban on trading or working in securities.

Mr. Chavady and Mr. Hallgrimson were key players in the Fund-a-Flip and Hassle-Free Landlord programs offered to investors by Epic Alliance. According to a report from bankruptcy trustee Ernst & Young Inc., investors gave Epic Alliance $170-million to buy rental properties in Saskatoon and North Battleford between 2014 and 2021. That investment was mainly in the form of mortgages that were “in excess of the properties’ purchase price in order to provide funding to renovate the properties.” The company collected more than $14-million in excess mortgage money.

Of the 700 homes, about 280 Fund-a-Flip properties were sold to other Epic Alliance investors for $72.6-million, typically with a conventional mortgage and 20-per-cent down payment from the buyers, who were represented by the same agent as the sellers. The 67 dual-agency sales referred to in the regulator’s disciplinary order were from this total.

According to EY , most of those properties sold as Hassle-Free landlord properties had received minimal renovations. In one case, it could find only $824 worth of renovation costs spent on a home purchased for $198,000 that was appraised for $265,000 one year later, even though “interior pictures of the kitchen and bathrooms showed outdated appliances, countertops and cupboards which were not indicative of a renovation occurring.”

The same day that home was listed, it was sold to an Epic investor for $260,000 – a $62,000 gain after $824 in renovations. The listing agents received $1,700 for the sale.

“This was a big deal, and I’m still waiting for someone to do something about it … to make sure it doesn’t happen again,” said lawyer Mike Russell, who represented 120 Epic Alliance investors through the court-ordered insolvency of the company. The investors collectively lost about $10-million, Mr. Russell said. He said the company had almost no money left to recover for his clients.

Ms. Guérette expressed frustration that the regulator’s consent agreements did not name Epic Alliance as the party that the two men dealt with, referring to the company only as “InvestCo.”

“The decision doesn’t say Epic Alliance, but it’s common knowledge in Saskatchewan. It is a failure of that consent order that it’s not very clear,” she said in an interview.

Mr. Chavady confirmed that the regulator had agreed to leave out the company’s name in the consent agreements. Speaking on behalf of himself and Mr. Hallgrimson, he said it was unfair to tie them to Epic Alliance, and disputed that the penalties were light. “It’s been quite a nightmare for us. Frankly, when weighed against what’s been published and what’s there, I would say it’s borderline heavy-handed,” he said in an interview.

Ms. Guérette said her association has moved quickly to close a loophole in its own rules that would have allowed either of the realtors to access its services and tools as “administrative assistant and business partner accounts (non-members)” while a suspension was pending.

Ms. Guérette said the real estate commission needs an overhaul so it can act more quickly and effectively on disciplinary matters. “You cannot have a weak structure and culture at the top and expect to have a strong corporation,” she said.

Editor’s note: Due to incorrect information provided by the source, a statement attributed to the Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission’s Aaron Tetu stated that Saskatchewan’s legislation requires proof of criminality to permanently revoke the licence of a realtor. Mr. Tetu advised the Globe after publication that proof of criminality is not required to permanently revoke the licence of a realtor.

Of the 700 homes, about 280 Fund-a-Flip properties were sold to other Epic Alliance investors for $72.6-million, typically with a conventional mortgage and 20-per-cent down payment from the buyers, who were represented by the same agent as the sellers. The 67 dual-agency sales referred to in the regulator’s disciplinary order were from this total.

According to EY , most of those properties sold as Hassle-Free landlord properties had received minimal renovations. In one case, it could find only $824 worth of renovation costs spent on a home purchased for $198,000 that was appraised for $265,000 one year later, even though “interior pictures of the kitchen and bathrooms showed outdated appliances, countertops and cupboards which were not indicative of a renovation occurring.”
The same day that home was listed, it was sold to an Epic investor for $260,000 – a $62,000 gain after $824 in renovations. The listing agents received $1,700 for the sale.

“This was a big deal, and I’m still waiting for someone to do something about it … to make sure it doesn’t happen again,” said lawyer Mike Russell, who represented 120 Epic Alliance investors through the court-ordered insolvency of the company. The investors collectively lost about $10-million, Mr. Russell said. He said the company had almost no money left to recover for his clients.
Ms. Guérette expressed frustration that the regulator’s consent agreements did not name Epic Alliance as the party that the two men dealt with, referring to the company only as “InvestCo.”
“The decision doesn’t say Epic Alliance, but it’s common knowledge in Saskatchewan. It is a failure of that consent order that it’s not very clear,” she said in an interview.

Mr. Chavady confirmed that the regulator had agreed to leave out the company’s name in the consent agreements. Speaking on behalf of himself and Mr. Hallgrimson, he said it was unfair to tie them to Epic Alliance, and disputed that the penalties were light. “It’s been quite a nightmare for us. Frankly, when weighed against what’s been published and what’s there, I would say it’s borderline heavy-handed,” he said in an interview.

Ms. Guérette said her association has moved quickly to close a loophole in its own rules that would have allowed either of the realtors to access its services and tools as “administrative assistant and business partner accounts (non-members)” while a suspension was pending.

Ms. Guérette said the real estate commission needs an overhaul so it can act more quickly and effectively on disciplinary matters. “You cannot have a weak structure and culture at the top and expect to have a strong corporation,” she said.

Mr. Tetu advised the Globe after publication that proof of criminality is not required to permanently revoke the licence of a realtor.

stories.title: Portion of Highway 3 reopens after crash involving police cruiser
stories.summary: A collision involving a police cruiser and a pickup truck closed a section of Highway 3 for several hours Tuesday evening.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A collision involving a police cruiser and a pickup truck closed a section of Highway 3 in Elgin County for several hours Tuesday evening.

Police said the crash occurred on Highway 3 between Heritage Line and Springer Hill Road. Initial reports indicated a three-vehicle collision, but investigators later confirmed the incident involved two vehicles, a police cruiser and a pickup truck.

One person was transported to hospital as a precaution.

The collision forced the closure of Highway 3 in both directions while emergency crews responded and investigators examined the scene. The roadway remained closed for approximately three hours before reopening around 9:20 p.m.

Police said the investigation remains ongoing. No further details have been released.

stories.title: Buyers in search of affordable homes willing to make trade-offs, survey finds
stories.summary: Amid market slowdown, Re/Max survey says 65% of Canadians are open to making concessions
stories.author: Daniel Johnson
stories.content:
Canadians are willing to make compromises to afford a home that better meets their needs, a new survey from Re/Max finds.

The survey, released Wednesday, said 65 per cent of respondents would compromise in at least one way to afford a larger or more suitable place to live. Such compromises might include living further away from city centres or choosing an older home that May need renovations.

“Rather than giving up on home ownership, Canadians are making different choices about how to get there. For some, that means looking outside their current community or reconsidering the type of home they buy,” Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said in a news release.

“For others, it means making different financial choices. Buyers are identifying what matters most and where they have room to be flexible.”

The survey found that 63 per cent indicated they would relocate for a home that better fits their needs, including 47 per cent who said they would move up to an hour from the community they currently live in.

Re/Max said the report comes amid a slowdown for the housing market. Data from its own brokers and agents shows home sales saw annual declines in 81 per cent of markets that were analyzed over the first half of the year. During the period, average home prices increased across 56 per cent of markets.

Slower sales and more choice in certain markets could provide more time to compare properties, Re/Max said, allowing buyers to keep focused on their top priorities.

“The market has not become easy for buyers, but in many regions, it is allowing for a more deliberate purchasing process,” said Kottick in the release.

“That matters for people who are already rethinking location, property type or condition to make the numbers work. More time and choice can help buyers compare their options and understand where their budget goes further without feeling like they have to compromise.”

Conditions favourable to buyers are also more common than anticipated heading into the year, Re/Max said, with 32 per cent of markets analyzed currently in buyers’ favour, compared with 15.2 per cent a year earlier.

Canadians were also willing to make trade-offs beyond the property itself in order to afford a home, Re/Max found. Forty-one per cent of respondents said they would reduce discretionary spending, like travel and dining out, while 24 per cent said they would extend their amortization period.

Seventeen per cent would take on a second job or another source of income to afford a home. Another 17 per cent said they would delay retirement or other longer-term savings.

The online survey was conducted by Leger between July 17 and July 19, and responses were taken from 1,532 Canadian adults.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

stories.title: FBI complaint depicts Tumbler Ridge shooter’s guns and how it May have been obtained
stories.summary: Killer told Washington state suspect on the Discord platform that she possessed a 3D-printed foregrip, firearm magazines and a ‘switch’ device for an SKS rifle
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter for months provides extensive new details about the guns that May have been used in the attack, and how the teenage killer May have obtained them.

The complaint sworn by an FBI agent in Seattle says James Bryant, who is charged with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country, told officers that Jesse Van Rootselaar stole firearms and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and hid them in her room “in preparation for a mass shooting.”

It also says in claims not tested in court that 18-year-old Ms. Van Rootselaar told Ms. Bryant in online chats that she had convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf, and that one of the weapons she intended to use had been returned after previously being confiscated by the RCMP.

Ms. Van Rootselaar killed eight victims on Feb. 10, including her mother and brother at their home, and five students and an educational assistant at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

The RCMP criminal investigation into the shooting is ongoing, despite Ms. Van Rootselaar having killed herself at the school.

Assistant RCMP Commissioner Elija Rain, who is acting commanding officer in B.C., says “investigators have made substantial progress in the criminal investigation.”

Commissioner Rain said in a statement that the RCMP’s release of information about the case has recently been limited “because of the need to ensure our investigative theories and actions were not compromised.”

The FBI complaint released on Tuesday says Ms. Van Rootselaar told Ms. Bryant on the Discord platform that she possessed a 3-D printed foregrip, firearm magazines and a “switch” device for an SKS rifle, which the FBI says likely referred to a “machine-gun conversion device.”

Ms. Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, Wash., allegedly told the FBI that Ms. Van Rootselaar “ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

A photo in the complaint depicts a person the FBI says is Ms. Van Rootselaar, posing on their knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings, while holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic sight on the morning of the attack.

On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, decorated in the blue, white and pink bands of the transgender Pride flag.

Ms. Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Ms. Bryant identifies as female.

The FBI says that in December, 2025, Ms. Van Rootselaar discussed a gun she said she was planning to use in the attack.

It also says in claims not tested in court that 18-year-old Ms. Van Rootselaar told Ms. Bryant in online chats that she had convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf, and that one of the weapons she intended to use had been returned after previously being confiscated by the RCMP.
Ms. Van Rootselaar killed eight victims on Feb. 10, including her mother and brother at their home, and five students and an educational assistant at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School.

stories.title: Matthews scores OT winner as Maple Leafs come back to beat Predators 5-4
stories.summary: McKenna also picked up an assist on Tavares' goal for his first professional point. Nylander chipped in two assists and Roslovic added one.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Auston Matthews scored at 4:46 of a chaotic overtime and added three assists in regulation as the Toronto Maple Leafs erased a 3-0 deficit to defeat the Nashville Predators 5-4 on Tuesday.

Matthews buried a rebound after William Nylander took the puck to the net in the extra period to end a wild night at Scotiabank Arena.

Nylander, No. 1 overall pick Gavin McKenna — with his first in the NHL — John Tavares and Jack Roslovic had the other goals for Toronto (2-2-0), which got 21 saves from Anthony Stolarz.

McKenna took a pass from Matthews and ripped his first in the NHL upstairs on Saros at 14:31 of the second before dropping to one knee in celebration. The 18-year-old also picked up an assist on Tavares’ goal for his first professional point. Nylander chipped in two assists and Roslovic added one.

Steven Stamkos scored twice to move into 17th place on the NHL’s all-time list for Nashville (1-1-1), while Nils Hoglander added two of his own. Juuse Saros made 33 stops. Filip Forsberg chipped in a pair of assists.

Stamkos opened the scoring at 7:13 of the first period on a power play after Stolarz made a couple of huge stops. Nashville doubled its lead at 9:08 when Hoglander collected a rebound off the end boards and slotted it home before making it 3-0 at 3:03 of the second on another tap-in.

Tavares got Toronto going off the rush at 4:56 of the middle period — McKenna picked up the primary assist — and Nylander connected on a man advantage at 6:58 to make it 3-2. Stamkos scored his second to restore a two-goal lead at 13:30, but McKenna buried his first in the NHL just 61 seconds later.

Roslovic tied things at 8:54 of the third when he went bar down on Saros to set up the late drama that included Toronto failing to connect a 3-on-0 in OT before Matthews fired past Saros for the victory.

stories.title: Group releases dictionary of 'highjacked' terms misused since outbreak of Israel-Hamas war
stories.summary: The attempt to "hijack" such terms is done to "demonize, delegitimize, and apply double standards to 'the Jew' among nations," says CEO.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
An advocacy group has released a dictionary full of terms that it says have been hijacked and misused, particularly for the past three years, since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war.

“The initiative emerges from a growing recognition that the erosion of language is not merely a semantic concern,” says Michal Cotler-Wunsh, the CEO of the International Legal Forum, the group behind the new online resource.

“When terms such as ‘genocide,’ ‘apartheid,’ ‘war crimes,’ and ‘crimes against humanity,’ are detached from their legal definitions and repurposed as political weapons, the consequences extend far beyond a specific conflict, article, post, or courtroom. The integrity of law itself is placed at risk.”

The dictionary not only defines the terms, but provides which countries the terms have been weaponized against. It provides real-world examples and examines how words have been misused. Its release falls on Oct. 7, the third anniversary of when Hamas terrorists murdered 1,200 people in Israel and took 251 hostage.

Following the outbreak of the war, there has been an anti-Israel movement in the form of protests, antisemitic incidents and rallies to “honour martyrs” in Canada and across the world. Several university campuses in Canada housed encampments that demanded support for Israel come to an end and called the war a genocide.

The term genocide was coined in the aftermath of the Holocaust, when six million Jewish people were targeted and systematically murdered by the Nazi regime in Europe.

Anti-Israel Oct. 7 event to 'honour martyrs' will not proceed on U of T campus: university

'You are going to die for the Jews,' said Belleville shooting suspect: police

“That ‘intent’ is not a technicality. It is the legal distinction between genocide and other crimes.”

She said the attempt to “hijack” such terms is done to “demonize, delegitimize, and apply double standards to ‘the Jew’ among nations.”

“It has enabled the unleashing of this unconventional weapon, the ultimate lie in the ‘progressive’ antisemitism playbook: accusing Israel of genocide, even as it defends itself from openly declared genocidal intent launched with Hamas’s pre-meditated war crimes and crimes against humanity,” she said.

The term was used against Israel immediately after October 7, even before they responded to the attack, she added.

In a 2025 report and again in 2026, the United Nations accused Israel of committing genocide. Many experts and Jewish advocacy groups strongly denied that claim. In response, a statement from Israel said the report “relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods, laundered and repeated by others.”

The dictionary lists Canada as a country that the term genocide is weaponized against.

“Canada continues to embolden genocidal terror and tyranny,” said Cotler-Wunsh.

“War is hell. Tragedies occur, especially when that is the intent of those who deliberately and systematically hide amongst and below civilians. That is precisely why these terms and their equal and consistent application are vital.”

According to the International Legal Forum, the dictionary is intended to make vital legal principles and terms accessible to a broad audience.

stories.title: Americans could lose access to cheap Canadian prescription drugs. Here's how much U.S. imports
stories.summary: Americans once spent US$1 billion on prescription drugs from Canada, but new import rules might mean they no longer spend anything at all.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Americans once spent US$1 billion on prescription drugs from Canada, but new import rules might mean they no longer spend anything at all.

It’s the consequence of a new rule published in the U.S. Federal Register on June 24, which enforces an indefinite suspension of the de minimis exemption that allows imports valued at $800 or less to arrive through the international postal network without formal customs paperwork.

And it could result in millions of Americans who use foreign mail-order pharmacies, mostly from Canada, having their supply cut off, according to the Canadian International Pharmacy Association (Cipa).

The text doesn’t specifically address prescription drugs, but it does say that formal entry is now required for any shipments regulated by Partner Government Agencies (PGA). This includes the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which has historically used enforcement discretion for personal-use medicines, with the agency’s personal importation guidance explaining that some shipments of medication May be allowed if the quantity is no more than a three-month supply.

National Post spoke to Tim Smith, general manager at Cipa, which represents licensed Canadian pharmacies that ship to U.S. patients. He explained that the FDA policy “allows agents to use their discretion when a package is coming in for personal use in a quantity not exceeding 90 days,” and that this is the way the system has operated for the past 25 years. “What goes into effect on October 22 is a new system that is much more complicated,” he said.

This is because, in most cases, drugs purchased from other countries have not been approved for use and sale in the U.S. by the FDA, making them illegal to import. It means that, from Oct. 22, medications mailed from abroad will go through a customs process requiring a licensed customs broker and a financial guarantee.

“The understanding we have at this point is that the FDA is no longer going to exercise the discretion that they have done traditionally,” said Smith.

And while recent data on the value of these purchases is limited, a Congressional Research Report published in 2007 said that, in 2003 alone, U.S. consumers bought more than $1 billion in prescription drugs from Canada.

The demand is largely due to Canada having generally lower prices for prescription medication because of government price controls. Smith explained that Americans who purchase medication from Canada can expect to save 50 to 80 per cent on drugs like Eliquis, which prevents blood clots, and Crestor, which lowers cholesterol.

Meanwhile, the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation (Cppi), an advocacy organization that campaigns for Americans’ access to prescription medications from Canada, recently published a price study comparing the cost of 10 commonly prescribed brand-name medications in the U.S. and Canada.

They found that American consumers could save an average of 65 per cent by purchasing these medications from licensed Canadian pharmacies. Savings were highest for Jublia, which is used to treat fungal infections and costs $2,422 for a 90-day supply, compared to $257.77 in Canada.

Xifaxan, which treats IBS, costs $11,919 for a 90-day supply in the U.S. compared to $2,325.78 in Canada, according to the Cppi study, while Rybelsus, which is prescribed for type 2 diabetes, cost $2,913 in the U.S. and $1,193.99 in Canada.

But Smith said that, following the rule change, Cipa expects the FDA to take a path of “complete enforcement” against all packages entering the U.S., meaning Americans should expect virtually all prescription orders mailed from Canada — and other international pharmacies — to be unable to reach them.

He is calling on the FDA, along with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), to assure the American public that their ability to purchase affordable medications for personal use will be maintained past Oct. 22.

Until then, Cipa is advising all U.S. patients to order refills before the deadline and start looking for alternative places to purchase their medication.

National Post has contacted the FDA and CBP for clarification, but did not receive a response before publication.

As for how the changes will impact Canadian online pharmacies, Smith says: “Because they’re in the mail order business for their service to the United States, some of our pharmacies have located themselves close to international mail facilities. As a result of that, they have less presence in neighbourhoods, shopping malls or areas where people live and would go to a pharmacy.”

He added that these pharmacies May need to make “adjustments” as a result of the change, but that all of Cipa’s members are licensed pharmacies in Canada and serve Canadians too, even if a large portion of their patients May be based in the U.S.

stories.title: Power restored in White Oaks area in London, Ont.
stories.summary: Over 1,300 London Hydro customers are without power Tuesday evening.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Over 1,300 Londoners in the city’s south end are without power Tuesday evening.

London Hydro took to social media, saying, “There are a number of elements impacting restoration including a pole down, pole fire, and grass fire.”

A large part of the White Oaks and Westminster areas are without power, including parts of White Oaks mall.

The estimated time of restoration is 10:30 p.m.

stories.title: The unsafe side effects of ‘safer supply’
stories.summary: Ontario’s prescription opioids program is flooding the streets with addictive drugs
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Ontario medical professionals thought they could help people with addictions by giving them prescription opioids to take on their own so they could avoid risky street drugs. But it’s now clear that this supposed solution carries big costs.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario will decide later this month if it will set stricter guardrails around the practice, which has become known as “safer supply.” The proposal includes many sensible measures, but it should go farther in integrating prescriptions into comprehensive treatment plans to help patients break their addictions.

Across Ontario, doctors are giving patients with substance-use disorders prescriptions for the powerful opioid hydromorphone. The practice began around a decade ago in an attempt to reduce overdose deaths from street drugs, such as fentanyl, which can be unpredictable as it is often mixed with other substances. These prescriptions don’t need to be integrated into broader treatment plans to address behavioural issues and other factors that influence substance use.

A recent Globe and Mail investigation revealed that for many users, the hydromorphone isn’t strong enough to ward off their cravings, so they sell it on the black market to get money for fentanyl. All too often, the hydromorphone ends up in the hands of young people seeking a cheap high.

These buyers sometimes mistakenly believe the pharmacy-provided drugs are “safe,” yet there is a high risk of addiction. Even small amounts of the drug can lead people to stop breathing and overdose. Some hydromorphone users, chasing a stronger high, move on to fentanyl. Instead of stemming the harms of addiction, these prescriptions give fentanyl users an easy way to support their destructive habits while flooding the market with cheap opioids that hurt others.

Last year, British Columbia reined in its prescription opioid program after leaked documents showed a significant portion was being trafficked. Patients now need to consume the pills in front of a medical professional or pharmacist. However in Ontario, patients are regularly allowed to take large amounts of their pills off site.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has been vocal about moving away from safe consumption sites and towards recovery-focused treatment. Yet there’s been less attention to pharmaceutical opioids, which are prescribed by individual doctors and promoted by specialty pharmacies. Some pharmacies have built lucrative businesses by having doctors dole out prescriptions online to walk-in patients, says Hamilton addictions doctor Lori Regenstreif.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is finally waking up to the issue. In May , it introduced changes that require doctors to see patients in person and offer other addiction medicines prior to starting them on prescription opioids. The doctors are also required to assess these patients in person every three months.

On Oct. 13, the College board will decide if it should enact further restrictions. The proposal includes a provision to require patients to take their pills at the pharmacy or clinic. It would bring in an eight-week limit for prescription opioids for drug users and require in-person clinical assessments once a month.

These measures would go a long way to limit the harms of prescription opioids, and they should be enacted. But the changes should go further. The College needs to work with the province to ensure that these prescriptions are integrated into long-term treatment plans with recovery as the goal. This is best achieved by having only doctors specializing in addictions offer prescription opioids for patients with substance use disorders.

The opioid crisis took off when Purdue Pharma flooded the market with addictive pills. It won’t end by flooding our communities with more opioids, such as hydromorphone, which was brought to Canada by Purdue under the name Dilaudid.

Prescription medications – particularly methadone and suboxone – have a role to play in treating people with addictions. But they work best as part of a comprehensive plan that helps patients work through trauma, reconnect with loved ones and find stable housing and employment. Instead of allowing prescription opioids to flood the streets, Ontario should expand treatment options to give people a chance to get clean and improve their lives.

stories.title: Live by the Blade, die by the Blade: How Mahershala Ali and Bassam Tariq carved their own action-movie path
stories.summary: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is wildly entertaining but also soulful and solemn
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
Over the past two decades, a number of Marvel Studios films have been announced with great fanfare, only to evaporate into the cinematic equivalent of the Negative Zone, a parallel universe where abandoned elements go to die.

For most of the discarded projects – which were scuttled for reasons as varied as stars getting criminally convicted (see Avengers: The Kang Dynasty ) or simply audience disinterest ( Inhumans , Armor Wars ), the creative teams simply move on and try to forget that they wasted however many months, or sometimes years, of their lives. But forgetting wasn’t an option for Mahershala Ali and Bassam Tariq, the one-time star and director, respectively, of Marvel’s Blade reboot.

After being attached for years to a fresh take on the “daywalker” superhero – that is, a half-man, half-vampire vigilante who wages a shadowy war on bloodsuckers with a giant samurai sword – Ali and Tariq got tired of waiting for a green light from Marvel and pivoted to a completely different project, which, while original in narrative, form, style and themes, carried over just a little more than a hint of their Blade groundwork.

The result is the wildly entertaining, yet at the same time soulful and solemn, action-drama Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother .

On the surface, a film following a devout Muslim family man named Latif, who moonlights as an assassin, might not seem very Marvel-y. And indeed, the Pakistani-born, American-raised Tariq conceived of the story’s bones long before he was ever attached to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. But the hero here also lives by a very Blade-like moral code, finds himself facing an army of eccentric villains who feel ripped out of the pages of an especially surreal comic book, and, well, he carries an extremely big and extremely sharp sword that might make the toughest vampire weak in the knees. It is both the best Marvel movie the studio never made and an inspiring story of a creative team using the ashes of a dashed dream to spark something entirely new.

“I think I can get bored easy, ON some level, so I’m always looking for something that if I’m going to commit to it, if it’s going to take me away from my family, it has to challenge me and be worthy of my time and my attention,” says Ali during an interview last month at the Toronto International Film Festival, where the movie made its world premiere. “You want to make sure that you’re immersed into something that has real value in the world.”

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother certainly has that real-world value, but crucially also real-world values, plural. The Oscar-winning Ali (whose last trip to Tiff for the premiere of Green Book ended up going pretty well) portrays a kind of hero that has simply never been seen on screen before.

Latif is a man of great contradictions, whose life revolves around his local mosque and community, but whose desire for vengeance constantly and violently pulls him away from those who he values and loves the most. And when Latif’s world is further upended by the arrival of a gun-toting, fundamentalist Christian militia leader named Pastor Yoon (played by John Cho in the best kind of gonzo-villain performance), Tariq’s film swirls with frenzied tensions between faith and family, justice and righteousness.

“I definitely had some questions when I saw the script for the first time, like how do you fit all these worlds together? If it’s not executed well, it could be a really bad movie, even if it reads beautifully on the page,” Ali recalls. “As far as the arc of the character, that was beautiful to me. But it was more trying to understand Latif’s world, and Pastor Yoon’s world, and navigating the mosque and the action scenes – how does it all stitch together seamlessly?”

On that level, Tariq enlisted a team of close collaborators to make Latif’s world feel both recognizable to members of the American South’s Muslim communities – the film takes place in the suburbs of Houston, but was informed by the director’s time living in Atlanta – and slightly fantastical.

“Filmmaking is not just one person, and I’ve tried to do it before on projects where I had to educate everybody, and it was just so daunting,” says the director, whose previous feature was the 2020 drama Mogul Mowgli about the travails of a British-Pakistani rapper played by Riz Ahmed. “This time around, I made sure that I had people who knew the community or had a way into it.”

“I think the Atlanta Muslim community played a really important role, to get that tapestry correct,” Tariq continues. “And I think it’s just incredible to have a partner in this with Ali, who is also Muslim. We never really talked about, like, what does it mean to be Muslim? We’re just in it. We just live it. Because we have that shorthand, we didn’t have to explain anything. It was only about getting more details correct.”

Those details are woven into Latif’s onscreen journey in perhaps more deeply personal ways than Tariq or Ali initially conceived.

The film – whose title is taken from an Islamic hadith in which a man asks the Prophet Muhammad who in his life most deserves his attention and devotion – is just as much about a superhero-like hit man as it is about a man reckoning with how much time he spends supporting his family versus how much time he actually spends with them. Much like, well, a movie star who is pulled out of the family unit for months at a time.

“I have another movie at the festival called Wildwood , and I got to screen an unfinished version of that film with my daughter – and I’m now starting to see a look on her face where she’s registering what my work is and some of my responsibilities that push me away from her,” Ali says.

“We’re starting to develop a language around me being able to share what I’m doing. If I’m going to do it, I don’t want it to be just because I’m getting a cheque. There’s been a few times when I just really needed a job, like no doubt. I could go on my resume and show you those, if we’re being honest. But in general, I really try to push my energies into something that is going to feel larger than me.”

Or, as the saying goes: Live by the Blade , die by the Blade .

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother opens in Toronto Oct. 9, expanding to additional cities Oct. 16.

stories.title: ‘Not much of a benefit’: Grocery payments fall short of making difference, readers say
stories.summary: Eligible Canadians have begun receiving their second payment under the new Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, but some say the extra money does little to ease the pressure of rising food and household costs.
stories.author: Tammy Ibrahimpoor
stories.content:
Eligible Canadians have begun receiving their second payment under the new Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit , but some say the extra money does little to ease the pressure of rising food and household costs.

The benefit, formerly known as the GST/HST credit, provides quarterly payments to lower-income Canadians based on factors including income, marital status and the number of children in a household.

A single person without children can receive up to $679 annually, while households with four or more children can receive up to $1,826.

CTVNews.CA asked readers if the benefit helped their families make ends meet. Through email responses, some said it was not enough to make a meaningful difference, while others said they do not qualify, despite facing financial pressure.

‘Spit in the ocean’

For some seniors and people living on disability benefits, the extra money is welcome, but quickly disappears.

“This barely helps me at all,” Allen Mayes of Armstrong, B.C., wrote, adding that the maximum annual benefit for a single person amounts to only a handful of grocery trips for him.

The 73-year-old said he lives on both the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and Old Age Security (OAS), and spends about $150 every two weeks on basic food.

“(The payment is) less than 20 per cent of my basic food for the year. That’s not a drop in the bucket — it’s spit in the ocean,” Mayes wrote. He said he relies on inexpensive staples such as beans, frozen peas and corn, rice and flour, and bakes his own bread to save money.

Guy Helwig, of Southampton, Ont., said the benefit helps “somewhat,” but argued that rising costs extend far beyond groceries.

Helwig, who said he is retired and living on a fixed income, pointed to higher rent, property taxes, water and sewer rates, as well as phone, cable and internet costs.

“People are drowning in higher bills!” he wrote.

‘Tired of never being heard’

Jodie McAuley of Vancouver Island said the amount she received is far too little to make a significant difference.

“$127 for groceries for a senior is just sad,” she wrote. “If you do the math, that works out to $1.41 a day between payments. A can of soup is more expensive.”

It’s a similar situation for Liz Carter.

“While I am appreciative of any extra money I get it really is just ‘a drop in the bucket’,” the native of Red Deer, Alta. wrote.

The 72-year-old said she has little food in her fridge and pantry, and has had to cut back on what she eats because of rising prices.

“I primarily live on canned light tuna and frozen grilled chicken strips,” she wrote.

Mike Van Damme, of Sarnia, Ont., said he receives about $1,200 a month through CPP.

He said people living on disability benefits are struggling to afford basic necessities and deserve more dignity.

“I never asked to be born with a genetic defect that affected my heart,” he wrote. “We all talk about affordability, but little is done, and people on disability are tired of never being heard.”

‘I feel the government left us out’

For some readers, geography and circumstance adds another layer to the problem.

Arlene Campbell, who is from Patuanak, Sask., said residents in her northern Saskatchewan community do not have access to large grocery chains such as Walmart or Superstore.

“We have to buy from Northern Store, and the price of freight is included in the prices, which (comes at an) extremely higher cost,” Campbell wrote.

She said a jug of milk can cost nearly $14, while a box of diapers can go for $64.

While Campbell appreciates the grocery rebate, she said it’s ”not much of a benefit.”

Not everyone who responded to the callout receives the benefit.

Cindy Hitch, based out of Winnipeg, said she was laid off in 2025 after her employer went bankrupt and has been living on employment insurance.

She said she believes the benefit calculation, based on her previous income, has left people like her behind.

The benefit, formerly known as the GST/HST credit, provides quarterly payments to lower-income Canadians based on factors including income, marital status and the number of children in a household.
A single person without children can receive up to $679 annually, while households with four or more children can receive up to $1,826.

CTVNews.CA asked readers if the benefit helped their families make ends meet. Through email responses, some said it was not enough to make a meaningful difference, while others said they do not qualify, despite facing financial pressure.

stories.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to mirror molecule explorers Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai
stories.summary: Scientists made key contributions to the understanding of ‘chirality’ in the 1990s, discoveries that proved important for the development of pharmaceuticals
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Two scientists who studied the properties and production of molecules that are mirror images of one another have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

On Wednesday, members of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced that Henri Kagan of Université Paris-Sud, Orsay and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science will share this year’s chemistry Nobel.

Both made key contributions to the understanding of “chirality,” a property that means some molecules can have left- and right-handed versions.

Their discoveries have proved important for the development of pharmaceuticals, many of which require the production of only one version of a molecule and not its mirror twin.

For example, in some cases, the mirror version of a molecule is not only ineffective but harmful. When the drug thalidomide was marketed as a morning sickness pill starting in the 1950s, the consequences were tragic. The mirror image of the active drug turned out to cause severe birth defects.

“How can a reaction be designed to spontaneously create only one of the two mirror images without involving any other chiral molecule? It is this puzzle that this year’s laureates have solved,” Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry said during Wednesday’s announcement.

The work also helps to illuminate why life on Earth is based only on left-handed versions of certain key organic molecules.

Dr. Kagan was born in 1930 in Boulogne-Billancourt, France, and received his PhD from the College of France in Paris in 1960.

Through the 1970s and 1980s he developed reactions in which catalysts enhanced the production of one version of a mirror molecule relative to the other.

The work was recognized as a breakthrough for its practical applications, including for the development of flavour and scents, in which only one version of a chiral molecule can be sensed.

Dr. Kagan was awarded the prestigious Wolf Prize in Chemistry 2001. Now 95, he is among the oldest winners of a chemistry Nobel.

Dr. Soai was born in 1950 in Hiroshima, Japan, and received his PhD from the University of Tokyo in 1979.

In the 1990s he discovered a chiral substance known as 5-pyrimidyl alkanol which acts as an autocatalyst, a molecule that can create itself.

By 2003 he had developed a chemical reaction in which chiral molecules formed from nonchiral percursors. He then showed how a very small excess of one version of the mirror molecule would eventually grow in proportion to take over the reaction, until it was the sole version remaining.

Apart from the origin of life more than four billion years ago, which produced a biology with exclusively left-handed chemistry, no other such examples are currently known.

At Wednesday’s announcement, Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee, said Dr. Soai’s discovery is “probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry.”

Each year the Chemistry prize marks the third in a series of Nobel prize announcements.

On Monday, Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for creating the field of optogenetics, a method of genetically modifying neurons to react to light that has transformed brain research.

On Tuesday, Francis Halzen, who leads a giant neutrino detection experiment in Antarctica, was named this year’s winner of the Nobel Prize in Physics .

Recipients of the Nobel Prize in Literature and the Nobel Peace Prize are scheduled to be announced on Thursday and Friday, respectively. The winner of this year’s Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.

stories.title: Why Quebec’s independence debate is back
stories.summary: Among his plans for the province, he eyes holding a referendum in a push to separate Quebec from Canada.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has been voted in as Quebec’s newest Premier.

His party, Parti Québécois, secured their minority government on Monday night’s election with 59 seats, up from three seats back in 2022. Among his plans for the province, he eyes holding a referendum in a push to separate Quebec from Canada. And although Plamondon promised to wait until US President Trump left the White House, the new Premier would still need to gain the support from the other provincial parties.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to André Lecours, a political science professor at the University of Ottawa to discuss what PSPP’s win means for the province, its future in Canada, and for Prime Minister Carney’s tenure.

You can subscribe to The Big Story podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

stories.title: Sunshine returns after weak front moves through southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: A weak weather system moving through southwestern Ontario Wednesday could bring a few brief showers to parts of the region before skies clear and sunshine makes a strong return.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
A weak weather system moving through southwestern Ontario Wednesday could bring a few brief showers to parts of the region before skies clear and sunshine makes a strong return heading into the Thanksgiving holiday weekend.

“We could see a few spotty showers this morning, particularly across parts of midwestern Ontario, but most of the rain will be light and short-lived,” CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison said. “By this afternoon, many areas, including London, should see a return to sunshine.”

The forecast calls for a high of 21 degrees Wednesday.

While a few isolated showers could linger near Grey and Bruce counties into Thursday, Atchison said much of the region is set for a stretch of dry and seasonably warm weather.

Thursday is expected to be sunny with a high of 19, followed by full sunshine on Friday. A mix of sun and cloud is forecast for Saturday.

“Right now, the probability of showers on Sunday is fairly low, around 30 per cent,” Atchison said. “There May be a bit more cloud cover Sunday evening and into Monday, but at this point we’re not expecting anything significant.”

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Wednesday: Mainly cloudy. 30 per cent chance of showers early in the morning and late in the afternoon. Wind becoming southwest 20 km/h in the morning. High 21. UV index 4 or moderate.

Wednesday night: Partly cloudy with 30 per cent chance of showers. Low 8.

Thursday: Sunny. High 19.

Friday: Sunny. High 18.

Saturday: Sunny. High 19.

Sunday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 20.

stories.title: Character study: Century home renos balance heritage details with modern comforts
stories.summary: Plus, expert tips on how to update an older home without breaking the bank
stories.author: Silvana Longo
stories.content:
The door to designer Jessica Cinnamon’s 1920s Tudor home is new. The stone arch around it is not.

The Toronto neighbourhood, Old Mill, is one of the city’s coveted pockets. Its century-old houses have been largely left alone or are at least still recognizable, notable in a city where sprawling new builds increasingly dominate.

Cinnamon’s home makes the case for a hybrid approach to renovating an older property; one that respects the place’s history while reinventing its interior for 21st-century life.

Much of Toronto’s older housing stock, including Cinnamon’s home, has been altered by decades of piecemeal updates. The house had been carved into a duplex years earlier, according to the designer, who moved in this year with her husband and two young children after a two-year renovation.

By the time they bought the place, in 2024, the Tudor exterior was intact and the original windows were still in place, though they were cracked and deteriorating. Opening the walls revealed asbestos, a discovery that halted their plans until a full remediation could happen.

“It added another layer to the process,” Cinnamon said, “but it also reinforced the importance of taking the house back to its fundamentals.”

The updated home features original corbels, salvaged where possible; windows in their original dimensions, now black, mullioned and triple-paned; and fireplaces in their original locations. The remodel also reinstated the staircase’s curved bull-nose detail, which had been lost during the duplex years.

Cinnamon didn’t increase the property’s footprint, which she felt would have altered its Tudor character. Instead, she found space in what was already there: a vaulted ceiling opened up in her daughter’s bedroom once the house was stripped to its frame, and an attic converted into usable space on the third floor.

The interior design is textured, restrained and contemporary while still reflecting the original home’s character. A fluted black marble archway, backlit, frames the entry to the family room. Warm oak floors run underfoot. Gunmetal hardware carries through every room.

“The goal was never to recreate a 1920s interior,” said Cinnamon, who led the design. “It was to preserve the architectural soul of the home while creating an interior that felt relevant to how we live today.”

Others prefer a different approach.

Designer Kate Stuart of Toronto’s TOM Design Collective works with clients who want history running through every room. Original medallions, cornices, stained glass, fireplaces and woodwork aren’t just nostalgic details; homeowners “are coming to us because they want that history to inform the house as a whole,” she said.

For a residence in Saint-Lambert, Que., that philosophy was the starting point.

At Résidence Victoria, a Second Empire and neo-Georgian home built in 1892 and renovated by Montreal’s Blanc Marine Intérieurs, led by Mélanie Cherrier and Laurence Pons Lavigne, the architecture and original interior remain remarkably intact. The home belongs to Kimberley Pontbriand, marketing director and partner at Blanc Marine, and her husband, Samuel Finn, the firm’s president.

“We weren’t interested in reducing the house to a particular architectural label or recreating a period interior,” said Cherrier. “We wanted to understand what gave it its character, preserve those elements and allow the new interventions to enter into a dialogue with them.”

Blanc Marine leaned into the home’s layered identity. Second Empire influences are reflected in its mansard roof and decorative detailing, while classical elements such as fluted pilasters, carved rosettes and layered mouldings speak to its Georgian Revival lineage.

Contemporary changes weren’t designed to imitate either era but to complement them.

Original stained glass runs above the front door and through nearly every window. A gilded chandelier hangs beneath a ceiling medallion in the entryway. The main staircase, crafted entirely from solid wood, carries its own classical language: an intricately carved newel post, turned balusters, fluting and rosettes, with the original warm-wood tone still intact. In the sitting room, woodland wallpaper wraps a fireplace framed in original woodwork.

“We believe contrast can actually make heritage architecture more powerful,” Cherrier said. “We allowed the home’s classical architecture to become the backdrop, introducing cleaner contemporary lines alongside vintage and antique pieces, natural materials and layers of texture.”

Even the kitchen, the most updated room in the home, feels cohesive, with warm wood cabinetry, an apron sink and a country-style stove.

Quebec’s Cultural Heritage Act can extend protection to a home’s interior, whereas in Ontario, heritage rules generally apply only to what’s visible from the street. Résidence Victoria has no formal heritage designation; the preservation reflects Blanc Marine’s design philosophy, not a legal requirement.

“Our clients rarely want an older home to feel new again,” Cherrier says. “They want to preserve what made them fall in love with it in the first place.”

In Halifax, designer Natalie Owens, principal of Stil James, sees a version of that same instinct. “There is a bit of a forced hand when it comes to buying a property,” she said. “It is just too costly to be knocking down homes.” She also pointed to something more emotional: a younger generation, she’s noticed, has developed a real appreciation for layered, traditional design.

“I do think there is something attractive about these homes that are reminiscent of my generation’s childhood. Most of us grew up in a traditional-style home. Modern, super-contemporary homes weren’t a thing in Atlantic Canada. There is something that pulls you in as a prospective buyer: Wouldn’t it be great if I could raise my kids in a home like the one I was raised in?”

She also pushed back on the notion that heritage work costs 20 to 30 per cent more than a new build. “If you’re comparing apples to apples,” she said, “you’re still going to be spending more on a new build” of matching quality. Cherrier and Stuart agreed: The premium isn’t a heritage tax. It’s simply what quality materials cost with any renovation.

The designers have all observed a growing pull toward the past. “It does feel as though heritage is having a moment again,” said Stuart. “What’s old is new.”

The shift May point to something larger than just design preference. “I think the broader state of the world plays into this,” Stuart said. “Between uncertainty, constant screen time, technology and the speed at which everything changes, people are craving warmth and comfort at home. There is something grounding about living in a house that has a history.”

Natalie Owens, Stil James: Before ripping out original hardwood, sand and refinish it. Stripping a yellowed oil finish and recoating the wood with a water-based clear finish restores the original wood tone for roughly half the cost of replacing the floor outright. Owens also recommended phasing the work: do the kitchen, dining room and mud room first, and hold off on secondary spaces such as a dated bathroom.

Mélanie Cherrier, Blanc Marine Intérieurs: Prioritize what’s genuinely hard to recreate today: original woodwork, floors, mouldings, doors and staircases. “Sometimes the most respectful design decision, and even the most economical one, is to leave something beautiful exactly where it is.”

Kate Stuart, TOM Design Collective: When budgets are tight, protect the elements that give the house its character – original millwork, doors, plasterwork, fireplaces and good-quality flooring – rather than trying to save everything. A cheaper replacement isn’t always a more economical choice if it will need to be redone in a decade. “The perception that preservation is automatically prohibitively expensive can push people toward a full renovation when a more strategic approach might serve the house better.”
