stories.title: It's already going around: Ontario's flu season is getting an early start
stories.summary: The good news is that early signs suggest this year’s vaccine could be a good match for the H1N1 strain now circulating.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Anyone with colleagues calling in sick or kids home with a fever May have suspected it already: Ontario’s flu season is getting an early start.

Influenza tests are coming back positive more often than at this point in recent years, and the rates for children are even higher. It’s too soon to say how severe the season will be, but early signs suggest this year’s vaccine could be a good match for the strain now circulating, Public Health Ontario says.

If trends continue, Ontario will hit the threshold that officially marks flu season within a couple weeks, and typically it takes five to six weeks after that to reach peak flu season, said Dr. Richard Mather, a public health physician with Public Health Ontario.

Positivity captures only people who get tested, and flu isn’t the only virus going around.

High-risk groups are eligible Sept. 28, followed by the general public at pharmacies and doctors on Oct. 26.

Influenza positivity — the portion of lab tests that come back positive — reached three per cent for the week ending Sept. 26, according to the agency’s respiratory virus tracker. Influenza detections were higher among children: a 6.8 per cent positivity rate for children ages five to 11 and 5.3 per cent for kids ages one to four.

Children “are sort of efficient at spreading viruses,” Mather said. “We typically see a higher per cent positivity in kids at the start, and then in other age groups it starts to increase as well.

“It’s important, as we are seeing some increased activity, to get the vaccine as soon as it’s available for you.”

In Ontario, the influenza vaccine is technically already available for those over 65 and under five, health-care workers, residents in long-term care homes and other high-risk populations. But finding a shot depends on the availability of initial supplies.

Last year, there was a lot of concern about a possible mismatch between the flu vaccine and H3N2, a mutated strain of influenza A that was common. But Mather says the latest data from the Sentinel Practitioner Surveillance Network, which analyzes how well the vaccine worked in Canada each year, shows it was better than expected and reduced the risk for that strain by over one-third.

Right now, the most commonly circulating strain is influenza A, H1N1. That was also the strain that was prominent at the end of the flu season in the Southern Hemisphere and a factor in the World Health Organization’s choice of strains for this year’s Northern Hemisphere vaccine, he said.

“It’s somewhat reassuring that the vaccine is anticipated to be a good match,” he said.

Dr. Isaac Bogoch, an infectious diseases specialist at Toronto General Hospital and the University of Toronto, said Canada has weathered two years of challenging flu seasons. He’s hoping this season will be better.

“But hope, of course, is not a strategy,” Bogoch said. “And we need to prepare by getting vaccines and ensuring people remember about staying home if they’re sick.

“It’s not widespread just yet, but it will be, it absolutely will be.”

This early on, it’s impossible to project how severe the respiratory virus season, which includes influenza, COVID-19 and RSV, will be, or just how much protection the flu vaccine will provide, he said.

“People might say, ‘oh, the shot’s not perfect, I might not get it.’ But … influenza, I’m not talking about the sniffles or a cough or a cold, true influenza can knock even a healthy young person on their butts for a few days and they will feel absolutely miserable.”

Dr. Pierre-Philippe Piché-Renaud, a physician in the infectious diseases division at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, said the hospital is seeing what it would expect at this point in the season.

But with Thanksgiving celebrations and long-weekend gatherings coming up, it’s important to keep in mind that influenza is already floating around, Piché-Renaud said.

“It’s an excellent time to think about how to protect children and vulnerable individuals,” he said, “especially in the context of these kind of celebrations. If people do have symptoms, it’s probably best to stay at home and take care of yourself as opposed to spreading these kind of viruses.

“We’ve been repeating that message for some time now. And again, as soon as vaccines become available, to get vaccinated to prevent getting the infection in the first place.”

stories.title: Former defence chief warns Canada must defend its North or risk U.S. intervention
stories.summary: Wayne Eyre says Canada must "ensure that it doesn't receive sovereignty-violating help" with the region.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa — The military’s former top soldier says there is a risk the United States will step in to defend the Canadian Arctic under the pretext Canada isn’t up for the job — one reason that he argues the federal government must maintain increases in military spending, even if it means sacrificing social programs.

In a wide-ranging interview with the Star on Tuesday, retired Gen. Wayne Eyre said Canada must, by showing it is capable of protecting the North, defend against “help” that would violate the country’s sovereignty over the vast region. While multibillion-dollar plans to do that are in the works, including through the construction of new over-the-horizon radar stations, icebreaker ships and military support hubs in the Arctic, “speed of execution” is now key, Eyre said.

ByEdward Keenan Columnist

Good morning. This is the Wednesday, Oct. 7 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

I was up Tuesday night moderating a mayoral debate. You may have heard how at the last minute it turned from a three-candidate debate into a twosome. (If you haven’t heard, we’ll get to that news in a moment.) Here’s what our team thought the key takeaways from the night were. Lots more Toronto mayoral election news below.

But first up, here are six things to know on Wednesday morning:

The Tumbler Ridge shooter plotted with a U.S. resident who advised her on weapons and even planned to livestream the killings, police allege.

Mississauga mayoral candidate Alvin Tedjo says a volunteer for his campaign was attacked with a knife while putting up election signs.

“Much more than names”: More details on Canadian crew of missing air ambulance as Transportation Safety Board says it will investigate what happened.

Flu season is set to start early. But it looks like this year’s vaccine might be a good match.

Fighting has escalated in Yemen while U.S.-Iran tensions remain high. Here’s a breakdown of what’s going on.

There’s a possible case of pneumonic plague after a lab worker died in Russia. Here’s how the country and the WHO are responding.

Pitter patter, let’s get at ’er.

Just half an hour before early voting opened Tuesday morning, the former immigration minister ended his campaign for mayor of Toronto, saying he lost faith he’d find the path to victory. The announcement leaves Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford as the two main contenders. Quick recap: Alexander failed to garner much support in nearly 10 weeks of campaigning, despite robust policy proposals. At single digits in recent polling, some questioned why he was even running. Alexander missed the deadline to officially withdraw, so his name will remain on the ballot for the Oct. 26 vote.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Image 20Image 21

A puzzled Matt Gurney asks: What was the point of all that, Chris Alexander?

Does Chow have a problem? Is Bradford’s record credible? Our columnists weighed in on Tuesday night’s mayoral debate.

Think you can bring your favourite Niagara red down to grandma’s condo in Florida? Think again. Experts say there appears to be no personal exemption from Trump’s Canadian alcohol import ban.

Recap: Star reporters answered reader questions Tuesday about Canada’s push for closer ties with the EU. Catch up here.

Carney flexed his own popularity after Quebec’s election results, saying a strong sovereign Canada is what Quebecers and Canadians need.

The federal government remains confident in the Alto high-speed rail project despite the PQ election victory.

Éric Blais’s take: Why fear won’t contain the Parti Québécois — and how federalists should respond to Quebec separatists.

Canada’s foreign influence commissioner says his office has contacted Alberta separatist groups about U.S. meetings.

Doug Ford reminded Quebec’s incoming sovereigntist premier that Canada faces an existential threat from Trump.

Ontario’s so‑called “Crypto King” has begun facing down the investors he’s accused of defrauding, representing himself in his criminal trial.

Sometimes when you’re a journalist, finding news is easy: Someone holds a big press conference, or sends you an email making a big announcement, or there’s a scheduled event like a parliamentary session, a mass protest or a hockey game going on and you just show up to be an eyewitness.

But sometimes that’s not the most valuable kind of journalism. Especially in the age of livestreaming and social media, when people often hear the planned announcement and witness the event for themselves.

Sometimes journalists need to look in unexpected places, and read the fine print, to find the story. Our contributing city hall columnist Matt Elliott has made a career out of examining the fine print in municipal budgets, council votes, staff reports and the lobbyist registry and explaining what he finds there. Ana Pereira was able to discover that Scotiabank had laid off almost 15,000 employees over six years by scouring the fine print in annual reports. And then there’s the new story from investigative reporter Brendan Kennedy about a provincial rule change that critics fear could clear the way for “triple-bunking,” crowding more inmates into already overcrowded cells.

The story is controversial enough. But what jumped out at me is when Kennedy writes:

“The change to the provincial building code was quietly made public late Friday evening in a government newsletter for building industry stakeholders. No explanation was provided in the brief description of the change, which simply removes a requirement for at least 4.7 square metres of sleeping area space, per person, in adult correctional facilities.”

Kennedy did pose questions about the policy change to the government, and to watchdogs and interest groups, to try to flesh out what it might mean. Good thing he looked at the building industry stakeholder newsletter, right?

But it does raise the question of why he would have to. Isn’t a policy change like this — eliminating the minimum space requirements for warehousing people — the kind of thing we should have some public discussion on?

What do you think? If a policy like this is likely to be controversial — or at least consequential — shouldn’t it be discussed in a more public forum before being implemented? Is it okay with you when governments try to slip things through in the fine print? Are you concerned about what other changes might slip by unremarked? Let us know in the comments section here.

ALOK MUKHERJEE:In sports, a hit to the head is a known danger. Why is it accepted by Ontario police?

GILLIAN STEWARD:Alberta Premier Danielle Smith finds out that playing both sides of the fence is a losing strategy.

Cole Escola’s award-winning dark comedy, “Oh, Mary!” is on its way to Toronto. Here’s which “RuPaul’s Drag Race” alum is playing Mary Todd Lincoln.

Cannibalism, murder-suicide and Boca Raton’s seedy underbelly: Our book reviews this week have something for every crime novel enthusiast, including the latest from Toronto Star alumnus Linwood Barclay.

Hockey: The Leafs defeated the Nashville Predators 5-4 in overtime on Tuesday night, thanks in part to Gavin McKenna’s first NHL goal.

Soccer: Canada’s men’s soccer team lost to the U.S. in St. Paul, Minn. on Tuesday night. At least two lingering World Cup weaknesses were exposed.

Basketball: The Raptors know what they want from a second unit when the NBA season begins, but they still don’t know who’ll be in it.

Althia Raj’s column on the Quebec election results drew a lot of interesting takes about this moment in the political landscape and the comparison to Alberta’s separatist movement. Some recalled a painful past:

“The main reason they vote for sovereigntist parties is to have more leverage within Canada, despite flirting with disaster. I find it sad that Quebecers have chosen this particular time in Canada’s history to threaten to go there once again.” — Dave

While others simply said let them go:

“They, like Alberta, will learn separation doesn’t mean what they think it does. No, it won’t be a financial win. And no, they don’t have sovereignty over all the provincial lands — Indigenous peoples have rights to it.” — John

Before you go: Today’s word of the day could be “luxury.” What does it mean to you? How does it apply to recovering from addiction? At one Muskoka resort, Kevin Donovan recently reported, the definition of luxury rehab didn’t include an on-site doctor or properly licensed nursing staff. As the facility he wrote about faces bankruptcy, Donovan will join readers Wednesday at noon to answer questions. Find him in the comments section here.

Thanks for starting your day with us. If you enjoy First Up, please share it with a friend. And let us know what you think of the changes we’ve made, and what you’d like to see. Email firstup@thestar.ca. I’ll see you back here tomorrow morning.

content_blocks.text: THE CONVERSATION
Finding news in those hard-to-reach places

Sometimes when you’re a journalist, finding news is easy: Someone holds a big press conference, or sends you an email making a big announcement, or there’s a scheduled event like a parliamentary session, a mass protest or a hockey game going on and you just show up to be an eyewitness.

But sometimes that’s not the most valuable kind of journalism. Especially in the age of livestreaming and social media, when people often hear the planned announcement and witness the event for themselves.

Sometimes journalists need to look in unexpected places, and read the fine print, to find the story. Our contributing city hall columnist Matt Elliott has made a career out of examining the fine print in municipal budgets, council votes, staff reports and the lobbyist registry and explaining what he finds there. Ana Pereira was able to discover that Scotiabank had laid off almost 15,000 employees over six years by scouring the fine print in annual reports. And then there’s the new story from investigative reporter Brendan Kennedy about a provincial rule change that critics fear could clear the way for “triple-bunking,” crowding more inmates into already overcrowded cells.
The story is controversial enough. But what jumped out at me is when Kennedy writes:

“The change to the provincial building code was quietly made public late Friday evening in a government newsletter for building industry stakeholders. No explanation was provided in the brief description of the change, which simply removes a requirement for at least 4.7 square metres of sleeping area space, per person, in adult correctional facilities.”

Kennedy did pose questions about the policy change to the government, and to watchdogs and interest groups, to try to flesh out what it might mean. Good thing he looked at the building industry stakeholder newsletter, right?

But it does raise the question of why he would have to. Isn’t a policy change like this — eliminating the minimum space requirements for warehousing people — the kind of thing we should have some public discussion on?

What do you think? If a policy like this is likely to be controversial — or at least consequential — shouldn’t it be discussed in a more public forum before being implemented? Is it okay with you when governments try to slip things through in the fine print? Are you concerned about what other changes might slip by unremarked? Let us know in the comments section here.

stories.title: Boler Road construction continues with work progressing through final phase
stories.summary: Boler Road closed between Byron Baseline Road and Norman AvenueFrom October 13 to October 30, Boler Road will
stories.content:
From October 13 to October 30, Boler Road will be fully closed between Byron Baseline Road and just north of Norman Avenue while work continues on the Boler Road Cycling and Watermain Improvements project.

A full closure will allow crews to work in the area more efficiently and complete this section of the project sooner, rather than having several shorter closures.

Crews will work longer hours, with the goal of completing the roadway, bike path, and sidewalks this fall.

A signed detour will be in place, and the Byron Baseline Road intersection will remain open.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

The project will replace the aging watermain under Boler Road, which broke 13 times last year and required repairs that caused short-term closures or reduced the road to one lane. Replacing it now will help prevent these repeated disruptions.

The project will also add a two-way bike path, giving people cycling a dedicated route through Byron where there is currently limited cycling infrastructure. It also includes upgraded sidewalks, pedestrian crossings, traffic signals, and repairs to the road, including new pavement, curbs and gutters.

Most of the work is expected to be completed by the end of fall 2026, with some remaining work continuing into spring 2027.

The project is being completed in three phases:

Phase 1: Byron Baseline Road to Griffith Street is complete, including replacement of the watermain and water services.

Phase 2: Griffith Street to Southdale Road is nearing completion, including the new bike path and other road improvements.

Phase 3: Commissioners Road to Byron Baseline Road is underway, including the new bike path, pedestrian crossings, and road improvements.

For information about the Boler road project including construction updates, project timelines, visit the City’s Get Involved webpage.

You can also subscribe to receive project updates by clicking the Follow button at the top of the page.

stories.title: Suspect sought after hydro pole cut down
stories.summary: London, ON (October 7, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) are investigating after a London Hydro pole was cut down in the south end of the city last night.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 7, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) are investigating after a London Hydro pole was cut down in the south end of the city last night.

On Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at approximately 5:45 p.m., a citizen in the area of Exeter Road and Meg Drive heard a loud noise and observed smoke and flames near a hydro pole.

The citizen called 9-1-1, and officers attended with members of the London Fire Department, and London Hydro.

Multiple downed power lines and a hydro pole were located, and it was determined that the base of the pole had been intentionally cut. The damage is estimated at approximately $10,000.

As a result of the incident, a number of London Hydro customers were without power. London Hydro has since completed the repairs, and all power has been restored.

There were no reported injuries.

The investigation has been re-assigned to members of the LPS Patrol Operations Investigative Section.

Images of the suspect and suspect’s vehicle are being released in hopes that someone can identify him.

The suspect is described as a white male wearing a ball cap, a black hoodie with writing across the chest and grey pants.

The suspect vehicle is described as a grey SUV, believed to be a 2019 Honda CR-V or similar model.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:20 p.m. and 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, and witnessed the incident, or who May have dashcam, residential or business surveillance footage, to contact the London Police Service.

Anyone with information in relation to these types of incidents is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Barricaded male
stories.summary: London, ON (October 7, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after an investigation in the south-east end of the city earlier this week.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 7, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after an investigation in the south-east end of the city earlier this week.

On Monday, October 5, 2026, members of the London Police Service responded to a residence on Frontenac Road in relation to checking the welfare of an individual.

At approximately 6:05 a.m., officers attended the area and learned that the suspect male had barricaded himself inside the home. Members of the Emergency Response Unit (ERU) were called to assist, and nearby roads were closed for a period of time while police attempted to negotiate with the suspect male.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the suspect exited the residence and threw an object toward officers. No injuries were reported. The suspect then threw another object at the front windshield of the London Police Service's Light Armoured Vehicle (LAV), before retreating back inside the residence.

The vehicle did not sustain any damage.

At approximately 7:10 a.m., the suspect exited the residence, armed with a knife. He uttered threats toward officers. Negotiations continued while police maintained containment of the residence.

At approximately 10:05 a.m., the suspect exited the residence and was taken into custody without injury.

As a result of the investigation, Ara Husni, 20, of London, has been charged with:

Two counts of assault a peace officer with a weapon;

Fail to comply with release order; and

Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.

The accused is expected to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

At approximately 6:05 a.m., officers attended the area and learned that the suspect male had barricaded himself inside the home. Members of the Emergency Response Unit (ERU) were called to assist, and nearby roads were closed for a period of time while police attempted to negotiate with the suspect male.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the suspect exited the residence and threw an object toward officers. No injuries were reported. The suspect then threw another object at the front windshield of the London Police Service's Light Armoured Vehicle (LAV), before retreating back inside the residence.
The vehicle did not sustain any damage.
At approximately 7:10 a.m., the suspect exited the residence, armed with a knife. He uttered threats toward officers. Negotiations continued while police maintained containment of the residence.
At approximately 10:05 a.m., the suspect exited the residence and was taken into custody without injury.
As a result of the investigation, Ara Husni, 20, of London, has been charged with:
Two counts of assault a peace officer with a weapon;
Fail to comply with release order; and
Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.
The accused is expected to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: A Toronto cancer patient applied for pricey out-of-country funding. Now Ontario is tightening the rules
stories.summary: Funding will now only be available for drug treatments when “specific conditions” are met, Health Ministry says.
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
The Ford government has tightened its policy on when it will fund out-of-country treatments, in the wake of a high-profile court fight by a Toronto man with terminal cancer.

The Ministry of Health says amendments to Ontario’s Health Insurance Act mean funding will now only be provided for drug treatments that are already in use and approved for public coverage in the province but are temporarily unavailable.

The regulatory amendments — announced this week — essentially close the door to patients like Alex Shved, a 37-year-old with metastatic melanoma , who has been fighting to have Ontario fund a last-resort therapy in the U.S. He argues that his terminal diagnosis means he can’t wait for the personalized cell treatment to make its way through Canada’s lengthy drug funding process.

Shved called Ontario’s move “a betrayal” and said he’s “incredibly frustrated” the province has blocked access to the out-of-country program for drug treatments that have been given the green light by Health Canada but not approved for public coverage.

Last month, a panel of the Ontario Divisional Court directed the provincial government to reconsider its earlier denial to fund Shved’s treatment in the U.S., citing his immediate need.

The Health Ministry states the new Health Insurance Act amendments were put in place to “protect Ontario patients’ access to affordable, life-saving medication here at home.”

In its Tuesday announcement, the ministry states the province’s out-of-country drug funding program, which has been in place since 2011, will now only fund drugs that have gone through Ontario’s “rigorous, consistent, transparent, evidence-based and expert-led process.”

The ministry said it needed to act to prevent the Ontario Health Insurance Plan from paying out an additional $5.2 billion each year. It also said the policy, as previously written, created “a back door for global pharmaceutical companies to avoid negotiating directly with the province to achieve more competitive pricing.”

Sylvia Jones, deputy premier and minister of health, said in the news release that the government is “protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price-gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas.”

“This change supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions, protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process and will help avoid up to $5.2 billion in additional costs to Ontario’s health-care system every year,” Jones said.

The amendments are to Regulation 552 of the Health Insurance Act. The conditions for funding now include that the drug treatment is performed and publicly funded in the province; access to the drug is temporarily unavailable in Ontario; and delay in access “makes it necessary that the insured person travel out of Canada to avoid death or medically significant irreversible tissue damage.”

The province pointed to the need to protect Canada’s ability to negotiate fair drug prices with pharmaceutical companies as a main reason to make the regulatory change. The Health Ministry also said it needed to limit a recent but “significant increase” in out-of-country treatment requests that would otherwise lead to “up to $170 million” in additional annual costs.

Steven J. Hoffman, professor of global health, law, and political science at York University’s Global Strategy Lab, said in an email statement that the regulatory clarification “makes good sense for promoting value-for-money in Ontario’s health-care system and protecting efforts to ensure Canadians pay some of the world’s lowest prices for patented medicines.”

He said the executive officer of the Ontario Public Drug Programs will likely continue to decline Shved’s request for out-of-country drug coverage. Shved confirmed Wednesday the province has again denied his application.

Hoffman said that provinces must be effective stewards of limited health-care resources and noted that how pharmaceutical companies set their prices also deserves scrutiny.

“Companies developing new drugs and charging prices that only multi-millionaires can afford is not helpful,” Hoffman said. He described Shved’s case as “tragic.”

Shved was diagnosed with melanoma in 2020 and is running out of treatment options. Doctors have recommended he undergo tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, or TIL therapy, which uses a patient’s own cells to train their immune system to find and attack cancer.

Produced by an American biotechnology company, the therapy is marketed as lifileucel, also known by its brand name Amtagvi, and is only available at authorized centres in the U.S. Shved said a Florida hospital quoted $1.3 million for the therapy, which requires chemotherapy and time in hospital, in addition to producing the personalized cell treatment.

In its September ruling, the three-justice panel of the Ontario Divisional Court underscored that medical experts had recommended Shved get access to TIL therapy as part of its reasoning for directing the province to reassess its earlier denial.

“The record discloses that he will likely be dead by Christmas if he does not receive the requested treatment within a few weeks,” the panel wrote in its ruling.

The Health Ministry’s news release stated it’s “exploring all available options” for the court ruling, including an appeal “and/or seeking a mutually satisfactory resolution” with Shved.

On Wednesday, Shved said he has yet to receive any settlement details and is unsure what he will do next.

“I don’t know what this (amendment change) means for me, or for all the other people who are in the queue,” he said. “This is a blanket rejection of all applications now and in the future.”

stories.title: An Ontario Trillium Benefit payment is coming soon. Here’s what you need to know to get it
stories.summary: The OTB is comprised of three credits, but you only need to qualify for at least one to receive it.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin; Joshua Smith; Jake Ross
stories.content:
For those whose bank balances could use a boost after the back-to-school season and ahead of the holidays, the next Ontario Trillium Benefit payment is going out to eligible Ontarians on Oct. 9 .

The provincial government started issuing the payments in 2012 after including it in the 2011 budget.

Here’s what you should know about the money that could be coming your way.

The Ontario Trillium Benefit (OTB) combines three credits — the Northern Ontario Energy Credit, the Ontario Energy and Tax Credit, and the Ontario Sales Tax Credit — to help offset energy, sales and property tax expenses.

In order to qualify for the benefit, you need to have filed an income tax return and filled out the Ontario Trillium Benefit application form.

The Canada Revenue Agency will determine if you’re eligible to receive the benefit based on the information you provided.

You can receive the benefit if you’re eligible for at least one of the three credits noted in the previous section.

To estimate your amount, use the child and family benefit calculator. Taxpayers entitled to more than $500 could’ve opted for either a monthly payout starting this past June or a lump sum that’ll be issued next June.

If your 2026 OTB annual entitlement is $500 or less, it would’ve been issued in one lump-sum payment in the first payment month, which is usually July.

To apply for the Ontario Trillium Benefit, you have to fill out the ON‑BEN Application for the 2026 Ontario Trillium Benefit and Ontario Senior Homeowners’ Property Tax Grant form.

The CRA will send you a notice if you are deemed eligible for the Ontario Trillium Benefit.

In order to continue receiving the benefit, you have to file income tax annually and reapply by filling out the form each year. If you were previously deemed ineligible for the benefit in a previous year, you can reapply for it.

If you already receive your income tax refund or other benefits or credits by direct deposit, you will also receive your OTB payments by direct deposit. Otherwise, you’ll get your payments by cheque.

The federal government is encouraging people to sign up for direct deposit. Wildfires in Ontario have delayed the delivery of a small number of benefit and credit cheques, the government says .

The first payment is typically received four to eight weeks after applying.

The payments are issued monthly, unless you qualify to receive the aforementioned lump sum.

The funds have been issued on the 10th day of every month this year, except when the 10th falls on a weekend. That’s why the money will arrive on Oct. 9.

Subsequent payments will be sent out on Nov. 10 and Dec. 10.

stories.title: Toronto Zoo announces baby wombat’s name in a sweet nod to the little joey’s mother
stories.summary: More than 16,000 people voted on the name for the new female southern hairy-nosed wombat, who was known as #TZpouchpotato.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
The Toronto Zoo’s newest wombat finally has a name, and it’s one her mother would approve of.

After more than 16,000 votes , the zoo announced Wednesday that the baby southern hairy-nosed wombat is now called Clover, a nod to one of her mother’s favourite foods.

The joey, previously known as “#TZPouchPotato,” is the first wombat reared at the zoo in more than 30 years.

Clover was chosen as the baby wombat’s name after 16,000 votes.

Clover was one of four names put to a public vote alongside Nellie, Melba and Matilda. The zoo said the winning name honours her mother, Matilba, who enjoys munching on clover in her outdoor habitat.

Toronto Zoo CEO Dolf DeJong said the response to the contest shows how people have taken the baby wombat to heart.

“To reach out to our community and have 16,000 people weigh in on the name, I think really shows how this species and this individual has captured the community’s imagination,” DeJong told the Star.

Clover is only the second wombat successfully reared at the Toronto Zoo. The first, a female named Nan who lived from 1994 to 2018, was Clover’s great-grandmother, according to the zoo.

Toronto Zoo CEO Dolf DeJong compared watching Matilba dig while Clover gets in the way to “a parent trying to vacuum and the toddler at their feet.”

At the name unveiling Wednesday, visitors gathered around the habitat hoping to catch a glimpse of Clover. She was initially shy around the larger crowd, DeJong said, but eventually emerged after people stepped back.

“She stays close to mom Matilba,” he said. “You get all these amazing little moments with mother and daughter interacting.”

DeJong compared watching Matilba dig while Clover gets in the way to “a parent trying to vacuum and the toddler at their feet.”

Clover spent close to 10 months developing in and around her mother’s pouch. She is now too big to stay inside it and started exploring the habitat more independently, though the zoo says she is still nursing.

Matilba was “incredibly protective,” during Clover’s early development, DeJong said. Even as Clover begins venturing farther away, she still tends to stay close.

“Baby was right in the shadow of mom,” he said.

The naming process was supported by the Australian Consulate-General in Toronto, which helped select the options put to the public vote.

“Wombats hold a special place in the hearts of Australians, and it is heartwarming to see Canadians welcome this little ambassador to the Toronto Zoo,” Kate Hogan, Australian High Commissioner to Canada, said in the zoo’s news release.

Visitors hoping to see Clover can find her in the Australasia Pavilion. DeJong said their best chance of spotting her is near the beginning or end of the day.

stories.title: Ottawa tracking allegations of foreign interference in Alberta referendum, Carney says
stories.summary: "It's exceptionally important that all elections that are held in Canada and all votes are held are free and fair," the prime minister said.
stories.author: Tonda MacCharles
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday his government is closely tracking allegations of foreign interference in the Alberta referendum campaign, adding it is critical that votes are “free and fair.”

His first public comments came the day after a federal watchdog office revealed it notified a leading Alberta separatist group, among 60 others, about legal obligations to report foreign influence.

Asked about allegations of foreign interference in Alberta, where an Oct. 19 referendum will test the public demand for a vote on independence, Carney told the Star, “We follow these things closely, and it’s exceptionally important that all elections that are held in Canada and all votes are held are free and fair.”

Carney’s comments also came on a day when Elon Musk posted on X — the social media platform formerly known as Twitter that he owns — that Quebec , Alberta and Saskatchewan “should separate.” Musk, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, wrote, “they would be better off.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe responded on X in a terse reply: “No.”

Late Wednesday, Steven MacKinnon, the federal minister of democratic reform, issued a further statement on the Alberta referendum, saying the government is committed to “protecting the integrity of our democratic processes and institutions, and “the risk of foreign interference is real.”

He said Ottawa is working alongside Alberta provincial authorities including its elections office and local police “to ensure the integrity of the referendum.”

Albertans “can trust that their rights will be protected and that action will be taken against any attempts to undermine our democracy.”

The question of foreign influence (which refers to overt attempts to sway public opinion) and interference (which refers to covert activity to affect debates) in Canada’s elections and other fundamental votes has taken on greater urgency with the rise of technology and powerful online tools.

Canada’s foreign influence commissioner, Anton Boegman, said Tuesday his office reached out last month to Alberta Prosperity Project, one of the most vocal advocates of Alberta separatism, whose organizers travelled last year to Washington to meet with unnamed U.S. State Department officials.

The group, which is not registered as a third-party advertiser in the provincial referendum but advocates for Alberta independence and closer ties with the U.S., is among 60 organizations or individuals Boegman said his office contacted using a list compiled with assistance from Elections Alberta regarding activities related to the Oct. 19 vote.

Alberta Prosperity Project organizers met with Republican party political strategists from Michigan who developed a voter mobilization app that was credited with helping Trump win that state in the 2024 U.S. presidential election, according to reports published by the Globe and Mail and Press Progress.

Earlier this year, the Alberta group’s leaders acknowledged they travelled to Washington in 2025 to meet with officials at the U.S. State Department. The Globe, citing one organizer, reported Saturday that the Alberta separatists discussed greater American access to Alberta’s oil and fresh water resources in exchange for American financial support for Alberta’s independence.

Alberta separatists gather at the Alberta Legislature in Edmonton on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026, for a protest organized by the Alberta Prosperity Project.

One of the group’s leaders who acts as counsel for the group, Jeffrey Rath, has disputed the Globe’s characterization of the talks in Washington, and told the Star the group does not have any obligation to submit its contacts to the foreign influence transparency registry.

“We do not meet any of the criteria under the (Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act). The very first criteria is that you have an arrangement with a foreign principal ... we have no arrangement with anybody. Our contacts with the United States were purely informal,” he told the Star’s Stephanie Taylor.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, left, waits to deliver a speech on Alberta Day in Calgary, Alta., Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026.THE Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh

It’s not known who else Boegman has contacted, or what specific kind of foreign influence his office is worried about.

At first, the watchdog office refused to even publicly disclose the number of groups it contacted, with the commissioner only revealing that to a handful of reporters who pressed him following an appearance Tuesday at a parliamentary committee.

The number of those notified by Boegman’s office exceeds the number of groups that Elections Alberta has registered as third-party advertisers in the campaign, with 28 listed on its website.

Premier Danielle Smith’s government has asked Albertans to cast votes — on 10 separate ballots, one for each question — on whether the province should demand more power on immigration levels and services offered to newcomers, more say in judicial appointments, and the ability to opt-out of federal programs, as well as the final, potentially most explosive question: whether to trigger a second binding vote on taking Alberta out of Canada.

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to journalists as he makes his way to a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Oct. 7, 2026.

Carney has articulated a pro-unity argument in the past week — after announcing a major pipeline construction project would be fast-tracked, and after Quebec voters elected a minority separatist Parti Québécois government on Monday — that centres on the notion that “Canada is working.”

On Tuesday, he touted his government’s trade diversification agenda and Ottawa’s drive to build major capital-intensive resource and infrastructure projects. “You know, this is a crucial time for our country. It’s a crucial time for Quebec,” Carney said. “This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness.”

stories.title: Stephen Galloway tells court he was shocked by rape allegations
stories.summary: The former UBC professor believed his two-year relationship with his student had ended amicably, he told the court
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway acknowledged his two-year affair with a University of B.C. creative writing student was “inappropriate, ill-advised and stupid” during testimony on the second day of a trial where this woman and three others are defending themselves against accusations that they later defamed him.

Mr. Galloway told B.C. Supreme Court on Tuesday that he believed the relationship had ended amicably. And so, he said, he was surprised to learn shortly afterward that his former partner had filed a sexual harassment complaint with the school’s administration – an allegation which would eventually publicly explode and torpedo his personal and professional life.

“Without being crass, there was enthusiastic and ongoing consent at all times,” he said when his lawyer Daniel Burnett asked him about their sex life.

The high-profile trial is more than a decade in the making. Ubc’s announcement of a formal investigation of “serious allegations” involving Mr. Galloway in 2015 led to an online firestorm over the CanLit luminary’s rights to due process versus the rights of his alleged victim. UBC fired Mr. Galloway in 2016, but a retired judge hired by the university to investigate the complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established he committed sexual assault or assault.

He was never charged by police. In 2018, he sued nearly two dozen people for defamation, saying they had falsely claimed online that he had sexually and physically assaulted the woman. She is known publicly as A.B. because her identity is protected by a publication ban until 45 days after Justice Neena Sharma makes her final judgment.

Only A.B. and three other defendants remain: Mandi Gray, Dana Kagis and Glynnis Kirchmeier.

At the start of proceedings Monday, A.B.’s lawyer Arden Beddoes told the court she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment – but not admitting she spread lies about her former romantic partner – explaining that she had tried to kill herself twice in recent months because of the stress of the lawsuit. She is not testifying.

During Tuesday’s afternoon court session in Vancouver, Mr. Galloway’s lawyer directed the 51-year-old to explain how the student first began joining him for post-lecture drinks with a fellow professor in one of their offices before the pair began a sexual relationship around April 2011.

Mr. Galloway testified that he and A.B. initially had fun together, even if he now realizes their relationship was not appropriate given the power dynamic between a professor and a master’s student.

“I’d never had moments where I thought this person’s not enjoying this relationship,” he said.

After their affair ended in April, 2013, Mr. Galloway testified, they kept texting regularly and remained cordial. But his lawyer told the court that in July of that year A.B. filed a formal sexual harassment complaint with the university, alleging that Mr. Galloway repeatedly gave her several drinks of scotch in his office and propositioned her for sex.

Upon learning of this complaint, nearly three years later during the university’s investigation, Mr. Galloway testified that he had two reactions: shock that she was complaining even as she was texting him regularly asking him to go to concerts and other social events, and a feeling that her allegations were ridiculous since their relationship had ended cordially.

He also testified how in 2013, he dealt with a similar sexual harassment complaint from A.B. against a visiting scholar. She alleged the academic, who was a candidate for a professorship, had groped and choked her in an elevator while touring the campus, Mr. Galloway testified. After hearing her account and her refusal to file a formal complaint, Mr. Galloway stated that he and two of his colleagues decided to do what they could to stop him from being hired.

“Shamefully, the three of us lowered our interview scores to the point where the candidate dropped out,” he said.

Mr. Galloway said he was about to go on stage in Dayton, Ohio, for a speaking engagement when Ubc’s Dean of Arts first notified him he was being suspended in November, 2015, pending an internal review of an allegation of sexual assault.

He began his testimony detailing how he rose from an arts undergrad at his hometown college in Kamloops to become one of only a handful of Canadian authors with a New York agent, with lucrative speaking engagements across North America.

He had sold over a million copies of 2008’s The Cellist of Sarajevo across more than 30 countries and commanded as much as US$10,000 for an appearance, he testified. All of that vanished when the university’s investigation of A.B.’s allegations of sexual assault became public, the court heard.

He is expected to testify for the remainder of the week.

stories.title: Elections Alberta notifies thousands of referendum voters about invalid mail-in ballot packs
stories.summary: Agency has been working to assuage concerns about election integrity in the home stretch of the referendum campaign
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Thousands of Albertans May not have their ballots counted for the province’s coming referendum after Elections Alberta said more than 3,000 voters failed to properly identify themselves in the mail-in voting process.

The provincial elections agency said it has reached out to those electors, most of whom incorrectly filled out the voter declaration form that must be submitted alongside their ballots, asking them to resubmit documentation over e-mail.

“If they provide the required information, by email, we can process their special ballot,” Maia Hanrahan, spokesperson for Elections Alberta, said in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail.

“If they do not, we cannot process their special ballot, and it will be rejected.”

The agency has been working to assuage concerns about election integrity in the home stretch of the referendum campaign.

Elections Alberta has verified nearly 221,000 completed mail-in ballots, Ms. Hanrahan said, representing roughly one-third of the 652,000 electors who have been sent voting packages ahead of the province’s Oct. 19 referendum.

The errors add to a list of problems that have plagued the mail-in voting process, just one component of a referendum that Elections Alberta says is one of the biggest electoral events in Canadian history.

The referendum centres around 10 questions – all designed by Premier Danielle Smith’s government – asking voters to weigh in on provincial separation, immigration and constitutional issues.

The sweeping vote has forced Elections Alberta to order 45 million ballots for the 10 separate questions, more than twice the number of ballots cast nationwide in the 2025 federal election.

It has also hired more than 41,000 election workers and received roughly 65,000 applications, Ms. Hanrahan said on Tuesday. The agency is hoping to hire an unprecedented 60,000-plus election workers – more than four times the number who helped in Alberta’s 2023 provincial general election.

Nearly one-fifth of Alberta voters, meanwhile, have seized the opportunity to vote by mail, the first time Albertans have had unrestricted access to the process for a provincewide election.

The agency is asking voters to mail their ballots by Oct. 9 to ensure their votes are counted.

In order to vote by mail, Alberta requires electors to request a special ballot package and return the ballots along with a copy of their valid identification, and a declaration form containing their personal information and signature.

Ms. Hanrahan wrote that some voters filled out their declaration incorrectly by putting their birthdate in the signature line, not signing the declaration, or failing to fill out the entire form. She added that other voters either neglected to send a copy of their ID or there were other issues with the document.

Elections Alberta is asking those voters to rectify those issues by e-mailing the agency a new declaration form or copy of their ID.

“Without these two pieces of information, we are unable to verify and count their submitted special ballot, and it would be rejected,” she wrote.

The agency has been proactively responding on social media to voters who were notified that they need to send in more documentation.

Elections Alberta has been forced to address a crop of issues in the lead up to the referendum. Some of the first declaration forms sent to electors, for example, incorrectly included a section asking voters to testify that they’re unable to vote in person. Alberta voters were previously prohibited from voting by mail unless they could prove they were unable to.

Elections Alberta also found 313 mail-in packages sent to electors that were missing ballots.

Some observers have pointed to repeated warnings from Elections Alberta – an arm’s-length government agency – that it is underfunded and understaffed.

The provincial elections agency said it has reached out to those electors, most of whom incorrectly filled out the voter declaration form that must be submitted alongside their ballots, asking them to resubmit documentation over e-mail.
“If they provide the required information, by email, we can process their special ballot,” Maia Hanrahan, spokesperson for Elections Alberta, said in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail.
“If they do not, we cannot process their special ballot, and it will be rejected.”
The agency has been working to assuage concerns about election integrity in the home stretch of the referendum campaign.

Elections Alberta has verified nearly 221,000 completed mail-in ballots, Ms. Hanrahan said, representing roughly one-third of the 652,000 electors who have been sent voting packages ahead of the province’s Oct. 19 referendum.

The errors add to a list of problems that have plagued the mail-in voting process, just one component of a referendum that Elections Alberta says is one of the biggest electoral events in Canadian history.
The referendum centres around 10 questions – all designed by Premier Danielle Smith’s government – asking voters to weigh in on provincial separation, immigration and constitutional issues.
The sweeping vote has forced Elections Alberta to order 45 million ballots for the 10 separate questions, more than twice the number of ballots cast nationwide in the 2025 federal election.

It has also hired more than 41,000 election workers and received roughly 65,000 applications, Ms. Hanrahan said on Tuesday. The agency is hoping to hire an unprecedented 60,000-plus election workers – more than four times the number who helped in Alberta’s 2023 provincial general election.
Nearly one-fifth of Alberta voters, meanwhile, have seized the opportunity to vote by mail, the first time Albertans have had unrestricted access to the process for a provincewide election.
The agency is asking voters to mail their ballots by Oct. 9 to ensure their votes are counted.

In order to vote by mail, Alberta requires electors to request a special ballot package and return the ballots along with a copy of their valid identification, and a declaration form containing their personal information and signature.

Ms. Hanrahan wrote that some voters filled out their declaration incorrectly by putting their birthdate in the signature line, not signing the declaration, or failing to fill out the entire form. She added that other voters either neglected to send a copy of their ID or there were other issues with the document.
Elections Alberta is asking those voters to rectify those issues by e-mailing the agency a new declaration form or copy of their ID.
“Without these two pieces of information, we are unable to verify and count their submitted special ballot, and it would be rejected,” she wrote.
The agency has been proactively responding on social media to voters who were notified that they need to send in more documentation.

Elections Alberta has been forced to address a crop of issues in the lead up to the referendum. Some of the first declaration forms sent to electors, for example, incorrectly included a section asking voters to testify that they’re unable to vote in person. Alberta voters were previously prohibited from voting by mail unless they could prove they were unable to.

That report was published roughly three months before Ms. Smith unveiled her plans for the October referendum. In May, Mr. McClure told a legislative committee that he’s “drinking from a firehose.”

Last month, lawyer and pro-independence organizer Keith Wilson said it’s critical his supporters vote at the mailbox. Prominent separatist leader Mitch Sylvestre, meanwhile, said he has “no faith in the system at all.”

stories.title: Rally calls on council candidates to pledge support for expanded licensing of landlords’ buildings
stories.summary: Members of tenants’ advocacy group London Acorn held a rally outside City Hall on Tuesday, calling on council candidates to pledge that they will support expanding municipal licensing of rental properties operated by landlords.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Members of tenants’ advocacy group London Acorn held a rally outside City Hall on Tuesday, calling on council candidates to pledge that they will support expanding municipal licensing of rental properties operated by landlords.

Currently, only residential buildings with up to four units, and converted dwellings with five or more units, require a Residential Rental Unit License.

“That leaves out the majority of landlords, all of the large landlords, and all of the corporate landlords,” said Jordan Smith, chair of London Acorn’s East of Adelaide Chapter. “So, that’s obviously really ineffective as a policy.”

The municipal licenses are intended to provide regulations for rental units, protect the safety of renters, and ensure property standards are maintained.

However, Acorn wants landlords to pay annual per-unit fees to fund a broader licensing program that would include proactive inspections and public reporting of the results.

Smith says with less than three weeks to go until the municipal election, candidates are being asked to pledge their support for the changes, “We’ve been presenting to the city for the last six years, literally that resolve this issue, you know, so we’re looking for a little bit of common sense here. We’re looking for a champion coming into it with our new council.

Mayoral candidate Tariq Khan was among a small number of candidates who attended the rally, “The rental protection office is not working, or there is a lack of accountability. There is a lack of supervision, and I just want to fix it.”

Following a meeting of the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc) on Tuesday afternoon, CTV News asked incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan and mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson about potentially expanding rental unit licensing.

“I wouldn’t make any changes without a robust consultation on the extent of the licensing regime,” Morgan said. “What I will say is, there are costs and enforcement implications of licensing widely. Often those costs get passed on to tenants. So I think we’d want to be cautious about that.”

He added, “I do think we need to continue to work with community partners on modernizing our rules. We brought in a renoviction by-law. We’ve made other changes to protect renters, and I’m always open to discussion about things that we could do.”

Stevenson acknowledged the concerns expressed by Acorn, “We’re hearing a lot of concern about apartment buildings where people have gone a long period of time without elevators, without heat, access to hot water, or water itself. So, I think that’s the underlying issue. I wouldn’t want to go broad and create a lot of red tape and costs in areas where it’s not needed. We want to focus all the efforts on the problems.”

She added that consultation would be important, “Getting people involved and listening to what the issues are, where are they, and at what level of government are we able to make a difference.”

A list of all 12 candidates for mayor can be found on the City of London website along with the registered candidates in all 14 wards.

Election day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: Hanover shooting leaves man injured, suspect arrested
stories.summary: At least three schools and the town’s hospital were placed in a “hold and secure” Tuesday after gunshots were heard in Hanover.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
One person has been taken into custody following a shooting investigation in Grey County.

According to police, one person was injured in the shooting shortly before noon at a residence in the 300 block of 14th Avenue in Hanover, Ont.

Police said a 37-year-old man was taken to Hanover and District Hospital by Grey County paramedics with gunshot wounds that were not considered life-threatening.

Investigators said a 50-year-old suspect was arrested a short time after the incident, however they have not released details on any charges. Officers also recovered a firearm near the scene.

Hanover police are asking for the public’s help identifying and locating a black van that was seen leaving the area immediately after the shooting.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Hanover Police Service investigators or Crime Stoppers.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Cost of living on the minds of Fanshawe students, housing staff as London Hydro proposes rate hike
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/wC3221JkUhs With the recent proposed price increase for electricity by London Hydro, students...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
With the recent proposed price increase for electricity by London Hydro, students at Fanshawe and staff at student residencies are concerned about the impact it could have on the cost of living in the city.

The concerns come after London Hydro announced yesterday that it intends to raise rates in the city by approximately $6 per month or $72 per year, citing cost of business and infrastructure upgrades as the reason why.

Meanwhile at Fanshawe, many students haven’t heard of the proposed price raises. However, when informed, they expressed concern about how it May add to larger financial problems that students face.

“The cost of living for people is absolutely nightmarish right now,” said first-year pharmacy technician student Charley Crann.

While Crann lives at home still, she says she understands the problems students living in residence face with paying for utilities.

For other students, an increase in hydro prices May be difficult to budget for. First-year environmental technologies student Avery Clarkson said he believes students May have to rework their monthly budgets.

Hydro lines running through Kestrel Court. The proposed increase in London Hydro rates could have long-term consequences on student finances. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“As someone who just recently moved to London and is living in an apartment myself, that’s an additional $72 I could spend on food,” said fellow first-year environmental technologies student Lukas Krikstaponis. “I’d rather have the funds available to have more food than pay for hydro unnecessarily.”

Elliott Anderson, another environmental technologies student, added that as a lifelong London resident, a potential hike in hydro prices would add to the list of things she’s seen become more expensive.

“On top of Doug Ford cutting Osap, the grocery prices rising, everything on top of that, it just makes everything a lot harder,” she said.

Anderson also voiced questions about whether or not the proposed price raises were necessary, believing the provincial government should eat the cost.

For people working in student residency, the long-term effects of a price raise on hydro also pose concerns. Leasing agent at Foundry First Ariel Sparks compared the potential consequences to the metaphor of a frog not noticing it’s being boiled in a pot of water as the temperature is gradually increased.

“I think at first it’ll be nominal, and you won’t be able to tell until at the end of the year you’re like ‘oh, I’ve spent way more than I thought on the utilities’,” said Sparks. “That’s going to trickle down into their books and their tuitions.”

Sparks also believes that hydro prices May influence the rental market for off-campus student housing, especially since she is unaware of any incentives or assistance that Foundry or Fanshawe provides to students for housing. She added that she thinks a flat rate or cap rate for students and student housing would help students with hydro prices.

“That’s just one idea that could be tossed in the pot,” she said.

If approved, the price increase would take effect on May 1, 2027.

stories.title: Parti Québécois Leader says independence vote won’t be early priority for incoming minority government
stories.summary: Mark Carney played down the separatist threat from the PQ’s win and emphasized the benefits of co-operation
stories.author: Maura Forrest, Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon vowed to work with opposition parties and played down the potential for conflict with Ottawa on his first day as premier-designate of Quebec after securing a minority government.

The PQ’s pledge to hold an independence referendum has been complicated by the low level of popular support the party earned from voters in Monday’s provincial election, a result that revealed a divided province deeply ambivalent about the separatist project.

Election night saw the governing Coalition Avenir Québec wiped off the political map, losing all of its seats. Outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette resigned as leader of the party on Tuesday.

In a Quebec City press conference earlier in the day, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon suggested sovereignty won’t be a top priority in the first part of his mandate, and repeated a promise not to hold a referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump is in the White House.

“We’ve got time. We’ve got plenty of urgent problems to solve, so I think the upcoming months will more be about … things that are urgent,” he said.

The PQ’s 59 seats put it five shy of its hoped-for majority, and its 28 per cent share of the popular vote is the lowest of any government in Quebec history. A five-way race splintered the 70 per cent of Quebeckers who say they don’t want a referendum.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon did not waver on his commitment to sovereignty, though he acknowledged his minority government would need the support of opposition lawmakers to launch a referendum.

“Once we make a commitment during a campaign, we work to carry it out,” he said, brushing off questions about the strength of his mandate to pursue Quebec’s independence.

On Parliament Hill, Prime Minister Mark Carney sought to play down the separatist threat from the PQ’s win and emphasized the benefits of co-operation.

“It’s a crucial time for Quebec. It’s a crucial time for our country. This is not a time to wait for something a few years down the road. It’s a time to act. It’s a time for boldness,” Mr. Carney told reporters on his way into a cabinet meeting.

The Prime Minister is navigating a delicate moment for national unity, with a referendum in Alberta less than two weeks away, and persistent threats to Canada’s sovereignty and economy by the Trump administration.

Asked if the Parti Québécois had a mandate to separate with just 28 per cent of the vote, the Prime Minister did not answer the question but noted that he won last year’s federal election with a 43 per cent mandate from voters.

Mr. Carney spoke Tuesday with the premier-designate, and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon described their conversation as “perfectly respectful and constructive.” He said he will meet soon with the Prime Minister.

The PQ Leader said he is ready to collaborate with the federal government and the other provinces “provided that it serves Quebec’s interests,” but cautioned that collaboration “doesn’t mean asking for nothing and then agreeing to anything.”

“The federal government’s position, in principle, must follow the will expressed by the people of Quebec – not the other way around,” he said.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon repeated his desire to abolish the office of lieutenant-governor in Quebec, a move to buck the British monarchy that critics see as an attempt to foment conflict with Ottawa. He said he has sought a legal opinion on the matter.

The premier-designate said one of his first moves in office will be to assemble a negotiating team to protect key sectors of Quebec’s economy during the trade dispute with the United States.

Upon announcing her resignation Tuesday, Ms. Fréchette said her party needs someone to lead the CAQ into the next election and beyond, although it is unclear whether the once-dominant party can be revived after being shut out of the National Assembly.

The Caq’s “third way” nationalism, which seeks to defend Quebec’s identity and powers without the disruption of independence, is still the best option after eight years in government, Ms. Fréchette said.

“We allowed our nation to affirm itself,” she said.

Meanwhile, other opposition party leaders spoke about their plans for wielding the balance of power in a possibly short-lived minority parliament.

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard was upbeat after his party more than doubled its caucus by winning 40 seats, and called on former CAQ supporters to “come home” to the federalist party.

“We’re the only ones who can realistically block the PQ’s referendum project,” he said.

The left-wing separatist party Québec Solidaire did not rule out supporting the PQ in launching a referendum, which would require a majority vote in the National Assembly. The nine seats won by QS in the downtowns of Montreal and Quebec City would be enough to help the PQ trigger an independence vote, but the two separatist parties differ widely on immigration and identity issues, as well as the economy.

Ruba Ghazal, the co-leader of QS, remained vague about her intentions but suggested that cost-of-living issues were more urgent for many Quebeckers, and that holding a referendum would be more promising when a larger share of the population wants one. Currently, just 30 per cent of Quebeckers say they support independence, a historically low level.

“Anything is possible,” Ms. Ghazal said of supporting a PQ referendum initiative in the National Assembly. “We’ll do everything to rally a majority of the population to this beautiful project.”

“Quebec isn’t 70 per cent federalist. 70 per cent of people are anxious, or don’t know. There are those who have an attachment to Canada – it’s very diversified.”

The new PQ government will also have to contend with the wild card of the Quebec Conservative Party, which enters the National Assembly for the first time with a flourish after winning 19 seats.

Leader Éric Duhaime, the election’s breakout star, campaigned on aggressively shrinking the size of the Quebec state and sharply cutting immigration levels, which the province partly controls.

A self-described nationalist, Mr. Duhaime also opposes a referendum and has said his party will vote against one, but with a surprisingly large and mostly inexperienced caucus, controlling his troops will be a tall order.

“Our first challenge is to show Quebeckers we’re capable of taking on the functions we’ve been given … to play our role of watchdog well,” he said in a press conference Tuesday. “We’ll have a steep learning curve.”

With a file from Marieke Walsh

stories.title: Universities in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver brace for Oct. 7 protests
stories.summary: Jewish groups have decried the demonstrations as insensitive and deliberately provocative
stories.author: Colin Freeze, Kelly Grant
stories.content:
University officials in Canada’s largest cities say they are working with police and security services to prepare for protests Wednesday, the third anniversary of Hamas ’s deadly Oct. 7 attacks on Israel .

Protests are being planned at or near the University of Toronto, Montreal’s McGill University, and the University of British Columbia in Vancouver, as campuses continue to be flashpoints for demonstrations over conflicts in the Middle East.

About 1,200 Israelis and foreigners were killed and 250 people taken hostage when Hamas, which has been designated a terrorist entity by the Canadian government, invaded Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s subsequent invasion of Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in the territory.

In Canada and the United States, pro-Palestinian protesters have set up encampments on university campuses, demanding that the institutions divest from weapon manufacturers connected to the Israeli military and sever ties with Israeli universities that operate in the occupied territories.

Meanwhile, Jewish groups and students have demanded protection from alleged antisemitism on campus and demonstrations they say include threats and intimidation.

Pro-Palestinian groups in Canada organizing the campus protests have said they are intended to honour those killed in Gaza by Israel, while some Jewish groups have decried the demonstrations as insensitive and deliberately provocative.

McGill says it is in contact with the Service de Police de la Ville de Montréal ahead of a planned rally by pro-Palestinian groups outside the gates of that campus. “The university’s security services will enhance their staffing and are working closely with the Spvm,” said Katherine Cuplinskas, a spokeswoman for the school.

In an e-mail, Ms. Cuplinskas said the university has “dedicated intervention teams available to address unauthorized occupations, property damage, safety concerns, or significant operational disruptions.”

In Toronto, pro-Palestinian groups have been planning what they call an “honouring our martyrs” event at the University of Toronto’s downtown campus. The university has told student groups among the protesting factions that this event should not take place on campus.

An unsigned U of T statement says safety concerns are paramount and include “physical safety risks to participants and to members of the broader university community.” The statement says those concerns have been heightened by “the online promotion of counter-protests to take place at the same time.”

Some protest activity is still expected to take place on or around the downtown campus. The Toronto Police Service said it will be on hand Wednesday to monitor events. “We are aware and will be present,” said Nadine Ramadan, the force’s spokeswoman.

Protest activity is also being planned in Vancouver, according to UBC officials.

While the B.C. RCMP would not say whether they will be monitoring that event, university spokeswoman Thandi Fletcher said some security measures will be in place. “UBC is aware that two pro-Palestinian groups are organizing gatherings on the Vancouver campus on Oct. 7,” she said in an e-mail.

In October, 2024, McGill officials restricted access to the campus and asked professors to move classes online, citing an elevated potential for disruption on the first anniversary of the Hamas attacks.

And pro-Palestinian groups held an “honouring our martyrs” event last Oct. 7 on U of T’s Mississauga campus.

In an unsigned statement, the Boycott, Divest and Sanction caucus of the U of T graduate students union said the use of the term “martyrs” for the Oct. 7 protest refers to Palestinians killed in Gaza during the Israeli invasion.

However, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs counters that the term is a provocation meant to glorify Hamas.

“People are out there celebrating what happened,” said Danielle Keenan, a spokeswoman for Cija. “It would be more credible if these events were not taking place on Oct. 7 … This is the day that 1,200 people lost their lives.”

The concerns over this year’s Canadian campus protests coincide with mounting fears in Jewish communities worldwide. With the U.S. and Israel still at war with Iran, the Israeli government is warning Jews around the world that they May be at heightened risk of attacks this Oct. 7.

stories.title: Santé Québec releases report touting nearly $2-billion in savings
stories.summary: The report was released after the election victory of Parti Québécois, which has promised to dismantle the provincial health authority
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Hours after the election of the Parti Québécois, which pledged to dismantle Santé Québec, the provincial health authority released a Deloitte Canada report stating it had achieved nearly $2-billion in cost savings since it started operations in December, 2024.

PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose party will form a minority government, promised during the campaign to abolish Santé Québec, calling it “a bureaucratic monster.”

The Deloitte report was officially released Tuesday morning although it had been leaked to La Presse previously. Santé Québec wanted to wait until the end of the election campaign so it wouldn’t interfere in the political debate, Catherine Brousseau, the health authority’s spokeswoman, said.

The report was commissioned by Santé Québec’s board of directors in July. It said the organization had saved $1.9-billion since its creation, mostly by reducing the use of travel nurses and other agency temporary staff, which saved $1.7-billion in almost two years.

Many of those savings can be traced back to the outgoing Coalition Avenir Québec government, which made it a priority to eliminate agency personnel and reduce health care staffing – but the Deloitte report includes updated numbers.

The total time worked by temporary agency staff in Quebec’s health care system has shrunk by 86 per cent in nearly two years and overtime costs are also down, according to the report. Furthermore, the increase in health care personnel slowed from an annual average of 4.7 per cent in the 2019-2023 period to 0.8 per cent for 2025-2026.

The Deloitte analysis added that there were also unquantified savings from having Santé Québec act as a sole purchaser on behalf of the 30 regional health authorities and university hospital networks that it oversees.

“The initiatives undertaken have generated tangible benefits. In light of trends observed during major mergers and integrations, additional investments could support the continued realization of synergies and benefits,” the report said.

During the election campaign, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon floated different scenarios to replace Santé Québec, with either a smaller agency, a task force or a branch of the provincial Health Department.

Meeting reporters following the election, he said a “governmental efficiency secretariat” would be created to reduce bureaucracy and “superfluous programs.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has said that abolishing Santé Québec would save up to $100-million a year and complained that its staffing was bloated, calling it “a second mammoth” since it took over some of the functions previously handled by the province’s Health Department.

The Deloitte report, however, noted that 94 per cent of the 1,192 headquarter’s employees had been transferred from the Health Department and only 66 were new hires.

Santé Québec has been the public body providing health care services and managing the system daily since it was formed, while the Health Department sets strategic goals.

Contacted for comments on Tuesday, Christian Dubé, the former CAQ health minister who initiated Santé Québec, referred The Globe and Mail to the findings in the Deloitte report and to an open letter he made public in September.

“Quebeckers want a better healthcare system, not another reform,” Mr. Dubé wrote in the open letter, arguing that the changes he initiated in 2024 couldn’t show its full impact within a four-year electoral cycle.

Santé Québec was created by legislative act and abolishing it would require another law.

The PQ is five seats short of a legislative majority. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon acknowledged that his government will need the collaboration of opposition parties to pass its bills.

He noted that he shared similar views on tightening public spendings with Eric Duhaime’s Conservatives, who won 19 seats. “Our desire to better manage public finances after years of wastage should find a friendly ear among the Conservatives,” the premier-designate said.
