stories.title: Who is Conservative Party of Quebec Leader Éric Duhaime?
stories.summary: Quebec Conservative Party Leader Éric Duhaime and 18 members of his party emerged as winner in Monday's general election.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Heading into Monday’s Quebec general election, leader Éric Duhaime hoped to see a dozen Conservative Party of Quebec (CPQ) candidates, including himself, elected to the National Assembly — the minimum for official party status.

By night’s end, however, he and the party had “written a page” in the province’s history, winning 19 seats, the third most in a crowded field.

Duhaime committed to working with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s minority Parti Québécois government “to cut bureaucracy, put money back in families’ pockets and reform the old Quebec model” and said the CPQ would not “support a referendum that will weaken Quebec.”

Before Monday’s result, the CPQ was represented by lone MNA Maïté Blanchette Vézina (La Peltrie), who joined after leaving the Coalition Avenir Québec in the spring following extensive discussions with Duhaime.

Here’s what to know about the leader who led the party to claim its first seats in the provincial legislature in more than 90 years.

“He has said that from a young age he wanted to get involved in politics to give a voice to ordinary people, whom he believes are too often overlooked by the political elite,” it reads.

He attended the Université de Montréal, earning a bachelor’s in political science, and later obtained a master’s degree in public administration from the École nationale d’administration publique (Enap).

Éric Duhaime is hoping to make 'history' with Quebec Conservatives. Will he?

Marc-Olivier Fortin: PQ referendum hopes rest on support from hard left Québec Solidaire

Duhaime is also gay, having come out in a 2017 book, La fin de l’homosexualité et le dernier gay (The end of homosexuality and the last gay man), his first of five books to date.

In the 1990s, Duhaime worked as a political advisor to Bloc Québécois leaders Lucien Bouchard and Michel Gauthier. At the provincial level, he was also a Parti Québécois activist. He later joined Reform Party Leader Preston Manning’s “United Alternative” movement, before throwing his support behind Stockwell Day’s successful leadership bid for the Canadian Alliance party. He then served as an advisor to the leader from 2000 to 2002.

From 2003 to 2008, he was an advisor to Mario Dumont, leader of the Action démocratique du Québec (ADQ), and Bloc leader Gilles Duceppe.

In 2009, he joined the National Democratic Institute as a consultant — a U.S.-based non-governmental organization that promotes democratic institutions — and worked in Morocco, Mauritania and Iraq.

He told National Post’s Catherine Lévesque he returned from the latter suffering from Ptsd, but the media attention from having been there led to more opportunities to provide commentary. He later joined Québecors stable of columnists.

While still writing columns, he became a regular radio host in 2012, finding a wider audience on stations such as Noovo, Télé-Québec and Radio X, “a pillar of what in Quebec is called ‘radio poubelle’ — trash radio,” according to The Breach.

In 2003, before working for Dumont, a then-34-year-old Duhmaine entered Quebec’s general election under the ADQ, but finished third.

He told National Post that current Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre, also a political staffer at the time, helped him canvass suburban neighbourhoods that summer while he was visiting Montreal.

He remained on the periphery of the political world until 2021, when his notoriety helped him cruise to victory in the Cpq’s leadership race to succeed Adrien Pouliot, capturing 96 per cent of the vote conducted entirely online due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

But a seat in the legislature evaded him in the 2022 election, as he fell to the Caq’s Sylvain Levesque in the riding of Chauveau.

He also failed to get elected in the 2025 by-election for the Arthabaska riding (now redrawn as Arthabaska-L’Érable), losing to the Parti Québécois’ Alex Boissonneault by more than 4,000 ballots.

Monday night was a different story, however, with preliminary results indicating Duhaime steamrolled the competition by capturing 63 per cent of the Bellechasse riding vote. The PQ’s Jerome Couture was a distant second (15 per cent).

His first book offered a criticism of homosexual victimhood and, according to the jacket synopsis , aimed “to show that it is possible to be gay and happy in Quebec” without being a “martyr.”

It was followed by 2012’s L’État contre les jeunes: Comment les baby-boomers ont détourné le système (The State versus Youth: How Baby Boomers Hijacked the System), Libérez-nous des syndicats! (Free us from the Unions) a year later, and La SAQ pousse le bouchon! (The SAQ pushes the envelope!) in 2014, a criticism of the province’s liquor authority.

His fifth book, Destination Autonomie, in which he discusses how Quebec can gain more autonomy within Confederation, was released in April.

Just days before the election, he admitted that he used AI to help write the book after Quebecor media outlets reported last week that 62 per cent was machine-generated, according to The Canadian Press.

“AI is important to us. It’s part of reality,” he said Friday. “That said, it has to be done under human supervision. And that’s exactly what happened.”

— With files from Catherine Levesque

It was followed by 2012’s L’État contre les jeunes: Comment les baby-boomers ont détourné le système (The State versus Youth: How Baby Boomers Hijacked the System), Libérez-nous des syndicats! (Free us from the Unions) a year later, and La SAQ pousse le bouchon! (The SAQ pushes the envelope!) in 2014, a criticism of the province’s liquor authority.
His fifth book, Destination Autonomie, in which he discusses how Quebec can gain more autonomy within Confederation, was released in April.

Just days before the election, he admitted that he used AI to help write the book after Quebecor media outlets reported last week that 62 per cent was machine-generated, according to The Canadian Press.
“AI is important to us. It’s part of reality,” he said Friday. “That said, it has to be done under human supervision. And that’s exactly what happened.”

stories.title: Will the latest Canada grocery benefit payment help you ahead of Thanksgiving?
stories.summary: Eligible Canadians began receiving their second Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit payment on Monday.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Eligible Canadians began receiving their second payment on Monday under the new Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit .

Previously known as the GST/HST credit, the quarterly payments for lower-income Canadians can range from a few hundred dollars to nearly two thousand dollars annually, depending on income, marital status and the number of children in a household.

A single individual without children, for example, can receive up to $679 a year while those with four or more children can receive up to $1,826. Meant to help offset the rising cost of living , the payment comes as the annual inflation rate stood at three per cent in August .

Have you received a Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit payment? Is it helping you or your family make ends meet? How will you use it ahead of Thanksgiving? Do the payments help with the rising cost of groceries and other essentials? Or are the payments just a drop in the bucket?

stories.title: London robot pizza maker wins prestigious food tech award
stories.summary: The company is one of 40 recipients of a Foodtech Frontier Award from the Canadian Food Innovation Network.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London-based food technology company Appetronix has received a food industry award recognizing its work in robotics and automation.

The company is one of 40 recipients of a Foodtech Frontier Award from the Canadian Food Innovation Network. Appetronix was recognized for its fully automated robotic pizza oven technology designed for food-service environments. One of the systems is currently operating at John Glenn Columbus International Airport in Ohio.

Appetronix is also expanding into autonomous coffee and burrito bowl technology, with deployments planned in Toronto later this year.

Co-founder and chief innovation officer Ray Schott said the technology is designed to help restaurant operators address staffing and profitability challenges.

“From labour shortages to shrinking profit margins, to just being able to staff it, and to be able to do these on the off-peak hours, that’s a challenge,” Schott said. “This technology allows them to bridge that gap. I don’t need anybody to be manning this machine, so it’s available to be used 24 hours a day, seven days a week.”

Canadian Food Innovation Network CEO Dana McCauley said Canadian food technology firms continue to be leaders in innovation, despite often receiving limited recognition.

“There are so many Canadian innovators that are so under the radar and so unrecognized right here in Canada,” McCauley said. “As these companies start to work globally, it’s even more difficult to get their names out there. We hope the Foodtech Frontier list brings awareness to these concepts and adds credibility to their work.”

stories.title: Dog blamed for crash, St. Thomas driver charged
stories.summary: A driver has been charged after a single-vehicle crash in Huron East that police said was caused by a dog distracting the person behind the wheel.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A driver has been charged after a single-vehicle crash in Huron East that police said was caused by a dog distracting the person behind the wheel.

Huron County OPP, along with paramedics, responded to the collision on Kippen Road shortly after 7 p.m. on Sunday.

Police said an SUV left the roadway and struck a tree stump. The impact deployed the vehicle’s airbags and left the SUV heavily damaged and inoperable.

The driver, a 66-year-old from St. Thomas, was treated at the scene for minor injuries.

According to investigators, a dog in the vehicle had jumped into the front seat, distracting the driver. Police said the driver then lost control of the SUV, left the roadway and collided with the tree stump.

The driver has been charged with careless driving under Ontario’s Highway Traffic Act.

Police are reminding motorists travelling with pets to ensure animals are properly secured and do not interfere with the safe operation of a vehicle.

stories.title: Canada’s new foreign agents database has received just 30 registrations
stories.summary: Canada’s first foreign influence commissioner says he’s focused on raising awareness of requirements for foreign agents to register with his office.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s new foreign influence commissioner says only 30 people have disclosed working for foreign governments or foreign principals with his office as of Tuesday.

That’s a far cry from the roughly 2,422 foreign agents Public Safety Canada has estimated are active in Canada, raising questions from opposition MPs about how effective the Liberals’ registration scheme will be.

The registry of foreign influence activities was created by the Liberal government in response to concerns about foreign governments and entities covertly meddling in domestic politics. It allows people or organizations in Canada doing legitimate work with foreign countries to publicly disclose those activities.

But as of the Oct. 3 deadline, there were only two names on the public registry, and roughly 30 more being vetted by Foreign Influence Commissioner Anton Boegman’s office.

Conservative MP Michael Cooper noted that, if Public Safety Canada’s estimates were accurate, that would mean just one per cent of foreign agents complied with the law.

“This is a complete and utter failure,” Cooper told reporters after the meeting.

“And it’s deeply concerning, because the very point of the registry is to provide sunlight and transparency. And what we have is Canadians who are being left in the dark about persons who are engaging with public officials, engaging in political and governmental processes on behalf of foreign actors.”

Under opposition questioning, Boegman noted that the requirement to register with his office is new. Now that the deadline to register has passed, Boegman said he was focused on raising awareness and encouraging voluntary compliance with the registration scheme.

“We’re really working to communicate to people so that they have a good understanding of what the requirements are. We’re working with many different sectors across Canada. So we’re going to look at what we have,” Boegman told Global News.

“We’re going to look at where, if we need to do more on the outreach side, and we’re going to try to make sure that the register is capturing the activities that it needs to capture.”

Failing that, Boegman noted that his office does have “teeth” — including imposing monetary penalties of up to $1 million — to ensure foreign agents register with his office.

In January, Public Safety Canada published an analysis about the new foreign registration requirements, noting that it would apply to individuals and entities that “enter into arrangements with a foreign principal … for the purpose of conducting influence activities targeting Canada’s political or governmental processes.”

Those “influence activities” can be perfectly legal and above-board, such as traditional lobbying. Foreign “principals” is broadly defined, and can mean states or economic entities.

Based on a similar scheme already in place in Australia, the federal government estimated that 2,422 entities (872 individuals and 1,550 businesses) would register with Boegman’s office.

Patrick Lennox, a former RCMP intelligence analyst, told Global News that the number of registrants so far seemed “surprisingly low.”

“I thought that the thresholds for signing up were actually themselves pretty low. So most people would have had to if they had ongoing relationships with foreign states, including allied states,” Lennox said in an interview.

“I think maybe it’s just off to a slow start and people are not clear on the reporting requirements and need to kind of get their paperwork in order.”

Lennox noted that the foreign influence registry May take time to be integrated into the wider Canadian security and intelligence community, but there are opportunities —through working with agencies like the RCMP and Csis — to help fill the gaps.

“(The office) has to find its way in terms of information sharing with Csis and with the RCMP and with other agencies in Canada to figure out, okay, are we missing anybody here?,” said Lennox, who has been writing on foreign interference and Alberta separatist movements.

“What do we know from the intelligence side of things that doesn’t align with what’s been proactively reported?”

Boegman is Canada’s first foreign influence commissioner, a position ultimately created after a flurry of media reporting in 2023 and 2024 about foreign countries allegedly attempting to covertly meddle in Canadian political affairs.

The articles detailed how adversarial foreign countries — particularly China and India — have allegedly engaged in the transnational repression of diaspora communities in Canada, including assassination plots, as well as allegations of funneling money or influence into Canadian politics behind the scenes.

Foreign interference is not new. But in the wake of those stories, it was thrust to the forefront of Canadian national security discourse. The then-Trudeau government launched a public inquiry, led by Commissioner Marie-Josee Hogue, former attorney general of Canada.

The Hogue inquiry found that while foreign interference did not change the outcomes of federal elections in 2019 and 2021, it nevertheless undermined some voters’ rights and presents a significant threat to Canadian democratic institutions.

Those “influence activities” can be perfectly legal and above-board, such as traditional lobbying. Foreign “principals” is broadly defined, and can mean states or economic entities.
Based on a similar scheme already in place in Australia, the federal government estimated that 2,422 entities (872 individuals and 1,550 businesses) would register with Boegman’s office.
Patrick Lennox, a former RCMP intelligence analyst, told Global News that the number of registrants so far seemed “surprisingly low.”

“I thought that the thresholds for signing up were actually themselves pretty low. So most people would have had to if they had ongoing relationships with foreign states, including allied states,” Lennox said in an interview.
“I think maybe it’s just off to a slow start and people are not clear on the reporting requirements and need to kind of get their paperwork in order.”

Lennox noted that the foreign influence registry May take time to be integrated into the wider Canadian security and intelligence community, but there are opportunities —through working with agencies like the RCMP and Csis — to help fill the gaps.

“(The office) has to find its way in terms of information sharing with Csis and with the RCMP and with other agencies in Canada to figure out, okay, are we missing anybody here?,” said Lennox, who has been writing on foreign interference and Alberta separatist movements.
“What do we know from the intelligence side of things that doesn’t align with what’s been proactively reported?”

Boegman is Canada’s first foreign influence commissioner, a position ultimately created after a flurry of media reporting in 2023 and 2024 about foreign countries allegedly attempting to covertly meddle in Canadian political affairs.

The articles detailed how adversarial foreign countries — particularly China and India — have allegedly engaged in the transnational repression of diaspora communities in Canada, including assassination plots, as well as allegations of funneling money or influence into Canadian politics behind the scenes.

Foreign interference is not new. But in the wake of those stories, it was thrust to the forefront of Canadian national security discourse. The then-Trudeau government launched a public inquiry, led by Commissioner Marie-Josee Hogue, former attorney general of Canada.

The Hogue inquiry found that while foreign interference did not change the outcomes of federal elections in 2019 and 2021, it nevertheless undermined some voters’ rights and presents a significant threat to Canadian democratic institutions.

stories.title: Joly presses Stelco’s U.S. owner to present job-saving plan in 5 days
stories.summary: The federal government is turning up the heat on the U.S. owner of Stelco Holdings Inc. over impending layoffs at the Hamilton-based steel plant.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The federal government is turning up the heat on the U.S. owner of Stelco Holdings Inc. over impending layoffs at the Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday laying out her “extreme disappointment” over the company’s plan to lay off up to 500 workers in response to U.S. tariffs and other market pressures.

Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the go-ahead to purchase Stelco back in 2024 under the Investment Canada Act, which regulates foreign takeovers.

Canada’s approval of the deal was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions, Joly said.

0:33 If Stelco ‘is honest, they’ll get back to us,’ Joly says as layoffs begin in Hamilton

Those conditions don’t expire just because “business strategy or market conditions have changed,” she wrote in the letter.

“This is particularly relevant here, where Cleveland-Cliffs has cited trade disruptions as affecting its operations at Hamilton Works, notwithstanding its chief executive officer’s public support for Section 232 tariff measures,” Joly said.

Lourenco Goncalves, the chief executive of Cleveland-Cliffs, has publicly supported U.S. steel tariffs, saying they are a “necessary step” to curb dumped steel imports.

In the letter, Joly said she wants to see Cleveland-Cliffs’ plan to comply with all undertakings of the original acquisition. She asked for a response within five business days or the government could consider legal action.

If the steelmaker does not comply, Ottawa could go to superior court where a judge could order the company to meet its obligations, impose penalties or even order a sale of the business, Joly said.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers local 1005, which represents workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant, said he is pleased the federal government acted “very swiftly.”

“They were very slow to react last time,” he said, referring to an earlier dispute involving the steel mill under a different owner. “We actually had to lobby to get them to react.”

U.S. Steel began laying off hundreds of workers at the former Stelco operations in November 2008 and announced temporary shutdowns affecting another roughly 1,500 jobs the following March.

Then-industry minister Tony Clement did not issue a formal demand under the act until May 5, 2009 — roughly nine weeks after the larger shutdown was announced.

In that case, Ottawa rejected the company’s explanation for falling short of its labour and production commitments and took U.S. Steel to court.

The case was ultimately settled in 2011 after the company agreed to a new set of undertakings.

However, the steel mill entered creditor protection in 2014 and was acquired by Bedrock Industries in 2017, returning to the Stelco name, before Cleveland-Cliffs acquired the company in 2024.

“Cleveland-Cliffs knew exactly what they were agreeing to when they bought the place,” Wells said, referring to the five-year commitments the company made when it purchased the operations.

“We’re hoping that they will recant the layoff,” he said. “But I’m not holding my breath.”

“They’ll drag this through court and try to provide their rationale for how this was out of their control. But they’re all in favour of the tariffs so it’s contradictory.”

The existence of Joly’s letter was first reported by the Toronto Star.

stories.title: Clapping Music composer Steve Reich celebrates his 90th birthday – and what’s not to applaud?
stories.summary: On Oct. 6, Reich will be celebrated with a concert at Toronto’s Koerner Hall
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
The great American composer Steve Reich turned 90 on Saturday. Speaking to him a couple of weeks before, I had wished him an early happy birthday.

“I think you’re the first to actually say the words,” he said from New York. “Ninety years.”

When I suggested to the minimalist that slow harmonic rhythm wins the race, he laughed.

“I don’t know if you can characterize my life as slow harmonic rhythm.”

On Oct. 6, Reich will be feted with a concert at Toronto’s Koerner Hall, presented by Soundstreams in collaboration with the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Music. Gary Kulesha will conduct an all-star ensemble.

Soundstreams, founded in 1982 by artistic director Lawrence Cherney, is in the business of presenting and commissioning new works. For the 90th birthday of the man hailed by The New York Times as “our greatest composer,” they are presenting the North American premiere of In All Your Ways , his piece for 14 instruments co-commissioned by Soundstreams, Carnegie Hall, Edinburgh Festival, Philharmonie de Paris and others.

Reich finished it earlier this year. He’s happy with it.

“I think it’s one of the best things I ever did,” he says. “What can I tell you? It’s about 18 minutes long and it’s built around four different key signatures, each of which could be major, minor or modal.”

Sounds pretty loose.

“Well, there’s organization harmony, but, yes, it’s very loose. Looser than I tend to organize. Rhythmically it’s laid out in 16ths, eighths and triplets. I got about 15 minutes into it and said to myself, ‘slow down, I gotta have some slow movements.’ So, I wrote three separate slow movements. It makes a big difference.”

Slowing down isn’t in Reich’s nature. But, other than a yearly flight to Los Angeles to visit his son, he doesn’t travel much and he no longer appears in concert.

A few years ago, Canadian filmmaker Atom Egoyan arranged the filming of Reich performing one half of his four-handed Clapping Music piece from 1972. In concert, the audience watches a film projection of Reich’s rhythmic hands, while another clapper handles the other phrases in person.

“The idea was to create a permanent record of Steve Reich’s clapping,” Egoyan told The Globe and Mail in 2023. “In the future, anyone could perform the song with the composer. You will literally be linked to the origin of the piece.”

Reich thinks the idea is a little funny. “It’s an oddity,” he says, chuckling. “But I was getting old and infirm.”

The taped/live Clapping Music hybrid was presented as part of Soundstreams’ celebration of Reich’s 86th birthday. On hand, as it were, for that concert was the composer’s longtime collaborator, Toronto percussionist Russell Hartenberger. He’ll perform at the 90th as well.

Hartenberger is a founding member of the legendary Canadian percussion ensemble Nexus and a professor emeritus with the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Music. He also wrote the book on Reich: Performance Practice in the Music of Steve Reich , published in 2016 by Cambridge University Press

Hartenberger was part of the ensemble in the mid-1970s that helped develop Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians, a composition organized in 11 sections, each based on a single chord. The piece is part of this week’s Soundstreams concert. Reich composed it in New York over a period of two years, at the same time the ensemble rehearsed the work in progress.

“He would come in with pieces of manuscript paper with some patterns we were to play, and we would tack it on to what we did before,” Hartenberger explained. “It was an exciting time. There were a lot of musicians who were interested in playing Steve’s music and were willing to basically volunteer their time, because we weren’t paid for the rehearsals.”

Music for 18 Musicians premiered at New York’s Town Hall on April 24, 1976. Reich turned 40 that year and married video artist Beryl Korot. He was establishing himself as an innovative composer who changed the trajectory of classical music by widening its appeal to different kinds of music listeners.

He’s not finished composing, but this moment in his life could be described as one of those slower movements he spoke about. This spring he broke a rib and his right wrist in a fall. He says the recovery for his wrist is “taking forever,” and that the physical therapy can be painful.

“It has definitely inhibited my creative juices to be sure,” he admits. “But I was in high creative mode before the injury. After that? TBA. We’ll figure it out.”

Celebrating Steve Reich at 90 , Oct. 6, at Toronto’s Koerner Hall.

“I think it’s one of the best things I ever did,” he says. “What can I tell you? It’s about 18 minutes long and it’s built around four different key signatures, each of which could be major, minor or modal.”
Sounds pretty loose.

“Well, there’s organization harmony, but, yes, it’s very loose. Looser than I tend to organize. Rhythmically it’s laid out in 16ths, eighths and triplets. I got about 15 minutes into it and said to myself, ‘slow down, I gotta have some slow movements.’ So, I wrote three separate slow movements. It makes a big difference.”
Slowing down isn’t in Reich’s nature. But, other than a yearly flight to Los Angeles to visit his son, he doesn’t travel much and he no longer appears in concert.

A few years ago, Canadian filmmaker Atom Egoyan arranged the filming of Reich performing one half of his four-handed Clapping Music piece from 1972. In concert, the audience watches a film projection of Reich’s rhythmic hands, while another clapper handles the other phrases in person.

“The idea was to create a permanent record of Steve Reich’s clapping,” Egoyan told The Globe and Mail in 2023. “In the future, anyone could perform the song with the composer. You will literally be linked to the origin of the piece.”
Reich thinks the idea is a little funny. “It’s an oddity,” he says, chuckling. “But I was getting old and infirm.”

The taped/live Clapping Music hybrid was presented as part of Soundstreams’ celebration of Reich’s 86th birthday. On hand, as it were, for that concert was the composer’s longtime collaborator, Toronto percussionist Russell Hartenberger. He’ll perform at the 90th as well.

Hartenberger is a founding member of the legendary Canadian percussion ensemble Nexus and a professor emeritus with the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Music. He also wrote the book on Reich: Performance Practice in the Music of Steve Reich , published in 2016 by Cambridge University Press

Hartenberger was part of the ensemble in the mid-1970s that helped develop Reich’s Music for 18 Musicians, a composition organized in 11 sections, each based on a single chord. The piece is part of this week’s Soundstreams concert. Reich composed it in New York over a period of two years, at the same time the ensemble rehearsed the work in progress.

“He would come in with pieces of manuscript paper with some patterns we were to play, and we would tack it on to what we did before,” Hartenberger explained. “It was an exciting time. There were a lot of musicians who were interested in playing Steve’s music and were willing to basically volunteer their time, because we weren’t paid for the rehearsals.”

Music for 18 Musicians premiered at New York’s Town Hall on April 24, 1976. Reich turned 40 that year and married video artist Beryl Korot. He was establishing himself as an innovative composer who changed the trajectory of classical music by widening its appeal to different kinds of music listeners.

He’s not finished composing, but this moment in his life could be described as one of those slower movements he spoke about. This spring he broke a rib and his right wrist in a fall. He says the recovery for his wrist is “taking forever,” and that the physical therapy can be painful.
“It has definitely inhibited my creative juices to be sure,” he admits. “But I was in high creative mode before the injury. After that? TBA. We’ll figure it out.”

stories.title: Cyclist transported to hospital following collision with police cruiser
stories.summary: A London police cruiser was involved in a collision with a cyclist Tuesday morning, between Pegler Street and ...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
A London police cruiser was involved in a collision with a cyclist Tuesday morning, between Pegler Street and Smith Street on Hamilton Road. London police spokesperson Gavin Dell said that the cyclist was taken to the hospital after the crash.

“The accident involves a cyclist and a marked line police service cruiser,” said Dell. “The cyclist was transported to the hospital with unknown injuries.”

A Major Collision Investigation truck later appeared on the scene to gather evidence and pictures related to the crash.

Dell had also said that road will remain closed at this time, as the investigation continues.

“Obviously the road will remain closed for right now,” he said. “We will update online once it’s reopened.”

Photos taken by Kelly Nicol.

stories.title: Carney government tables legislation to turn Defence Investment Agency into Crown corporation
stories.summary: As Canada builds its military industrial complex to spur the economy and meet its Nato commitments, Mark Carney’s government is transforming the fledgling Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
As Canada builds its military industrial complex to spur the economy and meet its Nato commitments, Mark Carney’s government is transforming the fledgling Defence Investment Agency (DIA) into a Crown corporation.

The Liberals are trying to accelerate the pace of military procurement by tabling Bill C-40 – called the Strengthening Canada’s Defence Sector Act.

The legislation was introduced in the House of Commons Tuesday.

In a backgrounder, the DIA says becoming a Crown corporation would provide the agency “with a clear mandate, a permanent structure and dedicated ministerial leadership focused on defence procurement production” to support National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces.

The new organization aims to give the DIA the ability to make decisions more quickly, reduce, fragmentation and provide predictability across defence acquisitions.

“With the introduction of this legislation, we are making clear that large-scale, agile defence production and procurement is here to stay. Procurement and investment must live together, by connecting the capabilities our armed forces need with the investments that will deliver them and the industrial capacity that will sustain them,” said Joel Lightbound, the minister of government transformation, public works and procurement. Lightbound sponsored the bill in Parliament.

Since it was created over a year ago, the DIA has selected Tkms of Germany as the preferred supplier to replace Canada’s aging submarine fleet. The contract for 12 submarines, once finalized, could be valued at about $100 billion over the lifespan of the fleet. It has also announced smaller contracts.

The draft legislation would change the name of the DIA to the Canadian Corporation for Defence Investment. It would operate at arm’s length under the national defence portfolio reporting to a new Associate Minister of National Defence of Procurement.

The bill would allow the DIA to operate more like a company and less like a federal department. According to a background briefing, the Crown corporation would have its own board of directors and have greater independence and authority to manage defence-related investments, procurement, and production activities.

Currently, Stephen Fuhr, a former fighter pilot and Liberal MP, is the Secretary of State for Defence procurement.

“Canada is making a generational investment in our defence and security and we need institutions built to match the scale and urgency of that ambition,” Fuhr said in a news release announcing the transition.

As part of its commitment to Nato, Canada plans to substantially increase defence spending over the next decade. Canada currently spends two per cent of GDP on defence. By 2030, that will increase to four per cent and rise to five per cent by 2035.

According to new analysis by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer, the federal government would have to spend $164.6 billion in 2035-36 to meet the five per cent target. This fiscal year, Canada is spending approximately $75 billion on defence. In a decades time, the PBO projects, Canada will have to more than double its military spending to meet its Nato commitments.

stories.title: Ontario’s medical regulator proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply
stories.summary: The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is looking to clamp down and is set to hold a board of directors meeting next week to decide on the proposed changes.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator is proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply drugs, The Canadian Press has learned.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is looking to clamp down on the practice and is set to hold a board of directors meeting next week to decide on the proposed changes.

Safer supply refers to prescribing medications as an alternative to opioids obtained on the streets to those who are at high risk of overdose.

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain. Fentanyl is often found laced with other drugs such as benzodiazepines, a depressant, and xylazine, often used to tranquilize animals.

One change the regulator has proposed in a document tucked away on its website is that “physicians must only prescribe safer supply medications in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.” The therapy uses medications such as methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The college is also proposing an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply, and mandating that it be consumed in front of health-care professionals.

The regulator previously made changes to its drug prescription policy in May that mandated physicians to perform an in-person assessment before prescribing narcotics for safer supply, as well as making it mandatory for doctors to offer opioid agonist therapy before prescribing safer supply drugs and perform followups every three months.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

The rationale behind the new proposed changes centres largely on diversion of patients’ prescription pills to the black market.

“The proposed amendments build on targeted changes introduced in May and respond to ongoing concerns about the diversion of safer supply medication and the resulting risks to patients and communities,” Mickey Cirak, spokesperson for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, wrote in an email.

“In response, the college has proposed amendments intended to strengthen oversight of safer supply prescribing and enhance safeguards related to physician prescribing practices, consistent with its role as Ontario’s medical regulator.”

The college said it has consulted with a broad range of people and organizations, including physicians, municipalities and health-care partners, as well as the office of Ontario’s chief medical officer of health, Dr. Kieran Moore.

Moore’s office did not respond to a request for comment or an interview. Moore has never granted The Canadian Press an interview about the province’s opioids crisis, despite more than a dozen requests since he took the role in 2021.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons said the initiative to change safer-supply prescription rules is its own and did not come from the provincial government.

Cirak said the college also received feedback from doctors with expertise in addiction medicine.

The proposal has the support of Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“Our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs, including the illicit use of hydromorphone masked as ‘safer supply,'” said Satnam Grewal, a spokesperson for Jones.

“We welcome any action from Ontario’s 27 regulatory colleges who set standards and obligations for health-care professionals, including the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, to crack down on the predatory prescribing of addictive drugs.”

Ontario has moved to an abstinence-based model under Premier Doug Ford in its approach to the ongoing opioid crisis. The province closed provincially funded supervised consumption sites and passed a law banning them within 200 metres of schools and daycares.

The province has since opened 29 homelessness and addiction recovery treatment hubs, which the government calls Hart hubs. It has spent more than $500 million on that plan, which offers primary and mental health care, addiction services and peer supports.

Word of the proposed changes has reached some people who depend on safer supply, said Lorraine Lam, an organizer with the Shelter and Housing Justice Network and a longtime harm reduction worker.

“The changes are really dangerous and very destabilizing,” Lam said.

“People are really, really scared and people are really, really anxious and very angry.”

She said some people using safer supply got jobs or returned to school and she’s worried what will happen to them when they’re cut off.

“The reality is people who are on safe supply are going to be de-prescribed really, really quickly, which will increase the chances of people turning to the street unregulated supply, which will then therefore increase the risk of overdoses and deaths,” Lam said.

The college’s board of directors is set to meet on Oct. 13, when it is expected to vote on the proposed changes.

“Our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs, including the illicit use of hydromorphone masked as ‘safer supply,'” said Satnam Grewal, a spokesperson for Jones.

“We welcome any action from Ontario’s 27 regulatory colleges who set standards and obligations for health-care professionals, including the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, to crack down on the predatory prescribing of addictive drugs.”

Ontario has moved to an abstinence-based model under Premier Doug Ford in its approach to the ongoing opioid crisis. The province closed provincially funded supervised consumption sites and passed a law banning them within 200 metres of schools and daycares.

The province has since opened 29 homelessness and addiction recovery treatment hubs, which the government calls Hart hubs. It has spent more than $500 million on that plan, which offers primary and mental health care, addiction services and peer supports.
Word of the proposed changes has reached some people who depend on safer supply, said Lorraine Lam, an organizer with the Shelter and Housing Justice Network and a longtime harm reduction worker.
“The changes are really dangerous and very destabilizing,” Lam said.
“People are really, really scared and people are really, really anxious and very angry.”
She said some people using safer supply got jobs or returned to school and she’s worried what will happen to them when they’re cut off.

“The reality is people who are on safe supply are going to be de-prescribed really, really quickly, which will increase the chances of people turning to the street unregulated supply, which will then therefore increase the risk of overdoses and deaths,” Lam said.

stories.title: Two teenagers die in head-on collision in eastern New Brunswick: RCMP
stories.summary: The Mounties say they believe a car carrying five people from Moncton crossed the centre of the road and collided with a SUV just before 7:30 p.m.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted October 6, 2026 12:42 pm

New Brunswick RCMP say two teenagers are dead after a head-on collision last night in Moncton.

The Mounties say they believe a car carrying five people from Moncton crossed the centre of the road and collided with a SUV just before 7:30 p.m.

An 18-year-old man and 16-year-old girl in the car were both pronounced dead at the scene.

The 25-year-old man driving the car was taken to hospital and later arrested, though there’s no word on charges.

A 16-year-old boy in the car was taken to hospital in critical condition, while a 14-year-old boy received minor injuries.

The SUV was carrying five people from Arkansas between the ages of 24 and 72, and police say they were all treated in hospital for minor injuries.

stories.title: N.B. public advocate pitches non-profit co-ordination unit to fix social services
stories.summary: New Brunswick’s public advocate says the province should create a new unit to bridge the gaps between its social services and the community organizations that deliver them.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
New Brunswick’s public advocate is proposing the provincial government create a new body he says would allow for more cost-effective delivery of social services.

Provincial advocate Kelly Lamrock, in a report published Tuesday, proposed the creation of a Non-Profit Opportunities Unit that would measure success by tracking human results, such as vulnerable people receiving housing.

Lamrock writes the unit would co-ordinate the province’s social services strategy while leaving service delivery to the government’s partners in non-government organizations.

He says the unit aims to make the social welfare system more nimble and responsive by empowering local problem solvers, rather than relying solely on rigid government bureaucracy.

“It’s a way for communities to spot problems and propose solutions — and get government to fund the solution closer to the community,” Lamrock said by phone Tuesday.

He compared social services to a boat, saying the government “should steer, but not row — the rowing should happen closer to the community and closer to the individual.”

He wrote the current system heavily depends on social services workers following manuals and checklists rather than tracking whether a person’s life actually improves.

In two separate reports released earlier this year, Lamrock blamed the deaths of a 16-year-old boy and an elderly woman on systemic failures by the province’s Department of Social Development.

In his 50-page report released Tuesday, Lamrock criticizes the department for being too rules-bound in its approach to social services.

The proposed non-profit unit, he wrote, would track human quality-of-life outcomes as a new way of measuring the value of taxpayer-funded programs.

To accomplish that, he proposed “social entrepreneurship contracts” that could provide savings for government by focusing on preventative measures and tracking their progress.

Lamrock suggests in his report that spending more on social services can lead to savings later by preventing crises.

For example, he says investing more in programs for at-risk teenagers, such as those who are recovering from addictions, can decrease costs down the road by reducing the number of youth who enter the justice system.

He points out massive amounts of taxpayer dollars are spent on emergency rooms, police and the courts — which can be costly routes for dealing with social welfare problems such as addictions or mental health crises.

Lamrock said his proposed unit could also work to connect the bureaucratic dots for the community organizations by streamlining grant applications.

“The resources are all with the folks who move slowest,” Lamrock said.

“And maybe there’s a way to get the resources in the hands of the most nimble problem solvers.”

Lamrock said he believed the Liberal government could establish the unit, along with some of his other recommendations, in the near future.

As well, he pointed out that if the province is going to run deficits, as it’s projected to do for the next couple of years, it needs to use that extra spending efficiently before a period of deep cuts to social services.

“We actually have to … make sure we get results now that have fewer crisis expenditures later and that transforms the system into something effective,” he said.

“If we don’t do that … we’re just going to downsize a very dysfunctional status quo.”

Cindy Miles, the social development minister, didn’t immediately commit to implementing the recommendations in the report, but said they deserved “careful review.”

“We will take the time necessary to thoroughly assess the recommendations before determining next steps,” Miles said in a statement.

The Liberal minister said her department agreed with having “strong partnerships with the non-profit sector, a focus on better outcomes, and efforts to strengthen prevention and early intervention.”

stories.title: Mpox cases on the rise in Toronto, public health officials urge vaccine for those eligible
stories.summary: Fourteen cases of the viral illness have been confirmed since September
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto public health officials say they are seeing a rise in mpox infections in the city and are urging eligible residents to get vaccinated.

Toronto Public Health says 14 cases of the viral illness have been confirmed since September, and wastewater monitoring by the Public Health Agency of Canada has also “consistently detected mpox” in the city.

Public health officials say the risk to the public remains low, as mpox is most commonly spread through close or sexual contact with someone who has the virus.

Mpox symptoms include a rash, fever, swollen lymph nodes, headache, muscle aches and fatigue.

People eligible for vaccination include men who have sex with men and have more than one partner; men who have sex with men who have gone to venues for sexual contact; people who work in those venues; and sex workers, regardless of gender.

Toronto Public Health says the city has seen 41 confirmed mpox cases so far this year, compared to 118 confirmed cases during the same time period in 2025, which saw a total of 158 cases.

stories.title: Buy Canadian sentiment May withstand holiday spending squeeze, survey finds
stories.summary: The ‘Buy Canadian’ sentiment seems to be withstanding the holiday spending squeeze, a survey by PricewaterhouseCoopers found on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The cost of living is squeezing Canadians ahead of the holiday shopping season, but many say they’d be willing to spend more under one condition – if they’re buying Canadian.

The ‘Buy Canadian’ sentiment seems on track to withstand the holiday spending squeeze, a survey by PricewaterhouseCoopers found on Tuesday.

Nearly three out of four (72 per cent) say they are seeking alternatives to U.S.-made goods, with more than half (54 per cent) saying they will be willing to pay more for goods made in Canada, PwC’s 2026 Canadian holiday outlook said.

This is despite budget pressures, which have meant Canadians plan to spend 11 per cent less on holiday shopping overall, it added.

Canadians plan to spend an average of $1,487 this holiday season, the report said.

“Canadians are cutting back, but they’re drawing a hard line on where their money goes,” said Adam Boutros, partner and national consumer markets leader at PwC Canada.

This year’s budget squeeze is coming primarily from older Canadians. Gen X Canadians are planning to spend 21 per cent less, while baby boomers are cutting back by 18 per cent.

In contrast, Gen Z Canadians are planning to spend eight per cent more this year than they did last year.

Households with children continue to be the main driver of holiday spending, with those households planning to spend twice as much over the holidays compared to child-free households.

Canadians are also changing where they look for deals, with more than a quarter (28 per cent) planning to use AI tools to shop for the holidays. This is up sharply from 17 per cent in 2025.

Shoppers are planning to use AI tools to research products, compare items, discover gift ideas and, in some cases, make purchases.

However, stores remain the top way to shop, with 40 per cent saying they plan to use both physical and online stores.

stories.title: Greater Toronto home sales in September down from year ago, average price also lower
stories.summary: Renewed tensions with the United States and a surge in gas prices amid an ongoing war in the Middle East have kept potential buyers on the sidelines in recent months.
stories.author: Ritika Dubey
stories.content:
Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area were down in September from a year ago, while average prices continued to decline.

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said on Tuesday sales totalled 5,040 in September, down nine per cent year-over-year.

The result came as the average selling price for the month was $1,006,409, down from $1,060,036 a year earlier.

The composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.7 per cent year-over-year in September.

The board says homebuyers were in a holding pattern in September, as uncertainty surrounding the economy, inflation and borrowing costs weighed on sales.

Renewed tensions with the United States and a surge in gas prices amid an ongoing war in the Middle East have kept potential buyers on the sidelines in recent months.

Slowing home sales come as municipalities across Ontario, including the GTA, hold a ballot on Oct. 26.

“Housing is one of the biggest issues on voters’ minds, and the upcoming municipal election will help shape housing policy across the GTA and Simcoe County for the next four years,” said Daniel Steinfeld, Trreb president, in a statement.

“The decisions our next mayors and councillors make on affordability, housing supply and the costs associated with buying a home can also influence buyer demand and confidence in the market.”

New listings in September totalled 16,500, down 14.4 per cent year-over-year.

stories.title: Canadian actor Simu Liu marries Allison Hsu in France: reports
stories.summary: Marvel actor Simu Liu began dating Allison Hsu in 2022 and the pair announced their engagement in May 2025 after a trip to Paris together.
stories.author: Katie Scott
stories.content:
Canadian actor Simu Liu reportedly married his longtime girlfriend Allison Hsu over the weekend, according to multiple U.S. reports.

The Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings star and his fiancée Hsu tied the knot in France, according to People .

TMZ was first to report the news of the wedding.

4:42 Simu Liu reveals who kicked him in the face on the set of “The Copenhagen Test”

Global News has reached out to Liu’s representatives for further comment, but has not received a response.

Liu began dating Hsu in late 2022, making their red carpet debut at the Violent Night premiere in Los Angeles wearing holiday sweaters.

In August 2023, Liu shared a birthday message to Hsu on Instagram, writing, “Happy birthday to the girl who truly does it all. She inspires me in her passion for music (well… one musician specifically), teaches me how to balance a busy and chaotic schedule with grace, and touches me in how she cares for each and every person in her life. Most importantly, she shows me that the people we love are always worth fighting for.”

Liu proposed to Hsu, who works at Interscope Records as vice president of digital marketing, in May 2025 during a trip to Paris.

Hsu shared some pictures from their engagement to Instagram at the time, with the caption, “Us forever.”

Liu also shared an Instagram post from his engagement with the caption, “From weekends in Paris, day trips to Palm Springs, long nights on set, afternoons vegging on the couch and everything in between, I choose you forever and always.”

During an appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon later that year, Liu said that he asked Taylor Swift to surprise Hsu with a message because “she grew up a Swiftie.”

“I’ll preface this by saying my fiancée works in music, so she’s a digital marketing executive, and she grew up a Swiftie. She loves Taylor Swift,” the 37-year-old actor said.

“Taylor Swift’s songs and her music, that was a big part of the beginning of our relationship, was getting to know her through those songs, and why they meant so much to her,” he continued.

“I was like, ‘Well, there’s one person that would make this engagement so special,’ and I reached out — as if we’re BFFs, no I mean I met her a couple of times, she’s fantastic,” Liu said.

The Barbie actor revealed that he reached out to Swift through her publicist.

“I said, ‘Hey, is there any way that I could convince you to make like a two-second video just to say congrats?’ And she literally two days later sent it over, and I was able to play it for her. And so Taylor Swift was the cherry on top,” Liu shared.

He said that Hsu was “really emotional before” he played the video but once he shared Swift’s congratulatory message Hsu “completely lost it.”

stories.title: Porter Airlines expands service at London airport with five new domestic routes
stories.summary: The airline announced Tuesday it will offer direct service from London to Edmonton, Halifax, Montreal Metropolitan Airport, Ottawa and Vancouver.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Porter Airlines says it will add five new year-round domestic routes from London International Airport in spring 2027.

The airline announced Tuesday it will offer direct service from London to Edmonton, Halifax, Montreal Metropolitan Airport, Ottawa and Vancouver.

Porter president Kevin Jackson said the expansion builds on the airline’s recently announced winter sun service from London to destinations in Florida, Mexico and Jamaica.

“We are building on the strong passenger response to our recent winter sun destinations announcement by introducing five nonstop domestic routes,” Jackson said in a statement. “This expansion demonstrates that Porter is committed to making London a meaningful part of our network.”

According to the airline, service to Halifax and Vancouver will begin April 12, 2027, with Edmonton flights launching May 6, 2027. Routes to Ottawa and Montreal Metropolitan Airport will also begin April 12.

At peak service, Porter plans to operate daily flights between London and Halifax, seven weekly flights to Edmonton, and 11 weekly flights to Vancouver. Ottawa and Montreal routes will operate up to 20 times weekly, including as many as three daily round trips.

Scott McFadzean, president and chief executive officer of London International Airport, described the announcement as a significant investment in the region.

“These five domestic non-stop routes represent a transformational investment in our region, strengthening access for travellers and businesses while enhancing London’s position as a growing centre for aviation and aerospace,” he said in a statement.

At peak service, Porter plans to operate daily flights between London and Halifax, seven weekly flights to Edmonton, and 11 weekly flights to Vancouver. Ottawa and Montreal routes will operate up to 20 times weekly, including as many as three daily round trips.
Scott McFadzean, president and chief executive officer of London International Airport, described the announcement as a significant investment in the region.

“These five domestic non-stop routes represent a transformational investment in our region, strengthening access for travellers and businesses while enhancing London’s position as a growing centre for aviation and aerospace,” he said in a statement.

stories.title: Ottawa pushed to extend Lgbtq+ funding that is set to expire in spring
stories.summary: Ottawa has given no commitment to extending the action plan, and the office of Gender Equality Minister Rechie Valdez has not yet provided a comment in response.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Groups serving Lgbtq+ people are urging the Carney government to extend funding and programming aimed at growing mental health and security concerns.

“Without core funding and material commitments to help uphold the Charter rights of 2SLGBTQIA+ people, we are facing a dire crisis across the sector,” Lgbt YouthLine head Lauren Pragg told reporters Tuesday on Parliament Hill.

“We are facing a dire crisis across the sector. Many organizations have been forced to close,” Pragg said.

The organization has seen its funding drop by half since the Trudeau government launched an action plan in 2022 to support Lgbtq+ Canadians. That plan included funding for increasing security at Pride parades and boosting research programs.

That programming is set to expire in the spring, prompting multiple Lgbtq+ groups to take to Parliament Hill on Tuesday to press for the funding to be renewed and expanded.

Ottawa has given no commitment on extending the action plan.

“We are reviewing the Action Plan, and decisions regarding the next steps for the program will be announced at the appropriate time,” wrote Erin Quevillon, a spokesperson for Gender Equality Minister Rechie Valdez, in a statement.

“The Federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan has delivered important results, including strengthening community organizations and advancing the rights and inclusion of 2SLGBTQI+ people.”

Egale Canada said there are rising needs as minorities face online threats. The organization has also advocated against new provincial policies affecting transgender youth.

Alberta Sen. Kristopher Wells says the Liberal government should put dollars behind its pledge to not abandon sexual and gender minorities, and match its rhetoric by expanding existing programs to confront rising threats.

“It’s about the direction that this government wants to set,” he said. “That starts at home, by providing the necessary resources that support communities on the ground.”

The Dignity Network coalition says Canada needs to speak out for people abroad facing repression, including in Turkey. Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Tuesday he’d be visiting that country later this month.

The Turkish government has launched a recent series of raids on Lgbtq organizations, HIV-advocacy groups, nightclubs and the homes of activists.

Human Rights Watch has called it the widest crackdown on Lgbtq+ people in recent years, but Canada has been silent. It is in the midst of negotiating a new trade deal with Turkey.

“This is about more than Lgbtiq rights. Attacks on our communities are increasingly part of a broader assault on civil society, human rights, and democracy itself,” coalition head Doug Kerr said.

“These movements, these narratives, these politics, disinformation (all) cross borders, and have impact even here at home.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Cooking turkey for Thanksgiving? It’s going to cost you more this year
stories.summary: Aside from a main protein, such as turkey or ham, the menu includes potatoes, carrots, dinner rolls, pumpkin pie, cranberries, stuffing, and gravy as sides.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A turkey dinner for Thanksgiving is going to cost you a lot more this year, a report by the the Agri-Food Analytics Lab at Dalhousie University found on Tuesday.

The cost of cooking your family a Thanksgiving meal has been rising steadily since 2024, with a small increase of 0.6 per cent for a turkey dinner in 2025, compared to 2024.

This year, however, the cost went up 10 per cent from $32.48 in 2025 to $35.72 in 2026 for a Thanksgiving meal for four with turkey as your main meat.

The menu includes potatoes, carrots, dinner rolls, pumpkin pie, cranberries, stuffing, and gravy as sides, but the rise in the cost is mainly due to the cost of turkey rising from $10.43 to $12.53.

How much do sides cost this year?

Side dishes got more expensive too.

There was a slight $0.74 rise in the cost of a pound of carrots from $0.91 in 2025 to $1.65 in 2026.

The price of a 10-pound sack of potatoes remained the same at $6.99.

8:29 Global food prices at three-year high: UN

The combined price of the five other sides – dinner rolls, pumpkin pie, cranberries, stuffing, and gravy – went up by 2.8 per cent, the report said.

Overall, it will cost $23.19 to put together the whole array of sides. In 2025, the same side dishes cost $22.05 and in 2024, they cost $20.61.

While the cost of turkey has seen the sharpest rise, you’ll be paying more this year regardless of what meat you use as your main course.

The rise in the price of turkeys has meant that the cost of a ham dinner would be in the same ballpark range.

The price of a ham Thanksgiving dinner went up 4.3 per cent from $34.87 in 2025 to $36.37 this year.

2:18 Thanksgiving amid record demand

The cost of lamb and lobster meals will depend on the cut of the meat, but the report estimates that both those proteins also went up in price.

A lamb meal for four has gone up 3.5 per cent from $77.77 in 2025 to $80.47 in 2026.

Lobster meals have seen the smallest increase in price but remain the most expensive protein in a Thanksgiving meal for four. It went up 3.4 per cent from $85.23 in 2025 to $80.47.

stories.title: Is Canada’s new grocery benefit helping you make ends meet?
stories.summary: Eligible Canadians began receiving their second Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit payment on Monday.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Eligible Canadians began receiving their second payment on Monday under the new Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit .

Previously known as the GST/HST credit, the quarterly payments for lower-income Canadians can range from a few hundred dollars to nearly two thousand dollars annually, depending on income, marital status and the number of children in a household.

A single individual without children, for example, can receive up to $679 a year while those with four or more children can receive up to $1,826. Meant to help offset the rising cost of living , the payment comes as the annual inflation rate stood at three per cent in August .

Have you received a Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit payment? Is it helping you or your family make ends meet? How will you use it ahead of Thanksgiving? Do the payments help with the rising cost of groceries and other essentials? Or are the payments just a drop in the bucket?

stories.title: Canada needs ‘substantial’ defence spending to reach Nato 5% targets: PBO
stories.summary: The Liberal government has yet to detail their plans to hike defence spending to five per cent of GDP by 2035, a massive increase over a tight timeline.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada will need “substantial and sustained” defence spending increases to meet its Nato obligations by 2035, a new report from the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO) states.

The Liberal government has not yet revealed how it intends to reach the target of spending five per cent of GDP on defence within the next decade — a significant jump that would see core defence spending increase from $95.7 billion in 2030 to $163.7 billion in 2035-36.

Pulling that off, the PBO report suggests, will depend on how well the federal government handles complex procurement projects in a relatively short timeline — historically, a challenge for Ottawa.

The promised increase in defence spending would have significant implications on the federal budgetary picture, the PBO report noted.

“The PBO estimated that the additional core defence spending would increase the budgetary deficit by $63.7 billion, or 1.4 per cent of GDP, in 2035-36 relative to the (status quo scenario, and) federal debt would be 5.7 percentage points of GDP higher,” the report says.

But the budget watchdog also noted that the massive boost in military spending would have implications for Canada’s “economic activity, industrial capacity” and the domestic defence industry.

“While many aspects of the government’s defence expenditure strategy remain in development, current defence spending already supports economic activity across a range of industries and regions and can inform potential forward dynamics for the Canadian defence industrial base and wider economy,” the report noted.

Canada has for years been a laggard in Nato spending commitments. The military alliance set a target of countries spending two per cent of GDP on defence in 2006 — and Canada consistently failed to meet that target.

Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to change that, and Canada is expected to hit that longstanding two per cent Nato spending target for the first time this year. But the Carney government has been less clear about how it intends to reach the new benchmark of spending five per cent of GDP on defence— or how Ottawa will pay for it.

Asked recently about the lack of transparency around defence spending plans, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said more details are expected in the government’s 2026 budget.

“Obviously when we’re going to present Budget 2026 … we’ll be looking at measures to make the Canadian economy strong and make sure that, you know, the systems and procurement we’re doing to meet the Nato requirement, but at the same time that the Canadian economy can finance these big investments,” Champagne told reporters in July.

stories.title: Police warn of cold-water dangers after Goderich Harbour rescue
stories.summary: A 66-year-old canoeist is expected to recover after spending about 20 minutes in the cold waters of Goderich Harbour before being rescued.
stories.content:
Police are reminding boaters and paddlers about the dangers of cold-water exposure following the rescue of a canoeist in Goderich Harbour over the weekend.

Emergency crews were called at about 11:26 a.m. after a citizen reported seeing a person in distress in the water near the Goderich salt mine.

According to police, two people in a nearby inflatable dinghy came to the aid of the lone canoeist and pulled the individual from the water.

The 66-year-old paddler had been in the water for approximately 20 minutes before being rescued. The person was treated at the scene by paramedics and then transported to hospital suffering from hypothermia. Police said the person is expected to make a full recovery.

The incident has prompted police to remind recreational water users that cold-water conditions can pose a serious risk, even during the fall boating season.

Before heading out on the water, the OPP advises people to check weather forecasts, wind conditions, currents and water temperatures, and to ensure they are properly prepared for changing conditions.

Police also encourage outdoor enthusiasts to travel in groups whenever possible, noting that having others nearby can improve safety and response times in the event of an emergency.

stories.title: Toronto advance voting has begun. What you should know
stories.summary: It's advance voting in Toronto with people able to go cast their vote for the mayoral race, as well as city councillors and school board trustees.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Advance voting has begun in the City of Toronto, even as Chris Alexander says he’s dropping out of the mayoral race.

From Oct. 6 to Oct. 11, Torontonians can head to their designated polling places from 10 a.m. until 7 p.m. daily to cast their vote for mayor, city councillor and school board trustees.

Many residents will have likely received their voter information card in the mail which gives the locations of both advance and election day voting locations.

But people can also check out the city’s MyVote website to confirm, add or update voters’ list information, find out polling locations, and see who their candidates are. People can also call 311 to do the same if they cannot access MyVote.

In order to vote, people must show identification that includes their name and a Toronto address.

If you plan to vote in this year’s municipal election, you must be a Canadian citizen, at least 18 and a resident in the city. Alternatively, if you aren’t a resident of Toronto, you can vote if you or your spouse own or rent property in Toronto.

Whether you own or rent one or more properties, the city stresses you can only vote once and you must vote in the ward where you live.

A person cannot vote if they are prohibited from voting under any law. This includes someone serving a sentence of imprisonment in a penal or correctional institution; a person acting as executor or trustee or in another representative capacity, except as a voting proxy; or are a corporation.

The City of Toronto requires identification to vote, but there is a wide range of ID you can bring in order to cast that ballot though it adds you cannot use your voter information card or passport as ID.

Among the acceptable forms of ID include an Ontario issued photo card such as a driver’s licence or motor vehicle permit, a bank account statement, a mortgage statement or lease agreement, or any other document from the federal, Ontario or municipal government.

Also allowed is a utility bill for hydro, any document from a Band Council in Ontario established under the Indian Act (Canada), or a document showing residence in a long-term care home issued by the home’s administrator.

A full list of acceptable ID, including electronic ID, is on the city’s voting website.

I May need help to vote, what can I do?

For voters with accessibility needs or those who are out of the city on voting day, there are still many ways you can vote including Voter Assist Terminals available at all advance voting locations and two election day locations.

If you require assistance at the voting place, you can bring a friend along or ask an election official for assistance. The city they will need to make a declaration if you want them to accompany you behind the voting screen.

Torontonians can also appoint another voter or proxy to vote on your behalf if you, for any reason, are unable to attend any of the voting days.

A proxy must be eligible to vote as well and is someone you trust and only one person can be a proxy. A voting proxy appointment form must be completed and signed by both the person and the proxy and then certified by the city clerk.

Contact the city if you have questions about accommodations at 416-338-1111 extension 6. You can also email accessibleelections@toronto.CA.

I'm working election day, can I vote?

If you can’t make advance voting and are working election day, Oct. 26, you are still entitled to time to vote. Election day polls are open from 10 a.m. until 8 p.m.

You are allowed three hours to cast your ballot, the City of Toronto says, which means you’re allowed to be absent to give yourself three hours to vote.

The city gives an example of this stating if you work 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., you are entitled to leave one hour early so you would have from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m.

People should also speak with their employer if they need time, as the city says an employer could offer you time to vote. For example, if you work 12 p.m. until 6 p.m., your employer could have you start your shift at 1 p.m. instead of leaving work at 5 p.m.

No. Torontonians had until Sept. 24 to request a vote by mail package. Those who have received their package have until 12 p.m. on Oct. 14 to return their package and they can also track the status of their package online.

When people get behind the voting screen, they’ll be casting their vote for mayor, a city councillor and school board trustees.

The ballots are in place for the election, meaning former federal cabinet minister Chris Alexander will still appear as a mayoral candidate even though he announced Tuesday he was no longer running for the role.

People can still vote for Alexander, but he will not become mayor even if you cast your vote for him. He has also not endorsed another candidate.

stories.title: Carney touts Canadian sovereignty in first comments on Parti Québécois win in Quebec
stories.summary: Carney said he spoke with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and promised to work with him towards increasing sovereignty for Canadians.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Hours after the Parti Québécois was elected to a minority government, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he spoke with premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and promised to work with him towards increasing sovereignty for Canadians.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday morning, Carney said he had just congratulated the incoming Quebec premier and discussed ways to work together in the future.

On Monday evening, Quebecers elected a minority Parti Québécois government to replace the Coalition Avenir Quebec, which was completely eradicated from the electoral map.

St-Pierre Plamondon committed to hold a referendum on Quebec’s sovereignty within his first mandate if elected, but only after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the Oval Office.

In the meantime, Carney said he wanted to extend his philosophy of “cooperative federalism” to the separatist leader and argued for the need for a “strong Quebec within a strong Canada.”

Asked if he was concerned about a Quebec referendum, Carney retorted that he too was working towards sovereignty, but for Canada.

“We take advantage of the real opportunities that exist for our country because of Canadians, because of Canadian values, because of Canadian strengths to expand our trading network and to become more sovereign in Canada,” Carney told reporters Tuesday morning.

“It’s sovereignty, but it’s Canada’s sovereignty. It’s Canada’s independence.”

St-Pierre Plamondon was elected with only 28 per cent of the vote, raising questions about if he has a legitimate mandate to hold a plebiscite on the province’s independent.

When the question was put to Carney, the prime minister simply responded with his party’s election numbers in the 2025 federal election.

stories.title: Amendments would let Manitoba cannabis stores drop window coverings for safety
stories.summary: Cannabis stores across Manitoba May soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.
stories.author: Brittany Hobson
stories.content:
Cannabis stores across Manitoba May soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.

The Manitoba government introduced amendments to the provincial Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Control Act on Monday that would eliminate window coverings on all cannabis storefronts amid safety concerns.

The province said the change would increase visibility from outside the store and help make sure workers are not hidden from public view.

Current legislation requires retailers to ensure that cannabis and cannabis products are not visible to people who are not legally allowed to purchase the products.

“We’re still mandating that the cannabis product will not be visible because we want to protect kids, and so we’re finding that balance,” said Justice Minister Matt Wiebe.

“We don’t want cannabis displayed in window fronts. We don’t want kids riding by and seeing cannabis and being enticed into trying a product that’s not appropriate for them, but at the same time we have to prioritize workers’ safety.”

Labour groups have long expressed concerns about the special problems that cannabis stores pose, because they sell a controlled substance and are required by government rules to cover all windows to the outside.

An attack on a cannabis store employee who was working alone at night in May renewed calls from unions for improved worker safety.

Police arrested a man after he allegedly entered a retail store, waiting for a customer to leave, and then locked himself inside with a woman working alone.

They said he sexually assaulted the 24-year-old, who was able to flee the store and call police.

The province is also proposing changes to the act that would allow mandatory minimum staffing levels during certain hours to ensure that workers are not alone during times when there May be a higher risk of violence.

The United Food and Commercial Workers union welcomed the province’s proposals.

It surveyed its members and non-unionized staff on worker safety concerns and found that staffing levels was one of the biggest issues.

“Loud and clear, not working alone was by far the No. 1 issue that they raised,” said Marie Buchan, secretary-treasurer of Local 832.

Wiebe said the proposed amendments would give the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority the ability to mandate how many employees May be on a shift at a given period.

The Opposition Progressive Conservatives said they would have to review the bill before commenting.

Other provinces, including Ontario, have scrapped similar rules around window coverings to address safety concerns expressed by employees.
