paragraphs: Edmonton — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s office is distancing itself from one of her party presidents who met in Calgary with U.S. Republican strategists looking to assist the province’s separation movement.
Smith’s spokesperson Sam Blackett, in a statement Monday, said the premier “is not affiliated with these individuals’ activities and has no knowledge of these alleged meetings.”
Blackett added, “She also opposes separation or becoming a U.S. state.”
Blackett’s statement declined to answer questions put to him on what, if anything, Smith will do about Mitch Sylvestre’s presence at the meeting.

Sylvestre is the president for the Bonnyville-Cold Lake UCP constituency association. He also heads up the pro-separation Alberta Prosperity Project and spearheaded a petition that ultimately gathered enough signatures for a provincewide separation vote before a judge quashed it in court earlier this year.

On the weekend, the Globe and Mail reported and quoted him being among a group that met with U.S. Republican strategists in Calgary in January to look at software designed to identify and mobilize supporters.
Sylvestre told the Globe and Mail he was uncomfortable with the meeting and balked at using the Alberta Prosperity Project membership list to power the project, citing legal and privacy concerns.
The article also said separatist leaders reportedly suggested exchanging water and oil for U.S. support when it met with State Department officials in Washington, D.C., last year.
Sylvestre on Monday denied any discussion about access to water or oil taking place during the three meetings in Washington, though he said he only attended one meeting in September.
“We have no authority to do any of that,” he said in an interview.
“We’re not in government. We can’t go down there and have that conversation.”
Jeff Rath, another leading face in the separatist movement who had attended all of the Washington meetings, also denied that oil and water were on the table in any meaningful way.
“The story is completely false,” he said.
“The whole water thing is inflammatory and the suggestion of a U.S. royalty on Alberta oil is just ludicrous.”

Asked if he would support an exchange of oil and water, Sylvestre said he had never thought about it but that he thinks there’s enough homegrown support for Alberta independence to make U.S. support unnecessary.
Sylvestre also said that he only attended one of the Washington meetings because he didn’t see them as being useful given how far away Alberta is from seceding.
“We’re in a question-to-ask-a-question phase,” he said referring to the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum.
The Globe and Mail report has raised concerns about foreign involvement as Albertans prepare to vote in two weeks on whether to stay in Canada or launch a second, binding referendum on quitting.
In Ottawa, the Conservative MP leading his party’s efforts to convince Albertans to stay in Canada says he is concerned by reports of the Washington meeting.
“Absolutely nobody has a right to promise away Alberta’s birthright, which is our natural resources,” Dane Lloyd said.
Lloyd said he wouldn’t speculate on whether the reported activity amounted to foreign interference or how the matter should be investigated.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree deferred questions about the reporting to Canada’s security agency Csis. But he said they expect democratic events “to be governed under democratic principles.”
In Calgary, Mayor Jeromy Farkas, a staunch critic of Alberta’s separatist movement, said the report shows independence leaders are putting the province’s future at risk.
“They say (separation) is about taking back control, then go begging to Washington for support,” Farkas said in a video posted to social media.
“That’s not taking back Alberta. That’s selling Alberta out.”
Elections Alberta is projecting a record turnout on Oct. 19. Public opinion polls suggest a large majority will vote to stay in Canada.

Smith has said separation is a burning issue in the province that must be addressed. The premier has repeatedly cited hundreds of thousands of citizens signing petitions for and against staying in Canada.

Critics, including Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, say there is no burning separatist sentiment and that Smith is exploiting fringe grievances to placate separatists in her United Conservative Party in order to keep her job and keep the party from fracturing.
This is the second time in a week Smith has been asked about taking action against those within her United Conservative caucus and party.

Last week, Smith declined to take action against caucus member Jason Stephan, who represents Red Deer-South, after Stephan confirmed to CBC he is voting in favour of a second referendum on separation. In a social media post last week, Stephan said voting for a binding referendum was “the right way.”
Smith said her party tolerates differences of opinion but that their official position is for Alberta to stay in Canada.
Sylvestre said he hasn’t faced any pressure from Smith or her office to change course since he launched a petition, or in the wake of the meetings in Washington or with Republican strategists.
“And it wouldn’t matter. I’m a UCP member, same as her,” he said.
On Friday, Nenshi said Smith’s refusal to act in response to Stephan is telling.
“She’s not focused on your priorities, she’s focused on keeping her party together, cheating to win and keeping the separatists happy,” Nenshi said.
“But most of all, she’s focused on protecting her own political skin.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.
— With files from Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa and Timon Johnson in Edmonton
Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Liberals ask Ontario auditor to probe spending, oversight of Osap at career colleges
stories.summary: Toronto - The Ontario Liberals are asking the auditor general to investigate provincial student financial aid spending at private career colleges.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Ontario Liberals are asking the auditor general to investigate provincial student financial aid spending at private career colleges, after reporting by The Canadian Press showed a rapid increase concentrated within a small number of schools.

Liberal colleges and universities critic Tyler Watt requested a value-for-money audit, looking at the spending increases and whether the government was properly overseeing the Ontario Student Assistance Program.

“This has all the makings of Doug Ford’s next billion-dollar scandal,” Watt said Monday at a press conference.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that in 2024-25, career college students received nearly $1 billion in Osap grants. Just seven career colleges accounted for $385 million of that funding.

Between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 academic years, the province spent $465 million more on Ontario Student Assistance Program grants, and 95 per cent of that went to private career college students, the data showed.

Auditor general Shelley Spence’s office said all 2026 audits are underway, but it would take Watt’s request into account for future audit planning.

The request comes after a series of stories by The Canadian Press showed that Osap applications at a few career colleges far outpaced the rest of those institutions and publicly funded colleges and universities, and that Career Colleges Ontario has warned the provincial government for years about that.

The association representing career colleges raised concerns with the ministry about “indicators consistent with suspicious activity” in Osap applications in January 2023, according to a letter filed in court in a case involving three schools.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn earlier this year said the cost of Osap was becoming “unsustainable” and dramatically reduced the amount of grants that students at universities and publicly funded colleges can receive, while also making career college students only eligible for loans.

Watt said the evidence seems to suggest the issue of rapidly growing Osap costs was limited to a small number of private career colleges, and raises the question of why the government response involves students at all publicly funded institutions taking on more debt to fund their education – or in some cases delaying their schooling.

“Instead of cracking down on the dozen or so private career colleges at the centre of Osap spending increases, the government took a hatchet to a problem that required a scalpel, and it ruined Osap for everyone,” he said.

“That’s either a government that is grossly incompetent, or one that has something it desperately wants to hide.”

Zain Baig, president of the Toronto Metropolitan Students’ Union, said the government has penalized students across the province.

“Slashing Osap for everybody May be the easy thing to do, and it’s simple and straightforward for the higher-ups like Doug Ford and Minister Quinn,” he said.

“But maybe the right thing to do would have been to dedicate more resources to do an independent investigation, look into these things thoroughly, and address the issue on a case-by-case basis, as opposed to just a one-size-fits-all type of solution.”

Quinn earlier this year made five career colleges ineligible even for Osap loans, and three of the schools – which share a parent company – have asked the courts for a judicial review of that decision, alleging it was procedurally unfair.

Ministry inspection reports filed in court as part of that case show inspectors alleged they found evidence suggesting third parties were completing the coursework, and students who completed all of a course’s quizzes and exams in a single day.

The three Academy of Learning locations deny most of the ministry’s allegations, saying they have taken concerns seriously. None of the findings and allegations from either level of government have been proven in court.

A statement from the schools said it has implemented dozens of corrective actions, including stricter admission and identity verification controls.

“These include two-factor authentication and investigation of unusual login activity,” the Academy of Learning wrote. “We have co-operated extensively with both reviews and will continue to strengthen our controls wherever issues are identified.”

The instances of unusually rapid completion of courses warrants review, the Academy acknowledged, and said it has implemented additional monitoring of files before exam codes are issued.

By The Canadian Press

David Lepofsky filed a human rights complaint more than seven years ago after an incident during the 2018 Ontario election.

Lepofsky says he had tried to vote using Elections Ontario’s assistive voting terminal for voters with disabilities, but a poll worker inadvertently saw who he voted for.

Lepofsky argues Elections Ontario did not take sufficient action to ensure accessible voting, including before, during and after the incident.

He had said he also experienced barriers to accessible voting in Ontario elections since that June 2018 incident and that constitutes a continuing human rights violation.

Lepofsky argues that Elections Ontario violated his rights under the Ontario Human Rights Code to equal treatment with respect to services and facilities without discrimination because of his total blindness.

The hearing is set to take place over several days this week, with Lepofsky and Elections Ontario expected to provide final submissions later this month.

stories.title: Capitals legend Alex Ovechkin to retire at end of season
stories.summary: This season will be Alex Ovechkin’s last. The Washington Capitals captain and NHL all-time leading scorer made the announcement to teammates in a video posted by the team on Monday. “I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision,” Ovechkin said in a statement. “I am excited about […]
stories.author: Cole Fortner
stories.content:
This season will be Alex Ovechkin’s last.

The Washington Capitals captain and NHL all-time leading scorer made the announcement to teammates in a video posted by the team on Monday.

“I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision,” Ovechkin said in a statement. “I am excited about this season with my teammates, and we will do everything we can to make this year special. I am going to enjoy every moment with my family, my boys, our fans and everyone who has been part of my hockey career.”

Ovechkin, the 41-year-old Russian, is underway in his 22nd NHL season after being drafted first overall by the Capitals in 2004.

He has spent his entire career in Washington, highlighted by winning the 2018 Stanley Cup.

Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky’s all-time goals record in April 2025 when he scored his 895th against the New York Islanders. He currently sits at 929 career tallies, plus 77 more in the playoffs.

That total of 1,006 puts him 10 goals shy of Gretzky’s combined goals record of 1,016.

His 1,688 career regular-season points rank 10th, with a chance to pass Mario Lemieux (1,723) and Steve Yzerman (1,755) in his final season.

Ovechkin and the Capitals are set to play their home opener Wednesday against longtime rival Sidney Crosby and the Pittsburgh Penguins.

stories.title: Trial begins for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport
stories.summary: A man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history has pleaded not guilty to two charges as his trial begins in Brampton, Ont.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history has pleaded not guilty to two charges as his trial begins in Brampton, Ont.

Parmpal Sidhu is charged with theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist that took place at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

The trial comes soon after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial later this fall.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Sign on off-campus property perpetuated rape culture: St. Francis Xavier University
stories.summary: Antigonish, N.S. — Two Nova Scotia universities are condemning a sign that was displayed at an off-campus property in Antigonish on the weekend, saying it perpetuated rape culture.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Antigonish, N.S. — Two Nova Scotia universities are condemning a sign that was displayed at an off-campus property in Antigonish on the weekend, saying it perpetuated rape culture.

Tara Taylor, a professor at St. Francis Xavier University, posted a photo on social media Friday that showed a sheet draped over the window of a home in Antigonish with a spray-painted message that read: “Drop-off zone: Acadia girlfriends.”

The sign appeared outside the property during the university’s annual homecoming celebrations. The property is used for student housing.

“When I saw it … it felt like a slap in the face,” Taylor said in an interview Monday. “I just thought it was incredibly tone-deaf.”

Elizabeth Yeo, the university’s vice president of student life, issued a statement Saturday calling the sign “offensive,” adding that the university was investigating the incident.

Taylor said the sign was taken down Saturday morning, but it was displayed again that night.

In a statement released Sunday, university president Andrew Hakin said the school made sure the sign was taken down again, adding that the sign’s message was “degrading and deeply concerning.”

“St. F.X. unequivocally rejects misogyny, sexualized and gender-based violence, and the attitudes and behaviours that contribute to rape culture,” the statement said.

Meanwhile, Acadia University in Wolfville, N.S., issued a news release Sunday that said the sign encouraged sexual violence against its students.

“What happened in Antigonish is a symptom of a society-wide problem,” it said. “It is our collective responsibility as higher education institutions to speak out against violence against women and rape culture specifically.”

Coined in the 1970s, the term rape culture refers to behaviour and beliefs that encourage or normalize sexual violence.

Mariana Paludi, who has researched the views of students at Canadian universities about the issue, said she believes the sign is promoting sexual violence against women.

“It’s portraying … this gender imbalance and degrading women … and objectifying women,” said Paludi, an assistant professor at the Universidad Técnico Federico Santa Maria in Chile

Paludi published research earlier this year that looked at how Canadian post-secondary students interpreted rape culture following two high-profile incidents at Nova Scotia universities — a Saint Mary’s University student chant about sexually assaulting underage girls in 2013 and a 2015 Dalhousie University dentistry student group-chat that contained violent sexual messages about female classmates.

Paludi said the new sign posted over the weekend demonstrates how slow society has progressed, more than a decade after those two scandals.

Taylor said it was shocking to see the sign in light of recent online discourse surrounding a high-profile lawsuit in the United States that alleges seven members of the Chi Pi fraternity at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., sexually assaulted a woman in October 2024.

The professor said the St. F.X. students who displayed the sign must have been aware of the lawsuit, adding that the timing was “very triggering” for her.

“They can’t possibly be ignorant. It’s on social media everywhere,” she said.

Taylor said she shared the photo to raise awareness about a “party culture” at the university that she says contributes to sexual violence.

“I’ve been at St. F.X. for 22 years and I’ve had students every year come to me and say that they are dealing with the consequence of being sexually assaulted,” she said. “And I’m not unique in that.”

In 2018, students at the university criticized its handling of a reported case of sexual assault and called for a review of its sexual violence policy. And in 2023, a student sued the university, alleging she was sexually assaulted while attending the school in 2022.

Taylor said the university has taken steps to address sexual violence on campus and improve support for victims, but more needs to be done.

“There are people at the university who have worked very hard for a long time to make it safer, so it is deeply frustrating that these incidents still happen.”

According to the university’s website, its sexual violence response policy was approved in 2019 and reviewed in 2025. The policy states that the school is committed to fostering a culture where “behaviours that perpetuate sexual violence are discouraged and rejected.”

In his statement, Hakin said the most recent incident has been referred to the university’s disciplinary process, which will be guided by the school’s sexual violence response policy.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026

— By Tori Fitzpatrick in Halifax.

stories.title: Trial begins for man accused in Pearson gold heist
stories.summary: Parmpal Sidhu charged with theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A trial is set to begin today in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu is charged with theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist that took place at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

The trial comes soon after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22-million in restitution.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20-million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial later this fall.

stories.title: Toronto’s Harbourfront Centre names arts leader Gideon Arthurs as CEO
stories.summary: Veteran performing-arts administrator Gideon Arthurs’s hiring follows a period of intense restructuring at the cultural centre
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Toronto’s Harbourfront Centre has hired veteran performing-arts administrator Gideon Arthurs as its next chief executive officer, after years of financial struggle and concerns from the local arts community that its future as a cultural centre could be diminished.

Arthurs has been the executive director of Soulpepper Theatre Company and the Young Centre for the Performing Arts since 2022, announcing last month that he would soon step away from the job. He was previously CEO of the National Theatre School of Canada, executive director of the Toronto Fringe Festival and general manager of Tarragon Theatre.

Arthurs’s hiring follows a period of intense restructuring at Harbourfront Centre, a federally funded cultural complex on the shore of Lake Ontario in downtown Toronto that’s operated for more than five decades. Soon after long-time CEO Marah Braye quietly exited Harbourfront in 2023, Ottawa began warning that the centre lacked a “sustainable operating foundation” and would need to grapple with $106-million in deferred maintenance.

The new CEO said in an interview that he hoped to bridge both Harbourfront’s artistic and civic histories. “Cultural organizations become sustainable when they’re relevant, and they are relevant when they’re able to reimagine their value and purpose in the lives of the people they’re serving,” he said.

Harbourfront has a special role in Arthurs’s own history: he saw his first-ever play there at age 5, performed there at 8, and both he and his children have attended camps there.

Arthurs will begin the job Dec. 1. Ronald McDonald House Charities Canada executive Cathy Loblaw took over Harbourfront after Braye’s exist and quickly began restructuring . She cut staff levels by 25 per cent and stopped leasing the neighbouring Fleck Dance Theatre.

Soon after, the centre’s long-time tenant, the Toronto International Festival of Authors, left the complex to become independent , and the on-site Power Plant Contemporary Art Gallery became financially independent as well.

Harbourfront has always been a multifaceted complex, with a beloved outdoor skating rink and a variety of programming; it is currently home to portions of the shuttered original Ontario Science Centre.

But changes over the last few years shook Toronto’s arts community, many members of whom worried that the storied waterfront complex would reduce its arts programming.

Arthurs said this is top of mind, while he plans to make the 10-acre campus accessible to a broad swath of Torontonians, too. “We need to broadly push ourselves to find ways for artists and the public to meet in ways that maybe are not as intimidating, not as behind a paywall, and we need to find ways to make sure that artists have the conditions that they need to thrive,” he said.

Tenio Evangelista, president of Harbourfront’s board, said that three candidates were finalists to become CEO. While Arthurs had the most experience in arts administration, Evangelista said that he also had the right connections with governments and local stakeholders. He said that “a lot of the financial challenges have been fixed,” giving Arthurs a foundation upon which to broaden public access to Toronto’s waterfront.

Loblaw, who had described her work as CEO as that of a turnaround agent, said last year that she would step down as Harbourfront searched for a permanent chief executive.

The institution has made some inroads in replacing the cultural organizations it’s severed ties with, particularly with its announcement last December that the Shaw Festival repertory theatre company would launch a three-year artistic residency there .

Harbourfront said in a press release that last summer was one of its most successful ever in terms of visitors, with attendance of 4.2 million.

stories.title: University of Toronto launches $100 million scholarship program targeting PhD talent
stories.summary: The University of Toronto says it's launching a new $100 million scholarship program designed to attract PhD talent to Canada.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The University of Toronto is launching a new $100 million scholarship program to attract PhD talent from around the world including those leaving the United States, said president Melanie A. Woodin on Monday.

Woodin said the school is appealing to scholars who are looking for the best place to conduct research and those choosing to leave the U.S. because it’s not providing an environment to ask certain questions including on topics like climate change and gender.

“The attacks on higher education in general and the loss of funding to many institutions is certainly a push factor for many individuals,” she said.

“It also means that certain top talent that might have otherwise thought about going to the U.S. is now reconsidering it and looking for other academic institutions where they can make their next discoveries.”

Woodin said the situation in the U.S. creates “an exceptional opportunity” for Canadian institutions to focus on attracting talent.

The university said the Presidents’ Impact Scholarship Program will provide $80,000 funding per year for 50 scholars for a total of $320,000 of funding over four years.

The school said the program is the largest of its kind in Canada and is comparable to scholarship funds in other world-leading research universities in the United States and United Kingdom.

“It is the most lucrative PhD funding package in Canada and it ranks amongst the highest in the world, above Princeton, Harvard, Cambridge, and Oxford,” Woodin said.

“When you want the best in the world, first of all, you need to be competitive and recognize that many individuals May not currently be in school. They might be already out, have done their undergraduate or master’s training or another program, might be out working in the field.”

Woodin said the university wants to have the PhD students engage in an interdisciplinary approach to solve the biggest problems facing the world and produce future leaders.

“The world right now is facing many complex challenges, whether they be climate change, the role of AI for humanity, the list goes on,” she said.

“In order for us to address these complex challenges facing Canada and the world, we need to be producing leaders who have a real interdisciplinary perspective in how they tackle these challenges.”

She said the program will be run by the school of graduate studies and there will be activities that bring the cohort together around working on the complex problems to solve.

“You can think about academic conferences. We’ll also be providing them with a lot of networking opportunities to maximize, as a collective group, their public impact, external to the academy,” she said.

“There are big professionalism activities for them to help them engage again in that knowledge mobilization for both social and economic impact.”

The university said a Canadian family foundation with a long history of supporting the university and high education in the country provided a $50 million endowed gift for the program and the university matched its annual payout to create the $100 million fund.

The school said a total of 12 or 13 new scholarship recipients will receive four years of funding each year starting in September 2027.

The program will have a total of 50 scholars by the beginning of its fourth year and that number of recipients will be maintained in perpetuity.

stories.title: ‘It’s a cloud’: Sovereignty questions loom over Quebec firms as PQ leads the polls
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec's business community is taking notice as polls show the Parti Québécois seizing a firm lead with the provincial election in full swing.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec’s business community is on alert as polls show the separatist Parti Québécois with a firm lead heading into Monday’s election day, with some sensing early jitters over the prospect of sovereignty — but “no panic” in the offing.

PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has pledged to hold a referendum within his first mandate, though not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office in 2029.

“It’s a cloud. We have uncertainty on tariffs, we have uncertainty on counter-tariffs,” said Sébastien Lachaine, Quebec director at lobbying firm Sussex Strategy.

“The uncertainty of a referendum, even if the PQ is a minority, will add a cloud in the business community.”

Concerns over the possibility of independence could dampen investment, discourage immigration and trigger a rise in interest rates on government bonds, Lachaine said.

However, the PQ platform promises to lower corporate tax rates, an apparent boon for businesses in the province and part of a perceived rightward shift in the party’s policies.

For investors, a lot hinges on whether the would-be government emerges as a minority or a majority. The latter would increase the odds of a vote on separation, said Louis Hébert, a management professor at Montreal’s HEC business school.

“That will make a big difference,” he said. “If it’s a minority government, the likelihood of a new election within two years is pretty high, if you look at the past history.”

Investors outside the province have already factored a potential separatist regime into their calculations, with secession a farther-off risk compared to the clear and present crises of the U.S.-Canada trade war and artificial intelligence, he said.

Moreover, sovereigntist sentiment is nothing new in la belle province.

“In French we say something: better the devil you know than the devil you don’t know. And I think that the sovereignty risk in Quebec is a known devil,” Hébert said.

“People are taking it seriously, but no panic.”

Worries over referendum rumblings’ effect on Quebec businesses would not be unprecedented.

In the four years between Parti Québécois founder René Lévesque’s election in 1976 and the 1980 referendum on sovereignty-association, about 350 companies left the province and many more gutted their Montreal head offices. Some 200,000 residents also pulled up stakes, according to Statistics Canada.

In 1995, the narrow margin of a referendum vote — a 50.6 to 49.4 per cent split — left executives uneasy about the consequences for the provincial economy.

Recent polls show that support for independence — and for the PQ — hovers at around 30 per cent. In a fractured election battle with five major parties potentially poised to win seats, that threshold is still likely to translate to a win for the Parti Québécois, if not a yes on sovereignty.

Millions of voters across Quebec are casting their ballots on Monday.

Eric Girard, Quebec’s outgoing finance minister, warned last week that an “independent, sovereign Quebec would be poorer” and could lose up to $65 billion in economic activity in the first five years after leaving. He cited a University of Calgary study that pegged the cost of Alberta separation at between $50 billion and $170 billion over five years.

As a cautionary tale, Girard also pointed to the United Kingdom, where economic output wound up six to eight per cent below where it would have been had the country decided to stay in the European Union, according to a 2025 study from the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research.

For its part, the PQ states that independence would yield between $13 billion and $16 billion in administrative savings by scrapping or merging most of the roughly 230 federal agencies now operating in Quebec, according to the party’s costed platform. However, the cost of creating a stand-alone military, border services and other potential expenses are not covered in the document.

Given the relatively low support for secession, many entrepreneurs are focusing on more immediate concerns.

Some are fed up with the tangle of red tape they feel the province sticks them with and want more tax cuts and, for big companies, fewer cash injections, said François Vincent, vice-president for Quebec at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.

A September survey from the federation found that four in five respondents want the provincial government to balance the budget before launching new programs.

On Friday, a group of prominent Quebec business leaders called on the future government to “regain” the province’s economic ambition and foster the conditions for entrepreneurship to flourish.

“Today, Quebec finds itself ‘uninvestable,’ or much less attractive than other markets around the world,” said billionaire Andrew Lutfy, chairman and CEO of fashion retailer Groupe Dynamite Inc.

Others in the group included Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. founder and executive chairman Alain Bouchard, Laurent Beaudoin — widely credited with turning Bombardier Inc. into a transportation giant in the late 20th century — and Paul Desmarais III, senior vice-president of Power Corp. of Canada.

The event where two of the four business luminaries delivered their message to hundreds of executives and entrepreneurs last week was a “non-partisan, non-political gathering.” But the timing, days ahead of an election where the PQ is poised to win, was hard to miss.

“Businesses need to have clarity,” Lachaine said. “They are waiting to be reassured.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Michelle Good makes Giller Prize short list for 100K award for Canadian fiction
stories.summary: Toronto - Order of Canada member Michelle Good is among the five finalists for Canada's richest fiction award.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - When Michelle Good woke up at 4 a.m., an hour before she was scheduled to receive word on whether her book had been shortlisted for the prestigious Giller Prize, she knew there was no going back to sleep.

But the early morning wait was worth it, when the author was notified that she was among the five first-time finalists vying for Canada’s richest fiction award, which hands out $100,000 to the winner and $10,000 to the finalists.

“It’s almost heart-stopping,” Good said when reached in Winnipeg. “It’s so incredible to not only have your work receive popular approval, but critical approval as well, through the Giller. It’s just so satisfying and really phenomenal.”

Good was nominated for “Eliza Sunshine,” a multi-generational family saga that follows three Cree women and the storytelling tradition that connects them. The novel draws from Good’s mother and great-grandmother’s lives, which is why she said “it was an extremely personal and emotional book to write.”

“There’s so many things in this book that are actually factual and it was very important for me for people to understand it,” Good said. “For people to not miss the point. In particular, my mother’s story and my mother’s approach or feelings about identity. It’s a very touchy subject. And I think I hit the right note and that’s a big sigh of relief for me.”

The Cree lawyer, activist and Order of Canada member had previously been longlisted for her 2020 novel, “Five Little Indians.”

Meanwhile, Prince Edward Island-based author Nicholas Herring was nominated for his second novel “Your Breath in Charcoal” which follows a directionless young Islander who drives to New Brunswick to pick up an acquaintance’s brother from a mental health hospital.

When reached by video call while at his day job as a carpenter, Herring called the honour “very humbling and validating.”

“It means a lot obviously to have this kind of recognition,” he said. “Every Canadian writer probably sort of would hope that this would happen with their work, so in that sense I’m very grateful and very fortunate.”

Herring has previously received recognition for his writing, winning the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize for his debut novel “Some Hellish” in 2022. Herring said the $60,000 prize money helped him carve out the necessary time to write his latest book, of which he said, “I was kind of swinging for the fences with this one.”

“I say this with as much humility as I can muster, but I just thought it’s a pretty unique book. It’s a pretty unique story,” said the author. “I’m probably the only person on planet Earth who could write this book. I didn’t know if it was good or not, but I knew it was definitely unique and singular.”

Herring said he was also hoping he’ll get to meet Canadian comedian Rick Mercer, who is scheduled to host the Giller’s televised awards ceremony on Nov. 16 in Toronto.

The Vancouver-based author Nazanine Hozar, who was nominated for her novel “The Small Ones,” was asleep when the short list was announced, but she woke up to a celebratory text from her girlfriend.

“It was just a series of happy sunshine emojis and stuff,” she said.

The Iranian-Canadian writer’s second novel draws from historical facts and tells the story of children caught up in a military insurgence along the Iran-Iraq border in the early 1980s. Hozar’s first novel, the national bestseller “Aria,” centred on moms and motherhood, so in her second book, she said she wanted to explore fathers and sons.

“And what it means to be a man in a world that seems to embrace violence and aggression and what would it mean to raise a son, to have sons, and what fathers and sons might mean to each other,” she said.

“The Small Ones” was only released in Canada last week, but Hozar said she’s grateful for the Giller recognition, especially after she said “it’s been very hard to crack the American market” with this title.

“There was a point there where I was thinking, ‘Oh, but did I write a bad book? Or have I got something wrong here?’” And I was really questioning certain things about my writing or my storytelling,” she said. “And it puts it a little bit into perspective that, OK, maybe you’re on the right track. Maybe you can even write another book. You have some ability, or at least people are recognizing something.

“It’s just a bit of encouragement and a more internal sense of knowing that I can do this and I can continue to do this.”

Rounding out the contenders are Regina-based Tara Gereaux for “Wild People Quiet,” which explores the repercussions of a woman’s decision to hide her Métis identity while living in a small prairie town in the 1940s and Toronto-based Patmeena Sabit for her debut national bestseller “Good People,” which tells the story of how a family’s private tragedy thrusts them into the court of public opinion.

The Giller has faced controversy and financial uncertainty in recent years.

In 2023, hundreds of book workers — including past winners — boycotted the award, in part objecting to its previous title sponsor Scotiabank and its ties to a subsidiary that held shares in Elbit Systems, an Israeli arms manufacturer. The subsidiary has since divested from the arms company.

The Giller and Scotiabank parted ways in February 2025. The boycott ended earlier this year.

In September, the Giller announced new funding from Hilary and Galen Weston Foundation, which would donate $4 million to the prize in a multi-year gift, in addition to $1 million the Weston family quietly gave a year ago, when the award was in dire financial straits.

In response to recent backlash, the organization created the Giller Prize Writers’ Circle, a new advisory council that it said will work to support the literary community.

A nine-member jury panel of independent booksellers representing all five regions of Canada selected this year’s short list from an initial list of more than 140 titles.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario air ambulance company says 6 aboard missing flight presumed dead
stories.summary: Authorities had been searching waters off the coast of Nantucket after the aircraft vanished early Saturday morning.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Six people aboard a medical evacuation flight that disappeared off the U.S. East Coast while travelling from Bermuda to Boston are now presumed dead after the search-and-rescue effort was called off , according to the Ontario-based company that operated the aircraft.

Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance issued a statement saying the United States Coast Guard has concluded active search-and-rescue operations and transitioned to recovery efforts following the disappearance of Heartbeat 104 Medevac.

Authorities had been searching waters off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., after the aircraft vanished early Saturday morning.

The company said the decision means it must now confront “the heartbreaking reality” that the six people on board are presumed dead.

Those aboard the Gulfstream G100 included four Latitude crew members, a patient being transported from Bermuda to Boston, and a family escort accompanying the patient, the company said.

The aircraft disappeared around 1:30 a.m. ET Saturday while en route to Boston. Earlier Sunday, the Coast Guard said search crews were focusing their efforts around a debris field that had been located in the search area, but did not indicate at the time whether the mission had shifted from rescue to recovery.

Air traffic audio indicates that the plane May have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.

Latitude said its four crew members were carrying out their mission of providing care to people during difficult moments when the tragedy occurred.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family,” the company said in its statement. “They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives.”

In a statement, Latitude president Peter Byl called the loss “unimaginable” and said the company’s immediate focus is supporting the families of those on board and assisting investigators.

The company said it will continue to cooperate with the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada and other authorities involved in the recovery effort and investigation.

No cause has been released, and Latitude said it will not speculate while investigators work to determine what happened.

With files from John Marchesan and Denio Lourenco, CityNews

stories.title: Cohere unveils latest AI platform with more agentic features for businesses
stories.summary: Toronto-based company hopes to win more corporate and government customers with new version of North
stories.author: Joe Castaldo
stories.content:
Cohere Inc. is releasing a new version of its North artificial-intelligence platform in a bid to win more corporate and government customers in the fiercely competitive market for enterprise AI applications.

The Toronto-based company, which builds large language models, released the first version of North last year. Cohere chief AI officer Joëlle Pineau said the initial version functioned largely as a chatbot that could pull internal documents and handle some automated workflows.

“It was essentially a generative model,” she said. “Today, we’ve actually put in a lot of the features that allow agentic behaviour.”

Customers can use the latest version, called North 2, to build agents to carry out more complex multistep actions, such as resolving customer issues, conducting financial analysis and coding. Ms. Pineau said some features of North 2 have already been shipped to customers.

North acts as a kind of software layer around AI models, and at its core is what’s called an agent harness, an increasingly common term in the industry. The harness manages agents and connects with other applications to complete tasks.

“The model is like the engine, and the harness is like the vehicle,” Ms. Pineau said. “If you have a motor, you’ve got a ton of power. But without a vehicle, you’re not going anywhere.”

Cohere has scored Bell Canada , LG CNS Co. Ltd. and Dell Inc. as North customers, but the company declined to identify how many clients it has in total. “We have dozens of companies, and some of them are up to tens of thousands of users,” Ms. Pineau said.

Founded in 2019, Cohere focuses on businesses, regulated industries and public-sector clients for whom privacy, security and control are crucial. Rivals OpenAI and Anthropic are gunning for these clients, too.

OpenAI, for one, offers ChatGPT Enterprise for businesses and is rolling out a new agent product called Dots, which the company says can monitor customer feedback and suggest improvements, fix software bugs and update documents, among other tasks. Microsoft Corp. is selling its 365 Copilot product suite, while French AI company Mistral is making inroads with Canadian businesses.

Cohere is much smaller than its U.S. competitors, too, though it is bulking up through a merger with German AI company Aleph Alpha, giving it more access to the European market.

AI agents have dominated headlines in recent months for misbehaving and attempting to hack into organizations during evaluations, and sometimes succeeding. In the corporate world, companies want assurance that agents will carry out work correctly, access the right documents and tools, and not corrupt anything in the process.

Cohere said multiple security features are built into North. Agents can be designed to take only authorized actions and seek human input for more critical tasks. Customers can set parameters around the information agents can access and which employees can deploy certain agents.

Companies can also monitor costs and set usage limits, reflecting concerns about rising AI expenses . The issue is compounded by AI agents, which can spend a lot of time trying to complete a task – and not necessarily in the most efficient way – pushing up usage costs.

North is model-agnostic, meaning customers can use it with any AI model, even those from Cohere’s competitors. “We actually derive a sizable portion of our revenue from the harness,” Ms. Pineau said.

Training AI models is an expensive endeavour, with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google spending billions and racing to develop more sophisticated LLMs. Ms. Pineau said Cohere sees value in continuing to train models and build the agent harness around them. “The hypothesis is you do a much better version of both when you develop both,” she said.

stories.title: Trial to start where former UBC professor alleges defamation
stories.summary: A trial is expected to start Monday in B.C. Supreme Court where author and former professor Steven Galloway says he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted October 5, 2026 8:45 am

A trial is expected to start Monday in B.C. Supreme Court where author and former professor Steven Galloway says he was defamed by false accusations of sexual assault.

Galloway was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at the University of British Columbia when rumours swirled and spread online that he had assaulted one of his students.

He was never charged, but was fired, though a report that was later produced for the university by former judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the accusations against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

The defendants in the defamation suit, including his accuser known only as A.B., and those who repeated the allegations online, took the defamation case to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming their accusations were protected speech.

The High Court refused to hear the case, after a lower court said that if the defendants’ arguments held, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

Chelsea Rooney, one of the defendants in the case, issued a lengthy apology to Galloway over the weekend, saying she was genuinely sorry for the part she played in causing harm to him.

stories.title: Clocks stay in daylight saving, but analysis backs permanent standard time
stories.summary: Ralph Mistlberger's light is adjustable, allowing him to have the full spectrum of options depending on what his internal clock needs.
stories.author: Ashley Joannou
stories.content:
Ralph Mistlberger’s light is adjustable, allowing him to have the full spectrum of options depending on what his internal clock needs.

“You want cool in the morning. You want warm in the evening or warm in the afternoon,” he said.

“And so, it goes from being more bluish in the morning to more reddish in the evenings. Both of those are important because artificial light affects your clock.”

Mistlberger knows real sunlight is better than a lamp, but after more than 40 years as a neuroscientist studying sleep and the body’s circadian rhythms, he’s preparing for what’s to come Nov. 1.

That’s when clocks would normally have turned back an hour for most of Western Canada. But they’re staying where they are, putting residents on permanent daylight time.

Mistlberger said it’s a mistake and he and other researchers from British Columbia have released an analysis warning of the potential risks to health, the economy and students’ well-being with the darker mornings on the way.

The analysis by economic, mental health and sleep experts was published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal and examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight saving — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

Mistlberger, a psychology professor at Simon Fraser University, said people May think they want more sun in the evening, but the impact of starting your winter day in the dark is far-reaching.

“You’re actually waking up at an earlier circadian phase. Your clock May still be telling your brain and your body that this is the sleep period. It’s not time to wake up yet,” he said.

“The same is going to happen in the evening. It’s going to be telling you this is still the wake period, it’s not time to go to bed yet.”

He said not being able to get consistent sleep can lead to what scientists call “social jet lag,” when someone’s life and social calendar doesn’t line up with their biological clock.

Small amounts of sleep deprivation can be reversed with a good, long snooze, he said, but if the issue becomes chronic it can lead to health concerns.

That can include more cases of metabolic disorders, like obesity and diabetes, as well as cardiovascular disease. He said epidemiological studies of large populations have found increases in cancer and some mood disorders.

B.C., Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Manitoba all announced this year that they would adopt permanent year-round daylight time.

The B.C. government pitched that the move would “improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”

It said more than 223,000 people participated in a 2019 online survey and 93 per cent preferred a change to year-round daylight time.

Both Mistlberger and Patrick Baylis, a co-author of the analysis, said the government survey didn’t give the public the option to choose permanent standard time.

“The survey gave two options, which were comparing a switching regime, which is what we have previously had, to permanent daylight time. But those are the only two options. Baylis said.

Baylis, an associate professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia, said one of the biggest concerns is what it will mean for students going to school in the dark.

A study of students around the time zone boundary in Florida showed an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores among adolescents. The analysis said it was “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions and largest at puberty when circadian rhythms are most sensitive.”

“At minimum we should be thinking about monitoring for some of these negative effects on schooling outcomes, particularly among adolescents,” Baylis said in an interview.

While there is limited economic research, Baylis said some studies suggest exposure to sunlight can affect productivity.

A study that looked at variation in sunset timing within U.S. time zones found that an hour of later sunset reduces earnings over the long run by about five per cent.

Some countries that tried to make the switch to permanent daylight saving have not fared well.

Russia made the move in 2011 but reversed it three years later.

“Public dissatisfaction grew rapidly, particularly in northern regions, where winter morning darkness was even more prolonged, with critics citing disrupted biological rhythms, morning travel risks and effects on daily functioning,” the study said.

Most of Chile’s decision to change in 2015 was also reversed “after complaints about reduced school attendance, scheduling disruption and agricultural effects,” it said.

In 1974, all of the United States adopted permanent daylight saving as an energy-conservation measure.

“The policy was abandoned within the year after widespread opposition to dark winter mornings, concerns about children travelling to school before sunrise, workplace safety concerns and limited evidence of meaningful energy savings,” the analysis said.

The study recommends that choosing to stay with permanent daylight time should include steps to reduce the potential health effects and to evaluate the change.

Baylis said that could mean more flexible or later school start times or helping schools supplement the lack of real light in the morning.

Mistlberger said educating people on the potential impact is important, using bright lights in morning with adjustable bulbs to dim them by the evening.

“You want to get as much light exposure as you can as early as possible in the day when you go outside. So, even though the sunrise is going to be later than usual, it’s going to help you to get outside as soon as there is some sunrise.”

stories.title: Carney’s major projects bill up for debate as MPs return to Parliament
stories.summary: The government's key piece of economic legislation, Bill C-39, proposes measures to create a one-year timeline for federal project decisions.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Parliamentarians are back in Ottawa where debate is set to continue on the government’s 243-page economic and labour bill, with plans to introduce legislation focused on national defence and security procurement.

The government’s key piece of economic legislation, Bill C-39 , proposes measures to create a one-year timeline for federal project decisions, create zones of “national interest” where certain projects are pre-approved and change when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute — a move aimed at reducing the number of work stoppages.

The legislation is expected to be pushed for committee study. Instead of going to a regular standing committee, the House of Commons will create a special committee to study the wide-ranging bill.

Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has warned the government against “abusing” its majority powers to pass the bill as it could affect First Nations rights if it limits mandatory consultation.

The bill has also faced pushback from labour groups, including the Canadian Labour Congress, who say the proposed powers threaten the right to strike.

2:11 Environmentalists blast Liberal ‘Building Canada Strong’ act

Bea Bruske, Canadian Labour Congress president, says the International Trade Union Confederation has written a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the proposed labour regulations are “highly likely to violate” Canada’s international labour obligations.

“Canada has a long history of standing up for fundamental labour rights,” Bruske said in a statement. “It should concern all of us when the international labour movement is warning that legislation before our Parliament could put those commitments at risk. This is an opportunity for the government to reconsider these provisions and get this right.”

Cupe, one of Canada’s largest union’s, has pledged to defy Bill C-39 should it pass without amendment. Members of the business sector, meanwhile, have said the bill doesn’t go far enough to stave off job action.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the bill will put “guardrails” around ministerial powers to intervene in a strike or lockout and force people back to work.

Procurement Minister Joel Lightbound put a piece of legislation on the notice paper Friday, entitled “an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security.”

Lightbound’s portfolio includes the Defence Investment Agency, meant to overhaul defence procurement, that was created a year ago.

The government has been quickly increasing its defence spending with the goal of meeting the Nato target of putting five per cent of GDP into defence spending annually.

On the opposition benches, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has put a notice on motion that his party will call on the government to set a goal of Canada producing one-million barrels of diesel per day amid high fuel prices.

2:01 Mark Carney reiterates Indigenous partnerships for major projects in Ndtr speech

He said in a video released Sunday this would be done with emergency permits and tax relief for refining, storage and transportation.

The Conservative motion also calls on the government to extend the fuel excise tax exemption until at least July 1, 2027.

Poilievre added the government should create a strategic energy reserve so there are stockpiles in the event of shortages driving up prices.

“We are the only G7 country that has no such reserve, even though we have the most oil right beneath our feet. So we could be joining them to release the 100 million barrels of oil they’re putting on the market right now,” Poilievre said.

2:15 Mixed reactions to Carney, Smith’s ‘Pacific Link’ pipeline announcement

The International Energy Agency stipulates that member nations must maintain a 90-day supply of their net fuel imports that can be used in the event of shortages. Canada is exempt from this rule because it exports more fuel than the country consumes.

This comes as last week closed with near record-high diesel prices, with the Canadian average being about $2.60 per litre.

The current fuel excise tax pause, which was extended last month until Jan. 31, 2027, will see the tax gradually climbing back to being fully in place on April 1, 2027.

Parliamentarians will be in Ottawa until Friday, when they return to their ridings for another constituency week to coincide with Thanksgiving.

stories.title: U.S. Coast Guard suspends search for missing Ontario air ambulance
stories.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard suspended the search for six people, including four Canadians, who were aboard a missing medical transport aircraft off the coast of Nantucket.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard suspended the search for six people, including four Canadians, who were aboard a missing medical transport aircraft off the coast of Nantucket.

A statement released Sunday said the coast guard and other agencies searched more than 7,000 kilometres for the plane that went missing Saturday with the Canadians and two Bermuda nationals on board.

Rear Admiral Matthew Lake said in the statement that suspending a search was not an easy decision and offered his condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy.

Coast guard officials earlier told reporters that a debris field was found about 32 kilometres off the island of Nantucket, in waters approximately 24 to 27 metres deep, which was confirmed to be from the missing Canadian air ambulance jet.

The coast guard search began around 2 a.m. Saturday after they were notified the Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the plane as it flew from Bermuda to Boston.

The medical evacuation jet, belonging to Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance, was carrying a patient, their family member and four Canadian crew members when it went dark.

Latitude Air, in a statement late Sunday, said it faces a “heartbreaking reality” that all six souls are presumed dead.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family. They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred,” the statement says.

“We are grieving their loss deeply and will continue to support their families and our employees through the difficult days ahead.”

The company said it was co-operating with authorities and asked for privacy for the families involved.

Lt.-Cmdr. Kastriot Kastrati from the coast guard earlier told reporters that he couldn’t provide details about the debris that was recovered. Lake said the coast guard was working with Massachusetts authorities to get sonar-equipped craft to search the sea floor around the debris field.

Lake said search efforts were being aided by fixed-wing aircraft, boats and a helicopter, and that next of kin for the six missing people were being updated as the search continued.

He said a black box, a recording device found in airplanes used to investigate accidents, has yet to be recovered.

According to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net, the pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.

The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

Mary Schiavo, a former inspector general of the U.S. Transportation Department, told The Associated Press she thinks the plane May have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar.

“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”

Lake said at Sunday’s news conference that he didn’t want to speculate if electrical problems or weather played a factor.

“That’s up to the investigative efforts later,” he said.

Latitude Air Ambulance offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, according to its website. Operations manager Clarence Togeretz told The Canadian Press on Saturday that this was the first time the company lost contact with one of its planes.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said on social media before the search was suspended that she was “deeply concerned” by the disappearance of the air ambulance.

She said Global Affairs consular officials were in contact with the relevant authorities.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their loved ones. I thank the U.S. Coast Guard and all those involved in the search and rescue efforts for their tireless work,” Anand wrote.

The coast guard search began around 2 a.m. Saturday after they were notified the Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the plane as it flew from Bermuda to Boston.
The medical evacuation jet, belonging to Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance, was carrying a patient, their family member and four Canadian crew members when it went dark.
Latitude Air, in a statement late Sunday, said it faces a “heartbreaking reality” that all six souls are presumed dead.

“Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family. They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred,” the statement says.
“We are grieving their loss deeply and will continue to support their families and our employees through the difficult days ahead.”
The company said it was co-operating with authorities and asked for privacy for the families involved.

Lt.-Cmdr. Kastriot Kastrati from the coast guard earlier told reporters that he couldn’t provide details about the debris that was recovered. Lake said the coast guard was working with Massachusetts authorities to get sonar-equipped craft to search the sea floor around the debris field.
Lake said search efforts were being aided by fixed-wing aircraft, boats and a helicopter, and that next of kin for the six missing people were being updated as the search continued.
He said a black box, a recording device found in airplanes used to investigate accidents, has yet to be recovered.
According to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net, the pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.
“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.
The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

Mary Schiavo, a former inspector general of the U.S. Transportation Department, told The Associated Press she thinks the plane May have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar.

“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”
Lake said at Sunday’s news conference that he didn’t want to speculate if electrical problems or weather played a factor.
“That’s up to the investigative efforts later,” he said.

Latitude Air Ambulance offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, according to its website. Operations manager Clarence Togeretz told The Canadian Press on Saturday that this was the first time the company lost contact with one of its planes.
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said on social media before the search was suspended that she was “deeply concerned” by the disappearance of the air ambulance.
She said Global Affairs consular officials were in contact with the relevant authorities.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their loved ones. I thank the U.S. Coast Guard and all those involved in the search and rescue efforts for their tireless work,” Anand wrote.

stories.title: Trial set to begin for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport
stories.summary: A trial is set to begin Monday in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A trial is set to begin Monday in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu is charged with theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist that took place at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

The trial comes soon after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial later this fall.

stories.title: Art installation highlights Canada-EU ties beyond trade and defence
stories.summary: Abandoned grain silos May not seem like an obvious place for a diplomatic mission. But for the Delegation of the European Union to Canada, it served as a perfect blank canvas on which to showcase shared priorities between this country and the economic bloc.
stories.author: Michael Serapio
stories.content:
Toronto - Abandoned grain silos May not seem like an obvious place for a diplomatic mission. But for the Delegation of the European Union to Canada, it served as a perfect blank canvas on which to showcase shared priorities between this country and the economic bloc.

“We want to reinforce the connection between the Canadian and European,” said Geneviève Tuts, the EU’s Ambassador to Canada. “In my view, culture and art should be part of this conversation.”

The Canada Malting Silos are former malting towers that sit unused at the base of Toronto’s Bathurst Street along Lake Ontario.

But on Saturday, those two towers came to life, as two art installations were projected onto the structures for Toronto’s Nuit Blanche Festival , an annual art celebration that transforms the nighttime city into a giant exhibition space.

Presented by the Ontario College of Art and Design (Ocad) University and the EU Delegation, the two works featured images that explore nature and the impacts of climate change.

They are works that explore a shared human experience, as well as an opportunity for the EU to help bring that art to a Canadian public.

“I was in Strasbourg two weeks ago, and I had the chance to listen carefully to our two leaders, and they were determined and committed to build, as we say, a new partnership. And this new partnership will cover a wide range of topics,” said Tuts. “This is not just about economic issues or trade issues or digital. This is also about people-to-people ties.”

It’s the kind of language that’s getting more attention these days.

Just last month, the European Commission president invited Canada to explore becoming the first associate member of the EU.

It’s not clear what associate membership would look like, since it is not an established status within the political and economic bloc.

But Prime Minister Mark Carney accepted the invitation, open to deepening economic and security ties with the European Union but also stating he’s not seeking membership.

Rather, Carney says he’s looking for a unique alliance.

However, the relationship is defined, Canada and the European Union are already working more closely together, drawn together by the defence of Ukraine and decisions made by the United States since the re-election of Donald Trump.

A shifting alliance

“The United States, which pushed that multilateral system after the Second (World) War has pulled out of it,” said Jeremy Kinsman, Canada’s former ambassador to the EU from 2002 to 2006. “They’re not supporters of it. In fact, they’re resentful of the European Union’s multilateralism.”

It was that past commitment to multilateralism and the liberal democratic order that led Europe and Canada to rely on the United States as a security backstop.

But that relationship has changed, and the shift extends beyond defence.

The Trump administration has also upended U.S. trade policy, imposing tariffs on products from both friends and foes.

“The events of the last two years — and call them Trump — have focused everybody on the value of this relationship,” Kinsman said.

Deepening economic ties

Over the past year, Canada and European partners have taken steps to deepen their economic ties.

The federal government announced over the summer that it had selected Germany’s ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems , or Tkms, as Canada’s preferred supplier to build up to 12 new state-of-the-art submarines.

European buyers have also expressed interest in purchasing more water bombers from Canadian aircraft manufacturer De Havilland, while German energy company Uniper has finalized a deal to buy liquefied natural gas from the future Ksi Lisims LNG project in British Columbia. First deliveries are expected in 2032.

Those developments underscore a point Kinsman says should guide the debate over the future of Canada-EU relations, regardless of whether Canada becomes an associate member.

“What is going to determine this relationship is not what it’s called, and it’s not all the words to describe why we need the relationship,” he said.

“It’s going to be concrete evidence of real capital projects, you know, between the two countries. And we’re doing them.”

The evolving relationship will come into sharper focus later this month.

Global Affairs Canada says Carney will welcome von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa to Montreal on Oct. 29 for a two-day summit.

There is already speculation that the leaders could announce agreements aimed at strengthening co-operation on critical minerals, supply chains and low-carbon energy.

“We have a lot to do together. We are sharing the same values. We are two democratic countries. We are respecting fundamental laws, the rule of law,” Tuts said. “We are fighting for multilateralism.”

Those shared ideals are helping Canada and Europe find common ground on a growing number of fronts — including an art project that lit up Toronto’s waterfront.

“It’s going to be concrete evidence of real capital projects, you know, between the two countries. And we’re doing them.”
The evolving relationship will come into sharper focus later this month.
Global Affairs Canada says Carney will welcome von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa to Montreal on Oct. 29 for a two-day summit.
There is already speculation that the leaders could announce agreements aimed at strengthening co-operation on critical minerals, supply chains and low-carbon energy.
“We have a lot to do together. We are sharing the same values. We are two democratic countries. We are respecting fundamental laws, the rule of law,” Tuts said. “We are fighting for multilateralism.”
Those shared ideals are helping Canada and Europe find common ground on a growing number of fronts — including an art project that lit up Toronto’s waterfront.

stories.title: Teen charged after vehicle plunges down Georgian Bay embankment
stories.summary: A 15-year-old faces several charges after a vehicle with three people inside, crashed down an embankment and came to rest along the shoreline of Georgian Bay in Owen Sound early Sunday morning.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 15-year-old faces several charges after a vehicle with three people inside, crashed down an embankment and came to rest along the shoreline of Georgian Bay in Owen Sound early Sunday morning.

Emergency crews were called to the 2900 block of 3rd Avenue West at about 2:05 a.m. where police said the vehicle left the roadway, crossed a grassy shoulder and plunged about 20 feet down an embankment before coming to rest near the water’s edge.

Investigators said two of the people inside fled the scene before emergency crews arrived but were quickly found by responding officers.

A 15-year-old was charged with operation while impaired by alcohol and drugs, operation while impaired with a prohibited blood-alcohol concentration, dangerous operation, taking a motor vehicle without consent and driving without a licence.

Under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, the accused cannot be identified. The youth was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in court in November.

Two of the vehicle’s occupants were assessed and treated at the scene by paramedics. A third occupant was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
