stories.title: Nobel prize awarded to researchers who learned how to light up the brain
stories.summary: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel share prize for work leading to the development of the field known as optogenetics
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
A discovery that began with algae and turned into a powerful method for investigating the brain is the subject of this year’s Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

On Monday, the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden announced this year’s prize has been has awarded to three scientists, one in the United States and two in Germany, for work leading to the development of the field known as optogenetics.

Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University of Berlin and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg, also in Germany, will share equally in the prize, worth approximately $1.7-million dollars.

The story of this year’s medical Nobel begins in the 1980s, when Dr. Hegemann, a biophysicist, was working at the Max Planck Institute of Biochemistry in Martinsried, Germany, and became fascinated with the ability of pond algae to sense and respond to sunlight. Algae rise or sink depending on the amount of light they are exposed to. By doing so they can regulate photosynthesis.

The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists who created a tool using light to help unravel how the brain works. Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

The Associated Press

The phenomenon led to the discovery of a class of proteins called channelrhodopsins, which the algae use to turn light into electrical signals. Dr. Hegemann found the underlying gene associated with channelrhodopsin in algae, which Dr. Nagel was then able to produce in frog egg cells to study the protein’s function.

“Nagel and Hegemann realized exactly what they had found. They had just discovered the switch neuroscientists had long dreamed of,” said Abdel El Manira, a member of the Nobel Committee, during Monday’s announcement.

The practical value of the discovery was realized in 2005, when Dr. Deisseroth and Ed Boyden, then a postdoctoral researcher in Dr. Deisseroth’s lab at Stanford, showed how a channelrhodopsin gene obtained from Dr. Nagel could be inserted into the DNA of a rat neuron . This effectively created brain cells that could be switched on or off with exposure to light. With that innovation, optogenetics was born.

Researchers have now used the technique to activate individual cells within networks of neurons to understand how brains are wired. The method has opened a new window into a range of complex neural functions including perception, memory and emotion.

More recently, the tool has been extended beyond neuroscience to develop therapies that harness light to activate cells to treat retinitis pigmentosa, a form of blindness, as well as cancer and diabetes.

Over the years, the advancements made possible by optogenetics have been widely celebrated. In 2016, Dr. Deisseroth and Dr. Boyden, now at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, received the Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for their contributions.

In 2018, Dr. Deisseroth, Dr. Boyden and Dr. Hegemann were among the winners of the Canada Gairdner International Award .

In an interview with The Globe and Mail that year, Dr. Hegemann said the unlikely combinations of knowledge from areas such as aquatic biology and neuroscience is “the beauty and the stimulating factor in science” that can lead to unexpected advancements.

“This is how the big jumps are produced,” he said.

Monday’s announcement kicks off a week of Nobel prize reveals, with the recipient or recipients of the physics prize to be named on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday.

The prizes were first awarded in 1901, with categories stipulated in the will of Swedish businessman and inventor Alfred Nobel.

A sixth prize for economics, added in 1969, is set to be announced on Oct. 12.

The science, literature and economic prizes are bestowed annually at a special ceremony held in Stockholm on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896, while the Nobel Peace Prize is given on the same day in Oslo.

stories.title: London seniors turn decades of knitting into a way to give back
stories.summary: A group of seniors in their 80s and 90s are turning a lifelong passion for knitting and crocheting into a way to give back to their community.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A group of seniors in their 80s and 90s are turning a lifelong passion for knitting and crocheting into a way to give back to their community.

Residents at Masonville Manor Retirement Residence sold their handmade creations on Oct. 4, with proceeds going to the London Food Bank.

Among them is 95-year-old Sophia Lustberg, who learned to knit and crochet from her mother as a child and has continued the craft ever since.

For the past decade, she has donated handmade blankets and other creations to organizations including Ronald McDonald House and Anova in London, buying the supplies herself.

She began donating blankets to a women’s shelters, she later asked her daughter she wanted to do more.

Sophia’s daughter suggested the Ronald McDonald house, and ever since she has been donating blankets, scarves and booties for children.

Sophia has made hundreds of pieces over the years, but she doesn’t use patterns. Instead, she creates her own designs and colour combinations, making each piece unique.

She’s joined by other residents with decades of experience.

Nancy Herrington, 90, once owned a children’s knitwear business with her daughter, while 87-year-old Lilliana, who was born in Italy, turns leftover pieces of yarn into bookmarks, scarves and washcloths without using patterns.

Betty Smuck, 95, continues to knit alongside the group.

For the residents, the craft is about more than creating handmade items. Knitting and crocheting can engage skills such as hand-eye coordination, counting, memory and creative problem-solving, while also providing opportunities for social connection and creativity.

“We know there are many people in our community who are struggling to put food on the table,” Sophia said. “We’re fortunate that we can use something we love doing to help.”

The group hopes its handmade creations will raise money while putting skills developed over a lifetime to use for a cause close to home.

stories.title: Does Canada punish murder too harshly? B.C.’s top court wades into the debate
stories.summary: The province considers the revival of faint hope for first-degree murderers
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
A twisted fever for vengeance gripped Luciano Mariani. He planned to kill his former girlfriend after she had an abortion.

In August, 2021, he bought a baseball bat at a Value Village in Vancouver and travelled to Vancouver Island. According to court records, Mr. Mariani stalked Caroline Bernard’s home in the hours before dawn. In previous weeks, he had scoped out details of his plan online. His searches included “what to do if you believe an eye for an eye and your child was killed” and “time needed to kill someone with a baseball bat.”

He broke through a sliding glass door at Ms. Bernard’s home a little after 4 a.m. He beat her to death in her bed. Her four-year-old daughter was there beside her. Ms. Bernard was 41.

Two years later, the 45-year-old Mr. Mariani pleaded guilty to first-degree murder. His lawyers, however, challenged Canada’s long-standing punishment for first-degree murder, killings that are planned and deliberate: a life sentence with no possibility of parole for at least 25 years.

They argued that the mandatory minimum sentence levied on all people convicted of first-degree murder, without any exceptions, violated the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

In the past, there had been a small exception. The faint-hope clause offered an opening to apply for early parole after 15 years. But in 2011, the Conservative federal government eliminated that option. Mr. Mariani’s lawyers made the case that scrapping faint hope meant the one-size-fits-all minimum for first-degree murder was, under the Charter, cruel and unusual punishment.

In mid-2025, when Mr. Mariani was sentenced, Justice Robin Baird of the British Columbia Supreme Court described the murder as one of obscene brutality, “exceptionally violent” and “committed in cold blood.” It inflicted profound and permanent pain on Ms. Bernard’s family, he said.

But Justice Baird also concluded the absence of faint hope violated the Charter.

Faint hope, the judge said, was “part of a legislative compromise that led to the abolition of capital punishment.” He called it an “important element of the balance” in the punishment of first-degree murder.

The judge’s ruling, applicable only in B.C., restored the faint hope of parole at 15 years for people convicted of first-degree murder, including Mr. Mariani. The judgment is now under the scrutiny of three judges on B.C.’s top bench, the Court of Appeal, after they heard arguments in June.

A ruling from the appeal court is expected this fall. If the top provincial court affirms the restoration of faint hope, it would likely presage a high-profile showdown at the Supreme Court of Canada.

Ms. Bernard’s family is still reeling from her murder. That Mr. Mariani could get out of prison earlier than the 25 years just doesn’t make sense to them.

“I cannot understand the law,” Margarita Bernard, Caroline’s mother, said in an e-mail. “My life was destroyed and I will never recuperate from this. I will live with this pain until I die.”

Now, what started as a murder case has morphed into a constitutional reckoning and vaulted a philosophical question of crime and punishment into an unexpected spotlight at a top court. It’s a question that has long been debated by a small group of lawyers and legal academics: Does Canada punish murder too harshly?

Parliament instituted the mandatory minimum for first-degree murder a half-century ago when the country abolished the death penalty.

From Confederation in 1867 to 1962, Canada executed 710 people. The last two hangings happened at the Don Jail in Toronto, a few weeks before Christmas.

A Globe and Mail investigation the next year revealed major questions in one of those executions, helping to propel mounting public opposition against the hangman’s noose.

The legal questions involved in such a determination, where a harsh sentence escalates into cruel and unusual, include whether a mandatory minimum punishment is “grossly disproportionate” in some cases. Research from the Library of Parliament in 2011, when faint hope was ended, showed that people convicted of first-degree murder in Canada served an average of 28 years. stories.title: Meet the five novelists shortlisted for the 2026 Giller Prize
stories.summary: The writers were considered by a jury which for the first time was not made up of mostly authors
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
A fisherman from Prince Edward Island, a bestselling author born in Tehran, a Métis television and film writer, an Order of Canada member from Red Pheasant Cree Nation in Saskatchewan and a Kabul-born first-time novelist who took 10 years creating her book are the shortlisted novelists for the 2026 Giller Prize.

They were considered by a jury which for the first time was not made up of mostly authors. The nine-member panel is composed exclusively of owners, managers and staffers from independent Canadian booksellers representing seven provinces and one territory.

Established in 1994 by Toronto businessman Jack Rabinovitch , the $100,000 award is the country’s richest for fiction.

Of the five shortlisted authors, only one, Michelle Good of Saskatchewan, has been nominated previously. The Cree writer, lawyer and Order of Canada member was longlisted in 2020 for Five Little Indians , a debut novel (about residential school survivors) that won the Governor General’s Literary Award for Fiction.

She is shortlisted for Eliza Sunshine , a multigenerational story which considers the loss of the buffalo.

“Just imagine everything gone, all of a sudden,” Ms. Good told The Globe and Mail recently. “Food, clothing, shelter, medicine, tools – everything suddenly gone. How would you survive in the world? How could you possibly survive?”

The Giller jury cited the novel, published by Random House Canada, as a “masterful, deeply personal snapshot of a tragic chapter of Canadian history, navigating readers with unflinching honesty through a story of hope and strength.”

The four other nominated authors are Nicholas Herring, for Your Breath in Charcoal (Goose Lane Editions); Nazanine Hozar, for The Small Ones (Knopf Canada); Tara Gereaux, for Wild People Quiet (Scribner Canada); and Patmeena Sabit, for Good People (Crow).

PEI author Mr. Herring’s Your Breath in Charcoal is about a rudderless young Islander who heads to New Brunswick to retrieve an acquaintance’s brother from a mental hospital. It is the second novel from the well-educated fisherman based in Murray Harbour. His first, Some Hellish , won the 2022 Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.

The Giller jury described Your Breath in Charcoal as an “uproarious, undeniably Maritime tale” and a “deeply philosophical narrative filled with pop culture references, literary allusions, and mordant, quotable witticisms.”

The Small Ones , by the Tehran-born, Vancouver-based Ms. Hozar is a fable about child martyrs used as front-line shields in the Iran-Iraq War. Ms. Hozar’s first novel, 2019’s Aria , a saga set in the lead-up to the Iranian revolution, was hailed by Margaret Atwood on X (then Twitter) as the “ Doctor Zhivago of Iran.”

The Giller jury said The Small Ones “ transforms the experiences of children caught in conflict into a deeply affecting examination of sacrifice, power, survival, and the enduring humanity of those whom society deems expendable.”

Wild People Quiet comes from the Regina-based Métis author Ms. Gereaux, who has worked as a writer and story editor for film and television. Her novel explores the repercussions of a woman’s decision to hide her Métis identity while living in a small, predominantly white prairie town in the 1940s.

“A stunning exploration of colonial trauma, self-acceptance, and the sacredness of community,” the jury wrote about the book.

The fifth finalist is Toronto-based Ms. Sabit, who was born in Kabul a few years after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. Her family sought refuge in Pakistan and then the United States. Ms. Sabit grew up in Virginia, the setting for Good People , a debut novel about the American Dream and the death of an Afghan-American teenager.

The jury cited the book as “polyphonic, layered, and brilliant.”

The Giller Prize will be presented at a Toronto gala hosted by Rick Mercer and televised and streamed across CBC platforms on Nov. 16.

Globe and Mail reporter and photojournalist Jesse Winter is shortlisted for Canada’s Balsillie Prize for Public Policy , an annual $70,000 award that recognizes books which advance policy discussions on social, political, economic and cultural topics. His Wild Fire: Dispatches from a Country Ablaze covers three Canadian wildfires from the front lines.

The four other nominees are Dennis Molinaro, for Under Assault: Interference and Espionage in China’s Secret War Against Canada; Moira Welsh, for The Astonishing Lives of Older Women: How to Create Pleasure Over Peril in Peak Longevity; Rick Westhead, for We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada’s Troubled Hockey Culture; and Tim Wu, for The Age of Extraction: How Tech Platforms Conquered the Economy and Threaten Our Future Prosperity.

The winner will be revealed on Nov. 24.

The Cundill History Prize , administered by McGill University, announced its three finalists: Jonathan Cheng, for Korean Messiah: Kim Il Sung and the Christian Roots of North Korea’s Personality Cult ; Alexander Lee, for The First Ghetto: Venice and the Jews ; and Beth Lew-Williams, for John Doe Chinaman: A Forgotten History of Chinese Life Under American Racial Law .

The winner of the US$75,000 prize will be revealed on Oct. 23 as part of the Cundill History Prize Festival in Montreal.

stories.title: MPs to debate economic and labour bill, plus new plans for national defence and security procurement
stories.summary: Bill C-39 proposes to create one-year timeline for federal project decisions, and change when jobs minister can intervene in labour disputes
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Parliamentarians are back in Ottawa, where debate is set to continue on the government’s 243-page economic and labour bill, with plans to introduce legislation focused on national defence and security procurement.

The government’s key piece of economic legislation, Bill C-39, proposes measures to create a one-year timeline for federal project decisions, create zones of “national interest” where certain projects are pre-approved and change when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute – a move aimed at reducing the number of work stoppages.

The legislation is expected to be pushed for committee study. Instead of going to a regular standing committee, the House of Commons will create a special committee to study the wide-ranging bill.

Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has warned the government against “abusing” its majority powers to pass the bill as it could affect First Nations rights if it limits mandatory consultation.

The bill has also faced pushback from labour groups, including the Canadian Labour Congress, who say the proposed powers threaten the right to strike.

Bea Bruske, Canadian Labour Congress president, says the International Trade Union Confederation has written a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the proposed labour regulations are “highly likely to violate” Canada’s international labour obligations.

“Canada has a long history of standing up for fundamental labour rights,” Bruske said in a statement. “It should concern all of us when the international labour movement is warning that legislation before our Parliament could put those commitments at risk. This is an opportunity for the government to reconsider these provisions and get this right.”

Cupe, one of Canada’s largest unions, has pledged to defy Bill C-39 should it pass without amendment. Members of the business sector, meanwhile, have said the bill doesn’t go far enough to stave off job action.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the bill will put “guardrails” around ministerial powers to intervene in a strike or lockout and force people back to work.

Procurement Minister Joel Lightbound put a piece of legislation on the notice paper Friday, entitled “an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security.”

Lightbound’s portfolio includes the Defence Investment Agency, meant to overhaul defence procurement, that was created a year ago.

The government has been quickly increasing its defence spending with the goal of meeting the Nato target of putting five per cent of GDP into defence spending annually.

On the opposition benches, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has put a notice on motion that his party will call on the government to set a goal of Canada producing one-million barrels of diesel per day amid high fuel prices.

He said in a video released Sunday this would be done with emergency permits and tax relief for refining, storage and transportation.

The Conservative motion also calls on the government to extend the fuel excise tax exemption until at least July 1, 2027.

Poilievre added the government should create a strategic energy reserve so there are stockpiles in the event of shortages driving up prices.

“We are the only G7 country that has no such reserve, even though we have the most oil right beneath our feet. So we could be joining them to release the 100 million barrels of oil they’re putting on the market right now,” Poilievre said.

The International Energy Agency stipulates that member nations must maintain a 90-day supply of their net fuel imports that can be used in the event of shortages. Canada is exempt from this rule because it exports more fuel than the country consumes.

This comes as last week closed with near record-high diesel prices, with the Canadian average being about $2.60 per litre.

The current fuel excise tax pause, which was extended last month until Jan. 31, 2027, will see the tax gradually climbing back to being fully in place on April 1, 2027.

Parliamentarians will be in Ottawa until Friday, when they return to their ridings for another constituency week to coincide with Thanksgiving.

Bea Bruske, Canadian Labour Congress president, says the International Trade Union Confederation has written a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney saying the proposed labour regulations are “highly likely to violate” Canada’s international labour obligations.

“Canada has a long history of standing up for fundamental labour rights,” Bruske said in a statement. “It should concern all of us when the international labour movement is warning that legislation before our Parliament could put those commitments at risk. This is an opportunity for the government to reconsider these provisions and get this right.”

Cupe, one of Canada’s largest unions, has pledged to defy Bill C-39 should it pass without amendment. Members of the business sector, meanwhile, have said the bill doesn’t go far enough to stave off job action.
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the bill will put “guardrails” around ministerial powers to intervene in a strike or lockout and force people back to work.

Procurement Minister Joel Lightbound put a piece of legislation on the notice paper Friday, entitled “an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security.”
Lightbound’s portfolio includes the Defence Investment Agency, meant to overhaul defence procurement, that was created a year ago.
The government has been quickly increasing its defence spending with the goal of meeting the Nato target of putting five per cent of GDP into defence spending annually.

On the opposition benches, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has put a notice on motion that his party will call on the government to set a goal of Canada producing one-million barrels of diesel per day amid high fuel prices.
He said in a video released Sunday this would be done with emergency permits and tax relief for refining, storage and transportation.
The Conservative motion also calls on the government to extend the fuel excise tax exemption until at least July 1, 2027.
Poilievre added the government should create a strategic energy reserve so there are stockpiles in the event of shortages driving up prices.

“We are the only G7 country that has no such reserve, even though we have the most oil right beneath our feet. So we could be joining them to release the 100 million barrels of oil they’re putting on the market right now,” Poilievre said.

The International Energy Agency stipulates that member nations must maintain a 90-day supply of their net fuel imports that can be used in the event of shortages. Canada is exempt from this rule because it exports more fuel than the country consumes.
This comes as last week closed with near record-high diesel prices, with the Canadian average being about $2.60 per litre.
The current fuel excise tax pause, which was extended last month until Jan. 31, 2027, will see the tax gradually climbing back to being fully in place on April 1, 2027.
Parliamentarians will be in Ottawa until Friday, when they return to their ridings for another constituency week to coincide with Thanksgiving.

stories.title: Supreme Court to open judicial year with ceremony in temporary new building
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada is set to mark the opening of the judicial year with a ceremony in its temporary new building today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Supreme Court of Canada is set to mark the opening of the judicial year with a ceremony in its temporary new building today.

The top court’s nine justices are settling in at the West Memorial Building in Ottawa while the court’s permanent home across the street undergoes extensive renovations.

Refurbishing the stately Supreme Court building is expected to take at least 10 years.

Chief Justice Richard Wagner plans to make remarks at the ceremony, which will include current and former members of the court.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Kristen Boon, president of the Council of Canadian Law Deans, are among the other scheduled speakers.

A formal welcome for the court’s newest member, Glenn Joyal, is expected to take place later this month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Can Canada actually deliver universal childcare?
stories.summary: Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Martha Friendly, the Executive Director of the Childcare Resource and Research Unit, about how the system is working, how it's not, and how Canada can better fulfil the promises of its newest large social program.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
In today’s The Big Story podcast, Ontario has become the latest province to extend their $10-a-day childcare deal with the federal government. It’s a policy that’s undoubtably reduced prices for Canadians, but that doesn’t mean it’s become more accessible. A crisis of affordability has become one of availability, as the number of open spots across the province is far fewer than the demand for them. So, what needs to happen to make Canada’s “universal childcare” program actually universal?

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Martha Friendly, the Executive Director of the Childcare Resource and Research Unit, about how the system is working, how it’s not, and how Canada can better fulfil the promises of its newest large social program.

You can subscribe to The Big Story podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

stories.title: Designing a solution to homelessness
stories.summary: Spring House, Toronto’s new supportive and transitional housing building, sets an important example of how to serve a marginalized population while attending to the details that make a good home
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
If you ask Dr. Andrew Boozary about design, he has a simple formula: “Good design is rooted in human dignity,” he says. The doctor, who treats unhoused people through University Health Network, has helped deliver new buildings that provide dignified conditions to an underserved population.

At Spring House, a new supportive and transitional housing building in Toronto’s Parkdale neighbourhood, the hospital and three governments will bring that ideal home. The roughly 40,000-square-foot building will include 54 apartments along with supportive services. It sets an important example of how to serve a marginalized population while attending to the details that make a good home.

The building, designed by Toronto’s Montgomery Sisam Architects, builds on the precedent of nearby Dunn House, which opened in 2024. Both rely on a simple insight: The best way to treat homelessness is with housing.

Last Thursday, Build Canada Homes, the City of Toronto and the UHN Foundation announced a total of $64-million to expand the program over three more sites, providing about 200 more homes.

The model works well. Dunn House serves unhoused people who were frequent UHN emergency-department patients. After one year, residents saw emergency visits drop by 52 per cent and their days in hospital drop 79 per cent, for reported savings of more than $2-million.

Dr. Boozary, who treats Dunn House residents, has seen results that can’t be captured on a spreadsheet. “The community that’s emerged there is one of the most powerful and beautiful things that I’ve witnessed,” he says. “There’ll be someone in their 20s knocking on my clinic door, saying, ‘You know, I’m worried about Miss So-and-So, who’s in her 70s. I went to get her groceries, and she’s not her usual self. I think you might want to check in on her.’

“This person – someone that we would stigmatize and push away – is here banging on my door to look out for an older adult.”

That is medicine.

Spring House is designed in two parts. The main eight-storey block is compact and repetitive, suited to the mass-timber construction systems being encouraged by Build Canada Homes. Wood panels and beams provide a rational structural grid. Down at the ground, a two-storey triangular wing reaches its arm out to meet the street.

The architects have also paid close attention to Parkdale itself. The building takes its material cues from the area’s Victorian brick and sandstone. Proposed hand-laid brick surrounds large arched windows. At the entrance, green glazed brick provides a flash of colour.

At Dunn House, some benches proved less useful than expected, while a covered porch seat became a popular place to stop and talk. At Spring House that experience has informed a more informal public edge, with opportunities for what Dr. Boozary calls “micro-interactions.”

Inside, the front desk is tucked around a corner, allowing staff to see what is happening without making the entrance feel like a checkpoint.

The second floor offers a lounge and terrace at the level of the surrounding trees. “People who have experienced homelessness often feel very scrutinized,” says Kevin Hutchinson, the partner at Montgomery Sisam who is leading the design. A resident can use the front porch to interact with people on the street, he explained, or go upstairs for a private moment.

For Dr. Boozary, such intentional design marks a contrast to the punishing conditions of the shelter system. “I just refuse to call shelters housing,” he told me. The uncertainty, instability and lack of privacy are “not a way to live.”

Spring House provides an answer, but also a puzzle of governance and fundraising. The building is supported by the federal government through Build Canada Homes, the province and the City of Toronto – municipal real estate agency CreateTO acts as development manager.

This means many mandates and many cooks in the kitchen.

The growth of the program suggests that UHN, and Dr. Boozary’s team, have been canny in designing and managing the place. They have taken input from their housing fellows program ; one fellow, the British social-housing architect Paul Karakusevic, provided feedback on the Spring House design.

And Montgomery Sisam are being hired by the clients directly, rather than through the complicated lawyerly alliances that define most health care buildings in Canada today.

That, Mr. Hutchinson says, has made it easier to protect the little things that might be seen as dispensable but which in fact give a place soul: a porch, a garden, a better street edge, an extra window, a room where people can gather to simply exist, in dignity.

stories.title: How Canada's retaliatory tariffs could drive up your winter heating costs
stories.summary: New tariffs on U.S.-made Hvacr goods are raising costs for Canadian distributors — pushing some to seek alternatives in Asia.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — In the past week, the trade war saw new U.S. import restrictions on $1 billion in Canadian goods, fresh pain for Canadian steel workers, and more fiery rhetoric from the White House.

Last Monday, hundreds of Stelco workers in Ontario learned of looming layoffs and a plan to halt operations at the Hamilton Works plant. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump announced a massive, $15 billion mega-steel plant project for Iowa, touting hundreds of new jobs for the region.

“These are your 232 tariffs, the steel tariffs, at work,” U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said during that announcement, referring to the Section 232 tariffs Washington has imposed to support U.S. steel. “Without those tariffs, this mine doesn’t get built, and this steel plant doesn’t get built.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney laughed off U.S. President Donald Trump’s comment that Canada would say “sorry” for its retaliatory tariffs, but as trade tensions heat up, industry leaders are finding the tariffs anything but funny. That’s especially true in the heating, ventilation, air conditioning, and refrigeration (Hvacr) field, where costs are rising just in time for the colder months.

This has led to an unusual cross-border response by the Hvacr industry, with Canadian and U.S. groups that represent contractors, distributors, and manufacturers working together to push Ottawa and Washington to preserve the tariff-free trade arrangement under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (Cusma). They warn that duties on equipment and components are driving up costs, disrupting tightly integrated supply chains, and even pushing buyers to look for offshore suppliers.

“In a few weeks, it’s going to get cold, and people are going to need to turn on their furnaces. Those furnaces that are old and need to be replaced are being tariffed,” said Victor Hyman, executive director of ClimateCare Canada, an Hvac contractor cooperative in Ontario.

A Trump adviser's outburst and a new poll suggest Canada’s tariff strategy is landing

Trump administration muses about hitting Canada with EU-style tariffs over Carney’s EU pivot

“For the homeowner that needs to replace their furnace or heat pump or air conditioner this year, they’re going to pay a lot more than they would have pre-trade war,” he added, noting that a job that would’ve cost $5,000 two years ago is now $5,700 or $5,800.

Because the Canadian and U.S. Hvacr markets are so integrated, with some parts and appliances crossing the border multiple times during production, industry leaders in both countries are asking Washington and Ottawa to “prioritize a return to free, fair, and predictable trade,” according to the Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Institute (Hrai) of Canada.

Hrai recently announced that it was “joining its American counterparts in calling for the preservation of the benefits of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma/Usmca),” according to a press release.

Its U.S. counterpart, Heating, Air-conditioning, and Refrigeration Distributors International (Hardi), alongside the Air Conditioning Contractors of America, the Air-Conditioning, Heating, and Refrigeration Institute, and the Plumbing-Heating-Cooling Contractors Association, wrote a similar message to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in early September. They wrote to “express our strong support for the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (Usmca) and urge the Office of the United States Trade Representative to protect the agreement’s benefits to the heating, ventilation, air conditioning, refrigeration, and water heating (Hvacr) industry.”

Martin Luymes, VP of government and stakeholder relations at Hrai, which represents roughly 1,200 member companies nationwide, says the industry’s concerns are more urgent now that the tariff exposure has expanded. In 2025, in response to the 232 tariffs, Canada responded with a retaliatory set of tariffs that impacted U.S.-origin gas furnaces coming north. This led Canada’s industry to campaign for tariff relief, which was granted in June, Luymes explained.

But now, following the introduction of Washington’s Section 338 tariffs on hundreds of Canadian imports this August, Ottawa has imposed new retaliatory tariffs that are raising the prices on Hvacr equipment and components being shipped into Canada — and now the impact is close to universal.

“Air conditioning products, heat pumps, and a variety of others are included, including refrigeration components, parts … and are all within scope of different levels of tariffs, anywhere from 15 to 25 to 50 per cent,” Luymes explained.

Tariffs increasing the cost of products that are very necessary — whether it is heating in winter, air conditioning in summer … have a dramatic impact on people’s lives

Because Canada imports more Hvacr equipment from the U.S. than it exports, Luymes said Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs are hitting Canada’s side harder than the original U.S. tariffs.

“The impacts on the Canadian economy, in our sector at least, are greater — are more driven by the Canadian response than by the original U.S. tariffs,” he said.

That’s why Hyman and others want the retaliatory tariffs, at least on Hvacr products, lifted.

“As much as we would like to stand up to U.S. trade aggression, we shouldn’t do it despite ourselves,” Hyman said.

Without a policy change, he anticipates sticker shock for customers this winter. “If your furnace dies this winter, you need to replace it this winter. You can’t wait a couple of years to replace it,” he said.

In the U.S., Alex Ayers, Hardi’s VP of government affairs, also sees the tariffs and price increases as unfair to consumers, especially given that heating and cooling are essential goods.

“Tariffs increasing the cost of products that are very necessary — whether it is heating in winter, air conditioning in summer … and then very specifically refrigeration … have a dramatic impact on people’s lives,” he said.

A return to Cusma free trade, meanwhile, would restore much-needed certainty the industry has been lacking, he said.

“We as an industry view Usmca as successful. We want to continue to see it be successful,” Ayers said.

The goal of Trump’s tariffs was to foster more domestic manufacturing, but they have not succeeded in expanding U.S. domestic Hvac production, and the supply chain issues and higher costs have simply added more uncertainty.

Ayers noted that the fluctuating tariffs are wreaking havoc on operations.

“A product being manufactured anywhere in the world can take weeks to get to its final destination for a contractor to install it. So, when tariffs are constantly changing, it’s hard to say what the price of that product is going to be,” Ayers said.

Tariff uncertainty and the higher costs for parts, plus the administrative costs companies have had to absorb to ensure they’re keeping up with the duties, are also beginning to change business behaviour, with some suppliers looking elsewhere for products so they can avoid the red tape and higher prices.

Luymes and Hyman said this has Hvacr suppliers already starting to turn toward offshore suppliers for heat production and supplies of other components.

Luymes said he knows of a member company, a large contractor who buys tens of thousands of units each year, that has already shifted suppliers. The owner, he said, told him, “‘I’m not buying anything from the United States any more.’” That owner has since started sourcing his supplies from China instead, he said.

Businesses are looking for supply relationships that they can count on for years. “They don’t want to commit to a supplier and then suddenly have a 25 per cent increase,” Luymes added.

Luymes, Hyman and Ayers believe these decisions to pivot to Asian suppliers will increasingly be made throughout the industry the longer the tariff war continues.

“With products being produced within North America being tariffed on either side of the border,” said Luymes, “it does suggest that there will be a shift in purchasing away from Canadian or American producers and to Asian producers who are not subject to those tariffs.”

stories.title: Quebec voters heading to the polls for provincial general election
stories.summary: Montreal - Voters in Quebec's 127 ridings are heading to the polls today to choose a new provincial government.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Parti Québécois has won a minority government, completing a dramatic political comeback and paving the way for an eventual third sovereignty referendum.

The party captured 59 seats after the votes were counted late Monday, falling short of the 64 needed to form a majority in Quebec’s legislature.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, which has governed the province for the past eight years, was wiped off the map. Even leader Christine Fréchette, who took over after former premier François Legault’s resignation earlier this year, failed to win a seat in her hometown of Trois-Rivières.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon gave a victory speech in Montreal after his party was projected to form a minority government in Quebec. In the Eastern Townships region, Liberal party leader Charles Milliard promised to be a unifying force and a balance to the new government's promise of a referendum. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Charles Milliard’s Liberals were elected in 40 ridings and form the official Opposition for the third straight election, while the Quebec Conservatives led by Éric Duhaime make a historic entry into the legislature and gain official party status with 19 elected members.

A crowd of PQ supporters exploded with cheers at a watch party in Montreal as they learned their party was declared elected, with supporters dressed in blue and white chanting “Quebec, a country,” in French.

“There is a new chapter in our nation that is starting over the next few years,” PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon told a boisterous crowd Monday.

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to launch a referendum to separate Quebec from Canada, but not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

The premier-designate said a future independent Quebec would be rich, modern and democratic.

“A referendum is an opportunity to decide for ourselves,” he told the crowd, some of whom sported merchandise from the “Yes” campaign in the 1995 referendum. “It’s an act of democracy. It’s not up to anyone but us, as a people, to decide our national future.”

However, his path is complicated by the fact that both the Liberal and Conservative leaders have said their parties would fight to stop a sovereignty vote. Québec solidaire, another sovereigntist party, could hold the balance of power and support the PQ’s plans for a referendum. Québec solidaire elected nine members to the legislature.

The PQ has also promised to more than halve temporary immigration in Quebec and table legislation to abolish the monarchy, diverting funds used to pay the lieutenant-governor to tackle homelessness.

In his speech Monday, St-Pierre Plamondon pledged to include elements from the other parties’ platforms in his future budget. He also promised to work with the province’s English speakers and Prime Minister Mark Carney — when it serves Quebecers.

“I want to tell him that every time he’ll defend the interests of Quebec, he’ll find in me a partner in dialogue and collaboration,” he said.

Carney congratulated the PQ leader for his victory, pledging to work with the new government in Quebec City.

“Building a stronger Québec is core to our mission of building a stronger Canada,” Carney said in a statement on social media. “I look forward to working with you to support Québec’s businesses and workers impacted by tariffs, create more good jobs, work to end homelessness, and get more homes built across Québec.”

Carney also thanked Fréchette for her service, noting they had accomplished a lot together.

The Parti Québécois won only three seats in 2022, the lowest total ever since the party was founded in 1968. That number increased to seven by the start of the campaign, after four straight byelection wins.

The sovereigntist party capitalized on Quebecers’ desire for change after eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule. The outgoing governing party struggled to connect with voters due to a series of scandals, unpopular decisions and high-profile departures from its caucus in recent years, culminating in Legault’s resignation in January.

The Liberals also more than doubled their seat count, finishing with about 24 per cent of the popular vote, close behind the PQ, which finished the evening with about 28 per cent of the votes that were counted.

Milliard, the 47-year-old former pharmacist-turned-politician, warned St-Pierre Plamondon that the PQ would need to secure support beyond its own ranks to govern, and said he was open to collaborating on matters that improve Quebecers’ lives.

“But to prepare your referendum, you’ll find a determined opposition,” he said.

Duhaime and the rest of his Conservative team are the first candidates to be elected under the Conservative banner in modern history, although the party has had a recent presence in the legislature in former CAQ member Maïté Blanchette Vézina, who joined the party.

Under Duhaime’s leadership, the party surged from a marginal formation that captured less than two per cent of the vote in 2018 to a main player. The party ran a campaign that was largely targeted on key ridings, after failing to capture a seat in 2022 despite getting close to 13 per cent of the vote.

Duhaime has promised to use his leverage to act as a “guard dog” that would protect taxpayer interests and attempt to block a referendum vote.

“The voice of Quebecers who no longer recognize themselves in the old parties and who want to modernize the old bureaucratic model will finally be heard,” Duhaime said.

It was a quiet night at a Coalition Avenir Québec watch party in Trois-Rivières, where more than half the tables remained empty. The party entered the campaign with 79 seats, and ended the night with none.

Fréchette, who replaced Legault as leader and premier in April, took the blame for her party’s crushing defeat.

“Quebecers wanted change, and I respect their choice,” Fréchette said.

She spent much of her campaign warning of the dangers of a referendum at a time when the U.S. trade war is destabilizing the economy, and argued that her party was best placed to guide the province through the storm.

Despite an early boost in the polls, she largely failed to make the case that she could offer Quebecers a change in leadership without a change in government.

Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal was declared elected in her Montreal riding, as the left-wing sovereigntist party appeared poised to hold onto most of its seats.

She told supporters that her party’s results prove that “the left is still alive and well in the province,” and promised to fight the “four shades of right” that the other parties offer.

The same cheers of “Quebec, a country” — heard at the PQ watch party — also echoed through Québec solidaire’s gathering in Montreal, as Ghazal said the sovereigntist party was looking forward to building a country inclusive of everyone, including immigrants, Indigenous people and English speakers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: MPs return for break with debate set on key legislation and new bill on the table
stories.summary: Parliamentarians are back in Ottawa where debate is set to continue on the government's 243-page economic and labour bill, with plans to introduce legislation focused on national defence and security procurement.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Parliamentarians returned to Ottawa on Monday and Opposition members of Parliament had their sights trained firmly on the government’s 243-page economic and labour bill.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also squared off in question period Monday over whether the government has done enough to prioritize Canadian materials in its sweeping infrastructure agenda.

Key to that agenda is the Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, which was introduced on the first day of the fall sitting on Sept. 21.

The government’s landmark economic legislation proposes measures to create a one-year timeline for federal project decisions, create zones of “national interest” where certain projects are pre-approved, and change when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute — a move aimed at reducing the number of work stoppages.

Conservative MPs speaking to the legislation as debate resumed Monday were broadly supportive of getting projects built more quickly but questioned whether Bill C-39 would help Canada do that.

Conservative MP David McKenzie, who represents the riding of Calgary Signal Hill, said Liberal promises to approve projects with one assessment within one year are not the same as the government getting out of the way and letting private proponents build.

Bill C-39’s proposed “regions of national interest” — zones where pre-emptive consultations can pave the way for project pre-approvals and exemptions from certain laws — are akin to letting the government prioritize certain developments above others, he argued.

“It is an uncertainty, it’s a political process, and it is not going to be helpful in moving things forward,” McKenzie said.

Conservatives have largely criticized Bill C-39 since its introduction but have yet to say whether they would support the legislation or seek to amend it.

The bill’s passage is not in doubt, as the Liberals hold a majority of seats in the House of Commons now.

Bloc Québécois MP Christine Normandin criticized the bill’s proposed centralization of powers.

Speaking in French, Normandin compared the “national interest” exemptions to U.S. President Donald Trump bypassing the checks and balances of the United States Congress. She said Canada should not imitate Trump as it responds to the economic crisis he caused.

Liberal MPs argued in response that Bill C-39 is about giving businesses and private investors the certainty they need to get projects moving.

The legislation is expected to go before a committee for study, however instead of sending it to a regular standing committee, the House of Commons will create a special committee to study the wide-ranging bill.

Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations, has warned the government against “abusing” its majority powers to pass the bill, adding it could affect First Nations rights if it limits mandatory consultation.

The bill has also faced pushback from labour groups, including the Canadian Labour Congress, which says the proposed powers threaten the right to strike.

People in the business sector, meanwhile, have said the bill doesn’t go far enough to stave off labour disruptions.

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the bill will put “guardrails” around ministerial powers to intervene in a strike or lockout and force people back to work.

Poilievre has said his party will call on the government to set a goal for Canada to produce one million barrels of diesel per day in response to high fuel prices.

He said in a video released Sunday that target could be reached through emergency permits and tax relief for refining, storage and transportation.

The Conservative motion also calls on the government to extend the fuel excise tax exemption until at least July 1, 2027.

Poilievre added the government should create a strategic energy reserve so there are stockpiles in the event of shortages driving up prices.

“We are the only G7 country that has no such reserve, even though we have the most oil right beneath our feet. So we could be joining them to release the 100 million barrels of oil they’re putting on the market right now,” Poilievre said.

The International Energy Agency stipulates that member nations must maintain a 90-day supply of their net fuel imports that can be used in the event of shortages. Canada is exempt from this rule because it exports more fuel than the country consumes.

Last week closed with near record-high diesel prices, while the Canadian average was about $2.60 per litre.

The Conservatives have two opposition days this week. The first is Tuesday, when they could introduce a motion that would be voted on Wednesday. They’ll be able to bring forward another motion Thursday that would go to a vote on Oct. 19.

The current fuel excise tax pause, which was extended last month until Jan. 31, 2027, will see the tax gradually rise until it’s fully in place on April 1, 2027.

Procurement Minister Joel Lightbound put a piece of legislation on the notice paper Friday entitled “an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security.”

Lightbound’s portfolio includes the Defence Investment Agency, created a year ago to overhaul defence procurement.

The government has been ramping up its defence spending with the goal of meeting the Nato target of investing five per cent of annual GDP in defence.

Parliamentarians will be in Ottawa until Friday, when they return to their ridings for another constituency week to coincide with Thanksgiving.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

— With files from Alessia Passafiume.

stories.title: Author Steven Galloway 'destroyed' by sex assault allegations, lawyer says
stories.summary: Vancouver - The lawyer for author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says his life and career were “destroyed” by sexual assault allegations, while his defamation lawsuit has been delayed for years as he tried to clear his name.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The lawyer for author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says the man’s life and career were “destroyed” by sexual assault allegations, while his defamation lawsuit has been delayed for years as he tried to clear his name.

Daniel Burnett told a B.C. Supreme Court judge on Monday that Galloway’s case is mostly about how to calculate damages against the defendants, who spread unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against Galloway.

Burnett said Galloway was once “a star in the literary world” with a bright future that was “cut very short” when the allegations were made publicly by a former student, and were then spread by others in the academic and literary world.

He said at the opening of the defamation trial that Galloway’s reputation was “tarnished to a degree that is incomparable.”

The sexual assault accusations were made against Galloway in late 2015, and since then, his accusers have fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming their accusations were protected speech.

The high court refused to hear the case, after a lower court said that if the defendants’ arguments held, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

In the months after the information came out, dozens of high-profile representatives in Canada’s literary community, including Margaret Atwood and Yann Martel, signed a letter that raised concerns about the university’s process to investigate the complaints against Galloway, calling them secretive and unfair.

Galloway was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at the University of British Columbia when rumours swirled and spread, and while he was never charged, he was fired from the university.

A report that was later produced for the university by former judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the accusations against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

The defamation trial was originally scheduled for 60 days, but Justice Neena Sharma said it will likely take 20 days.

Nine of the people who accused Galloway or repeated accusations against him online have apologized, all of which have been posted on the website gallowayapologies.com .

Chelsea Rooney, one of the original defendants, issued a lengthy apology to Galloway over the weekend, saying she was genuinely sorry for the part she played in causing harm to him.

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know if the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them, and she has come to better understand his position and commitment to clear his reputation.

“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets or my participation in the process,” her statement said, much of which was published in the National Post newspaper on Saturday.

Rooney is no longer a defendant in the case.

The court heard that four defendants remain, including his accuser only known as A.B., who isn’t going to attend court to testify.

Glynnis Kirchmeier, who is representing herself as a defendant, told the judge that the court will hear evidence about “how UBC utterly failed to have any reporting mechanisms available” for the proper reporting of sexual assault and that A.B. did “as best she could in a context where it was impossible to do so in the right way.”

Author Mandi Gray and Dana Kagis are also defendants.

After Burnett completed his opening on Monday, Galloway’s wife, Katie Wagner, told the court that Galloway was taken to a mental health facility in Ohio when the allegations came to light in 2015.

She testified that Galloway would become physically ill; he would cry, shake and vomit; and was distraught after the “outlandish” allegations went public in news articles and spread over social media.

Wagner became emotional during her testimony, telling the court that Galloway had panic attacks and sleep troubles that were “horrible.”

When they returned home to Vancouver, she said reporters started calling and showing up to their home with cameras, and the family retreated to Vancouver Island “for a long time” to avoid the publicity.

After the Boyd report came out and found the allegations against Galloway unsubstantiated, she said the faculty association at the university indicated that he should get his job back, but he didn’t.

She said Galloway would withdraw and she became a sort of caretaker for him, driving him to therapy and medical appointments and portioning out medications, taking a toll on her life for the last 10 years.

“I would feel torn. I want to go out and take care of my kids, or do normal things, or go to things, and he would be in there, you know, obsessing over the situation that was so horrible and couldn’t just be dropped. He couldn’t just shed it all, like go downstairs and, you know, live life.”

She said Galloway reacted with “hopelessness” and defeat as the allegations would be repeated, and she tried shielding him from social media.

Wagner told the court that she brought Galloway to a writer’s festival event, insisting that he go, and he “sat in the corner” and later told her how “absolutely awful it felt to go there and see his former life that way.”

The defamation trial continues in Vancouver on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: University of Toronto launching $100-million scholarship fund to attract PhD students
stories.summary: New program aims to help school compete for bright minds at a time when elite U.S. universities are under attack by the Trump administration
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The University of Toronto is launching a $100-million scholarship fund for PhD students that will double the pay of recipients and help the school compete for bright minds at a time when elite U.S. universities are under attack by the Trump administration.

The new U of T program, unveiled Monday, will see the university recruit 12 or 13 new PhD candidates a year to conduct cross-disciplinary research on a predetermined theme, such as sovereignty and the Arctic, or health and artificial intelligence.

Winners will be paid $80,000 a year for four years, twice the current minimum base funding for PhD candidates at U of T. Half of the $100-million endowment comes from an anonymous donation, the rest from the university.

“We’ve got an unprecedented opportunity right now to bring back Canada’s best and keep Canada’s best here,” U of T president Melanie Woodin said in an interview. “The Prime Minister has spoken about the prioritization of talent as it relates to Canada’s economic resiliency and sovereignty, and as Canada’s flagship university, we’re fully aligned because we’re in the talent business.”

The new U of T awards are called the Presidents’ Impact Scholarships. If the name sounds familiar, it could be because Mark Carney’s Liberal government last year promised $1.7-billion over 12 years for an academic recruiting blitz with a similar moniker – The Canada Global Impact+ Research Talent Initiative.

That federal campaign is part of a wider push by Canada’s top-flight universities and hospitals to capitalize on uncertainty at postsecondary institutions south of the border. Donald Trump’s government has cut funding for scientific and scholarly research, sued top universities and expressed a general disdain for science.

The infusion of public funding and attention for science and scholarship in Canada is also something of a departure from the past.

In 2023, an advisory panel’s report on the federal research support system found the funding dispersed by Canada’s three main granting councils – the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada; and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada – had “not kept pace with evolving needs” or with Canada’s international competitors.

One of the shortfalls the report singled out was pay to graduate students, which they often receive via their professors’ grants.

The panel, led by Frédéric Bouchard, dean of the faculty of arts and sciences at the University of Montreal, concluded that financial support for graduate students in Canada was “at a breaking point.” The value of Ottawa’s awards for university research trainees had been stagnant for two decades, the panel’s report noted.

The new U of T scholarship program is an acknowledgment that paltry pay for graduate students can be a barrier to doctoral research, especially for those who have racked up debt as undergraduates or who are considering leaving the private sector to pursue a PhD, Dr. Woodin said.

She added that the Presidents’ Impact Scholarships will be, to U of T’s knowledge, the most lucrative PhD funding package in Canada. “Globally, it puts us pretty close to the top – so above Princeton, Harvard, Cambridge and Oxford,” Dr. Woodin said.

All that said, pay packages are just one of many factors that promising PhD candidates weigh when choosing a university.

U of T is hoping candidates for the new scholarship will be enticed by the interdisciplinary nature of the awards, which require doctoral students to work with two faculty supervisors from different disciplines.

For stem cell scientist Derrick Rossi, a Canadian co-founder of the pharmaceutical company Moderna Inc., money didn’t matter as much as living somewhere interesting and finding a PhD program that was the best fit for him.

He studied at U of T before moving to Paris and ultimately getting his PhD at the University of Helsinki.

More important, Dr. Rossi said in an interview, is the message that U of T is sending with a large scholarship for doctoral students.

“The U.S. government right now is very anti-science,” he said. “The signal that [U of T] is sending to the globe is that Canada is not anti-science and we’re serious about science.”

stories.title: PM Mark Carney pledged to ‘Buy Canadian.’ Since then, $7.8 billion in contracts went to American corporations
stories.summary: A Star analysis reveals U.S. firms dominated federal contracts despite PM Mark Carney’s ‘Buy Canadian’ promise.
stories.author: Frédérik Plante
stories.content:
Since assuming office a year and a half ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney has repeatedly promised that his government would “build Canadian and buy Canadian .”

But American-controlled multinational corporations have dominated the most lucrative federal contracts under Carney’s leadership, a Toronto Star analysis of government data shows. The share of government contract dollars going to U.S. companies also increased.

Since Carney was sworn in as Prime Minister in March 2025 and up to the end of July 2026 — the latest available data — Ottawa awarded $25 billion in contracts to buy everything from cloud services to military vehicles and office furniture.

The vast majority of it, $22.4 billion, went to Canadian companies, according to federal contract data. United States businesses come at a distant second place, with nearly $1.2 billion.

But that’s not the full picture; procurement data does not distinguish between a homegrown shop and the locally-incorporated subsidiary of an American corporation. This is how well-known U.S. brands such as defence contractor Lockheed Martin , which has received about $86 million in contracts under Carney, or tech giant Amazon, which has received about $49 million, sometimes show up in procurement data as Canadian companies.

The Star cross-referenced procurement data with another federal data set, the Inter-corporate Ownership (ICO) review’s index , which includes information on more than 50,000 companies and their “country of control” — where the people controlling the firm live. That metric is used to measure “the extent and impact of foreign control within the Canadian economy,” according to the ICO review, which reports on its findings to Parliament.

The Star also reviewed reports filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, company websites and other public records to confirm American ties among some of Ottawa’s largest contractors. Where there was no ICO match for smaller contractors, the Star used procurement data to establish an organization’s country.

The results show that while Carney has promised to uphold Canadian sovereignty and make the country’s economy less dependent on the U.S., his government has been reliant on its businesses. They also illustrate the limits of Ottawa’s Buy Canadian Policy, which went into effect in December to give “priority to Canadian businesses and Canadian-made content for large federal purchases.”

In its first 16 months in power, the Carney government gave an estimated $7.8 billion in federal contracts to American-controlled corporations. Contracts with Canadian companies over the same period amounted to $14.9 billion.

Public Services and Procurement Canada did not answer the Star’s questions on the proportion of contract dollars going to U.S.-controlled companies. Spokesperson Jean-François Létourneau said that the government “continues to take action to increase domestic participation, strengthen Canadian supply chains, and support Canadian workers, businesses, and communities.” He said that since December, 34 contracts worth $1.5 billion have been awarded under the Buy Canadian Policy.

The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment.

The share of federal contract dollars heading south went from one-fifth in the 16 months before Carney took office to nearly a third under his watch.

Canada’s secretary of state for defence procurement defended a decision on Wednesday to narrow the contest for at least 1,600 new light utility

Don Davies, the Vancouver Kingsway MP and New Democratic Party finance critic, said that this level of contracting with U.S.-controlled firms is “completely unacceptable” and “wrong in the current situation.”

“But it’s consistent with the Carney approach to (U.S. President Donald Trump) from the beginning of his election, which is to talk tough and act weakly,” Davies said. “If we can’t find Canadian companies” for procurement contracts, “then I think we should be looking for non-U. S. sources,” he added.

Shuvaloy Majumdar, the Calgary Heritage MP and Conservative Shadow Minister for Canada-U. S. Relations, said that the federal government should favour Canadian companies in procurement and be more transparent about contractors’ origins.

“If Mark Carney wants the world to choose Canada, maybe his own Liberal government should start by choosing Canadian,” Majumdar said, in reference to the Prime Minister’s push to attract investment.

“Canadians should be able to clearly see whether their tax dollars are supporting Canadian businesses and workers who are being hit hardest by unjustified U.S. tariffs, or if they are being funneled out to American companies,” he said.

The four highest-grossing federal contractors under Carney are all American-controlled. Tech giants IBM and Microsoft charged Ottawa more than $1 billion each for software license fees and IT services, among other things. Defence contractor L3Harris earned more than $1.2 billion, the majority of it for aircraft parts and engineering services, while General Dynamics got $846 million, mostly for ammunition and engineering consultants.

Canadian company Bombardier closes the top five with $710 million in contracts, mainly for aircraft parts.

The Department of National Defence, which is responsible for some of the largest contracts with U.S.-controlled companies, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did Minister of National Defence David McGuinty, nor Joël Lightbound, the minister responsible for procurement.

David Macdonald, a senior economist at the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, a progressive think tank, said the biggest risk of relying on American tech lies in “Canadians’ data sovereignty.”

“Those American corporations are beholden to a U.S. government that has become increasingly erratic,” Macdonald said. “They seem perfectly willing to intrude upon their own citizens and likely our citizens’ data for their own ends, whatever those might be.”

Other countries have been moving away from U.S. tech. In June, the European Commission proposed a series of measures to “strengthen Europe’s capacity in semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud and open source.”

At Shared Services Canada, the department responsible for federal IT infrastructure, spokesperson Nick Wells said that the government “ensures data is protected and governed under Canadian laws and meets stringent government requirements for security, privacy and accountability.” This includes maintaining classified data in Canadian facilities or within consular and diplomatic premises abroad, he said.

Macdonald said the Star’s analysis shows that the Buy Canadian Policy — which does not consider suppliers’ country of control in establishing whether they’re Canadian — is not enough. “It would take a concerted effort, particularly on the technology side, to move away from American dominance.”

paragraphs: Since assuming office a year and a half ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney has repeatedly promised that his government would “build Canadian and buy Canadian .”

But American-controlled multinational corporations have dominated the most lucrative federal contracts under Carney’s leadership, a Toronto Star analysis of government data shows. The share of government contract dollars going to U.S. companies also increased.

Since Carney was sworn in as Prime Minister in March 2025 and up to the end of July 2026 — the latest available data — Ottawa awarded $25 billion in contracts to buy everything from cloud services to military vehicles and office furniture.
The vast majority of it, $22.4 billion, went to Canadian companies, according to federal contract data. United States businesses come at a distant second place, with nearly $1.2 billion.

But that’s not the full picture; procurement data does not distinguish between a homegrown shop and the locally-incorporated subsidiary of an American corporation. This is how well-known U.S. brands such as defence contractor Lockheed Martin , which has received about $86 million in contracts under Carney, or tech giant Amazon, which has received about $49 million, sometimes show up in procurement data as Canadian companies.

The Star cross-referenced procurement data with another federal data set, the Inter-corporate Ownership (ICO) review’s index , which includes information on more than 50,000 companies and their “country of control” — where the people controlling the firm live. That metric is used to measure “the extent and impact of foreign control within the Canadian economy,” according to the ICO review, which reports on its findings to Parliament.

The Star also reviewed reports filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, company websites and other public records to confirm American ties among some of Ottawa’s largest contractors. Where there was no ICO match for smaller contractors, the Star used procurement data to establish an organization’s country.

The results show that while Carney has promised to uphold Canadian sovereignty and make the country’s economy less dependent on the U.S., his government has been reliant on its businesses. They also illustrate the limits of Ottawa’s Buy Canadian Policy, which went into effect in December to give “priority to Canadian businesses and Canadian-made content for large federal purchases.”

In its first 16 months in power, the Carney government gave an estimated $7.8 billion in federal contracts to American-controlled corporations. Contracts with Canadian companies over the same period amounted to $14.9 billion.

Public Services and Procurement Canada did not answer the Star’s questions on the proportion of contract dollars going to U.S.-controlled companies. Spokesperson Jean-François Létourneau said that the government “continues to take action to increase domestic participation, strengthen Canadian supply chains, and support Canadian workers, businesses, and communities.” He said that since December, 34 contracts worth $1.5 billion have been awarded under the Buy Canadian Policy.
The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment.
The share of federal contract dollars heading south went from one-fifth in the 16 months before Carney took office to nearly a third under his watch.

Don Davies, the Vancouver Kingsway MP and New Democratic Party finance critic, said that this level of contracting with U.S.-controlled firms is “completely unacceptable” and “wrong in the current situation.”

“But it’s consistent with the Carney approach to (U.S. President Donald Trump) from the beginning of his election, which is to talk tough and act weakly,” Davies said. “If we can’t find Canadian companies” for procurement contracts, “then I think we should be looking for non-U. S. sources,” he added.

Shuvaloy Majumdar, the Calgary Heritage MP and Conservative Shadow Minister for Canada-U. S. Relations, said that the federal government should favour Canadian companies in procurement and be more transparent about contractors’ origins.
“If Mark Carney wants the world to choose Canada, maybe his own Liberal government should start by choosing Canadian,” Majumdar said, in reference to the Prime Minister’s push to attract investment.

“Canadians should be able to clearly see whether their tax dollars are supporting Canadian businesses and workers who are being hit hardest by unjustified U.S. tariffs, or if they are being funneled out to American companies,” he said.

The four highest-grossing federal contractors under Carney are all American-controlled. Tech giants IBM and Microsoft charged Ottawa more than $1 billion each for software license fees and IT services, among other things. Defence contractor L3Harris earned more than $1.2 billion, the majority of it for aircraft parts and engineering services, while General Dynamics got $846 million, mostly for ammunition and engineering consultants.
Canadian company Bombardier closes the top five with $710 million in contracts, mainly for aircraft parts.

The Department of National Defence, which is responsible for some of the largest contracts with U.S.-controlled companies, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Neither did Minister of National Defence David McGuinty, nor Joël Lightbound, the minister responsible for procurement.

“Those American corporations are beholden to a U.S. government that has become increasingly erratic,” Macdonald said. “They seem perfectly willing to intrude upon their own citizens and likely our citizens’ data for their own ends, whatever those might be.”

At Shared Services Canada, the department responsible for federal IT infrastructure, spokesperson Nick Wells said that the government “ensures data is protected and governed under Canadian laws and meets stringent government requirements for security, privacy and accountability.” This includes maintaining classified data in Canadian facilities or within consular and diplomatic premises abroad, he said.

Macdonald said the Star’s analysis shows that the Buy Canadian Policy — which does not consider suppliers’ country of control in establishing whether they’re Canadian — is not enough. “It would take a concerted effort, particularly on the technology side, to move away from American dominance.”

“I mean, there isn’t a Canadian Microsoft Word, right? It just doesn’t exist now,” he said. However, “you might want to mandate the federal government move toward open source alternatives, which certainly do exist.”
