By The Canadian Press

Hometown: Lévis, Que.

Before politics: A pharmacist by training, Milliard worked as an executive at pharmacy chain Uniprix and at public relations firm National before becoming president and CEO in 2020 of the Fédération des chambres de commerce du Québec, an organization advocating for economic growth and supporting businesses.

Education: He obtained a bachelor’s degree in pharmacy from Université Laval in 2002 and a master’s from HEC Montréal in 2007.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Family: Milliard is openly gay and has a partner.

Political record: Milliard joined the party in 2010 and announced a bid for the Quebec Liberal leadership in 2024, saying he was committing himself to Quebec politics for the next decade. He finished a close second to Pablo Rodriguez in the 2025 vote, taking 47.7 per cent of the points on the second ballot compared with Rodriguez’s 52.3 per cent.

After Rodriguez resigned in December 2025, Milliard entered the race to replace him and was crowned the party’s 17th leader on Feb. 13, 2026, after no other candidate qualified. He has described himself as a nationalist, regionalist and federalist and has made the economy, public services, regions, culture and housing his main priorities.

Milliard was approached by the federal Liberals to run in a 2024 byelection in the Montreal riding of LaSalle—Émard—Verdun but declined to focus on provincial politics.

Riding: Orford, in Quebec’s Eastern Townships.

Quote: “Learning to live with people who aren’t exactly like you — to me, that’s exhilarating; it’s positive. Uniting two peoples, two nations — I find that beautiful. Some people find it complicated; I find it beautiful,” Milliard told The Canadian Press in an interview about his views on federalism on Oct. 1, days before the Oct. 5 election.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Charles Milliard: The pharmacist who caught the political bug
stories.summary: Montreal - On Monday, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard will try to join the ranks of the provincial legislature as the province's premier and turn the tide for the Liberal party, which has been plagued by poor showings and scandals for years.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - On Monday, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard will try to join the ranks of the provincial legislature as the province’s premier and turn the tide for the Liberal party, which has been plagued by poor showings and scandals for years.

Milliard became the party’s leader in February 2026 acclamation, following an earlier attempt he lost. Along with Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, Milliard is one of the two major party leaders campaigning from outside the walls of the national assembly, having never held elected office.

“I want to be premier of Quebec … to create wealth in Quebec, to redistribute it, to finance our social model, to support our regions and to nurture our culture,” Milliard said when he announced his second leadership bid. “I also want to reunite Quebecers. I want everyone to feel at home here, and to put an end to the divisions that slow us down and that frankly bother me.”

In debates, Milliard has presented himself as the only federalist among Quebec’s major party leaders. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon of the Parti Québecois and Ruba Ghazal of Québec solidaire run sovereigntist campaigns. The Coalition Avenir Québec’s Christine Fréchette and Duhaime have described themselves as “autonomist” and have closed the doors to a third independence referendum.

Milliard told The Canadian Press on Thursday that he wasn’t a die-hard federalist and that he also identified as a nationalist.

“For some people, the maple leaf is the most sacred thing on earth. For others, Canada is a good ‘deal’ or a convenient political arrangement. I lean much more towards the ‘Quebec-first’ end of the spectrum. But I’m convinced that Canada is something exceptional to which we have to contribute,” he said.

In his run for the Liberal leadership, he promised to renew the party, which had fallen out of favour with large swaths of the francophone majority.

Although Milliard caught the political bug at a very young age, he waited until his 40s before running for office.

Born in 1979 in Lévis, ON the south shore of Quebec City, he began his career as a pharmacist. He quickly rose through the ranks at the pharmacy Uniprix, notably by writing health columns in Quebec media. In 2013, at age 33, he was named executive vice president of the pharmacy chain.

After a stint at the public relations firm National, he was appointed CEO of the federation of Quebec chambers of commerce in 2020. There, he voiced the concerns of the business community to the Coalition Avenir Québec government.

His work at the federation allowed him to broaden his focus beyond healthcare to include the economy, entrepreneurship, education, transportation and the environment.

He finally entered partisan politics in 2024, announcing his intention to run for the leadership of the Liberal party.

During the race, he defied the odds by giving the front-runner a run for his money. Former federal minister Pablo Rodriguez narrowly won in the second round.

A few months later, the expulsion of House Leader Marwah Rizqy and the “brownies scandal,” during which Rodriguez was accused of paying for votes, shook Rodriguez’s leadership, leading to his resignation.

Milliard won the leadership role by acclamation in a second leadership race.

“We have gone through a difficult period, but today we look forward,” Milliard said a few days after becoming the party’s leader. “Under my leadership, integrity, transparency, and accountability will be the watchwords because the party I want to lead must be above reproach, and trust is earned, not requested.”

If the Liberals emerge victorious from the election campaign, Milliard would become the first openly gay leader of a Quebec government.

An art lover, Milliard has served on the board of directors of the Montreal Symphony Orchestra and the TransAmérique Festival.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

By The Canadian Press

Birthplace: Beirut, Lebanon

Early years: Ghazal was born to a Palestinian family in Lebanon. She immigrated to Quebec when she was 10 years old.

Before politics: Ghazal worked in environmental management for manufacturing companies including Bombardier and Church & Dwight. When she was elected for Québec solidaire, she was director of health, security and environment for American glass-manufacturing company O-I.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Education: Ghazal studied business administration at HEC Montréal for her bachelor’s degree, which she obtained in 2000. In 2003, she got a master’s degree in environment at the Université de Sherbrooke.

Family: Ruba Ghazal is in a relationship with actor Hubert Proulx.

Political record: Ghazal was a founding member of Québec solidaire in 2006. She was elected in the Montreal riding of Mercier in 2018.

She became co-spokesperson of the party on Nov. 16, 2024, when she was the only candidate in the race to replace Émilise Lessard-Therrien, who resigned months after replacing Manon Massé in the role.

Ghazal became the party’s parliamentary leader on March 21, 2025, after her co-spokesperson, Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois, resigned. She is going into the elections alongside Sol Zanetti, who replaced Nadeau-Dubois.

Riding: Mercier, in Montreal

Quote: “Our independence project should not depend on the Trumps of the world. This is the new normal, and we don’t know who will replace Trump.”

stories.summary: Former political commentator Éric Duhaime has led the Conservative Party of Quebec for five years. Duhaime has never held a political office, and the Conservatives did not win any seats at the last general elections, despite collecting close to 13 per cent of the popular vote.

Former political commentator Éric Duhaime has led the Conservative Party of Quebec for five years. Duhaime has never held a political office, and the Conservatives did not win any seats at the last general elections, despite collecting close to 13 per cent of the popular vote.

By The Canadian Press

Hometown: Montreal

Early years: Duhaime is an only child and grew up in the Montreal suburb of Laval. His mother was a bus driver and his father worked at a factory. Duhaime began to follow the news in primary school, reading the daily newspaper and watching nightly news broadcasts.

Before politics: Duhaime worked as a talk radio host, political commentator, newspaper columnist and author. He has also worked for the National Democratic Institute, a United States-based non-governmental organization that promotes democratic institutions.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 9Image 10Image 11

Education: Duhaime studied political science at Université de Montréal for his bachelor’s degree and got a master’s degree in public administration from École nationale d’administration publique.

Family: Duhaime is openly gay and has been in a relationship for many years.

Political record: In the 1990s, Duhaime was a parliamentary aide and researcher for the Bloc Québécois and an adviser to the party’s leader. From 2000 to 2002, he was an adviser to the federal Canadian Alliance leader, Stockwell Day.

In 2003, Duhaime ran for provincial office in a Montreal-area riding as a member of the right-of-centre Action démocratique du Québec, coming third. He then worked as an adviser to the party’s leader until 2008.

Duhaime became the leader of the Conservative Party of Quebec in 2021, winning nearly 96 per cent of the vote in the leadership race.

His party did not win any seats in the 2022 general election.

Duhaime had another shot at a seat at the Quebec national assembly in the 2025 Arthabaska riding byelection, but lost to the Parti Québécois candidate.

Riding: Bellechasse, south of Quebec City.

Quote: “This year is our year. 2026 is the year of the Conservatives.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Canada must weigh creation of new spy service with ‘eyes wide open,’ study warns
stories.summary: Ottawa — Espionage is a deadly serious and generally misunderstood business, and it's critical for Canadian politicians thinking about starting a foreign spy service to decide "with their eyes wide open," a new study says.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Espionage is a deadly serious and generally misunderstood business, and it’s critical for Canadian politicians thinking about starting a foreign spy service to decide “with their eyes wide open,” a new study says.

“Virtually no Canadian knows how espionage is actually done,” says the paper by former Canadian intelligence officials Alan Barnes and Geoff St. John.

“Romantic, facile notions predominate. Those bemused — or deceived — by the fictions of page and screen would benefit by learning how espionage is really done.”

The study is being published this month on the website of the Policy Insights Forum, the research wing of the lobbying firm Samuel Associates.

The federal government is preparing a long-awaited update of its national security strategy while the National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians examines Canada’s foreign intelligence gathering capabilities.

Barnes, who worked as an analyst and manager in the Canadian intelligence community for over 25 years, is a senior fellow at Carleton University’s Norman Paterson School of International Affairs. St. John, a retired member of the Canadian Forces Intelligence Branch, is director of the national security studies program at the Policy Insights Forum.

Drawing on their own experience and the literature, the authors attempted to go beyond familiar arguments about setting up an espionage agency to look at what such spy services actually do, along with the full range of factors politicians need to consider.

First and foremost, they write, policymakers must set aside the exploits of fictional spies like James Bond.

“Ninety-nine per cent of all espionage fiction is pure junk,” the paper says. “Only a few fictional works have any merit. Those of John le Carré are the best examples, but professionals have even found fault with some of his characterizations of espionage. Ian Fleming’s Agent 007 exploits are pure fantasy. Bond films are not documentaries.”

Espionage, the clandestine collection of information by people, involves hostile, undercover acts to learn things otherwise unknowable — actions that break the laws of the country where agents operate, the paper notes.

The authors take pains to distinguish the intelligence officers who work for espionage agencies from the agents they recruit abroad to ferret out secrets.

“Imagine you run an espionage agency tasked with finding out what senior generals say about invading a neighbouring country,” the paper suggests.

“In the Hollywood version, one of your intelligence officers would infiltrate the meeting and report what was said. This is rank nonsense. The obstacles are insurmountable.”

Even if an officer with the right background and language fluency could be assigned — and even if they could find a way into the meeting — they would be instantly recognized as a fraud, the authors write.

“No, much, much better to have one of the generals tell you what was said. Far better to suborn one of them, or perhaps the note taker, or an official who gets the meeting notes, to learn what transpired.”

Canada already has some eyes and ears on the world.

The Communications Security Establishment, Canada’s cyberspy agency, collects foreign intelligence through electronic means. Global Affairs Canada contributes diplomatic reporting, while the military gathers defence-specific intelligence.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service is permitted to gather intelligence in Canada and abroad about security threats such as terrorism and espionage. It is allowed to gather foreign intelligence — information about the activities, capabilities and intentions of foreign people, organizations and states — only within Canada, not overseas.

Since the end of the Second World War, Canada has regularly considered creating its own version of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency or Britain’s Secret Intelligence Service, better known as MI-6.

The fundamental question is what purpose a Canadian espionage agency would serve, the paper says.

Often the question takes a back seat to enthusiasm for simply having a spy agency, the authors lament.

“Instead, the discussion should start by identifying the fundamental requirement — ‘Canada has a vital need for information on X which can only be obtained through espionage’ — before proceeding to consideration of the practical issues of actually establishing a new agency for this purpose,” the paper says.

No espionage agency that Canada can afford could ever produce enough reports to replace the flood of raw information Canada receives from allies, the paper adds.

“A Canadian espionage agency might be able to generate several hundred reports a year. And then it could only report on selected, narrow areas of Canadian interest, not all our interests.”

The exposure of Canadian espionage operations would have diplomatic, political and economic repercussions, the authors warn.

The foreign affairs minister and Canadian diplomats would have to deal with the fallout and try to limit the effect on Canada’s interests, the paper says.

“In some cases the diplomatic response might be limited to the expulsion of diplomats. But the repercussions could be more severe if the foreign country targeted by Canada’s spies was otherwise considered a friend.”

And the agents — the foreigners spying for Canada — would face very real physical, legal and psychological risks, the authors point out.

“At best, if caught passing on secret material to a Canadian intelligence officer, he or she can expect a long prison sentence. At worst, the agent May be tortured and executed. It is a certainty that one or more agents spying for Canada will be found out eventually,” the paper says.

“Canadian espionage officers would face risks as well. Those operating under embassy cover will have some protections but could still face physical abuse before the diplomatic protocols are enforced.”

Espionage officers operating under some non-official cover, such as a business, would face greater dangers, the paper adds.

Foreign governments might also use the existence of a Canadian espionage agency as a pretext for arresting Canadian citizens and claiming they were spies, it says.

The authors say getting espionage right is very difficult.

“It can succeed only with lots of political grit, the right strategic targets, willingness and ability to act on intelligence, tough tactics and very carefully selected, extremely well-trained espionage officers,” they write.

“And even then, espionage May not uncover an enemy’s darkest secrets. There is simply no guarantee. But if it does work well, the value of its information May exceed considerably its costs and risks.”

The “opportunity cost” of a Canadian espionage agency needs to be carefully considered, Barnes told The Canadian Press.

“Investments in Canada’s neglected intelligence analysis capacity would likely have a bigger payoff in bolstering Canada’s ability to form an independent view of international developments than collecting more secret information at considerable risk and expense,” he said.

Ottawa should create a foreign espionage agency only if it intends it to be highly effective, St. John said.

“An ineffective agency would be an embarrassment to Canada and an expensive white elephant.”

stories.title: Parti Québécois heads a crowded election field into provincial election vote
stories.summary: Montreal — Quebec's campaign trail has been more crowded than ever in 2026, with five parties potentially in a position to have members elected to the legislature for the first time in 50 years.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — Quebec’s campaign trail has been more crowded than ever in 2026, with five parties potentially in a position to have members elected to the legislature for the first time in 50 years.

But it’s Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon who has appeared to pull away from the pack, at the tail end of a campaign that has been dominated by questions of economic uncertainty, cost of living and the looming prospect of a third sovereignty referendum.

While St-Pierre Plamondon has said he isn’t taking the result for granted, his talk has turned in recent days towards asking voters to help his party reach a majority, and looking beyond the Oct. 5 vote.

“In my mind, it is very clear that once the election is over, if people give you the mandate to be premier, you have a moral obligation to be the premier for absolutely everyone,” he said Friday in Quebec City.

A victory on Monday would represent a stunning comeback for a party that won only three seats in 2022, the lowest total ever since the party was founded in 1968.

André Lamoureux, a political science professor at the Université du Québec à Montreal, says the latest PQ momentum has come at the expense of the Coalition Avenir Québec, which has dropped in the polls in recent days.

He attributes the shift in part to a mistake by Leader Christine Fréchette, who suggested that Americans were trying to help sovereigntists take control of the province — a claim she was nearly immediately forced to walk back.

But while the Parti Québécois might be the biggest beneficiary of the CAQ drop, he stresses that there are still multiple players in the race.

“It still comes down to five parties, even though there have been significant changes over the last five or six days,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum in the next four years if his party forms government, despite polls showing most Quebecers don’t favour separation.

But Lamoureux says the PQ has become a “party of refuge” for nationalist and French-speaking Quebecers who want change from CAQ.

Lamoureux says another beneficiary of the waning support for the governing Coalition Avenir Québec could be Éric Duhaime’s Conservatives, who have focused their campaign around the Quebec City area.

Throughout the campaign, Duhaime has relentlessly hammered his rivals for being too bureaucratic and wasteful, while promising to address Quebecers’ cost of living through large tax cuts and slashing the cost of government.

The former right-wing radio host has been asking electors to give him the balance of power, which he has promised to use to block St-Pierre Plamondon’s planned sovereignty referendum.

On Friday, Duhaime and his candidate Maïté Blanchette-Vézina posed in front of a couple of buses branded with the “Yes” and “No” signs used in the 1995 referendum, symbolically slamming the garage door shut.

“We’re going to make sure that the ‘Yes’ bus and the ‘No’ bus remain nothing more than a fantasy of Charles Millard and Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, and that they certainly don’t become a nightmare for Quebecers over the next four years,” he said, attacking both the PQ and Liberal leaders.

Liberal Leader Milliard, meanwhile, has portrayed himself as the only federalist leader in the race, and the one who is best positioned to oversee an economic resurgence.

On Friday, Milliard suggested the Coalition Avenir Québec was “game over,” and suggested the vote was a race between his party and PQ. He suggested the CAQ had been an “empty chair” and that St-Pierre Plamondon “wants to take the chair away” from discussions with other provinces and Ottawa, as the PQ makes a bid for sovereignty.

However, Lamoureux says Milliard has struggled to increase his support among francophones, making it difficult to expand his base. Left-wing Québec solidaire, which has proposed ideas such as a wealth tax and public grocery stores, has also failed to make an impact outside their base in urban Montreal.

Fréchette entered the race as outgoing premier and what looked like an upswing in momentum. She has worked to present her team as the best-positioned to defend Quebec businesses amid an ongoing trade war, and has stated that U.S. President Donald Trump is her main adversary.

But Fréchette, who took over the party following François Legault’s resignation earlier this year, has also faced attacks from rivals who have accused her government of having wasted Quebecers’ money and failing to deliver on its promises during eight years in government.

Whoever wins will almost certainly preside over a very different legislature than the one that was elected four years ago, when the Coalition Avenir Québec captured 90 of 125 seats.

A minority scenario would force the winner to make partnerships and seek out cooperation, Lamoureux notes, meaning that any of the parties that are represented will still have their chance to make a mark.

stories.title: Quebec on the cusp of electing separatist government promising referendum
stories.summary: A victory for the PQ would give new life to a decades-old debate over sovereignty that took a back seat during the Caq’s eight years in power
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Quebec appears poised to elect a separatist government for the first time in more than a decade, even though most of the province has little interest in a promised vote on independence.

The Parti Québécois, polls show, will likely take the reins of power from the governing Coalition Avenir Québec on Monday after a lacklustre campaign in which voters expressed a desire for change but little enthusiasm for any of their options.

A victory for the PQ would give new life to a decades-old debate over sovereignty that took a back seat during the CAQ’s eight years in power. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum on independence within a first mandate, though not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

The separatist party could claim a majority of the 127 seats in the province’s National Assembly despite the fact that support for the PQ – and for sovereignty – has not climbed above 30 per cent during the campaign. The CAQ, meanwhile, is lagging in polling, with forecasters suggesting the party could find itself with few, if any seats.

After a six-week campaign in which none of the five viable parties managed to capture the imagination of voters, the Parti Québécois stands to win because the alternatives appeared to be even less inspiring.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s pitch – three years of good government followed by a referendum once Mr. Trump leaves office – has not rallied any new support.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, under new Leader Christine Fréchette, briefly benefited from a Trump bump when Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down and Prime Minister Mark Carney – enduringly popular in the province – unveiled a series of funding announcements alongside the Premier. She tried to make the campaign about the trade war and called the U.S. President her main adversary.

But Quebeckers quickly turned the page, seemingly persuaded by rival parties who argued that Ms. Fréchette was not at the table in tariff negotiations and could not influence their outcome. The perception that she was not consulted on Mr. Carney’s countertariffs, some of which hurt Quebec businesses, further undermined her standing on the issue.

An attempt in the late stages of the campaign to warn of the potential for U.S. interference in the election, based on a blog post from a right-wing think tank proposing American funding for sovereigntists in Canada, backfired.

The most full-throated federalist party, the Quebec Liberals, struggled to find their voice under new leader Charles Milliard until late in the campaign, when the CAQ’s collapse positioned them as the most plausible alternative to the separatist PQ. They will likely remain the Official Opposition, a role they have occupied since 2018.

The election revealed a province preoccupied by the cost of living, homelessness, crumbling infrastructure, immigration and emergency-room waiting times, but unsure of how to fix any of it. The existential questions of Mr. Trump’s aggression and independence from Canada largely failed to become defining issues.

The big questions of the future received little attention. The dangers and possibilities of artificial intelligence were barely discussed until Friday, when it emerged that Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime had used AI to write his latest book. The other parties mocked him, while Mr. Duhaime countered that it was “a tool like any other.”

Perhaps the most ambitious policy agendas were put forward by the two parties who were never in the running to form government – the left-wing Québec solidaire (QS), which proposed publicly owned grocery stores and raising taxes on the very rich, and the Conservatives, who campaigned on sweeping tax cuts and easier access to private health care.

Despite a well-liked co-leader in Ruba Ghazal, QS has remained marginal in the campaign and is working to hold on to its handful of seats. But Mr. Duhaime’s promises to rein in government spending have struck a chord with voters who feel the CAQ government has played fast and loose with their money. For the first time, his party will likely win several seats in the National Assembly and become a real political force.

Quebec appears to have little appetite for grand projects, preferring help with making ends meet. One of the campaign’s most popular ideas – proposed by the Conservatives and péquistes alike – was to abolish the provincial sales tax on used goods.

Cuts were also prominent on the menu – both to the immigration rate and the size of the state. A majority of the five parties proposed substantial cuts to the number of newcomers coming in and the size of the public-sector work force, differing only on how many thousands.

The well-known Montreal businessman Andrew Lutfy roughly captured the state of Quebec’s self-image on Friday when he declared that the province had become “uninvestable” because of excess red tape and needed 6-per-cent annual growth to fix its hospitals, schools and roads.

But with the province legally required to balance its budget by the end of the decade, the three main parties had little room to propose big ideas, said political analyst Raphaël Melançon. “Basically, what we are selling is the status quo,” he said. “We’re just going to keep governing the province as it is.”

“It’s been a pretty boring and beige campaign.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s pitch – three years of good government followed by a referendum once Mr. Trump leaves office – has not rallied any new support.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, under new Leader Christine Fréchette, briefly benefited from a Trump bump when Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down and Prime Minister Mark Carney – enduringly popular in the province – unveiled a series of funding announcements alongside the Premier. She tried to make the campaign about the trade war and called the U.S. President her main adversary.

But Quebeckers quickly turned the page, seemingly persuaded by rival parties who argued that Ms. Fréchette was not at the table in tariff negotiations and could not influence their outcome. The perception that she was not consulted on Mr. Carney’s countertariffs, some of which hurt Quebec businesses, further undermined her standing on the issue.

An attempt in the late stages of the campaign to warn of the potential for U.S. interference in the election, based on a blog post from a right-wing think tank proposing American funding for sovereigntists in Canada, backfired.

The most full-throated federalist party, the Quebec Liberals, struggled to find their voice under new leader Charles Milliard until late in the campaign, when the CAQ’s collapse positioned them as the most plausible alternative to the separatist PQ. They will likely remain the Official Opposition, a role they have occupied since 2018.

The election revealed a province preoccupied by the cost of living, homelessness, crumbling infrastructure, immigration and emergency-room waiting times, but unsure of how to fix any of it. The existential questions of Mr. Trump’s aggression and independence from Canada largely failed to become defining issues.

The big questions of the future received little attention. The dangers and possibilities of artificial intelligence were barely discussed until Friday, when it emerged that Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime had used AI to write his latest book. The other parties mocked him, while Mr. Duhaime countered that it was “a tool like any other.”

Perhaps the most ambitious policy agendas were put forward by the two parties who were never in the running to form government – the left-wing Québec solidaire (QS), which proposed publicly owned grocery stores and raising taxes on the very rich, and the Conservatives, who campaigned on sweeping tax cuts and easier access to private health care.

Despite a well-liked co-leader in Ruba Ghazal, QS has remained marginal in the campaign and is working to hold on to its handful of seats. But Mr. Duhaime’s promises to rein in government spending have struck a chord with voters who feel the CAQ government has played fast and loose with their money. For the first time, his party will likely win several seats in the National Assembly and become a real political force.

Quebec appears to have little appetite for grand projects, preferring help with making ends meet. One of the campaign’s most popular ideas – proposed by the Conservatives and péquistes alike – was to abolish the provincial sales tax on used goods.

Cuts were also prominent on the menu – both to the immigration rate and the size of the state. A majority of the five parties proposed substantial cuts to the number of newcomers coming in and the size of the public-sector work force, differing only on how many thousands.

The well-known Montreal businessman Andrew Lutfy roughly captured the state of Quebec’s self-image on Friday when he declared that the province had become “uninvestable” because of excess red tape and needed 6-per-cent annual growth to fix its hospitals, schools and roads.

But with the province legally required to balance its budget by the end of the decade, the three main parties had little room to propose big ideas, said political analyst Raphaël Melançon. “Basically, what we are selling is the status quo,” he said. “We’re just going to keep governing the province as it is.”
“It’s been a pretty boring and beige campaign.”

stories.title: Military veterans twice as likely to develop ALS, researchers seek answers
stories.summary: Military Veterans are twice as likely to develop ALS, and researchers have been trying to figure out why.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Guelph, Ont. - Military Veterans are twice as likely to develop ALS, and researchers have been trying to figure out why.

“It’s a great mystery that we’re trying to unravel, is it something about enlisting with the military or is it something about exposures experienced during the military,” questions Harvard University researcher Marc Weisskopf.

Retired Royal Canadian Air Force pilot, Bob Gibson wants answers too.

Gibson spent 12 years serving his country, flying into “sketchy” areas.

“The Gaza Strip, Cyprus, Damascus, Addis Ababa flying the Hercules for sometimes up to 18 hours a day,” Gibson said.

For six years, Gibson shared his troubling symptoms to a rolodex of different doctors across Canada.

Then in 2023, he finally received a difficult diagnosis.

“We got the bad news, I had ALS,” Gibson said.

There is no cure for the progressive neurodegenerative disease that attacks the nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has affected Gibson’s mobility, but it hasn’t slowed down his quest to understand why military veterans such as himself are at a higher risk of developing the disease.

Speaking to CTV News from his home in Guelph, Gibson said he suspects his exposure to different chemicals while serving with the military May be a driving factor.

“We’d be in the Gaza Strip, and they’d have a pit fire where they’d be burning off excess fuels,” the retired pilot recalled.

A recent study published in the Journal Neurology, conducted in part by Weisskopf, found that the risk of developing ALS varies within military divisions.

The journal’s summary stated that “those serving in the Air Force, Navy, or Coast Guard May incur exposure to military environments that increase risk of ALS. It is imperative to identify relevant exposures to reduce harm to service members and, potentially, civilians with similar exposures.”

In the United States, the Department of Defense has committed millions to ALS research , .

Now, the ALS Society of Canada is calling on the federal government in Ottawa to do the same.

“Every Canadian needs to be concerned about ALS because they too are at risk of this disease, and we need answers for our veterans,” said Tammy Moore, CEO, of the ALS Society of Canada.

Gibson and the ALS Society of Canada are calling on Ottawa to come to the table with $50 million dollars to help fund critical research that is already underway.

“When you see how much we’re spending on our military today in Canada, $50 million is a drop in the bucket,” Gibson said.

CTV News asked Veterans Affairs Canada if the federal government was open to helping fund the research, but the department did not clearly answer our question.

In an email, a spokesperson for Veterans Affairs Canada wrote, “the department expedites requests for benefits, services and supports related to ALS, recognizing the significant and rapidly changing needs that can accompany this diagnosis.

This includes financial support, health care, home care, caregiver support, long-term care and other services a veteran May need, such as additional care in the home, assistance for caregivers, respite and palliative care.”

For Gibson, the funding he and others are requesting isn’t just to help researchers understand the cause of his disease, it’s also to help future generations. Gibson’s son, Kyle, is also a Canadian Armed Forces veteran, and he worries about others being diagnosed in the years ahead.

“The reality is, our military is growing, and if we don’t solve this mystery, more and more veterans are going to be diagnosed with ALS,” Kyle Gibson added.

The elder Gibson has already made a trip to Parliament Hill to petition the federal government to fund the important research. He plans to make another trip to speak with lawmakers this October.

Researchers believe if they can find out why members of the military are developing ALS, it will lead to a greater understanding of the disease for everyone.

stories.title: ‘We will build this pipeline for the people of Canada’: Hodgson promises Pacific Link will get built
stories.summary: Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson is promising the new Pacific Link oil pipeline to the West Coast will get built, regardless of potential future market shifts and geopolitical changes
stories.author: Spencer Van Dyk
stories.content:
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson is promising the new Pacific Link oil pipeline to the West Coast will get built, regardless of potential future market shifts and geopolitical changes.

On Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the Pacific Link pipeline will be the first officially designated national interest project under the Building Canada Act.

The designation is meant to speed up the process of building the pipeline, with both the premier and prime minister setting a September 2027 timeline for construction to get underway.

Carney on Thursday also insisted: “The Canadian taxpayer is going to make a lot of money off this pipeline.”

In the meantime, taxpayers are footing much of the bill for the pipeline, despite promises it needed a private backer. According to a government official in a technical briefing ahead of the announcement on Thursday, the early process is estimated to cost $4 billion between the two levels of government.

The Pembina Pipeline Corp. has expressed interest in a 10 per cent private sector stake and has the option of up to another 10 per cent once the pipeline is in operation.

In an interview on CTV Question Period airing Sunday, host Vassy Kapelos asked Hodgson why Canadians should trust that the pipeline will get built when the prime minister said less than a year ago it would not go forward without a private proponent.

“We’re in the middle of the worst energy crisis in the history of the modern world, as defined by the International Energy Agency (IEA),” Hodgson said, adding he thinks “Canadians understand a lot has changed in the last year.”

“That was all really brought on by a war that had not started a year ago,” Hodgson also said. “We are in a very different world today. The Trans Mountain Expansion Project (TMX) has proven to be a very good investment for Canadians, and I believe this project will be as well.”

Hodgson then pointed to the number of foreign markets that have expressed an interest in Canadian oil.

When pressed by Kapelos on the federal government’s commitment to the Pacific Link pipeline — considering geopolitical contexts are constantly changing and many European markets remain committed to transitioning away from conventional energy — Hodgson said his impression from the president of the IEA is that “demand for oil to continue well into the future.”

Pressed again on much of Europe’s commitment to reaching net zero and how that could affect the demand for Canadian oil down the line, Hodgson said: “I think the market will speak.”

“The proponents here will have an open season, likely next spring, and in that open season, shippers will be asked to commit to long-term contracts to take oil over that pipeline,” he added.

If shippers do not commit to the pipeline, Hodgson said: “We’ll deal with that at the time.”

“But if I were a betting person today, looking at what we’ve just seen happen on the TMX, where shippers increased their contracted portion of the pipeline, and where I hear from everyone (that) they would like more, if I were a betting person, I think that’s a pretty good bet for the Canadian taxpayer,” Hodgson said.

Hodgson reiterated the prime minister’s election promise to turn Canada into an energy superpower, saying the federal government is “highly confident” that’s the best path forward for the country.

“The good news is there are shovels in the ground,” Hodgson said, pointing to two other projects that are currently underway, such as the 89-kilometre Taylor to Gordondale pipeline to move diluent from British Columbia to Alberta, and the $4-billion Sunrise pipeline expansion.

“We are building pipelines, and we will build this pipeline for the people of Canada,” Hodgson insisted.

You can watch Energy and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson’s full interview on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

With files from CTV News’ Rachel Aiello

When pressed by Kapelos on the federal government’s commitment to the Pacific Link pipeline — considering geopolitical contexts are constantly changing and many European markets remain committed to transitioning away from conventional energy — Hodgson said his impression from the president of the IEA is that “demand for oil to continue well into the future.”
Pressed again on much of Europe’s commitment to reaching net zero and how that could affect the demand for Canadian oil down the line, Hodgson said: “I think the market will speak.”
“The proponents here will have an open season, likely next spring, and in that open season, shippers will be asked to commit to long-term contracts to take oil over that pipeline,” he added.
If shippers do not commit to the pipeline, Hodgson said: “We’ll deal with that at the time.”

“But if I were a betting person today, looking at what we’ve just seen happen on the TMX, where shippers increased their contracted portion of the pipeline, and where I hear from everyone (that) they would like more, if I were a betting person, I think that’s a pretty good bet for the Canadian taxpayer,” Hodgson said.
Hodgson reiterated the prime minister’s election promise to turn Canada into an energy superpower, saying the federal government is “highly confident” that’s the best path forward for the country.

“The good news is there are shovels in the ground,” Hodgson said, pointing to two other projects that are currently underway, such as the 89-kilometre Taylor to Gordondale pipeline to move diluent from British Columbia to Alberta, and the $4-billion Sunrise pipeline expansion.
“We are building pipelines, and we will build this pipeline for the people of Canada,” Hodgson insisted.

stories.title: When two cars are trying to move into the same lane on a highway, who has the right of way?
stories.summary: While the rules vary by province, they’re similar across Canada: Neither driver has a right of way and both have to make sure it’s safe before switching lanes
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
When changing lanes on a multilane road such as Highway 401, does any lane have right of way over other lanes? If there are three lanes and the car from the left lane and a car from the right lane are trying to move into the middle lane at the same time, which car has the right of way? Does the faster left lane have priority over the slower right lane? Or vice versa? – Jonathan, Toronto

When two cars are trying to get into the same lane, nobody gets dibs.

“Neither has an automatic right of way to that lane,” said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop. “Both drivers have an obligation to make sure their lane change can be completed safely before they move.”

There’s no general rule in Ontario giving a driver in a particular lane the right of way when changing lanes.

Ontario’s law states that “a vehicle shall not be driven from one lane to another lane … unless the driver first ascertains that it can be done safely.”

While the rules vary by province, they’re similar across Canada: you have to make sure it’s safe before switching lanes.

British Columbia’s law goes a step further. It states that you can’t change lanes unless “the movement can be made with safety and will in no way affect the travel of another vehicle.”

Also, you generally need to signal before making your move.

The lane truth?

So how do you make sure it’s safe – especially if you’re trying to get into a middle lane?

“Don’t just check the lane immediately beside you,” Angelo DiCicco, chief executive officer of the Ontario Safety League, a nonprofit that focuses on driver education, said in an email. “You also need to be aware of what is happening two lanes over because another driver may be trying to enter the same space at exactly the same time.”

That means checking your mirrors – and making sure they’re properly adjusted in the first place – and doing a shoulder check .

Aside from watching out for drivers farther back in the next lane who might be speeding, you’re looking for cars two lanes over that might be signalling a move into that lane – or already making it, DiCicco said.

“The objective isn’t simply to see where the other vehicles are,” he said. “It’s to anticipate where they may be going.”

And, if there’s a car driving parallel to you in that far lane, it might be a good idea to wait until they’re clear – just in case they decide to get into that centre lane and don’t see you moving or signalling.

“Two drivers can both make what appears to be a perfectly normal lane change and still end up competing for exactly the same piece of pavement,” DiCicco said.

Crossed signals?

When you signal to move over, it doesn’t mean the lane is yours, Shapiro said.

“A turn signal communicates your intention,” he said. “It doesn’t reserve the lane for you, and it doesn’t give you the right of way.”

And other drivers might not even be paying attention to your signal.

“Never assume another driver has seen your signal, seen your vehicle or understood what you intend to do,” DiCicco said.

So what if, despite all the precautions, two drivers both still try to get into the same lane at the same time?

“They both have an obligation to react and avoid the collision,” Shapiro said.

If one car gets there first, the other car has to abandon the move, he said.

“The other driver is now attempting to enter an occupied lane and must make sure that movement can be made safely,” Shapiro said.

Who would be at fault if you both move into that lane at the same time and cause a crash?

Most provinces have rules to determine who’s at fault in many common collision scenarios.

For instance, in Ontario, those rules say if you change lanes and hit a car that’s already there, you’re entirely at fault.

But if you’re both changing lanes when you hit each other, fault is generally split 50/50 – no matter who started moving first, Rob de Pruis, the national director of consumer and industry relations at the Insurance Bureau of Canada, said in an email.

If you were already fully in the lane when the other driver hit you, you would likely need video evidence – for instance, from a dash cam – or witnesses to prove it, de Pruis said.

The rules in other provinces are similar, he said.

Rules only go so far

Even if there were clear rules for right of way when switching lanes, they wouldn’t magically prevent a crash, DiCicco said.

Some drivers might not know them or they might just ignore them. And, even when there are clear rules for right of way in other situations on the road, you always have to make sure it’s safe before making a move.

“We naturally want a clean rule or formula that tells us who has the right of way,” he said. “But the bigger question is ‘Does that other driver see me, and what are they about to do?’”

stories.title: A rainy late summer and early fall is good news for Nova Scotia farmers
stories.summary: With haunting memories of a record-breaking dry growing season in 2025, farmer Josh Oulton is now enjoying Nova Scotia’s recent rainy trend.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Wolfville, N.S. - With haunting memories of a record-breaking dry growing season in 2025, farmer Josh Oulton is now enjoying Nova Scotia’s recent rainy trend.

“This year we had good rains in September, and no hurricanes,” said Oulton.

Last year’s drought wiped out many crops and almost put some farmers out of business.

“Look at blueberries in Nova Scotia as a good example,” said Dalhousie University professor and food researcher Sylvain Charlebois.

“The drought was so severe, it forced many blueberry buyers to go elsewhere beyond Nova Scotia and to other places. Sometimes when farmers lose customers, it is not just for one year, but several years and that is a big problem for farmers.”

This year, timely late summer and early autumn rainfall has allowed crop yields to rebound in Nova Scotia.

“For all crops it was great and we had good bean crops, good corn crops, and our fields are still full of great vegetables,” said Oulton. “We had forgotten how much an apple will size up in the month of September if it has adequate rain like we received.”

CTV Atlantic chief meteorologist Kalin Mitchell said Prince Edward Island and the central and eastern parts of Nova Scotia , received the most rainfall in late summer.

There was major and destructive flooding, especially in Cape Breton, but in other areas the rain had a restorative impact on the soil and many farming fields during growing season.

“Most of the Maritimes saw near-to-well-above average amounts of rain for September, this year,” said Mitchell.

But it is not all good news for farmers. As they continue to recover from the drought of 2025, they are also dealing with the high cost of diesel fuel.

In fact, escalating overhead prices have driven up the overall cost of farming production.

“It all has made our margins that much smaller,” said Oulton.

Fuel, labour, packaging, and electricity costs are being passed onto consumers and not just in Nova Scotia.

“The price of wheat is up 42.8 per cent, soybean oil is up 31.6 per cent, rice is up 25.6 per cent, and the price of corn has climbed 20.8 per cent,” said Charlebois.

“Diesel costs, which are double of what they were last year, are impacting the bottom line hard right now and it is impacting farmers and their margins, which will also impact consumers.”

Oulton said the prices of the food he grows and sells have also increased, but he is hopeful that a healthy growing season this year with a bumper crop could be the first step towards seeing prices return to lower levels in time for 2027.

stories.title: New remote testimony room aims to make court less traumatic for London-area children
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: October 4, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 5 hours ago
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A new remote testimony suite at the London Family Court Clinic is giving children and youth involved in the justice system another option when they have to testify. The clinic says providing a safer, more comfortable environment can reduce stress and help young people give a fuller account of what happened.
· Posted: Oct 04, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago
For children involved in the justice system, testifying in court can be intimidating.
The London Family Court Clinic has developed a new remote testimony suite that lets young people give evidence from a safe, trauma-informed environment without having to enter a courtroom.

The suite uses Cctv technology to connect children with court proceedings. Joelene Bamford, the clinic's executive director, said the goal is to reduce some of the anxiety associated with the justice system.
"They don't have to go to the courthouse, they don't have to go into courtrooms," Bamford said. "They're able to provide that testimony from a safe place that's trauma-informed."
Bamford said research shows children can provide better evidence when they feel safer and less stressed.
"The literature certainly shows that when children feel safer, they're better able to speak in their own words," she said. "They're better able to provide a full and candid account of the evidence."

Research reviewed by the Department of Justice Canada has found that testimonial aids such as closed-circuit television can reduce stress for child witnesses, while studies have found children's accuracy is either improved or not significantly different compared with in-person testimony.
The clinic is also home to Beacon House, its Child and Youth Advocacy Centre, where young people can meet with police in a child-friendly environment.
Bamford said having a space away from a police station or courthouse can reduce stress and retraumatization.
"That safety reduces the amount of stress, reduces the amount of retraumatization," she said.
The clinic also has a specially trained facility dog, NSD Virgil, who can accompany children during court preparation, attend court with them and be present when they meet with police.
"He's definitely the star of the show," Bamford said.

The clinic also supports young people who are navigating the youth justice system themselves, including through counselling and assessments. Bamford said the court system can be overwhelming regardless of a young person's role.
"The court system can be extremely intimidating whether you're a victim, whether you're a witness, or whether you're an accused person," she said.
The London Family Court Clinic is a non-profit that has been serving children, youth and families involved in the justice system for more than 50 years.
The clinic is holding its second annual fundraiser, Stronger Together: Lfcc at the Met, ON Wednesday, Nov. 25, at Metropolitan United Church, from 7 to 9 p.m.
Organizers say proceeds will directly support the clinic's clinical services for children and youth.
With files from Kate Dubinski.

stories.title: Slugs gone, bugs gone, strawberries thriving as invasive lizards boom in B.C.
stories.summary: Tracy Menzies had been at war with slugs in her backyard garden as they've always managed to beat her to the harvest, but not this year.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Tracy Menzies had been at war with slugs in her backyard garden as they’ve always managed to beat her to the harvest, but not this year.

The strawberries in her garden this season turned out to be “absolutely beautiful.”

It turns out the slugs are facing a formidable foe — the invasive European wall lizard, which experts say are spreading fast and eating everything in their path, from insects and spiders to slugs.

Menzies, who lives near the Gorge Waterway in Saanich, said she started noticing the lizards in her yard in growing numbers a few months ago, darting through her garden and scurrying under foot.

“I don’t have a slug in my yard, so I can only assume, given the start of me seeing the wall lizards, that they’re feasting on the slugs,” said Menzies.

Most of them are just a few inches long, and many are even smaller, she said.

“However, I have seen them in North Saanich to be at least eight- to 10-inches, and I’ve seen them in crawl spaces,” said Menzies, who is a real estate agent.

Gavin Hanke, curator of vertebrate zoology at the Royal BC Museum, said it’s estimated that there are about 800,000 to a million European wall lizards in B.C., mostly on Vancouver Island, and they have spread as far as Campbell River, 260 kilometres north of Victoria.

He worries their rapid spread could have a “serious impact” on the environment.

“They’re spreading fast and furious, and we’re stuck with them,” said Hanke. “We will have to learn how to live with them.”

“The unfortunate thing is these lizards are impacting invertebrate populations. They do kill baby garter snakes. Every lizard eating something every day is really impacting the insects and spiders on Vancouver Island,” he added.

Biologist Nicholas Wong, science and operations manager with the Invasive Species Council of BC, said there aren’t any official management programs to oversee the population growth.

Wong said the lizards are “competing with some of our native lizards for food and space as well.”

Hanke, who lives in Victoria, said the lizards reached his garden around 2019, when he saw a few that year, but they have surged to about 100 lizards thriving in his front and back yards.

Male lizards have black and green marks on their bodies with a whip-like tail, while the smaller females are brassy with a wash of green over them.

Hanke said the population explosion in B.C. originated from an intentional release of 12 lizards in 1970 after a roadside zoo, Rudy’s Pet Park, in Central Saanich closed following the death of its owner. Southern Vancouver Island’s cooler winters mixed with its hot, dry summers make these lizards from Italy feel at home.

The Invasive Species Council of BC said they typically spread at a rate of about 100 metres every year, although they can spread much further by hitchhiking on vehicles or on firewood and building materials to help expand their footprint.

“I do know someone who cut open a bale of hay to use for mulch in their garden, and five lizards came out of that,” said Hanke.

The lizards are omnivores, feeding on a variety of insects, spiders and other invertebrates.

Slugs, ants, termites, earwigs, mason bees, honey bees and bumble bees are also part of their diet, along with fruit.

“If a fig falls to the ground and it’s ripe, they will eat that,” said Hanke.

Although the wall lizards helped to safeguard her strawberries this year, Menzies said she’s has concerns about their spread.

“I don’t want to exterminate them. But I also don’t want them in my house,” she said.

“Now, I haven’t seen one in my house yet, but the first time I do see one in my house, I’m probably going to feel differently about killing them.”

Hanke said the best way to get rid of the lizards is to have a “really boring” garden.

“A very plain, closely cut lawn, that’s the kind of habitat they don’t want,” said Hanke.

Wong said the tricky thing is that if you try and remove them from your backyard and your neighbours don’t, they’ll just re-invade from your neighbours’ property.

“It needs to be quite a collective effort in the location,” said Wong.

Hanke said the reality is it’s too late to exterminate the lizards.

“If we were gonna wipe them out, we should have done it probably about 1972, 1973, because once they were outside of that initial release point, it’s impossible,” he said.

He said humans have done a lot of damage to our ecosystem, and ironically, these lizards thrive in manufactured environments.

“It’s no surprise that, as an invasive, they can just occupy any sort of habitat that’s available, as long as we’ve messed up the original habitat that was available,” he said.

“So, we’re to blame, and we’re also to blame for bringing them here.”

Hanke said people should not catch the lizards and bring them to new locations because there is a risk they could spread further south.

“I think it’s a matter of years before we see them in Washington State.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version said that the lizard’s spread at a rate of about 160 kilometres a year.

stories.title: Olympian Clara Hughes on menopause and psychedelic therapy: 'I had to go hard'
stories.summary: The six-time Olympic medallist pushed her body. But menopause broke through her defences, she writes in her memoir.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Clara Hughes spent two decades teaching her body to obey her — through pain, exhaustion and sheer force of will — on her way to becoming the only athlete in history to win multiple medals at both the Summer and Winter Olympics.

Then, in her late 40s, her body stopped listening.

Exhaustion. Insomnia. Sudden rages. Joint pain. Hot flashes. Trouble remembering names, trouble coping with the smallest stress. “I was losing my mind. I really felt like I was losing my grip on reality,” Hughes said in a video interview from her home north of Nanaimo on Vancouver Island. “What I was feeling inside was so intensely frightening and destabilizing, initially, I didn’t link it with menopause .”

It’s a transition every woman eventually faces. But after two doctors prescribed antidepressants to treat her symptoms — not the hormone therapy she needed — Hughes set off on a tumultuous path of alternative therapies with psychoactive compounds in search of relief.

Left to fend for herself, she turned to a medicine cabinet no doctor would prescribe: Mdma, ketamine, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT, 3-MMC, golden halo mushrooms and San Pedro cactus — none of them legal to buy or use in Canada. She had never even heard of some of them but, as she puts it: “I had to go hard — scary hard — in order to become gentler with myself.”

What started as a way to treat menopause took her to places she hadn’t expected. That journey is detailed in her new memoir, “Learning to Breathe,” out Oct. 13.

It’s a hair-raising ride through punishing hiking trips, knee surgery (she stayed awake for it), life-altering menopause, guided psychedelic experiences, and surfacing memories of abuse by her late father.

Learning to Breathe publishes Oct. 13.

“I’ve been very nervous about this book, very afraid of this book because it’s so exposing and I do feel very vulnerable in it,” she said.

But looking out her window at Douglas fir trees and the Salish Sea, Hughes is also quick to smile and laugh. She’s embracing who she is — not who she’s long thought she should be — for the first time in her life.

“I want to share those things. And I know there’s a risk — obviously the illegality of this. Everything I did was underground; it was not a clinical study. There are risks in how people come at you after sharing those things, and it’s worth the risk if this can touch one woman out there and help her come back to life.”

To be clear, Hughes is not suggesting readers should do what she did, quite the opposite: it’s a “path that I would not recommend for anyone.”

But the power of a good storyteller is to inspire others to think more deeply about their own lives.

“For me, connection has always been the goal, and I feel many people May relate to the new me: people who’ve been broken down and found ways to build themselves back up,” she writes in the book. “People who need to know they’re not alone. More than anything, I hope my story can help people connect back to themselves.”

The six-time Olympic medallist in cycling and speed skating turned 54 last week. She was 23 at her first Olympics in Atlanta in 1996, and weeks shy of her 40th birthday at her last, the 2012 London Games.

She moved on to public speaking and broadcasting, and was the founding spokesperson for the Bell Let’s Talk campaign , designed to break down stigma around mental health. In 2015, she published her first memoir, Open Heart, Open Mind , detailing her challenging childhood in Winnipeg , rise through sport and struggles with depression.

In 2017, she shelved much of her career and spent the next three years backpacking thousands of kilometres a year, trying to “walk away” from physical and emotional feelings she didn’t understand. “‘I can’t do this anymore’ was actually perimenopause, which I didn’t know about at the time,” she said.

“It’s a place that is confusing, is terrifying, is frustrating and is annoying, and so misunderstood and underserved,” she said about mid-life hormonal transitions.

That’s what prompted this second memoir.

“Feeling all these things and then trying to get help that wasn’t there, I had this deep sensation and realization that if I’m going through this in this way and this feels impossible — absolutely impossible — what are other women experiencing? It ended up going on some pretty extreme tangents that I didn’t expect at the time, but it was really about opening up the conversation and the experience of a woman in this season of life.”

Hughes did eventually get to see a women’s health specialist who prescribed menopause hormone therapy, which helped her and eliminated the hot flashes that had left her soaking and embarrassed in the middle of speaking engagements: “I can wear wool again! I can wear nice blazers when I do speeches.”

Just as an athlete only fully appreciates brutal training once standing on the podium, Hughes now appreciates the search for menopause relief that led her to psychoactive-assisted therapies. That exploration, she says, helped her dredge up memories and fears about her father, which she says she had locked in a vault, and, ultimately, let them go.

Now, she finds gratitude in what nearly broke her:

“I’m even beginning to feel grateful for menopause,” Hughes wrote. “Sure, it’s a physical and emotional s—-storm. But on the other side lies a meadow blooming with empathy. When our bodies slow down, we naturally turn inward. And we find a whole universe in there. Without menopause I wouldn’t have tried psychedelics, and without psychedelics I wouldn’t have spied the Vault. I guess I’m grateful that menopause f—-ed me up, because it also cracked me open.”

stories.title: After a devastating cancer diagnosis, a 21-year-old Ontario college student fought to save her fertility
stories.summary: A transplant was needed. But the patient learned it would risk her fertility and there was no time for egg retrieval.
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
Within weeks of getting diagnosed with cancer, Ishtar Samano was already tallying her losses.

She was just 21 when doctors told her she had advanced Hodgkin lymphoma, forcing her to drop out of her London, Ont., college. The gruelling treatment left her too exhausted to keep up with friends.

Soon she was unable to walk into the hospital without help. She lost her appetite, then her thick, waist-length hair.

After two failed attempts, doctors still believed they could treat the cancer, but it would take a risky stem cell transplant. That’s when Samano learned the treatment could threaten her fertility.

“It was very hard to hear,” Samano said. “It felt like cancer was throwing away my future.”

For young cancer patients, the diagnosis is just the first blow as they navigate a devastating disease. Beyond survival, experts say fertility is an urgent concern, yet too many patients still miss out on the chance to have a biological family.

Canadian guidelines recommend all cancer patients of reproductive age receive counselling on fertility preservation before treatment. But research suggests only about half report having that conversation, though many therapies can harm reproductive organs.

Ovarian tissue cryopreservation through Mount Sinai and SickKids has become an option for patients as young as 1.

As more hospitals introduce specialized cancer programs for younger adults, there are signs family planning is becoming part of treatment plans. But experts say greater awareness is needed, especially as researchers track a worrying global increase in early-onset cancers .

Dr. Jennia Michaeli, a reproductive endocrinology and fertility specialist at Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic in Toronto, said it’s critical that fertility preservation becomes a pillar of oncology care. She said survivors who weren’t offered fertility protection tell her they feel robbed and suffer lasting grief.

“It’s irreversible and it often changes the course of a person’s life.”

Samano first experienced unexplained fatigue in the spring of 2025. She was enrolled in the pre-health sciences program at Fanshawe College but soon struggled to keep up.

In May, after switching to a less-demanding program, Samano developed back pain so severe it disrupted her sleep and noticed swollen lymph nodes in her groin.

Samano went to her family doctor but said her symptoms were dismissed. When the pain persisted, she went to her local hospital’s emergency department. Diagnostic imaging and bloodwork suggested she had cancer.

“When I heard the doctor say, ‘This May be lymphoma,’ I immediately just felt numb,” Samano said.

A few weeks later, doctors confirmed Samano had advanced Hodgkin lymphoma and admitted her to Victoria Hospital, part of London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), for emergency treatment. Samano said she was told the chemotherapy could harm her ovaries, but agreed with her hematologist there was not enough time to pursue fertility preservation.

“When you’re facing a challenge like this, you just want to get better,” she said. “I didn’t want to delay my treatment.”

Over the next few months, doctors tried two different chemotherapy regimes, but both failed. Immunotherapy cleared the cancer but Samano also needed a stem cell transplant.

Samano recalled Dr. Uday Deotare, LHSC’s assistant director of the blood and marrow transplant program, explaining that the high-dose chemotherapy in preparation for the transplant had significant fertility risks. While the chemo would eradicate the cancerous stem cells in her bone marrow, it would also severely damage her ovaries. The chance of becoming permanently sterile following a bone marrow transplant is about 60 per cent, Deotare said.

Ishtar Samano and Dr. Uday Deotare at Victoria Hospital in London, Ont.

Samano said Deotare encouraged her to think of her future and connected her with the hospital’s adolescent and young adult cancer program. Because she was so ill, Samano didn’t have enough time to undergo standard egg retrieval, which can take weeks. Instead, she had ovarian tissue cryopreservation , a new option for Ontario patients.

In early 2026, three weeks before her stem cell transplant, Samano had one ovary removed. The tissue was transported to the Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic in Toronto to be processed and cryo-preserved.

Though she initially struggled to consider fertility options when her own life was at risk, Samano said her dream of becoming a mom overtook her fear.

“Even if I never end up having kids, I just wanted to know that I did something to try to preserve that chance. I didn’t want to have regrets if I didn’t do anything at all.”

Dr. Karen Glass, director of fertility preservation at CReATE Fertility Centre in Toronto, has been helping cancer patients for more than 20 years. She said in her clinic, one of Canada’s largest oncofertility clinics, about 60 per cent of patients choose preservation following a consultation.

“Even those who are unsure about having children choose to freeze gametes (sperm or eggs) because they do not want the choice permanently taken away from them,” she said.

Glass said streamlining referrals and connecting patients to fertility specialists as early as possible — even before a diagnosis is confirmed — will help ensure the most options for younger adults.

She said patients could “multi-task” fertility procedures alongside testing for cancer rather than waiting until chemotherapy is imminent, forcing them to give up on preservation.

Ontario, unlike some other provinces, funds one treatment cycle of egg freezing or sperm freezing per patient before any medical treatment that May cause infertility.

Experts say this funding is welcome but stress that patients still need to pay out-of-pocket for fertility drugs, storage fees and travel to clinics, often concentrated in the largest cities. They note these extra costs, which can be thousands, can price out patients.

In a statement, the Health Ministry pointed to the Ontario Fertility Treatment Tax Credit , which provides families a refundable tax credit worth 25 per cent of eligible fertility treatment expenses, up to a maximum of $5,000 a year. Eligible expenses include fertility drugs, egg and embryo freezing and storage, travel and diagnostic testing, the ministry said.

Currently, the government does not fund ovarian tissue cryopreservation. Michaeli, who leads Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic’s ovarian tissue cryopreservation and cancer survivorship programs, said the clinic pays “pro bono” for patients anywhere in the province to access their program. Though the clinic organizes safe transport for the tissue, patients must pay those costs.

Both Glass and Michaeli say their clinics have chosen to subsidize storage fees for cancer patients and note pharmaceutical companies offer cancer patients compassionate access to fertility drugs.

“We need to keep advocating for better awareness and access,” Michaeli said.

Dr. Jennia Michaeli, a physician with Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic, said cancer survivors who weren’t offered fertility protection tell her they feel robbed.

It’s been nine months since her stem cell transplant and Samano has regained most of her strength, though it could take almost a year for her immune system to fully recover.

Deotare said Samano is currently in remission but must be closely monitored because the risk of lymphoma returning is highest in the first two years post-transplant. He said her experience highlights why oncologists must never forget there is more to cancer care than cutting-edge treatments.

“I see the patient as a whole,” said Deotare, adding that all patients of child-bearing age have the right to fertility preservation.

Samano, who wants to be a nurse, said she’s sharing her story to encourage young adults to not let doctors dismiss initial cancer symptoms, and to raise awareness of fertility risks.

“I don’t want them to be overlooked, just because they’re young.”
paragraphs: Within weeks of getting diagnosed with cancer, Ishtar Samano was already tallying her losses.
She was just 21 when doctors told her she had advanced Hodgkin lymphoma, forcing her to drop out of her London, Ont., college. The gruelling treatment left her too exhausted to keep up with friends.
Soon she was unable to walk into the hospital without help. She lost her appetite, then her thick, waist-length hair.
After two failed attempts, doctors still believed they could treat the cancer, but it would take a risky stem cell transplant. That’s when Samano learned the treatment could threaten her fertility.
“It was very hard to hear,” Samano said. “It felt like cancer was throwing away my future.”

For young cancer patients, the diagnosis is just the first blow as they navigate a devastating disease. Beyond survival, experts say fertility is an urgent concern, yet too many patients still miss out on the chance to have a biological family.

Canadian guidelines recommend all cancer patients of reproductive age receive counselling on fertility preservation before treatment. But research suggests only about half report having that conversation, though many therapies can harm reproductive organs.
Ovarian tissue cryopreservation through Mount Sinai and SickKids has become an option for patients as young as 1.

As more hospitals introduce specialized cancer programs for younger adults, there are signs family planning is becoming part of treatment plans. But experts say greater awareness is needed, especially as researchers track a worrying global increase in early-onset cancers .

Dr. Jennia Michaeli, a reproductive endocrinology and fertility specialist at Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic in Toronto, said it’s critical that fertility preservation becomes a pillar of oncology care. She said survivors who weren’t offered fertility protection tell her they feel robbed and suffer lasting grief.
“It’s irreversible and it often changes the course of a person’s life.”
Samano first experienced unexplained fatigue in the spring of 2025. She was enrolled in the pre-health sciences program at Fanshawe College but soon struggled to keep up.
In May, after switching to a less-demanding program, Samano developed back pain so severe it disrupted her sleep and noticed swollen lymph nodes in her groin.

Samano went to her family doctor but said her symptoms were dismissed. When the pain persisted, she went to her local hospital’s emergency department. Diagnostic imaging and bloodwork suggested she had cancer.
“When I heard the doctor say, ‘This May be lymphoma,’ I immediately just felt numb,” Samano said.

A few weeks later, doctors confirmed Samano had advanced Hodgkin lymphoma and admitted her to Victoria Hospital, part of London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), for emergency treatment. Samano said she was told the chemotherapy could harm her ovaries, but agreed with her hematologist there was not enough time to pursue fertility preservation.
“When you’re facing a challenge like this, you just want to get better,” she said. “I didn’t want to delay my treatment.”
Over the next few months, doctors tried two different chemotherapy regimes, but both failed. Immunotherapy cleared the cancer but Samano also needed a stem cell transplant.

Samano recalled Dr. Uday Deotare, LHSC’s assistant director of the blood and marrow transplant program, explaining that the high-dose chemotherapy in preparation for the transplant had significant fertility risks. While the chemo would eradicate the cancerous stem cells in her bone marrow, it would also severely damage her ovaries. The chance of becoming permanently sterile following a bone marrow transplant is about 60 per cent, Deotare said.

In early 2026, three weeks before her stem cell transplant, Samano had one ovary removed. The tissue was transported to the Mount Sinai Fertility Clinic in Toronto to be processed and cryo-preserved.
Though she initially struggled to consider fertility options when her own life was at risk, Samano said her dream of becoming a mom overtook her fear.
“Even if I never end up having kids, I just wanted to know that I did something to try to preserve that chance. I didn’t want to have regrets if I didn’t do anything at all.”
