stories.title: U.S. Coast Guard searches for survivors of Hamilton air ambulance jet that disappeared off Nantucket coast
stories.summary: The plane went missing early Saturday carrying four staff and crew from the GTA and Hamilton areas, along with a patient and family escort.
stories.author: Raju Mudhar
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard is still searching for the six people who were on Latitude Air Ambulance jet that went missing early Saturday morning.

Authorities held a press conference on Sunday morning giving an update on the debris found in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Nantucket where the jet went missing and said their search and rescue efforts are continuing.

“At this point, we are still conducting a search for the missing personnel,” said Rear Admiral Matt Lake. “I want you to know that my thoughts, and those of every Coast Guard crew member, are with the families on that aircraft, are with people on that air craft. Their families, their friends, and their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time.”

A search pattern conducted by a U.S. Coast Guard airplane.

The press conference was held at Coast Guard Base Boston, where officials detailed the ongoing search efforts and refused to say when the search and rescue would end, or turn into a recovery effort.

The missing Gulfstream G100 jet C-Grjp, operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, was travelling from Bermuda to Boston carrying two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and a family escort. All four crew were Canadian, while the passengers were Bermudan. The coast guard said that next of kin had been notified of the search efforts.

The Coast Guard said they had covered 7,355 square kilometres over the 53 hour search period, and were looking for survivors.

Lake said the depth of the water where the debris field was found was approximately 80 to 90 feet.

Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance’s Gulfstream G100 jets. The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for jet C-Grjp, second from the bottom.

“We’re in the process of working with Massachusetts authorities to get some craft out there that are equipped with sonar to be able to do some detection on the seabed floor,” said Lake.

Officials said that the debris had been found has been secured for further investigation, but at this point, the jet’s black box recorder had not been recovered.

Lake would not give any further information about the crew or passengers.

On Saturday evening, the Coast Guard confirmed it found debris from the plane. The search involved several planes, helicopters and lifeboats. The U.S. National Guard also provided a plane and two helicopters.

“Coast Guard search crews located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft. Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night,” they said in a release.

The missing Gulfstream G100 jet is operated by Latitude Air Ambulance in Hamilton. It was was travelling from Bermuda to Boston carrying two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and a family escort when it disappeared off the coast of Nantucket early Saturday morning.

“We’re dealing with a lot here at home base and working closely with the families of the crews, so need some space and privacy right now,” said Clarence Togeretz, Latitude Air Ambulance’s operation manager, via email on Sunday morning.

Many of Latitude’s staff rushed to the office on Saturday, when they heard of the incident, working through the night, hoping for the best for as the search continued for their lost colleagues.

The flight had the call sign “Heartbeat 104,” which left Bermuda at 11:42 p.m. Friday, reported apparent problems at 12:46 a.m. Saturday as they approached Nantucket, telling air traffic control they were “coming in blind,” according to audio posted online.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind, is that what you said?” a New York-based air traffic controller asks, according to recordings from the website liveatc.net . “Are you declaring an emergency or no?”

The flight lost contact around 1:30 a.m., ON Saturday morning, about 20 minutes outside its destination, Boston Logan International Airport. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration also lost contact with the flight early Saturday morning.

After its departure from Bermuda, Flight Aware data shows the plane climbing for 10 minutes to 24,000 feet, at 11:51 p.m., and remaining at that altitude until 1:04 a.m. The jet then apparently descends over several minutes to 11,000 feet and continues there until it disappears.

During the search, Flight tracking showed US Coast Guard planes conducting search patterns and then repeatedly circling over certain areas in the ocean.

Officials said that the debris had been found has been secured for further investigation, but at this point, the jet’s black box recorder had not been recovered.
Lake would not give any further information about the crew or passengers.

On Saturday evening, the Coast Guard confirmed it found debris from the plane. The search involved several planes, helicopters and lifeboats. The U.S. National Guard also provided a plane and two helicopters.

“Coast Guard search crews located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft. Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night,” they said in a release.

The missing Gulfstream G100 jet is operated by Latitude Air Ambulance in Hamilton. It was was travelling from Bermuda to Boston carrying two pilots, two medical staff, a patient and a family escort when it disappeared off the coast of Nantucket early Saturday morning.

“We’re dealing with a lot here at home base and working closely with the families of the crews, so need some space and privacy right now,” said Clarence Togeretz, Latitude Air Ambulance’s operation manager, via email on Sunday morning.
Many of Latitude’s staff rushed to the office on Saturday, when they heard of the incident, working through the night, hoping for the best for as the search continued for their lost colleagues.

The flight had the call sign “Heartbeat 104,” which left Bermuda at 11:42 p.m. Friday, reported apparent problems at 12:46 a.m. Saturday as they approached Nantucket, telling air traffic control they were “coming in blind,” according to audio posted online.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind, is that what you said?” a New York-based air traffic controller asks, according to recordings from the website liveatc.net . “Are you declaring an emergency or no?”

The flight lost contact around 1:30 a.m., ON Saturday morning, about 20 minutes outside its destination, Boston Logan International Airport. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration also lost contact with the flight early Saturday morning.

After its departure from Bermuda, Flight Aware data shows the plane climbing for 10 minutes to 24,000 feet, at 11:51 p.m., and remaining at that altitude until 1:04 a.m. The jet then apparently descends over several minutes to 11,000 feet and continues there until it disappears.
During the search, Flight tracking showed US Coast Guard planes conducting search patterns and then repeatedly circling over certain areas in the ocean.

stories.title: Debris from missing Ontario-based air ambulance located: U.S. Coast Guard
stories.summary: Debris associated with an Ontario-based air ambulance that was carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been located hours after it went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.
stories.author: Bryann Aguilar, Joshua McGinnis
stories.content:
Debris associated with an Ontario-based air ambulance that was carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been located hours after it went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.

The U.S. Coast Guard said in a news release on Saturday night that crews discovered the debris field off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., where they had been conducting a search all day.

“Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night,” the release read, noting that 1,644 square miles have been searched over approximately 27 hours.

The U.S. Coast Guard added that next of kin have been notified.

The Coast Guard said the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration notified them around 2 a.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 with the tail number C-Grjp and owned by Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance.

#Breaking : @uscg is searching for a Gulfstream aircraft with 6 persons on board. @FAANews reported losing contact w/the aircraft early Saturday morning. #Uscg air & surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft. Updates will be provided here as info becomes available.… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Clarence Togeretz, the air ambulance company’s operations manager, told The Canadian Press on Saturday morning that the aircraft was transporting a patient and family member, who were Bermuda nationals.

He said the two pilots and two medical staff aboard were Canadians.

Togeretz also shared that his company had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. as it was approaching Boston. Togeretz said Latitude reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard when the aircraft failed to reach the tarmac.

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

Togeretz noted that this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

Pilot declared emergency: ATC audio

The aircraft bound for Boston Logan International Airport departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport at 12:41 a.m. The air ambulance arrived in Bermuda from Hamilton the previous night.

Air traffic control audio captured by LiveATC.net indicates that the flight declared an emergency before it went missing.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot, who cannot be heard in the audio.

The controller then asked the pilot if they were declaring an emergency.

“You’re coming in a little weak. I didn’t hear your response was if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the controller heard telling the pilot.

A short time later, the controller got a confirmation from the pilot that they were indeed declaring an emergency.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, data shows that one hour and 23 minutes into the flight, the aircraft dropped from an altitude of 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in two minutes and then levelled off before it vanished.

The search for the jet included crews in the air and on the water, the U.S. Coast Guard said, noting that it was using two planes, a search and rescue lifeboat, a helicopter, and a cutter.

The Coast Guard noted that crews

#Update Uscg assets responding include: - HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew from AirSta Cape Cod - HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City - MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod - 47-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point - FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154)… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Latitude Air Ambulance’s website says that it currently has four G100 jets in its fleet, each with a range of 5,000 km.

In a statement posted to X , Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge said that “Our thoughts are with our colleagues at Latitude Air Ambulance at this time.”

“All of us at Ornge are hopeful the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Ornge noted that the flight was not related to its operations.

Canadian government ‘closely monitoring the situation’

Canada’s Transportation Minister, Steven MacKinnon, said his department is aware of the situation and that they “are closing monitoring” in a post to X.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time.”

“We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue. I want to thank all first responders involved for their ongoing efforts.”

I am aware of reports of a Canadian-registered air ambulance aircraft that went missing while travelling from Bermuda to Boston. Four Canadians are among the six people on board. My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during… — Steven MacKinnon (@stevenmackinnon) October 3, 2026

Global Affairs Canada said it was aware of reports of Canadians on board the missing Latitude Air Ambulance.

“Consular officials stand ready to provide consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities. Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be disclosed,” Global Affairs said in a statement to CTV News.

Bermuda government releases statement

A spokesperson on behalf of the Bermuda government confirmed the air ambulance’s departure from Bermuda to Boston this morning in a post to X.

Officials said they’ve been in contact with the families of those on board as well as the U.S. Coast Guard conducting the search.

In a statement, Bermuda’s Premier David Burt said that “his thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time.”

“We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

The Government of Bermuda confirms that an air ambulance which departed Bermuda for Boston early this morning, carrying six people, has been reported missing after contact was lost with air traffic control. The United States Coast Guard is conducting search and rescue… pic.twitter.com/yYEwWXMdQQ — Bermuda Government (@BdaGovernment) October 3, 2026

With files from The Associated Press and The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. politicians talk groceries, seniors amid election campaign
stories.summary: Grand Forks - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby says his election promise to cap unfair increases on grocery staples is aimed at multiple major grocers in the province and was not deliberately targeting one company.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Grand Forks - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby says his election promise to cap unfair increases on grocery staples is aimed at multiple major grocers in the province and was not deliberately targeting one company.

Eby says the distribution of food in the province is highly centralized, which means British Columbians have seen an increase in the cost of groceries beyond the rate of inflation.

stories.title: Steven Galloway accuser apologizes ahead of defamation trial, regrets role in spreading unproven allegations
stories.summary: Chelsea Rooney says she communicated serious allegations she could not verify and regrets the harm caused to the former UBC professor’s reputation
stories.author: Terri Theodore
stories.content:
One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says she now understands her conduct toward him was “serious and harmful” as she apologized just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.

Chelsea Rooney’s statement said she communicated serious and unproven allegations against Galloway and that she was involved in collecting complaints in an attempt to build a case against him.

“I recognize that statements and communications about allegations of this nature can cause profound harm to a person’s reputation, work, personal life, and family, and did in fact do so to Mr. Galloway. I deeply regret my role in contributing to the harm Mr. Galloway has suffered in this regard,” her statement said.

Much of Rooney’s apology appeared in the National Post newspaper on Saturday and the entire statement is posted on the website gallowayapologies.com, along with eight other apologies from those who say they regret communications or actions that accused Galloway of sexual assault.

Rooney, who is a defendant in the B.C. Supreme Court case due to start Monday, said she recognizes the communications she circulated about Galloway caused others to believe they were true, and she’s aware he firmly denies that he sexually assaulted a student only know as A.B.

The apology is the latest occurrence in what began as an accusation against Galloway in November, 2015. He sued numerous people in 2018, alleging he was defamed with false sexual assault allegations by fellow professors, a former student and others who repeated the statements on social media and elsewhere.

The Supreme Court of Canada in 2024 dismissed an appeal by his accusers , clearing the way for the defamation trial.

Galloway is the author of novels including The Cellist of Sarajevo and The Confabulist and was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at UBC.

He was never charged, though he was fired from his job .

A report commission by the University of B.C. by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, could not be immediately reached for comment on Saturday, although he said in an interview after the High Court’s ruling that his client’s “reputation and life were devastated by the criminal allegations.”

Rooney is among the defendants who fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming the accusations of sexual assault must be protected speech, true or not, and “regardless of the circumstances in which the statement was published.”

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Elaine Adair said in her ruling on the case in 2021 that if the defendants arguments were true, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

“It is difficult to see how something so extreme and potentially reckless would be in the public interest,” her decision said.

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them or posted them publicly on social media.

She said she has reflected on Galloway’s steadfast efforts over the years and she has come to better understand the basis for his position and his commitment to clearing his name and reputation.

“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets, or my participation in the process.”

Rooney said Galloway considered her a friend before A.B. made the allegations, and on multiple occasions went out of his way to help her, with nothing asked in return, she said.

“In my 2014 book, I thanked him as someone ‘who encouraged me to commit to writing at a very important time in my life.’ That was a true statement,” her apology said.

“I know that nothing I say now can undo the harm or give back the years affected by these events, but I am genuinely sorry for the part I played in causing that harm.”

stories.title: France has not issued new snow crab licence, Ottawa says
stories.summary: Canada’s fisheries minister says France has not issued a new snow crab licence off Newfoundland, despite a surprising promise last month by French President Emmanuel Macron.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s — Canada’s fisheries minister says France has not issued a new snow crab licence off Newfoundland, despite a surprising promise last month by French President Emmanuel Macron.

Joanne Thompson said Friday evening that the Canadian government has been in contact with French officials to confirm they had not issued a new license, after news outlets including franceinfo and Radio-Canada reported Macron had pledged to grant an exploratory snow crab licence along Canada’s continental shelf to a fishing company in St-Pierre-Miquelon, a small French archipelago off the southeast coast of Newfoundland.

Macron’s promise appeared to catch Canadian officials off guard, especially as it was reported a day after Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Macron in the French islands, marking the first official visit to St-Pierre-Miquelon by a Canadian prime minister.

“Canada affirms our claim to the extension of Canada’s continental shelf, which includes all snow crab in this area,” Thompson said in a statement. “Canada does not agree with any foreign snow crab fishing in this area.”

Any licensing matters would be discussed by the countries through formal, well-established processes, and no such talks have taken place, she added.

The countries have been jockeying for territory in the Atlantic for decades and it appears Macron was hoping to revive some of those discussions. According to footage published by franceinfo, he told fishers during his visit in St-Pierre-Miquelon he hoped to initiate “calm but constructive debates” with Canada about the continental shelf.

Fishing is a main economic driver of St-Pierre-Miquelon, which is home to roughly 5,800 people.

Both Canada and France are signatories to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea which, according to Fisheries and Oceans Canada, says coastal states have sovereign rights over the natural resources of the seabed extending from a country’s coastline and into the ocean basin.

If this seabed area, called the continental margin, extends beyond 200 nautical miles from a country’s coasts, that country can make a submission to the United Nations’ Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf to claim rights over that extended area.

Canada made such a submission for the area around its Atlantic coast, including Newfoundland, in 2013. France made a submission for the area around St-Pierre-Miquelon in 2014, saying the area had overlap with Canada’s claim, particularly in a region off Nova Scotia. Under the commission’s rules, the two countries would need to come to an agreement, France said.

In the meantime, a separate ruling from 1992 gave the French islands a 24-nautical-mile zone and added a narrow 10.5-mile strip, known as the French Baguette, which extends south and stops short of Canada’s 200-nautical-mile limit.

Canada responded to France’s 2014 submission to the United Nations, saying it rejected any French claims to maritime areas outside of the 1992 decision.

The area in which Macron reportedly promised a snow crab licence to a French company is beyond Canada’s 200 nautical-mile-limit, but within its extended continental shelf, said Kevin Anderson, head of the School of Fisheries at the Marine Institute of Memorial University in St. John’s, N.L.

And though France and Canada’s continental shelf submissions to the United Nations are unresolved, Canada still has a strong claim to Macron’s proposed French fishing area, he said.

“Canada has been fishing these crab in this area for a long time,” Anderson said in an interview, adding that past court cases have established Canada’s jurisdiction over the snow crab in the region.

“We have the legal structure, we have history, and I think, generally speaking, the precedent,” he added. “That’s the Canadian confidence, I think, that this is ours.”

It is also helpful that snow crab live on the sea bed, which is precisely what the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf deals with, he said.

In her statement Friday, Thompson said Newfoundland and Labrador and Saint-Pierre-Miquelon have been close partners and she hopes that will continue.

However, she said, “Canada will always defend the interests of the harvesters, families, and communities in Newfoundland and Labrador who count on the snow crab fishery.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

stories.title: ‘This monument is to honour our veterans’: Dedication ceremony draws hundreds to Springbank Park
stories.summary: The unveiling of the Byron Springbank Veterans Monument honours those who have fallen, those who served and returned and a legacy for future generations.

stories.content:
It’s a Veterans monument to represent the past, present and future.

The unveiling of the Byron Springbank Veterans Monument honours those who have fallen, those who served and returned and a legacy for future generations.

Two decades ago, Padre Frank Mantz had a dream to bring this space to West London.

Photo Gallery: Unveiling of Byron Springbank Veterans Monument

“My grandfather always said, ‘Don’t start something unless you can finish it,’” said Mantz at the dedication ceremony on Oct. 3, 2026.

“Without Frank, there is no monument, let’s be absolutely clear,” said Ed Holder, chair of the consortium.

“It’s been his vision for 19 years. This monument is to honour our veterans, those who made supreme sacrifices and those who came back - some not whole - and some to make great contributions to their communities, especially in London here. So how could we not do this to honor our veterans?”

Honouring them is what they did Saturday. With veterans from Parkwood Hospital in attendance, hundreds of people packed Springbank Park for the ceremony to dedicate the site.

“This is a place where families come to play, where different groups come to have picnics,” said London Mayor Josh Morgan.

“They’re going to be able to see this space, know what’s happened and pay their respects all at the same time. It’s really about awareness. If ‘Lest We Forget’ is going to be an actual thing, we need to continue to build monuments in public spaces where people will never forget the sacrifices and services that have occurred.”

The day had multiple fly overs by Canadian Harvard Aircraft, acts of remembrance, poetry readings and music.

This site will be the future home of Remembrance Day ceremonies by the Byron Legion.

“I want people to come here when they walk by or ride by and look at this,” said Mantz.

“I want them, if they’re tired in their life, to come and sit down on a bench and look at it and remember what these veterans have done for them out of the love of their hearts. I want it to rekindle their spirits, just sitting here and knowing that these guys and gals were there for them and will always be here. That’s the way our country is. We’re there for each other.”

stories.title: Three dead, four injured in crash on rural Saskatchewan road
stories.summary: A woman and two young girls were killed when a truck attempting to pass a semi collided with an SUV near Foam Lake, RCMP say
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mounties in Saskatchewan say a woman and two girls are dead, and a man from the United States is facing charges, after a truck trying to pass a semi collided with an SUV.

RCMP say they responded to a call for the crash on a rural road near Foam Lake, a small town located southeast of Saskatoon, at around noon on Friday.

Three people in the SUV – including the 40-year-old woman driving the car, an eight-year-old girl and a five-year-old girl – were pronounced dead at the scene.

Police say a man who was also in the SUV was taken to hospital by helicopter in serious condition, and the semi driver was not injured.

The truck driver and a truck passenger were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries while a second passenger, also in the truck, was flown to hospital with serious injuries.

RCMP say a 40-year-old man from Sumter, South Carolina, has been arrested and charged with three counts of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing death and three counts of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing bodily harm.

He is set to appear in court on Monday.

stories.title: France hasn't issued crab licence off Newfoundland, despite surprising pledge: Ottawa
stories.summary: ST. John's - Canada's fisheries minister says France has not issued a new snow crab licence off Newfoundland, despite a surprising promise last month by French President Emmanuel Macron.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Canada’s fisheries minister says France has not issued a new snow crab licence off Newfoundland, despite a surprising promise last month by French President Emmanuel Macron.

Joanne Thompson said Friday evening that the Canadian government has been in contact with French officials to confirm they had not issued a new license, after news outlets including franceinfo and Radio-Canada reported Macron had pledged to grant an exploratory snow crab licence along Canada’s continental shelf to a fishing company in St-Pierre-Miquelon, a small French archipelago off the southeast coast of Newfoundland.

Macron’s promise appeared to catch Canadian officials off guard, especially as it was reported a day after Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Macron in the French islands, marking the first official visit to St-Pierre-Miquelon by a Canadian prime minister.

“Canada affirms our claim to the extension of Canada’s continental shelf, which includes all snow crab in this area,” Thompson said in a statement. “Canada does not agree with any foreign snow crab fishing in this area.”

Any licensing matters would be discussed by the countries through formal, well-established processes, and no such talks have taken place, she added.

The countries have been jockeying for territory in the Atlantic for decades and it appears Macron was hoping to revive some of those discussions. According to footage published by franceinfo, he told fishers during his visit in St-Pierre-Miquelon he hoped to initiate “calm but constructive debates” with Canada about the continental shelf.

Fishing is a main economic driver of St-Pierre-Miquelon, which is home to roughly 5,800 people.

Both Canada and France are signatories to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea which, according to Fisheries and Oceans Canada, says coastal states have sovereign rights over the natural resources of the seabed extending from a country’s coastline and into the ocean basin.

If this seabed area, called the continental margin, extends beyond 200 nautical miles from a country’s coasts, that country can make a submission to the United Nations’ Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf to claim rights over that extended area.

Canada made such a submission for the area around its Atlantic coast, including Newfoundland, in 2013. France made a submission for the area around St-Pierre-Miquelon in 2014, saying the area had overlap with Canada’s claim, particularly in a region off Nova Scotia. Under the commission’s rules, the two countries would need to come to an agreement, France said.

In the meantime, a separate ruling from 1992 gave the French islands a 24-nautical-mile zone and added a narrow 10.5-mile strip, known as the French Baguette, which extends south and stops short of Canada’s 200-nautical-mile limit.

Canada responded to France’s 2014 submission to the United Nations, saying it rejected any French claims to maritime areas outside of the 1992 decision.

The area in which Macron reportedly promised a snow crab licence to a French company is beyond Canada’s 200 nautical-mile-limit, but within its extended continental shelf, said Kevin Anderson, head of the School of Fisheries at the Marine Institute of Memorial University in St. John’s, N.L.

And though France and Canada’s continental shelf submissions to the United Nations are unresolved, Canada still has a strong claim to Macron’s proposed French fishing area, he said.

“Canada has been fishing these crab in this area for a long time,” Anderson said in an interview, adding that past court cases have established Canada’s jurisdiction over the snow crab in the region.

“We have the legal structure, we have history, and I think, generally speaking, the precedent,” he added. “That’s the Canadian confidence, I think, that this is ours.”

It is also helpful that snow crab live on the sea bed, which is precisely what the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf deals with, he said.

In her statement Friday, Thompson said Newfoundland and Labrador and Saint-Pierre-Miquelon have been close partners and she hopes that will continue.

However, she said, “Canada will always defend the interests of the harvesters, families, and communities in Newfoundland and Labrador who count on the snow crab fishery.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Bradford closing in on Chow in Toronto mayoral race: new research
stories.summary: Bradford leads Chow by 7 per cent with voters between 55 and 64 and trails by just 2 per cent among voters over 65.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
A little more than three weeks from Toronto’s municipal election, Brad Bradford is closing on incumbent mayor, Olivia Chow.

The other candidates trail far behind. Chris Alexander sits at 7.2 per cent, Sarah McVie at 2 per cent, then Odessa Paloma Parker at 1.8 per cent, and finally the other candidates deemed by Mainstreet as “someone else” (2.7 per cent) rounding out the field.

With 16% undecided and 14% of voters reporting they might change their minds, including more than a quarter of Chris Alexander voters, the race is close.

Chow leads more comfortably among voters under 55 years-old, with a lead of 7 points among those under 35. She leads by 11 points among voters between 35 and 44, and 17 points among those between 45 and 54.

Among older voters, however, Bradford leads Chow by 7 per cent with voters between 55 and 64. He trails by just 2 per cent among voters over 65, which Mainstreet says is a statistical tie.

With turnout expected to be higher among older voters, Bradford’s edge could be a significant factor in the final outcome.

With regard to election issues, over three quarters of voters point to affordability as extremely or somewhat important (78 per cent). The affordability concerns for almost 3 in 10 include spending on public and transit safety (29.8 per cent). A plurality of voters said any tax increases should go toward paying for affordable housing and fighting homelessness (23.9 per cent).

“The race remains Olivia Chow’s to lose,” said Quito Maggi, President & CEO of Mainstreet Research. “With 16 per cent remaining undecided and another 14 per cent saying they might change their minds on how to vote, the next Mayor of Toronto is far from certain at this point” he added.

“We will keep a close eye on this important race and other as we approach election day” he concluded.

stories.title: Search continues for missing Ontario air ambulance carrying 6 people, including 4 Canadians
stories.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard says search efforts for a missing Ontario-based air ambulance carrying six people, including four Canadians, will continue throughout the night.
stories.author: Joshua McGinnis, Bryann Aguilar
stories.content:
The search for an Ontario-based air ambulance carrying six people, including four Canadians, that went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston early Saturday morning has stretched into the night.

The U.S. Coast Guard, which has been scouring the waters off Nantucket, Mass., all day, said in an update that search efforts for the medical aircraft would continue throughout the night, led by its CGC William Sparling ship.

#Update : The CGC William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night for the 6 people aboard the Gulfstream Aircraft that went missing this morning. — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 4, 2026

The Coast Guard said the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration notified them around 2 a.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 with the tail number C-Grjp and owned by Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance.

Clarence Togeretz, the air ambulance company’s operations manager, told The Canadian Press that the aircraft was transporting a patient and family member, along with two pilots and two medical staff.

The four crew onboard are Canadians, while the passengers are Bermuda nationals, Togeretz said.

He shared that his company had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. as it was approaching Boston. Togeretz said Latitude reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard when the aircraft failed to reach the tarmac.

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

Togeretz noted that this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

Pilot declared emergency: ATC audio

The aircraft bound for Boston Logan International Airport departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport at 12:41 a.m. The air ambulance arrived in Bermuda from Hamilton the previous night.

Air traffic control audio captured by LiveATC.net indicates that the flight declared an emergency before it went missing.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot, who cannot be heard in the audio.

The controller then asked the pilot if they were declaring an emergency.

“You’re coming in a little weak. I didn’t hear your response was if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the controller heard telling the pilot.

A short time later, the controller got a confirmation from the pilot that they were indeed declaring an emergency.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, data shows that one hour and 23 minutes into the flight, the aircraft dropped from an altitude of 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in two minutes and then levelled off before it vanished.

The search for the jet included crews in the air and on the water, the U.S. Coast Guard said, noting that it was using two planes, a search and rescue lifeboat, a helicopter, and a cutter.

#Update Uscg assets responding include: - HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew from AirSta Cape Cod - HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City - MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod - 47-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point - FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154)… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Latitude Air Ambulance’s website says that it currently has four G100 jets in its fleet, each with a range of 5,000 km.

In a statement posted to X , Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge said that “Our thoughts are with our colleagues at Latitude Air Ambulance at this time.”

“All of us at Ornge are hopeful the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Ornge noted that the flight was not related to its operations.

Canadian government ‘closely monitoring the situation’

Canada’s Transportation Minister, Steven MacKinnon, said his department is aware of the situation and that they “are closing monitoring” in a post to X.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time.”

“We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue. I want to thank all first responders involved for their ongoing efforts.”

I am aware of reports of a Canadian-registered air ambulance aircraft that went missing while travelling from Bermuda to Boston. Four Canadians are among the six people on board. My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during… — Steven MacKinnon (@stevenmackinnon) October 3, 2026

Global Affairs Canada said it was aware of reports of Canadians on board the missing Latitude Air Ambulance.

“Consular officials stand ready to provide consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities. Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be disclosed,” Global Affairs said in a statement to CTV News.

Bermuda government releases statement

A spokesperson on behalf of the Bermuda government confirmed the air ambulance’s departure from Bermuda to Boston this morning in a post to X.

Officials said they’ve been in contact with the families of those on board as well as the U.S. Coast Guard conducting the search.

In a statement, Bermuda’s Premier David Burt said that “his thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time.”

“We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

The Government of Bermuda confirms that an air ambulance which departed Bermuda for Boston early this morning, carrying six people, has been reported missing after contact was lost with air traffic control. The United States Coast Guard is conducting search and rescue… pic.twitter.com/yYEwWXMdQQ — Bermuda Government (@BdaGovernment) October 3, 2026

With files from The Associated Press and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Defendant says sorry to former UBC professor days before defamation trial to start
stories.summary: One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway has issued a lengthy apology just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver — One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says she now understands her conduct toward him was “serious and harmful” as she apologized just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.

Chelsea Rooney’s statement said she communicated serious and unproven allegations against Galloway and that she was involved in collecting complaints in an attempt to build a case against him.

“I recognize that statements and communications about allegations of this nature can cause profound harm to a person’s reputation, work, personal life, and family, and did in fact do so to Mr. Galloway. I deeply regret my role in contributing to the harm Mr. Galloway has suffered in this regard,” her statement said.

Much of Rooney’s apology appeared in the National Post newspaper on Saturday and the entire statement is posted on the website gallowayapologies.com, along with eight other apologies from those who say they regret communications or actions that accused Galloway of sexual assault.

Rooney, who is a defendant in the B.C. Supreme Court case due to start Monday, said she recognizes the communications she circulated about Galloway caused others to believe they were true, and she’s aware he firmly denies that he sexually assaulted a student only know as A.B.

Galloway was never charged

The apology is the latest occurrence in what began as an accusation against Galloway in November 2015. He sued numerous people in 2018, alleging he was defamed with false sexual assault allegations by fellow professors, a former student and others who repeated the statements on social media and elsewhere.

The Supreme Court of Canada in 2024 dismissed an appeal by his accusers, clearing the way for the defamation trial.

Galloway is the author of novels including “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” and was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at UBC.

He was never charged, though he was fired from his job.

A report commission by the University of B.C. by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, could not be immediately reached for comment on Saturday, although he said in an interview after the High Court’s ruling that his client’s “reputation and life were devastated by the criminal allegations.”

Rooney is among the defendants who fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming the accusations of sexual assault must be protected speech, true or not, and “regardless of the circumstances in which the statement was published.”

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Elaine Adair said in her ruling on the case in 2021 that if the defendants arguments were true, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

“It is difficult to see how something so extreme and potentially reckless would be in the public interest,” her decision said.

‘Nothing I say now can undo the harm’

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them or posted them publicly on social media.

She said she has reflected on Galloway’s steadfast efforts over the years and she has come to better understand the basis for his position and his commitment to clearing his name and reputation.

“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets, or my participation in the process.”

Rooney said Galloway considered her a friend before A.B. made the allegations, and on multiple occasions went out of his way to help her, with nothing asked in return, she said.

Chelsea Rooney’s statement said she communicated serious and unproven allegations against Galloway and that she was involved in collecting complaints in an attempt to build a case against him.

“I recognize that statements and communications about allegations of this nature can cause profound harm to a person’s reputation, work, personal life, and family, and did in fact do so to Mr. Galloway. I deeply regret my role in contributing to the harm Mr. Galloway has suffered in this regard,” her statement said.

Much of Rooney’s apology appeared in the National Post newspaper on Saturday and the entire statement is posted on the website gallowayapologies.com, along with eight other apologies from those who say they regret communications or actions that accused Galloway of sexual assault.

Rooney, who is a defendant in the B.C. Supreme Court case due to start Monday, said she recognizes the communications she circulated about Galloway caused others to believe they were true, and she’s aware he firmly denies that he sexually assaulted a student only know as A.B.
Galloway was never charged

The apology is the latest occurrence in what began as an accusation against Galloway in November 2015. He sued numerous people in 2018, alleging he was defamed with false sexual assault allegations by fellow professors, a former student and others who repeated the statements on social media and elsewhere.
The Supreme Court of Canada in 2024 dismissed an appeal by his accusers, clearing the way for the defamation trial.
Galloway is the author of novels including “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” and was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at UBC.
He was never charged, though he was fired from his job.
A report commission by the University of B.C. by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, could not be immediately reached for comment on Saturday, although he said in an interview after the High Court’s ruling that his client’s “reputation and life were devastated by the criminal allegations.”

Rooney is among the defendants who fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming the accusations of sexual assault must be protected speech, true or not, and “regardless of the circumstances in which the statement was published.”

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Elaine Adair said in her ruling on the case in 2021 that if the defendants arguments were true, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.
“It is difficult to see how something so extreme and potentially reckless would be in the public interest,” her decision said.

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them or posted them publicly on social media.
She said she has reflected on Galloway’s steadfast efforts over the years and she has come to better understand the basis for his position and his commitment to clearing his name and reputation.

stories.title: One person in custody after vehicle rollover in London
stories.summary: One person has been taken into custody after a vehicle rollover in Euclid Avenue.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
One person has been taken into custody after a vehicle rollover on Euclid Avenue in London.

Witnesses say a vehicle made an illegal left turn onto Euclid Avenue at a high rate of speed from Wharncliffe Road before slamming into two parked cars and turning onto its roof.

A neighbour, who wished not to be identified, says he sprung from his living room when he heard the crash and found a man upside down in the vehicle.

When the driver tried to flee the scene, the neighbour tackled him, and made a citizen’s arrest until police arrived.

Once police arrived on scene, the driver of the vehicle was arrested and charges are pending as the investigation remains in its early stages.

When the driver tried to flee the scene, the neighbour tackled him, and made a citizen’s arrest until police arrived.

stories.title: Fanshawe to deliver aircraft maintenance training at CFB Borden
stories.summary: Fanshawe College will deliver aviation maintenance training to hundreds of military members under a $34 millio...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
Fanshawe College will deliver aviation maintenance training to hundreds of military members under a $34 million contract with the Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf). T he four-year deal is one of the largest contract ever awarded a Canadian college.

Starting in January, instructors from Fanshawe’s Norton Wolf School of Aerospace, Information & Defence Technologies will deliver the curriculum to nearly 300 armed forces members a year at the CFB Borden military base near Barrie.

Military graduates will get the same credentials as Fanshawe students throughout the fast-tracked 16-month program which aims to prepare aviation and aircraft technicians for “ increasingly sophisticated aerospace capabilities in the years ahead,” Fanshawe said in Friday’s announcement.

“Together, we are helping develop the highly skilled aerospace and defense workforce that Canada needs today and in the future,” said Fanshawe President Peter Devlin.

The new contract means an easier pipeline between students and the military, with Rcaf members now having the option to use their credits earned at the School of Aerospace Technology in Borden in a civilian manner with Fanshawe College.

“This partnership between Borden and the Aerospace Department at Fanshawe will provide future airmen and women with valuable credentials while strengthening Canada’s airpower,” said Canada’s defence minister, David McGuinty.

The deal is in keeping with Fanshawe’s position as a military-connected college that offers numerous supports for military personell, veterans and their families.

Police identify the victim as Gabriel-Simon Akokane and say he has a criminal record.

stories.title: Warm, sunny weekend ahead for London
stories.summary: London is in for a warm and mostly sunny weekend, with temperatures reaching 17 C Saturday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London is in for a warm and mostly sunny weekend, with temperatures reaching 17 C Saturday.

Mainly sunny skies are expected throughout the day.

Clear skies will continue Saturday night, with temperatures falling to a low of 6 C.

Sunday will begin with sunshine before clouds move in. There will be a 40 per cent chance of showers late Sunday morning, with a high of 20 C.

Sunday night will see cloudy periods, with a low of 7 C.

stories.title: U.S. Coast Guard searching for Canadian air ambulance missing off Nantucket
stories.summary: Jet was on trip from Bermuda to Boston and had four crew members and two passengers aboard
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Debris from a missing Ontario air ambulance that had been carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been spotted off the coast of the United States.

The U.S. Coast Guard said search crews found a debris field roughly 150 kilometres southeast of Boston and confirmed it belonged to the missing aircraft.

A statement said the search continues for the occupants, and that Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will spearhead the effort throughout the night.

The frantic search began after the Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the plane early Saturday as it travelled from Bermuda to Boston.

The aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 jet, belongs to Latitude Air Ambulance, a Hamilton-based medical evacuation company.

Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, told The Canadian Press that the missing aircraft was transporting a patient and their family member, with two pilots and two medical staff on board.

The four crew members are Canadian, he said, while the two passengers are Bermuda nationals.

Togeretz said Latitude had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. Saturday as it was approaching Boston.

When the plane failed to reach the tarmac, the company reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard, Togeretz said.

Togeretz said the company is “dealing with the situation with as much positivity and optimism as we can.”

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

The operations manager said this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

The company offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, according to its website.

According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 lost contact very early Saturday morning. Air traffic audio indicates that it May have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.

That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane May have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon wrote on social media that the government is closely monitoring the situation and working with authorities as the search continues.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time,” he wrote.

Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement that the government is in contact with the families of those on board and U.S. searchers.

Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge reacted to the news of the missing plane on Saturday, writing in a social media post that it hopes “the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Togeretz said Latitude Air Ambulance is in contact with Transport Canada. The Canadian Press reached out to the federal agency for comment but did not immediately hear back.

stories.title: Ontario air ambulance carrying six people missing off Nantucket: U.S. Coast Guard
stories.summary: An Ontario air ambulance carrying six people, four of them Canadians, has gone missing off the coast of the United States.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Debris from a missing Ontario air ambulance that had been carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been spotted off the coast of the United States.

The U.S. Coast Guard said search crews found a debris field roughly 150 kilometres southeast of Boston and confirmed it belonged to the missing aircraft.

A statement said the search continues for the occupants, and that Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will spearhead the effort throughout the night.

The frantic search began after the Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the plane early Saturday as it travelled from Bermuda to Boston.

The aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 jet, belongs to Latitude Air Ambulance, a Hamilton-based medical evacuation company.

Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, told The Canadian Press that the missing aircraft was transporting a patient and their family member, with two pilots and two medical staff on board.

The four crew members are Canadian, he said, while the two passengers are Bermuda nationals.

Togeretz said Latitude had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. Saturday as it was approaching Boston.

When the plane failed to reach the tarmac, the company reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard, Togeretz said.

Togeretz said the company is “dealing with the situation with as much positivity and optimism as we can.”

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

The operations manager said this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

The company offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, according to its website.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon wrote on social media that the government is closely monitoring the situation and working with authorities as the search continues.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time,” he wrote.

Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement that the government is in contact with the families of those on board and U.S. searchers.

Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge reacted to the news of the missing plane on Saturday, writing in a social media post that it hopes “the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Togeretz said Latitude Air Ambulance is in contact with Transport Canada. The Canadian Press reached out to the federal agency for comment but did not immediately hear back.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

stories.title: Ontario-based air ambulance carrying 6 missing off U.S. coast
stories.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration told Global News in a statement it issued a Search and Rescue Alert for a Gulfstream G-100 around 1:20 a.m. Saturday.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard is searching for a Hamilton-based air ambulance carrying six people that went missing off the coast of Nantucket.

The Federal Aviation Administration told Global News in a statement it issued a Search and Rescue Alert for a Gulfstream G-100 around 1:20 a.m. Saturday.

The flight departed from L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda and was headed to Boston Logan International Airport, a spokesperson said. It was scheduled to arrive in Boston around 1:30 a.m.

A spokesperson for the Massachusetts Port Authority, which operates Boston Logan International Airport, confirmed to Global News in an email that the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled.

“Our thoughts are with those on board and their loved ones as the search continues,” the spokesperson said.

According to data from Flight Aware, the plane took off around 11:40 p.m. Friday. Data shows the aircraft slowing down as it dropped from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet around 1:05 a.m. before losing contact.

In a post on social media, the Coast Guard said it had launched air and surface crews in search of the aircraft.

Authorities are engaging in what is called a pattern search, John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University, told Global News.

“These aircraft are typically equipped with a transponder that basically beeps out to the world about location. So I’m not sure whether that transponder got deployed or not,” he said, adding it does not appear authorities have a pinpointed location.

The Nantucket Police Department told Global News in a statement that they were requested to check the Nantucket Memorial Airport and the southern shoreline for the plane but it was not located.

“We have been monitoring the southern shore on ATV with both police and Harbour Master’s Office Staff since sunrise,” a spokesperson said.

The jet is registered to Latitude Air Ambulance, a company based in Hamilton, Ont., according to data from FlightRadar 24.

The company’s website states it operates four Gulfstream G-100 jets, the “longest range dedicated medevac aircraft in North America.”

Gradek said the company has been around for a while, calling it the “premier long distance air ambulance service in North America.”

“They’ve been around a few years, they fly high quality, good maintenance airplanes, and are very reliable,” he added.

Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, told The Canadian Press this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

He said the missing aircraft was transporting a patient and their family member, with two pilots and two medical staff on board.

The four medical staff are Canadian and the two passengers are Bermuda nationals, he added.

The Bermuda government said in a post on social media it has been in contact with the families of those on board.

The jet’s previous flight was Friday, travelling from Hamilton to Bermuda.

– With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: OPP Auxiliary officers looking to support local food banks Saturday
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police will be at select grocery stores Saturday helping address food insecurity across the province.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police will be at select grocery stores Saturday helping address food insecurity across the province.

The event is called ‘Operation Full Plate’ and it is a one-day food drive looking to help support local food banks and address food insecurity.

“It’s a time when people can give back to our communities throughout our food banks by donating non-perishable goods and toiletries,” said Sgt. Marty Salliss of the OPP.

In the West region, officers will be at 14 different locations including Dorchester, Exeter, Goderich, Mitchell, Tillsonburg, Petrolia and Forest.

“Food insecurity continues to affect individuals and families in communities throughout Ontario,” OPP said in a release .

“Operation Full Plate provides an opportunity for OPP Auxiliary members and the public to work together in support of local food banks and the people who rely on them.”

Hundreds of volunteers will be at these locations to help collect essential goods. The food drive runs from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

stories.title: London Food Bank celebrates 40th anniversary
stories.summary: Over the past 40 years the London Food Bank has seen plenty of changes, however the main aim remains the same, to help those in need in our community.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Over the past 40 years the London Food Bank has seen plenty of changes, however the main aim remains the same, to help those in need in our community.

The two co-founders Jane Roy and Glen Pearson are still with the food bank, now acting as co-executive directors.

“In October 1986 imagine us in 600 sq. ft. on Dundas Street and we served 360 families a month,” said Roy. “Today we have 22,000 sq. ft., thirteen staff members, walk-in freezers and we serve fifty-seven hundred families a month.”

The food bank was initially meant to be temporary but that changed over time with Roy saying, “Back 1986 or 1987, CTV or A Channel or whatever it was did a piece on hidden hunger and that’s when we understood that there was two London’s and we started to understand there was a greater need.”

Along the way, Glen Pearson says the London Food Bank has been able to obtain an army of helpers.

“We have four thousand volunteers and that would stand out in anybody’s book and we don’t go out and recruit them,” says Pearson “They just come in because these are citizens who want to play their role in these troubling times.”

To mark the 40 years, the community is invited to come out to the Leathorne Street facility on Saturday, Oct. 3 starting at 11 a.m.

Roy says they want people to come on in and they’d like to show them around and show them what happens.

The Celebration coincides with the 38 annual Thanksgiving Food Drive which got underway Thurday.

“The drive lasts until Thanksgiving Monday,” said Roy. “There’s no goal but whatever people can give, a can of tuna or a bag of groceries can be dropped off at any grocery store or fire hall.”

The London Food Bank has grown to become is one of the most successful in Canada mainly due to the generosity of the London community.

“When you think of what the Business Cares community has done with over a thousand businesses it’s amazing,” said Pearson. “I can tell you with every challenge that we face, every pandemic or recession we don’t sit around and worry because Londoners will hear about that and they will support their food bank because it’s about them.”

stories.title: B.C. judge declares dad guardian after mom returns to Ukraine with toddler
stories.summary: Couple who never lived together while she was in Vancouver on visitor's visa now face court battle from two continents
stories.author: Susan Lazaruk
stories.content:
A toddler born to a Vancouver man and a woman visiting Canada from Ukraine is now at the centre of an international court battle over where he’ll live.

Edward Ronald Boney, 51, who was recently declared a legal guardian of “E.N.B.” by a B.C. Supreme Court judge, is seeking to have the child returned to Canada after the mom returned to Ukraine in February with the boy without his knowledge, according to the decision.

In March, Boney filed an application for the boy’s return through a provincial office, citing the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The following month, he filed a separate claim in B.C. Supreme Court seeking shared guardianship and parenting responsibilities and the return of the boy to B.C.

Oksana Melnychaiko, 38, began her own family law proceedings in March in a court in Ternopil in Western Ukraine. She is seeking an order that would allow her to raise their child — who turns two in December — in Ukraine with child support from Boney.

In his ruling declaring Boney a legal guardian of E.N.B., Justice Richard Fowler wrote that the mother and father met on a dating site in January 2024. Melnychaiko had arrived in Canada in 2022 or 2023 on a work visa. Their child was born in December 2024.

While Boney never lived with Melnychaiko and their child, he regularly cared for him, including feeding him, changing his diaper, reading to him and taking him swimming and on other outings, according to the decision.

Boney, who had a paternity test done after the baby was born, used a spreadsheet to show the court he had spent $17,000 on baby items in his first 14 months and said he’d spent time with his son on 303 days of the first 432 days of his life.

He said he’d helped move her to a new apartment before the birth and picked up her and the baby when they got out of hospital. And he has regularly taken them shopping and to medical appointments, and did the laundry and other chores.

Dad faces contempt of court penalty after failing to pay Vancouver ex or disclose finances

Mac's treatment of temporary foreign workers 'callous,' B.C. judge rules

Boney had also taken the boy to family gatherings where he got to know his grandparents, aunt and uncle and Boney’s childhood friends, according to the decision.

E.N.B. had a B.C. Care Card, a Canadian social insurance number, Canadian passport, bank account, registered education savings plan account and medical coverage through Boney’s extended health plan at work, court heard.

For three months in mid-2025, Melnychaiko took the boy to Europe to visit family and friends. She did so again from December 2025 to January 2026. For both trips, Boney provided letters of consent required for international travel.

But when she left again with the child in February 2026, it was without his knowledge. She used Boney’s still-valid letter of consent from the December-January trip, according to the decision.

After Melnychaiko failed to return to Canada as planned in March, she told Boney in a lengthy text she was finding it difficult to live in Canada and that she was making a “life-changing” decision to stay in Ukraine. She accused him of not supporting her or their child, Fowler wrote.

Melnychaiko had taken the position a B.C. court didn’t have jurisdiction, or shouldn’t have exercised it, to hear Boney’s application on guardianship.

But Fowler found otherwise after concluding that the boy was “habitually resident” in B.C. when the father filed his claim for guardianship.

Fowler said it was “undisputed” that Boney regularly cared for the child before his removal from Canada and therefore is a guardian.

Fowler noted it would be “difficult” to establish the removal of E.N.B. violated his custody rights under the Hague Convention unless he was guardian at the time the child left Canada.

Melnychaiko provided little evidence during the two-day hearing to counter Boney’s version of events.

She provided no reason to the court for why she left Canada. But the ruling notes she didn’t have family in Canada, her immigration status was temporary and there’s no evidence she applied for or considered applying for more permanent status.

In Ukraine, the Justice Ministry has notified the court in Ternopil it has to wait for the Hague Convention decision on whether the child should be returned to Canada before issuing its custody decision, according to Fowler’s ruling.

That Hague Convention hearing by law takes place in the country to which the baby was taken. If the child is returned to B.C., a court here would then decide parenting arrangements, such as a parenting schedule and decision-making rights.

stories.title: Four Canadian wines for October entertaining
stories.summary: Whether you’re on a budget or willing to splurge, these bottles are perfect for celebratory dinners and parties this fall
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
There are many reasons to get together this month, with celebrations, such as Thanksgiving, Oktoberfest and Halloween punctuating the social calendar. Here are four reliable Canadian wines to have on hand for celebratory dinners and parties this month, including the special occasion-worthy Osoyoos Larose red from the Okanagan.

Henry of Pelham Baco Noir 2025 (Canada), $16.95

Henry of Pelham’s early interest in the unassuming baco noir has given the Speck family a unique selling opportunity around the world. This fruity, full-bodied red, which balances a mix of tart and sweet red fruit and peppery flavours, has become one of Niagara’s biggest exports. This has 13-per-cent ABV and 12 g/litre r.s. Drink now. Available at the above price in Ontario, $14.95 direct, henryofpelham.com, various prices in Alberta and Saskatchewan, $17.99 in Manitoba, $17.95 in Quebec, $23 in New Brunswick, $23.49 in Prince Edward Island, $22.21 in Newfoundland.

Osoyoos Larose Le Grand Vin 2022 (Canada), $60.95

Osoyoos Larose has produced collectible and age-worthy red wine from the southern Okanagan since its first vintage in 2001. Originally a joint venture between Bordeaux’s Groupe Taillan and Canada’s Vincor International, it is now entirely French-owned and has just updated its packaging. The 2022 vintage of its flagship red blend, made from mostly merlot with cabernet sauvignon, cabernet franc, petit verdot and malbec, is made in a medium-bodied fragrant and fruity style. There’s a distinctive Okanagan sage note that adds local character to its core of juicy dark fruit and floral flavours. This has 14.5-per-cent ABV and 3 g/litre r.s. Drink now to 2036. Available at the above price in Ontario, $59.99 in British Columbia, various prices in Alberta and Saskatchewan, $64.99 in Manitoba, $67 in New Brunswick.

Peller Family Reserve Secco Bubbles (Canada), $14.95

This Niagara take on Prosecco comes with a screw cap closure, which might cause confusion by lacking the traditional mushroom-shaped cork and wire cage, but makes opening and serving a breeze. A blend of vidal, gewurztraminer and other grape varieties, this enjoyable sparkling wine features a crowd-pleasing mix of peach, apple and pear flavours. This has 12-per-cent ABV and 12 g/litre r.s. Drink now. Available at the above price in Ontario, various prices in Alberta, $17.99 in Manitoba, $16.49 in New Brunswick, $19.42 in Newfoundland.

Sandhill Sovereign Opal 2025 (Canada), $20.95

The sovereign opal grape variety was bred in 1966 in Summerland, B.C., to withstand the Okanagan’s harsh winters. A cross between maréchal foch and golden muscat, the hybrid grape produces white wines with distinctive floral, peach and tropical flavours. Sandhill continues to be the only producer of this made-in-Canada rarity, offering a light and juicy version in the 2025 vintage with some citrusy acidity that balances the natural sweetness. This has 11.7-per-cent ABV and 12.5 g/litre r.s. Drink now. Available at the above price in British Columbia, various prices in Alberta.

stories.title: Anti-Israel Oct. 7 event to 'honour martyrs' will not proceed on U of T campus: university
stories.summary: Other Canadian campuses are still set to have anti-Israel rallies on Oct. 7, including one in Vancouver and one in Montreal.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
An anti-Israel event intended to “honour martyrs” at the University of Toronto on Oct. 7 will no longer be permitted.

A spokesperson for the university told National Post that it has told the recognized student groups involved in organizing the event — one of several planned on Canadian campuses — that it “cannot proceed because of significant safety and operational concerns.”

“These concerns include physical safety risks to participants and to members of the broader university community due to the unsuitability of the space for large gatherings and the online promotion of counter-protests to take place at the same time,” the spokesperson said.

Oct. 7 marks the third anniversary of the Hamas terrorist attack in which 1,200 Israelis were murdered. It was the deadliest attack on Jewish people since the Holocaust. Canadian leaders and Jewish advocacy groups called on U of T and other universities to shut down anti-Israel Oct. 7 events.

“On some Canadian campuses, the third anniversary of October 7 will be marked by protests glorifying the heinous attacks, honouring the terrorists as ‘martyrs’ and calling for intifada — which many of Canada’s allies consider incitement to violence against Jews,” the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs said in a statement shared with National Post.

“This glorification of violence and terrorism has no place on campuses and administrations have a responsibility to ensure safe places for learning free from hate, particularly when such events are organized or supported by student groups and unions.”

'Disgusting' antisemitic flyers distributed in Belleville weeks after synagogue shooting

What we know about the Flydubai suspect who allegedly 'refused to shake hands with women'

“Choosing October 7th as a date for ‘honouring our martyrs’ isn’t random. It’s purposefully provocative,” he wrote.

The U of T event was expected to take place at 5:30 p.m. at the steps of Sidney Smith Hall, located at the university’s St. George campus. The university will “act swiftly to enforce its policies should it become aware of potential violations,” said the U of T spokesperson.

Other events are still planned across Canada, including a “gathering” at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and a rally at McGill University in Montreal.

A UBC spokesperson told National Post it was aware of a “range of activities on the Vancouver campus” being hosted by “Jewish and Palestinian student groups” on Oct. 7. None of them are “official” UBC events.

“UBC is committed to free inquiry, the free exchange of ideas and opinion, and the ability of all members of our community to engage in peaceful expression,” the spokesperson said. “We expect everyone exercising these freedoms to do so respectfully and within the boundaries of university policy and the law. Hate and intolerance have no place at UBC.”

An Oct. 7 rally is set for 2 p.m. at McGill’s Roddick Gates.

A McGill spokesperson said the university “denounces all forms of antisemitism and anti-Jewish hatred and reaffirms its dedication to preventing and combating such discrimination.”

“Every member of our campus community deserves to work and learn in a respectful, inclusive, and supportive environment,” said the spokesperson. “At the same time, McGill is committed to freedom of expression and has no issue with lawful activism and protest that ensure campus access remains unobstructed and academic activities continue without disruption.”

The concern from the Jewish community about the safety of such events stems largely from recent antisemitic incidents, including a hate-motivated, targeted shooting at a Belleville, Ont. synagogue and the arrest of two individuals in Ontario for making antisemitic threats online.
