stories.title: Experts eye Alberta referendum as case study on impacts of artificial intelligence
stories.summary: Edmonton - On any given day, says Aengus Bridgman, if you ask a popular artificial intelligence chatbot and a search engine whether taxes in an independent Alberta would be higher, it might say yes.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - On any given day, says Aengus Bridgman, if you ask a popular artificial intelligence chatbot and a search engine whether taxes in an independent Alberta would be higher, it might say yes.

A few hours later, it could be no.

Responses from Google AI Overview and OpenAI’s ChatGPT can change, because data used to predict responses is always changing. ”(It’s) not because any of the underlying reality has changed,” said Bridgman, director of Media Ecosystem Observatory.

In a report released last month, the Ontario-based initiative documented mixed responses to questions about what an independent Alberta could look like.

“We asked, ‘Will my taxes go up?’ ‘Will my pension go up?’ ‘Is this fiscally advantageous to me?’” Bridgman said.

The report tracks how AI technologies are being harnessed in the online discourse ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum.

Albertans are voting on 10 questions, including whether they want to stay in Canada or to have a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

The report says the vote is a case study in how AI could influence future elections when it comes to where people get their news.

“Year over year, online influencers have been accumulating relevance and engagement at the expense of news media and elected officials,” says the report.

“We now have a case study of what a democratic vote looks like squarely in the influencer era.”

Bridgman said social media and AI have vastly expanded debates on separation.

“It’s good in terms of a lively democracy.”

But, he added, technologies have also made tracking the referendum, and elections generally, more complex.

It’s likely because of the maxim: garbage in, garbage out.

Elections Alberta says on its website that AI-powered chatbots and search engines are increasingly being used to find and summarize information found online.

The agency warns: “They are not official sources of election information and frequently cite incorrect information sources.”

OpenAI and Google didn’t respond to requests for comments on Media Ecosystem’s report.

OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans shared a May blog the company posted on its website outlining what technologies the company has partnered with to ensure its chatbot produces accurate information during votes.

“This year is the world’s second major election year since generative AI became widely available, and we’re continuing to build on the foundation we laid in 2024 to help protect elections in countries and territories around the world,” the post said.

The Media Ecosystem study also found an uptick in content about Alberta separation produced in other countries, including the United States. But there’s not enough evidence of foreign interference, Bridgman said.

The study says foreign actors are producing content largely for financial profit, and the millions and millions of views they get suggest they are cashing in.

Pro-separation influencers also dominate the online discourse, the study found, despite polls showing a large majority of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada.

Bridgman said it’s unclear why there are more pro-separation social media accounts than federalist accounts.

“My attribution of this is generally because these (separatist) voices have not felt represented in more traditional media.”

Many influencers are also using AI to generate content, the study found.

University of Alberta political science professor Blair Attard-Frost said the increased use of AI in the separation debate is concerning.

The AI chair with Canadian Institute for Advanced Research said when search engines became popular in the early 2000s, so did information campaigns about media literacy.

With the advancement in AI, a new wave of media literacy needs to be implemented because of how big tech markets its search engines and services.

“These are really deceptive products,” Attard-Frost said. “They’re marketed as intelligent tools.”

She said she’ll be paying attention to how the current technologies might affect the referendum results and the future of Alberta’s separation movement.

“A lot of people could be getting incomplete, inaccurate, false or misleading information about the potential consequences of separatism, and using that information to make decisions about how to vote,” she said.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, asked this week whether she’s concerned about AI-generated misinformation swaying votes, said her government has turned to traditional media to get out information.

It recently launched an ad campaign and mailed out booklets outlining and explaining the 10 referendum questions.

The first nine ask if the government should have more authority to push for Constitutional reform and impose limitations and financial guardrails around some newcomers.

The last question is about separation.

“We are making sure that Albertans know exactly what the questions are and some of the context for them,” Smith said Monday.

On Friday, Alberta Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said anyone looking for misinformation should look no further than Smith’s United Conservative Party government.

Nenshi pointed to the booklets that arrived at homes this week as an example of the government putting its thumb on the scale.

The booklet uses uncontextualized numbers and information to urge voters to give the government a mandate for the first nine questions, while it’s silent on the 10th

For example, said Nenshi, the booklet says temporary residents cost Alberta taxpayers $1 billion a year in health care and education. It doesn’t say where the number comes from or that temporary workers, by definition, have to have a job to stay and must also pay taxes.

“For the first nine questions, (Smith) tells you how to vote,” Nenshi said. “That doesn’t feel like direct democracy to me. It feels like propaganda.

“This (booklet) is garbage — $4 million worth of taxpayer-funded garbage.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

University of Alberta political science professor Blair Attard-Frost said the increased use of AI in the separation debate is concerning.

stories.title: How the game of chess became cool
stories.summary: At swanky bars and trendy coffee shops across the country, the board game is shedding its stuffy image
stories.author: Alex Robert Ross, Photography by Nina Ricci Lu
stories.content:
Zelko Odorcic is a celebrity at Knightcap Chess Club. When he walks into Soho House Toronto one Friday night in August, a dozen people half his age greet him as if he’s a returning hero. His tucked-in T-shirt displays a blacked-out mantra: Discipline = Freedom. But this is not his approach to chess, which he plays only for fun.

He was once a competitive club player, hosting tournaments for the Croatia Chess Club in Mississauga. But now he agrees with 19th-century grandmaster Paul Morphy, who said that playing chess made a gentleman but playing well was the sign of a wasted life.

Odorcic is here to play only a couple of casual games. He spends the rest of the time drinking chardonnay and making conversation. “Besides family and business, you want some other place where you can come and have a friendly chat and play some games,” he says, sweeping back his thick white hair.

Tonight, the ordinarily exclusive Soho House is just that. On the third-floor Pretzel Bell Bar, table lamps throw warm light onto roll-up boards and plastic pieces, and a sultry modern R&B playlist lingers in the background as players chat between moves in untimed games.

Knightcap is one of a new generation of chess clubs that have grown rapidly across Canada over the past few years. Unlike conventional chess clubs, which developed a reputation as serious and stuffy, these groups run informal, open events for players of all levels. They’re taking over some of the most sought-after bars and social spaces in their cities – and spawning communities that extend far beyond the board.

These groups, Knightcap founder Taylor Harrison says, want to “switch up the atmosphere for chess – because it is a very social game when you’re with the right people.”

The over-the-board events grew from the online chess explosion of the early pandemic lockdowns. Tiger King and The Last Dance ate up only so many hours, and Zoom-based “hangouts” quickly lost their novelty. Chess, ON the other hand, was – and remains – inexhaustible; there are more possible unique game variations on the board than there are particles in the known universe. The website chess.com , which offers anyone the chance to play for free against a similarly skilled opponent, exploded. At the start of March, 2020, it had 280,000 daily users; by the end of the month, more than one million people were logging on every day.

That fall, Netflix released The Queen’s Gambit , a miniseries in which a chess prodigy grapples with her own genius. It was an immediate success, streamed by 68 million households worldwide. Chess.com’s daily users doubled in the space of a month, and the number of chess products sold on eBay in the lead up to the holidays was up 215 per cent on the previous year.

“A lot of people who were locked up were looking for something to do that felt fun but also meaningful,” says Sam Copeland, chess.com ’s head of community. “You feel like you’re using your brain. You’re getting something out of it. You’re participating in a lineage and tradition that goes back over a millennium.”

Knightcap’s Harrison was among those who picked the game up in earnest during the pandemic. Before the first quarantine he was a manager at a high-end Italian restaurant. As the hospitality industry continued to suffer, he worried that he might never go back to hosting.

“I really missed taking care of people: handling the ambience, setting the music, the mood, the candlelight,” he says. As restrictions eased, he thought of combining his new hobby with his old passion: a chess event emphasizing vibes, not expertise. He hosted the first Knightcap at Toronto’s industrial-chic Annex Hotel Wine Bar in November, 2023, expecting it to be a one-off for a few friends. Sixty people showed up.

Since then, Knightcap has grown quickly. Harrison has taken it to some of the city’s most luxurious locations, including the Park Hyatt and the Ace Hotel. It’s also expanded beyond Toronto, with regular events in three major U.S. cities–Austin, Miami, and Chicago–as well as Mexico City and Milan. Wherever they are in the world, Knightcap events are open to everyone, regardless of skill level.

Nadine Hassan, who works in corporate law and moved to Toronto from the suburbs two years ago, credits Knightcap with helping her find her footing in the city.

“I feel like now we’re all sharing our own Toronto experience. I feel like I’m from Toronto now,” she says over a 30-minute game at Soho House in which we both keep forgetting whose turn it is. “I have my little spots that I go to, which I’ve learned about through the different chess events and the people I’ve met through chess.”

At 915 Dupont, a Japanese-inspired coffee shop and listening bar with one of the best vintage sound systems in the city, informal chess events are held every Monday night.

Chess is a natural fit, the bar’s manager, Dan Courtice, explains from behind the turntables. Typically, 915 Dupont attracts a breed of audiophile who cares about the styles of specific jazz pianists in Japan – another inexhaustible universe that rewards time and patience.

“Music nerds and chess nerds are the same breed,” Courtice says, adding that he’s seen countless people arrive alone, play games with strangers and form long-lasting friendships.

Such connections are happening across the country. Kurtis Formosa, who runs the Vancouver Beer & Chess night, says his events have resulted in at least half a dozen couples. In Calgary, Araz Zarghami believes the more relaxed atmosphere surrounding the game is key. He started attending the city’s Downtown Chess events as pandemic restrictions eased, and eventually took over organizing the group last year.

“I think it’s changing as people see more and more that ordinary people are playing it, having a beer and not needing to sit down in a quiet room where all you can hear is the air conditioning,” he says.

Meanwhile, the online game continues to grow and develop more chess-curious newcomers. Sign-ups at chess.com were twice as high in the summer of 2023 as in the immediate aftermath of The Queen’s Gambit, with more than eight million players joining every month. This past February, the number of accounts on the site hit 250 million. According to chess.com’s data, more than 7.5 million belong to players who identify as Canadian – the eighth highest participation rate per capita in the world.

A new generation of engaging and media-savvy chess personalities has also emerged to guide players through tactics previously relegated to dusty strategy books. Five-time U.S. Chess Champion and grandmaster Hikaru Nakamura and international master Levy Rozman, better known as GothamChess, each have millions of followers on Instagram and YouTube.

On livestreaming platform Twitch, the average number of people watching chess-related content rose 20-fold in the first year of lockdowns. This coincided with the dominance of Magnus Carlsen, statistically the greatest chess player of all time and a natural celebrity: young, handsome and surprisingly relatable. He is so famous among chess players of every level that he’s usually referred to by just his first name.

In 2023 he twice appeared at the Madison, an old bar by the University of Toronto, for Pub Chess. The world’s top-ranked player was invited by Chessbrah, a Toronto-based streamer, and those visits are still spoken about in awed tones. Over the din by the pool table on a recent Wednesday night, one young customer can be heard telling the story to a group of disbelieving friends.

A few feet away, 32 chessboards, each with a clock at its side, are laid out along two long rows of tables. The playlist is mostly pop, the Blue Jays are on four different televisions and Neil Goel is standing on a table shouting as loud as he can to announce the matchups for the next round of games.

Pub Chess has been a fixture at the Madison since 2015, but it has exploded in the past four years, after co-founder Liza Orlova moved to Vancouver and handed over the reins. Unlike Orlova, who played competitively as a teenager before effectively retiring, Goel was another pandemic-era online newcomer. He had only been playing at the Madison for a few weeks before agreeing to run the event temporarily. Four years later he’s still here, asking a packed room of beer drinkers to clap twice if they can hear him.

In a brief quieter moment, while guests focus on their games, Goel says the event has quadrupled in size since he took charge. The nights used to be more competitive, but he was determined to lower the barrier to entry.

“Toronto’s had more newcomers to Canada than most cities in the country,” he says. “Chess functions as a sort of universal language. We get tons of people coming from all walks of life, and they sometimes find it hard to communicate. But through chess they’re able to make friends. They’re able to build community.”

Pub Chess is now held twice weekly, with Tuesday’s sessions taking place at a brewery in Liberty Village. The events attract highly rated players as well as complete rookies. Every guest is paired according to their self-reported Elo rating – most people who’ve played more than a few times online know theirs – with winners facing a greater challenge in their next game and losers getting an easier match.

Harrison says he can spot people new to playing in person (myself included) by the way they lean over the board. Regardless of ranking, the view from one side is radically different from the top-down perspective shown online. At the Madison, under time pressure and faced with another human, it feels like driving on a highway for the first time after learning about cars exclusively from arcade racing games .

A few stops farther west on the subway, ON a humid Thursday night, the Secretaries Shirley International Chess Club hosts an event at Nile, a trendy new coffee shop in the shell of an old Portuguese sports bar. Parker Murchison, Jack Perros and Nick Collini – who started the events, like so many others, as pandemic restrictions eased – are all 24 (and all run fashion brands). The vast majority of attendees tonight, sipping Super Bock and bespoke cocktails, are well-heeled younger millennials or members of Gen Z.

“I think people want to seem smart right now,” Perros says over the sound of DJ Jiynx, who is more accustomed to playing underground venues and warehouses. “It’s like having good taste. People want to have good taste that differentiates them.”

When they put on their first event three years ago, the three friends wanted to explore the growing trend of people going out for hands-on activities such as game nights and scrapbooking meets. They stumbled into chess without thinking about it too hard, and Ssicc is now a monthly event in Toronto. They’ve also hosted nights in Los Angeles, London and Paris.

One striking thing at all of these events is how few phones are on the tables. Face-to-face interaction is clearly part of building these real-life communities. “You can’t be on your phone and play chess” over the board, Collini says. “I think people are looking for that right now.”

Chess’s most magnetic quality is, it seems, its inexhaustibility – its resistance to perfection. When the IBM computer Deep Blue beat then world champion Garry Kasparov for the first time in 1996, The Globe and Mail’s editorial board argued that a computer, no matter how advanced, would always be inferior to humans, with all their flaws and impulses.

“The manipulation of sums evinces intelligence, but reams of numbers in columns and rows do not add up to humanity. … We are our minds, and we are our passions,” the piece read.

Now, inside all these rowdy pubs and bars littered with chessboards, every person carries in their pocket a computer orders of magnitude more powerful than Deep Blue, and it feels utterly irrelevant to what’s happening at the table. As Daniel Rensch, the co-founder of chess.com , said in a recent interview, “neural nets are better than Magnus Carlsen, but it has nothing to do with the fact that we keep playing the game.”

On International Chess Day in July, Knightcap hosted an event at the Well, a multipurpose complex in downtown Toronto. Khrystyna Boyko, 19, happened to wander past with her boyfriend. Back in Ukraine, her dad had taught her how to play when she was a child, but she was never a fan until playing online during the pandemic.

“I just really love to win, and I was always trying to win, but I was losing,” she said over a game in which we both blundered away our pieces. “I feel like that’s the way I learned.” At a table nearby, Arthur Calugar, an international master and a regular at casual events in the city, patiently walked an aspiring player through the complexities of an obscure opening.

As the game’s continued democratization shows, chess is not about perfection. It’s about the ability to blunder away a queen, miscalculate an endgame or launch an audacious attack on little more than mad confidence. It allows people to fail, learn, improve and fail again – all while sipping drinks in a dimly lit room – for no more complex purpose than seeing those same human traits in others.

At 915 Dupont, a Japanese-inspired coffee shop and listening bar with one of the best vintage sound systems in the city, informal chess events are held every Monday night.

Chess is a natural fit, the bar’s manager, Dan Courtice, explains from behind the turntables. Typically, 915 Dupont attracts a breed of audiophile who cares about the styles of specific jazz pianists in Japan – another inexhaustible universe that rewards time and patience.
“Music nerds and chess nerds are the same breed,” Courtice says, adding that he’s seen countless people arrive alone, play games with strangers and form long-lasting friendships.

Such connections are happening across the country. Kurtis Formosa, who runs the Vancouver Beer & Chess night, says his events have resulted in at least half a dozen couples. In Calgary, Araz Zarghami believes the more relaxed atmosphere surrounding the game is key. He started attending the city’s Downtown Chess events as pandemic restrictions eased, and eventually took over organizing the group last year.

“I think it’s changing as people see more and more that ordinary people are playing it, having a beer and not needing to sit down in a quiet room where all you can hear is the air conditioning,” he says.

Meanwhile, the online game continues to grow and develop more chess-curious newcomers. Sign-ups at chess.com were twice as high in the summer of 2023 as in the immediate aftermath of The Queen’s Gambit, with more than eight million players joining every month. This past February, the number of accounts on the site hit 250 million. According to chess.com’s data, more than 7.5 million belong to players who identify as Canadian – the eighth highest participation rate per capita in the world.

A new generation of engaging and media-savvy chess personalities has also emerged to guide players through tactics previously relegated to dusty strategy books. Five-time U.S. Chess Champion and grandmaster Hikaru Nakamura and international master Levy Rozman, better known as GothamChess, each have millions of followers on Instagram and YouTube.

On livestreaming platform Twitch, the average number of people watching chess-related content rose 20-fold in the first year of lockdowns. This coincided with the dominance of Magnus Carlsen, statistically the greatest chess player of all time and a natural celebrity: young, handsome and surprisingly relatable. He is so famous among chess players of every level that he’s usually referred to by just his first name.

In 2023 he twice appeared at the Madison, an old bar by the University of Toronto, for Pub Chess. The world’s top-ranked player was invited by Chessbrah, a Toronto-based streamer, and those visits are still spoken about in awed tones. Over the din by the pool table on a recent Wednesday night, one young customer can be heard telling the story to a group of disbelieving friends.

A few feet away, 32 chessboards, each with a clock at its side, are laid out along two long rows of tables. The playlist is mostly pop, the Blue Jays are on four different televisions and Neil Goel is standing on a table shouting as loud as he can to announce the matchups for the next round of games.

Pub Chess has been a fixture at the Madison since 2015, but it has exploded in the past four years, after co-founder Liza Orlova moved to Vancouver and handed over the reins. Unlike Orlova, who played competitively as a teenager before effectively retiring, Goel was another pandemic-era online newcomer. He had only been playing at the Madison for a few weeks before agreeing to run the event temporarily. Four years later he’s still here, asking a packed room of beer drinkers to clap twice if they can hear him.

In a brief quieter moment, while guests focus on their games, Goel says the event has quadrupled in size since he took charge. The nights used to be more competitive, but he was determined to lower the barrier to entry.

“Toronto’s had more newcomers to Canada than most cities in the country,” he says. “Chess functions as a sort of universal language. We get tons of people coming from all walks of life, and they sometimes find it hard to communicate. But through chess they’re able to make friends. They’re able to build community.”

Pub Chess is now held twice weekly, with Tuesday’s sessions taking place at a brewery in Liberty Village. The events attract highly rated players as well as complete rookies. Every guest is paired according to their self-reported Elo rating – most people who’ve played more than a few times online know theirs – with winners facing a greater challenge in their next game and losers getting an easier match.

Harrison says he can spot people new to playing in person (myself included) by the way they lean over the board. Regardless of ranking, the view from one side is radically different from the top-down perspective shown online. At the Madison, under time pressure and faced with another human, it feels like driving on a highway for the first time after learning about cars exclusively from arcade racing games .

A few stops farther west on the subway, ON a humid Thursday night, the Secretaries Shirley International Chess Club hosts an event at Nile, a trendy new coffee shop in the shell of an old Portuguese sports bar. Parker Murchison, Jack Perros and Nick Collini – who started the events, like so many others, as pandemic restrictions eased – are all 24 (and all run fashion brands). The vast majority of attendees tonight, sipping Super Bock and bespoke cocktails, are well-heeled younger millennials or members of Gen Z.

“I think people want to seem smart right now,” Perros says over the sound of DJ Jiynx, who is more accustomed to playing underground venues and warehouses. “It’s like having good taste. People want to have good taste that differentiates them.”

When they put on their first event three years ago, the three friends wanted to explore the growing trend of people going out for hands-on activities such as game nights and scrapbooking meets. They stumbled into chess without thinking about it too hard, and Ssicc is now a monthly event in Toronto. They’ve also hosted nights in Los Angeles, London and Paris.

One striking thing at all of these events is how few phones are on the tables. Face-to-face interaction is clearly part of building these real-life communities. “You can’t be on your phone and play chess” over the board, Collini says. “I think people are looking for that right now.”

Chess’s most magnetic quality is, it seems, its inexhaustibility – its resistance to perfection. When the IBM computer Deep Blue beat then world champion Garry Kasparov for the first time in 1996, The Globe and Mail’s editorial board argued that a computer, no matter how advanced, would always be inferior to humans, with all their flaws and impulses.
“The manipulation of sums evinces intelligence, but reams of numbers in columns and rows do not add up to humanity. … We are our minds, and we are our passions,” the piece read.

Now, inside all these rowdy pubs and bars littered with chessboards, every person carries in their pocket a computer orders of magnitude more powerful than Deep Blue, and it feels utterly irrelevant to what’s happening at the table. As Daniel Rensch, the co-founder of chess.com , said in a recent interview, “neural nets are better than Magnus Carlsen, but it has nothing to do with the fact that we keep playing the game.”

On International Chess Day in July, Knightcap hosted an event at the Well, a multipurpose complex in downtown Toronto. Khrystyna Boyko, 19, happened to wander past with her boyfriend. Back in Ukraine, her dad had taught her how to play when she was a child, but she was never a fan until playing online during the pandemic.

“I just really love to win, and I was always trying to win, but I was losing,” she said over a game in which we both blundered away our pieces. “I feel like that’s the way I learned.” At a table nearby, Arthur Calugar, an international master and a regular at casual events in the city, patiently walked an aspiring player through the complexities of an obscure opening.

As the game’s continued democratization shows, chess is not about perfection. It’s about the ability to blunder away a queen, miscalculate an endgame or launch an audacious attack on little more than mad confidence. It allows people to fail, learn, improve and fail again – all while sipping drinks in a dimly lit room – for no more complex purpose than seeing those same human traits in others.

stories.title: Smith, Nenshi ramp up political attacks as Alberta referendum campaign enters home stretch
stories.summary: Premier takes a swipe at the NDP Leader over federal counterpart Avi Lewis’s opposition to the West Coast pipeline
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party and Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi ramped up their political attacks on each other this week as the province entered the home stretch of its referendum campaign.

On Thursday, while Ms. Smith basked in the afterglow of a West Coast pipeline being declared a project of national interest , she also took a swipe at Mr. Nenshi over federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis’s strong opposition to the proposed conduit.

Mr. Nenshi piped back with criticism of his own after it emerged earlier this week that one of Ms. Smith’s caucus members had voted by mail in favour of a second, binding vote on secession, as separatist leanings within her party continue to cause turmoil and weigh down the Premier’s popularity.

While the Oct. 19 referendum has consumed Alberta’s political scene this fall, Ms. Smith and Mr. Nenshi are preparing to spend much of the next year in campaign mode ahead of the October, 2027, provincial election.

Recently, Ms. Smith has lagged in polls and continues to deal with the fall-out of a by-election loss in Calgary’s conservative heartland. Inside her party, she is managing an uprising of separatist sentiment and pockets of discontent among UCP membership over her federalist stand.

Mr. Nenshi, ON the other hand, has been buoyed by the Ndp’s surprise by-election win. But Mr. Lewis’s disapproval of the West Coast pipeline and earlier vows to stop the expansion of oil and gas development have forced Mr. Nenshi to respond, opening his own party to familiar attacks from conservatives.

On Thursday, Ms. Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney met their shared deadline to designate a proposed pipeline to the West Coast a project of national interest.

The Premier has heralded the pipeline as proof of Alberta’s renewed relationship with Ottawa, less than three weeks before Albertans decide on remaining in Canada or working toward a binding secession vote.

But the announcement was overshadowed by news that one of Ms. Smith’s caucus members, Jason Stephan, had voted for holding a second, binding referendum on separation.

He described the choice as one that “puts Ottawa on notice,” while voting to remain in Canada “affirms the status quo, a nation in decline, dragging Alberta down with it.”

On Thursday, Ms. Smith – who says she will vote to remain in Canada – said she welcomes a variety of opinions in her party.

Mr. Stephan remains a member of caucus. He did not respond to a request for comment.

The pipeline announcement, meanwhile, reignited a dormant conflict between the federal and provincial NDP, which have long warred over their positions on oil-and-gas development.

Mr. Lewis criticized the plan as a “pipeline to the courts” and “another gift to the oil industry,” while Mr. Nenshi applauded the news: “I’m looking forward to actually getting it built in conjunction with the strongest environmental safeguards in the world,” he said on Friday.

Ms. Smith latched on to Mr. Lewis’s comments, calling on Mr. Nenshi to break with the federal NDP – “right down to the name of their party,” she wrote.

Asked about Ms. Smith’s call to change the party name, Mr. Nenshi said: “If you’re giving me advice on my party, I’ll give you some on yours: Kick out the separatists.”

Mr. Lewis’s stand against oil-and-gas development has appeared to widen the chasm between the national party and its provincial counterparts, many of whom are competing to win their respective governments. Mr. Nenshi and Saskatchewan NDP Leader Carla Beck both denounced his plans for the sector when he was elected party leader in March.

“We’ve cut that tie with the federal NDP, and fundamentally, he can say what he likes,” Mr. Nenshi said of Mr. Lewis on Friday, referring to the provincial party’s decision in 2025 to make federal party membership optional.

Mr. Nenshi had previously appealed to Mr. Lewis and the other contenders running for federal party leadership to not damage his 2027 election campaign.

On Friday, Mr. Nenshi dismissed Ms. Smith’s efforts to link him to the federal party leader.

“They would like nothing more than to tie me to Avi Lewis, and it’s been completely unsuccessful so far, and it will continue to be completely unsuccessful,” he said.

Anne McGrath, principal secretary to former Alberta NDP premier Rachel Notley, said in an interview that tension between the federal and Alberta NDP over pipeline development is an enduring feature of New Democratic politics.

Ms. McGrath, also a former campaign director for the federal NDP, said she believes the public understands the differences between the national and provincial parties.

“I think that they understand that tension. They live in that tension,” said Ms. McGrath of the Alberta NDP.

“But they, I don’t think are going to spend a lot of time raising hell about it or anything like that.”

stories.title: Catholic nuns end affiliation with Nova Scotia hospital, clearing way for Maid, abortion services
stories.summary: No changes to services have been made at the renamed Antigonish Memorial Regional Hospital as it undergoes a transition period
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
The crucifixes are gone. The masses are done. And the carved wooden statues of nuns have been relocated to a local museum, marking the end of an era at a regional hospital in the northeastern Nova Scotia town of Antigonish.

A congregation of aging Roman Catholic nuns, who founded St. Martha’s Regional Hospital more than a century ago, will no longer sponsor the facility, clearing the way for the health facility to offer medical assistance in dying and abortion services under one roof.

The historic change for the Nova Scotia hospital is happening at a time of powerful religious opposition to MAID and intense debate in the courts over who should be allowed access to the procedure.

“We’re not closing doors, we’re not dying yet,” said Sister Brendalee Boisvert, the Congregation Leader of the Sisters of St. Martha, known as “the Marthas,” in an interview.

“We’re just choosing where we can put our best energies, and we felt that administration and hospital – because it’s so litigious too now – that it’s not an area that we have a lot of members’ expertise in. So we decided this is a good time.”

On Oct. 1, the hospital officially became Antigonish Memorial Regional Hospital – no longer a Catholic hospital, where abortion and MAID were prohibited. The hospital, which serves about 100,000 people from Antigonish, Guysborough and surrounding communities, was the only publicly funded hospital in Nova Scotia where access to health care was restricted because of a religious affiliation.

The Nova Scotia Health Authority, meanwhile, says no changes to services have been made at the hospital, as it’s undergoing a transition period.

During a visit to France late last month, Pope Leo XIV blasted the legalization of medically assisted death as immoral, calling it “false compassion.”

The faces of MAID

The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has been hearing a challenge to the federal government’s decision to bar MAID in cases of mental illness.

In B.C., a Charter challenge in April was centred around the case of the late Samantha O’Neill, who was diagnosed with Stage 4 cervical cancer at age 34 and transferred from a faith-based facility for a MAID procedure. According to Dying With Dignity Canada, which was part of the court challenge, she “went through a painful, undignified forced transfer” and “suffered needlessly in her final days because of the religious beliefs of a publicly funded health care organization.”

The decision from the Supreme Court of B.C. is expected this fall and could determine whether publicly funded religious health facilities banning MAID is a violation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

For the past 30 years, the Nova Scotia nuns have been a sponsor of the Mission Assurance Agreement, a partnership with the province designed to ensure the hospital operates under Catholic values. Prior to that, the Sisters of St. Martha had run the hospital since its founding in 1906.

When MAID became legal a decade ago, the Catholic hospital prohibited its use. Advocates argued that a publicly funded hospital enforcing a religious-based ban violated the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Then in 2019, after mounting public and legal pressure, the Nova Scotia Health Authority quietly allowed MAID to take place at a local health clinic nearby.

With the Catholic influence now removed, it eliminates the need for the transfer of fragile patients to the clinic, which could cause unnecessary pain or even the loss of access to MAID if they aren’t stable enough for the transfer, said Jocelyn Downie, Schulich School of Law professor emerita in Dalhousie University’s faculties of law and medicine. Ms. Downie was a member of the legal team for the landmark Supreme Court of Canada decision Carter vs. Canada, which paved the way for MAID.

“More dramatically, it now means that abortion, gender affirming care, surgical sterilization, birth control etc. can now be provided at that hospital,” she wrote to The Globe and Mail in response to questions.

“People in Antigonish requiring and desiring these services will no longer be told that they must leave their community for health care just because the Catholic Church disapproves of it.”

Patients in some other provinces, including B.C., Alberta and Ontario, face challenges and even absolute barriers to access to care simply because it violates the beliefs of some protected religious institution, Prof. Downie added.

The Nova Scotia Health Authority, which runs the hospital, did not answer whether abortion or MAID would be offered on site. Spokesperson Jennifer Lewandowski said “access to care and services continues to be our priority.” Changes would be made in collaboration with physicians and staff, she added.

“As part of that transition, we are looking carefully at the hospital’s services and policies and how they will more closely align with other hospitals across Nova Scotia,” she said in a statement.

The Marthas, whose median age is 87, had arranged for another group, Catholic Health International of New Brunswick, to take over as sponsor of the Mission Assurance Agreement when they announced earlier this year that they were stepping back. The provincial government and the health authority declined the proposal.

“After much discussion it was determined that in the Sisters’ absence, it no longer made sense to have a new sponsor,” Nova Scotia Health Minister Michelle Thompson wrote in a statement to The Globe and Mail.

While deconfessionalization – the removal of religious influence – occurred in Quebec health facilities years ago, Dying With Dignity Canada chief executive Helen Long said the change in Nova Scotia represents a shift in people’s beliefs.

“I think people are very focused on their own autonomy, their own choice, their own suffering and they’re continuing to want access to the care they need regardless of the institutions,” she said.

Nearly 60 per cent of the population of Antigonish County identifies as Catholic, according to Statistics Canada. And Catholicism is woven into the community and local institutions because of the Sisters of St. Martha.

They started as a congregation in 1900, cooking and cleaning for the students and faculty at St. Francis Xavier University.

As a tuberculosis epidemic raged and with no health care institution for hundreds of kilometres, the nuns established a cottage hospital with six beds in 1906.

In 1926, a new state-of-the-art brick building opened, and St. Martha’s School of Nursing became affiliated with St. FX, a collaboration that ended in 1995.

In 1996, a regional health authority, accountable to the province, took over running the hospital from the sisters. In 2015, it became province-run as part of a provincewide amalgamated health authority.

The legacy of the Sisters of St. Martha won’t be completely wiped out, said Sister Boisvert. A stone carving “legacy piece” is in the works for the entrance to the hospital to remember their contributions. Both she and the health authority spokesperson say the word “memorial” in the hospital’s new name recognizes the history, care and compassion that the sisters helped establish in the town 120 years ago.

“It’s a new beginning,” Sister Boisvert said.

Then in 2019, after mounting public and legal pressure, the Nova Scotia Health Authority quietly allowed MAID to take place at a local health clinic nearby.

With the Catholic influence now removed, it eliminates the need for the transfer of fragile patients to the clinic, which could cause unnecessary pain or even the loss of access to MAID if they aren’t stable enough for the transfer, said Jocelyn Downie, Schulich School of Law professor emerita in Dalhousie University’s faculties of law and medicine. Ms. Downie was a member of the legal team for the landmark Supreme Court of Canada decision Carter vs. Canada, which paved the way for MAID.

“More dramatically, it now means that abortion, gender affirming care, surgical sterilization, birth control etc. can now be provided at that hospital,” she wrote to The Globe and Mail in response to questions.
“People in Antigonish requiring and desiring these services will no longer be told that they must leave their community for health care just because the Catholic Church disapproves of it.”

Patients in some other provinces, including B.C., Alberta and Ontario, face challenges and even absolute barriers to access to care simply because it violates the beliefs of some protected religious institution, Prof. Downie added.

The Nova Scotia Health Authority, which runs the hospital, did not answer whether abortion or MAID would be offered on site. Spokesperson Jennifer Lewandowski said “access to care and services continues to be our priority.” Changes would be made in collaboration with physicians and staff, she added.
“As part of that transition, we are looking carefully at the hospital’s services and policies and how they will more closely align with other hospitals across Nova Scotia,” she said in a statement.

The Marthas, whose median age is 87, had arranged for another group, Catholic Health International of New Brunswick, to take over as sponsor of the Mission Assurance Agreement when they announced earlier this year that they were stepping back. The provincial government and the health authority declined the proposal.

“After much discussion it was determined that in the Sisters’ absence, it no longer made sense to have a new sponsor,” Nova Scotia Health Minister Michelle Thompson wrote in a statement to The Globe and Mail.

While deconfessionalization – the removal of religious influence – occurred in Quebec health facilities years ago, Dying With Dignity Canada chief executive Helen Long said the change in Nova Scotia represents a shift in people’s beliefs.
“I think people are very focused on their own autonomy, their own choice, their own suffering and they’re continuing to want access to the care they need regardless of the institutions,” she said.

Nearly 60 per cent of the population of Antigonish County identifies as Catholic, according to Statistics Canada. And Catholicism is woven into the community and local institutions because of the Sisters of St. Martha.
They started as a congregation in 1900, cooking and cleaning for the students and faculty at St. Francis Xavier University.
As a tuberculosis epidemic raged and with no health care institution for hundreds of kilometres, the nuns established a cottage hospital with six beds in 1906.
In 1926, a new state-of-the-art brick building opened, and St. Martha’s School of Nursing became affiliated with St. FX, a collaboration that ended in 1995.

In 1996, a regional health authority, accountable to the province, took over running the hospital from the sisters. In 2015, it became province-run as part of a provincewide amalgamated health authority.

The legacy of the Sisters of St. Martha won’t be completely wiped out, said Sister Boisvert. A stone carving “legacy piece” is in the works for the entrance to the hospital to remember their contributions. Both she and the health authority spokesperson say the word “memorial” in the hospital’s new name recognizes the history, care and compassion that the sisters helped establish in the town 120 years ago.
“It’s a new beginning,” Sister Boisvert said.

stories.title: Byline or bot? AI-generated 'journalists' start to appear in Canada
stories.summary: Quebec correspondent “Geneviève Tremblay” — who has been reporting on multiple news stories a day lately — seemed to be experiencing a glitch.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec correspondent “Geneviève Tremblay” — who has been reporting on multiple news stories a day lately — seemed to be experiencing a glitch.

She wasn’t the only one. All of We News’ reporters and editors seemed to be malfunctioning on Friday, sending out error messages whenever The Canadian Press tried to ask them questions via chat.

That can happen when your “journalists” are — like the virtual staffers at We News — just fake personas generated by artificial intelligence.

AI has infiltrated news media in Canada and around the world. In early September, Nunatsiaq News published a story about an AI persona posing as an Inuk journalist in Nunavut — one of many personas used to repurpose work from legitimate news sources, including The Canadian Press, for We News.

The site describes itself as a “round-the-clock news portal covering Canada and the world.” But while it remains online, it appears to have been delisted from Google’s search results.

In late September, the story of “Daniel Robson” emerged. Canadian news outlets pulled his work from their websites after being told Robson appeared not to be a real person.

Policy Options editor-in-chief Les Perreaux was the first to sound the alarm in Canada. In an online post on Sept. 24, Perreaux wrote that an editor at Türkiye Today contacted him to ask him to vouch for Robson — and he realized he couldn’t.

“The key moment where my heart sank was when the Turkish journalist told me that Daniel Robson refused to do a video call,” Perreaux said in an interview.

Perreaux said he reviewed the correspondence and material Robson sent and spotted signs of AI product. He said the bigger issue was the attempt to deceive news editors and readers, while AI merely acted as an “accelerant.”

“AI is definitely part of the story, but it’s a smaller part than the deception part where there was a human behind this, pretending to be someone he’s not, or at least refusing to be who he really is,” he said.

In a story published on Sept. 29, Türkiye Today said the purpose of the Robson persona seems to be to attack Moroccan dissidents.

We News isn’t hiding its use of AI and clearly labels its “journalist” profiles — including photos of what appear to be human beings — as AI generated.

The AI personas at We News, which include grey-haired editor-in-chief “Gordon Halloway,” repurpose international, national, provincial and local news in more than 100 cities across Canada.

The Canadian Press did attempt to reach a human behind the site, but the contact email address listed on the site bounced back.

When the AI detection company Originality.ai analyzed just over 200 articles by “Geneviève Tremblay,” it identified them as AI-generated.

Originality.ai CEO Jon Gillham said the articles were rewritten versions of stories published by legitimate news media outlets like CBC, CTV, CityNews, Global and the Montreal Gazette. The Canadian Press also found its own reporting among the sources.

“I think industrial-scale AI slop (sites) like this one run the risk of degrading the trust in the news,” Gillham said.

The phenomenon isn’t limited to Canada. On Sept. 17, the U.S.-based website Futurism published a story about Brown Brothers Media, a company Futurism said bought up legitimate news sites and flooded them with AI-generated content — and claimed to pull 50 million page views a month.

Ahmed Al-Rawi, a professor of news, social media and public communication at Simon Fraser University, said sites with fake AI journalists are trying to monetize content.

“A lot of players, whether they are bad players or just profiteers, people who are really trying to get money, are exploiting the hard work of real journalists in order to repackage news content,” he said.

Al-Rawi said social media platforms “should also be blamed for enhancing the popularity of these fake websites.”

Western University assistant professor of journalism Chris Arsenault said it’s difficult to regulate these websites.

“You can get a free or very cheap AI model to pump out this kind of nonsense, and you can always find somebody to host it,” he said. “So it’s a very hard thing to legislate around or to respond to in terms of effective policy.”

Paul Deegan, president of the publishers group News Media Canada, said while news content is covered by copyright, it’s very difficult for publishers to sue.

“It’s expensive, it takes a long time, whether or not they are in fact in Canada,” he said. (We News says it’s based in Hong Kong.)

News Media Canada is calling on the federal government to state publicly that it does not intend to introduce a broad exception to copyright law for text and data mining.

AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office said in a media statement that “Canadians deserve to know when the information they consume has been generated or altered by AI.”

“Generative AI can be a useful and powerful tool, but Canadians should not be deceived by content that impersonates journalists or conceals how it was created,” the statement said.

Solomon’s office pointed to a recently-concluded consultation on AI transparency and said it recognizes “the concerns raised by journalists and other creators about consent, compensation, attribution and transparency when their work is used to train AI systems.”

There May be no silver bullet to solve the problem, but Arsenault said there is one antidote: old-fashioned reporting.

He noted the “Daniel Robson” case came to light because “of an old-school editor in Turkey who had the temerity and good sense to just, God forbid, pick up a telephone and do some basic journalism, just do some due diligence on a would-be contributor.”

Futurism reported on Sept. 30 that the Brown Brothers Media sites now appear to have stopped publishing and were delisted or significantly downranked by Google.

In Canada, We News also appears to have been delisted. When The Canadian Press searched for the website using Google’s search engine, it got no results — but the site immediately popped up as the top result on another search engine.

Google did not directly answer questions about whether it has delisted We News from its search results, when it May have done so, and whether that was the result of news coverage about its AI “journalists.”

A spokesperson said in a statement the company’s policies for search and Google News “prohibit producing low-value content at scale to game our ranking systems.”

“While we generally don’t comment on individual sites, we act on policy violations to keep 99 per cent of search visits spam-free,” the spokesperson added.

Deegan said it’s in Google’s interest to “make sure that when people go to Google for information that they’re getting accurate information … For them to de-rank and remove these sites that are clearly involved in theft makes sense.”

But Arsenault questioned whether Big Tech companies should be “playing hall monitor and being arbiters of truth.”

“They have a role to play in taking down stuff that’s clearly untrue … But I don’t know if we want them making those editorial judgments.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

In late September, the story of “Daniel Robson” emerged. Canadian news outlets pulled his work from their websites after being told Robson appeared not to be a real person.

Policy Options editor-in-chief Les Perreaux was the first to sound the alarm in Canada. In an online post on Sept. 24, Perreaux wrote that an editor at Türkiye Today contacted him to ask him to vouch for Robson — and he realized he couldn’t.
“The key moment where my heart sank was when the Turkish journalist told me that Daniel Robson refused to do a video call,” Perreaux said in an interview.

Perreaux said he reviewed the correspondence and material Robson sent and spotted signs of AI product. He said the bigger issue was the attempt to deceive news editors and readers, while AI merely acted as an “accelerant.”

“AI is definitely part of the story, but it’s a smaller part than the deception part where there was a human behind this, pretending to be someone he’s not, or at least refusing to be who he really is,” he said.
In a story published on Sept. 29, Türkiye Today said the purpose of the Robson persona seems to be to attack Moroccan dissidents.
We News isn’t hiding its use of AI and clearly labels its “journalist” profiles — including photos of what appear to be human beings — as AI generated.
The AI personas at We News, which include grey-haired editor-in-chief “Gordon Halloway,” repurpose international, national, provincial and local news in more than 100 cities across Canada.
The Canadian Press did attempt to reach a human behind the site, but the contact email address listed on the site bounced back.
When the AI detection company Originality.ai analyzed just over 200 articles by “Geneviève Tremblay,” it identified them as AI-generated.

Originality.ai CEO Jon Gillham said the articles were rewritten versions of stories published by legitimate news media outlets like CBC, CTV, CityNews, Global and the Montreal Gazette. The Canadian Press also found its own reporting among the sources.
“I think industrial-scale AI slop (sites) like this one run the risk of degrading the trust in the news,” Gillham said.

The phenomenon isn’t limited to Canada. On Sept. 17, the U.S.-based website Futurism published a story about Brown Brothers Media, a company Futurism said bought up legitimate news sites and flooded them with AI-generated content — and claimed to pull 50 million page views a month.
Ahmed Al-Rawi, a professor of news, social media and public communication at Simon Fraser University, said sites with fake AI journalists are trying to monetize content.

“A lot of players, whether they are bad players or just profiteers, people who are really trying to get money, are exploiting the hard work of real journalists in order to repackage news content,” he said.
Al-Rawi said social media platforms “should also be blamed for enhancing the popularity of these fake websites.”
Western University assistant professor of journalism Chris Arsenault said it’s difficult to regulate these websites.

“You can get a free or very cheap AI model to pump out this kind of nonsense, and you can always find somebody to host it,” he said. “So it’s a very hard thing to legislate around or to respond to in terms of effective policy.”
Paul Deegan, president of the publishers group News Media Canada, said while news content is covered by copyright, it’s very difficult for publishers to sue.
“It’s expensive, it takes a long time, whether or not they are in fact in Canada,” he said. (We News says it’s based in Hong Kong.)
News Media Canada is calling on the federal government to state publicly that it does not intend to introduce a broad exception to copyright law for text and data mining.
AI Minister Evan Solomon’s office said in a media statement that “Canadians deserve to know when the information they consume has been generated or altered by AI.”
“Generative AI can be a useful and powerful tool, but Canadians should not be deceived by content that impersonates journalists or conceals how it was created,” the statement said.

Solomon’s office pointed to a recently-concluded consultation on AI transparency and said it recognizes “the concerns raised by journalists and other creators about consent, compensation, attribution and transparency when their work is used to train AI systems.”
There May be no silver bullet to solve the problem, but Arsenault said there is one antidote: old-fashioned reporting.

He noted the “Daniel Robson” case came to light because “of an old-school editor in Turkey who had the temerity and good sense to just, God forbid, pick up a telephone and do some basic journalism, just do some due diligence on a would-be contributor.”
Futurism reported on Sept. 30 that the Brown Brothers Media sites now appear to have stopped publishing and were delisted or significantly downranked by Google.

In Canada, We News also appears to have been delisted. When The Canadian Press searched for the website using Google’s search engine, it got no results — but the site immediately popped up as the top result on another search engine.

Google did not directly answer questions about whether it has delisted We News from its search results, when it May have done so, and whether that was the result of news coverage about its AI “journalists.”
A spokesperson said in a statement the company’s policies for search and Google News “prohibit producing low-value content at scale to game our ranking systems.”
“While we generally don’t comment on individual sites, we act on policy violations to keep 99 per cent of search visits spam-free,” the spokesperson added.

Deegan said it’s in Google’s interest to “make sure that when people go to Google for information that they’re getting accurate information … For them to de-rank and remove these sites that are clearly involved in theft makes sense.”
But Arsenault questioned whether Big Tech companies should be “playing hall monitor and being arbiters of truth.”
“They have a role to play in taking down stuff that’s clearly untrue … But I don’t know if we want them making those editorial judgments.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.
Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. candidates and voters scramble to get their minds around two elections, one week apart
stories.summary: The races are on for the municipal and provincial elections, but the turnout could suffer
stories.author: Mike Hager, Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The mess of 14 large election signs featuring the faces of dozens of municipal and provincial politicians that sat along one of Surrey’s major thoroughfares became a symbol this week of the confusion permeating many parts of B.C.

The tangle of typography at the intersection – with five massive signs inside the yard of the corner house towering over the others zap-strapped onto the family’s fence – illustrated the difficult duty confronting British Columbians in the coming weeks. A handful of school trustee candidates’ signs had been shunted to the edge of the property, laying in a tidy sidewalk pile.

This month will see the first overlap of municipal and provincial elections since British Columbia’s Election Act was passed in 1995.

The homeowners didn’t want to speak on the record Thursday, but told The Globe and Mail the signs would soon be gone after learning their house had gained infamy online.

In Surrey alone, more than 380,000 eligible voters will be asked to cast a ballot for a mayor, eight councillors and six school trustees on Oct. 17 before returning the next weekend to select their preferred MLA. In total, voters in the Vancouver suburb and B.C.’s second biggest city will have to sift through nearly 100 candidates for the municipal elections. On Oct. 24, there’s expected to be a total of at least 20 candidates, likely more, running across Surrey’s 10 provincial ridings.

Many in B.C. say they are burdened by the mental math needed to identify and choose their preferred candidates in the concurrent contests. The splintering and subsequent partial reunification of the provincial Conservatives has created a more crowded political landscape, which now includes two upstart rightwing parties promising they will compete in the majority of the 93 ridings.

Experts warn voter turnout could suffer, especially in municipal races planned years before Premier David Eby called a snap election on Sept. 22 .

On Vancouver Island, Saanich resident Robert Randall, who himself ran unsuccessfully for Victoria council in 2008, said he finds the overlapping elections especially confusing because many of voters’ biggest concerns – such as affordability, homelessness and housing development – are being discussed at both levels, with both sets of politicians giving many of the same answers.

“I feel annoyed because researching a new mayor and a full slate of council candidates is a hard enough job without having an unscheduled provincial election dropped in the middle of it,” Mr. Randall said.

“I won’t take it out on the party in charge as I’m still a likely NDP voter, but I won’t be going to the polling booth with a skip in my step.”

Two weeks ago, at the weeklong Union of B.C. Municipalities convention in Vancouver, mayors and councillors from cities and towns across B.C. pleaded for things to be different. The group united to pass an emergency resolution urging Mr. Eby to hold off on calling a provincial election until after municipal voting on Oct. 17, to avoid interfering with local campaigns.

Cori Ramsay, an incumbent Prince George council candidate who just finished her term as Ubcm president, said she is worried that too many of the temporary workers needed to pull off the local election in her northern city will chase the slightly-higher wages offered by the provincial election agency.

“If we don’t get the required [staffing] turnout then it’s going to be really long lines, it’s going to run the risk of people not wanting to go line up for the provincial poll and then come over to the municipal polls – because we got the advanced poll day for the province the exact same day as the municipal election,” she told The Globe.

The twin elections have also created the unusual situation of candidates running in both contests.

Kevin Acton has been the mayor of the Village of Lumby in the north Okanagan since 2009. He is simultaneously seeking re-election and running as the Conservative candidate in Vernon-Lumby. Should he win both races, B.C. law would automatically deem him to have resigned as mayor once the writ confirming his provincial election is returned, triggering a mayoral by-election.

Mr. Acton said the early election call created “a lot of confusion and angst” among community members, including some concerned that he would abandon his mayoral bid and hand challenger Bradley Weston a “free seat.”

If, instead, he wins both elections, the resulting mayoral by-election – which he has pledged to pay for personally – could draw new candidates, including long-time councillor Randal Ostafichuk, who declared his interest on Tuesday.

Keeping his two candidacies straight has required some careful choreography. Mr. Acton said his coffee-shop campaign stops in Lumby remain focused on village issues, provincial events are clearly identified, and he will wait until after the municipal election to expand his door-knocking beyond Lumby.

“I can tell you, for the first few days, my head was spinning,” Mr. Acton said.

Others – including Courtenay councillor Will Cole-Hamilton, Terrace councillor Sarah Zimmerman and Central Saanich Mayor Ryan Windsor – withdrew from their local contests before running provincially.

Less than two weeks ago, Andrew Weaver, the climate scientist and former leader of the BC Green Party, was serving as campaign manager for his wife, Jordan Weaver, who is running for a seat on Saanich council.

Mr. Weaver felt compelled to return to provincial politics when nearly all the group of Conservative defectors who had joined the upstart CentreBC party returned to their old party. That left behind new CentreBC leader Elenore Sturko, whom he felt needed his support.

“I have no financial agent. I haven’t raised a penny. I have no rack cards. I have no signs,” Mr. Weaver told The Globe on Sept. 23, his first day as a CentreBC candidate in his old riding of Oak Bay-Gordon Head.

Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer at the University of B.C., said he expects the advantage incumbent candidates often enjoy in municipal elections to be heightened in this chaotic atmosphere because it will be harder for aspiring first-time politicians to “break through” and ingratiate themselves to enough voters.

Darin Nesbitt, a political science instructor at Douglas College, said voters are being asked to navigate two sets of candidates, ballots, polling places and voting dates, potentially compounding existing uncertainty about which level of government does what. And, he said, with bigger budgets, higher profile leaders and more media coverage, provincial campaigns risk drowning out municipal issues such as housing approvals, transit and police.

“When voting starts to feel like homework, some people simply opt out,” Prof. Nesbitt said.

stories.title: Poilievre's popularity lags behind his party, but few options on the horizon, new poll finds
stories.summary: The Conservative Party of Canada is more popular with Canadian voters than party head Pierre Poilievre.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Conservative Party of Canada is more popular with Canadian voters than party head Pierre Poilievre, according to a new poll that suggests one-third of potential Tory supporters don’t do so simply because they don’t like the leader.

But the poll from U.K.-based firm Lord Ashcroft Polls also suggests that swapping Poilievre for another leader is far from a panacea for Conservative woes.

That’s because while certain groups of voters say they would more likely vote for the Conservatives under an unnamed different leader, the change would also correlate with losses among the current Tory base, the poll finds.

“Switching leadership would bring its own risks,” reads the report.

“Changing leader could… mean alienating core supporters while at best standing still among softer voters and potential converts. The costs are therefore clearer than the uncertain reward.”

The poll surveyed a representative sample of 10,098 Canadians online between July 31 and Aug. 17 and hosted 16 focus groups held in B.C., Alberta, Quebec and Ontario.

Notably, 47 per cent of respondents thought Canada is headed in the wrong direction, compared to 40 per cent who said the country is on the right track.

And yet, the poll found that Prime Minister and Liberal Leader Mark Carney was the only leader of a major federal political party whose personal popularity exceeded that of his party.

That poses a particular challenge for Poilievre because the current federal landscape suggests an election would be a two-way battle between Liberals and Conservatives while Avi Lewis’s NDP looks to re-emerge from the ashes of the devastating 2025 vote.

“The PM was also a less polarizing figure than his opponent. While Poilievre is rated –64% by Liberal voters, Carney is only rated –33% among Conservatives,” Lord Ashcroft Polls found.

According to the poll, 60 per cent of respondents had a positive impression of Carney while 55 per cent said the same of the Liberal party. For Poilievre, 43 per cent of those surveyed viewed him positively (compared to 50 per cent negatively), six points below the Conservative party as a whole (49 per cent).

But the report notes the effect is even more pronounced among crucial voter groups for Conservatives.

During polling, “potential but currently unlikely Conservative voters” pegged not liking Poilievre (34 per cent) and the party feeling too close to U.S.-style politics (29 per cent) as the two top reasons they were put off from voting Tory.

More than half (53 per cent) of another key group, “persuadable Liberals” (recent Liberal voters who identified the Tories as their “clear second choice”), told Lord Ashcroft they were more likely to vote Conservative under a different leader than Poilievre.

That group is most likely to peg U.S. trade as one of three top issues facing Canada today, an issue poll respondents largely said they trust Carney to deal with better than Poilievre.

When combined with the fact that Conservatives’ current popularity challenges with the electorate are also tied to perception of it being “too American,” the prospect of another election centred around U.S. President Donald Trump could be terrible for Tories, according to the report.

“In Australia as well as Canada, incumbent governments pulled off upset victories by framing their national elections as referendums on President Trump’s trade policies and portraying the centre-right party as a proxy for the Americans,” reads the report.

“Allowing the Liberals to repeat the trick would give them the opportunity to galvanize the Carney coalition and leave the Conservatives trapped at their previous ceiling, inviting the same result.”

But there are chinks in Carney’s seemingly impenetrable polling armour too, the report notes. Respondents offered “mixed feelings” about Carney’s dealing with Trump, and fewer than half of respondents said the Carney government is “making progress and doing some good things.”

Furthermore, 45 per cent of respondents said they felt worse off compared to one year ago, whereas only 17 per cent said they were doing better.

stories.title: From ‘political orphan’ to probable premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is going 'all-in' on separatism
stories.summary: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon once described himself as a disappointed federalist. Now, he’s prepared to hold a third referendum.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
This story was first published on Oct. 3

Quebec City — “To the sovereigntists, I say this: your obsession with holding and winning a referendum harms the progressive cause and feels like psychological harassment to a majority of the population. Many voters share my view.”

These words May seem like they would come out of the mouth of a federalist politician in Quebec, but they were written by Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon in his book Les Orphelins politiques (The Political Orphans) published in 2014.

Twelve years later, St-Pierre Plamondon has been elected premier of a PQ government, promising to hold the referendum that he once deplored despite his party’s minority status.

St-Pierre Plamondon has pulled off a stunning political metamorphosis. He claims to have voted “Yes” in the 1995 referendum when he turned 18 but decamped to federalist circles when he attended law school at McGill University and when he was a young lawyer.

In fact, the PQ leader was friends with Sacha Trudeau and even attended his wedding in 2009. St-Pierre Plamondon also co-founded Génération d’idées, a think tank dedicated to young people aged 20 to 35, with now Industry Minister Mélanie Joly.

St-Pierre Plamondon also donated $2,300 to the Liberal Party of Canada between 2004 and 2008, when working as a junior lawyer at the Montreal firm Stikeman Elliott.

Asked by National Post if he was once a federalist, the PQ leader replied: “Yes, I guess you can say that.”

But he added it is not an anomaly for leaders of the sovereigntist party to have a change of heart. PQ founder René Lévesque was once a federalist, as was Jacques Parizeau, he said. Both men still ended up becoming the face of the 1980 and 1995 referendums.

“Our greatest leaders have all been (federalists),” said Claude Villeneuve, a former speechwriter for the last PQ premier, Pauline Marois. He also unsuccessfully ran a candidate for St-Pierre Plamondon’s team in Quebec City.

Like Lévesque and Parizeau, the PQ leader experienced a “rupture” with federalism, said Villeneuve.

St-Pierre Plamondon has claimed it was his work at Stikeman for Groupe Polygone — one of the firms involved in what came to be known as the sponsorship scandal — that helped revive the sovereigntist political convictions he had as a young adult.

Frédéric Bérard, a constitutional lawyer who is one of St-Pierre Plamondon’s fiercest critics, was working at the firm at the time. He said the math does not add up.

He noted that St-Pierre Plamondon donated to the federal Liberals until 2008, years after the start of the Gomery Inquiry.

“It’s funny, actually. The sovereigntists I know don’t donate money to the Liberal Party of Canada. It’s crazy like that,” Bérard said.

It is unclear what led to the falling out between St-Pierre Plamondon and Joly, although one rumour is that Joly accepted an invitation to go to one of Quebec’s biggest talk shows in 2008 to talk about Génération d’idées without first informing her co-founder.

Joly did not respond to a request for comment for this article, nor did Sacha Trudeau.

As a “political orphan” circa 2014, St-Pierre Plamondon spent his time lambasting the traditional political parties in Quebec that, according to him, had nothing new to offer.

He was critical of the PQ for its “obsession” about holding another referendum, which he said alienated many progressives in the province, and said many Quebecers, allergic to corruption and cronyism, wanted nothing to do with the Quebec Liberals.

So, it was a surprise to many when, in 2016, St-Pierre Plamondon decided to first run for the leadership of the PQ. “The orphan-in-chief has found himself a foster family,” wrote at the time Vincent Marissal, then a columnist at La Presse .

In this leadership bid, the young politician described himself as a “disappointed federalist.” He proposed to hold a third referendum only in a second mandate, and only if 20 per cent of the population of Quebec signed a register demanding it.

St-Pierre Plamondon ended the race with seven per cent of the vote, which was considered a fair result for a political rookie who was a relatively unknown figure.

The winner of the 2016 PQ leadership race, Jean-François Lisée, decided to task the young recruit with holding consultations on the state of the party. St-Pierre Plamondon took that task to heart, criss-crossing the province, and delivering his report in 2017.

“Osez repenser le PQ” (“Dare to Rethink the PQ”) was a scathing assessment of the party that was too old and too white. The internal reaction to the report was terrible, to say the least, and its author reportedly got a dressing-down from the PQ caucus.

After failing to win a seat in the 2018 election, St-Pierre Plamondon left the political scene to go back to practicing law in a small firm in the Outaouais region.

Louis Lyonnais was part of a small group of supporters who would drive to St-Pierre Plamondon’s home in Buckingham, Quebec, to try to convince him to consider running again to become PQ leader. Lisée had resigned the night of the election.

“He didn’t say yes right away, but the idea simmered,” said Lyonnais.

“Finally, we convinced him.”

St-Pierre Plamondon ran for leader a second time. But this time, he would promise to hold a referendum in a first mandate. And he hasn’t changed his mind since.

He published another book, “Rebâtir le camp du OUI” (“Rebuilding the Yes camp”) during that race in which he explained that Quebec separating from the rest of Canada in a first mandate is “a matter of linguistic and cultural survival for Quebec.”

“Quebec’s independence is not only legitimate but necessary, because Canada condemns us to decline — linguistically, culturally, and economically. It also condemns us to a culture of dishonesty, as well as to chronic instability,” he wrote.

I think people told themselves, ‘This guy won’t bullsh-t us’

Lyonnais, who now acts as one of St-Pierre Plamondon’s most trusted aides, said the change of heart on the timing of a referendum was in part because of the perceived setbacks in terms of language and culture under the Trudeau years.

St-Pierre Plamondon, even though he was polling third at the start of the race, became leader of the party in 2020. And because it took place during the pandemic, he pronounced his victory speech without an audience.

He was elected in the eastern Montreal riding of Camille-Laurin in 2022, in part thanks to a Québec Solidaire candidate who withdrew after she was caught stealing PQ flyers from mailboxes to replace them with flyers of her own party.

St-Pierre Plamondon was one of three members of his party who won seats in that election, the worst score in the party’s history. But that didn’t stop him.

He made his mark immediately in the National Assembly of Quebec when he and the other elected members of his party refused to swear allegiance to King Charles.

Lyonnais said that moment “unlocked” something for the new leader.

“It gave him, I think, credibility in front of Quebecers,” he said. “I think people told themselves, ‘This guy won’t bullsh-t us. If he says something, he will see his idea through to the end.’”

A former PQ staffer, who spoke on a not-for-attribution basis, said that when St-Pierre Plamondon has an idea in mind, he cannot take his eyes off the ball.

“Paul can’t be told that something is impossible.”

It could be a good or a bad thing in a premier, said the staffer. He will be the type of person who can break the mould and do things differently. But the government is a slow machine, resistant to changes, and he might come up against challenges.

St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum in a first mandate that a majority of Quebecers don’t want. But only after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office, he said, which would push it to 2029 at the soonest.

Lyonnais admits that it would have been easier to drop that promise and that the party would probably have had better poll numbers if that were the case.

“But we’re not doing that because it would not be responsible.”

Bérard said he also thinks St-Pierre Plamondon will go “all in” with his promise.

“The problem with guys like him is that it’s never enough. So, becoming president of the Republic of Quebec, succeeding where Parizeau and Lévesque have failed?”

“Of course he’ll do it.”
