stories.title: Quebec political leaders make final pitch as election campaign nears end
stories.summary: Montreal - The leaders of Quebec's five main parties will make their last pitches to undecided voters over the weekend, with the election set for Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec’s political parties are making a final push for undecided voters as the provincial election campaign enters its last weekend before Monday’s vote.

The leaders of the five main parties made multiple appearances in the province Saturday, appealing to voters in key regions as they sought to shore up support and make last-minute gains.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette used a campaign stop in Saint-Hubert, south of Montreal, to urge voters to stick with what she called the Caq’s “third way” between federalism and sovereignty.

For decades, she said, Quebecers were forced to define themselves politically as either federalists or sovereigntists, a divide the CAQ sought to move beyond when it came to power in 2018.

“We thought we had moved past it, but no, it has come back in recent days,” Fréchette said.

The question of Quebec sovereignty has returned to the forefront in the final days of the campaign, with the Parti Québécois leading in the polls and promising to hold a referendum in 2029.

Fréchette said many voters are still undecided and argued that Quebecers who don’t want to return to the federalist-sovereigntist divide should support the CAQ.

“There are still two days, and for many Quebecers, those are two days for reflection,” she said.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard also turned his attention to the sovereignty question Saturday, warning voters tempted by the PQ against entering what he called a “spiral” that could lead Quebec to its own version of Brexit.

Speaking in Lachute, Que., Milliard pointed to the economic consequences of the United Kingdom’s departure from the European Union and argued the current geopolitical climate favours greater co-operation among middle powers.

“Faced with the world’s giants, there is strength in unity for our farmers, for our entrepreneurs,” he said, calling PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s sovereignty project “archaic compared with the economic reality.”

Milliard, whose Liberals have been polling behind the PQ, later told supporters in Trois-Rivières that “absolutely nothing is decided,” noting that roughly three-quarters of eligible Quebecers have yet to cast a ballot.

“This is anything but over,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon, meanwhile, made his own appeal to undecided voters, asking Quebecers to give his party a majority government and what he called a “real chance” to make a difference.

“There really is a dilemma in the minds of several voters who have not yet decided,” the PQ leader said.

St-Pierre Plamondon argued a minority government would make it more difficult for the PQ to carry out its promises and could send Quebecers back to the polls within a year or 18 months.

“We’re electing a government on Monday, not an opposition,” he said.

His rivals have increasingly targeted the PQ’s promise to hold a sovereignty referendum during a first mandate, but St-Pierre Plamondon said Saturday his opponents had “more than overused” the issue.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime raised his ambitions after a Léger poll for Quebecor media put his party at 20 per cent support, up two percentage points from the previous poll.

The online survey by the market-research firm was conducted Sept. 30 to Oct. 1 among 1,000 Quebec residents aged 18 and older who are eligible to vote.

Duhaime previously focused on electing at least 12 members to the National Assembly, but said Saturday that reaching 20 per cent of the provincewide vote would also allow the Conservatives to be recognized as a parliamentary group under the legislature’s rules.

“I had only talked about 12 because I didn’t think the other one was attainable, very honestly,” he said.

Duhaime urged Quebecers to vote Monday, saying several ridings could be decided by a small number of ballots.

The PQ has spent much of the campaign on the offensive, with St-Pierre Plamondon visiting almost every region of the province, while the other parties have concentrated much of their attention on areas where they hope to protect or gain seats.

About 1.6 million Quebecers, or 25.59 per cent of eligible voters, have already cast a ballot ahead of election day, according to Élections Québec.

The PQ, the Quebec Liberals, the Quebec Conservatives, Quebec solidaire and the Coalition Avenir Québec are all expected to win seats on Monday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

— With files by Caroline Plante in Quebec City and Frédéric Lacroix-Couture in Montreal

stories.title: Toronto’s budget hole looms over mayoral race
stories.summary: Mayoral contenders offer their own solutions for the operating shortfall, but experts say the way cities are funded needs an overhaul
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Every year, the City of Toronto faces a fresh $1-billion-plus shortfall in its operating budget, an issue its main mayoral contenders have all vowed to fix. But experts say the city and other municipalities across Canada will be left perennially begging for cash without major changes to the way they are funded.

Toronto’s budget hole – city bureaucrats prefer the term “opening pressure,” pegging this year’s at $1.3-billion – must be filled each year, as municipalities in Ontario cannot borrow to cover operating deficits. The annual scramble usually ends with the use of tax hikes, reserve funds, spending reductions and varying amounts of financial support from Queen’s Park.

Mayor Olivia Chow – who took office in 2023, with a $1.8-billion gap looming for the following year – imposed two large property-tax hikes in a row, outpacing any others in recent memory. However, she was also able to win a “new deal” with Premier Doug Ford that provided important financial relief. Whoever assumes the mayor’s chair after the Oct. 26 municipal election will inevitably be seeking a New Deal 2.0 to shore up the city’s books.

Cities, as creatures of provincial legislation, have been set up across Canada with similar financial structural problems. In Ontario, municipalities are in worse shape because they’re required to cover more of the costs of social programs that are delivered by the province in other jurisdictions. And Toronto, with the country’s largest public transit system and busiest network of homeless shelters, is in a class by itself. In all, the annual bill to run Toronto has now hit $18.9-billion – more than several provinces spend.

“This is not a case of extravagant Toronto crying poor,” said Myer Siemiatycki, professor emeritus in the department of politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University. “There is a systemic underfunding of municipalities right across this country.”

The problem, many experts and municipal leaders have argued over the years, is that municipalities largely rely on property taxes, which do not grow with the economy and inflation the way taxes on income do. (They also don’t sag the same way in a recession.)

Meanwhile, costs for Toronto and other municipalities – transit, homeless shelters, road repairs – often rise faster than the general rate of inflation, requiring hotly debated, highly visible property-tax rate hikes to keep up.

In years past, the annual budget process has seen Toronto council twist itself in knots. It has passed budgets that were only balanced with money still to come from other governments. It has resorted to arcane accounting tricks, such as selling all of its lamp posts to its own hydro utility in 2005 to raise $60-million. In 2017, then-mayor John Tory had to renege on a social media pledge to Olympic swimming gold-medalist Penny Oleksiak to keep city-funded lessons at her childhood pool, an $85,000 line item.

The deal that Ms. Chow struck with Mr. Ford provided a total of $1.2-billion over three years for operating costs, money that runs out this year and was enough to shrink, but not eliminate, the city’s annual budget shortfall. The province also agreed to take over two major expressways, the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway, taking billions of dollars of capital spending off the city’s books.

While they do not dispute the need for some sort of renewed deal with the province, Ms. Chow’s leading challengers in the upcoming election, city councillor Brad Bradford and former federal Conservative cabinet minister Chris Alexander, also accuse the sitting mayor, a former councillor and NDP MP, of not doing enough to contain spending.

They have taken aim at her first two years, when, despite pledging “modest” hikes, she oversaw residential tax-rate increases of 9.5 and 6.9 per cent. That was just after her predecessor Mr. Tory had raised taxes by 7 per cent in 2023, as the city faced a pandemic-induced financial crisis amid high inflation. (For decades, property-tax hikes in Toronto were usually around or below the rate of inflation.)

But property-tax hikes cannot solve the problem. Every percentage point that Toronto increases property taxes means it takes in an added $49-million. Filling a billion-dollar hole with just property taxes would mean a pitchfork-prompting rate hike of more than 20 per cent.

Ms. Chow has said future hikes, if she is re-elected, would look more like this year’s hike of 2.2 per cent, and would be at or near inflation. Even with the increases, Torontonians’ property-tax burden remains lower than in several surrounding municipalities.

On average, according to 2025 figures compiled by the city that account for Toronto’s user-fee system for waste collection, Toronto households paid less property tax than those in Hamilton, Markham, Mississauga, Vaughan and Brampton. (Most municipalities fund their garbage collection through property taxes, but not Toronto.) Part of the reason for discrepancy in tax bills is Toronto’s large commercial and industrial tax base, which has historically allowed it to keep residential taxes lower.

Both of her challengers have pledged to freeze property taxes in their first year in office, a move that might be popular but would add to – not reduce – the annual budget shortfall. (In decades past, mayors Mel Lastman and Rob Ford made similar moves, but returned to increasing taxes as cost pressures mounted.)

Mr. Bradford also says he would eliminate the city’s land-transfer tax on the first $1.1-million of a principal residence’s cost. He says doing so would cost the city $300-million a year, potentially making that gap wider once again.

But he also has promised to launch an external “line-by-line” review of city spending to find savings, while borrowing more money to cover infrastructure costs. Mr. Bradford accuses Ms. Chow of taking a record amount of money from other governments and still failing to deal with the city’s financial woes – while its transit system, parks and roads languish.

In an interview, Mr. Alexander said he would push city staff to find the $130-million needed to cover the cost of his tax freeze. He argued he would be a better negotiator in seeking a more comprehensive, permanent arrangement involving both Queen’s Park and Ottawa. He said that could perhaps involve some sort of constitutional change to give the city more power, an idea others have suggested but that has gone nowhere in the past.

“You want a super new deal,” Mr. Alexander said. “I think it should be a bridge to something that is institutionalized.”

Ms. Chow has pointed out that her recent budgets have already relied on hundreds of millions of dollars in belt-tightening and other adjustments, found through “line-by-line” scrutiny of the city’s books by its own staff. She also routinely mentions the 2024 upgrade that the city won from credit rating agency S&P Global Ratings, which boosted Toronto to a AA-plus rating – the first such upgrade for the city in more than 20 years.

Governments often bring in outside experts for a second look at their finances. But previous external audits – including one from 2011, when the now-Premier was on council and his late brother Rob was mayor – found too little in pain-free savings to solve Toronto’s budget problems without requiring large service cuts.

Under former mayor David Miller, who launched an unsuccessful campaign for a share of sales-tax revenue, the city managed to convince then-premier Dalton McGuinty to give Toronto its own menu of potential “revenue tools” in 2007. Most were politically hard to swallow, such as a sales taxes on booze, or the vehicle-registration tax that Mr. Miller imposed, but that his successor Mr. Ford had council agree to scrap.

The city’s land-transfer tax on property sales, piggybacking on the province’s similar levy, survived, generating about $800-million this year. It has served as a lifeline that allowed subsequent mayors to avoid much larger property-tax hikes. But it also rendered Toronto’s budget vulnerable to swings in the real estate market. (Ms. Chow recently brought in a steeper rate for homes worth more than $3-million.)

Riley Brockington, president of the Association of Municipalities of Ontario and an Ottawa city councillor, said local governments across the province face a similar mismatch between their revenues and their responsibilities, along with a wave of aging infrastructure – everything from roads to hockey arenas – they cannot afford to fix.

“There just aren’t the revenues, Mr. Brockington said. “There’s a massive deficit in this province that we need addressed.”

stories.title: Sadly, we might be repeating Britain’s high-speed rail mistakes
stories.summary: Before we get carried away with the high-speed rail line from Toronto to Quebec City, we should take a look across the pond
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
The federal government’s plan to build a high-speed rail line from Toronto to Quebec City is rushing ahead.

Alto, the Crown corporation quarterbacking the effort, is getting ready to present its proposed route for the first stage of the 1,000-kilometre line: between Ottawa and Montreal. It has already started buying the land required to make it happen.

The Prime Minister is fired up. He says the project will add $35-billion to the economy and create more than 50,000 jobs. “It’s more cost-effective, it’s more sustainable, it’s connecting our communities, it’s going to be faster,” Mark Carney said last spring.

All this is exciting news for rail enthusiasts. After years – no, decades – of talk, this project finally has unmistakable momentum.

But before we get too carried away, we might want to take a look across the pond at a similar effort in Britain. It’s a cautionary tale if there ever was one.

Like Canada, the United Kingdom is far behind other countries when it comes to fast trains. Spain, France, Italy, Germany – all have good, efficient networks. China has more than 50,000 kilometres of high-speed track, the biggest system in the world. Though the British invented the modern railway, they still have just one true high-speed line: the one that carries the Eurostar train from London to the coast en route to Paris. Even that one took years to get up and running.

So it seemed to make perfect sense for Britain to join the high-speed party and build a second line: HS2, a successor to the HS1 train that goes to Paris. Approved in 2012, it was to link London with Birmingham and Manchester in the north, with an eastern leg reaching as far as Leeds. The cost would be about 32-billion pounds, or around $60-billion at today’s exchange rate. Trains would start running in 2026, whipping along their tracks at 360 km an hour, faster than any other similar high-speed railway using conventional technology.

It wasn’t long, though, before cost estimates started rising and opening dates receding. In their zeal to get cracking, authorities underestimated how much it would cost to push such a line through England’s green and pleasant land. It meant building a giant rail bridge, the Colne Valley Viaduct, the biggest in the country, and a massive tunnel, 16 km long, under parts of the lovely Chiltern Hills.

Complaints from residents and activists about the impact on the English countryside led planners to make design changes, adding extra tunnels and, in one forested section, a special arched shield to prevent protected species of bats from being killed by the onrushing trains. By the time construction started in 2020, the estimated cost had soared to 80 billion pounds and a parliamentary committee was warning that the project was “badly off course.”

To get it back on track, the government axed first the leg to Leeds (in 2021) and then the one to Manchester (in 2023). The trains will now stop at Birmingham, which is only an hour and half from central London on the current train service. To save more money, it reduced the planned top speed to 320 km an hour.

Still, the cost has continued to grow, with estimates reaching more than 100 billion pounds. The opening has been pushed back yet again to somewhere between 2036 and 2039.

Britain’s Labour government naturally blames the previous Conservative one. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander told the House of Commons in May that the government had inherited a “litany of failures.”

Of course, other countries have managed to build high-speed rail lines without making such a hash of it. The Paris-Bordeaux line, for example, whisks you to the southwest of France in just over two hours.

Sadly, there are reasons to think we might repeat Britain’s high-speed mistakes.

Farmers and homeowners are already complaining the line would gobble up valuable agricultural land and shatter the peace and quiet in rural communities. Politicians are already mucking about with the plans. Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said in June that the federal government would like the line to have a stop in Kingston, which would add billions to the cost and add to the length of the route.

The projected cost is already rising. The Parliamentary Budget Officer said this week it could be $75-billion to $113-billion, considerably more than the government’s estimate of $60-billion to $90-billion.

Then there is the issue of urban stations. One of the big challenges facing HS2 is getting the rail line into dense central London, which will require a tunnel and new station at Euston – immensely costly undertakings. When it first opens, the train will stop short of the city centre and passengers will have to transfer to subway or commuter rail to get into town.

Similarly, one of the big challenges for Alto is getting high-speed rail into central Toronto and Montreal. Union Station, the obvious Toronto terminus, is already the hub for VIA trains, GO commuter trains and the airport shuttle, UP Express. Even if Union could be redesigned to accommodate high speed as well, it would be hard to get the line into downtown along the existing, cramped the rail corridor. So Alto is talking, in a vague way, about an elevated or tunnelled route – enormously difficult and expensive options.

Of course, Alto could avoid these problems and build a whole new station instead, but that would defeat the purpose. High speed only makes sense if it goes straight from downtown to downtown. Who is going to ride a train that dumps them in the suburbs?

Mr. Carney’s enthusiasm for high speed is understandable. It is just the kind of nation-building project he wants the country to embrace at a time of confrontation with the United States.

But the same gung-ho, damn-the-torpedoes spirit gave Britain the national embarrassment that is HS2. Let’s not make the same mistake.

stories.title: In an Ontario steel town, the trade war and local elections spark conversations about change
stories.summary: Despite the recent wave of layoffs, residents of Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., see reason for optimism
stories.author: Patrick White, Photography by Deborah Baic
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections.

On Day 565 of a trade war that has bombarded Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., with bad news and pink slips, the city vibrates with an ear-splitting cover of Fat Bottomed Girls .

Down on Queen St., adult Saultites (pronounced SOO-ites) line up at a Northern Superior Brewing tent, drink tickets in hand, while the kids wait on face-painting and mini-putt.

About 4,000 locals will filter through this downtown block party on their way into the Soo Greyhounds season opener, many wearing the Hounds jersey that has graced the teenaged likes of Wayne Gretzky, Paul Coffey and Joe Thornton – all now Hockey Hall of Famers. Their opponents tonight are another junior hockey OHL team, Michigan’s Saginaw Spirit, whose logo is a bald eagle with stars and stripes for plumage. But nobody wants to call it a proxy battle.

The Canada-U.S. trade dispute is casting a long shadow over upcoming municipal elections in the city of 80,000, where Algoma Steel recently laid off 1,000 workers as it struggles for profitability in the face of punishing tariffs. But beyond the economic setbacks, many residents see a case for long-term optimism.

“We’re not gloomy people here, we’re very positive,” says Frank DeMarco, his plastic beer cup frothing as he offers up bear-hugs and handshakes to other party-goers, many of them steelworkers like him. Their kids go in for high-fives. Many call him Uncle Frank.

U.S. President Donald Trump has put that positivity to the test, slapping 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian steel in the spring of last year, doubling to 50 per cent by summer. The levies yanked Saultites onto the front lines of a trade war with the nation just across the St. Marys River.

The casualties piled up. Last December, Algoma Steel, the city’s molten economic heart for more than a century, issued Mr. DeMarco and 1,000 other steelworkers layoff notices, which took effect on March 23.

For Mr. DeMarco, the timing was awful. He and his wife, Maarit, had opened a restaurant, DeMarco’s Boots & Saddles Roadhouse, in 2025, the same week Trump announced the 50 per cent tariff.

“Boom, I think my career is over,” he says. “I’m massively under stress at that point.”

He wondered how they would endure without his Algoma cheque. And for that matter, how would his city fare with 1,000 fewer Algoma paycheques.

DeMarco’s Boots and Saddles opened just as new U.S. tariffs cast a pall over the Sault’s economy. The restaurant is co-owned by Mr. DeMarco and his wife, Maarit.

Six months on from the layoffs, the city is holding its own welfare check in the form of local elections on Oct. 26.

Incumbent mayor Matthew Shoemaker is pitching an economic Hail Mary – construction of a $250-million multimodal port estimated to support more than 2,000 jobs.

Challenger Joel Rowswell has focused on fixing the crime and disorder associated with lean times. His sense of the city clashes with the boosterish likes of Mr. DeMarco.

“Everybody is negative,” said Mr. Rowswell inside GFL Memorial Gardens, as the Hounds and Spirit headed for overtime. “I hear it every day when I go to the doors.”

It doesn’t take long to find what he’s talking about. A few pot-holed blocks from the Hounds arena, past broken windows and boarded-up homes, Connie Raynor Elliott has seen the lines outside her non-profit organization grow since the layoffs.

“The people who used to donate are now in our line-up,” says Ms. Raynor, who founded Save Our Young Adults in 2011. Dozens of volunteers provide free food, clothing and other support to the growing numbers of those in need. In the last three years, her clientele (she hates that word, preferring to call them ‘friends’) has grown from 350 to 600.

Mr. DeMarco’s own low point came shortly after the December layoff notice. Every year he runs a hockey tournament in January to raise money for local medical students who want to practise here. With massive job losses in the wind, he started making arrangements to cancel.

The Soo wouldn’t let him.

“A lot of laid-off guys came out, donated,” he says, his voice trembling. “It was … Sorry, I get a little emotional thinking about it. We’re a very interesting city. We support these things. Times can be low. Depressing times. But we still come. We still support one another.”

The city had seen worse. Many people here remember 1982, when around 4,500 steelworkers were laid off. Through the decade, the workforce shrunk from 13,000 to around 6,000. Multiple generations of local families had worked the mill. The cutbacks terminated paycheques and bloodlines at Algoma.

Mr. DeMarco’s bricklayer dad moved here from Italy in 1965 to work at Algoma, part of a wave of post-war Italian migration still evident in the many eponymous restaurants: Giovanni’s, Arturo’s, Gus’s. He brought an immigrant’s work ethic and a recipe for sublime chiff-choff, a kind of Italian chili. The son took after the father, laying brick all over the booming city before taking a position at Algoma 20 years ago. For the last five, he’s worked as a warehouse supervisor, everything from a 10-cent pencil to a million-dollar transformer passing through his hands.

His son and daughter worked at Algoma until the recent layoffs, too.

This time around, the layoff letters didn’t come as a complete surprise. Algoma had long planned to transition away from traditional coal-based blast furnaces and adopt a lower-cost electric arc system that requires about half its 3,000 workers. Heavy financial losses from the Trump tariffs only hastened the need for that transition.

Some workers resigned as soon as the layoff notices landed, preferring not to wait until their termination date. “I decided I was still at the right age to switch gears,” says Regis Emond, aged 57. He decided to resign with severance. He retrained for mining jobs before applying for 22 positions.

By mid-September, Mr. Emond said he still hadn’t heard any job offers.

Others had better luck. Chris Casagrande went for retraining shortly after the layoffs. In September, he started his first two-week shift at a northern gold mine. “A lot of guys are trying to ride out EI waiting to get called back to Algoma,” he said by phone from the mining camp. “I wanted to pivot. The industry is booming.”

Amid the gloom, something unexpected happened. Though Mr. DeMarco received a layoff notice, he was never let go. His job was extended beyond the layoff date, and then made permanent. He didn’t miss a shift. Many friends had the same experience. His son is back at the steel plant while his daughter found a new job within days of leaving Algoma.

At 5 p.m. on a recent Saturday, DeMarco’s Boots & Saddles Roadhouse was filling up. Uncle Frank stood at the front, kissing cheeks, shaking hands. The existential dread he once felt – for his family, his city, his country – has died down. This summer, there were line-ups out the door for Tuesday wing night. People can’t seem to get enough Big Frank burgers or Franktastics (a cocktail of coconut rum and pineapple) or his father’s chiff-choff recipe.

“It’s a slow incline up, but we’re getting there,” he says, taking a moment from seating tables to wipe his brow and down some water. “It’s a positive place.”

The Soo Greyhounds had a 3-1 victory in this game against the Saginaw Spirit, to the elation of the locals. Children lined up to greet Mr. DeMarco for bear hugs.

Vancouver: The population is shrinking in some neighbourhoods. What if we put more housing there?

stories.title: Calls for improved safety on road favoured by cyclists after 34-year-old fatally struck
stories.summary: As police investigate a crash east of London that left one cyclist dead, others who regularly bike in the area say the incident has left them rattled, and shows a need for better safety measures.
stories.author: Matthew Trevithick
paragraphs: As police investigate a crash east of London that left one cyclist dead, others who regularly bike in the area say the incident has left them rattled, and shows a need for better safety measures.
· Posted: Oct 03, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 41 minutes ago
Provincial police are continuing to investigate the cause of Wednesday's collision along Richmond Street, between Gore Road and Marion Street, north of Dorchester.(Ontario Provincial Police)
The collision happened over the noon-hour on Wednesday along Richmond Street, north of Dorchester, in Thames Centre, Ontario Provincial Police said.
A cause remains under investigation, but police said the cyclist, identified only as a 34-year-old Thames Centre resident, was seriously hurt and later died in hospital.

The stretch of Richmond where the crash occurred, between Gore Road and Marion Street, is similar to other rural routes near London — a municipal road with two lanes, no paved shoulder and a speed limit of 80 km/h.
However, of the few roads connecting Dorchester to Gore Road and beyond, many cyclists consider it safer than nearby Elgin and Shaw roads, which are busier and see more truck traffic.
Cyclist dies after being struck by vehicle in Thames Centre
Video This cycling app will help Londoners find safer routes through the city
Londoner Ivan Cernigoy says he regularly bikes east out of the city and through the Dorchester area, and had been on Richmond Street about an hour before the crash.
“I was dumbstruck because I just didn’t see how it could happen. The visibility was great that day, there was hardly any traffic,” he said.
“Short of a medical emergency, the only other way I could see it happening is not looking at the road.”Police did not have an update on the case on Friday, and Cernigoy did not know the victim.

The roadway isn’t typically busy around the time the crash happened, 12:20 p.m., Cernigoy said. He notes a paved shoulder running up Richmond and used by cyclists ends abruptly at Marion Street, forcing them to ride in traffic to get to Gore Road.

“There's always guys that are going to come too close to you. Usually, I try to take a good metre of road, but nothing really stands out to me about that road … and that's why that accident surprised me.” He said he avoids riding on Richmond after 3 p.m. because of increased traffic.
The crash won’t change how and where he rides, and he does everything he can to be safe, including using a helmet, lights and a radar camera, he said.
“But, you know, you can never account for some things, right?”
Location of Sept. 30, 2026 collision in Thames Centre:
Richmond Street is commonly used by cyclists travelling to and from Dorchester, and the crash has left the cycling community devastated, said Evan Jones, a cyclist from London.
“I can see myself in this situation ... The idea of not coming back is really heartbreaking. It’s unfortunately something that I think about while I’m riding,” he said.

Like Cernigoy, Evans said he does what he can to stand out, including using lights and high visibility clothing, but says almost every ride outside London has at least one dicey moment with passing vehicles.

“I don’t know if drivers are always familiar with what it feels like to be passed on a road like that,” he said. “Country roads are usually straight with great visibility. You would think that it’s not a problem ... but passing at high speed with a very limited amount of space is a really scary experience.”
Having more paved shoulders would take pressure off cyclists to ride in traffic, and provide a sense there is an area of the road that belongs to them, he said.

According to Thames Centre's trails and cycling master plan, paved shoulders can be considered accessible for bicycles if they “offer sufficient operating space, clear pavement markings ... and a smooth surface free from snow and debris."
Cyclist in critical condition after crash in London's core
Police investigating after cyclist, 25, fatally struck by motorist south of Strathroy
Bill Dowhaniuk, a cyclist living in Nilestown, west of Dorchester, also believes construction along Catherine Street and at nearby subdivisions has led to an increase in traffic, and close calls.

“I’ve had more close calls this year than other years,” he said. One came within the last two weeks as he turned south onto County Road 74 from Catherine Street. "A gentleman was turning left onto River Road and he did not see me at all."

Dowhaniuk didn't know the victim, and says while the crash has left him shaken up, he will likely continue using Richmond because Elgin and Shaw are too busy. He would like to see the paved shoulder extended north from Marion Street to Gore Road.
While he doesn’t think every road needs a paved shoulder, Cernigoy believes the 34-year-old would still be alive had there been one where the crash happened.
“I don’t think cyclists need to have every road catered to them. But there should be some roads where you can get to the same places and stay out of the way of cars,” Cernigoy said.
CBC News reached out to Thames Centre Coun. Tom Heeman, whose ward covers the crash scene, for comment, but did not receive a response before publication.

stories.title: 3 songs from London Morning to boost your weekend playlist
stories.summary: London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role and selects tunes for the show. That's about 25 songs each week. Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from the past week.
stories.author: Ryan Soulliere
paragraphs: London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role and selects tunes for the show. That's about 25 songs each week. Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from the past week.
· Posted: Oct 03, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 42 minutes ago
Drives The Common Man, Bahamas and Joce Reyome are three artists featured on London Morning(Instagram)

London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role, selecting tunes for the show. In any given week, that's about 25 songs.Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from the past week.
_WATCH | Swing Set:_Video 8

2026 marks 10 years since the debut of the animated short film The Secret Path, featuring a soundtrack by Gord Downie. A concert is planned this month in Toronto to mark the anniversary. A swath of Indigenous artists are performing their reprised versions of songs from The Secret Path, including London's Drives The Common Man. The local artist's version of Swing Set is calm, earnest and begs reflection. Drives The Common Man's take on Swing Set is stripped down to just guitar and vocals, making for a relaxing, but pensive listen.
_WATCH | The Bridge:_Video 9

Bahamas is performing in London Sunday night with Boy Golden. London Morning played the Bahamas' song The Bridge earlier this week. This track is chill yet still keeps a beat you can get into. The Bridge has a wonderful flute part woven through the song, creating a nice blend of calm vocals and airy instrumentation. The Bridge is a great song to kick off your weekend mornings.
_WATCH | Party Line:_Video 10

This 3-song roundup wraps up with a banger: Party Line by Charlottetown's Joce Reyome. It follows Reyome's recent EP, Smoke Break. Party Line is your go-to party track this weekend, delivering a foot-stompin' blues boogie that is sure to please. And a note for blues lovers: if you have time to check out Reyome's new 6-song EP, you're in for a treat with a variety of blues styles all in one place.
