stories.title: London Knights win against the North Bay Battalion
stories.summary: The London Knights hit the ice against the North Bay Battalion at Canada Life Place Friday night.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Knights remain perfect to start the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) season after a 4-1 win over the North Bay Battalion at Canada Life Place Friday.

Making his first start of the season after returning from Vancouver Canucks camp, Aleksei Medvedev stopped 38 of the 39 shots fired his way to earn first star honours.

Rookie Marcus Nordmark opened the scoring with his first OHL goal early in the second period before the Battalion answered back to tie it at one going to the third period.

Less than a minute into the final frame, Thomas Zocco took advantage of a defensive mistake and buried what would turn out to be the game winner.

Jaxon Cover scored in his first game back from Ottawa Senators camp by taking a rebound off the end boards and slipping it home. Cohen Bidgood would add an an insurance marker to round out the scoring.

London sits 4-0 to start the year to lead the Western Conference standings and will look to remain undefeated Sunday when they host the Flint Firebirds.

London will be without defenceman Maksim Sokolovskii Sunday and for the near future.

stories.title: London Mayoral debate raises questions about open drug use
stories.summary: 980 Cfpl hosted a London Mayoral debate. David Peacock moderated the nearly 90 minute debate and asked mayoral...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
London mayoral candidates discussed how they would tackle open drug use Friday, debate on 980 Cfpl.

Host Devon Peacock moderated the 90-minute event, which included candidates Kirsten Krose, a businessperson, Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson, and Mayor Josh Morgan.

The candidates were asked how they would deal with issues related to London’s homelessness, housing, construction and public safety.

One of the key talking points that was repeatedly mentioned in this debate was the use of open drug use in London.

“ We are currently under the harm reduction model which supports and uh tries to make illegal drug use safer in our city. It’s making the problems worse,” said Stevenson. “The province gave us an extra $8.5 million in 2023 and 5 million of that 8 and a half went to increased shelter costs with no additional beds. Money that we’re getting is not getting to the people who need it.”

Morgan pointed out London police’s open-air drug policy, Project Pathways, is approaching it’s second phase, which he expects to reduce the amount of open drug use in the city.

“ We know that there is a gap in the amount of service available to refer to and that creates a barrier,” he said. “But ultimately, all of this is meant to say we’ve got to make people safer. We’ve got to continue to not only drive the stats, but make sure that it’s a feeling for people out on the streets and in our core, in the downtown.”

Krose did not mention much of Londoner’s facing open-drug use, instead, she described how she would enact policies that would broadly help those in need, such as the homeless.

“T his is a very complex issue and I don’t think that it’s a one-size fits-all. This is something that is going to require many different solutions,” she said.

“I would like to implement a 10-year stabilization strategy. I built this strategy from consulting as many as I could. The front line organizations, so everything from Unity Project, London Cares, St.Leonard’s, Ark Aid, Paul’s Place, you name it. I want to make sure that we have a broad spectrum of services that meet everywhere, meet everyone from temporary transition all the way to long-term.”

stories.title: Another Marineland whale dies at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago
stories.summary: Another whale shipped out of Marineland has died at the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The aquarium says Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga, died on Wednesday despite efforts to save her.

It’s the sixth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., theme park to die after a massive relocation of whales and dolphins over the summer.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Four other belugas and one dolphin from Marineland have died since they were moved out of the former tourist attraction.

Shedd says Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels. The park added that her blood had become “dangerously acidic.”

The aquarium says those findings helped the veterinary care team understand how sick the beluga was, but they did not establish a cause of death.

Shedd says Caspian was on life support for nearly four hours before she died.

Shedd recently performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.

Shedd and four other aquariums in the United States and Spain helped Marineland relocate all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins over the course of six weeks this summer.

Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada.

A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

Four other belugas and one dolphin from Marineland have died since they were moved out of the former tourist attraction.
Shedd says Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels. The park added that her blood had become “dangerously acidic.”
The aquarium says those findings helped the veterinary care team understand how sick the beluga was, but they did not establish a cause of death.
Shedd says Caspian was on life support for nearly four hours before she died.
Shedd recently performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.
Shedd and four other aquariums in the United States and Spain helped Marineland relocate all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins over the course of six weeks this summer.
Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada.
A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

stories.title: Ontario's top court paves way to reopen challenge of Hamilton's anti-encampment law
stories.summary: Ontario’s top court has revived a constitutional challenge brought by a group of homeless people in Hamilton against the city’s anti-encampment bylaw.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The question of whether the bylaw is unconstitutional has been left for a new judge to decide after the Court of Appeal for Ontario found flaws in a lower court’s decision to dismiss the challenge.

The Appeal Court found the trial judge’s ruling leaned heavily on his finding that the city did not carry out overnight encampment evictions, contrary to the testimony of several residents.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Today’s ruling says the trial judge discounted that testimony based on stereotypes about mental illness and addictions.

The Appeal Court panel also says on key legal issues the trial judge’s reasons “lacked the depth of analysis that is required” when dealing with homeless encampments.

The city did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre speaks in the Foyer of the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Posted October 9, 2026 12:36 pm.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says he will be in Alberta next week to deliver a speech on Canadian unity ahead of the province’s referendum on separation.

Poilievre told a press conference in Burlington, Ont., today he will be doing “additional campaigning on the ground.”

When asked about tech industrialist Elon Musk saying recently that Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec should separate, Poilievre said “Canadians control their own destiny.”

The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan brushed off Musk’s comments, while Quebec’s new premier has said he won’t trigger a separation vote while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Poilievre did not say where and when he will deliver his speech on national unity.

Albertans will vote on the prospect of a future separation referendum, along with nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues, ON Oct. 19.

stories.title: Top court sets sentencing framework for cases involving Indigenous offenders, victims
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada says in cases where an Indigenous offender commits an offence against an intimate partner who is an Indigenous woman, a judge must apply sentencing principles related to both Indigenous offenders and victims of crime in a harmonious way.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Supreme Court of Canada says in cases where an Indigenous offender commits an offence against an intimate partner who is an Indigenous woman, a judge must apply sentencing principles related to both Indigenous offenders and victims of crime in a harmonious way.

In a 5-4 judgment Friday, the top court provided guidance and set out a new framework for determining an appropriate sentence in such cases.

The court said Indigenous people are disproportionately and excessively imprisoned, while Indigenous women and girls suffer from unacceptably high levels of violence and abuse.

“Both of these pressing issues have been shaped by the experiences of colonization, and addressing them together is central to the ongoing process of reconciliation,” Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin wrote on behalf of the majority.

Parliament has tried to address both concerns through the criminal sentencing process, the top court noted.

In light of the phenomenon of Indigenous over-incarceration, a Criminal Code provision that took effect in the 1990s directs judges to consider sanctions other than prison that are reasonable in the circumstances. The court pointed out particular attention is to be paid to the circumstances of Indigenous offenders.

The court also underscored the importance of two provisions added to the Criminal Code more recently. One requires a sentencing judge to squarely consider the objectives of denunciation and deterrence when the offence involves the abuse of a person who is vulnerable because, for example, they are an Indigenous woman or girl.

Another section directs a judge sentencing an offender for abuse of their intimate partner to consider the increased vulnerability of women and girls, and to pay particular attention to those who are Indigenous, the court noted.

Sentencing circles may include participants such as the offender, lawyers, the sentencing judge, Elders, the victim or their proxy and community members with knowledge of the offender. The top court said information gleaned from a circle can help the sentencing judge properly apply the principles specific to Indigenous offenders and victims.

The court said although the sentencing provisions invite engagement with distinct Indigenous perspectives on crime and punishment, they do not create a parallel regime for Indigenous offenders, and the consideration of Indigenous perspectives cannot displace a sentencing judge’s authority and responsibility under the Criminal Code.

The court said the sentencing judge must take three specific steps in such cases.

First, the judge must assess the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender in light of the Indigenous backgrounds of the parties.

Second, the judge must sensitively identify the relevant criminal sentencing objectives, emphasizing denunciation and deterrence, while still considering other relevant sentencing objectives.

Third, the judge must select the proportionate and just sentence in light of the Indigenous context, given that Parliament has expressly directed sentencing judges to consider all available sanctions other than imprisonment.

The top court added that the sentencing circle process can be relevant to understanding the availability of alternative sentencing options in the community, as well as the community’s perspective on the sentence that would best achieve the objectives.

The court said the sentencing methodology in such cases is not a mathematical formula but a guide to help judges take into account the circumstances of Indigenous offenders and the vulnerability of Indigenous women and girls to abuse and violence.

“Proportionality requires due attention to the circumstances of the offender and of the victim in light of relevant sentencing objectives,” O’Bonsawin wrote. “The appropriate balancing will inevitably vary depending on the specific circumstances of the offence.”

The ruling comes in the case of Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaq man with severe mental health challenges who was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty in 2022 to aggravated assault against his partner, a Mi’kmaq woman.

The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to three years. The Supreme Court ruled Friday the three-year sentence should stand.

The top court found the sentencing judge did not recognize that the offender’s mental illness contributed to the commission of the aggravated assault and did not consider the effect of that illness on the relevant sentencing objectives.

The sentencing judge would have settled on a shorter prison term had she properly considered the offender’s significant mental health issues, particularly when viewed in light of a sentencing circle’s recommendations in the case, the Supreme Court said.

The four dissenting Supreme Court judges said the Crown’s appeal should be allowed and the original sentence imposed by the sentencing judge restored.

They said the majority’s sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

The ruling comes in the case of Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaq man with severe mental health challenges who was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty in 2022 to aggravated assault against his partner, a Mi’kmaq woman.
The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to three years. The Supreme Court ruled Friday the three-year sentence should stand.

The top court found the sentencing judge did not recognize that the offender’s mental illness contributed to the commission of the aggravated assault and did not consider the effect of that illness on the relevant sentencing objectives.

The sentencing judge would have settled on a shorter prison term had she properly considered the offender’s significant mental health issues, particularly when viewed in light of a sentencing circle’s recommendations in the case, the Supreme Court said.
The four dissenting Supreme Court judges said the Crown’s appeal should be allowed and the original sentence imposed by the sentencing judge restored.

They said the majority’s sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls.

Braves will battle the Dolphins tonight while the Merchants visit the Firebirds and the Trojans host the Spitfires.

PJHL - All of Oxford County's Junior C hockey teams will kick off the Thanksgiving long weekend on the ice.

The Norwich Merchants will visit the New Hamburg Firebirds tonight, while the Tavistock Braves host the Dorchester Dolphins and the Thamesford Trojans host the Aylmer Spitfires. The Trojans will be looking for a comeback after suffering a 7-1 loss to the Petrolia Flyers last night.

The Braves and the Merchants will be back in action tomorrow with the Merchants visiting Dorchester and the Braves battling the Firebirds in New Hamburg.

All of the games have 7:30 p.m. start times.

The Braves are on top of the Doherty Division standings with 14 points, followed by the Wellesley Applejacks and the Firebirds with 10 points each. The Paris Mounties are in third place with seven points, only one ahead of the fourth place Merchants with six points. The Dolphins are in fifth place with four points and the Hespeler Shamrocks are at the bottom of the standings with three points.

The Trojans are tied with the Lucan Irish for fourth place in the Yeck Division standings with four points each, only one ahead of the last place Port Stanley Sailors. The Spitfires are tied with the Exeter Hawks for third place with eight points each and the Flyers are in second place with nine points. The North Middlesex Stars and the Mount Brydges Bulldogs are tied at the top of the standings with 12 points each.

The Navy Vets will host the Rockets tonight and visit the Redhawks tomorrow night.

WOODSTOCK/CAMBRIDGE - The Woodstock Navy Vets have two games scheduled for the Thanksgiving long weekend.

They will kick everything off with a home game against the Strathroy Rockets tonight. The puck will drop at 7:45 p.m. at Southwood Arena and it's also Breast Cancer Awareness Night, so fans are encouraged to wear pink to show their support.

The Vets will also be in Cambridge tomorrow to face the Redhawks. That game will get underway at 7:00 p.m. at Galt Arena Gardens.

Woodstock is currently in a five-way tie for fifth place in the Western Conference standings. The Vets have eight points so far and the same goes for the Listowel Cyclones, the Elmira Sugar Kings, the LaSalle Vipers, and the Komoka Kings. The London Nationals are in fourth place with nine points, while the St. Thomas Stars and Chatham Maroons are tied for second place with 14 points each. The St. Marys Lincolns sit on top of the standings with 16 points.

The Sarnia Legionnaires are at the bottom of the standings with zero points, while the Strathroy Rockets have three points and the Stratford Warriors have four points.

stories.title: Hamilton rocked by 2 suspected home explosions, 3 people hospitalized
stories.summary: One victim who was in a garage at the time of the first blast suffered serious burns and was taken to hospital in serious condition.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Two suspected home explosions that sparked multi-alarm fires in Hamilton Thursday morning have sent three people to hospital and have resulted in significant damage to the affected homes, according to firefighters.

Hamilton Fire Chief David Cunliffe told reporters Thursday afternoon that fire crews are investigating both incidents, and the Office of the Fire Marshall was on scene to determine the cause of the explosions. The two blasts are not linked, he said.

The first explosion occurred just after 7:30 a.m. at 182 Springside Drive on Hamilton Mountain. Cunliffe said a garage exploded, causing the house to collapse on itself and a fire was sparked.

A victim, who was in the garage at the time of the blast, suffered serious burns and was taken to hospital in serious condition, he said.

The explosion was felt at three fire stations across the city, said Cunliffe.

“People were calling from all over, it was a very significant blast,” he said.

Two neighbouring homes have also been significantly damaged, said Cunliffe, but no one else in that area has been injured. One of those homes had the blast travel through the kitchen and the debris field in the whole area is “very significant,” he said.

Then around 9 a.m., across town in Hamilton’s east end, another suspected home explosion happened at 8 Lampton Place. Cunliffe said a structure was “fully involved” when crews arrived and the fire was significant enough to send a large plume of smoke into the sky.

Neighbours rescued two residents who were inside the house while it was on fire, he said. One resident was sent to hospital in serious condition with burns and the other was sent in stable condition, also with burns.

One adjacent home was damaged by the fire. Cunliffe said there are some reports that neighbours were smelling gas prior to the explosion, but the cause is still being determined.

Damage to the home is valued at around $750,000, he said. The cause of each incident is under investigation.

stories.summary: Police say a transport truck left the road and went about 40 yards into the ditch.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Friday, 9 October 2026 06:44

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Police say a transport truck left the road and went about 40 yards into the ditch.

THAMES CENTRE - No one was hurt after a single vehicle crash involving a transport truck in the westbound lanes of Highway 401 in Thames Centre.

Sergeant Ed Sanchuk posted a video about on the OPP West Region X page at around 3:00 p.m. yesterday.

"Just shortly after 1:00 p.m. this afternoon, Middlesex County OPP officers responded a report of a transport truck that left the roadway and went approximately 40 yards into the ditch that you see over here."

He said one lane was closed so heavy tow truck operators could help retreive the transport truck. The other two lanes remained open, but the crash did cause some backups on the highway.

No further details have been released.

stories.title: Montreal mayor says city will offer 3,000 spots in emergency shelters for unhoused
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada says the city is planning to provide 3,000 beds in emergency shelters to address homelessness this winter.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the city is planning to provide about 3,000 spots in emergency shelters to address what she calls the biggest humanitarian crisis the city is facing: homelessness.

“I won’t leave anybody in the street to die from the cold. That’s my promise. So whatever we need to do, we’ll do it,” she said at a news conference Thursday.

The city will set up the 3,000 spots in nine winter warming centres, open 24/7, in seven of its boroughs. Martinez Ferrada says that shelters must be able to provide round-the-clock services, rather than requiring vulnerable individuals to move from one location to another throughout the day.

The mayor said some of the 3,000 spots would be chairs, and was unable to confirm how many would be beds.

She said the city purchased 350 new beds for the new emergency warming centres, which she said were needed since many people who used emergency shelters in recent years had to sleep on chairs.

“Everyone deserves to sleep in a bed,” she said.

The anticipated 3,000 spots are in addition to existing shelters and resources for the unhoused run by community organizations.

The city is not planning to add any new emergency beds in the Hochelaga neighbourhood in the east-end of Montreal, which currently has an encampment with about 200 tents.

It said it wants to ensure resources for those experiencing homelessness are distributed more evenly across the Montreal area.

Last November, the city had about 2,500 spots in emergency shelters and warming centres. Martinez Ferrada had said her administration added 500 added spaces by Christmas, for a total of about 3,000 spots.

“No other city in Quebec has this much capacity,” said the mayor.

The Quebec government estimated there were just over 12,000 people living on the street in the province in 2025, and that about 42 per cent of the province’s unhoused population lives in Montreal.

According to the mayor, Montreal needs about $20 million to put its emergency plans in place.

“I really do hope that this is the last winter that we’ll be waiting for funding, knowing that the winter comes every year. Community organizations need that certainty to retain their teams and workforce and plan ahead,” she said.

She added that she believes the city will get the funding it needs after the premier-designate, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, promised to make homelessness a top priority.

The city’s announcement comes after a woman died in an encampment in the Montréal-Nord borough early Wednesday following a fire.

“It kept me awake two nights in a row to think about what we can do more, and how to do it faster,” the mayor said.

St-Pierre Plamondon reacted to the news of the death on social media Wednesday, saying he is “making the fight against homelessness a personal matter.” He wrote that his government will provide the funding needed for this winter. At a separate news conference on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he would collaborate with the incoming Parti Québécois government on the issue.

Representatives of community organizations say they welcome the additional resources to tackle a problem they say is becoming increasingly complex. However, they say all levels of government need to commit to building more transitional housing and fund services like addiction treatment centres and mental health support to get people off the street.

The mayor called on the government to increase funding for transitional housing, adding that the city is working on building 2,000 units.

Sam Watts, CEO of the Welcome Hall Mission, told reporters that the city has been efficient at planning ahead but that there is a need for permanent solutions.

“We don’t want anybody to be born in the street or die in the streets, but I also don’t anybody to live in the street,” he said. “You heard the word transition housing over and over again. That is really the solution, to get people … back into permanent housing rather than a whole series of emergency measures, which are very costly.”

Émilie Fortier, director of homelessness services at the Old Brewery Mission, said that rent and housing prices are an additional barrier, with affordable units becoming harder to find.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Hamilton to pilot bylaw to protect downtown renters from extreme indoor heat
stories.summary: Hamilton city council has voted to pilot a bylaw intended to protect downtown tenants from stifling indoor temperatures, the first of its kind in Ontario.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Landlords in downtown Hamilton will soon face new requirements to protect renters from stifling indoor summer temperatures after local councillors backed a first-of-its-kind pilot in Ontario.

The pilot will require landlords in the city’s downtown Ward 2, where most residents are renters, to keep at least one room in each unit below 26 C, a threshold recognized by Health Canada.

The results will likely be watched closely by other cities, including Toronto, that are studying how to protect renters from rising temperatures driven by climate change.

The pilot is expected to inform staff recommendations, due in early 2029, on how to expand the bylaw Hamilton-wide.

“We recognize the significance of addressing the impacts of extreme heat on Hamilton residents and want to take a thoughtful approach to implementing this groundbreaking bylaw,” Mike Zegarac, the interim city manager, said in a statement.

The pilot is the first time a city in Ontario has voted to make landlords responsible for keeping rental units cool in the summer. The city’s health committee first directed staff to come up with a maximum temperature bylaw in 2023.

Ontario’s tenant laws require landlords to heat an apartment, but not to keep it cool in summer, a distinction some advocates say is increasingly untenable as climate change increases the frequency and intensity of dangerous heat waves across the province. Hamilton is expected to see roughly an extra 25 days above 30 C by mid-century, according to models based on current climate policies.

Toronto has also directed its city staff to come up with a similar bylaw by next summer.

The Hamilton pilot will start next year and run through September 2028. Exemptions are available to landlords who show there are structural, electrical or physical barriers to compliance, or if the only way to comply would require constructions or demolition. Tenants can also choose to opt out.

One of the recognized risks is the pilot’s possible impact on above-guideline rent increases sought by landlords to cover associated air conditioning costs, a staff report says. The report also notes there’s an overall lack of consistent funding programs available to property owners to complete retrofits.

Recent changes to provincial law give tenants the right to install air conditioners and allow landlords to pass off extra utility costs in seasonal rent increases, but do not provide for access to cooling as a minimum standard.

Tenant and environmental groups argued the pilot did not go far enough. At a minimum, it should be expanded to the other downtown wards and applied citywide by summer 2028, said a written submission co-signed by ACORN Hamilton, Environment Hamilton and the Canadian Environmental Law Association.

A landlord group, meanwhile, said a decision should be deferred and the bylaw studied further. The Hamilton and District Apartment Association said in its submission there was “no need to rush this decision.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Stelco begins issuing layoff notices as first job cuts set to take effect Sunday
stories.summary: The union representing workers at Stelco Holdings Inc.’s steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., says the company has started issuing individual layoff notices.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hamilton — The union representing workers at Stelco Holdings Inc.’s steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., says the company has started issuing individual layoff notices, with more expected before the end of the week.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers local 1005, says some workers received notices Wednesday telling them not to return for their next scheduled shift.

He says about 90 workers are expected to receive notices this week, with the first layoffs taking effect Sunday. The cuts are expected to unfold over roughly three weeks as operations are idled.

Latest updates on company news here

Wells says the layoffs at the Hamilton plant are expected to affect roughly 330 workers, with additional cuts expected among co-op workers and employees at the pickling operations at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont.

He says the company is describing the cuts as indefinite layoffs, while the union is treating them as temporary under its collective agreement.

Stelco, which is owned by U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., announced last week plans to cut up to 500 workers across its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has threatened legal action against Cleveland-Cliffs if it fails to provide a plan outlining how it will honour the job commitments made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Stelco begins issuing layoff notices as first job cuts set to take effect Sunday
stories.summary: Hamilton - The union representing workers at Stelco Holdings Inc.'s steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., says the company has started issuing individual layoff notices, with more expected before the end of the week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hundreds of southern Ontario steelworkers facing layoffs will be recalled if Canada and the United States reach a trade deal on steel, the head of Stelco’s U.S.-based parent company said Thursday.

Lourenco Goncalves, chairman and chief executive of Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs, said the Canadian market is too small to support galvanized steel production from both Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco, along with imports.

“There’s not enough orders there for us,” he said. “You can’t operate in an efficient and profitable way running at 50 or 55 per cent capacity. That’s what we have been facing with galvanized steel.”

He said he has spent more than a year and a half pushing Ottawa for stronger protections against foreign steel imports, arguing that measures adopted so far have helped the hot-rolled steel market but have not gone far enough to protect galvanized steel producers.

Stelco announced plans last week to lay off up to 500 workers across its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

Stelco’s Hamilton Works produces cold-rolled and galvanized steel. The company plans to idle both operations.

The company began issuing individual layoff notices in Hamilton on Wednesday, with about 90 workers expected to receive notices this week, said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers local 1005, which represents unionized workers at the Hamilton plant.

The first layoffs will take effect Sunday, with roughly 330 Hamilton workers expected to be affected over the next three weeks, along with additional cuts at Lake Erie Works and among co-op workers, Wells said.

“It’s a temporary layoff,” Goncalves said. “I do believe that one day we’re going to have a trade deal, I just don’t know when.

“Once this trade deal is reached and we’re back and able to produce and sell galvanized steel, we will bring back these people.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday demanding a plan outlining how Cleveland-Cliffs will honour the legally binding commitments it made when it acquired the steelmaker in 2024.

The commitments include maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees for five years.

Joly rejected the suggestion that U.S. tariffs and changing market conditions relieve the company of those obligations, noting that Goncalves has publicly supported the tariffs.

Goncalves called her comments “totally unfair” and “just playing with words.”

While he described U.S. Section 232 tariffs as “the most successful policy implemented on trade in the United States ever,” he also argued that Canada should adopt similar protections for its own steel industry.

Goncalves said he has long advocated for “Fortress North America,” an approach aimed at protecting steelmakers in both countries from foreign imports, while restoring U.S. market access for Canadian galvanized steel.

“What would be the goal?” he said. “To protect the Canadian steel industry the same way we’re protecting the American steel industry, and the consequences are all positive.”

Goncalves said Cleveland-Cliffs will respond to Joly’s letter by Tuesday, within the five-business-day deadline set by the minister.

He said the company is preparing two submissions: one responding to Joly’s demand for a plan to meet its commitments and a second, more detailed document containing commercially sensitive information that he said would be protected under the Investment Canada Act.

He declined to disclose the contents of either submission.

Meanwhile, at Stelco’s Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., John McElroy said between 40 and 50 workers could be laid off as early as Oct. 24 as the company reduces operations on its steel pickling lines.

Lake Erie Works produces steel from raw materials, including iron ore, and rolls it into coils that are sold to customers or sent to Hamilton for further processing and coating. Its pickling lines remove surface oxidation from hot-rolled steel.

“There’s no real good paying jobs out here and a lot of my co-workers are the breadwinner of the family,” said McElroy, president of United Steelworkers Local 8782, which represents unionized workers at the plant.

“They’re quite worried.”

McElroy said the union is working with management to reassign affected employees to other jobs normally performed by outside contractors.

Meanwhile, Wells said workers at the Hamilton plant feel betrayed.

“We feel we’re being used as pawns,” he said, referring to the ongoing trade dispute between Canada and the United States. “This is all done for political theatre.”

He added: “This is a manufactured crisis. They’re trying to get our federal government’s attention to get a favourable trade deal.”

Goncalves defended the layoffs as a temporary measure aimed at preserving more than 2,000 other jobs.

“I did not betray anyone,” he said. “I’m temporarily laying off 350 and I’m still hopeful that we’re going to have a trade agreement and I can bring these 350 workers back and continue to grow.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
stories.summary: Celebrated Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Nicole Thompson The Canadian Press

Anne Carson, the Toronto-born poet and scholar who’s said to have invented her own genre with work that blends the ancient and the avant-garde, has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

The famously private Carson became the 123rd Nobel laureate in literature on Thursday, thrusting her somewhat reluctantly into the limelight, according to Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy.

“We didn’t have much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland where she’s listening to the wind,” Carlberg said.

“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”

Carlberg said the academy rewarded Carson for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney commended Carson on social media, calling her win “a proud moment for Canada.”

“With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” Carney wrote on X.

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica. She’s defied literary conventions with a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts.

“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee for literature.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

Elizabeth Harvey, a retired English professor at the University of Toronto, described how Carson manages to “invent and reinvent form.”

“She takes things that don’t look like poetry, like a lecture or an essay, and makes it into poetry,” she said, pointing to Carson’s lyric essays.

“They look like prose pieces, but they’re really deeply poetic in their sensibility.”

But as Carson’s profile has grown over four decades, the particulars of her personal life have remained elusive.

Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”

Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and various accounts suggest she studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.

The Swedish Academy confirmed her year and city of birth, but offered few other details.

Concetta Principe, an assistant professor of English at Trent University who wrote a book on Carson, recalled first reading the writer’s author bio.

“It was like two sentences. That’s unusual,” she said. “In that way, it signified humility — that’s how I saw it initially, and I do still feel that to be the case with her.”

But Principe said she also sees it as a statement about the role of the author.

“We associate what’s on the page with the writer. We think it’s the writer’s life story that we’re reading, and that brings us close to the writer,” she said.

“I think her resistance to sharing is a way of reminding us that even if we think we have found her, even if we had all her biography, we still wouldn’t grasp where she is in the text, (or) what of her life is really there.”

After Carson’s PhD thesis in 1981, she made her publishing debut in 1986 with academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

That book was formative for Louis Ruprecht, director of the Hellenic Studies Institute at Georgia State University.

He said he picked it up when he was a newly minted PhD studying Sappho.

“I was mesmerized and blown away by the book. And when I got back to Atlanta, I wrote her a fan letter,” Ruprecht recalled.

She responded, and they corresponded for a while, he said. They talked mostly about the work — “we had Sappho in common,” he said.

Carson gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Brontë sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.

Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography of Red,” which reimagines the 10th labour of Hercules, telling the life story of the monster he slays, Geryon.

Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Man in the Off Hours” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T.S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.

In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc>,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red.” It made her the first two-time winner of the prize.

At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

Scott Griffin, the award’s benefactor, said Thursday that Carson’s win is a win for Canada and Canadian poetry.

“Anne Carson has raised the profile of poetry to its rightful place, in my opinion, right to the pinnacle of literature,” he said.

Griffin got to know Carson a little bit when they travelled to Edinburgh together after she won the inaugural prize.

“On stage, she tends to come through — sometimes, for some people — as a little bit severe,” he said. “But she’s very warm and loves to have fun.”

Carson also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.

Among her more recent books is 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win.

The American playwright and novelist Saul Bellow, who was born in Montreal and grew up in Chicago, was awarded the Nobel in 1976.

The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Lawyer seeks order forcing Quebec legislature members to swear oath to the King
stories.summary: Montreal - Lawyers are asking Quebec Superior Court to grant an emergency order that would force the new crop of elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Lawyers are asking Quebec Superior Court to grant an emergency order that would force the new crop of elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.

Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group are asking the court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional.

The Quebec legislature adopted the law after Parti Québécois members were temporarily barred from taking their seats after they refused to swear allegiance to King Charles.

David argues that politicians who don’t swear the oath won’t be constitutionally entitled to sit in the legislature, and the laws they pass will have no legal effect.

David has already filed a challenge against the law, and believes its application should be suspended to make incoming legislature members take the oath until the case is heard on its merits.

The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Monday’s election, and leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already said he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to the King.

The PQ leader also said he’s seeking legal advice on how to further cut ties with the monarchy, including stripping the lieutenant-governor of her roles and funding.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he told reporters Tuesday. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”

Bill 4, adopted in 2022, amended a section of the 1867 Constitution Act to exempt Quebec from the section that requires the oath.

David argues that the law infringes on Quebecers’ right to vote and right to effective representation, because they’ll be represented by politicians “who are not constitutionally qualified to hold office and whose votes on legislation and other activities in the National Assembly are constitutionally void,” the stay application reads.

He believes the constitutional amendment included in the law requires the consent of the federal government and all Canadian provinces.

David said the hearing date for his stay request hasn’t yet been set, but he will ask for a decision to be delivered before the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

David is also prepared to file more legal challenges if the Parti Québécois follows up on its plans to break from the monarchy, “including any attempt to unilaterally abolish the office of lieutenant governor,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

David has already filed a challenge against the law, and believes its application should be suspended to make incoming legislature members take the oath until the case is heard on its merits.
The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Monday’s election, and leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already said he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to the King.
The PQ leader also said he’s seeking legal advice on how to further cut ties with the monarchy, including stripping the lieutenant-governor of her roles and funding.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he told reporters Tuesday. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”
Bill 4, adopted in 2022, amended a section of the 1867 Constitution Act to exempt Quebec from the section that requires the oath.

David argues that the law infringes on Quebecers’ right to vote and right to effective representation, because they’ll be represented by politicians “who are not constitutionally qualified to hold office and whose votes on legislation and other activities in the National Assembly are constitutionally void,” the stay application reads.
He believes the constitutional amendment included in the law requires the consent of the federal government and all Canadian provinces.
David said the hearing date for his stay request hasn’t yet been set, but he will ask for a decision to be delivered before the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

David is also prepared to file more legal challenges if the Parti Québécois follows up on its plans to break from the monarchy, “including any attempt to unilaterally abolish the office of lieutenant governor,” he said.

stories.title: FBI depicts Tumbler Ridge shooter's guns, including 'SKS' once confiscated by RCMP
stories.summary: An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter for months provides extensive new details about the guns that May have been used in the attack, and how the teenage killer May have obtained them.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - A Canadian gun control group says FBI documents filed in a Washington state court about the murders in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., reveal the gaps in federal government laws and shows what needs to be done to protect others from such mass killings.

The FBI complaint says the killer talked about having an SKS gun and a “switch,” likely referring to a machine-gun conversion device, which the group PolySeSouvient says should prompt the federal government to prohibit the gun and ban its sale immediately.

The group notes that the SKS is still legal and it’s a military-style weapon that has been used in several mass murders, as well as shootings of police officers.

It says “the Carney government cannot keep ignoring this weapon.”

The FBI complaint was filed to support a charge of conspiracy to murder in a foreign country against 30-year-old James Bryant, who’s accused of supporting and conspiring with Jesse Van Rootselaar for months as she planned then carried out the murders of eight people in February of this year.

The RCMP hasn’t said what kind of guns were used and Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree told reporters in Ottawa it would be “irresponsible” to disclose the information, saying it was “absolutely not” a political decision.

Anandasangaree said an expert panel is reviewing whether to ban semi-automatic SKS weapons.

PolySeSouvient says in a news release that “additional reviews and consultations will not change what everyone can plainly see: this is a highly lethal weapon that has no place in the hands of ordinary civilians.”

The FBI complaint against Bryant includes chats in which Van Rootselaar allegedly speaks of intending to carry out her “plan” for a mass killing using an SKS that police confiscated but then returned.

The complaint includes a photo said to be the killer posing with a rifle on the day of the attack, as well as pictures of other weapons she said she intended to use.

Gun expert Frank Grosspietsch, a retired RCMP weapons officer with the national weapons enforcement support team, identified a gun shown in one set of photos in the complaint as a KRISS Vector submachine-gun, which was banned in Canada in 2024.

The photos were sent to Bryant by Van Rootselaar in 2025, the FBI documents said.

PolySeSouvient said the complaint showed the shooter knew how magazines could make guns more deadly, with Van Rootselaar quoted as telling Bryant, “I think it’d be pretty hard to escape me with my extended magazines on my vector, the recoil is so light that I really don’t think I’d miss.”

“Large-capacity magazines are easy to get. Canada’s magazine regulations are riddled with loopholes and exemptions,” the group said in its statement issued on Wednesday.

The documents said Bryant told officers that Van Rootselaar stole firearms and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and hid them in her room “in preparation for a mass shooting.”

It also said in claims not tested in court that 18-year-old Van Rootselaar told Bryant in online chats that she had convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf.

The RCMP criminal investigation into the shooting is ongoing, despite Van Rootselaar having killed herself at the school.

Assistant RCMP Commissioner Elija Rain, who is acting commanding officer in B.C., said in a statement that “investigators have made substantial progress in the criminal investigation.”

Rain said the RCMP’s release of information about the case has recently been limited “because of the need to ensure our investigative theories and actions were not compromised.”

He attended a news conference in Seattle on Tuesday to discuss Bryant’s case, but he declined to answer questions about the guns, citing a publication ban in Canada.

Grosspietsch, who is a technical adviser to the Association of Firearm and Toolmark Examiners, said the KRISS Vector was designed to appeal to users who wanted the look of a military weapon.

“The firearms industry recognized that if they ‘sexied up,’ and I use that term liberally, firearms to look like military pattern-type firearms or have a bit of a mystique to it, they would sell. KRISS Vector is one of those types of firearms,” he said.

Grosspietsch said the same type of weapon could also be seen in a photo of a gun safe shared on social media by Van Rootselaar’s mother, who was killed along with Van Rootselaar’s younger brother before Van Rootselaar headed to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five students and an education assistant.

Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, Wash., allegedly told the FBI that Van Rootselaar used some of the weapons they discussed during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.

Another photo in the complaint shows a Canuck brand shotgun, decorated with a sticker in the transgender pride colours of blue, pink and white.

Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Bryant is also trans and identifies as female.

Bryant allegedly told Van Rootselaar: “Love the stickers … stickers would be so funny to be seen in photos of the incident.”

A photo in the Bryant complaint depicts a person the FBI says is Van Rootselaar, posing on their knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings, while holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic sight on the morning of the attack.

On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, also decorated in blue, white and pink bands.

The claims in the FBI complaint have not been tested in court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

— With files by Chuck Chiang in Vancouver

stories.title: Hanover shooting leaves man injured, suspect arrested
stories.summary: At least three schools and the town’s hospital were placed in a “hold and secure” Tuesday after gunshots were heard in Hanover.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
One person has been taken into custody following a shooting investigation in Grey County.

According to police, one person was injured in the shooting shortly before noon at a residence in the 300 block of 14th Avenue in Hanover, Ont.

Police said a 37-year-old man was taken to Hanover and District Hospital by Grey County paramedics with gunshot wounds that were not considered life-threatening.

Investigators said a 50-year-old suspect was arrested a short time after the incident, however they have not released details on any charges. Officers also recovered a firearm near the scene.

Hanover police are asking for the public’s help identifying and locating a black van that was seen leaving the area immediately after the shooting.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Hanover Police Service investigators or Crime Stoppers.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Separation is unpopular in Quebec. Why did the province elect sovereigntists?
stories.summary: Quebecers chose a new government on Monday, handing the Parti Québécois (PQ) minority power in the province’s legislature, raising questions about why a sovereigntist party was elected when polling shows little interest in separating from Canada.
stories.author: Jordan Fleguel
stories.content:
Quebecers chose a new government on Monday, handing the Parti Québécois (PQ) minority power in the province’s legislature, raising questions about why a sovereigntist party was elected when polling shows little interest in separating from Canada.

“I think for now, Quebecers wanted a divided government,” David Heurtel, political analyst and former Quebec cabinet minister, told CTV News Channel on Tuesday.

“They wanted to give the PQ a minority government, and I think right now, what Quebecers want most is to deal with the priorities, the same priorities you see across Canada.”

Quebec’s premier-designate, PQ Leader Paul-St Pierre Plamondon has said that his party will work towards holding a third Quebec sovereignty referendum, but that he will wait until U.S. President Donald Trump has left office .

Minority saves province from ‘fraught territory’

That timeline keeps a referendum off the table for the next two years, by which point Plamondon May no longer be in charge, Heurtel said, noting that minority governments typically only last between 18 and 24 months.

“It’s, for most Quebecers, a big sigh of relief that (the PQ) didn’t get a majority, because then we would have been in some very fraught territory,” Tom Mulcair, CTV News’ political commentator and former federal NDP leader told CTV News Channel Tuesday.

“The fact that they were held to a minority came as a surprise to the PQ but not to those of us who kept our eyes on one number, which was 70 per cent. That’s the percentage of Quebecers that didn’t want another referendum,” he said.

Heurtel made the same observation, noting that even as the PQ surged in the polls during the campaign, “support for sovereignty has not wavered.”

5 takeways from Quebec election as Parti Québécois forms minority government

“Seventy per cent of Quebecers, including 63 per cent of Francophones, do not want a referendum and do not want independence,” said Heurtel.

Mulcair argued that while the PQ’s overarching separatist message was attractive to some voters in Quebec, Plamondon’s campaign mainly revolved around a promise to govern differently than the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ), which formed majority governments in 2018 and 2022.

Even Plamondon said in the final stretch of the campaign that the election was going to be about who Quebecers trusted most to lead them through the turbulent economic and political times ahead.

“It’s not totally accurate to say that this election is only about whether we would hold a referendum in three years from now,” Plamondon told Cjad, The Canadian Press reported .

“It’s about changing or not changing a government that has catastrophic results in many areas of our society and choosing who could do a good job and who could be reliable in terms of what they do and what they say.”

Collapse of the CAQ

Despite the PQ’s victory, the party received just 28 per cent of the total number of votes cast on Monday, and it has very little representation in the province’s largest urban centres of Montreal and Quebec City.

The collapse of the (CAQ), which failed to win any seats in the legislature, helped other parties gain ground as well. The provincial Liberals maintained opposition status after receiving 24 per cent of the popular vote, while the provincial Conservatives got roughly 21 per cent.

While both parties have said they would not support a referendum, Quebec’s other sovereigntist party, Québec solidaire, won enough seats in the legislature to form a majority with the PQ.

“They’ve got nine seats, so they could support the PQ if it decides to go ahead with the referendum bill, but there’s a lot of differences; they don’t get along very well on the political level,” said Heurtel.

Another important aspect of the political landscape in Quebec to keep in mind, Heurtel argued, is the current popularity of the prime minister.

“So, it’s not like you have that dichotomy with a Justin Trudeau, a Stephen Harper, or even a Jean Chrétien. The dynamic is completely different, and Quebecers don’t have an appetite… for a referendum.”

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario's medical regulator proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's medical regulator is proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply drugs, The Canadian Press has learned.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Ontario’s medical regulator is proposing sweeping changes to prescribing safer supply drugs, The Canadian Press has learned.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario is looking to clamp down on the practice and is set to hold a board of directors meeting next week to decide on the proposed changes.

Safer supply refers to prescribing medications as an alternative to opioids obtained on the streets to those who are at high risk of overdose.

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain. Fentanyl is often found laced with other drugs such as benzodiazepines, a depressant, and xylazine, often used to tranquilize animals.

One change the regulator has proposed in a document tucked away on its website is that “physicians must only prescribe safer supply medications in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy.” The therapy uses medications such as methadone to treat opioid addiction.

The college is also proposing an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply, and mandating that it be consumed in front of health-care professionals.

The regulator previously made changes to its drug prescription policy in May that mandated physicians to perform an in-person assessment before prescribing narcotics for safer supply, as well as making it mandatory for doctors to offer opioid agonist therapy before prescribing safer supply drugs and perform followups every three months.

The rationale behind the new proposed changes centres largely on diversion of patients’ prescription pills to the black market.

“The proposed amendments build on targeted changes introduced in May and respond to ongoing concerns about the diversion of safer supply medication and the resulting risks to patients and communities,” Mickey Cirak, spokesperson for the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, wrote in an email.

“In response, the college has proposed amendments intended to strengthen oversight of safer supply prescribing and enhance safeguards related to physician prescribing practices, consistent with its role as Ontario’s medical regulator.”

The college said it has consulted with a broad range of people and organizations, including physicians, municipalities and health-care partners, as well as the office of Ontario’s chief medical officer of health, Dr. Kieran Moore.

Moore’s office did not respond to a request for comment or an interview. Moore has never granted The Canadian Press an interview about the province’s opioids crisis, despite more than a dozen requests since he took the role in 2021.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons said the initiative to change safer-supply prescription rules is its own and did not come from the provincial government.

Cirak said the college also received feedback from doctors with expertise in addiction medicine.

The proposal has the support of Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

“Our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs, including the illicit use of hydromorphone masked as ‘safer supply,’” said Satnam Grewal, a spokesperson for Jones.

“We welcome any action from Ontario’s 27 regulatory colleges who set standards and obligations for health-care professionals, including the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario, to crack down on the predatory prescribing of addictive drugs.”

Ontario has moved to an abstinence-based model under Premier Doug Ford in its approach to the ongoing opioid crisis. The province closed provincially funded supervised consumption sites and passed a law banning them within 200 metres of schools and daycares.

The province has since opened 29 homelessness and addiction recovery treatment hubs, which the government calls HART hubs. It has spent more than $500 million on that plan, which offers primary and mental health care, addiction services and peer supports.

Word of the proposed changes has reached some people who depend on safer supply, said Lorraine Lam, an organizer with the Shelter and Housing Justice Network and a longtime harm reduction worker.

“The changes are really dangerous and very destabilizing,” Lam said.

“People are really, really scared and people are really, really anxious and very angry.”

She said some people using safer supply got jobs or returned to school and she’s worried what will happen to them when they’re cut off.

“The reality is people who are on safe supply are going to be de-prescribed really, really quickly, which will increase the chances of people turning to the street unregulated supply, which will then therefore increase the risk of overdoses and deaths,” Lam said.

The college’s board of directors is set to meet on Oct. 13, when it is expected to vote on the proposed changes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Greater Toronto home sales in September down from year ago, average price also lower
stories.summary: Toronto - Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area in September were down nine per cent compared with a year ago as the average price also edged lower.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area were down in September from a year ago, while average prices continued to decline as soft conditions persist in some parts of the housing market.

The Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said in its monthly report Tuesday that homebuyers were in a holding pattern in September, as uncertainty surrounding the economy, inflation and borrowing costs weighed on sales.

Sales totalled 5,040 in September, down nine per cent year-over-year, it said.

The result came as the average selling price for the month was $1,006,409, down from $1,060,036 a year earlier. The composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.7 per cent year-over-year in September.

Home sales in the Greater Toronto Area in September were down nine per cent compared with a year ago as the average price also edged lower. (Oct. 6, 2026)

Renewed tensions with the United States and a surge in gas prices amid war in the Middle East have kept potential buyers on the sidelines in recent months.

Meanwhile, rising bond yields have pushed fixed mortgage rates higher over the past month, and buyers are expecting the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates, said John Pasalis, president of Move Smartly Realty Inc.

“Higher rates — and the idea of higher rates — is obviously straining on affordability, but also leading buyers to think that the market’s going to be a little bit softer in the future,” he said in an interview on Tuesday.

The slowdown is likely going to continue through the rest of the year, he said.

Slowing home sales come as municipalities across Ontario, including the GTA, hold an election on Oct. 26.

“Housing is one of the biggest issues on voters’ minds, and the upcoming municipal election will help shape housing policy across the GTA and Simcoe County for the next four years,” said Daniel Steinfeld, TRREB president, in a statement.

“The decisions our next mayors and councillors make on affordability, housing supply and the costs associated with buying a home can also influence buyer demand and confidence in the market.”

New listings in September totalled 16,500, down 14.4 per cent year-over-year.

Within the City of Toronto, TRREB said there were 1,937 sales last month, down 5.4 per cent from September 2025. Across the rest of the GTA, home sales decreased nine per cent to 5,040.

Townhouses saw the biggest drop in activity among all housing types, with 12.8 per cent fewer sales year-over-year. There were also 7.8 per cent fewer condos sold last month compared with a year ago.

The semi-detached markets grew 8.2 per cent year-over-year, while detached home sales were up 8.7 per cent.

Toronto real estate broker Cailey Heaps said while some segments of the market suffered, ultra-luxury buyers as well as first-time homebuyers were active.

“First-time homebuyers have accepted that the market that we’re in now is the new normal. It’s no longer about waiting to time a market,” she said.

“You’re going to make a buying decision when it feels right for you, whether that’s because you’re getting married or starting a family or relocating to a new city or because you can afford it.”

The move-up market, or homeowners who can upgrade to a bigger property, largely remained on the sidelines last month, Heaps said.

“They don’t want to take the risk when the economy is not as strong as it was, or they have some job insecurity. So, not many people are moving in that segment,” she said.

A muted market could pick up in the new year but Pasalis said a rebound hinges on economic certainty and market confidence.

That means no new tariff threats, easing tensions with the U.S. and a slight decline in bond yields.

“We don’t even need to see a dramatic change, but if (bond yields) dip a little bit in the new year where mortgage rates are closer to the four per cent range rather than the mid-to-high four per cent range, I think again that can shift buyers off of the sidelines,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 6, 2026.

stories.title: Crash between cyclist and London police vehicle closes section of Hamilton Road
stories.summary: Police have closed a section of Hamilton Road following a crash between a marked London police cruiser and a cyclist.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Police have closed a section of Hamilton Road following a crash between a marked London police cruiser and a cyclist.

According to police, the crash happened around 6:30 a.m. and has closed Hamilton Road between Pegler Street and Smith Street.

Motorists are being asked to avoid the area and use an alternate route as the road will remain closed for an undetermined period while the investigation continues.

Police said the cyclist was transported to hospital with unknown injuries.

No details have been released regarding the circumstances surrounding the collision.

Further updates are expected as more information becomes available.

stories.title: Amendments would let Manitoba cannabis stores drop window coverings for safety
stories.summary: Winnipeg - Cannabis stores across Manitoba May soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WINNIPEG - Cannabis stores across Manitoba may soon be able to remove window coverings that are required to prevent the public from seeing inside.

The Manitoba government introduced amendments to the provincial Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Control Act on Monday that would eliminate window coverings on all cannabis storefronts amid safety concerns.

The province said the change would increase visibility from outside the store and help make sure workers are not hidden from public view.

Current legislation requires retailers to ensure that cannabis and cannabis products are not visible to people who are not legally allowed to purchase the products.

“We’re still mandating that the cannabis product will not be visible because we want to protect kids, and so we’re finding that balance,” said Justice Minister Matt Wiebe.

“We don’t want cannabis displayed in window fronts. We don’t want kids riding by and seeing cannabis and being enticed into trying a product that’s not appropriate for them, but at the same time we have to prioritize workers’ safety.”

Labour groups have long expressed concerns about the special problems that cannabis stores pose, because they sell a controlled substance and are required by government rules to cover all windows to the outside.

An attack on a cannabis store employee who was working alone at night in May renewed calls from unions for improved worker safety.

Police arrested a man after he allegedly entered a retail store, waiting for a customer to leave, and then locked himself inside with a woman working alone.

They said he sexually assaulted the 24-year-old, who was able to flee the store and call police.

The province is also proposing changes to the act that would allow mandatory minimum staffing levels during certain hours to ensure that workers are not alone during times when there may be a higher risk of violence.

The United Food and Commercial Workers union welcomed the province’s proposals.

It surveyed its members and non-unionized staff on worker safety concerns and found that staffing levels was one of the biggest issues.

“Loud and clear, not working alone was by far the No. 1 issue that they raised,” said Marie Buchan, secretary-treasurer of Local 832.

Wiebe said the proposed amendments would give the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority the ability to mandate how many employees may be on a shift at a given period.

The Opposition Progressive Conservatives said they would have to review the bill before commenting.

Other provinces, including Ontario, have scrapped similar rules around window coverings to address safety concerns expressed by employees.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.
