stories.title: Trial begins for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport
stories.summary: A trial is set to begin today in Brampton for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
BRAMPTON — Prosecutors allege an Air Canada employee provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Toronto Pearson airport cargo bay in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu was one of the “inside men” with the knowledge and access to help carry out the 2023 heist, Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic told a Brampton, Ont., court Monday as Sidhu’s trial began.

The trial is expected to hear evidence that the fraudulent air waybill was printed on site the day before the operation using Sidhu’s profile, and the Crown alleges he was the one who printed it, Vlacic said in her opening statement.

The driver who picked up the gold had an air waybill for a fish shipment, but the document was altered with a handwritten number for the gold shipment, she said.

The Crown alleges the driver is Durante King-Mclean, an Ontario man who U.S. authorities say fled south shortly after the heist. He was arrested in Pennsylvania in September 2023 and has since pleaded guilty in a separate case to conspiring to traffic firearms, U.S. officials said.

“Whoever provided this air waybill to Mr. Durante King-Mclean … knew exactly what he needed to have and what needed to be changed,” Vlacic said.

Sidhu pleaded not guilty Monday to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.

Prosecutors allege Sidhu was working hand in hand with Simran Panesar, another Air Canada employee at the time, to facilitate the theft for the others accused.

Panesar resigned in the months that followed the heist and was interviewed by investigators that July, court heard. The next day, he and his family left Canada and never returned, according to an agreed statement of fact read in court. A Canada-wide warrant has been issued for his arrest.

The altered waybill was only one of the steps needed to pull off the theft without getting noticed immediately, Vlacic said. In the background, the shipment’s designation as high value was removed and notes about its breakdown were changed, she said.

Yelizaveta Zaritskaya, who was Air Canada’s cargo operations manager at the time of the heist, told court her profile was used to remove the high-value designation from the gold shipment on a day when she was not working. Under questioning from the defence later, she clarified it was a crucial change that meant the shipment would be treated as regular cargo that could “pass for fish.”

Back then, she said, there were shared computers in the managers’ offices and it wasn’t uncommon for people to conduct minor functions while the computer was still logged into someone else’s profile.

“It was a bad practice,” she said.

Anyone who had access to the offices would have access to managers’ computers, including Sidhu’s, she said, adding that a lot of Air Canada’s security protocols have changed since then.

Asked by the defence whether security was lax in those days, Zaritskaya paused, then said: “It clearly was lacking since we had stolen gold.”

Zaritskaya highlighted some “concerning” points on the waybill used to pick up the gold. For one thing, she said, the number linking it to the shipment was handwritten on two separate spots when it should be typed out. “Air Canada employees should not write on the air waybill,” she said.

It also specified in which area the shipment should be stored, namely the cold storage, which is not often marked on the waybill, she said. As well, there was a tear in the document that means it wasn’t maintained to standard, she said.

However, an inexperienced attendant may not notice these issues, she said.

Earlier Monday, Peel regional police Const. Clayton Asano, testified about his role in investigating how the air waybill made its way through the cargo facility.

Court watched surveillance video from the cargo facility that showed a white truck back into the loading bay and the driver, dressed in reflective gear and a face covering, go inside and interact with Air Canada staff.

The driver handed over documents including the waybill and eventually an employee with a forklift came with the shipment and helped load it onto the truck. The truck then drove away, with the entire process playing out within an hour, court heard.

Prosecutors said the identity of the driver is not in dispute in this trial.

During cross-examination, Sidhu’s lawyers asked Asano whether handwriting analysis was conducted on the waybill. Asano said no, but clarified under re-examination by the Crown that such an analysis had been considered and ruled out because there wasn’t enough writing on the waybill or enough of a sample to compare it to.

The trial comes after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Chaudhary, who is considered one of the architects of the heist, is expected to testify for the prosecution in Sidhu’s trial.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial next month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Clocks stay in daylight saving, but analysis backs permanent standard time
stories.summary: An analysis by economic, mental health and sleep experts has concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time, not daylight saving. Here's why.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver — Ralph Mistlberger’s light is adjustable, allowing him to have the full spectrum of options depending on what his internal clock needs.

“You want cool in the morning. You want warm in the evening or warm in the afternoon,” he said.

“And so, it goes from being more bluish in the morning to more reddish in the evenings. Both of those are important because artificial light affects your clock.”

Mistlberger knows real sunlight is better than a lamp, but after more than 40 years as a neuroscientist studying sleep and the body’s circadian rhythms, he’s preparing for what’s to come Nov. 1.

That’s when clocks would normally have turned back an hour for most of Western Canada. But they’re staying where they are, putting residents on permanent daylight time.

Mistlberger said it’s a mistake and he and other researchers from British Columbia have released an analysis warning of the potential risks to health, the economy and students’ well-being with the darker mornings on the way.

The analysis by economic, mental health and sleep experts was published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal and examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight saving — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.

Mistlberger, a psychology professor at Simon Fraser University, said people May think they want more sun in the evening, but the impact of starting your winter day in the dark is far-reaching.

“You’re actually waking up at an earlier circadian phase. Your clock May still be telling your brain and your body that this is the sleep period. It’s not time to wake up yet,” he said.

“The same is going to happen in the evening. It’s going to be telling you this is still the wake period, it’s not time to go to bed yet.”

He said not being able to get consistent sleep can lead to what scientists call “social jet lag,” when someone’s life and social calendar doesn’t line up with their biological clock.

Small amounts of sleep deprivation can be reversed with a good, long snooze, he said, but if the issue becomes chronic it can lead to health concerns.

That can include more cases of metabolic disorders, like obesity and diabetes, as well as cardiovascular disease. He said epidemiological studies of large populations have found increases in cancer and some mood disorders.

B.C., Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Manitoba all announced this year that they would adopt permanent year-round daylight time.

The B.C. government pitched that the move would “improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”

It said more than 223,000 people participated in a 2019 online survey and 93 per cent preferred a change to year-round daylight time.

Both Mistlberger and Patrick Baylis, a co-author of the analysis, said the government survey didn’t give the public the option to choose permanent standard time.

“The survey gave two options, which were comparing a switching regime, which is what we have previously had, to permanent daylight time. But those are the only two options. Baylis said.

Baylis, an associate professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia, said one of the biggest concerns is what it will mean for students going to school in the dark.

A study of students around the time zone boundary in Florida showed an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores among adolescents. The analysis said it was “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions and largest at puberty when circadian rhythms are most sensitive.”

“At minimum we should be thinking about monitoring for some of these negative effects on schooling outcomes, particularly among adolescents,” Baylis said in an interview.

While there is limited economic research, Baylis said some studies suggest exposure to sunlight can affect productivity.

A study that looked at variation in sunset timing within U.S. time zones found that an hour of later sunset reduces earnings over the long run by about five per cent.

Some countries that tried to make the switch to permanent daylight saving have not fared well.

Russia made the move in 2011 but reversed it three years later.

“Public dissatisfaction grew rapidly, particularly in northern regions, where winter morning darkness was even more prolonged, with critics citing disrupted biological rhythms, morning travel risks and effects on daily functioning,” the study said.

Most of Chile’s decision to change in 2015 was also reversed “after complaints about reduced school attendance, scheduling disruption and agricultural effects,” it said.

In 1974, all of the United States adopted permanent daylight saving as an energy-conservation measure.

“The policy was abandoned within the year after widespread opposition to dark winter mornings, concerns about children travelling to school before sunrise, workplace safety concerns and limited evidence of meaningful energy savings,” the analysis said.

The study recommends that choosing to stay with permanent daylight time should include steps to reduce the potential health effects and to evaluate the change.

Baylis said that could mean more flexible or later school start times or helping schools supplement the lack of real light in the morning.

Mistlberger said educating people on the potential impact is important, using bright lights in morning with adjustable bulbs to dim them by the evening.

“You want to get as much light exposure as you can as early as possible in the day when you go outside. So, even though the sunrise is going to be later than usual, it’s going to help you to get outside as soon as there is some sunrise.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Ashley Joannou, The Canadian Press

“You’re actually waking up at an earlier circadian phase. Your clock May still be telling your brain and your body that this is the sleep period. It’s not time to wake up yet,” he said.
“The same is going to happen in the evening. It’s going to be telling you this is still the wake period, it’s not time to go to bed yet.”
He said not being able to get consistent sleep can lead to what scientists call “social jet lag,” when someone’s life and social calendar doesn’t line up with their biological clock.
Small amounts of sleep deprivation can be reversed with a good, long snooze, he said, but if the issue becomes chronic it can lead to health concerns.

That can include more cases of metabolic disorders, like obesity and diabetes, as well as cardiovascular disease. He said epidemiological studies of large populations have found increases in cancer and some mood disorders.
B.C., Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Manitoba all announced this year that they would adopt permanent year-round daylight time.

The B.C. government pitched that the move would “improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”
It said more than 223,000 people participated in a 2019 online survey and 93 per cent preferred a change to year-round daylight time.
Both Mistlberger and Patrick Baylis, a co-author of the analysis, said the government survey didn’t give the public the option to choose permanent standard time.
“The survey gave two options, which were comparing a switching regime, which is what we have previously had, to permanent daylight time. But those are the only two options. Baylis said.

Baylis, an associate professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia, said one of the biggest concerns is what it will mean for students going to school in the dark.

A study of students around the time zone boundary in Florida showed an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores among adolescents. The analysis said it was “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions and largest at puberty when circadian rhythms are most sensitive.”
“At minimum we should be thinking about monitoring for some of these negative effects on schooling outcomes, particularly among adolescents,” Baylis said in an interview.
While there is limited economic research, Baylis said some studies suggest exposure to sunlight can affect productivity.
A study that looked at variation in sunset timing within U.S. time zones found that an hour of later sunset reduces earnings over the long run by about five per cent.
Some countries that tried to make the switch to permanent daylight saving have not fared well.
Russia made the move in 2011 but reversed it three years later.

“Public dissatisfaction grew rapidly, particularly in northern regions, where winter morning darkness was even more prolonged, with critics citing disrupted biological rhythms, morning travel risks and effects on daily functioning,” the study said.
Most of Chile’s decision to change in 2015 was also reversed “after complaints about reduced school attendance, scheduling disruption and agricultural effects,” it said.
In 1974, all of the United States adopted permanent daylight saving as an energy-conservation measure.

“The policy was abandoned within the year after widespread opposition to dark winter mornings, concerns about children travelling to school before sunrise, workplace safety concerns and limited evidence of meaningful energy savings,” the analysis said.
The study recommends that choosing to stay with permanent daylight time should include steps to reduce the potential health effects and to evaluate the change.
Baylis said that could mean more flexible or later school start times or helping schools supplement the lack of real light in the morning.
Mistlberger said educating people on the potential impact is important, using bright lights in morning with adjustable bulbs to dim them by the evening.

“You want to get as much light exposure as you can as early as possible in the day when you go outside. So, even though the sunrise is going to be later than usual, it’s going to help you to get outside as soon as there is some sunrise.”

stories.title: Trial set to begin for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto's Pearson airport
stories.summary: A trial is set to begin today in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Brampton — A trial is set to begin today in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu is charged with theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist that took place at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

The trial comes soon after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial later this fall.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Supreme Court to open judicial year with ceremony in temporary new building
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada is set to mark the opening of the judicial year with a ceremony in its temporary new building today.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canada’s democratic institutions need protection in the face of unrelenting pressures, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said Monday as the Supreme Court of Canada opened a new judicial year.

Wagner said the world feels increasingly uncertain due to deepening polarization, the non-stop pace of events and the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence.

When seas grow rough an anchor keeps a vessel from drifting, and democratic institutions play the same role in society, Wagner said.

“The strength of an anchor is not measured in calm waters,” he added. “It is measured in a storm. The same is true for the rule of law.”

Wagner, flanked by the other members of the Supreme Court, spoke at a ceremony in the court’s temporary new building.

The top court is settling in at the West Memorial Building, not far from Parliament Hill, while the court’s permanent home across the street undergoes extensive renovations.

Refurbishing the stately Supreme Court building is expected to take at least 10 years.

A formal welcome for the court’s newest member, Glenn Joyal, is set to take place next month.

Kristen Boon, president of the Council of Canadian Law Deans, said during the ceremony Monday that, like many judges, those who lead law schools have been watching with concern the threats to the rule of law around the world.

“We believe that future generations of lawyers will understand their duties as citizens to be central to their professional identity,” Boon said.

“Our classrooms and our campuses should model what reasoned debate and evidence-based decision making looks like. Law faculties protect academic freedom and give professors the space to teach, to research and to debate difficult ideas openly.”

Justice Minister Sean Fraser told the courtroom full of dignitaries that provinces, communities and groups of people are asking questions about their roles within the Canadian federation.

“If we expect to preserve national unity, we must constantly improve the public’s belief that the systems that we enjoy serve their interests over time,” Fraser said. “The law has an important role to play in this regard.”

He said that at a time “when it’s difficult to discern between truth and fiction, particularly with the rise and deployment of artificial intelligence, the truth-seeking function of this court and courts across Canada could never be more important.”

Fraser said that, as a Nova Scotian, he appreciated Wagner’s seafaring analogy about the strength of an anchor being tested in choppy waters.

But the justice minister reflected on one even more familiar to the court.

“It’s been nearly a century since Canadian law was first referred to as a living tree. If we’re to accept that doctrine as part of the laws of this nation, we must similarly accept the obligation placed upon us as caretakers of that tree,” he said.

“And as the branches grow, sometimes in unruly ways to address the changing nature of modern reality, I know and take great comfort in the fact that the court will be here to ensure that its roots remain strong for a generation to come.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

paragraphs: VANCOUVER - Ralph Mistlberger’s light is adjustable, allowing him to have the full spectrum of options depending on what his internal clock needs.
“You want cool in the morning. You want warm in the evening or warm in the afternoon,” he said.
“And so, it goes from being more bluish in the morning to more reddish in the evenings. Both of those are important because artificial light affects your clock.”
Mistlberger knows real sunlight is better than a lamp, but after more than 40 years as a neuroscientist studying sleep and the body’s circadian rhythms, he’s preparing for what’s to come Nov. 1.
That’s when clocks would normally have turned back an hour for most of Western Canada. But they’re staying where they are, putting residents on permanent daylight time.

Mistlberger said it’s a mistake and he and other researchers from British Columbia have released an analysis warning of the potential risks to health, the economy and students’ well-being with the darker mornings on the way.

The analysis by economic, mental health and sleep experts was published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal and examined multiple studies and concluded that health evidence favours moving to permanent standard time — not daylight saving — in part because it better aligns with the body’s rhythm.
Mistlberger, a psychology professor at Simon Fraser University, said people may think they want more sun in the evening, but the impact of starting your winter day in the dark is far-reaching.
“You’re actually waking up at an earlier circadian phase. Your clock may still be telling your brain and your body that this is the sleep period. It’s not time to wake up yet,” he said.
“The same is going to happen in the evening. It’s going to be telling you this is still the wake period, it’s not time to go to bed yet.”
He said not being able to get consistent sleep can lead to what scientists call “social jet lag,” when someone’s life and social calendar doesn’t line up with their biological clock.
Small amounts of sleep deprivation can be reversed with a good, long snooze, he said, but if the issue becomes chronic it can lead to health concerns.

That can include more cases of metabolic disorders, like obesity and diabetes, as well as cardiovascular disease. He said epidemiological studies of large populations have found increases in cancer and some mood disorders.
B.C., Alberta, the Northwest Territories and Manitoba all announced this year that they would adopt permanent year-round daylight time.

The B.C. government pitched that the move would “improve people’s overall health, reduce disruptions for families, simplify scheduling and provide an extra hour of evening light during the winter months.”
It said more than 223,000 people participated in a 2019 online survey and 93 per cent preferred a change to year-round daylight time.
Both Mistlberger and Patrick Baylis, a co-author of the analysis, said the government survey didn’t give the public the option to choose permanent standard time.
“The survey gave two options, which were comparing a switching regime, which is what we have previously had, to permanent daylight time. But those are the only two options. Baylis said.

Baylis, an associate professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia, said one of the biggest concerns is what it will mean for students going to school in the dark.

A study of students around the time zone boundary in Florida showed an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores among adolescents. The analysis said it was “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions and largest at puberty when circadian rhythms are most sensitive.”
“At minimum we should be thinking about monitoring for some of these negative effects on schooling outcomes, particularly among adolescents,” Baylis said in an interview.
While there is limited economic research, Baylis said some studies suggest exposure to sunlight can affect productivity.
A study that looked at variation in sunset timing within U.S. time zones found that an hour of later sunset reduces earnings over the long run by about five per cent.
Some countries that tried to make the switch to permanent daylight saving have not fared well.
Russia made the move in 2011 but reversed it three years later.

“Public dissatisfaction grew rapidly, particularly in northern regions, where winter morning darkness was even more prolonged, with critics citing disrupted biological rhythms, morning travel risks and effects on daily functioning,” the study said.
Most of Chile’s decision to change in 2015 was also reversed “after complaints about reduced school attendance, scheduling disruption and agricultural effects,” it said.
In 1974, all of the United States adopted permanent daylight saving as an energy-conservation measure.

“The policy was abandoned within the year after widespread opposition to dark winter mornings, concerns about children travelling to school before sunrise, workplace safety concerns and limited evidence of meaningful energy savings,” the analysis said.
The study recommends that choosing to stay with permanent daylight time should include steps to reduce the potential health effects and to evaluate the change.
Baylis said that could mean more flexible or later school start times or helping schools supplement the lack of real light in the morning.
Mistlberger said educating people on the potential impact is important, using bright lights in morning with adjustable bulbs to dim them by the evening.

“You want to get as much light exposure as you can as early as possible in the day when you go outside. So, even though the sunrise is going to be later than usual, it’s going to help you to get outside as soon as there is some sunrise.”

stories.title: Trial set to begin for man accused in massive gold heist at Toronto's Pearson airport
stories.summary: Brampton - A trial is set to begin today in Brampton, Ont., for a man accused in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
BRAMPTON - Prosecutors allege an Air Canada employee provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Toronto Pearson airport cargo bay in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Parmpal Sidhu was one of the “inside men” with the knowledge and access to help carry out the 2023 heist, Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic told a Brampton, Ont., court Monday as Sidhu’s trial began.

The trial is expected to hear evidence that the fraudulent air waybill was printed on site the day before the operation using Sidhu’s profile, and the Crown alleges he was the one who printed it, Vlacic said in her opening statement.

The driver who picked up the gold had an air waybill for a fish shipment, but the document was altered with a handwritten number for the gold shipment, she said.

The Crown alleges the driver is Durante King-Mclean, an Ontario man who U.S. authorities say fled south shortly after the heist. He was arrested in Pennsylvania in September 2023 and has since pleaded guilty in a separate case to conspiring to traffic firearms, U.S. officials said.

“Whoever provided this air waybill to Mr. Durante King-Mclean ... knew exactly what he needed to have and what needed to be changed,” Vlacic said.

Sidhu pleaded not guilty Monday to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence.

Prosecutors allege Sidhu was working hand in hand with Simran Panesar, another Air Canada employee at the time, to facilitate the theft for the others accused.

Panesar resigned in the months that followed the heist and was interviewed by investigators that July, court heard. The next day, he and his family left Canada and never returned, according to an agreed statement of fact read in court. A Canada-wide warrant has been issued for his arrest.

The altered waybill was only one of the steps needed to pull off the theft without getting noticed immediately, Vlacic said. In the background, the shipment’s designation as high value was removed and notes about its breakdown were changed, she said.

Yelizaveta Zaritskaya, who was Air Canada’s cargo operations manager at the time of the heist, told court her profile was used to remove the high-value designation from the gold shipment on a day when she was not working. Under questioning from the defence later, she clarified it was a crucial change that meant the shipment would be treated as regular cargo that could “pass for fish.”

Back then, she said, there were shared computers in the managers’ offices and it wasn’t uncommon for people to conduct minor functions while the computer was still logged into someone else’s profile.

“It was a bad practice,” she said.

Anyone who had access to the offices would have access to managers’ computers, including Sidhu’s, she said, adding that a lot of Air Canada’s security protocols have changed since then.

Asked by the defence whether security was lax in those days, Zaritskaya paused, then said: “It clearly was lacking since we had stolen gold.”

Zaritskaya highlighted some “concerning” points on the waybill used to pick up the gold. For one thing, she said, the number linking it to the shipment was handwritten on two separate spots when it should be typed out. “Air Canada employees should not write on the air waybill,” she said.

It also specified in which area the shipment should be stored, namely the cold storage, which is not often marked on the waybill, she said. As well, there was a tear in the document that means it wasn’t maintained to standard, she said.

However, an inexperienced attendant may not notice these issues, she said.

Earlier Monday, Peel regional police Const. Clayton Asano, testified about his role in investigating how the air waybill made its way through the cargo facility.

Court watched surveillance video from the cargo facility that showed a white truck back into the loading bay and the driver, dressed in reflective gear and a face covering, go inside and interact with Air Canada staff.

The driver handed over documents including the waybill and eventually an employee with a forklift came with the shipment and helped load it onto the truck. The truck then drove away, with the entire process playing out within an hour, court heard.

Prosecutors said the identity of the driver is not in dispute in this trial.

During cross-examination, Sidhu’s lawyers asked Asano whether handwriting analysis was conducted on the waybill. Asano said no, but clarified under re-examination by the Crown that such an analysis had been considered and ruled out because there wasn’t enough writing on the waybill or enough of a sample to compare it to.

The trial comes after prosecutors dropped the charges against two other men accused in the case.

Last month, the Crown withdrew charges against Ali Raza, a jeweller who had been accused of knowingly receiving some of the stolen gold, and Amit Jalota.

Meanwhile, a man who admitted his role in the heist was sentenced this spring to four years in prison.

Arsalan Chaudhary, who was arrested earlier in the year as he flew back from Dubai, pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 and was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

Chaudhary, who is considered one of the architects of the heist, is expected to testify for the prosecution in Sidhu’s trial.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from Pearson on April 17, 2023, and had a value of more than $20 million.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from a refinery in Zurich, Switzerland, and were transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said two years ago as they released more details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K.

The gold and currency were then offloaded and brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Another man accused in the case, Archit Grover, is expected to face trial next month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 5, 2026.

stories.title: What Florida’s property tax vote means for Canadian snowbirds
stories.summary: A Florida ballot measure would sharply increase property tax exemptions for many permanent residents while keeping non-homesteaded properties in the tax base. Gov. Ron DeSantis has explicitly said snowbirds, including Canadians, could continue paying property taxes as Florida homeowners receive relief.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Florida voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to approve Amendment 3 , a constitutional measure that would substantially increase the homestead property-tax exemption for qualifying homeowners.

For Canadian snowbirds, who own property in Florida, the proposed tax overhaul comes with a twist: the biggest break would go to permanent Florida residents, while seasonal homeowners, including Canadians, could remain part of the tax base.

The proposal in May grew out of Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ campaign to reduce, and eventually eliminate, property taxes on homesteaded homes. He said that Florida could afford the change because “Property tax revenue collected by local governments has nearly doubled in the past seven years.”

He also made clear who would remain outside the main relief.

“We are focusing on homestead. Obviously they tax property that are non-homestead: Residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial,” DeSantis said in an interview with Fox News in June.

In 2025 , while arguing against a sales-tax cut, he said he wanted “Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists” to help subsidize Florida while residents received tax relief.

That is significant for Canadians, who make up a large share of Florida’s seasonal property owners.

The amendment , approved by Florida lawmakers, would increase the non-school homestead exemption from the current US$50,000 to US$150,000 in 2027 and US$250,000 in 2028. It would also reduce the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homesteaded properties from 10 per cent to five per cent.

In other words, the measure does not create a tax specifically targeting Canadians. Rather, Canadians who own properties that do not qualify for the permanent-resident homestead exemption would not receive the main tax break.

If approved by at least 60 per cent of Florida voters, Amendment 3 would take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Property taxes are local, not state. So we’d need to do a constitutional amendment (requires 60% of voters to approve) to eliminate them (which I would support) or even to reform/lower them… We should put the boldest amendment on the ballot that has a chance of getting that… https://t.co/WpOQmjNl0X — Ron DeSantis (@GovRonDeSantis) February 13, 2025

For Canadians, who own a winter home in Florida, the issue is therefore less about a new Canadian-specific tax than about who qualifies for the largest property tax relief and who remains responsible for local property taxes as Florida reshapes its tax base.

stories.title: Debris from missing Ontario-based air ambulance located: U.S. Coast Guard
stories.summary: Debris associated with an Ontario-based air ambulance that was carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been located hours after it went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.
stories.author: Bryann Aguilar, Joshua McGinnis
stories.content:
Debris associated with an Ontario-based air ambulance that was carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been located hours after it went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.

The U.S. Coast Guard said in a news release on Saturday night that crews discovered the debris field off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., where they had been conducting a search all day.

“Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night,” the release read, noting that 1,644 square miles have been searched over approximately 27 hours.

The U.S. Coast Guard added that next of kin have been notified.

The Coast Guard said the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration notified them around 2 a.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 with the tail number C-Grjp and owned by Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance.

#Breaking : @uscg is searching for a Gulfstream aircraft with 6 persons on board. @FAANews reported losing contact w/the aircraft early Saturday morning. #Uscg air & surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft. Updates will be provided here as info becomes available.… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Clarence Togeretz, the air ambulance company’s operations manager, told The Canadian Press on Saturday morning that the aircraft was transporting a patient and family member, who were Bermuda nationals.

He said the two pilots and two medical staff aboard were Canadians.

Togeretz also shared that his company had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. as it was approaching Boston. Togeretz said Latitude reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard when the aircraft failed to reach the tarmac.

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

Togeretz noted that this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

Pilot declared emergency: ATC audio

The aircraft bound for Boston Logan International Airport departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport at 12:41 a.m. The air ambulance arrived in Bermuda from Hamilton the previous night.

Air traffic control audio captured by LiveATC.net indicates that the flight declared an emergency before it went missing.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot, who cannot be heard in the audio.

The controller then asked the pilot if they were declaring an emergency.

“You’re coming in a little weak. I didn’t hear your response was if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the controller heard telling the pilot.

A short time later, the controller got a confirmation from the pilot that they were indeed declaring an emergency.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, data shows that one hour and 23 minutes into the flight, the aircraft dropped from an altitude of 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in two minutes and then levelled off before it vanished.

The search for the jet included crews in the air and on the water, the U.S. Coast Guard said, noting that it was using two planes, a search and rescue lifeboat, a helicopter, and a cutter.

The Coast Guard noted that crews

#Update Uscg assets responding include: - HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew from AirSta Cape Cod - HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City - MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod - 47-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point - FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154)… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Latitude Air Ambulance’s website says that it currently has four G100 jets in its fleet, each with a range of 5,000 km.

In a statement posted to X , Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge said that “Our thoughts are with our colleagues at Latitude Air Ambulance at this time.”

“All of us at Ornge are hopeful the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Ornge noted that the flight was not related to its operations.

Canadian government ‘closely monitoring the situation’

Canada’s Transportation Minister, Steven MacKinnon, said his department is aware of the situation and that they “are closing monitoring” in a post to X.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time.”

“We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue. I want to thank all first responders involved for their ongoing efforts.”

I am aware of reports of a Canadian-registered air ambulance aircraft that went missing while travelling from Bermuda to Boston. Four Canadians are among the six people on board. My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during… — Steven MacKinnon (@stevenmackinnon) October 3, 2026

Global Affairs Canada said it was aware of reports of Canadians on board the missing Latitude Air Ambulance.

“Consular officials stand ready to provide consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities. Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be disclosed,” Global Affairs said in a statement to CTV News.

Bermuda government releases statement

A spokesperson on behalf of the Bermuda government confirmed the air ambulance’s departure from Bermuda to Boston this morning in a post to X.

Officials said they’ve been in contact with the families of those on board as well as the U.S. Coast Guard conducting the search.

In a statement, Bermuda’s Premier David Burt said that “his thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time.”

“We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

The Government of Bermuda confirms that an air ambulance which departed Bermuda for Boston early this morning, carrying six people, has been reported missing after contact was lost with air traffic control. The United States Coast Guard is conducting search and rescue… pic.twitter.com/yYEwWXMdQQ — Bermuda Government (@BdaGovernment) October 3, 2026

content_blocks.text: “Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night,” the release read, noting that 1,644 square miles have been searched over approximately 27 hours.
The U.S. Coast Guard added that next of kin have been notified.

The Coast Guard said the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration notified them around 2 a.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 with the tail number C-Grjp and owned by Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance.

#Breaking : @uscg is searching for a Gulfstream aircraft with 6 persons on board. @FAANews reported losing contact w/the aircraft early Saturday morning. #Uscg air & surface crews have launched in search of the aircraft. Updates will be provided here as info becomes available.… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Clarence Togeretz, the air ambulance company’s operations manager, told The Canadian Press on Saturday morning that the aircraft was transporting a patient and family member, who were Bermuda nationals.
He said the two pilots and two medical staff aboard were Canadians.

Togeretz also shared that his company had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. as it was approaching Boston. Togeretz said Latitude reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard when the aircraft failed to reach the tarmac.
“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.
Togeretz noted that this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.
Pilot declared emergency: ATC audio
The aircraft bound for Boston Logan International Airport departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport at 12:41 a.m. The air ambulance arrived in Bermuda from Hamilton the previous night.
Air traffic control audio captured by LiveATC.net indicates that the flight declared an emergency before it went missing.
“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot, who cannot be heard in the audio.
The controller then asked the pilot if they were declaring an emergency.
“You’re coming in a little weak. I didn’t hear your response was if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the controller heard telling the pilot.
A short time later, the controller got a confirmation from the pilot that they were indeed declaring an emergency.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, data shows that one hour and 23 minutes into the flight, the aircraft dropped from an altitude of 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in two minutes and then levelled off before it vanished.
The search for the jet included crews in the air and on the water, the U.S. Coast Guard said, noting that it was using two planes, a search and rescue lifeboat, a helicopter, and a cutter.
The Coast Guard noted that crews

#Update Uscg assets responding include: - HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew from AirSta Cape Cod - HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City - MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod - 47-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point - FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154)… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026
Latitude Air Ambulance’s website says that it currently has four G100 jets in its fleet, each with a range of 5,000 km.
In a statement posted to X , Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge said that “Our thoughts are with our colleagues at Latitude Air Ambulance at this time.”
“All of us at Ornge are hopeful the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”
Ornge noted that the flight was not related to its operations.
Canadian government ‘closely monitoring the situation’
Canada’s Transportation Minister, Steven MacKinnon, said his department is aware of the situation and that they “are closing monitoring” in a post to X.
“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time.”
“We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue. I want to thank all first responders involved for their ongoing efforts.”

I am aware of reports of a Canadian-registered air ambulance aircraft that went missing while travelling from Bermuda to Boston. Four Canadians are among the six people on board. My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during… — Steven MacKinnon (@stevenmackinnon) October 3, 2026
Global Affairs Canada said it was aware of reports of Canadians on board the missing Latitude Air Ambulance.

“Consular officials stand ready to provide consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities. Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be disclosed,” Global Affairs said in a statement to CTV News.
Bermuda government releases statement
A spokesperson on behalf of the Bermuda government confirmed the air ambulance’s departure from Bermuda to Boston this morning in a post to X.
Officials said they’ve been in contact with the families of those on board as well as the U.S. Coast Guard conducting the search.
In a statement, Bermuda’s Premier David Burt said that “his thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time.”
“We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

The Government of Bermuda confirms that an air ambulance which departed Bermuda for Boston early this morning, carrying six people, has been reported missing after contact was lost with air traffic control. The United States Coast Guard is conducting search and rescue… pic.twitter.com/yYEwWXMdQQ — Bermuda Government (@BdaGovernment) October 3, 2026

stories.title: New remote testimony room aims to make court less traumatic for London-area children
stories.summary: New remote testimony room aims to make court less traumatic for London-area children CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: October 4, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 5 hours ago
London Family Court Clinic says new suite gives young witnesses a safe, trauma-informed alternative to court
For children involved in the justice system, testifying in court can be intimidating.
The London Family Court Clinic has developed a new remote testimony suite that lets young people give evidence from a safe, trauma-informed environment without having to enter a courtroom.

The suite uses CCTV technology to connect children with court proceedings. Joelene Bamford, the clinic's executive director, said the goal is to reduce some of the anxiety associated with the justice system.
"They don't have to go to the courthouse, they don't have to go into courtrooms," Bamford said. "They're able to provide that testimony from a safe place that's trauma-informed."
Bamford said research shows children can provide better evidence when they feel safer and less stressed.
"The literature certainly shows that when children feel safer, they're better able to speak in their own words," she said. "They're better able to provide a full and candid account of the evidence."

reviewed by the Department of Justice Canada has found that testimonial aids such as closed-circuit television can reduce stress for child witnesses, while studies have found children's accuracy is either improved or not significantly different compared with in-person testimony.
The clinic is also home to Beacon House, its Child and Youth Advocacy Centre, where young people can meet with police in a child-friendly environment.
Bamford said having a space away from a police station or courthouse can reduce stress and retraumatization.
"That safety reduces the amount of stress, reduces the amount of retraumatization," she said.
The clinic also has a specially trained facility dog, NSD Virgil, who can accompany children during court preparation, attend court with them and be present when they meet with police.
"He's definitely the star of the show," Bamford said.

The clinic also supports young people who are navigating the youth justice system themselves, including through counselling and assessments. Bamford said the court system can be overwhelming regardless of a young person's role.
"The court system can be extremely intimidating whether you're a victim, whether you're a witness, or whether you're an accused person," she said.
The London Family Court Clinic is a non-profit that has been serving children, youth and families involved in the justice system for more than 50 years.
The clinic is holding its second annual fundraiser,
Stronger Together: LFCC at the Met , on Wednesday, Nov. 25, at Metropolitan United Church, from 7 to 9 p.m.
Organizers say proceeds will directly support the clinic's clinical services for children and youth.

stories.title: Ed Seaward's London Gothic turns familiar city landmarks into a dark mystery
stories.summary: London-born author Ed Seaward has turned his hometown and surrounding area into the setting for London Gothic, a dark mystery about a teenage girl trying to uncover the truth about her mother's disappearance. The novel moves between the 1970s and 1984, exploring family secrets, violence, abuse and incest against a backdrop of familiar London locations.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London-born author Ed Seaward has turned his hometown and surrounding area into the setting for London Gothic, a dark mystery about a teenage girl trying to uncover the truth about her mother's disappearance. The novel moves between the 1970s and 1984, exploring family secrets, violence, abuse and incest against a backdrop of familiar London locations.
· Posted: Oct 04, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago
A London-born author is putting his hometown at the centre of a dark new gothic novel.

Ed Seaward’s London Gothic was released Friday and follows 17-year-old Bethany Caine, who has escaped her abusive father. Bethany's mother disappeared nine years earlier, and she begins pressing her older brother to reveal what really happened.

Seaward, who grew up in London and now lives in Georgetown, Ont., also wrote the 2020 novel Fair, which won a Silver Medal in Urban Fiction at the 2021 Independent Book Awards. London Gothic is published by DarkWinter Press.
The story moves between the 1970s and 1980s, gradually revealing the secrets surrounding the Caine family.
Seaward said the idea for the novel began with an image that came to him while he was out for a walk.
“This image of a father and son bearing a body popped into my head, as it will when you're out for a walk and you're a writer. I started to play with that and follow it through.”

Seaward said the concept of Southern Ontario Gothic, a literary tradition associated with dark themes and unsettling stories set in familiar Ontario communities, appealed to him because of his connection to London.
“That was coined by the late novelist Timothy Findley. When I came across that, I thought, ‘I like that idea,’ having been born and raised in London, Ontario.”
London Gothic by Ed Seaward was released on Oct. 2, 2026. (DarkWinter Press)
While the story is fictional, Seaward said the London setting is not.
“For people who read the book, all of the settings are real places," he said. "The story is fictionalized. Neither my father nor I buried a body."
"But all of the places are London, and my own experience growing up, like anyone's, you observe some darker things. So you pull on some of that, and then fictionalize it.”

That includes Victoria Park, which plays a role in the story. Seaward says using recognizable London locations also allowed him to play with the gothic tradition, which has roots in Victorian England.
“I had a lot of fun playing with some of these familiar tropes and things that are unfamiliar to some people, and teasing all that out.”
At the centre of the story is Bethany's search for answers about her mother. Her father and brother maintain that the woman abandoned the family, but Bethany isn't convinced.
Seaward said the novel's alternating timelines help readers understand how the family's secrets developed.
The novel explores violence, abuse and other disturbing family secrets. But Seaward said the Gothic elements ultimately explore what can haunt people long after events have happened.
“It's a story about the monsters in our life who are the real people in our life, and it's about the ghosts that are the memories that haunt us.”
Seaward will celebrate the release of London Gothic with a special book launch on Sunday, Oct. 4, from 4:30 to 6 p.m. at The Space, 23 Heather Cres.

stories.title: Defendant says sorry to former UBC professor days before defamation trial to start
stories.summary: Vancouver - One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway has issued a lengthy apology just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says she now understands her conduct toward him was “serious and harmful” as she apologized just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.

Chelsea Rooney’s statement said she communicated serious and unproven allegations against Galloway and that she was involved in collecting complaints in an attempt to build a case against him.

“I recognize that statements and communications about allegations of this nature can cause profound harm to a person’s reputation, work, personal life, and family, and did in fact do so to Mr. Galloway. I deeply regret my role in contributing to the harm Mr. Galloway has suffered in this regard,” her statement said.

Much of Rooney’s apology appeared in the National Post newspaper on Saturday and the entire statement is posted on the website gallowayapologies.com , along with eight other apologies from those who say they regret communications or actions that accused Galloway of sexual assault.

Rooney, who is a defendant in the B.C. Supreme Court case due to start Monday, said she recognizes the communications she circulated about Galloway caused others to believe they were true, and she’s aware he firmly denies that he sexually assaulted a student only know as A.B.

The apology is the latest occurrence in what began as an accusation against Galloway in November 2015. He sued numerous people in 2018, alleging he was defamed with false sexual assault allegations by fellow professors, a former student and others who repeated the statements on social media and elsewhere.

The Supreme Court of Canada in 2024 dismissed an appeal by his accusers, clearing the way for the defamation trial.

Galloway is the author of novels including “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” and was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at UBC.

He was never charged, though he was fired from his job.

A report commission by the University of B.C. by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, could not be immediately reached for comment on Saturday, although he said in an interview after the High Court’s ruling that his client’s “reputation and life were devastated by the criminal allegations.”

Rooney is among the defendants who fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming the accusations of sexual assault must be protected speech, true or not, and “regardless of the circumstances in which the statement was published.”

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Elaine Adair said in her ruling on the case in 2021 that if the defendants arguments were true, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

“It is difficult to see how something so extreme and potentially reckless would be in the public interest,” her decision said.

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them or posted them publicly on social media.

She said she has reflected on Galloway’s steadfast efforts over the years and she has come to better understand the basis for his position and his commitment to clearing his name and reputation.

“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets, or my participation in the process.”

Rooney said Galloway considered her a friend before A.B. made the allegations, and on multiple occasions went out of his way to help her, with nothing asked in return, she said.

“In my 2014 book, I thanked him as someone ‘who encouraged me to commit to writing at a very important time in my life.’ That was a true statement,” her apology said.

“I know that nothing I say now can undo the harm or give back the years affected by these events, but I am genuinely sorry for the part I played in causing that harm.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

He sued numerous people in 2018, alleging he was defamed with false sexual assault allegations by fellow professors, a former student and others who repeated the statements on social media and elsewhere.
The Supreme Court of Canada in 2024 dismissed an appeal by his accusers, clearing the way for the defamation trial.
Galloway is the author of novels including “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” and was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at UBC.
He was never charged, though he was fired from his job.
A report commission by the University of B.C. by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, could not be immediately reached for comment on Saturday, although he said in an interview after the High Court’s ruling that his client’s “reputation and life were devastated by the criminal allegations.”

Rooney is among the defendants who fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming the accusations of sexual assault must be protected speech, true or not, and “regardless of the circumstances in which the statement was published.”

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Elaine Adair said in her ruling on the case in 2021 that if the defendants arguments were true, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.
“It is difficult to see how something so extreme and potentially reckless would be in the public interest,” her decision said.
Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them or posted them publicly on social media.
She said she has reflected on Galloway’s steadfast efforts over the years and she has come to better understand the basis for his position and his commitment to clearing his name and reputation.
“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets, or my participation in the process.”
Rooney said Galloway considered her a friend before A.B. made the allegations, and on multiple occasions went out of his way to help her, with nothing asked in return, she said.
“In my 2014 book, I thanked him as someone ‘who encouraged me to commit to writing at a very important time in my life.’ That was a true statement,” her apology said.
“I know that nothing I say now can undo the harm or give back the years affected by these events, but I am genuinely sorry for the part I played in causing that harm.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.
